What Is CMA Intermediate?

CMA Intermediate is the second of the three stages of the Cost and Management Accountant qualification run by The Institute of Cost Accountants of India (ICMAI) — after Foundation and before Final. A candidate reaches it either by clearing CMA Foundation, or via other recognised entry routes ICMAI publishes (e.g. graduates in any discipline, or CAT-qualified students under the Institute's exemption scheme). Passing both groups of Intermediate is itself a recognised qualification and is also the gateway to CMA Final and to Practical Training.

Structure — Two Groups, Eight Papers

GroupPaperTitle
Group IPaper 5Business Laws and Ethics (BLE)
Paper 6Financial Accounting (FA)
Paper 7Direct and Indirect Taxation (DITX) — this document
Paper 8Cost Accounting (CA)
Group IIPaper 9Operations Management & Strategic Management (OMSM)
Paper 10Corporate Accounting and Auditing (CAA)
Paper 11Financial Management and Business Data Analytics (FMDA)
Paper 12Management Accounting (MA)

Paper 7 is unique among the eight papers: it is really two half-papers bound together — Section A, Direct Taxation (income-tax computation for individuals and HUFs), and Section B, Indirect Taxation (GST and Customs). ICMAI itself publishes them as two separate Study Notes books ("2 Books" per the official price notice), and this document keeps that same split — Modules 1–3 are Direct Taxation, Modules 4–6 are Indirect Taxation.

Exam Pattern, Timing and Passing Criteria (applies to every Intermediate paper, including this one)

Marks: each paper is 100 marks, split 30 marks Objective/MCQ + 70 marks Descriptive.

Descriptive section: typically 7 questions of 14 marks each, of which any 5 must be attempted (5 × 14 = 70).

Duration: 3 hours per paper, plus 15 minutes' reading time before writing begins. Offline, pen-and-paper mode.

Negative marking: none, on the MCQ portion.

Passing criteria: minimum 40% in each individual paper of a group, AND a minimum 50% aggregate across all four papers of that group, to pass the group.

Exam sessions: twice yearly — June and December.

Where Paper 7 Sits, and How to Approach It

Paper 7 rewards two different disciplines depending on which half you're in. Direct Taxation (Modules 1–3, 50%) is computation-heavy and Section-number-heavy: every answer traces back to a specific Section of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and marks come from correctly computing income under a head, then aggregating to total income and tax payable. Indirect Taxation (Modules 4–6, 50%) is equally computation-heavy but statute-different: CGST Act 2017 for GST, Customs Act 1962 for import/export duty, with its own Section-citation discipline and its own worked-computation style (GST liability, Input Tax Credit, assessable value of imported goods).

The single largest module in the whole paper is Module 5 (GST Laws, 35% on its own — more than a third of the entire paper) — it alone outweighs three of the six modules combined. Module 2 (Heads of Income, 25%) is the second-largest, covering five separate heads of income each with their own computation rules. Together, Modules 2 and 5 are 60% of Paper 7.

How to Use This Document

Paper 7 is a Section-citation-and-computation paper: marks come from naming the right Section, applying the right rate/threshold, and landing on the right figure — not from prose. Every computation statement, rate table, and worked illustration reproduced here follows ICMAI's own Study Notes exactly, and every figure has been checked for internal arithmetic consistency.

On sourcing: Every fact, Section number, rate, threshold, and worked illustration in this document is drawn exclusively from ICMAI's Paper 7 Study Notes (Syllabus 2022 — both the Direct Taxation and Indirect Taxation books) as supplied for this purpose. Nothing has been fetched from any external source, and no rate or slab has been "corrected" or updated against outside knowledge — tax law changes yearly, and this document reflects only what this edition of the source states. Presentation aids layered around that content — never new substantive content — are: the plain-language Glossaries before each module, the Mind Maps (which only re-arrange the module's own topics visually), and the exam-strategy notes (test-taking advice, not syllabus content).

Reading This Document

1. Module and topic numbering matches the source exactly. Section 5.4 in this document is Topic 5.4 in the ICMAI Study Notes — nothing renumbered.

2. Section numbers are reproduced, not paraphrased. Where the source cites "Sec. 54" or "Sec. 17(5) of the CGST Act," this document cites the same — the exam tests exact Section recall.

3. Every boxed formula IS the descriptive-answer skeleton. The 70-mark section rewards a structured working — these boxes are the structure to reproduce.

4. Worked illustrations carry the source's own figures. Follow the working line by line before checking the answer — that's how the method, not just the number, sticks.

5. One glossary sits before every module. Read it before the topics — it defines every technical term used in that module in plain words.

Exam Strategy for a 30% MCQ + 70% Descriptive, Two-Statute Paper

1. No negative marking on the MCQ portion. Attempt every objective question — an eliminated-down guess has positive expected value.

2. Identify which statute a question belongs to before you start. Direct Taxation and Indirect Taxation use entirely different Section-numbering schemes (Income-tax Act vs CGST Act/Customs Act) — citing the wrong Act's Section number under exam pressure is a very avoidable error.

3. Show the working, not just the answer. Descriptive marking in a computation paper is largely method-based — a correctly structured computation with one wrong figure still earns most of the marks; a bare final number does not.

4. Attempt exactly 5 of the 7 descriptive questions — choose fast. Skim all 7 stems first (2–3 minutes), rank by which computation you're most fluent in, and commit.

5. Weight your prep to Module 5. GST Laws alone is over a third of the paper (35 of 100 marks) — if time runs short anywhere in revision, it is never Module 5's turn to be cut. Module 2 (Heads of Income, 25%) is the second priority.

6. Distractors are engineered from classic mistakes. Wrong MCQ options are the numbers you get by making one specific error — every ⚠ TRAP block in this document names those errors.

MODULE 1 OF 6 · SECTION A · WEIGHT 10% · ≈10 MARKS

Basics of
Income Tax Act

This module builds application-oriented knowledge of the Income-tax Act, 1961 — the charging provisions and the meaning of Previous Year, Assessment Year, Person and Assessee; the tests for residential status and the resulting scope of total income; the meaning and tax treatment of agricultural income; and the categories of income Sec. 10 keeps outside total income altogether.

MUST NOT SKIP: the Sec. 6 residential-status test — Sec. 6(1)(a) 182 days in the previous year, OR Sec. 6(1)(c) 60 days in the previous year + 365 days in the 4 preceding previous years — since Sec. 5 makes the taxability of every rupee of an assessee's income turn on whether he lands as Resident & Ordinarily Resident, Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident, or Non-Resident.

1.1–1.4

Module Learning Objectives

After studying this module, the student will be able to – appreciate the various types of taxation and the sources of tax law; understand the meaning of terms such as Previous Year, Assessment Year, Person and Assessee; appreciate the provisions relating to residential status; apply that knowledge to ascertain the taxability of income in India; and appreciate the various incomes which are not liable to be taxed in India.

Glossary — Module 1, in Plain Words

The technical terms used across 1.1–1.4, explained simply.

Previous Year [Sec. 3]The financial year (1st April–31st March) in which income is earned. It is mandatory for every assessee — the year in which income is earned.
Assessment Year [Sec. 2(9)]The 12-month period commencing 1st April, immediately following the Previous Year, in which the Previous Year's income is assessed and taxed.
Financial YearPer Sec. 2(21) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 — the year commencing 1st April. Plays a dual role: it is the Assessment Year for one Previous Year and the Previous Year for the next Assessment Year.
Person [Sec. 2(31)]Seven categories: Individual, HUF, Company, Firm, AOP/BOI, Local authority, and every artificial juridical person.
Assessee [Sec. 2(7)]Anyone liable to pay tax/penalty/interest, anyone against whom proceedings have been taken, anyone assessable for another's income/loss, a deemed assessee, or an "assessee in default."
Hindu Undivided Family (HUF)All persons lineally descended from a common ancestor, plus their wives and daughters, governed by Hindu law (includes Jain and Sikh families). Arises from status, not contract.
Domestic Company [Sec. 2(22A)]An Indian company, or any other company that has made prescribed dividend-payment arrangements within India.
Foreign Company [Sec. 2(23A)]A company which is not a domestic company.
AOP / BOIAssociation of Persons: any persons (individuals, HUFs, companies, firms, etc.) who join for a common income-producing purpose. Body of Individuals: individuals only, joining for a common purpose whether or not to earn income.
Artificial Juridical PersonNot a natural person, but has a separate legal entity and can sue/be sued through the persons who manage it — e.g. deities, idols, a university, the Bar Council.
Income [Sec. 2(24)]An inclusive, not exhaustive, definition — covers cash and kind, includes negative income (loss), and treats capital receipts as taxable only where the Act specifically says so.
Heads of Income [Sec. 14]The five statutory buckets every item of income must fall into: Salaries, House Property, Business/Profession, Capital Gains, and the residual head, Other Sources.
Gross Total Income (GTI) [Sec. 80B(5)]The aggregate of income under all five heads, after set-off and carry-forward of losses — before Chapter VIA deductions.
Total Income (TI) [Sec. 2(45)]GTI minus deductions allowable under Chapter VIA (Sec. 80C to 80U). Tax is computed on this figure, rounded off under Sec. 288A.
Capital ReceiptNot taxable unless the Act specifically brings it to charge (e.g. Capital Gains u/s 45).
Revenue ReceiptTaxable unless the Act specifically exempts it.
Diversion of IncomeIncome diverted, by an overriding obligation, before it ever reaches the assessee — not taxable in his hands.
Application of IncomeIncome that reaches the assessee first and is then applied to discharge a self-imposed obligation — fully taxable.
Rebate u/s 87AA reduction of tax liability (not of income) available to a resident individual whose total income is within a specified limit — the limit and the rebate amount differ between the old and the default regime.
Marginal ReliefCaps the extra tax-plus-surcharge payable on income just above a surcharge threshold, so it never exceeds the amount by which income exceeds that threshold.
Health & Education Cess4% of tax liability after surcharge, payable by every assessee, on every regime.
Resident [Sec. 6(1)]An individual satisfying either the 182-day test [6(1)(a)] or the 60-day + 365-day test [6(1)(c)] for the previous year.
Resident & Ordinarily Resident (ROR)A resident individual who also satisfies both additional Sec. 6(6) tests: resident in at least 2 of the preceding 10 previous years, AND present in India for 730+ days in the preceding 7 previous years.
Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR)A resident individual who fails at least one of the two Sec. 6(6) tests.
Person of Indian OriginA person is deemed of Indian origin if he, or either of his parents or grandparents (paternal or maternal), was born in undivided India.
Place of Effective Management (POEM)Where key management and commercial decisions necessary for conducting the entity's business as a whole are, in substance, made — the test for company residence u/s 6(3).
Income deemed to accrue or arise in India [Sec. 9]Income taxable in India for every assessee irrespective of residential status — business connection, property/asset/source in India, transfer of a capital asset situated in India, and specified salary/dividend/interest/royalty/technical-fee/gift categories.
Agricultural Income [Sec. 2(1A)]Rent/revenue from land used for agricultural purposes in India, income from cultivation, income from processing the produce to make it marketable, income from sale of such produce, and income from a farmhouse fulfilling specified conditions.
Basic OperationHuman skill and labour applied to the land prior to germination — tilling, sowing, planting, irrigation. On its own, it is agricultural activity.
Subsequent OperationOperations after the produce sprouts — weeding, pruning, harvesting. Alone, it is NOT agricultural activity; it must follow a Basic Operation.
Partial IntegrationThe indirect method (since 1973) of taxing non-agricultural income at the tax-slab rate that would apply if agricultural income were added to it — agricultural income itself stays exempt.
Rule 7A / 7B / 8The fixed percentages that split composite income between agricultural and non-agricultural for rubber (65:35), cured coffee (75:25), roasted & ground coffee (60:40), and tea (60:40).
Income exempt u/s 10Income that does not form part of total income at all — distinguished from a deduction, which first enters GTI and is then subtracted.
Sec. 14ANo deduction is allowed for expenditure incurred to earn income that does not form part of total income — applies even if that income has not yet accrued or been received.
SEZ Unit Deduction [Sec. 10AA]A profit-linked deduction for eligible SEZ units on export turnover, at 100% for the first 5 years and 50% for the next 5 (subject to a reserve for the following 5) — not available under the default tax regime.

CONCEPT

1.1 Basic Concepts, Basis of Charge and Capital & Revenue Receipts ★★★ HIGH

The present Income-tax Act, 1961 has been in force from 1st April, 1962. It has 23 chapters covering 298 sections and 14 schedules and extends to the whole of India [Sec. 2(25A)]. Income tax is a Direct Tax — incidence and impact fall on the same person — as opposed to an Indirect Tax such as GST, where incidence and impact fall on two different persons.

Direct Tax vs. Indirect Tax

PointDirect TaxIndirect Tax
Incidence & impactFall on the same person — the assessee bears it himself.Fall on two different persons — the assessee passes the burden on.
Pinches the payer?Yes — it pinches the taxpayer.No — it does not pinch the collecting assessee, since it is passed on.
Levied onIncome.Goods and services — wider base, leads to inflation.
NatureProgressive — higher tax on higher income.Regressive — equal burden on all consumers of a good/service, irrespective of ability to pay.
ExampleIncome Tax.GST, Customs Duty.

Constitutional Validity & Administration

Article 265 bars levy/collection of tax except by authority of law. Article 246 read with Schedule VII splits legislative subject-matter into the Union List (Centre only), State List (State only) and Concurrent List (both) — a repugnant State law on a Concurrent-List entry is void to the extent of the repugnancy (Article 254).

List / ArticleContent
Union List, Entry 82Taxes on income OTHER THAN agricultural income — i.e., Income-tax.
State List, Entry 46Taxes on agricultural income — hence the Centre cannot tax it directly.
Article 270Taxes/duties (except specified) levied by the Centre and distributed between Union & States.
Article 271Parliament may levy a surcharge for Union purposes; the whole proceeds go to the Consolidated Fund of India.

CBDT (Central Board of Direct Taxes) deals with levy/collection of direct tax; CBIC (Central Board of Indirect Taxes & Customs) deals with central indirect tax — both constituted under the Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963, under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance.

Sources of Income Tax Law

  1. Income-tax Act, 1961 — provides "what to do": determination of taxable income and tax liability, assessment/appeal/penalty/prosecution procedure, and powers/duties of Income-tax authorities.
  2. Income-tax Rules, 1962 — provides "how to do it"; made by the Board u/s 295, notified in the Gazette of India.
  3. Annual Finance Act — the Finance Bill, part of the Union Budget presented on 1st Feb by the Finance Minister, becomes the Finance Act on Presidential assent and its amendments are incorporated into the Income-tax Act. Direct-tax amendments generally take effect from the next year unless stated otherwise. If, on 1st April of the Assessment Year, the new Finance Act is not yet enacted, the more beneficial of the old provisions or the proposed Bill applies until the new law takes effect [Sec. 294].
  4. Notifications, Circulars & Clarifications [u/s 119] — binding on Income-tax authorities but NOT on the assessee (though the assessee may claim benefit under them), and not binding on ITAT or the Courts.
  5. Judicial decisions — a Supreme Court decision binds all Courts/Tribunals/authorities/assessees till Parliament changes the law; between conflicting SC decisions, the larger Bench prevails (or, if equal-sized Benches, the later decision); High Court/ITAT decisions bind only assessees/authorities within their jurisdiction.

Sec. 4 — the Charging Section, the backbone of the Act: income of the previous year of a person is charged to tax in the immediately following assessment year, at the rate prescribed by that year's annual Finance Act (though certain incomes carry a rate fixed in the Act itself, e.g. lottery income @30% u/s 115BB). Tax liability arises at the CLOSE of the previous year; only its final quantification is postponed to the assessment year.

It is not a one-time tax — income chargeable to tax also attracts TDS or advance tax, wherever applicable.

Assessment Year, Previous Year & Financial Year

Assessment Year [Sec. 2(9)]: the period of 12 months commencing on 1st April every year — the year, immediately after the Previous Year, in which the Previous Year's income is charged to tax. Previous Year [Sec. 3]: the financial year immediately preceding the Assessment Year — the year in which income is earned. It is mandatory for every assessee to follow the financial year as Previous Year.

Financial Year [Sec. 2(21), General Clauses Act, 1897]: the year commencing 1st April. It plays a dual role — e.g. F.Y. 2025-26 is the Assessment Year for P.Y. 2024-25, and simultaneously the Previous Year for A.Y. 2026-27.

CaseFirst Previous Year is the period
Business/profession newly set upBeginning with the date of setting up, ending 31st March of that financial year.
New source of income arisingBeginning with the date the new source comes into existence, ending 31st March of that financial year.

The first Previous Year may run under 12 months, but never exceeds 12 months; every subsequent Previous Year is always a full 12 months. Where an assessee already has regular income and also starts a new source mid-year, his Previous Year runs from 1st April for existing income and from the new source's start date for the new income — but all income is aggregated and taxed in that one Previous Year.

Exceptions — Income Assessed in the SAME Year (not the following A.Y.)

To ensure smooth tax collection from taxpayers who might otherwise become untraceable, five categories are assessed in the same previous year:

  1. Income of a non-resident from shipping business [Sec. 172].
  2. Income of a person leaving India permanently or for a long period [Sec. 174].
  3. Income of bodies formed for a short duration [Sec. 174A].
  4. Income of a person likely to transfer property to avoid tax [Sec. 175].
  5. Income of a discontinued business [Sec. 176] — here the Assessing Officer has DISCRETION to assess in the same previous year or wait for the Assessment Year.

Assessee, Person & Types of Person

Assessee [Sec. 2(7)]: (a) anyone by whom tax/penalty/interest is payable, whether or not proceedings have been taken against him; (b) anyone against whom proceedings under the Act have been taken; (c) anyone assessable for another person's income/loss; (d) a deemed assessee under any provision; and (e) an "assessee in default" — e.g. a person who failed to deduct tax he was liable to deduct.

Person [Sec. 2(31)] includes: (i) an Individual; (ii) a HUF; (iii) a Company; (iv) a Firm; (v) an AOP or BOI, incorporated or not; (vi) a Local authority; and (vii) every artificial juridical person not covered above. On the settled principle that "the Crown cannot be charged to tax," the Union Government is not taxable unless specifically provided. An AOP/BOI/local authority/AJP is deemed a "person" whether or not formed with a profit motive. A firm includes a limited liability partnership.

  • Individual — a natural person; includes a minor or a person of unsound mind. Deities are assessable as artificial juridical persons. The trustee of a discretionary trust is assessed as an individual.
  • HUF — all persons lineally descended from a common ancestor, plus their wives and daughters, where Hindu law applies (includes Jain and Sikh families). Continues to be assessed as HUF until partition; arises from status, not contract.
  • Company [Sec. 2(17)] — any Indian company; any foreign body corporate; any institution/association/body assessed as a company for any A.Y. up to 1-4-1970; or any institution/association/body declared a company by the CBDT.
  • Indian Company [Sec. 2(26)] — a company formed and registered under the Companies Act (or predecessor company laws in J&K / the specified Union Territories), or a statutory corporation, or a body notified as a company by CBDT u/s 2(17) — provided its registered/principal office is in India.
  • Domestic Company [Sec. 2(22A)] — an Indian company, OR any other company that has made prescribed arrangements for declaration and payment of dividends within India out of its India-taxable income. Foreign Company [Sec. 2(23A)] — a company which is not a domestic company.
  • Company in which public are substantially interested [Sec. 2(18)] — a Government company, a Sec. 8 company under the Companies Act 2013, a mutual benefit finance company, a listed company, a company held by co-operative societies, or a company prescribed by CBDT.
  • Firm — per Sec. 4 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, the relationship between persons who agree to share profits of a business carried on by all or any acting for all. A firm is a separate TAXABLE entity apart from its partners, though not a separate legal entity generally; an LLP is treated at par with a firm (excluding Sec. 44AD/44ADA).
  • Local Authority — per Sec. 3(31) of the General Clauses Act: a municipal committee, district board, body of Port Commissioners, Panchayat, Cantonment Board, or other authority legally entitled to or entrusted with control/management of a municipal or local fund.
  • Artificial Juridical Person — not a natural person, has a separate entity in law, may be sued only through the person(s) managing it. E.g. Deities, Idols, University, Bar Council.
PointAOPBOI
MembersAny person — individuals, HUFs, companies, firms, etc.Individuals ONLY.
FormationMembers voluntarily come together with a common WILL for a common purpose.Such common will may, or may not, be present.

Income [Sec. 2(24)] — Points to Keep in Mind

PointRule
Cash vs. KindIncome in kind is valued as per prescribed rules, or at market price if none is prescribed.
Method of accountingIRRELEVANT for "Salaries", "House Property" and "Capital Gains" heads. RELEVANT for "Business/Profession" and "Other Sources" (other than Dividend) — taxed cash or accrual basis as regularly followed.
Notional incomeNo one can profit from a transaction with himself — goods transferred profit-wise between departments of the same business is NOT income.
Source of incomeMay be temporary or permanent.
Capital vs. Revenue receiptCapital receipt — not taxable unless specifically provided. Revenue receipt — not exempt unless specifically provided.
LossIncome includes negative income.
Disputed incomeAssessment cannot be withheld for a title dispute — normally taxed in the recipient's hands.
Lump-sum receiptNo difference between income received lump sum or in instalments.
ReimbursementMere reimbursement of expenses is NOT income.
LegalityThe Act makes no difference between legal and illegal income.
Double taxationSame income cannot be taxed twice.
Mutual activitySurplus of a mutual fund distributed among its own contributors is NOT income — except: (a) a trade/professional association's income from specific services to members [taxable u/s 28(iii)]; (b) mutual insurance business profits; (c) co-operative banking business with its own members.
Pin moneyMoney given by a husband for household expenses, and small savings a wife makes from it, is NOT income — but INCOME EARNED on investment out of pin money IS income.
AwardBusiness/profession-related award = income incidental to that business/profession. A non-professional's award is in the nature of a gift/testimonial, taxed per other provisions.
EmbezzlementMoney embezzled is a gain to the embezzler — falls within the wider definition of income.
Contingent incomeA contingent or anticipated income is NOT taxable.
SubsidyGovernment subsidy/grant/incentive/drawback is generally income, EXCEPT: (a) where taken into account for determining actual cost of an asset [Explanation 10 to Sec. 43(1)] — not taxed separately; (b) a Government subsidy for the CORPUS of a Government-established trust/institution — not taxable.

Heads of Income [Sec. 14]

All income of a person must be classified under one of five heads: (1) Salaries; (2) Income from house property; (3) Profits and gains of business or profession; (4) Capital gains; (5) Income from other sources — the RESIDUAL head, catching anything not covered by the first four. Income under one head cannot be charged under another; each head has self-contained computation provisions; charging income under the wrong head can cost the assessee a deduction he was entitled to under the correct head.

PointHeads of IncomeSources of Income
NumberOnly 5, fixed by Sec. 14.Not countable — unlimited.
SequenceA source is categorised under its head.Each source is classified into its head.
ProvisionThe Act has a distinct computation code per head.No separate code for each source.
OriginA mere classification of sources.Refers to WHERE income originates.

ILLUSTRATION 2 — Head under which income is taxable

(a) Tarun: ₹7,200 interest on fixed deposit with SBI → (b) Akash: ₹35,000 gain on sale of shares → (c) Atul: ₹2,700 as examiner remuneration from Calcutta University → (d) Barnali, a lawyer: ₹1,45,000 professional income → (e) Swarnli: ₹84,000 rent from letting out a flat.

Answer: (a) Income from Other Sources; (b) Capital Gains; (c) Income from Other Sources; (d) Profits & Gains of Business or Profession; (e) Income from House Property.

Gross Total Income, Total Income & Rounding Off

Gross Total Income [Sec. 80B(5)] is the aggregate of income under all five heads, after set-off/carry-forward of losses. Set-off means adjusting a loss from one source/head against income of another; an unabsorbed loss is carried forward subject to conditions (e.g. loss from other sources, other than horse-race losses, cannot be carried forward). Sec. 60 to 64 (clubbing provisions) can add another person's income to the assessee's GTI — e.g. certain minor-child income clubbed with a parent, or income from an asset transferred to a spouse for inadequate consideration.

Computation of Total Income for the A.Y. ____
ParticularsAmount
1. Salaries***
2. Income from house property***
3. Profits and gains of business or profession***
4. Capital gains***
5. Income from other sources***
Gross Total Income****
Less: Deduction u/s 80C to 80U****
Total Income****

Total Income [Sec. 2(45) r/w Sec. 80A(1)] = Gross Total Income – Deduction under Chapter VIA (Sec. 80C to 80U).

Tax is computed on TOTAL income as one figure — not as the sum of separate tax computed head-by-head. That is why income tax is called ONE tax, not a collection of taxes.

BasisGross Total IncomeTotal Income
MeaningAggregate of 5-head income after set-off/carry-forward of losses.GTI as reduced by Chapter VIA deductions [Sec. 2(45)].
Tax calculationTax is NOT calculated on this.Tax IS calculated on this.
Rounded offNot required to be rounded off.Rounded off u/s 288A.
ClubbingIncludes income subject to clubbing.Includes income subject to clubbing.
Set-off of lossesCurrent + b/f losses adjusted head-wise to arrive at GTI.No further adjustment needed.
Chapter VIA deductionsNOT considered while computing GTI.REDUCED from GTI to derive TI.

Rounding off Total Income [Sec. 288A]: rounded to the nearest multiple of ₹10 — a rupee-element of ₹5 or more rounds UP; the paise element is ignored.

Example: ₹7,41,645 → ₹7,41,650. But ₹7,41,644.98 → ₹7,41,640.

Rounding off Tax [Sec. 288B]: tax (including TDS/advance tax), interest, penalty and refund — all rounded to the nearest ₹10.

Example: ₹4,876.49→₹4,880; ₹6,452.50→₹6,450; ₹8,738.92→₹8,740; ₹5,132.75→₹5,130.

Procedure for Computation of Tax Liability (Individual)

  1. Residential status — determine it first.
  2. Compute income under each head, giving effect to clubbing.
  3. Aggregate to Gross Total Income, giving effect to set-off and carry-forward of losses.
  4. Chapter VIA deductions (Sec. 80C to 80U) from GTI → result is Total Income.
  5. Round off Total Income to the nearest multiple of ₹10, ignoring paise [u/s 288A].
  6. Compute tax — annually, at the rate for the relevant Assessment Year, per the annual Finance Act (or the Act's own special rates); based on the law as it stands on 1st April of the Assessment Year.
  7. Rebate u/s 87A — reduce it from the tax computed in Step 6, if the resident individual qualifies.
  8. Surcharge — if Total Income exceeds the specified limit, subject to marginal relief.
  9. Health & Education Cess @4% on (Step 6 – Step 7 + Step 8).
  10. Round off tax to the nearest multiple of ₹10, ignoring paise [u/s 288B], after reducing relief, TDS, TCS and advance tax.

Capital vs. Revenue Receipts

A capital receipt is not taxable unless the Act specifically provides otherwise; a revenue receipt is taxable unless the Act specifically exempts it. Capital receipts are chargeable (where taxable at all) under "Capital Gains"; revenue receipts under other heads. Judicial principles for telling them apart:

  1. Lump sum or instalments — makes NO difference to the receipt's nature.
  2. Nature is decided in the hands of the RECIPIENT, not by the source it came from.
  3. Accounting treatment/name given by the parties does not alter the true character.
  4. Income from wasting assets (e.g. royalties from mines/quarries) is taxable regardless of the capital consumed in earning it.
  5. Magnitude (big or small) of the receipt does not decide its nature.
  6. Nature is fixed at the TIME of receipt, not afterwards.
  7. Voluntary or legally-obliged receipt — makes no difference.
  8. Purpose of holding the article matters — e.g. a sculpture kept for personal decoration and later sold gives a capital receipt; the same sculpture sold by an art dealer gives a revenue receipt.

Capital-in-nature items SPECIFICALLY taxable: capital gains on transfer of a capital asset [Sec. 45]; compensation for termination/modification of service terms [Sec. 17(3)]; compensation covered u/s 28(ii)/28(va).

Capital vs. Revenue Expenditure — Judicial Tests

  • Acquiring an asset/advantage of an enduring nature points to capital expenditure ("enduring" ≠ "everlasting").
  • A capital asset belonging to a THIRD party → the expenditure to create it is still REVENUE.
  • Expenditure that is an integral part of the profit-EARNING process (not acquisition of an asset/right of permanent character) is revenue.
  • Fixed capital-related outlay → capital; circulating-capital/stock-in-trade-related outlay → revenue.
  • Removing a restriction/obstruction on an EXISTING business right (without acquiring a capital asset) → revenue.
  • Payment to a rival dealer to ward off competition → capital expenditure.
  • Part of ordinary commercial working expenses → revenue, not capital.
  • Initial outlay/extension of business/substantial replacement of equipment → capital; running the business/profit-making outlay → revenue.
  • Ensuring regular raw-material supply, even over several years → revenue.
  • Owner's expenditure on building additions that raise value → capital; a TENANT'S renovation expenditure on a rented building is ordinarily revenue (he acquires no asset of his own).
  • Purchase price of GOODWILL → capital, lump sum or instalments; but paying merely for the RIGHT TO USE goodwill → revenue.
  • Expenditure to create/cure/complete title → capital; expenditure merely to PROTECT an existing title → revenue.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: "LUMP SUM" AND "VALUE-ENHANCING" DO NOT MEAN CAPITAL

THE TRAP: students assume a large, one-time payment must be a capital receipt/expenditure, or that any expenditure which enhances an asset's value must be capital.

THE TWIST: the source is explicit — an employee agreeing to ₹3,60,000 lump sum instead of ₹10,000 p.m. for 3 years is STILL a revenue receipt (salary); and a TENANT's renovation spend on a rented building, even though it improves the building, remains revenue because the tenant acquires no capital asset of his own — only an OWNER's value-enhancing addition is capital.

Diversion vs. Application of Income

Diversion of income: where, by virtue of an obligation, income is diverted BEFORE it reaches the assessee — not taxable, even if the assessee collects it, because he collects it on behalf of another. Application of income: discharging a gratuitous or self-imposed obligation AFTER the income reaches the assessee — taxable.

Example: A, B and C are co-authors of a book. The publisher pays the whole royalty of ₹6,00,000 to A; A pays ₹2,00,000 each to B and C. That payment by A is DIVERSION of income, not application.

CONCEPT

1.2 Residential Status and Scope of Total Income ★★★ HIGH

Sec. 4 (the charging section) taxes total income; Sec. 5 defines the SCOPE of total income in terms of an assessee's residential status, tested by Sec. 6. Residential status is NOT the same as citizenship — an Indian citizen may be a non-resident for a year, and a foreign citizen may be resident in India for a year.

  • Different for each previous year — residential status can vary year to year.
  • Single status for each source — a person cannot be resident for one source of income and non-resident for another, in the same year.
  • Citizenship ≠ residential status — two different concepts entirely.
  • Country-specific — a person can hold the same residential status in more than one country.

Individual — Resident in India [Sec. 6(1)], if EITHER condition is satisfied (they are ALTERNATIVE, not cumulative):

(i) In India for 182 days or more in the previous year [Sec. 6(1)(a)]; OR
(ii) In India for 60 days or more in the previous year AND 365 days or more during the 4 previous years immediately preceding [Sec. 6(1)(c)].

For counting days in India, BOTH the date of arrival and the date of departure count as days present in India. Failing both conditions → Non-Resident.

ILLUSTRATION 3 — Sam, first year in India, P.Y. 2025-26

(i) Stayed 50 days → fails both conditions → Non-resident.
(ii) Stayed 183 days → satisfies 6(1)(a) → Resident.
(iii) Stayed 153 days → exceeds 60 days, but had NO stay in the preceding 4 years (first visit) → fails 6(1)(c) → Non-resident.

ILLUSTRATION 4 — Andy, British national, A.Y. 2026-27

Days in India: F.Y. 2021-22: 55; 2022-23: 60; 2023-24: 80; 2024-25: 160; 2025-26: 70. In the 4 years preceding P.Y. 2025-26 he stayed 55+60+80+160 = 355 days (under 365).

Answer: 70 days in the P.Y. fails 6(1)(a); 355 days in the preceding 4 years fails 6(1)(c) — Non-resident for the P.Y. 2025-26.

Exceptions to the Basic Test

(A) Sec. 6(1)(c) is IRRELEVANT for: an Indian citizen leaving India during the P.Y. for employment (in India or abroad), or as a crew member of an Indian ship — such a person is resident ONLY if he stays 182 days or more in the P.Y.

Case (Indian citizen / person of Indian origin visiting India)Modified 6(1)(c) test
Total income (excluding foreign-source income) exceeds ₹15 lakhs in the P.Y.Resident only if in India for 120 days or more (but <182 days) AND 365+ days in the preceding 4 years.
Total income (excluding foreign-source income) does NOT exceed ₹15 lakhs6(1)(c) is not applicable at all — only the 182-day test can make him resident.

(C) Deemed Resident [Sec. 6(1A)]: an individual is DEEMED resident (irrespective of days stayed) if he is (a) an Indian citizen; (b) his total income (excluding foreign-source income) exceeds ₹15 lakhs; (c) he fails BOTH basic conditions of 6(1); and (d) he is not liable to tax in any other country by domicile/residence/similar criteria. This exception does NOT apply to a foreign citizen, even if a person of Indian origin.

Rule 126 — for an Indian-citizen ship's crew member on an "eligible voyage," the period between the Continuous Discharge Certificate's joining date and signing-off date is EXCLUDED from his days-in-India count.

Example: joining 1st Jan 2026, signing off 31st Jan 2026 → the entire 31 days is excluded from his stay in India.

ILLUSTRATION 5 — Miss Pal, Indian citizen, left for a Tokyo job on 1-4-2025

Returned to India 11th Jan 2026; stayed 21+28+31 = 81 days in P.Y. 2025-26 (Jan+Feb+Mar).

Answer: since she left India for employment, 6(1)(c) is irrelevant and she needs 182 days to be resident; she stayed only 81 days → Non-resident for P.Y. 2025-26.

Points to Keep in Mind

  • Stay at the SAME place in India is not necessary.
  • CONTINUOUS stay in India is not necessary.
  • Presence on India's territorial waters (12 nautical miles from the coastal baseline) counts as presence in India.

Resident & Ordinarily Resident [Sec. 6(6)] — a resident individual must ALSO satisfy BOTH additional conditions: (a) resident [under 6(1)] in at least 2 of the 10 previous years immediately preceding; AND (b) present in India for 730 days or more during the 7 previous years immediately preceding.

Fails EITHER additional condition → Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR).

Exceptions — Deemed RNOR (even if both Sec. 6(6) conditions are met)

(A) Citizen of India, total income (excl. foreign-source) > ₹15 lakhs, not liable to tax elsewhere, deemed resident u/s 6(1A) → deemed RNOR. (B) Indian citizen/person of Indian origin visiting India, total income (excl. foreign-source) > ₹15 lakhs, present 120–181 days in the P.Y. and 365+ days in the preceding 4 years → deemed RNOR, even if he happens to satisfy both 6(6) conditions.

ILLUSTRATION 6 — Mr. X, 19, left India first time 31-5-2025

Stay in P.Y. 2025-26: April 30 + May 31 = 61 days. He was in India for 365+ days in the preceding 4 years (first departure).

Answer: (i) Left for employment → 6(1)(c) irrelevant, needs 182 days, has only 61 → Non-resident. P.Y. 2025-26 stay: 113 days. Preceding 4 years (2021-22 to 2024-25): 251+269+0+0 = 520 days — satisfies 6(1)(c). Resident for 2 of the preceding 10 years, but only 520 days (not 730+) in the preceding 7 years.

Answer: Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident, for BOTH a foreign citizen and an Indian citizen — because foreign citizens are never covered by the "leaving for employment" exception, and coming to India FOR employment is not itself an exception to 6(1)(c) either.

ILLUSTRATION 8 — X, foreign citizen, 83 days in P.Y. 2025-26

Preceding 4 years (2021-22 to 2024-25): 121+175+15+67 = 378 days → satisfies 6(1)(c), so Resident. For 6(6): resident in 8 of the preceding 10 years (satisfies condition 1); present 1,090 days during 2018-19 to 2024-25, well over 730 in the preceding 7 years (satisfies condition 2).

Answer: Resident and Ordinarily Resident for P.Y. 2025-26.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: TREATING "RESIDENT" AND "ORDINARILY RESIDENT" AS ONE TEST

THE TRAP: students apply Sec. 6(6)'s 2/10-year and 730/7-day tests directly to decide Resident vs. Non-resident, or stop after Sec. 6(1) and assume every resident individual is automatically "ordinarily resident."

THE TWIST: it is a strict TWO-STAGE test. Stage 1 [Sec. 6(1)] decides Resident vs. Non-resident. ONLY if Resident does Stage 2 [Sec. 6(6)] run — and BOTH its conditions must be met for "Ordinarily Resident"; failing even one gives "Not Ordinarily Resident." A Non-resident never reaches Stage 2 at all.

Income Received / Deemed Received in India

Income received in India is taxable in ALL cases, irrespective of residential status. "Receipt" means the FIRST occasion the recipient gets the money under his control, wherever that occurs — a later remittance/transmission of already-received income is NOT a fresh "receipt."

Example: Mr. X, non-resident, received dividend from an Italian company IN JAPAN on 15-12-2025; remitted it to India on 17-12-2025 — not taxable in India, since it was neither received nor accrued in India.

Deemed to be RECEIVED in India (taxable for all assessees, any residential status): (a) recognised-PF employer contribution in excess of 12% of salary, and interest credited above 9.5% [Sec. 7(i)]; (b) transferred RPF balance, to the extent taxable [Sec. 7(ii)]; (c) employer contribution to an 80CCD pension scheme [Sec. 7(iii)]; (d) Tax Deducted at Source [Sec. 198]; (e) income from undisclosed sources.

1.2.6 Income Deemed to Accrue or Arise in India [Sec. 9]

Taxable for EVERY assessee, irrespective of residential status:

  • Business connection in India [9(1)(i)] — income accruing through/from a business connection, a property/asset/source in India, or the transfer of a capital asset situated in India (regardless of the asset's movability, where the transfer document was registered, or where consideration was paid).
  • Salary for services rendered in India [9(1)(ii)] — including rest/leave periods that are part of an Indian service contract.
  • Salary from Government to an Indian citizen for services rendered OUTSIDE India [9(1)(iii)] — deemed to accrue in India (though allowances/perquisites so paid are exempt u/s 10(7), in both regimes).
  • Dividend paid by an Indian company outside India [9(1)(iv)].
  • Interest [9(1)(v)] — payable by Government (always); by a RESIDENT, unless the borrowed money is used for a business/profession or income-earning outside India; by a NON-resident, only if the money is used for business/profession/income-earning IN India.
  • Royalty [9(1)(vi)] and Fees for technical services [9(1)(vii)] — same Government/resident/non-resident logic as interest above.
  • Deemed receipt of gift [9(1)(viii)] — when a non-resident/RNOR/foreign company receives a sum covered u/s 56(2)(x), from a resident, outside India.

ILLUSTRATION A — Miss Monica, foreign national, comes to India 90 days every year since 2009-10

(a) 90 days/year: P.Y. 2025-26 stay 90 days; preceding 4-year stay 360 days — fails both 6(1) conditions.

Answer (a): Non-resident.

(b) 100 days/year: P.Y. stay 100 days; preceding 4-year stay 400 days — satisfies 6(1)(c) → Resident. But only 700 days (100×7) in the preceding 7 years — fails 6(6)'s 730-day test.

Answer (b): Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident.

ILLUSTRATION B — Mr. Sid, British national, joined an Indian company 1-5-2015

Days in India by year: 2025-26: 274; 2021-22: 61; 2016-17: 275; 2015-16: 336; all other years: 0.

Answer: 274 days in P.Y. 2025-26 satisfies 6(1)(a) → Resident. Resident (u/s 6(1)) in only 2 of the preceding 10 years (2016-17 and 2015-16), and present under 730 days in the preceding 7 years → fails 6(6) → Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident.

CONCEPT

1.3 Agricultural Income ★★★ HIGH

Agricultural income is exempt from CENTRAL taxation [Sec. 10(1)] because the Constitution reserves the power to tax agricultural income exclusively to the STATE Legislature (State List Entry 46).

Agricultural Income [Sec. 2(1A)]: (1) rent or revenue from land in India used for agricultural purposes; (2) income from cultivation of such land; (3) income from a process ordinarily employed by a cultivator/rent-in-kind receiver to render the produce marketable; (4) income from SALE by a cultivator/rent-in-kind receiver of produce where no process beyond making-it-marketable has been performed; and (5) income from a farmhouse building, subject to specified conditions.

Farmhouse Building Income — Conditions

  1. Occupied by the cultivator or rent-in-kind receiver.
  2. On, or in the immediate vicinity of, the agricultural land, situated in India.
  3. Used as a dwelling house, store-house or other out-building.
  4. The land is in a RURAL area, OR in an URBAN area but assessed to land revenue/local rates. (Urban = within a Municipality/Cantonment Board with population ≥10,000, or within a specified aerial distance of one: up to 2 km for population 10,000–1,00,000; up to 6 km for 1,00,000–10,00,000; up to 8 km for population above 10,00,000.)

Building used for a NON-agricultural purpose → not agricultural income, even on such land. Building let out merely for STORING crops → not agricultural income. The building must be owned AND occupied by the land-holder receiving rent/revenue; for a cultivator/rent-in-kind receiver, mere occupation suffices. Profit on TRANSFER of agricultural land is not agricultural income. There must be a close nexus between the agro-activity and the agro-income — e.g. income from selling silk-cocoons (grown from mulberry leaves) is NOT agricultural income, since silk-cocoons are a different commodity from what was raised.

Basic Operation: human skill & labour applied to land PRIOR to germination (tilling, sowing, planting, irrigation). On its own, IS agricultural activity. Spontaneous growth with no human effort is NOT.

Subsequent Operation: operations AFTER the produce sprouts, that foster growth/preserve the produce/render it market-fit (weeding, pruning, harvesting). Alone, is NOT agricultural activity — must accompany a Basic Operation.

Instances of Agricultural Income

  1. Growing trade/commercial products (jute, cotton).
  2. Growing flowers and creepers.
  3. Potted plants sold, PROVIDED basic operations were performed.
  4. A PARTNER's remuneration and interest-on-capital from a firm engaged in agricultural operations.
  5. Sale of trees on denuded forest land after replanting and subsequent operations.
  6. Insurance compensation for hail-storm damage to a tea garden's green leaf.
  7. Fee from land used for grazing cattle used in agricultural operation.
  8. Income from saplings/seedlings grown in a nursery.

Instances of NON-Agricultural Income

  • Salary from an agricultural business (paid to an employee).
  • Dividend from a company engaged in agriculture.
  • Salt produced by flooding land with sea-water.
  • Fisheries, poultry farming, dairy farming, butter/cheese making.
  • Breeding & rearing of livestock.
  • Interest received by a moneylender in the form of agricultural produce.
  • Profit on sale of standing crops PURCHASED (not grown) and then harvested.
  • Royalty income from mines.
  • A Director/Managing Director's remuneration from an agricultural company — even if based on a % of net profit.
  • Income from CONVERTING sugarcane (own-grown) to jaggery — to the extent related to the conversion, since sugarcane itself is marketable.
  • Interest on arrears of rent for agricultural land.
  • Income from land situated OUTSIDE India.
  • Annuity received for transferring agricultural land.
  • Income from supplying water for agricultural operations, even if received in agro-produce.
  • Income from sale of spontaneously-grown trees/grasses.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: "COMES FROM A FARM" ≠ AGRICULTURAL INCOME

THE TRAP: students assume anything earned on a farm — poultry, dairy, fisheries, livestock breeding — is agricultural income, or that any land-related income (mortgage interest, rent-arrears interest) automatically qualifies.

THE TWIST: the test is whether income is DERIVED FROM LAND by agricultural operations. Poultry/dairy/fisheries/livestock income is not derived from land at all — it is non-agricultural. And interest — whether on a mortgage of agricultural land, or on arrears of rent for such land — is a return on money, not on land, so it too is non-agricultural, even though the land itself is agricultural.

Partly Agricultural, Partly Non-Agricultural Income

RuleBusinessAgricultural %Non-Agricultural %
Rule 8Growing & manufacturing TEA60%40%
Rule 7AGrowing & manufacturing RUBBER65%35%
Rule 7B(1)COFFEE grown and cured75%25%
Rule 7B(1A)COFFEE grown, cured, roasted & grounded60%40%

A partner's remuneration/interest from a firm growing & manufacturing tea/coffee/rubber is split partly agricultural, partly business income on the same percentages. For any OTHER composite agri/non-agri business: prepare two separate Profit & Loss statements; debit agro-expenses to the agro P&L and non-agro expenses to the non-agro P&L; and treat the market value of any agricultural produce used as raw material as agro-INCOME and non-agro-EXPENDITURE.

Partial Integration (indirect taxation of agro-income via slab rate, since 1973): applies where (1) assessee is an Individual/HUF/BOI/AOP/AJP; (2) his NON-agricultural income exceeds the basic exemption limit (₹4,00,000 default regime; old regime ₹3,00,000 senior citizen / ₹5,00,000 super senior / ₹2,50,000 other); and (3) his agricultural income exceeds ₹5,000.

Step 1: Tax on (Non-agro income + Agro income). Step 2: Tax on (Agro income + Basic exemption limit). Step 3: Tax liability (before cess) = Step 1 – Step 2.

(a) A tills land as an agricultural EMPLOYEE, paid 50% of net profits → Salaries, NOT agro-income (but if A were a PARTNER, it would be agro-income). (o) ₹50,000 from land in Bangladesh → not agro-income. (p) ₹25,000 from a stone quarry → not agro-income (no agricultural operation).

CONCEPT

1.4 Income which do not form part of Total Income ★★ MEDIUM

Sec. 10 lists incomes that do NOT form part of total income at all — unlike a Chapter VIA deduction, which first enters Gross Total Income and is then subtracted, a Sec. 10 exemption never enters the computation. The exemptions relevant to Salaries and Capital Gains are cross-referred to those chapters; the ones below are examined here, grouped by theme for quick reference.

High-Yield Exemptions, in Full ★★★ HIGH

  • Agricultural Income [Sec. 10(1)] — see 1.3 above.
  • Member's Share in HUF Income [Sec. 10(2)] — any sum an individual receives as an HUF member, out of the family's income or of an impartible estate belonging to the family.
  • Partner's Share of Firm Profit [Sec. 10(2A)] — a partner's share in the firm's total income is exempt in his hands (the firm has already been taxed on it).
  • Minor's Income [Sec. 10(32)] — income up to ₹1,500 is exempt for EACH minor child whose income stands clubbed u/s 64(1A) in a parent's hands.

Sum received under a Life Insurance Policy [Sec. 10(10D)]: wholly exempt (including bonus) — EXCEPT: sums u/s 80DD(3)/80DDA(3); Keyman insurance policy sums; a policy issued on/after 1-4-2012 where premium in any year exceeds 10% of the actual capital sum assured (15% if insured is disabled u/s 80U / has a specified disease u/s 80DDB, for policies from 1-4-2013; 20% for policies issued 1-4-2003 to 31-3-2012); a ULIP issued on/after 1-2-2021 where any year's premium exceeds ₹2,50,000; and any OTHER (non-ULIP) life policy issued on/after 1-4-2023 where any year's premium exceeds ₹5 lakh.

Where premium is paid across multiple such policies, the exemption applies only to the policy/policies whose AGGREGATE annual premium stays within the limit. These premium-linked restrictions never apply to a sum received on DEATH, nor to a policy issued by the IFSC Insurance Office.

Charitable/Educational/Medical Institutions [Sec. 10(23C)]: income of specified funds (PM's National Relief Fund/PM CARES, PM's Fund for Folk Art, Swachh Bharat Kosh, Clean Ganga Fund, CM's/LG's Relief Fund, etc.), and of universities/hospitals existing solely for education/philanthropy AND NOT for profit, is exempt.

A university/hospital not substantially financed by Government must have annual receipts up to ₹5 crores to qualify [Explanation to (iiiad)/(iiiae)] — receipts from BOTH categories are aggregated for this ₹5 crore test. Where 85% of income is not applied in the year but accumulated for the objects, that accumulation escapes tax if a prescribed statement is filed (accumulation period capped at 5 years, funds kept in Sec. 11(5) modes). Anonymous donations covered u/s 115BBC remain taxable regardless.

Sec. 14A: no deduction is allowed for expenditure incurred in relation to income that does not form part of total income — even if that income has not yet accrued/arisen/been received in the relevant previous year.

Sec. 10AA — Deduction for Newly Established SEZ Units

NOT available under the default tax regime (nor, for companies/co-operative societies, if they opt for Sec. 115BAA/115BAB/115BAD/115BAE). Conditions: the assessee is an "entrepreneur" under the SEZ Act, 2005 with a Development Commissioner's letter of approval; manufacture/production/services began on/after 1-4-2005 but not after 31-3-2020 (extended to 31-3-2021, or a further notified date, if the approval itself was issued by 31-3-2020); the business is NOT formed by splitting up/reconstructing an existing business (subject to the Sec. 33B natural-calamity/riot/fire/war exception, if re-established within 3 years); plant & machinery is not substantially second-hand (old plant/machinery up to 20% of total value is allowed; imported, never-depreciated, first-used-in-India plant is treated as new); a chartered accountant's report is filed a month before the return due date; and the return is filed within the Sec. 139(1) due date, claiming the deduction in it.

Quantum of deduction = Profits of the SEZ undertaking × (Export turnover ÷ Total turnover of the undertaking).

100% of that amount for the FIRST 5 years from commencement; 50% for the NEXT 5 years; and, for a FURTHER 5 years, 50% again — but only if credited to a "SEZ Re-investment Allowance Reserve A/c," to be utilised within 3 years for new plant/machinery (until then, usable for the undertaking's business, but never for dividend/profit remittance abroad or creating an asset outside India). Reserve mis-utilised, or unutilised within the period, is deemed taxable profit of that year (or on expiry of the 3 years).

Export turnover excludes freight/telecom/insurance for delivery outside India and foreign-exchange expenses for technical services rendered outside India; proceeds must be received/brought into India (or credited to an RBI-approved foreign account) within 6 months of the year-end (or such further period as allowed). Where transactions between eligible and non-eligible units, or between the assessee and any other person, are NOT at market value, the Assessing Officer may recompute profit at market value. Double deduction (with Sec. 35AD) is not permissible; on amalgamation/demerger, the deduction carries forward to the amalgamated/resulting Indian company for the balance of the 10-year period.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SEC. 10AA UNDER THE DEFAULT REGIME

THE TRAP: students compute the SEZ export-profit deduction for a company/individual assessee without first checking which tax regime applies.

THE TWIST: the source is explicit — Sec. 10AA is NOT available under the default tax regime [Sec. 115BAC], and separately not available to a company/co-operative society that has opted for Sec. 115BAA/115BAB/115BAD/115BAE. The deduction survives only under the old regime (or for assessees who have not opted into those special company/co-op regimes).

  3. A foreign-incorporated company is resident in India if its place of effective management is _______ in India.
  4. A foreign company is liable to 5% surcharge if total income exceeds _______.

(2) Profit from growing and manufacturing tea in India is fully exempt from income tax under Sec. 10(1). (3) A prize given by the Madhya Pradesh Government for higher crop yield is agricultural income.

16 EXAM FACTS — BASICS OF INCOME TAX ACT (Module 1)

① Sec. 4 (Charging Section): tax on the PREVIOUS year's income is levied in the FOLLOWING Assessment Year, at the rate the annual Finance Act fixes for that A.Y. Liability arises at the close of the P.Y.; only quantification is postponed.

② Union List Entry 82 taxes income OTHER THAN agricultural income; State List Entry 46 taxes agricultural income — the constitutional root of Sec. 10(1)'s exemption.

③ "Person" [Sec. 2(31)] has 7 categories: Individual, HUF, Company, Firm, AOP/BOI, Local authority, Artificial juridical person. A firm includes an LLP; an AOP/BOI/local authority/AJP is a "person" whether or not profit-motivated.

④ Income [Sec. 2(24)] is inclusive: covers cash and kind, negative income (loss), embezzled money, and mutual-activity surplus is generally NOT income (3 named exceptions) — but pin money and mere reimbursement are never income.

⑤ 5 Heads of Income [Sec. 14]: Salaries, House Property, Business/Profession, Capital Gains, Other Sources (residual). GTI = 5-head aggregate after set-off/carry-forward; Total Income = GTI – Chapter VIA deductions [Sec. 2(45)].

⑥ Rounding: Total Income to nearest ₹10 [Sec. 288A, paise ignored, ≥₹5 rounds up]; Tax (and TDS/advance tax/interest/penalty/refund) to nearest ₹10 [Sec. 288B].

⑦ Capital receipt: NOT taxable unless the Act specifically says so. Revenue receipt: taxable UNLESS the Act specifically exempts it. Lump-sum vs. instalment, and value enhancement by a TENANT, never flip the classification.

⑧ Diversion of income (obligation intercepts income BEFORE the assessee) is not taxable; Application of income (obligation discharged AFTER income reaches the assessee) IS taxable.

⑨ Sec. 6(1) Resident test is ALTERNATIVE: 182 days in the P.Y. [6(1)(a)], OR 60 days in the P.Y. + 365 days in the preceding 4 P.Y.s [6(1)(c)]. For an Indian citizen leaving for employment/as ship's crew, 6(1)(c) drops out entirely — only the 182-day test can make him resident.

⑩ Sec. 6(6) Ordinarily-Resident test applies ONLY after a person is already Resident, and needs BOTH: resident in 2 of the preceding 10 P.Y.s, AND 730+ days present in the preceding 7 P.Y.s. Missing either → Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident.

⑪ Company residence [Sec. 6(3)]: an Indian company is ALWAYS resident; a foreign company is resident only if its Place of Effective Management for that year is in India. No ROR/RNOR split for companies, firms, AOPs or BOIs.

⑫ Sec. 5 Incidence of tax: income accrued OR received in India is taxable for everyone. Foreign business/profession income (controlled/set up outside India) is taxable for ROR only; income already received/accrued abroad in an earlier year stays untaxed for all three categories even if remitted later.

⑬ Agricultural income [Sec. 2(1A)] must be DERIVED FROM LAND in India by agricultural operations — poultry, dairy, fisheries and livestock income fail this test even on a farm; a Basic Operation (pre-germination) alone qualifies, a Subsequent Operation (post-germination) alone does not.

⑭ Partial integration taxes non-agricultural income at the higher slab rate agricultural income would otherwise push it to — applies only to Individual/HUF/AOP/BOI/AJP, only when non-agro income exceeds the basic exemption limit AND agro income exceeds ₹5,000. Rule 8 (tea) 60:40, Rule 7A (rubber) 65:35, Rule 7B(1) (cured coffee) 75:25, Rule 7B(1A) (roasted & ground coffee) 60:40.

⑮ Sec. 10 exemptions never enter the computation at all (unlike a Chapter VIA deduction, which enters GTI and is then subtracted). Sec. 14A denies any deduction for expenditure incurred to earn Sec. 10 income. Sec. 10AA's SEZ export deduction is NOT available under the default tax regime.

Check against the notes only after finishing — answering from memory is what converts today's reading into exam-day marks. Anything you could not retrieve, star it and re-attempt tomorrow morning. MODULE 2 OF 6 · SECTION A · WEIGHT 25% · ≈25 MARKS · THE SECOND-LARGEST MODULE

Heads of
Income

This module computes income under each of the five heads — Salaries, Income from House Property, Profits and Gains of Business or Profession, Capital Gains, and Income from Other Sources — fixing for each head the point of time at which income becomes taxable and the deductions that head allows. Together the five figures build the assessee's gross total income, and with it the tax audit and other compliances that attach to them.

MUST NOT SKIP: the head-wise computation proformas — and above all the Sec. 15 "due or receipt, whichever is earlier" basis for Salaries with the Sec. 10(13A) three-limb HRA test (actual HRA received / 50% of salary in a metro or 40% elsewhere / rent paid less 10% of salary — least of the three is exempt) and the Sec. 16 deductions that close every Salaries computation. A single mis-stated limb wrecks the whole statement, and every head in this module is examined as a statement, not as a sentence.

2.1–2.5

Module Learning Objectives

After studying this module, the student will be able to – appreciate the provisions of computing income under the different heads of income; appreciate the point of time at which income is taxable under each respective head; apply that knowledge to ascertain the gross total income of a person; and understand the various compliances, such as tax audit, that attach to these heads.

Glossary — Module 2, in Plain Words

The technical terms used across 2.1–2.5, explained simply. The Salaries vocabulary comes first because it is the heaviest and the most formula-driven.

Salary [Sec. 17(1)]An inclusive definition: wages, annuity or pension, gratuity, fees/commission/perquisites/profits in lieu of salary, advance salary, payment for leave not availed, the taxable part of the annual accretion and transferred balance in a Recognised Provident Fund, the employer's contribution to a Sec. 80CCD pension scheme, and the Central Government's contribution to the Agniveer Corpus Fund u/s 80CCH.
Employer-employee relationshipThe gateway test for this head. The employee must be bound to work under the employer's direction and supervision. No such relationship → the receipt is not "Salaries" but PGBP or Income from Other Sources.
Contract OF service vs. contract FOR serviceIn a contract OF service the employer directs both the duty and the manner of its performance — that is employment. In a contract FOR service the contractee can only set the target, not the method — that is not employment.
Basis of charge [Sec. 15]Salary is taxed on "due" basis or "receipt" basis, whichever is earlier. The employee's own method of accounting is irrelevant.
Advance salary vs. advance against salaryAdvance salary is taxable u/s 17(1)(e) in the year received. "Advance against salary" is merely a loan — not taxable under this head at all.
Arrear salaryA retrospective increment not taxed earlier. Taxed on receipt basis, in the year it is allowed; relief u/s 89(1) may be claimed.
Salary paid tax-freeWhere the employer bears the employee's tax: add the tax paid back into the employee's salary, then subtract it from his tax liability. Tax paid by the employer on non-monetary perquisites is itself exempt u/s 10(10CC).
Foregoing of salaryWaiving salary already earned does not make it exempt — it is an application of income. (Surrender to the Central Government under the Voluntary Surrender of Salaries (Exemption from Taxation) Act, 1961 is the one exception.)
AllowanceA fixed quantum of money paid regularly, over and above salary, to meet a particular requirement. Three families: fully taxable, partly exempt, fully exempt.
HRA [Sec. 10(13A), Rule 2A]House Rent Allowance. Exempt to the least of three limbs; available only under the old regime. Nothing is exempt if the employee lives in his own house or pays no rent.
Salary for HRA / retirement benefitsBasic + D.A. (only if it forms part of retirement benefit) + Commission as a fixed percentage of turnover. This narrow meaning recurs throughout the head.
Perquisite [Sec. 17(2)]A benefit or amenity attached to the office, in addition to salary. Taxable only if allowed by the employer to the employee or a member of his household, giving a personal advantage, derived by virtue of employment.
Specified employee [Sec. 17(2)(iii)]A director-employee, OR an employee beneficially holding 20% or more voting power in the employer company, OR an employee whose aggregate monetary salary from all employers exceeds ₹4,00,000 p.a. Certain perquisites are taxable ONLY in his hands.
Member of householdSpouse; parents; servants; children and their spouses (dependent or not); and dependants. Perquisites given to them are the employee's perquisites.
Rent-free accommodation (RFA)Housing given free. Valued at 10% / 7.5% / 5% of salary by city population where the employer owns it; at the lower of actual rent or 10% of salary where he hires it.
Profits in lieu of salary [Sec. 17(3)]Compensation on termination or modification of employment terms, Keyman Insurance receipts, and payments before employment or after its cessation — taxed as salary even though they are not "salary."
Commuted vs. uncommuted pensionUncommuted pension is the ordinary periodical payment (always fully taxable). Commuted pension is the lump sum present value of future pension (exempt in whole or in part, depending on who the employer is and whether gratuity is also received).
GratuityA retirement benefit for past service. Sec. 10(10) exempts it — wholly for a Government employee, and to a formula-capped extent for others.
Leave salary encashmentMoney received for waiving accumulated leave. Fully taxable during service; exempt u/s 10(10AA) on termination, wholly for Government employees and to a four-limb cap for others.
SPF / RPF / URPF / PPFStatutory (Provident Funds Act, 1925) / Recognised (approved by the Commissioner, Part A of Schedule IV) / Unrecognised (not approved) / Public (open to any member of the public) Provident Fund. Their four components — both contributions and both interests — are taxed quite differently.
Standard Deduction [Sec. 16(ia)]A flat deduction from gross salary allowed to every employee — ₹50,000 under the old regime, ₹75,000 under the default regime, but never more than gross salary itself.
Annual Value [Sec. 22]House Property head: it is the earning capacity of the building, not its actual income, that Sec. 22 charges in the owner's hands.
Composite rentOne combined sum received for the building plus assets or services. If it cannot be segregated, the whole becomes PGBP or Other Sources income — not house property income.
Block of assetsPGBP head: the grouping of assets of the same class and same depreciation rate on which Sec. 32 depreciation is worked out, rather than asset by asset.
Presumptive taxationPGBP head: schemes (Sec. 44AD / 44ADA / 44AE) that deem a percentage or a fixed sum as profit, sparing the eligible assessee from detailed books.
Capital asset [Sec. 2(14)] / Transfer [Sec. 2(47)]Capital Gains head: gain is charged only when a capital asset is transferred. Both words are separately defined, and both are separately tested.
IndexationCapital Gains head: scaling the cost of acquisition by the Cost Inflation Index so that only real, not inflationary, gain is taxed.
Residual head [Sec. 56]Income from Other Sources — where an income lands when it is chargeable to tax but fits none of the other four heads (family pension, casual income, gifts, dividend, interest on securities).
Gross Total IncomeThe sum of the five head-wise figures this module produces — the platform on which Module 3's Chapter VIA deductions then operate.

Module 2 Mind Map — read it now, redraw it from memory once you finish the module

CONCEPT

2.1 Salaries ★★★ HIGH

"Salary is the recompense or consideration given to a person for the pains he has bestowed upon another's business" — Stroud's Judicial Dictionary.

Salaries is the head every exam paper opens with, and the head that punishes imprecision hardest: almost every line of the computation carries either a statutory ceiling, a formula, or a "taxable in whose hands?" test. Work through it as three layers — what is salary (Sec. 17(1)), when is it taxed (Sec. 15), and what comes off it (Sec. 16) — with allowances, perquisites and retirement benefits sitting inside the first layer.

2.1.1 Basic Elements of Salary

Two elements must both be present before a receipt can be taxed under this head.

  1. The payer and payee must stand in an employer-employee (Master & Servant) relationship; and
  2. the payment must have been made by the employer in that capacity.

If either condition fails, the receipt is not taxable under "Salaries" but under "Income from Other Sources" or "Profits and Gains of Business or Profession."

Taxable as SalaryNOT taxable as Salary
Salary received by the Managing Director of a company.Salary received by an MP or MLA.
Salary received by a Minister of Government.Sitting fee received by a director.
Remuneration received by Judges — taxable under "Salaries" even though they have no employer.Salary paid to a partner by his firm.
  • Criterion for the relationship: the employee is always bound to work as per the direction and supervision of the employer.
  • Contract of service vs. contract for service: in a "contract of service" the employer can direct and control both the duties and the manner of their performance — the relationship exists. In a "contract for service" the contractee can only decide and quote the object or target to be achieved, not the manner of performance — no employment.
  • Agent and principal: commission or remuneration earned by an agent from his principal is not "Salaries," because an agent is not the employee of his principal.
  • Partner: salary received by a partner from his firm is not salary — there is no employer-employee relationship — and is taxed under "Profits & gains of business or profession."
  • Proprietor: salary received by a proprietor from his own proprietorship firm is not income at all — proprietor and firm are the same person, and no one can earn from himself.
  • Director: remuneration from his company is salary only if the director is an employee of the company; otherwise it is "Income from other sources." Directors' sitting fee is always "Income from other sources."
  • Widow / legal heir: pension received by the widow or legal heir of a deceased employee is not taxable as salary — no employer-employee relationship between payer and payee — but is taxable as "Income from other sources."

Concluding the point: a payment received for services rendered, from a person other than the employer, is never taxable under "Salaries" but may be taxed under PGBP or Other Sources.

ILLUSTRATION 1 — Is it salary or not?

ReceiptSalary?Reason
A teacher receives emoluments in kind from the school in which he teaches.YesIt is immaterial whether salary is received in cash or in kind.
A college teacher receives fees from a University for checking answer sheets.NoNo employer-employee relationship — a college teacher is not the University's employee. Taxable as "Income from other sources."
Payment made to a Member of Parliament or of the State legislature.NoNo employer-employee relationship; an MP/MLA is not treated as an employee of the Government. Taxable as "Income from other sources."

2.1.2 Section-wise Scheme

Three sections carry the whole head, and it pays to hold their division of labour in your head before any computation.

SectionRoleWhat sits under it
Sec. 15Charging sectionDue or receipt, whichever is earlier.
Sec. 16DeductionsStandard deduction u/s 16(ia); entertainment allowance to a Government employee u/s 16(ii); professional tax paid u/s 16(iii).
Sec. 17DefinitionsSalary [Sec. 17(1)]; Perquisites [Sec. 17(2)]; Profit in lieu of salary [Sec. 17(3)].

2.1.3 Definition of Salary [Sec. 17(1)]

As per Sec. 17(1), salary includes: (a) wages; (b) any annuity or pension; (c) any gratuity; (d) any fees, commission, perquisite or profits in lieu of, or in addition to, any salary or wages; (e) any advance of salary; (f) any payment received in respect of any period of leave not availed of by the assessee; (g) the portion of the annual accretion in any previous year to the balance at the credit of an employee participating in a recognised provident fund, to the extent it is taxable; (h) transferred balance in a Recognised Provident Fund to the extent it is taxable; (i) contribution made by the employer in the previous year to the account of an employee under a pension scheme referred to in Sec. 80CCD [National Pension Scheme and Atal Pension Yojana]; and (j) contribution made by the Central Government in the previous year to the Agniveer Corpus Fund account of an individual enrolled in the Agnipath Scheme referred to in Sec. 80CCH.

2.1.4 General Notes

  • Salary and wages are identical in the Income-tax Act.
  • Voluntary payments: the Act makes no difference between voluntary and contractual payment — both are taxable as salary.
  • Remuneration for extra work: extra payment by the employer (in that capacity) for work performed outside the duties of the office is taxable as salary.
  • Salary from more than one source: where an individual receives salary from more than one employer in the same previous year, salary from each employer is accumulated and taxed under "Salaries."
  • Former, present or prospective employer: salary from any of the three is chargeable under this head — e.g. pension from a former employer, advance salary from a prospective employer.
  • Salary paid tax-free: where tax on salary is borne by the employer, add the tax paid by the employer back to the amount received to compute income under "Salaries," then subtract that tax from the employee's tax liability. Further, u/s 10(10CC), income-tax paid by the employer on non-monetary perquisites on the employee's behalf is exempt in the employee's hands.
  • Foregoing of salary: once salary has been earned, a subsequent waiver does not exempt it — the waiver is an application of income. The one carve-out: salary surrendered to the Central Government u/s 2 of the Voluntary Surrender of Salaries (Exemption from Taxation) Act, 1961 is not taxable.

2.1.5 Basis of Charge [Sec. 15]

Salary is chargeable to tax on "DUE" basis or on "RECEIPT" basis — whichever is EARLIER.

Advance salary → taxed on receipt basis, in the year of receipt (and not again when it becomes due). Outstanding salary → taxed on due basis, in the year it falls due (and not again when received). Arrear salary → a retrospective increment not taxed in the past is taxed in the year it is allowed, on receipt basis.

Taxpoint: the method of accounting followed by the employee is irrelevant.

PROVISION ILLUSTRATED — arrear plus advance salary in one year

Find gross taxable salary.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SALARY "DUE" IS NOT SALARY "ACCRUED"

THE TRAP: Mr. X joins on 1st Dec. 2025 at ₹40,000 p.m.; students tax four months (December to March) in P.Y. 2025-26 because he "worked" four months.

THE TWIST: salary due is different from salary accrued — read the due date. Where salary falls due on the 1st day of every next month, December's salary is due 1/1/2026, January's on 1/2/2026 and February's on 1/3/2026 — three months' salary lands in P.Y. 2025-26 — but March's salary is due only on 1/4/2026 and therefore falls in P.Y. 2026-27. Related twin trap: "advance salary" is taxable u/s 17(1)(e), but an "advance against salary" is treated as a loan and is not taxable under this head at all.

Place of Accrual of Salary

Salary received in India or earned in India is taxable in the hands of every assessee, resident or non-resident. Salary is deemed to be earned in India where (a) the service is rendered in India, and (b) the rest period or leave period which is preceded and succeeded by service rendered in India and forms part of the service contract of employment.

Exception: salary paid to a Government employee being a citizen of India is deemed to accrue in India irrespective of the place of work [Sec. 9(1)(iii)]. Taxpoint: salary is earned at the place where the service is rendered.
