The Fully Taxable Core — Basic, DA, Fees, Commission, Bonus

  • Basic Salary — the sum paid by the employer as salary; fully taxable.
  • Pay-Scale (Grade system) — a payment system where the increment scale is pre-known. E.g. a scale of 15,000 – 5,000 – 30,000 – 8,000 – 46,000 means: initial pay ₹15,000 p.m., rising by ₹5,000 every year until it reaches ₹30,000 p.m., thereafter rising by ₹8,000 every year till it reaches ₹46,000. Basic salary is computed off that schedule.
  • Dearness Allowance (DA) / Dearness Pay (DP) — an extra amount to meet inflation or the increased cost of living. Fully taxable. Where the problem says DA/DP does not form part of retirement benefit, DA/DP is still fully taxable in the gross salary; it is simply excluded from "salary" when computing taxable leave encashment, pension, HRA, provident fund, etc.
  • Fees — extra remuneration for doing a specific job under the terms of employment; fully taxable.
  • Commission — whether a percentage of turnover or a percentage of profit, taxable in either case.
  • Bonus — contractual or voluntary, fully taxable either way. Contractual bonus is taxable as bonus; voluntary bonus is taxable as a perquisite. It is taxable in the year of receipt. Arrear bonus attracts relief u/s 89(1).

Retirement benefits — Gratuity, Leave Encashment, Pension, VRS compensation and other retirement receipts — are the exemption-bearing part of this head, and are taken next.

CONCEPT

2.1.6 Gratuity

Gratuity is a retirement benefit given by the employer in consideration of past services. Sec. 10(10) deals with its exemption, and that exemption can be claimed only by a salaried assessee — gratuity received by someone who is not an employee is not eligible. E.g. gratuity received by an agent of LIC of India is not eligible u/s 10(10), because agents are not employees of LIC.

Everything turns on five cases. Identify the case first; only then reach for a formula.

CaseSituationTreatment
AGratuity received during continuation of serviceFully taxable in the hands of all employees, Government or non-Government.
BOn termination of service, by a Government employeeFully exempt u/s 10(10)(i).
COn termination, by a non-Government (including foreign Government) employee covered by the Payment of Gratuity ActExempt to the minimum of three limbs u/s 10(10)(ii).
DOn termination, by a non-Government employee NOT covered by the Payment of Gratuity ActExempt to the lower of three limbs u/s 10(10)(iii).
EReceived after death of the employeeNot taxable in the hands of the recipient (see the taxpoint below).
"Government employee" for Case B includes an employee of the Central or State Government or a local authority, but does NOT include an employee of a statutory corporation.

CASE C — covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act [Sec. 10(10)(ii)]: exempt = MINIMUM of  (1) Actual gratuity received  |  (2) ₹20,00,000  |  (3) 15 working days' salary for every completed year of service, i.e. (15 ÷ 26) × Completed years of service × Salary p.m.

Completed year of service here INCLUDES any fraction in excess of 6 months — 7 years 9 months = 8 years; 7 years 5 months = 7 years; 7 years 6 months = 7 years. Salary here means Basic + DA, last drawn.

Seasonal establishment: 15 days is replaced by 7 days — (7 ÷ 26) × Completed years × Salary p.m. Piece-rated employee: 15 days' salary is computed on the average of total wages (excluding overtime) received for the 3 months immediately preceding termination.

CASE D — NOT covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act [Sec. 10(10)(iii)]: exempt = LOWER of  (1) Actual gratuity received  |  (2) ₹20,00,000  |  (3) ½ × Completed years of service × Average Salary p.m.

Completed year of service here IGNORES any fraction of a year — 7 years 9 months = 7 years only. Average salary means Basic + DA (only if DA forms part of retirement benefit) + Commission as a fixed percentage on turnover, being the average of the last 10 months immediately preceding the month of retirement. (Retirement on 18/11/2025 → the 10 months run from January 2025 to October 2025.)

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: THE TWO "COMPLETED YEAR" RULES ARE OPPOSITE

THE TRAP: the same service period — say 29 years 6 months 15 days — is rounded the same way in both gratuity formulas.

THE TWIST: under the Payment of Gratuity Act (Case C) a fraction in excess of 6 months counts as a full year, so 29 years 6 months 15 days = 30 years. Where the Act does not cover the employee (Case D) any fraction is simply ignored, so the very same service is 29 years. And the salary base differs too: last-drawn Basic + DA in Case C, but a 10-month average of Basic + DA + turnover commission in Case D.

Ashok, an employee of ABC Ltd., receives ₹8,05,000 as gratuity under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. He retires on 10th September 2025 after 35 years and 7 months of service. Last drawn salary ₹32,700 p.m. Calculate the gratuity chargeable to tax.

Gratuity — Three Notes You Will Be Tested On

  1. Gratuity may be paid on retirement, resignation, termination or death.
  2. The statutory ceiling is a lifetime ceiling. While claiming the ₹20,00,000, any amount earlier claimed as deduction u/s 10(10) is reduced from it. E.g. an assessee who left a job in 2001-02 and claimed ₹40,000 for gratuity, then left another organisation in 2025-26 receiving ₹19,80,000, gets a statutory limit of only ₹19,60,000 for A.Y. 2026-27.
  3. More than one employer: where gratuity is received from more than one employer in the same previous year, the aggregate exempt amount cannot exceed the statutory deduction.

Case E — gratuity received after the death of the employee. The Act is silent, but the position is settled by circulars: a lump sum paid gratuitously to the widow or legal heir of an employee who dies in service, by way of compensation or otherwise, is not taxable under "Salaries" [Circular No. 573, dated 21.08.1990]; unutilised deposit under the capital gains deposit account scheme is not taxable in the legal heir's hands [Circular No. 743 dated 6/5/1996]; a legal representative is not liable for tax on income that had not accrued to the deceased till his death; and leave salary paid to the legal heir of a deceased employee is not taxable as salary [Circular Letter No. F.35/1/65-IT(B), dated 5/11/1965], with leave salary to the legal heir of a Government employee who died in harness also not taxable [Circular No. 309, dated 3/7/1981].

Taxpoint — the timing test for a deceased employee: if gratuity becomes due BEFORE the death of the assessee (no matter when, or by whom, it is received) it is taxable in the hands of the employee. If gratuity becomes due AFTER the death, it is not taxable at all — not even in the hands of the legal heir.

CONCEPT

2.1.7 Leave Salary Encashment

Every employee is normally allowed a certain period of leave (with pay) each year. Unused leave may be availed later or encashed; the amount received for waiving leave lying to credit is leave salary encashment. Again, work by cases.

CaseSituationTreatment
ALeave salary received during continuation of serviceFully taxable for Government as well as other employees [Sec. 17(1)(va)].
BOn termination of service, by a Central or State Government employeeFully exempt u/s 10(10AA)(i).
COn termination, by a non-Government employee (including an employee of a foreign Government, local authority or public sector undertaking)Exempt to the minimum of four limbs u/s 10(10AA)(ii).
DLeave salary paid to the legal heir of a deceased employeeNot taxable [Circular Letter No. F.35/1/65-IT(B), dated 5/11/1965; Circular No. 309, dated 3/7/1981 for a Government employee dying in harness].
"Government employee" for Case B does NOT include an employee of a local authority, a public sector undertaking, or a foreign Government — those all fall into Case C.

CASE C — non-Government employee [Sec. 10(10AA)(ii)]: exempt = MINIMUM of the four — (a) Actual amount received as leave salary; (b) ₹25,00,000; (c) 10 × Average salary p.m.; (d) [{(1 × completed years of service) − leave actually taken in months} × Average salary p.m.], i.e. a maximum of 30 days (taken as 1 month) average salary for every completed year of service, less leave actually availed during the tenure.

Average salary = Basic + DA (only if it forms part of retirement benefit) + Commission as a fixed percentage on turnover, being the average of the last 10 months ending on the date of retirement or superannuation. (Retirement on 18/11/2025 → 19th Jan 2025 to 18th Nov 2025.) Completed years of service: ignore any fraction — 10 years 9 months = 10 years.

Two ceiling notes: (a) where leave encashment is received from more than one employer in the same previous year, the aggregate exempt amount cannot exceed ₹25,00,000; (b) any deduction claimed earlier for leave encashment is reduced from that ₹25,00,000.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: THE 10-MONTH WINDOW SHIFTS BETWEEN GRATUITY AND LEAVE ENCASHMENT

THE TRAP: the same 10-month average is used for both gratuity (Case D) and leave encashment.

THE TWIST: for gratuity not covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act, the 10 months are those preceding the month of retirement — retirement on 18/11/2025 gives January to October 2025. For leave encashment the 10 months end on the date of retirement — the same retirement gives 19th January 2025 to 18th November 2025. Under Sec. 3(35) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 a "month" is reckoned by the British calendar, so part-months are pro-rated by days, not rounded off.

(2) Per Sec. 3(35) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, a month is reckoned by the British calendar — 7th September to 6th October is one month. (3) Salary = Basic + DA + commission on turnover, being the last 10 months' average from the date of retirement.

ILLUSTRATION 6 — Deriving completed years from the leave entitlement

Mr. Das retired on 31/3/2026 with 18 months' leave to his credit and received leave encashment equal to 18 months' Basic salary, ₹1,26,000. His employer allows 1½ months' leave for every completed year of service; during his tenure he availed 12 months' leave. At retirement he also gets D.A. ₹3,000. His last increment of ₹1,000 in Basic was on 1/4/2025. Find taxable leave encashment.

Working 1 — completed years: he received 18 months' encashment and enjoyed 12 months' leave, so total leave benefit = 30 months. Since 1½ months' leave is allowed per completed year, completed service = 30 ÷ 1½ = 20 years.

Working 2 — average salary: Basic + DA + Commission, last 10 months' average from the date of retirement. There is no increment in the last 10 months (the last one was on 1/4/2025) and no commission, so average salary = ₹7,000 (₹1,26,000 ÷ 18) + ₹3,000 = ₹10,000 p.m.

CONCEPT

2.1.8 Pension [Sec. 10(10A)]

Pension is a periodical payment received by an employee after retirement. On some occasions the employer allows the employee to withdraw a lump sum being the present value of that periodical pension — the lump sum is fixed considering the age and health of the recipient, the rate of interest, and so on.

TypeMeaningTreatment
Uncommuted pension (Case A)Pension received periodically.Fully taxable in the hands of all employees, Government and non-Government alike.
Commuted pension — Government employee (Case B)Lump sum in commutation of pension.Fully exempt u/s 10(10A)(i).
Commuted pension — other employee who ALSO receives gratuity (Case C)Lump sum in commutation of pension.One-third of total pension the assessee is normally entitled to commute is exempt [Sec. 10(10A)(ii)].
Commuted pension — other employee who does NOT receive gratuity (Case D)Lump sum in commutation of pension.One-half of total pension the assessee is normally entitled to commute is exempt [Sec. 10(10A)(ii)].
For Case B, "Government employee" includes an employee of the Central or State Government, a local authority, AND an employee of a statutory corporation. Judges of the High Court and the Supreme Court are also entitled to the exemption [Circular No. 623 dated 6/1/1992]. For Case C it is immaterial whether the employee is covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act or not.
  • Pension received by a widow or legal heir of a deceased employee is not taxable as salary, but is taxable u/s 56 as income from other sources.
  • Where commuted pension is taxable, relief u/s 89 is available.
  • Pension received from the United Nations Organisation is not taxable; pension received by a widow of a UN ex-official from the UN Joint Staff Pension Fund is also exempt.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: THE FRACTION APPLIES TO 100% COMMUTATION, NOT TO THE AMOUNT RECEIVED

THE TRAP: where 80% of pension is commuted for ₹1,20,000, students exempt ½ or ⅓ of the ₹1,20,000 actually received.

THE TWIST: the exemption is a fraction of the total pension the assessee is normally entitled to commute, i.e. of the 100% figure. Gross it up first: if 80% commutation = ₹1,20,000, then 100% commutation = ₹1,50,000, and the exemption is ½ × ₹1,50,000 = ₹75,000 or ⅓ × ₹1,50,000 = ₹50,000. And do not forget that after commutation the uncommuted pension continues on the residual percentage only.

2.1.9 Retrenchment Compensation

Retrenchment means cancellation of the contract of service by the employer.

[Sec. 10(10B)] Compensation received by a worker at the time of retrenchment is exempt to the extent of the MINIMUM of — (a) Actual amount received; (b) ₹5,00,000; or (c) the amount calculated under Sec. 25F(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 — i.e. 15 days' average pay for every completed year of service or any part thereof in excess of 6 months.

Where the compensation is paid under any scheme approved by the Central Government, nothing is taxable at all. Compensation received by a workman at the time of closing down of the undertaking in which he is employed is treated as compensation received at the time of retrenchment.

2.1.10 Compensation Received at the Time of Voluntary Retirement [Sec. 10(10C)]

Where an employee accepts retirement willingly in exchange for compensation, that is voluntary retirement. The exemption is conditional on both: (1) the compensation is received from a specified employer, and (2) it is received under a Voluntary Retirement Scheme framed in accordance with the prescribed guidelines of Rule 2BA.

Exemption u/s 10(10C) = MINIMUM of — (a) Actual amount received as per the guidelines; or (b) ₹5,00,000.

Once in a lifetime: where the exemption is allowed in any assessment year, no deduction is allowed in any subsequent assessment year. Further, where relief has been allowed u/s 89 in respect of voluntary retirement, no exemption is allowed under this section.

Rule 2BA guidelines — the scheme must satisfy all five:

  1. The scheme applies to all employees (other than directors) who have either completed 40 years of age or completed 10 years of service. (This condition does not apply to an employee of a public sector company.)
  2. The scheme is framed to reduce the number of employees.
  3. The vacancy caused by the VRS is not to be filled up.
  4. The retiring employee is not to be employed in another company or concern belonging to the same management.
  5. The compensation does not exceed either (i) an amount equivalent to 3 months' salary for each completed year of service, or (ii) salary at the time of retirement multiplied by the balance months of service left. Salary here means Basic + DA (if it forms part of retirement benefit) + fixed percentage of commission on turnover, last drawn.

Specified employer: any company; an authority established under a Central, State or Provincial Act; a local authority; a co-operative society; a specified University; an Indian Institute of Technology; any State Government; the Central Government; a notified Institution of Management (IIM Ahmedabad, IIM Bangalore, IIM Calcutta, IIM Lucknow, and the Indian Institute of Foreign Trade, New Delhi); or any notified institution.

Taxpoint: voluntary retirement compensation received from an employer who is an individual, firm, HUF, AOP, etc. is fully taxable in the hands of the employee — such an employer is not a specified employer.

2.1.11 Annuity [Sec. 17(1)(ii)]

Annuity means a yearly allowance, income, or grant of an annual sum, for life or in perpetuity. Who pays it decides the head.

CaseTreatment
Annuity payable by a present employer, whether voluntarily or contractuallyFully taxable as salary.
Annuity received from an ex-employerFully taxable as profit in lieu of salary, u/s 17(3)(ii).
Annuity received from a person other than the employer, e.g. from an insurerTaxable under Sec. 56 as Income from other sources.

2.1.12 Salary Received in Lieu of Notice Period

When an employer retrenches an employee he must give proper notice. If he fails to, he must pay salary equivalent to the notice period, over and above retrenchment compensation. That amount is fully taxable — it does not share the Sec. 10(10B) exemption.

2.1.13 Profits in Lieu of Salary [Sec. 17(3)]

Five categories of receipt are taxable as profits in lieu of salary.

  1. Compensation due to or received by an assessee from his employer or former employer at or in connection with (a) the termination of his employment, or (b) the modification of the terms and conditions of employment.
  2. Any payment due to or received from the employer or former employer, except the following seven — gratuity exempted u/s 10(10); house rent allowance exempted u/s 10(13A); commuted pension exempted u/s 10(10A); retrenchment compensation exempted u/s 10(10B); payment from an approved Superannuation Fund u/s 10(13); payment from a statutory provident fund or public provident fund; and payment from a recognised provident fund to the extent exempt u/s 10(12).
  3. Any payment from an unrecognised provident fund or such other fund, to the extent it does not consist of the assessee's own contributions or interest on those contributions.
  4. Any sum received under a Keyman Insurance Policy, including the bonus allocated on such policy.
  5. Any amount due to or received by the employee (lump sum or otherwise) prior to employment or after cessation of employment.
CONCEPT

2.1.14 Allowances

Allowance means a fixed quantum of money given regularly, in addition to salary, to meet a particular requirement. The name of the allowance usually reveals the nature of that requirement — House Rent Allowance, Tiffin Allowance, Medical Allowance, and so on.

Sort every allowance in a problem into one of three families before you compute anything: fully taxable, partly exempt (either against actual expenditure or against a fixed statutory ceiling), and fully exempt. Then check the regime — most of these exemptions are casualties of the default tax regime.

SectionParticularsOld RegimeNew (default) Regime
10(13A)House Rent AllowanceAmount received in excess of the specified limits is taxable.No exemption.
10(14)(i)Special allowance/benefit, not being in the nature of a perquisite, granted to meet expenses wholly, necessarily and exclusively incurred in performing the duties of an office — Cat. A: Travel/Tour/Transfer, Daily and Conveyance Allowance; Cat. B: Helper, Uniform and Research/Training AllowanceExempt to the LOWER of (i) actual allowance received, or (ii) actual amount spent for the purpose.Same treatment for Cat. A only (Travel/Transfer, Daily, Conveyance). No exemption for Cat. B — Helper, Research and Uniform Allowance.
10(14)(ii)Special allowances to meet personal expenses at the place of duty or residence, or to compensate for the increased cost of living — e.g. City Compensatory, Tiffin, Medical, Servant and Transport AllowanceAmount received in excess of the limits specified under Rule 2BB(2) is taxable. Taxpoint: the deduction is available irrespective of actual expenditure.Partial exemption survives only for transport allowance to an employee who is blind / deaf and dumb / orthopaedically handicapped.
Allowance granted to meet the cost of travel on transfer includes any sum paid in connection with transfer, packing and transportation of personal effects on such transfer.

Fully Taxable Allowances

AllowanceMeaning
City Compensatory AllowanceTo meet personal expenses arising from special circumstances, or to compensate the extra expenditure of a posting at a particular place.
Tiffin AllowanceTo meet expenditure on tiffin, refreshment, etc.
Medical AllowanceTo meet expenditure on medical treatment, etc. (A fixed medical allowance is always fully taxable, however much is actually spent.)
Servant AllowanceTo meet the expenditure of a servant for personal purposes.
Non-practicing AllowanceGiven to professionals to compensate the restriction on private practice.
Warden or Proctor AllowanceGiven to employees of educational institutions for working as hostel warden or as proctor.
Deputation AllowanceGiven when an employee is sent on deputation for a temporary period from his permanent place of service.
Entertainment AllowanceTo meet expenditure on entertainment, by whatever name called. A Government employee can then claim a deduction u/s 16(ii) from gross salary.

House Rent Allowance [Sec. 10(13A) and Rule 2A]

An allowance to meet the expenses in connection with the rent of a house, by whatever name called. This is the single most examined formula in the head.

EXEMPT u/s 10(13A) = MINIMUM of the three limbs —
(a) Actual HRA received;
(b) 50% of salary if the house is in a METRO city, or 40% of salary if it is anywhere else, for the relevant period;
(c) Rent paid − 10% of salary.

Salary here = Basic + D.A. (only if it forms part of retirement benefit) + Commission as a fixed percentage on turnover. Available only if the assessee opts for the old regime.

Four working rules: (a) salary is determined on due basis, and only for the period during which the employee occupies rented accommodation and gets HRA; (b) no exemption at all if the employee lives in his own house, or in a house for which he pays no rent; (c) for the 50%/40% test what matters is where the house is situated, not where the employee is employed; (d) the deduction therefore turns on four variables — salary, amount of HRA, place of residence, and rent paid.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: PLACE OF EMPLOYMENT vs. PLACE OF THE HOUSE

THE TRAP: the employee works in a metro, so students apply 50% of salary to the whole year's HRA.

THE TWIST: the 50%/40% test looks only at where the rented house is situated. An employee posted in a metro but renting outside it gets 40%; an employee posted elsewhere but renting a metro house gets 50%. And when either the salary, the rent, the city or the fact of renting changes mid-year, the exemption must be computed separately for each segment of the year and the segment figures added — never on a single annual average.

Special Allowances Exempt u/s 10(14)(i) — Exemption Depends on ACTUAL Expenditure

AllowanceMeaning
Travel or Transfer AllowanceTo meet the cost of travel on tour. Cost of travel includes any sum paid in connection with transfer, packing and transportation of personal effects on such transfer.
Daily AllowanceGranted on tour (or for the journey period in connection with a transfer) to meet the ordinary daily charges incurred by the employee on account of absence from his normal place of duty.
Conveyance AllowanceTo meet expenditure on conveyance in the performance of the duties of the office, provided free conveyance is not provided by the employer. Taxpoint: the journey between office and residence is NOT expenditure in the performance of duties and is not covered here — that is Transport Allowance territory.
Helper / Assistant AllowanceTo meet the expenditure of an assistant or helper, provided the helper is appointed for the performance of the duties of an office. Taxpoint: Servant allowance is fully taxable.
Research AllowanceGranted to encourage academic, research and other professional pursuits. Also termed Professional Development / Academic allowance.
Uniform AllowanceTo meet expenditure on the purchase or maintenance of uniform worn during the performance of duties. Taxpoint: uniform allowance is different from Dress allowance — dress allowance is fully taxable.

Exempt u/s 10(14)(i) = MINIMUM of — (a) Actual amount received; or (b) Actual expenditure incurred for that purpose.

Taxpoint: under the default regime the exemption survives only for Travel or Transfer Allowance, Daily Allowance and Conveyance Allowance. There is NO exemption under the default regime for Helper Allowance, Research Allowance or Uniform Allowance.

Allowances Exempt u/s 10(14)(ii) — Exemption Does NOT Depend on Actual Expenditure

No benefit is available under the default tax regime for this family, except transport allowance.

CHILDREN EDUCATION ALLOWANCE [old regime only] — exempt to the MINIMUM of: (a) ₹100 per month per child, to a maximum of two children; or (b) actual amount received for each child, to a maximum of two children.

CHILDREN HOSTEL ALLOWANCE [old regime only] — exempt to the MINIMUM of: (a) ₹300 per month per child, to a maximum of two children; or (b) actual amount received for each child, to a maximum of two children.

"Child" includes an adopted child and a step-child, but not an illegitimate child or a grandchild; the child may be major or minor; and the deduction is available irrespective of actual expenditure incurred on the child's education.

TRUCK DRIVER'S ALLOWANCE [old regime only] — an allowance to an employee of a transport system to meet personal expenditure while on duty in the course of running that transport, provided he is not in receipt of a daily allowance. Exempt to the MINIMUM of: (a) 70% of the allowance; or (b) ₹10,000 p.m.

Taxpoint: if the assessee is in receipt of a Daily Allowance, this allowance is fully taxable.

TRANSPORT ALLOWANCE [available under BOTH regimes] — to meet the expenditure of travelling between the place of residence and the place of duty. Available only where the assessee is blind / deaf and dumb / orthopaedically handicapped. Exempt to the MINIMUM of: (a) actual amount received; or (b) ₹3,200 p.m.

Taxpoint: no exemption is available to any assessee other than those specified above — for everyone else transport allowance is fully taxable.

CONCEPT

2.1.15 Perquisite [Sec. 17(2)]

In common parlance a perquisite is any casual emolument or benefit attached to an office or position, in addition to salary or wages, which is availed by an employee — in short, the benefits over and above normal salary.

Per Sec. 17(2), "perquisite" includes — (i) the value of rent-free accommodation provided by the employer; (ii) the value of any concession in rent in respect of accommodation provided by the employer; (iii) the value of any benefit or amenity granted or provided free of cost or at a concessional rate to a specified employee; (iv) the amount paid by an employer in respect of any obligation which would otherwise have been payable by the employee; (v) any sum payable by the employer, directly or through a fund (other than a recognised provident fund, approved superannuation fund or deposit-linked insurance fund), to effect an assurance on the assessee's life or a contract for an annuity; (vi) the value of any specified security or sweat equity shares allotted or transferred, directly or indirectly, by the employer or former employer, free of cost or at a concessional rate; (vii) the aggregate of contributions made by the employer to the assessee's account in a Recognised Provident Fund, in the Sec. 80CCD(1) scheme (NPS) and in an approved superannuation fund, to the extent it exceeds ₹7,50,000 in a previous year; (viii) the annual accretion (interest, dividend, etc.) during the previous year to the balance at the credit of the aforesaid fund or scheme to the extent it relates to that contribution; and (ix) the value of any other fringe benefit or amenity as may be prescribed.

Two timing rules to memorise separately: an obligation of the employee met by the employer [17(2)(iv)] is taxable on CASH basis — in the year the employer pays it. A sum payable to effect an assurance/annuity [17(2)(v)] is taxable on ACCRUAL basis.

Example of the cash rule: an employer paying the employee's professional tax liability for 2025-26 in April 2026 creates a perquisite taxable in the previous year 2026-27, not 2025-26.

Combined ceiling: there is a single combined upper limit of ₹7,50,000 in a year for the employer's contributions to NPS, superannuation fund and recognised provident fund taken together — any excess is taxable, and so is the annual accretion attributable to it.

Three tests before anything is a perquisite under this head: it must be (a) allowed by an employer to his employee or any member of his household; (b) resulting in a personal advantage to the employee; and (c) derived by virtue of the employee's authority. A perquisite may be contractual or voluntary; but an unauthorised advantage taken without the employer's sanction is not a perquisite under "Salaries" (it is taxable as income from other sources). A perquisite may come from a former, present or prospective employer.

Member of household includes: spouse (dependent or not); parents (dependent or not); servants; children and their spouses (dependent or not); and dependants.

Specified Employees [Sec. 17(2)(iii)]

Several perquisites are taxable ONLY in the hands of a specified employee. Test all three gateways — any one is enough.

GatewayRuleTaxpoints and traps
1. Director-employeeAny employee who is a director.Immaterial whether he is a nominee of workers or financial institutions, whether full-time or part-time, or whether he was a director throughout the year. A director even for a day is a specified employee of that company. He is a specified employee of THAT company only — e.g. Manu, a director-employee of X Ltd. and merely an employee of Y Ltd., is a specified employee for X Ltd. alone.
2. Substantial interestAn employee who beneficially holds 20% or more voting power in the employer company.Specified employee of that company only. The criterion is beneficial, not legal, ownership. Substantial interest must be held by the assessee individually and not together with a relative — Mr. Mohan holding 18% and his wife 7% of X Ltd. is NOT a specified employee.
3. Salary ceilingAn employee whose aggregate salary from all employers together exceeds ₹4,00,000 p.a.If the aggregate exceeds the ceiling he is a specified employee of all his employers — Mr. Rohan with ₹2,36,000 from X & Co. and ₹2,45,000 from Y Ltd. is specified for both. Even DA not forming part of retirement-benefit salary is included for this ₹4,00,000 test.

Computing the ₹4,00,000: EXCLUDE / DEDUCT — (a) all non-monetary benefits; (b) non-taxable monetary benefits; (c) deductions u/s 16(ia), 16(ii) and 16(iii); and (d) the employer's contribution to Provident Fund.

So the test is applied to monetary salary net of Sec. 16 deductions — a large perquisite package can never by itself make an employee "specified."

Exempted Perquisites — the 21-item List

  1. Tea or snacks — tea, similar non-alcoholic beverages and snacks provided during working hours.
  2. Food provided by the employer at the working place.
  3. Recreational facilities extended to a group of employees.
  4. Goods sold to employees at concessional rate — goods manufactured by the employer and sold to employees at concessional (not free) rates.
  5. Conveyance facility — for the journey between office and residence and back, and to the Judges of the High Court and Supreme Court.
  6. Training — amounts spent on training of employees, including boarding and lodging for such training.
  7. Services rendered outside India — any perquisite allowed outside India by the Government to a citizen of India for rendering services outside India.
  8. Contributions to specified schemes — employer's contribution to a pension or deferred annuity scheme; to a staff group insurance scheme; and the annual premium paid by the employer on a personal accident policy in respect of his employee. (These are not perquisites because the employee has only an expectancy of the benefit.)
  9. Loans — a loan at nil or concessional interest where the aggregate amount of loan does not exceed ₹20,000; and an interest-free loan for medical treatment of the diseases specified in Rule 3A.
  10. Medical facility at office; and reimbursement of medical expenses for treatment of Covid-19. (But medical allowance is fully taxable.)
  11. Periodicals and journals required for the discharge of work.
  12. Privilege passes and privilege ticket orders granted by Indian Railways to its employees.
  13. Telephone, mobile phones — expenses actually incurred on the employee's behalf, whether by direct payment or reimbursement.
  14. Free education facility to children of the employee in an institution owned or maintained by the employer, provided the cost does not exceed ₹1,000 p.m. per child. Unlike Children Education Allowance, this is NOT restricted to two children.
  15. Computer or Laptop provided for use at office or at home, provided ownership is not transferred to the employee.
  16. Movable assets — sale or gift of any movable asset (other than a car and electronic items) to an employee after being used by the employer for 10 or more years.
  17. Leave Travel Concession, subject to conditions — exemption available only under the old regime.
  18. Rent-free accommodation — a rent-free official residence to a Judge of a High Court or the Supreme Court; and a rent-free furnished residence (including its maintenance) to an Official of Parliament, a Union Minister or a Leader of Opposition in Parliament.
  19. Accommodation provided on transfer of an employee in a hotel for a period not exceeding 15 days in aggregate; and accommodation in a remote area to an employee working at a mining site, onshore exploration site, project execution site, dam site, power generation site or offshore site.
  20. Tax on non-monetary perquisite paid by the employer on the employee's behalf — Sec. 10(10CC).
  21. Health club and sports club facility.
CONCEPT

2.1.16 Valuation of Perquisites — Rent-free Unfurnished Accommodation [Rule 3(1)]

Rent-free accommodation is taxable in the hands of all employees — except Judges of the High Court or Supreme Court, and Officials of Parliament, a Union Minister and a Leader of Opposition. "Accommodation" covers both a fixed structure (a house, flat, farm house or part of one, accommodation in a hotel, motel, service apartment, guest house) and a floating structure (a caravan, mobile home, ship).

For valuation, employees split into two categories.

CategoryValue of the perquisite
I. Central or State Government employee (including a military person), holding office or post in connection with the affairs of the Union or of that StateThe licence fee which would have been determined by the Central or State Government in accordance with the rules framed by that Government. (Academically, the taxable value is simply given in the problem.) Taxpoint: employees of a local authority or a foreign Government are NOT in this category.
II. Other employees (residual category)A percentage of salary, by city population — see the formula box.

CATEGORY II — accommodation OWNED by the employer: 10% of salary if the city's population exceeds 40 lakh as per the 2011 census; 7.5% of salary if it exceeds 15 lakh but not 40 lakh; 5% of salary for any other city — in each case for the period during which the employee occupied the accommodation.

CATEGORY II — accommodation NOT OWNED by the employer: rent paid or payable by the employer, OR 10% of salary, whichever is LOWER — regardless of the city's population.

Salary for RFA = Basic + Dearness allowance/pay (only if it forms part of retirement benefit) + Bonus + Commission + Fees + all other taxable allowances (taxable amount only) + any other monetary payment by whatever name called — EXCLUDING perquisites and lump-sum payments received at the time of termination, superannuation or voluntary retirement (gratuity, severance pay, leave encashment, voluntary retrenchment benefits, commutation of pension and similar payments), and EXCLUDING the employer's contribution to the employee's provident fund.

  • Salary for this purpose is determined on due basis.
  • Where the assessee receives salary from two or more employers, the aggregate salary for the period during which accommodation has been provided (by any of them) is taken.
  • Monetary payments that are not in the nature of a perquisite ARE counted — e.g. leave encashment received during continuation of service is included; leave encashment received at retirement is not.

CAP ON VALUATION IN SUBSEQUENT YEARS — where the SAME accommodation continues to be provided to the SAME employee for more than one previous year, the value is restricted to:
Amount calculated for the first P.Y. × (CII for the P.Y. for which the amount is calculated ÷ CII for the P.Y. in which the accommodation was initially provided)

CII = Cost Inflation Index as notified for the purposes of Sec. 48. "First previous year" means the previous year 2023-24, or the previous year in which the accommodation was provided to the employee, whichever is later. The value finally taken is the LOWER of the ordinary percentage-of-salary figure and this inflation-capped figure.

PROVISION ILLUSTRATED — the inflation-linked capping

ParticularsP.Y. 2023-24P.Y. 2025-26
Cost Inflation Index (CII)348376
Salary₹20,00,000₹28,00,000
Valuation of RFA, say 10% of salary [a]₹2,00,000₹2,80,000

RFA — Four More Rules

  1. Two houses on transfer — the 90-day exemption: where an employee is transferred and is provided with accommodation at the new place as well, the value of perquisite is taken for only one such house, the one having the lower value, for a period not exceeding 90 days. Thereafter, the values of BOTH houses are taxable.
  2. Site and remote-area accommodation: accommodation provided to an employee working at a mining site, on-shore oil exploration site, project execution site, dam site, power generation site or off-shore site is outside the charge where it is either (a) of a temporary nature, with plinth area not exceeding 1,000 sq. ft., located not less than 8 km away from the local limits of any municipality or cantonment board; or (b) located in a remote area. Remote area means any area other than one within the local limits of, or within an aerial distance of 30 kilometres from the local limits of, any municipality or cantonment board having a population of 1,00,000 or more based on the 2011 census.
  3. Deputation: where the Central or a State Government provides accommodation to an employee serving on deputation with a body or undertaking under its control, (i) the employer is deemed to be that body or undertaking, and (ii) the value is computed under residual category II as if the accommodation were owned by the employer.
  4. Concessional rent: value the accommodation exactly as if it were rent-free, then reduce the rent payable by the employee. Accommodation is deemed to be provided at a concessional rate where the computed value exceeds the rent recoverable from, or payable by, the assessee. This rule applies to Government employees too.

Concessional accommodation: Value of rent-free accommodation as usual *****  Less: Rent payable by employee to employer for the facility **** = Taxable value of perquisite ****

ILLUSTRATION 15 — Owned vs. hired accommodation in a 40-lakh-plus city

Mr. Chauhan (old regime): Basic Salary ₹75,000 p.m.; Entertainment Allowance ₹1,000 p.m.; Education Allowance ₹500 p.m. (he has 3 children); DA ₹3,000 p.m., of which only 60% forms part of retirement benefits; Fees ₹5,000 p.a.; Bonus ₹10,000 p.a.; professional tax of the employee paid by the employer ₹2,000 for the year. ⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: ALLOTTED vs. OCCUPIED

THE TRAP: a house is allotted with effect from 1/5/2025 but the employee could occupy it only from 1/6/2025; students charge the perquisite for 11 months from allotment.

THE TWIST: the percentage is applied "for the period during which the employee occupied the said accommodation" — so the charge runs for 10 months, not 11. Equally, remember which items are OUTSIDE salary for RFA: free refreshment, mobile/telephone facility and computer facility are exempt perquisites and never enter the RFA salary base; DA enters only to the extent it forms part of retirement benefit.

Rent-free FURNISHED Accommodation

Value of Furnished accommodation = Value of accommodation + Value of furniture

Value of furniture: 10% of the original cost where the furniture is owned by the employer; actual hire charges paid or payable where it is hired by the employer.

"Furniture" here includes a refrigerator, television, radio, air-conditioner and other household appliances. This rule applies to Government as well as non-Government employees.

Accommodation Provided in a Hotel

Value = MINIMUM of — (a) 24% of salary for the period such accommodation is provided; or (b) actual charges paid or payable to the hotel. Less any rent actually paid or payable by the employee.

Nothing is taxable where BOTH conditions hold: the accommodation is provided for a period not exceeding 15 days in aggregate, AND it is provided on transfer of the employee from one place to another.

"Salary" carries the same meaning as for rent-free accommodation. The rule applies to Government and non-Government employees alike. Where the facility runs for more than 15 days, the perquisite is exempt for the first 15 days and taxable thereafter — 45 days of hotel accommodation gives a taxable perquisite for the last 30 days only. "Hotel" includes licensed accommodation in the nature of a motel, service apartment or guest house.

2.1.17 Insurance Premium Payable by the Employer

Per Sec. 17(2)(v), sums payable by an employer — whether paid directly or through a fund other than a recognised provident fund, approved superannuation fund or deposit-linked insurance fund — to effect an assurance on the life of the assessee, or to effect a contract for an annuity, are a taxable perquisite in the hands of ALL employees.

Note: the employee can claim a deduction u/s 80C (if he opts for the old regime) for the LIC premium paid by the employer.

CONCEPT

2.1.18 Valuation of Sweat Equity Shares / Specified Securities (ESOP)

Specified security means securities as defined in Sec. 2(h) of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 — shares, scripts, stocks, bonds, debentures, debenture stock or other marketable securities of a like nature; derivatives; units or other instruments issued by a collective investment scheme; security receipts as defined in Sec. 2(zg) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002; units or instruments issued under a mutual fund scheme; any certificate or instrument issued to an investor by a special purpose distinct entity acknowledging beneficial interest in debt or receivables including mortgage debt; Government securities; such other instruments as the Central Government may declare; and rights or interest in securities. Where an employees' stock option has been granted under any plan or scheme, it includes the securities offered under that plan or scheme.

Sweat equity shares means equity shares issued by a company to its employees or directors at a discount, or for consideration other than cash, for providing know-how or making available rights in the nature of intellectual property rights or value additions, by whatever name called.

Taxpoint: if such shares are allotted or transferred for a reason OTHER than the above — e.g. an option granted against acquisition of immovable property by the company — the benefit is not a perquisite at all; the employee is instead liable to tax, if any, under the head "Capital Gains."

Three conditions must all be satisfied before the value becomes a perquisite: (a) the security or sweat equity shares are allotted or transferred on or after 01-04-2009; (b) they are allotted or transferred by the employer (former or present), directly or indirectly; and (c) they are allotted or transferred free of cost or at a concessional rate to the assessee.

Value of perquisite = Fair market value of the specified security or sweat equity shares on the date on which the OPTION IS EXERCISED by the assessee − the amount actually paid by, or recovered from, the assessee in respect of such security or shares.

Option means a right, but not an obligation, granted to an employee to apply for the specified security or sweat equity shares at a predetermined price.

Year of taxability: normally the year of exercising the option. But where the shares or securities are allotted by the current employer being an eligible start-up, the perquisite is taxable in the year that is EARLIEST of — (i) after the expiry of 48 months from the end of the relevant assessment year; (ii) the year in which the assessee sells such security or share; or (iii) the year in which the assessee ceases to be an employee of the employer.

ILLUSTRATION 20 — Which FMV date, and which assessment year?

Company 'X' grants an option to its employee 'R' on 1st April 2020 to apply for 100 shares, for making available rights in intellectual property to the employer-company, at a pre-determined price of ₹50 per share. Date of vesting 1st April 2021; exercise period 1st April 2021 to 31st March 2026. R exercises his option on 31st March 2025 and the shares are allotted/transferred to him on 3rd April 2025. FMV per share: 01-04-2020 ₹100; 01-04-2021 ₹180; 31-03-2025 ₹440; 03-04-2025 ₹470. Compute the taxable perquisite for A.Y. 2026-27.

Since the shares are allotted by the company AFTER 31-03-2025 (even though the option was exercised on 31-03-2025), the perquisite is taxable in A.Y. 2026-27.

Value of the perquisite in the hands of Mr. R
ParticularsAmount (₹)
FMV of shares on the date on which the option is exercised [₹440 × 100 shares]44,000
Less: The amount actually paid by the assessee in respect of such shares [₹50 × 100 shares]5,000
Value of perquisite39,000

For computing capital gain on a later transfer of these shares by Mr. R, ₹44,000 (i.e. ₹440 per share) is taken as their cost of acquisition — the amount already taxed as a perquisite is never taxed twice.

CONCEPT

2.1.19 Valuation of Perquisite in Respect of Motor Car [Rule 3(2)]

This grid is the most heavily examined perquisite in the paper. Read every problem as three questions in sequence: who owns the car; who maintains it; what is it used for. Only then read off the value — and only then ask in whose hands it is chargeable.

Owned byMaintained byUsed by employee forTaxable valueChargeable in whose hands
EmployerEmployerOffice purpose*Not a perquisiteNot applicable
Personal purposeM + DSpecified Employee
Both purposes₹1,800 or ₹2,400 p.m.
EmployerEmployeeOffice purpose*Not a perquisiteNot applicable
Personal purposeDSpecified Employee
Both purposes₹600 / ₹900 p.m.
EmployeeEmployerOffice purpose*Not a perquisiteNot applicable
Personal purposeMALL employees
Both purposesActual expenditure incurred by the employer, as reduced by ₹1,800 / ₹2,400 p.m. (with a further deduction of ₹900 p.m. for a driver), or a higher deduction if the prescribed conditions* are satisfied
EmployeeEmployeeAny purposeNot a perquisiteNot applicable

M = Maintenance cost.  D = Depreciation @ 10% of the actual cost of the car (but if the car is not owned by the employer, the actual hire charge incurred by the employer is taken instead).

₹2,400 p.m. applies to a higher-capacity car and ₹1,800 p.m. to a lower-capacity one; correspondingly ₹900 p.m. and ₹600 p.m. in the employer-owned/employee-maintained row. A higher capacity car means one whose engine cubic capacity exceeds 1.6 litres.

*Conditions for claiming a higher deduction or establishing office use: (i) the employer has maintained complete details of the journeys undertaken for official purposes — date of journey, destination, mileage and the amount of expenditure incurred; AND (ii) the employer gives a certificate that the expenditure was incurred wholly and exclusively for the performance of official duties.

Chauffeur / driver: where a chauffeur is also provided, the chauffeur's salary is ADDED to the value computed above. But where the car is used for both official and personal purposes, ₹900 p.m. — irrespective of the car's capacity — is taken as the value of the chauffeur perquisite.

  • If the car is provided at a concessional rate, charges paid by the employee are reduced from the value. However, where the statutory value (₹1,800 or ₹2,400 and ₹600 or ₹900) is taken as the taxable value, the amount charged from the employee is NOT subtracted.
  • "Month" denotes a completed month — any part of a month is ignored.
  • More than one car: where more than one car is provided otherwise than wholly and exclusively for office purposes, ONE car is valued as if provided partly for office and partly for private purposes (₹1,800 or ₹2,400 p.m., plus ₹900 p.m. for a chauffeur if provided), and the other car(s) are valued as if provided exclusively for private purposes.
  • Conveyance facility to Judges of the High Court or Supreme Court is not taxable.
  • Use of any vehicle provided to an employee for the journey from residence to workplace or back is not a taxable perquisite.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: DEDUCTING THE EMPLOYEE'S CONTRIBUTION FROM A STATUTORY VALUE

THE TRAP: the car is used for both purposes, the statutory value is ₹2,400 + ₹900 = ₹3,300 p.m. = ₹39,600, and the employee is charged ₹15,000 a year — so students answer ₹24,600.

THE TWIST: whenever the STATUTORY value (₹1,800/₹2,400 and ₹600/₹900) is the taxable value, the amount charged from the employee is NOT subtracted — the answer stays ₹39,600. The deduction for the employee's contribution applies only where the value is built up from actual maintenance and depreciation. And count only completed months: a car provided on 15/7/2025 gives 8 completed months, not 9.

ILLUSTRATION 26 — Three cars, and choosing the cheaper option

Mr. Vijay, a manager, has been provided the following cars by Kishan Ltd. (his employer), all owned by the employer. Car A: used for office as well as personal purpose, cost ₹3,00,000, maintenance by employer ₹50,000, capacity 1.8 ltr. Car B: used for office as well as personal purpose, cost ₹5,00,000, maintenance by employer ₹60,000, capacity 1.4 ltr. Car C: used for personal purpose, cost ₹2,00,000, maintenance expenditure of ₹40,000 incurred by the employee, capacity 1.6 ltr. Case (a): Mr. Vijay holds 17% of the equity share capital and 30% of the preference share capital of Kishan Ltd., and his wife holds 13% equity; his total salary during the year other than perquisites is ₹40,000. Case (b): Mr. Vijay holds 25% equity share capital of the employer company.

Case (a): voting power attaches to equity, and substantial interest must be held individually, not with a relative — 17% is below 20%, his salary is far below ₹4,00,000, and he is not a director. Since Mr. Vijay is NOT a specified employee and the employer owns all the cars, the car facility is not taxable at all.

Case (b): holding 25% equity, he holds substantial interest and IS a specified employee. Two cars are used for office as well as personal purposes, so he must nominate ONE as "office as well as personal" and treat the other as personal; Car C is personal in any case. That gives two options.

The Hon'ble Punjab & Haryana High Court in CIT v. Director, Delhi Public School (2011) 202 Taxman 318 held that if the value of the perquisite exceeds ₹1,000, the ENTIRE amount is taxable — an alternate view to the "excess only" reading.
  • The ₹1,000 p.m. per child exemption applies without any restriction on the number of children — unlike Children Education Allowance, which is capped at two children.
  • "Child" includes an adopted child and a step-child of the assessee, but does NOT include a grandchild or an illegitimate child.
  • Any amount charged from the employee for the facility is reduced from the above value.
  • Contribution made under an Educational Trust created for the children of a particular group of employees is not taxable.

Employer is engaged in the business of transportation of goods or passengersThe amount charged from the public for such facility is taxable in the hands of specified employees.
In any other caseThe actual cost to the employer is taxable in the hands of all employees.
Where the facility is provided to employees of Railways & Airlines, nothing is chargeable to tax. Any amount charged from the employee is reduced from the value. Conveyance facility for the journey between office and residence is not taxable.

2.1.25 Interest-free Loan or Loan at Concessional Rate [Rule 3(7)(i)]

NOT taxable where the aggregate amount of loan given by the employer (or any person on his behalf) to the employee or any member of his household does NOT exceed ₹20,000; and NOT taxable at all where the loan is for medical treatment of a disease specified in Rule 3A.

Otherwise, taxable value = interest at the rate charged by the State Bank of India as on the FIRST DAY of the relevant previous year in respect of loans for the same purpose, computed on the maximum outstanding monthly balance, LESS interest actually paid by the employee.

Maximum outstanding monthly balance means the aggregate outstanding balance for each loan as on the LAST day of each month.

  • Medical loan carve-out: the exempted loan does not include the amount that has been reimbursed by an insurance company under any medical insurance scheme.
  • Concessional interest: any interest paid by the employee to the employer is reduced from the computed value. If the rate charged by the employer is higher than the SBI rate, nothing is taxable as a perquisite.
  • The ₹20,000 is a threshold, not an exemption: if the loan amount exceeds ₹20,000, interest is levied on the total loan amount, not merely on the excess.
  • Interest on a loan taken before the insertion of this provision is also a taxable perquisite [Circular No. 15/2001 dated 12/12/2001].
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: TAXING ONLY THE EXCESS OVER ₹20,000

THE TRAP: a ₹5,00,000 interest-free loan is given, so students compute notional interest on ₹4,80,000 — the "excess" over the ₹20,000 threshold.

THE TWIST: the ₹20,000 is a gateway, not a deduction. Once the aggregate loan crosses it, notional interest is charged on the entire loan — on the maximum outstanding balance as at the end of each month — at the SBI rate prevailing on the FIRST day of the previous year for a loan of that same purpose, not the rate on the date the loan was taken.

2.1.26 Travelling / Touring / Holiday Home Expenditure on Holiday [Rule 3(7)(ii)]

Expenditure on travelling, touring, a holiday home, or any other expense paid, borne or reimbursed by the employer for any holiday availed by the employee or a member of his household is taxable in the hands of all employees.

CaseTaxable value of perquisite
Facility maintained by the employer and NOT available uniformly to all employeesThe notional cost of such facility — the value at which such facilities are offered by other agencies to the public.
Employee is on official tour and expenses are incurred for a member of his household accompanying himThe amount of expenditure incurred for the accompanying member of his household.
An official tour is extended as a vacationThe value is limited to the expenses incurred in relation to that extended period of stay or vacation.
In any other caseThe amount incurred by the employer.
Any amount charged from the employee is reduced from the value. These provisions do NOT apply to Leave Travel Concession, which has its own scheme u/s 10(5).

2.1.27 Free Meals [Rule 3(7)(iii)]

CaseTax treatment
Tea, snacks or other non-alcoholic beverages as light refreshment during office hours (including over-time)Nil
Free meals during office hours in a remote area (as defined for RFA), or at an offshore installationNil
Free meals and non-alcoholic beverages provided during office hours at office or business premises, or through paid vouchers which are non-transferable and usable only at eating jointsExpenditure on free meals in excess of ₹50 per meal is a taxable perquisite, to the extent of the excess, in the hands of all employees. [Available only under the old regime.]
In any other caseThe actual expenditure incurred by the employer, as reduced by the amount charged from the employee, is taxable in the hands of all employees.

Worked point from the source: a free meal worth ₹70 per meal, given through a non-transferable coupon 300 times in a year, gives a taxable perquisite of ₹6,000 [being (₹70 − ₹50) × 300]. An alternate view is possible — that where the value exceeds ₹50, the ENTIRE value is taxable — on which the perquisite would instead be ₹21,000. State the view you take.

2.1.28 Gift, Voucher or Token Given by the Employer [Rule 3(7)(iv)]

The value of any gift, voucher or token given to the employee (or any member of his household), on a ceremonial occasion or otherwise, is taxable in the hands of ALL employees — but gifts, vouchers or tokens up to ₹5,000 in aggregate during the previous year are exempted.

Where the worth of the gift exceeds ₹5,000, the amount in excess of ₹5,000 is taxable. No such ₹5,000 exemption is available on a gift made in cash or convertible into money.

ILLUSTRATION 28 — Gifts in kind, gifts in cash, and gifts to the spouse

Determination of taxable perquisite

If reimbursed by the employer: the amount reimbursed is taxable in the hands of ALL employees.

2.1.31 Use of Movable Assets [Rule 3(7)(vii)]

Where the employee or any member of his household uses any movable asset belonging to the employer (other than assets for which specific provisions exist), the value is — 10% of the original cost if the asset is owned by the employer, or the charges paid or payable by the employer if the asset is hired. Taxable in the hands of ALL employees.

Any sum charged from the employee is reduced. Use of a computer or laptop is an exempted perquisite. "Movable assets" here does NOT include a car — that has its own Rule 3(2).

2.1.32 Movable Assets SOLD by an Employer to an Employee [Rule 3(7)(viii)]

If the sale price is less than the written down value computed by the method and rate prescribed below, the difference is a perquisite taxable in the hands of all employees.

Type of assetRate of depreciationMethod of depreciation
Electronic items / Computer50%Reducing balance
Motor car20%Reducing balance
Any other asset10%Straight line
"Electronic items" here means data storage and handling devices such as computers, digital diaries and printers. They do NOT include household appliances like washing machines, microwave ovens or mixers — those fall into "any other," at 10% straight line.

Original cost to the employer *****  Less: Accumulated depreciation for each COMPLETED YEAR during which the asset was used by the employer **** = Written down value ****  Less: Amount charged from employee *** = Value of Perquisite (if positive)

Taxpoint: NO depreciation is charged for a part of the year — the depreciation clock runs in whole years from the date of purchase.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: CALENDAR-YEAR DEPRECIATION vs. FINANCIAL-YEAR DEPRECIATION

THE TRAP: depreciation on an asset bought on 1/7/2022 and sold on 18/8/2025 is charged for financial years 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25.

THE TWIST: completed years run from the date of purchase, not from 1st April. The computer bought on 1/7/2022 depreciates for 1/7/2022–30/6/2023, 1/7/2023–30/6/2024 and 1/7/2024–30/6/2025; the stub from 1/7/2025 to the 18/8/2025 sale date gets no depreciation because it is not a complete year. Second trap in the same rule: a Sofa set is "any other" asset at 10% straight line, so after 10 years its WDV is Nil — and a Nil WDV against a sale price of ₹5,000 gives a perquisite of Nil, never a negative figure.

2.1.33 Medical Facility [Proviso to Sec. 17(2)]

(a) Medical facility provided IN INDIA — six fully exempt cases.

No.CaseTreatment
1Medical facility provided to the employee or his family in a hospital, clinic, dispensary or nursing home maintained by the employer.Fully exempted
2Reimbursement of the medical bill of the employee or his family of any hospital maintained by Government or a Local Authority, or any hospital approved by the Government for its employees.Fully exempted
3Payment/reimbursement by the employer of medical expenses incurred by an employee on himself or his family in a hospital approved by the CCIT for the prescribed diseases (Cancer, TB, AIDS, etc.). The employee must attach to his return of income (i) a certificate from the approved hospital specifying the prescribed disease or ailment for which hospitalisation was required, and (ii) a receipt for the amount paid to the hospital.Fully exempted
4Approved group medical insurance (Mediclaim) obtained by the employer for his employees — approved by the Central Government or the Insurance Regulatory Development Authority.Fully exempted
5Any reimbursement by the employer of an insurance premium paid by the employee for insurance of his own health or that of a family member under a scheme approved by the Central Government or the IRDA.Fully exempted
6Reimbursement of the medical bill of the employee or his family for any illness relating to Covid-19, provided the employee submits: (a) the COVID-19 positive report, or a medical report where clinically determined positive through investigations in a hospital or in-patient facility by a treating physician; (b) all necessary documents of medical diagnosis or treatment for COVID-19 or a related illness suffered within 6 months from the date of being determined positive; and (c) a certification of all expenditure incurred on that treatment.Fully exempted

(b) Medical facility provided OUTSIDE INDIA — three lines, each with its own test.

CaseTreatment
Medical expenditureExempted to the extent permitted by RBI.
Cost of stay abroad (patient + one attendant/care-taker)Exempted to the extent permitted by RBI.
Cost of travel (patient + one attendant/care-taker)Exempted only where the gross total income of the employee, EXCLUDING this cost-of-travel perquisite, does not exceed ₹8,00,000 p.a. Taxpoint: in computing that GTI ceiling, the taxable value of the medical-treatment perquisite and of the cost-of-stay perquisite ARE included.
  • "Hospital" includes a dispensary, a clinic or a nursing home.
  • "Family" for this purpose means the spouse and children of the individual, and the parents, brothers and sisters of the individual wholly or mainly dependent on him.
  • Fixed Medical Allowance is fully taxable — the exemption is for a facility or a reimbursement, never for an allowance.
  • Expenditure on medical treatment by the employer may be by way of payment or reimbursement.
  • The perquisite is taxable in the hands of a specified employee; however, if the bills are issued in the name of the employee and reimbursed by the employer, it is taxable in the hands of all employees.

ILLUSTRATION 30 — Who counts as "family"?

(1) Y has been allowed a fixed medical allowance of ₹2,000 p.m. (2) Apart from reimbursement of petty medical bills of ₹25,000, Z and his family get medical treatment in a dispensary maintained by the employer, of the following values: Z ₹2,000; Mrs. Z ₹5,000; major son of Z (independent) ₹8,000; minor daughter of Z ₹25,000; dependent younger brother of Z ₹8,000; independent younger sister of Z ₹10,000; dependent sister-in-law ₹5,000.

(1) Medical allowance is fully taxable, so the taxable amount is ₹24,000.

(2) Taxable perquisite in the hands of Mr. Z
ParticularsAmount (₹)
(a) ZNil
(b) Mrs. ZNil
(c) Major son of Z (independent)Nil
(d) Minor daughter of ZNil
(e) Dependent younger brother of ZNil
(f) Independent younger sister of Z10,000
(g) Dependent sister-in-law5,000
(h) Reimbursement of medical bill25,000
Taxable Perquisite40,000

Spouse and children are "family" whether dependent or not — hence the independent major son is exempt. Brothers and sisters qualify ONLY if wholly or mainly dependent — hence the dependent brother is exempt but the independent sister is taxed. A sister-in-law is not "family" at all, dependent or otherwise. And the ₹25,000 of petty bills is a bare reimbursement outside the employer's own dispensary, so it is fully taxable.

2.1.34 Leave Travel Concession [Sec. 10(5)] [available only under the old regime]

If an employee goes on travel (on leave) with his family and the travelling cost is reimbursed by the employer, that reimbursement is fully exempted — subject to a tight set of conditions.

  1. The journey may be performed during service or after retirement.
  2. The employer may be present or former.
  3. The journey must be performed to any place within India.
  4. Where the journey is to various places together, the exemption is limited to the cost of the journey from the place of origin to the farthest point reached, by the shortest route — you cannot go to Manali first and then Goa on a Kolkata-to-Goa claim.
  5. The employee may or may not be a citizen of India.
  6. Stay cost is not exempt — the exemption is for travel cost only.

The exemption is limited to the amount actually incurred on the travel, to the extent below:

By Air → air economy class fare of the shortest route. By Rail → air-conditioned 1st class fare of the shortest route. Origin and destination connected by rail but journey by any other mode → same as by rail. Not connected by rail, but a recognised public transport system exists → first class or deluxe class fare, as the case may be, on such transport. Not connected by rail and no recognised public transport system exists → an amount equivalent to air-conditioned 1st class rail fare for the distance of the journey by the shortest route, as if the journey had been performed by rail.

  • No journey, no exemption: no exemption can be claimed without actually performing the journey and incurring expenses on it. Fixed leave travel allowance paid as a fixed sum is never exempt.
  • Block-period: the exemption is available for 2 journeys performed in a block of 4 calendar years commencing from 1st January 1986. Academically, for A.Y. 2026-27 the relevant blocks are January 2022 to December 2025 and January 2026 to December 2029.
  • Carry-forward: where the concession was not availed during the preceding block (on one occasion or both), any ONE journey performed in the first calendar year of the immediately succeeding block is additionally exempted — it is not counted against the two-journey limit.
  • Family here means the spouse and children of the individual, and the parents, brothers and sisters of the individual who are wholly or mainly dependent on him.
  • Restriction on number of children: the exemption may be claimed for any number of children born on or before 30/9/1998. In addition, it is available for only 2 surviving children born on or after 1/10/1998. Children born out of a multiple birth after the first child are treated as one child.
  • Leave travel concession provided to a High Court or Supreme Court Judge and members of his family is completely exempt without any conditions, under both regimes.

The value of any other facility, benefit, amenity, service, right or privilege not specifically dealt with above is determined on the basis of cost to the employer under an arm's length transaction, as reduced by the employee's contribution, if any.

CONCEPT

2.1.36 Provident Fund

A provident fund is a savings device for the salaried class and a retirement benefit scheme. A stipulated sum is deducted from the employee's salary as his contribution; the employer generally contributes a similar amount; both are invested in the fund and interest earned is credited to it. On termination or retirement the employee receives the whole accumulated fund, subject to conditions. So a provident fund has four components — employer's contribution, employee's contribution, interest on the employer's contribution, and interest on the employee's contribution — and each of the four is taxed differently in each of the four fund types.

TypeWhat it is
SPFStatutory Provident Fund — set up under the Provident Funds Act, 1925. Maintained by Government and semi-Government organisations, local authorities, railways, Universities and recognised educational institutions.
RPFRecognised Provident Fund — framed under the Employees' Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952; or an employer's own scheme recognised by the Commissioner of Income tax. Governed by Part A of Schedule IV to the Income-tax Act, 1961, which contains the rules on recognition of the fund, both contributions, and the treatment of the accumulated balance.
URPFUnrecognised Provident Fund — a scheme created by an employer that is NOT recognised by the Commissioner of Income tax.
PPFPublic Provident Fund — established by the Central Government to mobilise personal savings. Any member of the public (on his own behalf, or on behalf of a minor of whom he is guardian), salaried or self-employed, can open an account at any branch of the State Bank of India or its subsidiaries, other specified banks, or post offices. A salaried employee may simultaneously be a member of an employees' provident fund and of the PPF. For a deduction u/s 80C (old regime only) a member must contribute a minimum of ₹500 in a year; the maximum qualifying for deduction is ₹1,50,000 as per PPF rules. Interest is credited every year but payable only at maturity, and is exempt u/s 10(11).

SPF vs. RPF vs. URPF vs. PPF — the Master Comparison

ParticularsSPFRPFURPFPPF
Employer's ContributionNot taxableExempted up to 12% of Salary (salary = Basic + DA forming part of retirement benefit + Commission as a fixed percentage on turnover); the excess is taxableNot taxableNot Applicable
Employee's ContributionEligible for deduction u/s 80C [only under the old regime]Eligible for deduction u/s 80C [only under the old regime]NOT eligible for deduction u/s 80CEligible for deduction u/s 80C [only under the old regime]
Interest on employer's contributionNot taxable u/s 10(11)Exempted @ 9.5% p.a. u/s 10(12); any excess interest is taxable as salaryNot taxableNot Applicable
Interest on employee's contributionNot taxable u/s 10(11) (subject to Note 1)Exempted @ 9.5% p.a. u/s 10(12); any excess interest is taxable as salary (subject to Note 1)Not taxableNot taxable
Lump sum withdrawalExempt u/s 10(11)Exempt u/s 10(12) (subject to Note 3)See Note 2Exempt u/s 10(11)

NOTE 1 — the interest-on-own-contribution cap [Sec. 10(11)/(12), w.e.f. 01-04-2021]: interest accrued during the previous year in an employee's account shall NOT be exempted to the extent it relates to —

Where the employer IS giving a contribution: interest on the employee's contribution (made on or after 01-04-2021) in excess of ₹2,50,000 per year. Where the employer is NOT giving a contribution: interest on the employee's contribution (made on or after 01-04-2021) in excess of ₹5,00,000 per year.

Rule 9D — how it is computed: separate accounts within the provident fund account are maintained during P.Y. 2021-22 and all subsequent previous years for the taxable and non-taxable contribution, and the interest accrued in the taxable contribution account is not exempt. The non-taxable contribution account = closing balance as on 31-03-2021 + any contribution made during P.Y. 2021-22 and subsequent years not included in the taxable account + interest accrued on those balances, as reduced by withdrawals. The taxable contribution account = contributions in excess of the ₹2,50,000 / ₹5,00,000 threshold + interest accrued on them, as reduced by withdrawals.

Note 2 — Lump Sum Withdrawn from URPF: the Four-Way Split

ParticularsTax treatment
Accumulated employer's contributionFully taxable under the head "Salaries"
Accumulated employee's contributionNot taxable
Accumulated interest on the employer's contributionFully taxable under the head "Salaries"
Accumulated interest on the employee's contributionFully taxable as Income from Other Sources

Note 3 — lump sum withdrawn from RPF is NOT taxable if any of the following holds:

  1. The employee retires or terminates his job after 5 years of continuous service; or
  2. The employee has resigned before completing 5 years and joins another organisation which also maintains a recognised provident fund, and his fund balance with the current employer is transferred to the new employer; or
  3. The entire balance standing to the employee's credit is transferred to his account under the New Pension Scheme referred to in Sec. 80CCD; or
  4. The employee retires or terminates his job before 5 years of continuous service by reason of ill health, or by reason of contraction or discontinuance of the employer's business, or for any other reason beyond the control of the employee.

In any other case, the amount withdrawn is taxable exactly as in the case of a URPF — i.e. on the four-way split above.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: URPF WITHDRAWAL — ALL FOUR PIECES TAXED UNDER "SALARIES"

THE TRAP: on withdrawal from a URPF, students either exempt the whole thing (because "employer's contribution to URPF was never taxed") or push the whole thing into Salaries.

THE TWIST: split it four ways. The employer's contribution and the interest on it come to tax under Salaries; the employee's own contribution is not taxable at all (he never got a deduction for it); and the interest on the employee's contribution is taxable under Income from Other Sources — a different head, in the same year. Where the problem gives only a total, back out the interest as the residue and split it in the same ratio as the two contributions.

ILLUSTRATION 32 — The same contribution in an SPF, an RPF and a URPF

Mr. X: Basic pay ₹10,000 p.m.; DA ₹1,000 p.m.; Commission (fixed) ₹2,000; Entertainment allowance ₹2,000 p.m. X contributes ₹20,000 to a provident fund and the employer makes a matching contribution. ILLUSTRATION 33 — Withdrawal from URPF and RPF, four service histories

Sri Ramprasad retired on 1/7/2025 and received ₹3,00,000 as a lump sum from his provident fund, consisting of employer's contribution ₹1,25,000 and employee's contribution ₹1,25,000. State the treatment if (1) the fund is an Unrecognised Provident Fund; (2) the fund is a Recognised Provident Fund and (a) he retired after 23 years 7 months' service; (b) he retired after 4 years 7 months' service due to blindness; (c) he retired after 3 years 7 months and joined another company having an RPF, the old RPF balance being transferred to the new employer's RPF; (d) he retired after 3 years 10 months and started his own business.

(1) Lump sum received from a URPF
ComponentAmount (₹)Treatment
Employer's contribution1,25,000Taxable as salary
Employee's contribution1,25,000Not taxable
Interest on employer's contribution25,000Taxable as salary
Interest on employee's contribution25,000Taxable as income from other sources

Working: the total received is ₹3,00,000; the two contributions together are ₹2,50,000, so the balance ₹50,000 is interest. As the employer and employee contributed equal amounts, the interest is divided equally.

(2) Lump sum received from an RPF
CaseTreatment
(a) Retired after 23 years 7 monthsSince the employee retires after five years of service, the lump sum from the RPF is fully exempted — Sec. 10(12).
(b) Retired after 4 years 7 months due to blindnessSince he retires because of his incapability to work, the lump sum is fully exempted — Sec. 10(12).
(c) Retired after 3 years 7 months and transferred the balance to a new employer's RPFThough he left before five years, he joined another organisation maintaining an RPF and did not withdraw but transferred the balance — treated as a continuation of service, so fully exempted — Sec. 10(12).
(d) Retired after 3 years 10 months and started his own businessSince he left before five years of service, the amount received is taxable as in the case of a URPF — on the four-way split above.

Points to be Remembered — NPS, Agniveer and the ₹7,50,000 Cap

  1. The employer's contribution to the New Pension System (as specified u/s 80CCD) is fully taxable under the head "Salaries"; a deduction is then available u/s 80CCD. The deduction u/s 80CCD(2) for the employer's contribution is available irrespective of the regime; the deduction u/s 80CCD(1)/(1B) for the employee's contribution is available only under the old regime.
  2. The Central Government's contribution to the Agniveer Corpus Fund account forms part of salary. The deduction u/s 80CCH(2) for that Government contribution is available irrespective of the regime; the deduction u/s 80CCH(1) for the employee's contribution is available only under the old regime.
  3. The aggregate of the employer's contributions to (a) a Recognised Provident Fund, (b) the Sec. 80CCD(1) scheme (NPS), and (c) an approved superannuation fund, in excess of ₹7,50,000 in a previous year, is taxable — a single combined upper limit across all three.
  4. The annual accretion (interest, dividend, etc.) during the previous year to the balance at the credit of those funds, to the extent it relates to that excess contribution, is also taxable.

Payment from an Approved Superannuation Fund [Sec. 10(13)]

Any payment from an approved superannuation fund is exempt where it is made —

  • on the death of a beneficiary; or
  • to an employee in lieu of, or in commutation of, an annuity on his retirement at or after a specified age, or on his becoming incapacitated prior to such retirement; or
  • by way of refund of contributions on the death of a beneficiary; or
  • by way of refund of contributions to an employee on his leaving the service (otherwise than by retirement at or after a specified age or on becoming incapacitated prior to such retirement), to the extent that such payment does not exceed the contributions made prior to 1-4-1962 and any interest thereon; or
  • by way of transfer to the employee's account under a pension scheme referred to in Sec. 80CCD and notified by the Central Government.

Transferred Balance — Conversion of URPF into RPF [Rule 11(4), Part A of the Fourth Schedule]

An organisation maintaining a URPF may later obtain recognition from the Commissioner of Income tax, on which the accumulated URPF balance is converted into an RPF balance. A calculation is then made of all sums comprised in the transferred balance that would have been liable to income tax had the recognition of the fund been in force from the date of institution of the fund. (In case of serious accounting difficulty, the Commissioner may make a summary calculation of that aggregate.) That aggregate is deemed to be income received by the employee in the previous year in which the recognition of the fund takes effect.

Note: on the taxability of such a conversion, the assessee cannot claim relief u/s 89(1).
