CONCEPT

Deduction from Gross Salary [Sec. 16]

Only three deductions exist under this head, and two of the three vanish under the default regime. Write them in the order (ia), (ii), (iii) — the marking scheme follows that order.

2.1.37 STANDARD DEDUCTION [Sec. 16(ia)] — allowed to ALL employees, being the LOWER of:

OLD (regular) tax regime: (a) ₹50,000; or (b) the amount of gross salary.   |   DEFAULT tax regime: (a) ₹75,000; or (b) the amount of gross salary.

2.1.38 ENTERTAINMENT ALLOWANCE [Sec. 16(ii)] [available only in the old regime, and only to a GOVERNMENT employee] — deduction being the MINIMUM of:

(a) Actual Entertainment Allowance received; (b) ₹5,000; (c) 20% of Basic Salary. The deduction is allowed irrespective of the actual expenditure incurred, whether for office or personal purposes. NO deduction is available under this section to a non-Government employee.

2.1.39 TAX ON EMPLOYMENT OR PROFESSIONAL TAX [Sec. 16(iii)] [available only in the old regime] — tax on employment, profession, trade, etc. levied by a State under Article 276 of the Constitution, allowed as a deduction on CASH basis, whether paid by the employee or by the employer on his behalf.

Where the employer pays professional tax on behalf of the employee, it goes in TWICE: (a) first it is included as a taxable perquisite; and (b) then it is allowed as a deduction u/s 16(iii).

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: ENTERTAINMENT ALLOWANCE IS INCLUDED FIRST, THEN DEDUCTED

THE TRAP: students net the entertainment allowance off the gross salary, or grant the Sec. 16(ii) deduction to a non-Government employee.

THE TWIST: entertainment allowance is initially included in taxable allowances as fully taxable for every employee; the Sec. 16(ii) deduction is then given from gross salary — and only to a Government employee, and only under the old regime. Two more twists in the same box: the ₹5,000 limb is almost always the binding one, and "20% of Basic Salary" means Basic only — DA is not added, whether or not it forms part of retirement benefit.

A. Conversion of Net Salary into Gross Salary

Sometimes net basic salary is given after deducting TDS, loan repayment, PF deduction and so on, and must be grossed up.

Net Salary = Gross Salary − Employee's contribution to provident fund − TDS − loan repayment by employee − other deductions from salary (if any)

EXAMPLE — Grossing up a net basic salary

Find the basic salary of Mr. Singh: (a) Net Basic Salary received ₹1,00,000; (b) deduction from salary of 10% of basic salary as contribution to RPF; (c) TDS ₹9,000; (d) repayment of an earlier loan ₹35,000.

Net basic salary = Basic salary − TDS − Loan repayment − Contribution to RPF. Let the basic salary be X.

1,00,000 = X − 9,000 − 35,000 − 0.1X  →  1,44,000 = 0.9X  →  X = 1,60,000.

Answer: basic salary for the year is ₹1,60,000.

B. Meaning of "Salary" for Different Purposes — the One Table to Memorise

"Salary" wears seven different meanings inside this one head. More marks are lost to using the wrong meaning than to any arithmetic slip.

PurposeMeaning of "Salary"
FOR RETIREMENT BENEFITS
Gratuity (covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act)(Basic + DA) last drawn
Gratuity (NOT covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act)(Basic + DA1 + Commission2), being the average of the last 10 months preceding the month of retirement
Leave encashment(Basic + DA1 + Commission2), being the average of the last 10 months immediately from the retirement
Voluntary retirement(Basic + DA1 + Commission2) last drawn
FOR REGULAR BENEFITS
Rent Free Accommodation(Basic + DA1 + Commission2 + Bonus + Fees + any other taxable allowance + any other monetary benefit, excluding perquisites)
Specified employee (the ₹4,00,000 test)(Basic + DA + Commission2 + Bonus + Fees + any other taxable allowance + any other monetary benefit − deduction u/s 16)
Entertainment Allowance [Sec. 16(ii)]Basic only
Any other case(Basic + DA1 + Commission2)
1 DA only if it forms part of retirement benefit.   2 Commission as a fixed percentage on turnover. Note the two exceptions to 1: for gratuity covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act, and for the specified-employee test, DA is taken in FULL regardless of whether it forms part of retirement benefit.

CONCEPT

2.2 Income from House Property ★★★ HIGH

As per Sec. 22, the annual value of property consisting of any building or land appurtenant thereto of which the assessee is the owner — other than such portion of such property as he may occupy for the purposes of any business or profession carried on by him — is chargeable to tax under the head "Income from house property."

It is an exceptional feature of this head that rather than actual income from house property, the earning capacity of the house property is taxable. Sec. 22 taxes the "annual value" of the property, not its actual income (annual value is worked out later in this topic).

2.2.1 Chargeability [Sec. 22]

Annual value of the property is taxable under this head subject to three conditions.

Condition 1 — Building or land appurtenant thereto: "House property" is not defined in the Act; judicial interpretation construes it as (a) any land surrounded by a wall, having a roof or not, and (b) any land appurtenant to a building.

  • Building includes an enclosure of bricks, stone work, or even mud walls.
  • Building includes residential as well as commercial houses.
  • Vacant land is NOT a house property — income from letting vacant land is taxed as business income or income from other sources.
  • A roof is not necessary for a non-residential house property — a large stadium or an open-air swimming pool also counts as building.
  • It should be a permanent structure meant for a useful purpose.
  • If a building has several flats, each flat is a separate house property.
  • An incomplete, ruined, or demolished house cannot be termed house property.
  • Land appurtenant to a building includes car parking area, approach roads, backyards, courtyards, etc. attached to the building.

Condition 2 — Owner: annual value is assessed only in the hands of the owner, even if he receives no income; a person receiving rent who is not the owner is not taxed under this head. Hence income from sub-letting is taxable under "Income from other sources," not this head. E.g. Mr. X, tenant of Mr. Y at a monthly rent of ₹10,000, sub-lets to Mr. Z at ₹12,000 p.m.; the ₹2,000 p.m. profit is taxed as business income or income from other sources, not house property income.

Owner includes legal owner, beneficial owner, and deemed owner. A beneficial owner need not hold registered title — if he enjoys the property to the full extent of an owner, he is charged under this head.

Fictional owner or Deemed owner [Sec. 27]

In the following cases a person is treated as deemed owner and liable to tax (the legal/beneficial owner is then NOT further liable):

  1. Transfer to spouse or minor child [Sec. 27(i)]: where an individual transfers a house property to his/her spouse (not in connection with an agreement to live apart) or a minor child (not a married daughter) without adequate consideration, the transferor is deemed owner. Marriage must subsist both on the day of transfer and the day income arises. Transferred property must itself be a house property — if cash is transferred and the transferee buys a house with it, Sec. 27(i) does not apply (though the income is clubbed u/s 64(1)(iv)).
  2. Holder of an impartible estate [Sec. 27(ii)]: the holder of an impartible estate (not legally divisible, succeeded to by grant or covenant) is deemed owner.
  3. Property held by a member of a company, society or AOP [Sec. 27(iii)]: a member allotted/leased a building under a House Building Scheme of the company/co-operative society/AOP is deemed owner of that building, though not the legal owner.
  4. Person who acquired property u/s 53A of the Transfer of Property Act [Sec. 27(iiia)]: a person allowed to take/retain possession of a building in part performance of a contract u/s 53A of the TP Act, 1882 (part of the consideration paid/payable, contract in writing) is deemed owner.
  5. Lessee of a building u/s 269UA(f) [Sec. 27(iiib)]: a person acquiring a right u/s 269UA(f) by way of a lease agreement for a period not less than 12 years (including extension period) is deemed owner. Month-to-month leases or leases up to 1 year are excluded. E.g. a 9-year lease with a right to renew for 3 more years (11 total ≥ 12) makes the lessee deemed owner; but if renewal is conditional on 11-month cycles, the original owner remains taxable u/s 22.

Condition 3 — Property not used for business/profession carried on by the assessee: where a person carries on business/profession in his own house property, its annual value is not taxable u/s 22, provided such business income is chargeable to tax. Letting to employees (supporting smooth business flow), letting to Government agencies (bank branch, police station, post office, excise office, railway staff quarters, etc. for running the assessee's business more efficiently), and letting to ancillary units manufacturing components for the assessee are all deemed incidental to business — taxed as "Profits & Gains of Business or Profession," not house property. However, where the assessee's business itself IS letting out commercial properties, income is taxed as PGBP.

2.2.2 Some special cases

Assessee (foreign property)Condition for taxability
Ordinarily residentAlways taxable
Not ordinarily resident / Non-residentTaxable only if income is received in India
Annual value of a foreign property is computed as if the property were situated in India.

Disputed ownership: mere dispute over title cannot postpone assessment — the person in receipt of income or enjoying possession is assessed to tax.

Composite Rent = Rent for building + Rent for assets / Charges for various services

Where an owner receives one composite sum for the building plus other services/assets (furniture, machinery, etc.) provided in it.

Sum received forTaxable under the head
Use of the buildingIncome from house property
Other amenities / separable assetsPGBP, or Income from other sources
If segregation of composite rent is not possible, the WHOLE amount is taxed under PGBP or Income from other sources. Where letting of the building alone is not possible/acceptable (inseparable assets — e.g. hotel rooms, auditoriums), the whole rent is business/other-sources income even if segregable. Rent from a paying guest is, generally, taxable as Income from other sources.

Co-ownership [Sec. 26]: where two or more persons own a house property jointly with definite, ascertainable individual shares, each co-owner's share of income (computed per Sec. 22 to 25) is included in his own total income. Where a co-owned property is occupied by each co-owner, all of them can claim the Sec. 23(2)(a) self-occupation benefit, and interest on loan is allowed to each co-owner up to ₹30,000 / ₹2,00,000 as applicable. Sec. 26 is mandatory, not optional.

Partner's property used by the firm: business carried on by a firm is regarded as carried on by all partners — so the annual letting value of a property belonging to a partner but occupied by the firm is not includible in the partner's income u/s 22.

Property held as stock-in-trade [Sec. 23(5)]: where house property is held as stock-in-trade and not let out during any part of the previous year —

PeriodAnnual value
Up to 2 years from the end of the F.Y. in which the completion certificate is obtainedNil
After that periodComputed as per other provisions

2.2.3 Exempted properties

Income from the following house properties is exempt from tax:

  1. Any one palace (or part) of an ex-ruler, provided it is not let out [Sec. 10(19A)] — if partly self-occupied and partly let out, only the self-occupied part is exempt.
  2. House property of a local authority [Sec. 10(20)].
  3. House property of an approved scientific research association [Sec. 10(21)].
  4. House property of an educational institution [Sec. 10(23C)].
  5. House property of a hospital [Sec. 10(23C)].
  6. House property of a person resident of Ladakh [Sec. 10(26A)].
  7. House property of a political party [Sec. 13A].
  8. House property of a trade union [Sec. 10(24)].
  9. A farm house [Sec. 10(1)].
  10. House property held for charitable purpose [Sec. 11].
  11. House property used for own business or profession [Sec. 22].

2.2.4 Computation of Income

The chapter divides computation into six categories: Let-out property [Sec. 23(1)]; Self-occupied property [Sec. 23(2)(a)]; Deemed to be let out property [Sec. 23(4)]; Property not actually occupied by the owner [Sec. 23(2)(b)]; Partly let out and partly self-occupied property [Sec. 23(3)]; Recovery of arrears of rent and unrealised rent [Sec. 25A].

2.2.5 Let-out property [Sec. 23(1)] — Computation at a glance

Computation of Income from house property of ... for the A.Y. ...
ParticularsDetailsAmount
Gross Annual Value (GAV)****
Less: Municipal tax****
Net Annual Value (NAV)****
Less: Deductions u/s 24 — 24(a) Standard deduction (30% of NAV)****
  24(b) Interest on borrowed capital********
Income from house property****

Gross Annual Value (GAV) is determined from four factors

A. Actual Rent Receivable (ARR): computed on accrual basis; where tenant's rent is influenced by owner-provided benefits, it must be disintegrated — De facto rent = ARR − Cost of amenities. Outstanding rent is considered; advance rent received is NOT considered. Municipal tax paid by tenant and notional interest on tenant's deposit do NOT adjust de-facto rent.

B. Gross Municipal Value (GMV): the annual value fixed by the municipality for charging municipal tax. In metro cities (Chennai, Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai), tax is charged on Net Municipal Value after a repairs deduction (10% of GMV) and a service-tax allowance: NMV = GMV − 10% of GMV − Sewerage/Water Tax etc. (as % of NMV). In non-metro cities, GMV = NMV.

C. Fair / Notional rent: rent fetched by a similar property in the same/similar locality; inflated or deflated rent (emergency, relationship, etc.) must be adjusted to arrive at a reasonable fair rent.

D. Standard rent (Rent Control Act): the maximum rent a landlord can legally recover under the State's Rent Control Act. Reasonable Expected Rent (RER) cannot exceed Standard Rent, though it can be lower than Standard Rent. (RER is also called Annual Letting Value, ALV.)

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: STANDARD RENT IS A CEILING, NOT A TARGET

THE TRAP: students take RER as simply "higher of Municipal Value and Fair Rent," ignoring Standard Rent.

THE TWIST: RER = lower of [higher of (GMV, Fair Rent)] and [Standard Rent]. Standard Rent CAPS the RER; it can never push RER up, only down (or have no effect if it is the highest of the three).

Computation of Gross Annual Value (GAV) — step-by-step
StepParticularsAmount
1stGross Municipal Value (a)****
Fair Rent (b) — higher of (a) & (b) = [A]****
Standard Rent [B]; RER = lower of [A] and [B] = [C]****
2ndActual Rent Received/Receivable (ARR) − Unrealised Rent (UR) of the current year = [D]****
3rdGross Annual Value = higher of [C] and [D]****
4thHowever, where "ARR − UR" is LOWER only owing to vacancy, then "ARR − UR" (step 2) itself is treated as GAV.****

Unrealised Rent [Rule 4]: current-year unrealised rent is deducted in full from ARR only if — (i) tenancy is bona fide; (ii) the defaulting tenant has vacated (or steps have been taken to compel him to vacate); (iii) the defaulting tenant is not in occupation of any other property of the assessee; (iv) the assessee has taken all reasonable steps to sue for recovery, or has satisfied the Assessing Officer that legal proceedings would be worthless.

2.2.6 Taxes levied by local authority (Municipal Tax) [Proviso to Sec. 23(1)]

Tax levied by the municipality/local authority is deductible from GAV. As per Sec. 27(vi), "taxes levied by a local authority" includes service taxes (fire tax, water tax, sewerage tax, etc.) levied by that local authority. Computed as a % of Net Municipal Value, deduction is subject to three conditions: (1) actually paid during the previous year; (2) paid by the assessee; (3) related to the P.Y. or any year preceding the P.Y.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: WHO PAID, AND WHEN

THE TRAP: students deduct municipal tax that is outstanding, or that was actually paid by the tenant, or paid in advance for a future year.

THE TWIST: unpaid municipal tax and tax paid by the tenant are NOT deductible. Advance municipal tax is also NOT allowed — the Proviso to Sec. 23 deducts tax "irrespective of the previous year in which the liability was incurred," which presumes the tax has already been LEVIED; tax paid before it is levied cannot be deducted in the year of payment. Tax paid to a foreign local authority (property situated abroad) IS allowed. Refund of municipal tax already deducted is not taxable u/s 22. If cumulative tax paid (covering several past years) exceeds GAV, NAV can go negative.

The list u/s 24 is exhaustive — no deduction for expenditure not specified, e.g. no deduction for repairs, collection charges, insurance, ground rent, land revenue, etc.

ParticularsPre-construction periodPost-construction period
Starts fromDay of commencement of construction, or day of borrowing, whichever is later1st day of the P.Y. in which construction is completed
Ends on31 March immediately prior to the year of completion of constructionWhen the loan is fully paid
Tax treatmentAccumulated interest is allowed in 5 equal instalments from the year of completion of constructionInterest for the year (accrual basis) is allowed in the respective year
  • Interest on a fresh loan taken to repay the original (qualifying) loan is allowed.
  • Interest on a new loan taken to pay outstanding interest on the old loan is NOT deductible.
  • Brokerage/commission for arranging the loan is NOT deductible.
  • Interest on a loan taken for payment of municipal tax, etc. is NOT allowed.

Amount not deductible [Sec. 25]: interest payable outside India is not deductible if (a) tax has not been deducted at source (and paid per Chapter XVIIB), and (b) there is no agent in India for such interest u/s 163.

2.2.8 Self-occupied / unoccupied property [Sec. 23(2)]

Per Sec. 23(2)(a), a property is self-occupied where it (or part of it) — is in the owner's occupation for his own residence; is not actually let out during the whole or any part of the P.Y.; and no other benefit is derived by the owner from it. A residential house kept for self-occupation but that cannot actually be occupied by the owner for any reason is termed unoccupied property, treated the same as self-occupied. If an assessee occupies more than two houses as self-occupied, only two, at his option, can be treated as self-occupied; the rest are "deemed to be let out."

CombinationTreated as
Fully self-occupiedSelf-occupied property
Partly self-occupied & partly vacantSelf-occupied property
Partly self-occupied & partly let outPartly self-occupied & partly let out
Partly self-occupied & partly used for businessSelf-occupied to the extent used for self-occupation
  • Available to: only Individual and HUF; not available to a company, firm, etc.
  • Changing the option: the self-occupied choice may be changed every year without permission.
  • Owner occupying in another capacity: if the assessee occupies the house not as owner but, e.g., as an employee (owner let it out to his employer and got it back as rent-free accommodation), the self-occupation benefit CANNOT be claimed — the property is treated as let-out.
  • Combined units: where two-or-more residential units are self-occupied in a combined form (one property), annual value of the whole is nil, even though it has multiple units.
Computation at a glance — self-occupied property
ParticularsAmount
Net Annual ValueNil
Less: Interest on borrowed capital u/s 24(b) [available only if assessee opts for the old regime]***
Income from house property(***)

Standard deduction u/s 24(a) is NOT available for self-occupied property. The assessee can choose which two houses to treat as self-occupied to minimise tax — normally (not always) the house with the higher GAV is chosen as self-occupied, but it is advisable to compute total income under each option separately and pick whichever gives the lower income.

The ₹2,00,000/₹30,000 limit includes pre-construction period interest, and is the aggregate limit across ALL properties treated as self-occupied by that assessee.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: THE ₹2,00,000 CAP IS ONE CAP FOR ALL SELF-OCCUPIED HOUSES COMBINED

THE TRAP: students apply ₹2,00,000 separately to each of the two self-occupied properties.

THE TWIST: the ₹2,00,000 (or ₹30,000) ceiling is an AGGREGATE limit across both self-occupied properties taken together, not per property. Also, interest on self-occupied property is available only if the assessee opts for the OLD tax regime — under the default regime, it is not deductible at all.

2.2.9 Deemed to be let-out house property [Sec. 23(4)]

Where the assessee occupies more than two houses as self-occupied (or has more than two unoccupied houses), benefit u/s 23(2) can be claimed for any two of them (assessee's choice) — the remaining property/properties are treated as "deemed to be let out."

  • Gross Annual Value: since the assessee neither lets out the property nor receives rent, GAV is determined from Step 1 (RER) only — Steps 2, 3, 4 of the GAV computation are irrelevant.
  • Municipal taxes and deductions u/s 24(a) & 24(b) are available exactly as for let-out house property.

2.2.10 Partly self-occupied and partly let-out [Sec. 23(3)]

Where a house (or part of it) is self-occupied and let out during any part of the P.Y., the division may be Area-wise, Time-wise, or both.

Case 1 — Area-wise division: the property has two or more independent units, some self-occupied and some let out. Treatment: self-occupied and let-out portions are treated as two separate houses (Unit A / Unit B); common values (municipal value, fair rent, standard rent, municipal tax, interest) are proportionately divided; income of each unit is computed separately.

2.2.12 Recovery of Unrealised Rent and Arrears of Rent [Sec. 25A]

Applicability: the assessee has received arrears of rent, or unrealised rent realised subsequently, from a tenant.

Taxable amount = 70% × [Recovery of Arrear Rent or Unrealised Rent]

Taxable under "Income from house property" in the year of receipt, after deducting a standard deduction of 30% of the amount received.

  • No other deduction is allowed against this receipt except the 30% standard deduction — not even legal expenditure incurred to recover it.
  • The income is taxable on cash basis.
  • It is chargeable as income from house property even if the assessee is NOT the owner of that property in the year of receipt.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SELF-OCCUPIED BENEFIT AND THE DEFAULT TAX REGIME

THE TRAP: students deduct interest on a self-occupied house's loan regardless of which regime the assessee has chosen.

THE TWIST: interest u/s 24(b) on a self-occupied property is available only if the assessee opts for the old regime (Illustration 53, 63). Under the default regime u/s 115BAC, self-occupied NAV stays Nil and NO interest deduction is allowed against it — income from that house is simply Nil, never negative. A company/firm can never claim the self-occupied benefit at all (Illustration 60) — only Individuals and HUFs can.

CONCEPT

2.3 Profits and Gains of Business or Profession ★★★ HIGH

The most computation-heavy head of income — chargeability under Sec. 28, the deduction scheme of Sec. 29 to 43DB, and depreciation under Sec. 32 (block of assets, WDV method) are tested almost every attempt, frequently as full numerical problems.

2.3.1 Meaning of Business & Profession

Business [Sec. 2(13)]: Business includes — any trade, commerce or manufacture; or any adventure or concern in the nature of trade, commerce or manufacture.

Business generally means a recurring economic activity, but for income tax purposes an isolated activity may still be termed business depending on facts. Elements considered: nature of commodity, intention of the party, efforts applied in the transaction, periodicity of transaction, nature of transaction (whether incidental to a business or not).

Profession [Sec. 2(36)]: Profession includes vocation. Profession requires purely intellectual or manual skill based on special learning/qualification gathered through past training or experience (e.g. chartered accountant, doctor, lawyer). Vocation implies a natural ability to do particular work (e.g. singing, dancing) — it must have the earning feature, but unlike profession, does not require a degree or special learning.

AspectBusinessProfessionVocation
BasisTrade, commerce, manufacture, or adventure in the nature thereofIntellectual/manual skill from special learning & trainingNatural ability of the person
Qualification neededNone specificDegree/special learning, gathered through college/university/institute + experienceNo degree or special learning required
Tax treatmentSame treatment under the Act — both taxed as PGBPSame as profession for taxability, but "vocation" ≠ "hobby": it must have the earning feature
Segregation between business and profession still matters for applying Sec. 44AA, 44AB, 44AD, 44ADA (discussed later).

Note 1 — Profit motive: if the motive of an activity is pleasure only, it is not a business activity. Note 2 — Legality: illegal business income is still taxable (see General Points below), though a little segregation between business and profession is required for specific provisions.

2.3.2 Income Chargeable under PGBP [Sec. 28]

Sec. 28 enlists the incomes taxable under "Profits & gains of business or profession":

  1. Profits & gains of any business or profession [Sec. 28(i)]: including income from speculative transactions.
  2. Compensation to management agency [Sec. 28(ii)]: compensation/payment due to or received by a person managing the affairs of an Indian company or any company in India, on termination/modification of appointment terms; by an agent in India, on termination/modification of the agency; on vesting of management of property/business in Government/a corporation; or on termination/modification of any business contract.
  3. Income of trade/professional association [Sec. 28(iii)]: income from rendering specific services to members — an exception to the general principle that a mutual association's surplus is not taxable.
  4. Export incentive [Sec. 28(iiia)/(iiib)/(iiic)]: profit on sale of import licence/duty entitlement pass book, cash assistance from a Government of India scheme, and duty drawback receivable.
  5. Perquisite from business/profession [Sec. 28(iv)]: value of any benefit/perquisite arising from business or exercise of a profession, whether convertible into money or not, in cash or kind or partly both. E.g. a market-value car received by an authorised dealer over and above commission on achieving sale-target.
  6. Remuneration to partner [Sec. 28(v)]: interest, salary, bonus, commission or remuneration from a firm/LLP is business income in the partner's hands to the extent allowed in the firm's/LLP's hands u/s 40(b).
  7. Amount for non-compete/non-disclosure agreement [Sec. 28(va)]: any sum received/receivable for not carrying out any business activity, or for not sharing know-how/patent/copyright/trademark/licence/franchise or similar right — except (a) transfer of the right to manufacture/carry on business (taxable as Capital gains), and (b) compensation from the Montreal Protocol multilateral fund.
  8. Keyman Insurance Policy [Sec. 28(vi)]: any sum (including bonus) received under a Keyman policy — a life policy taken by a person on the life of another who is/was an employee, or connected in any manner with the business, of the first person [Sec. 10(10D)].
  9. Conversion of stock into capital asset [Sec. 28(via)]: the fair market value of inventory as on the date it is converted into/treated as a capital asset.
  10. Recovery on Sec. 35AD assets [Sec. 28(vii)]: sum received on a capital asset (other than land, goodwill or financial instrument) being demolished, destroyed, discarded or transferred, where the entire expenditure on it was allowed as deduction u/s 35AD.

General Points

  1. Chargeability [Sec. 145]: PGBP/Other Sources income is computed per the method of accounting (cash or accrual) regularly followed by the assessee [Sec. 145(1)] — except certain Sec. 43B expenditures, deductible only on cash basis. If the AO is unsatisfied about correctness/completeness/regularity of accounts or notified-standard compliance, Best Judgment Assessment u/s 144 may follow [Sec. 145(3)].
  2. Speculative transaction [Sec. 43(5)]: a transaction where a contract for purchase/sale of any commodity (incl. stock/shares) is periodically or ultimately settled otherwise than by actual delivery. Explanation 2 to Sec. 28 treats a speculation business as distinct and separate from any other business of the assessee.
  3. Deemed speculation — companies dealing in shares [Explanation to Sec. 73]: where part of a company's business is purchase and sale of shares of other companies, it is deemed a speculation business to that extent — except companies whose gross total income mainly consists of House Property/Capital Gains/Other Sources income, or whose principal business is trading in shares, banking, or granting loans/advances. (Covers shares only — not debentures or UTI/Mutual Fund units.)
  4. Not deemed speculative: hedging contracts (raw material/merchandise contracts to guard against price fluctuation on actual-delivery contracts; stock/share contracts by a dealer/investor to guard against holding losses; jobbing/arbitrage contracts by exchange members); eligible derivative trading on a recognised stock exchange (securities or commodity derivatives — commodities transaction tax requirement waived for agricultural commodity derivatives).
  5. Other Taxpoints: Income includes negative income (loss). Notional profit is not taxable — a person cannot do business with himself (e.g. proprietor withdrawing ₹10,000-cost goods at an agreed ₹12,000 value: the ₹2,000 "profit" is not taxable). Anticipated profit/loss is not considered. Legality of business is irrelevant — even illegal-business income is taxable, though expenditure for an offence/prohibited purpose is not deductible. Voluntary receipts received in the course of business/profession are income. Income from several businesses/professions of an assessee is merged. The business/profession must be carried on during the previous year (need not continue throughout the year).
SectionApplicability / Treatment
176(3A)/(4)Where a business/profession is discontinued and a sum is received after discontinuance, it is deemed income of the recipient in the year of receipt, if it would have been included in total income had it been received before discontinuance.
41(1)Recovery of any amount earlier allowed as a deduction.
41(2)Balancing charge in case of a power-sector unit.
41(3)Sale of an asset used for scientific research.
41(4)Bad debt recovery which was earlier allowed as deduction.
41(4A)Amount withdrawn from a reserve created u/s 36(1)(viii).
These are the exceptions where PGBP income can still arise even though the business is NOT carried on during the previous year.

2.3.3 Incomes NOT Taxable under PGBP

Though in the nature of business/profession profits, the following are NOT taxed under this head:

  1. Rent from residential house property — taxable u/s 22 under "Income from house property" even if the assessee's business is letting out properties, or the property is held as stock-in-trade.
  2. Dividend on shares — taxable u/s 56(2)(i) under "Income from other sources" even if the assessee deals in shares held as stock-in-trade (the rule does NOT extend to interest on securities held as stock-in-trade).
  3. Winnings from lotteries, races, etc. — taxable under "Income from other sources" even if derived through regular business. Exception: winnings from unsold lottery tickets held as stock-in-trade by a dealer are treated as incidental to business and taxed under PGBP.
  4. Income exempt by virtue of Sec. 10, 11 or 13A.
  5. Sum taxable under "Capital gains" for purposes of Sec. 28(va) — e.g. profit on sale of a route permit is not taxable under PGBP.

2.3.4 Expenditures Allowed as Deduction — General Notes

  1. Capital vs. Revenue expenditure: Capital expenditure is not allowed as deduction unless expressly allowed; revenue expenditure is allowed unless expressly disallowed.
  2. Expenditure of a non-assessable business is not allowed (e.g. expenditure for earning agricultural income cannot be set against an assessable business's income).
  3. Expenditure must relate to the assessee's own business — the mere fact that some other person also benefits does not deny admissibility.
  4. Anticipated loss/expenditure is not deductible, subject to exceptions (e.g. provision for bad & doubtful debts).
  5. Notional expenditure is not deductible — no one earns income from himself (rent/salary/interest on capital to a sole proprietor is not income in his own hands, hence not deductible from business income).
  6. Onus to prove that an expenditure is deductible lies on the assessee.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: CAPITAL vs. REVENUE — THE DEFAULT FLIPS

THE TRAP: students assume every expenditure is deductible "unless the Act says no," treating capital and revenue expenditure alike.

THE TWIST: the default direction is OPPOSITE for the two. Capital expenditure is disallowed BY DEFAULT — deductible only where expressly allowed (e.g. Sec. 35 scientific research capital expenditure, Sec. 35AD). Revenue expenditure is allowed BY DEFAULT — disallowed only where expressly barred (Sec. 40, 40A, 43B).

2.3.5 Specific Deductions [Sec. 29]: income under this head is computed considering the provisions of Sec. 30 to 43DB, which decide admissibility of expenditure.

2.3.6 Rent, Rates, Taxes, Repairs & Insurance for Building [Sec. 30]

  1. Use of building: must be used for business/profession. If not exclusively so used, deduction is restricted to a fair proportion determined by the AO [Sec. 38(2)].
  2. Notional rent: rent paid to the proprietor is disallowed, but rent paid by a firm to its partner for using his premises IS allowed.
  3. Current repair vs. capital repair: only current repairs are deductible, whether the assessee is tenant or landlord. Current repair (irrespective of amount) means a repair to preserve/maintain an existing asset, which does not create a new/fresh advantage, and is attended to as the need arises (not allowed to accumulate).
  4. Municipal taxes (land revenue, municipal tax, etc.) are deductible only on cash basis [Sec. 30 read with Sec. 43B].

2.3.7 Repairs & Insurance of Machinery, Plant & Furniture [Sec. 31]

  1. Use of asset: must be used for business/profession; if not exclusive, deduction restricted to a fair proportion determined by the AO [Sec. 38(2)].
  2. Current repair vs. capital repair: only current repairs deductible.
  3. Rent for the asset itself is NOT covered by Sec. 31 (only repairs & insurance are) — rent for use of plant/machinery/furniture is deductible u/s 37(1).
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SEC. 30/31 vs. SEC. 37(1)

THE TRAP: assuming Sec. 30 and Sec. 31 cover every building/asset-related cost — rent included.

THE TWIST: Sec. 30 and Sec. 31 cover ONLY rent/rates/taxes/repairs/insurance for buildings, and repairs/insurance for P&M/furniture. Rent paid to USE plant, machinery or furniture is not within Sec. 31 at all — it falls under the residuary Sec. 37(1).

2.3.8 Depreciation [Sec. 32] ★★★ HIGH

CategoryAssets Covered
Tangible assetsBuilding, Machinery, Plant and Furniture
Intangible assetsKnow-how, Copyright, Trade Mark, Patent, Licence, Franchise, or any other business or commercial right of similar nature acquired on or after 1/4/1998 (goodwill is NOT included)

Conditions for claiming depreciation: (1) the asset must be OWNED by the assessee, and (2) the asset must be USED for business/profession during the previous year.

  • Beneficial owner: need not be a registered owner — a beneficial owner can also claim depreciation.
  • Co-owner: joint ownership → depreciation allowed on a proportionate basis.
  • Hire purchase: the buyer can claim depreciation even before legal title passes (before the last instalment).
  • Lessee's capital expenditure on improvement/extension/super-construction of a business building — the lessee is entitled to depreciation on it.
  • Sec. 53A of Transfer of Property Act: a possessor under Sec. 53A can claim depreciation even without registered ownership.
  • Passive vs. active use: use includes both. Active use = actual use; passive use = "ready to use" — if a property was not actually used but was ready to use in the PY, depreciation can still be claimed.
  • Partly used for business [Sec. 38]: proportionate depreciation (as determined by the AO) is allowed.
  • Property let to employee/Government agency: where letting supports smooth running of the assessee's business (e.g. staff quarters, or a bank/police-station/post-office branch on the assessee's premises), the rent is PGBP income and the property remains eligible for depreciation u/s 32.

Method of Computing Depreciation (Other Than Power Units)

Block of Assets [Sec. 2(11)]: a group of assets of the same nature, in respect of which the same rate of depreciation is charged. Two conditions: assets must be of the same nature (tangible: building/machinery/plant/furniture; intangible: know-how/patents/copyrights/trademarks/licences/franchises or similar commercial rights acquired on/after 1-4-1998, excluding goodwill), and the depreciation rate must be the same.

Depreciation is allowed on the written down value (WDV) method at prescribed rates.

Calculation of Depreciation (at a glance)
ParticularsAmount
W.D.V. of the block at the beginning of the previous year***
Add: Assets (falling within the block) acquired during the previous year*** (A)
Less: Money payable* + scrap value of assets (within the block) sold, discarded, demolished or destroyed during the P.Y. [subject to max. of (A)](***)
Written Down Value [cannot be negative]XYZ
Less: Depreciation (as a % on XYZ)(***)
Opening WDV for 1st day of next year****

* Money payable [Explanation to Sec. 41] = insurance/salvage/compensation moneys, plus (where sold) the sale price. "Money" means actual money/cash only — not any other benefit evaluable in money [CIT v. Kasturi & Sons Ltd. (SC)]. Gross sale amount is deducted; transfer expenses may separately be claimed u/s 37(1).

Depreciation is NOT charged when…

(1) Sale proceeds exceed the (Opening WDV + Additions) — the excess is short-term capital gain.

(2) The value of the block before depreciation is positive, but no asset remains in the block — that positive balance is short-term capital loss.

180-Day Rule (effect of date of purchase)

Where an asset is ACQUIRED during the previous year AND put to use for LESS than 180 days in that same previous year → depreciation is restricted to 50% of the normal rate.

Taxpoint: there is NO significance of the DATE OF SALE for computing depreciation — and the 50% restriction applies only to an asset acquired in the current P.Y., never to one carried over from an earlier year.

Buildings10%Non-residential building, godown, office, factory, etc., including hotels and boarding

Illustration 66 — Tea Business: Correcting Depreciation Where Income Is Part-Agricultural

Mr. X, a grower and manufacturer of tea, purchased machinery (15%) on 10-4-2023 for ₹10,00,000. Error: Expl. 7 to Sec. 43(6) requires that, for computing WDV of assets acquired before the P.Y., the total depreciation be computed AS IF the entire income were business income — the 60:40 agriculture:business split is applied only AFTER depreciation is computed, not at every WDV step.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: THE 180-DAY RULE TESTS "ACQUIRED", NOT "USED"

THE TRAP: students see an asset used for less than 180 days anywhere in the computation and halve the depreciation on it, regardless of when it was actually bought.

THE TWIST: the ½-rate restriction applies ONLY where the asset was BOTH acquired during the current P.Y. AND used for less than 180 days in that same P.Y. (Illustration 65, Case K). An asset carried over from an earlier year that happens to be put to use late this year gets FULL depreciation. Similarly, the date of SALE is entirely irrelevant to the depreciation computation — only the date of acquisition/use matters.

2.3.9 Additional Depreciation [Sec. 32(1)(iia)] OLD REGIME ONLY

Applicable to all assessees engaged in manufacture/production of any article or thing, or in generation, transmission or distribution of power.

Conditions: (1) an industrial undertaking manufacturing/producing any article or thing, or a power-generation/transmission/distribution business; (2) a NEW plant or machinery acquired and installed after 31st March 2005, EXCLUDING — ships and aircraft; plant/machinery previously used (within or outside India) by any other person; plant/machinery installed in office premises/residential accommodation/guest house; office appliances or road transport vehicles; and plant/machinery eligible for 100% deduction in the same year.

Rate of Additional Depreciation = 20% of actual cost

If acquired & put to use for LESS than 180 days: 10% (i.e. 50% of 20%) in that P.Y., and the balance 10% in the immediately succeeding P.Y.

  • Additional depreciation is available ONLY on plant & machinery — not furniture, building, or any other asset.
  • Additional depreciation reduces the closing WDV of the block.
  • Not available if the new plant/machinery is sold in the year of acquisition itself.
  • Not available to a power unit claiming depreciation under the Straight-Line Method [u/s 32(1)(i)].
  • Printing / printing-and-publishing amounts to manufacture and IS eligible [Circular No. 15/2016 dt. 19-05-2016].

2.3.11 Depreciation in Case of Power Units

An undertaking engaged in generation, or generation and distribution, of power may choose (for assets acquired after 31/3/1997) — the WDV method (as for all other assessees), OR the Straight-Line Method at the prescribed rate in Appendix IA of the Income Tax Rules, on ACTUAL COST (not block value). The option must be exercised before the due date of furnishing the return, and once exercised applies to all subsequent A.Y.s. Additional depreciation is NOT available where SLM is opted.

Terminal DepreciationBalancing Charge
Applicable toAssessee engaged in generation or generation & distribution of power, following SLM, where the asset is sold/discarded/demolished/destroyed in a P.Y. OTHER THAN the year it was first brought into use.
Meaning+ve value of [WDV of asset – (Sale value or Scrap value)] — i.e. loss on transfer−ve value of [WDV of asset – (Sale value + Scrap value)] — i.e. profit on transfer, capped at accumulated depreciation
Excess over accumulated depreciation—Treated as capital gain (difference between sale price and actual cost)
TreatmentFully allowed as a business loss deduction; written off in the booksFully taxable as business income u/s 41(2) in the P.Y. it falls due — even if the business no longer exists that year; capped at accumulated depreciation claimed

2.3.12 Actual Cost of Assets [Sec. 43(1)]

In calculating actual cost, the following are INCLUDED besides the price of the asset: expenses directly related to acquisition (incl. travel), expenses to bring the asset to site/install/ready it for use (carriage inward, loading/unloading, installation, trial run), and expenses to increase the asset's capacity or make it fit prior to use.

Actual cost = actual cost to the assessee, REDUCED by that portion met directly or indirectly by any other person or authority. E.g. asset purchased for ₹5,00,000 with a ₹1,00,000 Government grant → actual cost for tax = ₹4,00,000.

SituationActual cost of acquisition
Assets acquired against cash payment >₹10,000 [in a day, to one person] otherwise than by account payee cheque/draft/ECS/other prescribed electronic modeSuch payment is IGNORED for determining actual cost.
Asset used for business after ceasing to be used for scientific research [Expl. 1]Actual cost to the assessee, LESS any deduction allowed u/s 35.
Asset acquired by gift or inheritance [Expl. 2]Actual cost to the previous owner, less depreciation that would have been allowable as if it were the only asset in the block; expenditure the assessee incurs (freight, installation, etc.) is also includible.
Interest on borrowed funds used to acquire an asset [Expl. 8]Before asset put to use: added to actual cost. After asset put to use: allowed u/s 36(1)(iii).
Subsidy/grant from Government or other authority [Expl. 10]Subtracted from cost of acquisition.
GST included in the invoice [Expl. 9]Actual cost is reduced by the input tax credit taken against GST (or other indirect tax).
Second-hand asset transferred mainly to reduce income-tax liability (via enhanced-cost depreciation claims) [Expl. 3]Actual cost determined by the AO, with prior approval of the Joint Commissioner.
Reacquisition of a transferred asset [Expl. 4]WDV at first transfer, OR price paid for reacquisition — whichever is LOWER.
Asset acquired from a person and leased back to the same person who had earlier claimed depreciation on it [Expl. 4A]WDV of the asset to the transferor. (Expl. 4A overrides Expl. 3.)
Building used personally, later brought into business [Expl. 5]Cost of purchase/construction, reduced by notional depreciation applying the rate applicable on the date of conversion.
Asset acquired outside India by a non-resident, later used in India [Expl. 11]Actual cost, reduced by depreciation calculated at the rate in force, as if used in India since the date of acquisition.
Asset transferred by a holding company to its 100% Indian subsidiary or vice versaSame actual cost as it would have been to the transferor company had it continued to hold the asset.
Asset transferred in amalgamation/demerger to an Indian amalgamated/resulting companySame actual cost as it would have been to the amalgamating/demerged company.
Sec. 35AD asset [Expl. 13]Deemed NIL. If gifted onward, cost stays Nil in transferee's hands. Where the asset is deemed income u/s 35AD(7B) (used for a non-specified purpose), actual cost = actual cost to assessee LESS depreciation that would have been allowable had it been used for business, at the rate in force, since acquisition.
Conversion of inventory into a capital asset [Expl. 1A]Fair market value of the inventory as on the date of conversion.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: THE "PERSONAL USE → BUSINESS" NOTIONAL-DEPRECIATION RULE IS BUILDING-ONLY

THE TRAP: students apply the Expl. 5 "cost less notional depreciation" formula to ANY personal asset (car, laptop, jewellery) converted to business use.

THE TWIST: Expl. 5 to Sec. 43(1) is worded specifically for BUILDINGS. For any other personal asset brought into business, the ORIGINAL COST is simply taken as the actual cost — market value and notional depreciation are irrelevant (Illustration 72).

2.3.13 Consequence of Changes in Rate of Exchange of Currency [Sec. 43A]

Conditions: (1) the assessee acquired an asset in a P.Y. from a country outside India; (2) due to a change in the exchange rate during any P.Y. after acquisition, there is an increase/decrease in the assessee's liability at the time of PAYMENT — towards the cost of the asset, or towards repayment of foreign-currency money borrowed specifically to acquire the asset (with interest).

Treatment: the amount of increase/decrease in liability at the time of payment (irrespective of accounting method) is added to or deducted from the actual cost (as reduced by depreciation already claimed).

Taxpoint: if the increase/decrease arises after the asset is transferred but the block still exists, it is adjusted in the WDV; if the block has ceased to exist, it is treated as a capital receipt/expenditure. Where the liability is met by another person/authority, that portion is ignored for Sec. 43A.

2.3.14 Taxation of Foreign Exchange Fluctuation [Sec. 43AA]

Any gain/loss, computed per ICDS, arising from a change in foreign exchange rates is treated as income/loss. This covers ALL foreign currency transactions: monetary and non-monetary items, translation of foreign-operation financial statements, forward exchange contracts, and foreign currency translation reserves (though ICDS itself does not deal with translation reserves). Sec. 43AA does NOT apply to cases already covered u/s 43A.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SEC. 43A vs. SEC. 43AA

THE TRAP: the near-identical section numbers get swapped in the exam.

THE TWIST: Sec. 43A is NARROW — it adjusts the ACTUAL COST of a specific imported asset when exchange-rate movement changes the liability at the time of payment. Sec. 43AA is GENERAL — it taxes/allows any forex gain or loss (per ICDS) across all foreign-currency transactions, and expressly steps aside wherever Sec. 43A already applies.

2.3.15–2.3.17 Unabsorbed Depreciation, Mandatory Provision & Succession Cases

2.3.15 Unabsorbed depreciation [Sec. 32(2)]: depreciation not fully deductible from current-year PGBP profits (insufficient profit) is "unabsorbed depreciation."

  1. It can first be deducted from income under any other head EXCEPT Casual income and Salaries, in the same A.Y.
  2. If still unabsorbed, it carries forward INDEFINITELY and can be set off against any income except Casual income and Salaries.
  3. Continuing the same business is NOT necessary.
  4. Set-off order: Current year depreciation → Brought forward business loss → Unabsorbed depreciation.
  5. Subject to Sec. 72/73, unabsorbed depreciation is added to the next year's depreciation allowance and treated as that year's depreciation, and so on.
  6. Carried forward even if the return of income was not filed.
  7. Under the default regime (Sec. 115BAC), unabsorbed additional depreciation attributable to a block from an earlier A.Y. (not given full effect before A.Y. 2024-25, and not set off in A.Y. 2024-25) increases the WDV of that block as on 1.4.2023.

2.3.16 Mandatory provision: from A.Y. 2002-03, if all Sec. 32 conditions are satisfied, depreciation is available WHETHER the assessee has claimed it or not.

2.3.17 Amalgamation, demerger or succession [Sec. 47(xiii)/(xiiib)/(xiv), Sec. 170]: depreciation u/s 32 in the year of amalgamation/demerger/succession is apportioned between the amalgamating and amalgamated company, the demerged and resulting company, or the predecessor and successor — in the ratio of the number of days each used the asset.

2.3.21 Deduction for Expenditure on Specified Business [Sec. 35AD]

For an individual/HUF/AOP/BOI carrying on specified business, Sec. 35AD is available only under the OLD REGIME. A company opting for Sec. 115BAA/115BAB is NOT eligible.

Specified businesses (each with its own "date of commencement on or after" threshold): cold-chain facility (1-4-2009); warehousing for agricultural produce (1-4-2010); cross-country natural gas/crude/petroleum pipeline network (1-4-2007, project approved by PNGRB & notified); 2-star+ hotel anywhere in India (1-4-2010); hospital with ≥100 beds anywhere in India (1-4-2010); notified slum-redevelopment housing project (1-4-2010); notified affordable-housing project (1-4-2011); fertilizer production in India (1-4-2011); inland container depot/container freight station under the Customs Act (1-4-2012); bee-keeping & production of honey/beeswax (1-4-2012); warehousing for storage of sugar (1-4-2012); slurry pipeline for iron-ore transport (1-4-2014); semi-conductor wafer fabrication unit, notified (1-4-2014); new infrastructure facility developed/maintained/operated by an Indian company (or consortium)/authority/board/corporation under a Government agreement (1-4-2017).

Cross-country oil pipelineOther specified business
Owned byAn Indian company/consortium, or an authority/board/corporation established under a Central/State ActAny assessee
Usage restrictionMust make available a PNGRB-specified proportion of total pipeline capacity for common-carrier use by others: Natural gas pipeline — 1/3rd; Petroleum product pipeline — 1/4thNo restriction
New business conditionMust NOT be set up by splitting up or reconstructing an existing business.
New plant/machinery conditionMust not be set up using P&M previously used for any purpose — EXCEPT imported P&M never depreciated in India where the assessee is the first Indian user, or where old P&M transferred in does not exceed 20% of total P&M value used.

Quantum of deduction: 100% of capital expenditure incurred during the P.Y., wholly and exclusively for the specified business — EXCLUDING expenditure on land/goodwill/financial instruments, and any payment (or aggregate to one person in a day) exceeding ₹10,000 made otherwise than by account payee cheque/draft/ECS/prescribed electronic mode. Pre-commencement capitalised expenditure is allowed in the year the business commences.

  • Optional: the assessee must affirmatively claim it.
  • No double deduction under any other section/year; also bars Sec. 10AA and 80HH–80RRB for the same specified business.
  • 8-year usage lock-in: the asset must be used ONLY for the specified business for 8 years from acquisition/construction. If diverted, [total deduction claimed – depreciation that would otherwise have been allowable u/s 32] is deemed PGBP income in the year of diversion (relief for a company that has become a sick industrial company u/s 17(1) of SICA, 1985).
  • Actual cost for depreciation of a Sec. 35AD asset is treated as NIL.
  • Realisation on demolition/destruction/transfer of a fully-Sec.-35AD-deducted asset is taxable as business income.
  • Carry forward of loss [Sec. 73A]: loss from a specified business can be set off ONLY against profit of another specified business; unabsorbed loss carries forward indefinitely against future specified-business profits.
  • Transfer of operation (e.g. a hotel built but its operation transferred to another person while ownership is retained) — the assessee is still deemed to be carrying on the specified business.
  • Inter-unit transfer between a Sec. 35AD-eligible unit and a non-eligible unit of the same assessee, at other than market value, is recomputed at MARKET VALUE.

"Associated person" = one who participates in management/control/capital of the assessee, holds ≥26% equity, appoints >half the Board (or one/more executive directors), or guarantees ≥10% of total borrowings. "Infrastructure facility" = road/toll road/bridge/rail system; highway project (incl. integral housing); water supply/treatment, irrigation, sanitation/sewerage or solid waste management project; port/airport/inland waterway/inland port/navigational channel.

2.3.22 Amortisation of Telecom Licence Fee [Sec. 35ABB]

Conditions: capital expenditure incurred to acquire a right to operate telecom services, AND the payment has actually been made (before or after commencement of business). Revenue telecom-licence expenditure is NOT eligible under Sec. 35ABB — it is claimed u/s 37(1) instead. NO depreciation is allowed on this capital expenditure.

CaseAmortisation period starts from
Licence-fee paid BEFORE commencement of business [Sec. 35ABB(1)]The P.Y. in which business commences
Licence acquired AFTER commencement of businessThe P.Y. in which the licence fee is actually paid

Deduction = actual expenditure incurred & paid, in EQUAL instalments over the period the licence remains in force. If the licence is sold in FULL [Sec. 35ABB(2)/(3)]: loss on sale → deductible as business loss in the year of sale; profit on sale, to the extent of aggregate deduction already allowed → business income; any excess of sale consideration over original cost (or indexed cost) → capital gain u/s 45. On amalgamation/demerger, the Indian amalgamated/resulting company continues the deduction for the residual period. A parallel deduction exists u/s 35ABA for spectrum-acquisition expenditure.

2.3.23–2.3.25 Rural Development, Agricultural Extension & Skill Development

  • 2.3.23 Sec. 35CCA — Rural development payments: full deduction for expenditure paid to (a) an association/institution undertaking an approved rural-development programme (certificate required); (b) an association/institution training persons to implement rural-development programmes (certificate required); (c) the National Fund for Rural Development; or (d) the National Urban Poverty Eradication Fund. No double deduction with Sec. 80G. Withdrawal of approval AFTER the contribution does not deny the deduction.

  • 2.3.25 Sec. 35CCD — Skill development project: full deduction to a COMPANY for expenditure (excluding cost of land/building) on a notified skill development project. No double deduction under any other provision.

2.3.26 Amortisation of Preliminary Expenses [Sec. 35D & Rule 6AB]

Preliminary expenses include: project/feasibility report preparation, market/other survey, engineering services for the business; legal charges for drafting business-setup agreements; legal charges for drafting/printing MOA/AOA (company only); Companies Act registration fees (company only); public-issue expenses (underwriting commission, brokerage, drafting/typing/printing/advertisement of prospectus — company only); and any other prescribed expenditure.

Non-corporate resident assesseeIndian company

Deduction = 1/5th of eligible preliminary expense, in 5 equal annual instalments, starting from the year business commences (or unit expansion/new unit commences production). Applicable to an Indian company or a resident non-corporate assessee only — NOT a resident foreign company. On amalgamation/demerger, the Indian amalgamated/resulting company claims the residual instalments [Sec. 35D(5)/(5A)].

Cost of Project = actual cost of fixed assets (land, buildings, leaseholds, plant, machinery, furniture, fittings, railway sidings) shown in the books as on the last day of the P.Y. business commences (or extension completes). Capital employed = issued share capital + debentures + long-term borrowings as on that same date, in connection with the business/extension.

2.3.27–2.3.29 Amalgamation/Demerger Costs, VRS, and Mineral Prospecting

2.3.27 Sec. 35DD: an Indian company incurring expenditure WHOLLY & EXCLUSIVELY for amalgamation/demerger (and not claimed under any other section) gets 1/5th of the expenditure deducted each year for 5 years, from the year amalgamation/demerger takes place.

2.3.28 Sec. 35DDA — VRS expenditure: any assessee paying VRS compensation to employees gets 1/5th deducted each year for 5 years, from the year of payment. On amalgamation/demerger the Indian successor company continues the residual instalments; on succession of a firm/proprietary concern by a company (Sec. 47(xiii)/(xiv)) or a private/unlisted-public company by an LLP (Sec. 47(xiiib)), the successor steps into the predecessor's shoes — but NO deduction is allowed to the predecessor/amalgamating/demerged entity in the very year of the amalgamation/demerger/succession, and no deduction is allowed under any other provision.

Sec. 10(10C) — "Salaries" headSec. 35DDA — PGBP head
Available toEmployees generally, but NOT employees of a partnership firm, HUF, or proprietorship firmALL assessees (as employer) can claim the deduction
Board approval of the VRS schemeExemption available ONLY if the scheme is Board-approvedDeduction available even if the scheme is NOT Board-approved

2.3.29 Sec. 35E — Mineral prospecting/development expenditure: available to an Indian company or any other resident assessee engaged in prospecting/extraction/production of a Seventh Schedule mineral. Qualifying expenditure = incurred in the year commercial production commences, or at any time during the 4 years preceding it, on prospecting or developing a mine/natural deposit. NOT qualifying: site/deposit acquisition cost; capital expenditure on building/plant/machinery/furniture already eligible for Sec. 32 depreciation; and any amount met by another person/authority. Non-corporate assessees need a CA audit report in Form 3AE, uploaded 1 month before the ROI due date. Deduction = total eligible expenditure in 10 equal instalments from the year of commercial production, capped each year at that year's mine-exploitation income (before this deduction); unabsorbed instalments carry forward up to the 10th year from commercial production. On amalgamation/demerger, the Indian successor continues the residual period (no deduction to the predecessor in the transfer year); no double deduction elsewhere.

2.3.30–2.3.41 Deductions under Sec. 36(1)

  • 2.3.30 Insurance premium for stocks & stores [36(1)(i)]: full deduction for premium against risk of damage/destruction of business stocks & stores. "Paid" = actually paid or incurred per the assessee's regular accounting method [Sec. 43(2)].
  • 2.3.31 Insurance premium for life of cattle [36(1)(ia)]: full deduction where paid by a federal milk co-operative society on cattle owned by members of an affiliated primary milk co-operative society.
  • 2.3.32 Insurance premium for employees' health [36(1)(ib)]: premium paid (other than by cash) as employer, under a scheme of the General Insurance Corporation approved by the Central Government, or of any other insurer approved by IRDA.
  • 2.3.33 Bonus or commission to employees [36(1)(ii)]: deductible if not in lieu of profit/dividend, and actually PAID before the return-filing due date [Sec. 43B].

2.3.34 Interest on Borrowed Capital [Sec. 36(1)(iii)]

Interest paid on capital borrowed for business/professional purposes is deductible, subject to: (a) money must have been borrowed; (b) it must be used for business/profession during the P.Y.; (c) interest must actually be incurred.

  1. Interest must be paid to ANOTHER person — interest on capital to a sole proprietor is disallowed; interest to PARTNERS is allowed u/s 40(b) instead.
  2. Interest paid by one unit of the assessee to another unit of the SAME assessee is not deductible.
  3. Interest to a relative is allowed, subject to Sec. 40A(2) — any excess over market rate is disallowed.
  4. Whether borrowed money was actually NEEDED is entirely the assessee's discretion — the AO cannot challenge the need, only that it was borrowed and applied in the business.
  5. Interest on share capital is not allowed.
  6. Interest on borrowings to acquire/install an asset: before commencement of business, or after commencement but before the asset is put to use — added to actual cost; AFTER the asset is put to use — allowed u/s 36(1)(iii).
  7. Interest on money borrowed and used to earn NON-ASSESSABLE income is not deductible.
  8. Interest on money borrowed to pay INCOME TAX is not allowed (interest on money borrowed to pay SALES TAX IS allowed).
  9. Interest paid outside India without TDS deduction is not allowed.
  10. Borrowed money may be applied to revenue OR capital expenditure — both qualify.
  11. Interest on money borrowed to invest as capital in a partnership firm IS allowed. Brokerage/commission to an agent for arranging the loan is NOT allowed under this section, but IS allowed u/s 37(1).
  12. Other interest (on deferred payment for a purchased asset, delayed electricity-charge payment, delayed raw-material payment, etc.) is claimed u/s 37(1), not u/s 36(1)(iii).
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: INTEREST TO PROPRIETOR vs. PARTNER vs. RELATIVE

THE TRAP: treating all "interest to a person connected with the business" as either uniformly disallowed or uniformly allowed.

THE TWIST: three DIFFERENT rules apply. Interest to a sole PROPRIETOR — fully DISALLOWED (a person cannot pay himself). Interest to a PARTNER — allowed, but only to the extent permitted in the firm's own hands u/s 40(b) (a firm-assessment-chapter cap, not Sec. 36(1)(iii)). Interest to a RELATIVE (any other lender) — fully allowed u/s 36(1)(iii), EXCEPT the portion above market rate, which is disallowed under Sec. 40A(2).

2.3.35–2.3.38 Zero Coupon Bonds, RPF/Superannuation, NPS & Gratuity Fund

2.3.35 Sec. 36(1)(iiia) — Discount on Zero Coupon Bonds: a "Zero Coupon Bond" [Sec. 2(48)] is issued by an infrastructure capital company/fund, public sector company, or scheduled bank on/after 1/6/2005, pays no amount/benefit before maturity/redemption, and is Central-Government notified. The discount on issue is allowed on a PRO RATA basis over the bond's life. ("Infrastructure capital company/fund" [Sec. 2(26A)/(26B)] = an entity investing by acquiring shares or providing long-term finance to enterprises under Sec. 80IA/80IAB, Sec. 80IB(10) housing projects, 3-star+ hotel projects, or 100+-bed hospital projects.)

2.3.36 Sec. 36(1)(iv) — Contribution to RPF/Superannuation Fund: employer's contribution, per the Fourth Schedule rules, is deductible IN FULL if actually paid before the return-filing due date [Sec. 43B]. Contribution to an UNRECOGNISED provident fund is NOT deductible; contribution to a STATUTORY provident fund is deductible u/s 37(1) instead.

2.3.37 Sec. 36(1)(iva) — Contribution to Notified Pension Scheme (NPS, Sec. 80CCD): employer's contribution is deductible up to 14% of the employee's "salary" for the P.Y. "Salary" here includes dearness allowance (if the employment terms so provide) but excludes all other allowances and perquisites.

2.3.38 Sec. 36(1)(v) — Contribution to Approved Gratuity Fund: employer's contribution to an approved gratuity fund set up under an irrevocable trust exclusively for employees is deductible, again subject to actual payment before the return-filing due date [Sec. 43B].

2.3.39 Employees' Contribution towards Staff Welfare Scheme [Sec. 36(1)(va)]

Any sum received by an employer from EMPLOYEES as their own contribution towards Provident Fund, Superannuation Fund, an ESI Act 1948 fund, or any other employee-welfare fund, is first treated as INCOME of the employer. It becomes deductible once the employer CREDITS it to the employee's account in the relevant fund on or before the due date prescribed under the relevant Act.

Timing of crediting employees' contributionTax treatment
Credited on or before the due date under the relevant ActNo separate treatment (netted off — effectively deductible)
NOT credited by that due dateTaxable as business income of the employer

"Due date" = the date the employer is required, under the relevant Act/rule/order/standing order/contract of service, to credit the employee's contribution. Example: under the ESI Act, 1948 and the EPF Scheme, 1952, contributions for wages of a given month must be deposited within 15 days of the close of that month.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: EMPLOYER'S OWN CONTRIBUTION vs. EMPLOYEES' CONTRIBUTION COLLECTED BY THE EMPLOYER

THE TRAP: assuming both the employer's PF/gratuity/superannuation contribution [Sec. 36(1)(iv)/(v)] and the amount deducted from EMPLOYEES' salaries towards PF/ESI [Sec. 36(1)(va)] follow the same "due date" — the return-filing due date under Sec. 43B.

THE TWIST: the EMPLOYER'S OWN contribution under 36(1)(iv)/(v) is deductible if paid any time before the RETURN-FILING due date [Sec. 43B]. But the money withheld from EMPLOYEES' wages under 36(1)(va) is first treated as the employer's income, and is deductible ONLY if credited to the employee's fund account by the due date FIXED UNDER THE RELEVANT WELFARE ACT (e.g. 15 days from month-end for EPF/ESI) — a much tighter, scheme-specific deadline, not the Sec. 43B return-filing date.

2.3.40–2.3.41 Dead/Useless Animals and Bad Debts

2.3.40 Sec. 36(1)(vi) — Allowance for dead or useless animals: applies where (a) the animals were used for business/profession, (b) they are NOT held as stock-in-trade, and (c) they have died or become permanently useless for that purpose. Deduction = difference between the animals' actual cost to the assessee and the amount realised (if any) on their carcasses/sale.

2.3.41 Sec. 36(1)(vii) — Bad Debts: any debt, or part of a debt, that becomes bad is allowed as a deduction. Taxpoint: it is the ASSESSEE who decides whether a debt has become bad — the Assessing Officer can never insist on proof that the debt actually became bad.

CONCEPT

Recovery of Bad Debts & Special Reserve ★★ MEDIUM

Where a deduction has been allowed for a bad debt (or part of it) u/s 36(1)(vii) and the amount subsequently recovered exceeds the un-allowed portion of that debt, the excess is deemed profits and gains of business or profession — taxable whether or not the business is continued.

Recovery of Bad Debts — Mathematically [Sec. 41(4)]
ParticularsAmount
Amount recovered₹ ******
Less: Bad debt claimed – Bad debt allowed as deduction₹ ******
Taxable bad debt recovery₹ ******

Provision for Bad and Doubtful Debts [Sec. 36(1)(viia)]

Unlike the general rule that a mere provision for bad debt is not deductible, specified financial persons are allowed a provision for bad and doubtful debts (PBDD) up to a statutory ceiling.

PersonExtent PBDD is allowed
A. Scheduled bank (not a foreign bank) or a non-scheduled bank or a co-operative bank — other than a primary agricultural credit society or a primary co-operative agricultural and rural development bank8.5% of total income (computed before this deduction and Chapter VIA)
B. Foreign bank or Public financial institution or State financial corporation or State industrial investment corporation or Non-banking financial company5% of total income (computed before this deduction and Chapter VIA)

Additional deduction for Person (A): (a) 10% of the aggregate average advances made by the rural branches of such bank; and (b) at option, a further deduction not exceeding the income derived from redemption of securities under a Central Government scheme, provided such income has been disclosed under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession."

  • Interaction with Sec. 36(1)(vii): for a person covered here, the bad-debt deduction u/s 36(1)(vii) is limited to the amount by which actual bad debts exceed the credit balance in the provision account; if actual bad debt is less than or equal to the provision, no separate bad-debt deduction is allowed.
  • Rural branch: a branch situated in a place with population not more than 10,000 as per the last preceding census whose figures were published before the first day of the previous year.

Special Reserve [Sec. 36(1)(viii)]

Deduction = LEAST of — (a) amount transferred to the special reserve during the P.Y.; (b) 20% of profits derived from the specified business of providing long-term finance; (c) twice the paid-up share capital + general reserve.

Specified EntitySpecified Business (providing long-term finance for)
A financial corporation u/s 2(72) of the Companies Act, 2013, or a financial corporation which is a public sector company or a banking company or a co-operative bank (other than a primary agricultural credit society or primary co-op agricultural and rural development bank)Industrial/agricultural development; development of infrastructure facility in India; or development of housing in India
A housing finance companyConstruction or purchase of houses in India for residential purposes
Any other financial corporation, including a public companyDevelopment of infrastructure facility in India

Long-term finance means a loan/advance repayable, along with interest, over a period of not less than 5 years.

Withdrawal from Special Reserve [Sec. 41(4A)]: any amount subsequently withdrawn from a special reserve on which deduction was allowed under this section is deemed profits and gains of business or profession, taxable in the year of withdrawal — even if the business no longer exists in that year.

CONCEPT

General Deductions [Sec. 37(1)] ★★★ HIGH

The residual, "catch-all" allowance: any expenditure not specifically covered elsewhere in the Act is deductible if it satisfies six conditions.

  1. Real, not notional/fictitious or a distribution of profit.
  2. Expended wholly & exclusively for the assessee's business or profession.
  3. Incurred in the previous year.
  4. Not a personal expenditure.
  5. Not a capital expenditure.
  6. Lawful — not incurred for a purpose that is an offence or prohibited under any law.

Expressly included as disallowed under this section: expenditure for a purpose that is an offence/prohibited by any law (in India or outside); to provide a benefit/perquisite whose acceptance violates any law/rule/guideline governing the recipient's conduct; to compound an offence; or to settle proceedings for contravention of such a law.

  • Corporate Social Responsibility: CSR expenditure under sec. 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 is NOT deemed incurred for business purposes — not deductible u/s 37. However, CSR spend that is by its nature already covered by sec. 30 to 36 remains deductible under those specific sections, subject to their own conditions [Explanatory Memorandum, Finance (No.2) Bill, 2014].
  • Keyman Insurance Policy: premium is an allowed business expenditure [Circular No. 762/1998]; in a firm, premium on a partner's Keyman policy (to protect the firm against business disruption) is admissible u/s 37 [Circular no. 38/2016].
  • Medical-sector freebees: expense on gifts/travel/hospitality/cash or similar freebees given in violation of the Indian Medical Council (Professional Conduct, Etiquette and Ethics) Regulations, 2002 is inadmissible u/s 37(1) in the hands of the pharmaceutical/health-sector assessee giving it; the value enjoyed by the medical practitioner/association is also taxable as business income or income from other sources [Circular 05/2012].
  • Expenditure to settle proceedings for contravention/default under the SEBI Act 1992, Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act 1956, Depositories Act 1996, or Competition Act 2002 is not deemed incurred for business purposes — no deduction.

Sec. 37(2B): expenditure on advertisement in any souvenir, brochure, tract, pamphlet or the like published by a political party is disallowed.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: CSR EXPENDITURE IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY DISALLOWED

THE TRAP: students assume ALL CSR spend under Companies Act sec. 135 is disallowed under the Income-tax Act.

THE TWIST: CSR spend is disallowed only under sec. 37(1) itself. If the very same expenditure would independently qualify under sec. 30 to 36 (e.g. a CSR donation that also fits a specific deduction section), it remains deductible under that specific section, subject to its own conditions.

Disallowed Expenditure [Sec. 40] ★★★ HIGH

Notwithstanding sec. 30 to 38, sec. 40 expressly disallows certain amounts while computing PGBP.

ClauseDisallowed
40(a)(i)Interest, royalty, fees for technical services or other sum chargeable under the Act, payable outside India, or in India to a non-resident (not a company) or a foreign company, on which TDS under Chapter XVII-B has not been deducted, or after deduction has not been paid by the due date of filing return u/s 139(1).
40(a)(ia)30% of any sum payable (or paid) to a resident on which TDS is applicable under Chapter XVII-B, where tax has not been deducted, or after deduction has not been paid on/before the due date of furnishing return of income.
40(a)(ii)Income tax (Indian or foreign), including any surcharge or cess by whatever name called — even tax paid by the assessee on a predecessor's income.
40(a)(iia)Wealth-tax.
40(a)(iib)Royalty, licence fee, service fee, privilege fee, service charge, or any other fee/charge levied exclusively on, or appropriated (directly/indirectly) from, a State Government undertaking, by the State Government.
40(a)(iii)Payment chargeable under "Salaries" if payable outside India or to a non-resident, and tax on it has not been paid in India nor deducted at source.
40(a)(iv)Payment to a provident/other employee-welfare fund without an effective TDS arrangement, where the payments are taxable under "Salaries."
40(a)(v)Tax on a non-monetary perquisite (exempt in employee's hands u/s 10(10CC)) actually paid by the employer on the employee's behalf.

Sec. 40(a)(i) — taxpoints: where tax is deducted in a subsequent year, or deducted during the year but paid after the sec. 139(1) due date, the sum is allowed as deduction in the year such tax is actually paid. Where the assessee fails to deduct tax but is not deemed "assessee in default" under the first proviso to sec. 201(1) — i.e. the payee has (a) filed return u/s 139, (b) included the sum in that return, (c) paid tax due thereon, and (d) the payer furnishes a CA certificate to this effect — the payer is deemed to have deducted and paid tax on the date the payee furnishes their return. Royalty and FTS carry the meanings in sec. 9(1)(vi) and 9(1)(vii) respectively.

Sec. 40(a)(ia) — taxpoints: the same deemed-deduction-date relief applies for resident payees, but is NOT available where the payer deducted tax but failed to deposit it. Where tax deducted late is deposited later, or deducted on time but deposited after the return due date, the 30% earlier disallowed becomes deductible in the year such tax is paid.

Where such tax has been deducted in any subsequent yearDisallowed amount (30%) shall be allowed as deduction in computing the income of the previous year in which such tax has been paid
Where such tax has been deducted in the relevant financial year but tax has been paid after the due date of furnishing return of the relevant assessment year

"Commission or brokerage" for this purpose includes payment received/receivable by a person acting on another's behalf for services rendered (other than professional services), or for services in buying/selling goods, or relating to any asset/valuable article/thing (not being securities).

ILLUSTRATION 81 — Sec. 40(a)(i)/(ia): Year of Allowability of TDS-Defaulted Expenditure

General rule pattern applied by the source across resident and non-resident deductees (interest expenditure, TDS due date 20-7-2025/deposit due date 7-8-2025 unless stated):

FactsAllowability
Resident deductee — TDS deducted on time and deposited by 2-9-2025 (after the due date of depositing TDS but the sum is still fully allowable in the year of accrual)100% allowed in the A.Y. 2026-27
Resident deductee — TDS deducted on time (20-7-2025) but deposited only on 12-12-202630% of such sum disallowed (70% allowed) in the A.Y. 2026-27; the 30% is allowed in the A.Y. 2027-28
Resident deductee — TDS deducted on time (20-7-2025) but deposited only on 3-4-202730% disallowed (70% allowed) in the A.Y. 2026-27; the 30% is allowed in the A.Y. 2028-29
Resident deductee — TDS deducted on time (17-6-2025) but not deposited; and a case where tax is not deducted at the correct time but deducted later (10-11-2025), still not deposited30% disallowed (70% allowed) in the A.Y. 2026-27; the 30% allowed in the A.Y. relevant to the P.Y. in which tax is actually paid
