Key contrast: for a NON-resident deductee, TDS default disallows 100% of the sum; for a RESIDENT deductee under sec. 40(a)(ia), only 30% is disallowed for the same kind of default.

CONCEPT

Payments to Related Persons [Sec. 40A(2)] ★★★ HIGH

Any payment to a related person is disallowed to the extent the Assessing Officer regards it as excessive or unreasonable.

"Relative" u/s 2(41) means the spouse, brother, sister, or any lineal ascendant or descendant of that individual. A person has "substantial interest" in a business/profession if — where it is carried on by a company, he is beneficial owner of equity shares carrying ≥ 20% voting power; in any other case, he is beneficially entitled to ≥ 20% of the profits of that business/profession.

For the assesseeRelated person means
An IndividualRelative; a person in whose business/profession the individual has substantial interest.
A CompanyDirector, or any relative of the director; a person in whose business/profession the company (or its director/director's relative) has substantial interest; any other company in which the aforesaid company has substantial interest.
A FirmPartner, or relative of partner; a person in whose business/profession the firm (or its partner/partner's relative) has substantial interest.
An AOPMember, or relative of a member; a person in whose business/profession the AOP (or its member/member's relative) has substantial interest.
An HUFMember of the family, or relative of such person; a person in whose business/profession the HUF (or its member/member's relative) has substantial interest.
Any assesseeAn individual/company/firm/HUF/AOP that has substantial interest in the assessee's business or profession, or a director/partner/member of such an entity, or any relative thereof — and vice-versa (an entity in whose business the assessee's director/partner/member has substantial interest).
  • Excessive or unreasonable is judged with reference to the fair market value of the goods/services/facilities, or the legitimate business need, or the benefit accruing to the assessee.
  • Where an assessee sells goods at a lower rate, no expenditure has been incurred by him — sec. 40A(2) is not invoked.

Cash Payments Exceeding ₹10,000 [Sec. 40A(3)/(3A)] ★★★ HIGH

Payment > ₹10,000 in a day, otherwise than by account payee cheque/DD, ECS, or other prescribed electronic mode → 100% disallowed [Sec. 40A(3)].

Exception: for payment to a Road Transport operator (plying/hiring/leasing goods carriages), the limit is raised to ₹35,000.

CaseMonetary Limit
Payment for plying, hiring or leasing goods carriages₹35,000
Payment for other expenses₹10,000
  • Sec. 40A(3A): where an allowance was made in an earlier assessment for a liability, and the assessee subsequently pays it in violation of sec. 40A(3), the payment so made is deemed profits and gains of business or profession of the year of payment.
  • A single bill paid in cash across different days to the same person does NOT attract sec. 40A(3), provided no single day's payment exceeds ₹10,000/₹35,000.
  • Where payment over the limit is made partly by account payee cheque and partly in cash, and the cash portion alone does not exceed ₹10,000/₹35,000, sec. 40A(3) is not attracted.
  • Sec. 40A(3) applies only where the expenditure is claimed as a deduction u/s 30 to 37.
  • Loan transactions are not covered by this section.

Exceptions under Rule 6DD — sec. 40A(3) is not attracted even for cash-mode payment above the limit, where payment is made:

  • To RBI, any banking company, SBI or a subsidiary bank, any co-operative/land mortgage bank, any primary agricultural/primary credit society, or LIC.
  • To Government where the rules require payment in legal tender.
  • By letter of credit through a bank; mail/telegraphic transfer through a bank; book adjustment between bank accounts; or a bill of exchange payable only to a bank.
  • By way of book adjustment against a liability incurred by the payee for goods supplied/services rendered by the assessee to the payee.
  • For purchase of agricultural/forest produce, animal husbandry produce (incl. livestock, meat, hides, skins) or dairy/poultry farming produce, fish/fish products, or horticulture/apiculture products, to the cultivator/grower/producer of such articles.
  • For purchase of products manufactured/processed without the aid of power in a cottage industry, to the producer.
  • In a village/town not served by any bank on the date of payment, to a person ordinarily residing or carrying on business there.
  • To an employee or their heir on retirement/retrenchment/resignation/discharge/death, by way of gratuity, retrenchment compensation or similar terminal benefit, where the aggregate does not exceed ₹50,000.
  • By way of salary after TDS to an employee temporarily posted 15+ continuous days away from their normal place of duty (or on a ship) who maintains no bank account there.
  • By a person to an agent required to make cash payment for goods/services on the person's behalf.
  • By a traveller/dealer/money changer purchasing foreign currency or travellers' cheques in the normal course of business.

EXAMPLE 13 — Applying Sec. 40A(3)

PointExample & Outcome
Same-day, different-time payments each under ₹10,000, but against a single bill of ₹50,000Entire ₹50,000 disallowed u/s 40A(3) (the "different days" relief does not apply to same-day splitting).
Single bill of ₹23,000 paid on different DAYS — ₹8,000 (7/12/2025), ₹9,000 (8/12/2025), ₹6,000 (9/12/2025) — none exceeding ₹10,000Nothing disallowed.
Bill of ₹50,000 paid as account payee cheque ₹42,000 + bearer cheque ₹3,000 + cash ₹5,000Nothing disallowed (cash portion alone does not exceed ₹10,000).
Goods of ₹14,000 purchased from brother in cash (market value ₹8,000)₹6,000 disallowed u/s 40A(2) (excess over FMV); nothing disallowed u/s 40A(3) since the allowed expenditure (₹8,000) does not exceed ₹10,000.
Cash paid to road transport operators — ₹23,000 (Bill 540), ₹32,000 (Bill 770), ₹37,000 (Bill 992), each on separate bills/datesOnly the ₹37,000 payment (exceeding the ₹35,000 road-carrier limit) is disallowed in full u/s 40A(3).
Goods purchased on credit (₹60,000) claimed as deduction in A.Y. 2026-27; paid in cash (₹60,000) in P.Y. 2027-28Since payment exceeds ₹10,000 in cash, the allowance originally made is deemed income of the P.Y. in which payment is made (P.Y. 2027-28) u/s 40A(3A).
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SPLITTING A CASH BILL

THE TRAP: assuming splitting a single large cash bill into pieces under ₹10,000 always escapes sec. 40A(3).

THE TWIST: the relief works only when the splits fall on DIFFERENT DAYS, each ≤ the limit. Splitting the SAME bill on the SAME day at different times still disallows the entire sum.

Provision for Gratuity [Sec. 40A(7)] & Certain Contributions [Sec. 40A(9)]

Sec. 40A(7): no deduction for any provision (by whatever name called) made for payment of gratuity to employees. Exception: a provision for contribution towards an approved gratuity fund, or for gratuity that has become payable during the P.Y., is allowed.

Sec. 40A(9): no deduction for any sum paid by an employer towards setting up/formation of, or as contribution to, any fund, trust, company, AOP, BOI, society or other institution for any purpose. Exception: contribution towards an approved superannuation fund, recognised provident fund, approved gratuity fund, or NPS, as required by law, IS allowed.

Taxpoint: contribution to an unrecognised provident fund is disallowed.

CONCEPT

Expenditures Allowed on Payment Basis [Sec. 43B] ★★★ HIGH

Category A — deduction for the following is allowed only if payment is made on or before the due date of furnishing return of income u/s 139(1) for the P.Y. in which the liability is incurred:

  1. Any sum payable by way of tax, duty, cess, fee (by whatever name called), under any law.
  2. Any sum payable as bonus or commission to employees for services rendered.
  3. Interest on loan/borrowing from public financial institutions, a State financial corporation, or a State industrial investment corporation.
  4. Interest on loan/borrowing from a notified class of non-banking financial companies, per the loan agreement.
  5. Interest on loans/advances from a scheduled bank or co-operative bank (other than a primary agricultural credit society or primary co-op agricultural and rural development bank), per the loan agreement.
  6. Any sum payable by an employer in lieu of leave at the credit of an employee (leave encashment).
  7. Employer's contribution to any provident fund, superannuation fund, gratuity fund, or other employee-welfare fund.
  8. Any sum payable to Indian Railways for use of railway assets.

Due date of furnishing return u/s 139(1): 31st October of the A.Y. where audit of accounts is compulsory under any law (30th November if transfer-pricing audit u/s 92E applies); otherwise 31st July of the A.Y.

  • If payment is not made by the above date, no deduction for the outstanding liability — deduction can be claimed only in the year of actual payment.
  • The assessee's method of accounting is irrelevant to this rule’s applicability itself — but see the cash-basis note below.
  • Sec. 43B applies only to expenditure otherwise allowable under the Act; timely payment of an already-disallowed item (e.g. income tax) does not make it deductible.
  • "Any sum payable" means a sum for which liability accrued in the P.Y., even if it was not yet legally due for payment within that year.

Notes:

  1. Sec. 43B applies only where the assessee follows the mercantile system. Under cash basis, deduction is allowed only in the year of actual payment, even if paid before the due date of filing return.
  2. The "pay by due date of return" rule applies only for the P.Y. in which the liability is incurred. If payment is made in a later year, deduction follows the year of actual payment, regardless of any due date.
  3. Where outstanding interest (bank/NBFC/PFI loans) is converted into a loan, debenture or other instrument deferring payment, such interest is NOT deemed as interest paid.
  4. A deduction already allowed on accrual basis in an earlier year cannot be allowed again on payment basis under this section.
  5. Per sec. 36(1)(va), employee contributions received by the employer towards PF/superannuation fund/ESI fund/other welfare fund are treated as the employer's income; deduction is allowed only when credited to the employee's account in the relevant fund by the due date prescribed under the relevant Act — if not deposited within that time, the deduction is NEVER allowed ("not now then never").

Example: professional tax of ₹10,000 relating to P.Y. 2022-23, paid on 7/5/2026, is deductible in P.Y. 2026-27 (year of actual payment), not P.Y. 2025-26.

Category B — Payments to Micro/Small Enterprises

Any sum payable by the assessee to a micro or small enterprise (other than a trading unit) beyond the time limit specified in sec. 15 of the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006 is allowed as deduction ONLY in the previous year in which it is actually paid.

For calculating investment in plant and machinery, the cost of pollution control, research and development, industrial safety devices and such notified items is excluded.

Example — Applicability of Sec. 43B (MSME limb)

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: CATEGORY A VS CATEGORY B TIMING RULE

THE TRAP: applying the "pay by the due date of filing return" relief to MSME dues too.

THE TWIST: Category A items (tax/bonus/specified interest/leave encashment/PF etc.) get relief if paid by the sec. 139(1) due date. Category B (MSME dues beyond the sec. 15 MSMED Act time limit) has NO such relief — deduction follows the P.Y. of actual payment regardless of the return due date, unless payment itself was within the MSMED Act's own 15/45-day limit.

CONCEPT

Deemed Profit Chargeable to Tax as Business Income ★★ MEDIUM

The following receipts are chargeable to tax as business income even if the related business no longer exists in the previous year.

SectionContents
41(1)Recovery against any deduction (detailed below)
41(2)Balancing charge
41(3)Sale of asset used for scientific research
41(4)Recovery of bad debts
41(4A)Withdrawal from special reserve created by financial corporation u/s 36(1)(viii)
176(3A) & (4)Recovery after discontinuance of business or profession (detailed below)

Recovery against any deduction [Sec. 41(1)] — Conditions: (1) an allowance/deduction was allowed in any A.Y. for loss, expenditure, or trading liability; and (2) the assessee subsequently obtains (in cash or otherwise) an amount in respect of it, or a benefit by way of remission/cessation of the trading liability. Treatment: the amount/benefit is deemed profits and gains of business or profession, taxable in the year obtained.

  • Applies whether or not the business/profession is in existence in that year.
  • Remission/cessation may be a unilateral act — e.g. the assessee simply writing off the liability in his books.
  • The essential precondition: an allowance/deduction must have been made previously while computing taxable income.
  • Successor in business is taxed if benefit is obtained by a successor: the amalgamated company (on amalgamation); the other firm (on succession of one firm by another); the other person (in any other succession); or the resulting company (on demerger).

Recovery after discontinuance [Sec. 176(3A) & (4)] — Condition: business/profession discontinued due to death or retirement of the person carrying it on. Treatment: any sum received after discontinuance is deemed income of the recipient, taxed in the year of receipt.

Maintenance of Books of Account [Sec. 44AA & Rule 6F] ★★ MEDIUM

CaseTurnover/income criteria (existing business)Turnover/income criteria (new business)Maintenance of Accounts
A — Persons carrying on specified professions¹Gross receipts > ₹1,50,000 in all of the 3 years immediately preceding the P.Y.Gross total receipts likely to exceed ₹1,50,000 for that yearMaintain books & documents as prescribed by Rule 6F²
B — Same personsGross receipts ≤ ₹1,50,000 in any one of the 3 preceding yearsGross total receipts not likely to exceed ₹1,50,000Maintain books & documents enabling the AO to compute taxable income
C — Persons carrying on a "non-specified profession or any business"Profit > ₹1,20,000 (₹2,50,000 for individual/HUF); OR sales/turnover/gross receipts > ₹10,00,000 (₹25,00,000 for individual/HUF), in any of the 3 preceding yearsIncome/total sales etc. likely to exceed the said amountMaintain books & documents enabling the AO to compute taxable income
D — Same personsLimit not exceeded in all 3 preceding yearsIncome and turnover not likely to exceed the said limitNot required to maintain any books of account
EAn assessee covered u/s 44AE, 44BB or 44BBB, claiming income from such business lower than the deemed income computed under the respective sectionMaintain books & documents enabling the AO to compute taxable income
FSec. 44AD(4) applies and the assessee's income exceeds the basic exemption limitMaintain books & documents enabling the AO to compute taxable income

¹ Specified Profession: legal, medical, engineering, architectural profession, or profession of accountancy, technical consultancy, interior decoration, information technology, company secretary, authorised representative, film artist, or any other Board-notified profession.

² Books required under Rule 6F: cash book; journal (if mercantile accounting followed); ledger; carbon copies of machine-numbered bills exceeding ₹25 issued by the assessee; original bills/receipts for expenditure incurred (or self-signed payment vouchers where no bill/receipt is issued and the expenditure does not exceed ₹50). A medical-profession assessee must additionally maintain a Daily Case Register in Form 3C and inventory records of drugs, medicines and consumable accessories.

  • Retention period [Rule 6F(5)]: 6 years from the end of the relevant assessment year.
  • Place of keeping: at the place of carrying on the profession (or the principal place, if more than one, unless separate books are kept per place).
  • Penalty [Sec. 271A]: ₹25,000 for non-compliance.
  • Per sec. 2(12A), "books of account" includes ledgers, day-books, cash books, account books, and similar records kept in written, electronic, or digital form, or as print-outs, or on any electro-magnetic data storage device.

Tax Audit [Sec. 44AB] ★★★ HIGH

The following assessees must get their accounts audited by a chartered accountant and electronically furnish the audit report one month prior to the due date of filing the return of income.

1. Assessee carrying on business — base condition: total sales/turnover/gross receipts for the P.Y. exceed ₹1 crore. Three escalating exceptions:

  • Exception 1: declares profits u/s 44AD AND turnover does not exceed ₹2 crore → tax audit not applicable.
  • Exception 2: declares profits u/s 44AD AND turnover does not exceed ₹3 crore AND aggregate cash receipts do not exceed 5% of turnover → tax audit not applicable.
  • Exception 3: the higher threshold of ₹10 crore applies to any business assessee (44AD declaration not required here) if aggregate cash receipts do not exceed 5% of total receipts AND aggregate cash payments do not exceed 5% of total payments.

Taxpoint: a non-account-payee cheque/bank draft is deemed a cash payment/receipt for this 5% test.

CaseApplicability
Turnover exceeds ₹10 croreApplicable
Turnover does not exceed ₹2 crore and assessee is covered u/s 44ADNot applicable
Turnover does not exceed ₹3 crore and cash receipt does not exceed 5% of total turnover and assessee is covered u/s 44ADNot applicable
Turnover does not exceed ₹10 crore and the 5%-cash conditions are satisfiedNot applicable
Turnover does not exceed ₹10 crore but exceeds ₹1 crore, and the above conditions are not satisfied (assessee not covered u/s 44AD)Applicable

2. Assessee carrying on profession — base condition: gross receipts > ₹50 lakh. Exception: declares profits u/s 44ADA AND gross receipts do not exceed ₹75 lakh AND cash receipts do not exceed 5% of gross receipts → not applicable.

3. Assessee covered u/s 44AE, 44BB or 44BBB, claiming income lower than the deemed income under the respective section.

4. Assessee covered u/s 44ADA claiming income lower than the presumptive income AND whose income exceeds the basic exemption limit.

5. Assessee covered u/s 44AD(4) whose income exceeds the basic exemption limit in any P.Y.

Penalty: failure to upload the audit report one month prior to the ROI due date attracts a penalty equal to the LOWER of ½% of turnover/gross receipt, or ₹1,50,000.

Audit report is generally due by 30th September of the A.Y.; where transfer-pricing audit u/s 92E applies, the date is 31st October of the A.Y.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: THERE IS NO SINGLE ₹1-CRORE AUDIT LINE

THE TRAP: assuming tax audit is triggered by a flat ₹1 crore turnover for every business assessee.

THE TWIST: the threshold rises to ₹2 crore, ₹3 crore, or ₹10 crore depending on whether the assessee declares income u/s 44AD and how much of their turnover moves through cash. Separately, even a presumptive-scheme assessee (44AD/44ADA/44AE) can still be dragged into audit — if they declare income LOWER than the presumptive figure AND their total income exceeds the basic exemption limit.

CONCEPT

Special & Method-of-Accounting Provisions ★ LOW

Sec. 43D — Income of public financial institutions, etc.: notwithstanding any other provision, interest income of a public financial institution, scheduled bank, co-operative bank (other than a primary agricultural credit society/primary co-op agricultural and rural development bank), State financial corporation, State industrial investment corporation, deposit-taking NBFC, or systemically important non-deposit-taking NBFC, relating to prescribed categories of bad or doubtful debts (per RBI guidelines), is chargeable to tax in the year it is credited to the P&L account OR actually received — whichever is earlier.

Sec. 145A — Method of accounting, valuation of stock: inventory is valued at the lower of actual cost or net realisable value per the ICDS. Purchase/sale of goods or services and inventory valuation must be adjusted to include tax/duty/cess/fee actually paid/incurred to bring goods/services to their location and condition. Unlisted securities (or listed-but-not-regularly-quoted securities) are valued at actual cost per ICDS; other securities at the lower of cost or net realisable value per ICDS; securities held by a scheduled bank/PFI per ICDS after considering RBI guidelines. The cost/NRV comparison for securities is done category-wise.

Sec. 145B — Taxability of certain income: interest received on compulsory acquisition (or on enhanced compensation) is deemed income of the year of receipt. Any claim for price escalation in a contract or export incentives is deemed income of the year reasonable certainty of realisation is achieved. Any subsidy/grant/cash incentive/duty drawback/waiver/concession/reimbursement (by whatever name called) is deemed income of the year of receipt, if not already charged to tax in an earlier year.

CONCEPT

Presumptive Taxation Schemes ★★★ HIGH

To relieve small taxpayers from maintaining books of account and getting them audited, the Act frames presumptive taxation schemes u/s 44AD, 44ADA and 44AE.

Computation of Business Profit on Presumptive Basis [Sec. 44AD]

Applicable to: a resident individual, resident HUF, or a resident partnership firm.

NOT applicable to: LLP; a person carrying on a profession referred to u/s 44AA; a person earning commission or brokerage income; a person carrying on any agency business; or a person carrying on the business of plying, hiring or leasing goods carriages under sec. 44AE.

  • Eligible business: any business other than those excluded above.
  • Maximum turnover — Option 1: total turnover/gross receipts ≤ ₹2 crore; OR Option 2: aggregate cash receipts ≤ 5% of total turnover, in which case total turnover/gross receipts may go up to ₹3 crore. (A non-account-payee cheque/DD is deemed a cash receipt for this test.)
  • Restriction: no deduction claimed u/s 10AA or 80HH to 80RRB for the relevant A.Y.
Where turnover/receipts are received byEstimated income
Account payee cheque/bank draft, ECS, or other prescribed electronic mode† during the P.Y. or before the ROI due date6% of such turnover/receipts
Any other case (cash, etc.)8% of such turnover/receipts

A taxpayer may voluntarily declare higher income. † Prescribed electronic modes: credit card, debit card, net banking, IMPS, UPI, RTGS, NEFT, and BHIM Aadhar Pay.

  1. No expense deduction: the estimated income is comprehensive — no further deduction for expenses.
  2. Depreciation is deemed already allowed; the asset's WDV is computed as if depreciation had been claimed.
  3. The estimated income is aggregated with the assessee's other income/heads; Chapter VIA deductions (other than the two restricted above) remain available.
  4. Brought forward loss is subtracted from the estimated income as usual.

Sec. 44AD(4) lock-out: where an eligible assessee (a) declares profit per this section for a P.Y., then (b) declares LOWER profit (below the specified %) for any of the 5 A.Y.s following that P.Y., he becomes ineligible to claim the scheme's benefit for 5 A.Y.s subsequent to the A.Y. of the lower-profit declaration.

Example: assessee opts for sec. 44AD for A.Y. 2025-26, continues to offer presumptive income for A.Y. 2026-27 and 2027-28, but does NOT opt for the scheme in A.Y. 2028-29. He is then ineligible for the scheme for the next 5 A.Y.s — A.Y. 2029-30 to 2033-34.

If sec. 44AD(4) applies and total income exceeds the basic exemption limit, the assessee must maintain books u/s 44AA AND get accounts audited u/s 44AB.

₹1 crore+ – ₹2 croreYesNot required if income offered u/s 44AD, else required
₹2 crore+ – ₹3 croreYes, subject to certain riderNot required if income offered u/s 44AD, else required
₹2 crore+ (conditions not satisfied) / ₹3 crore+ – ₹10 croreNoNot required if certain conditions are satisfied
₹10 crore+NoRequired

ILLUSTRATION 83 — Sec. 44AD Applied to a Firm

X Co., a firm engaged in cloth trading, has turnover for 2025-26 of ₹1,57,80,000, of which ₹25,00,000 was received by account payee cheque. It wants to claim: salary & interest to partners u/s 40(b) ₹60,000; salary to employees ₹4,90,000; depreciation ₹2,70,000; cost of materials ₹1,20,90,000; other expenses ₹13,45,000 (total expenses ₹1,42,55,000; net profit ₹1,57,80,000 − ₹1,42,55,000 = ₹15,25,000). Other data: taxable interest income ₹90,000; long-term capital gain ₹1,40,000; deduction u/s 80G ₹15,000.

Since turnover does not exceed ₹2 crore, sec. 44AD is applicable. Income computed under normal provisions (₹15,25,000) is LESS than the estimated presumptive income — so the firm may still be assessed at the lower, actual figure, but only if it (a) maintains books u/s 44AA and (b) gets accounts audited u/s 44AB.

Computation of Professional Income on Presumptive Basis [Sec. 44ADA]

Applicable to: any resident individual and resident firm (other than LLP).

  • Engaged in profession referred to u/s 44AA — legal, medical, engineering, architectural profession or profession of accountancy, technical consultancy, interior decoration, etc.
  • Maximum receipts — Option 1: gross receipts ≤ ₹50 lakh; OR Option 2: cash receipts ≤ 5% of gross receipts, in which case gross receipts may go up to ₹75 lakh. (Non-account-payee cheque/DD deemed cash.)

Estimated income = 50% of the gross receipts (voluntary higher declaration permitted).

  1. No further deduction u/s 30 to 38 — the estimated income is comprehensive.
  2. Depreciation is deemed already allowed; WDV computed as if allowed.
  3. Estimated income aggregated with other income/heads; Chapter VIA deductions available as usual.
  4. Brought forward loss subtracted as per Act provisions.
  5. If income is declared lower than the estimated figure: must maintain books u/s 44AA (if total income exceeds basic exemption limit) AND get accounts audited u/s 44AB (irrespective of the amount of turnover/gross receipts) if total income exceeds the basic exemption limit.

Note: the assessee can change this option from year to year.

Business of Plying, Leasing or Hiring Goods Carriage [Sec. 44AE]

Applicable to: all assessees engaged in the business of plying, hiring or leasing goods carriage.

Condition: assessee must not own more than 10 goods carriages at any time during the P.Y. (owner includes a hire-purchase/instalment buyer even if fully unpaid). "Goods carriage" means any motor vehicle constructed/adapted (or actually used) solely for the carriage of goods.

Type of Goods CarriagePresumptive Income (per month or part month)
Heavy₹1,000 per ton of gross vehicle weight/unladen weight
Other₹7,500

Income is calculated from the month the vehicle was acquired, whether put to use or not (any fraction of a month counts as a full month). A higher income may be declared. "Heavy goods vehicle" means gross vehicle weight exceeding 12,000 kg.

  1. No further deduction u/s 30 to 38 — the estimated income is comprehensive.
  2. For a firm, deduction for remuneration/interest to partners u/s 40(b) is further deductible from this income.
  3. Depreciation deemed already allowed; WDV computed as if allowed.
  4. Estimated income aggregated with other income/heads; Chapter VIA deductions available as usual.
  5. Brought forward loss adjusted as usual.
  6. An assessee estimating income per this section (or higher) is NOT required to maintain books u/s 44AA or get accounts audited u/s 44AB, in respect of this business — but must comply with both sections for any OTHER business. The gross receipts/income of this goods-carriage business are excluded when computing the 44AA/44AB monetary limits for those other businesses.
  7. If income is declared lower than the estimated figure: must maintain books u/s 44AA AND get accounts audited u/s 44AB, irrespective of turnover/gross receipts.

Note: the assessee can change this option from year to year.

ILLUSTRATION 84 — Sec. 44AE, Mr. Sukhvinder

On 1-4-2025, Mr. Sukhvinder owns 10 trucks (6 heavy goods vehicles, unladen weight 20 ton each). On 2-5-2025 he sells one heavy vehicle and purchases a light goods vehicle on 6-5-2025, which is put to use only from 15-6-2025. P&L data for the year: Freight charges collected ₹1,08,70,000; less operational expenses ₹99,25,000, depreciation u/s 32 ₹1,85,000, other office expenses ₹15,000 (total ₹1,01,25,000); Net Profit ₹7,45,000; other business/non-business income ₹70,000.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: 44AD's SPLIT RATE VS 44ADA's FLAT RATE

THE TRAP: applying a single flat presumptive rate across all three schemes, or forgetting that 44AD's rate depends on how receipts were collected.

THE TWIST: only sec. 44AD splits the rate by payment mode — 6% for turnover received through account payee cheque/DD/ECS/prescribed electronic modes, 8% for everything else (including cash). Sec. 44ADA is a FLAT 50% regardless of how the professional receipts were collected. Sec. 44AE isn't rate-on-turnover at all — it is a fixed rupee amount per vehicle per month.

CONCEPT

Income from Construction & Service Contracts [Sec. 43CB] ★ LOW

Profits and gains from a construction contract, or a contract for providing services, are determined on the basis of the percentage of completion method (POCM) in accordance with the ICDS.

Contract for providing servicesMethod
Duration not more than 90 daysProject completion method
Involving an indeterminate number of acts over a specific periodStraight line method

Under POCM: contract revenue includes retention money; contract costs are NOT reduced by any incidental income in the nature of interest, dividends, or capital gains.

Consequences of Undisclosed Income or Investment ★★ MEDIUM

SectionConditionsTax Treatment
68 — Cash CreditSum credited in the books; assessee offers no (or an unsatisfactory) explanation of its nature and source.The sum may be charged to tax as income of that previous year.
69 — Unexplained investmentsInvestments made in the P.Y. not recorded in the books; no (or unsatisfactory) explanation of nature/source.Value of investment may be deemed income for that P.Y.
69A — Unexplained money, etc.Assessee found owner of money/bullion/jewellery/valuable article not recorded in books; no satisfactory explanation of nature/source of acquisition.The money/value of the asset may be deemed income for that P.Y.
69B — Investments not fully disclosedAmount actually expended on investments/bullion/jewellery exceeds the amount recorded in the books; no satisfactory explanation for the excess.The excess amount may be deemed income for that P.Y.
69C — Unexplained expenditureAssessee has incurred expenditure with no (or unsatisfactory) explanation of source.Amount incurred (or part) may be deemed income for that P.Y.; proviso: such deemed income shall NOT be allowed as a deduction in any year under any head.
69D — Amount borrowed/repaid on hundiAny amount borrowed on a hundi from, or repaid to, any person otherwise than through an account payee cheque.Deemed income of the person borrowing/repaying, for the P.Y. of borrowing/repayment; if once taxed on borrowing, not taxed again on repayment (avoids double taxation); amount repaid includes interest paid.

Sec. 68 — company share capital/loan credits: where the assessee is a company (not one in which the public are substantially interested) and the sum credited consists of share application money/capital/premium (or a loan/borrowing), the company's explanation is deemed UNSATISFACTORY unless the resident person in whose name the credit is recorded also offers an explanation about its nature/source, and that explanation is found satisfactory by the AO. This two-tier requirement does not apply where the person is a venture capital fund/company referred to in sec. 10(23FB).

Sec. 115BBE — income referred to in sec. 68 to 69D is taxable @ 60% (+ surcharge @ 25% + cess), without any deduction for expenditure/allowance or set-off of any loss.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: NO SET-OFF AGAINST DEEMED UNEXPLAINED INCOME

THE TRAP: netting a business loss or brought-forward loss against sec. 68–69D income.

THE TWIST: sec. 115BBE taxes such income at a flat 60% (plus surcharge and cess), and expressly bars any deduction for expenditure/allowance AND any set-off of loss against it.

CONCEPT

Firm Assessment ★★★ HIGH

  1. A partnership firm has a separate identity apart from its partners and is taxed as a separate entity at a flat rate of 30% + applicable surcharge + Health & Education cess @ 4%. Unless stated otherwise, "partnership firm" includes an LLP, and "partner" includes an LLP partner.
  2. A partner's share in the firm's income is NOT taxable in the partner's hands [Sec. 10(2A)].
  3. Like any other assessee, firm income is assessed under all heads — House Property, PGBP, Capital Gains, and Other Sources. A firm CANNOT have income under "Salaries." Registration of the firm is not compulsory for tax-assessment purposes.

Deduction u/s 40(b) — Interest & Remuneration to Partners

In computing PGBP, a firm gets, in addition to all other deductions, deduction u/s 40(b) for interest and remuneration to partners — subject to conditions in sec. 184/185:

  1. Partnership must be evidenced by an instrument [Sec. 184(1)(i)].
  2. A certified copy of the instrument must accompany the return of income for the year firm-assessment is first sought [Sec. 184(2)].
  3. Individual partner shares must be specified in the instrument [Sec. 184(1)(ii)].
  4. No failure as specified u/s 144 on the firm's part.

Effect of non-fulfilment: per sec. 185, no deduction for interest or remuneration to partner is allowed for that A.Y.

Interest to partner (capital or loan) is allowed subject to: (1) authorised by the partnership deed; (2) pertains to a period after the deed. Deduction = the LOWER of actual interest per the deed, or 12% p.a. simple interest.

ILLUSTRATION 85 — Interest to Partners, Capped at 12%

Interest to Partner — Allowed vs. Disallowed
CaseCapital (₹)Rate per booksRate per deedWorkingsDisallowed
A20,00010%10%—Nil
B30,00015%12%(₹30,000/15)×36,000
C30,00015%Deed is silentInterest must be given as per deed30,000
D30,00020%18%(₹30,000/20)×812,000
E30,00015%10%(₹30,000/15)×510,000
F30,00030%30%(₹30,000/30)×1818,000

Rule illustrated: even where the deed AUTHORISES a higher rate, only 12% p.a. is allowed as deduction to the firm (subject to the deed's own lower ceiling, if any, and to the deed not being silent).

Interest to Partner — Further Rules

Applicability of sec. 40A(2): interest paid to a partner above the normal market rate is governed by sec. 40A(2), and the excess is disallowed under that section too.

Interest to representative partner — where an individual is a partner on behalf of, or for the benefit of, another person, he is a "representative partner." Interest paid by the firm to such an individual as partner in a representative capacity, AND to the person represented, is governed by sec. 40(b). Interest paid to the individual otherwise than in a representative capacity is governed by sec. 36(1)(iii) instead.

Interest on drawings charged by the firm from its partners is treated as taxable income (of the firm).

Remuneration to Partner

Remuneration includes salary, fees, commission, bonus etc. Conditions: (1) the partner must be a working partner; (2) authorised by the deed; (3) pertains to a period after the deed. "Working partner" = an individual actively engaged in conducting the firm's business/profession — time devotion is NOT the deciding factor.

Deduction (in total) = the LOWER of actual remuneration to all partners, or the maximum permissible limit u/s 40(b)(v):

In case of loss: maximum remuneration = ₹3,00,000.

In case of profit: on the FIRST ₹6,00,000 of book profit — 90% of book profit or ₹3,00,000, whichever is HIGHER; on the BALANCE book profit — 60%.

Computation of Book Profit: Step 1: net profit per the P&L A/c. Step 2: adjust per sec. 28 to 44DB (including adjustment for interest on partner's capital). Step 3: add back remuneration to partner, if debited to the P&L A/c. Step 4: subtract unabsorbed depreciation (but do NOT subtract brought-forward business losses) — the result is book profit. Note: after subtracting unabsorbed depreciation, the residual profit should not be reduced below the brought-forward losses to be set off in the current year.

Income from house property, income from other sources, and capital gains do NOT form part of book profit. Chapter VIA deductions (80C to 80U) are ignored for this purpose.

ILLUSTRATION 86 — Book Profit & Partner Remuneration, PP Traders

Uttar and Dakshin, partners of PP Traders. P&L for year ended 31-3-2026: Net profit ₹3,55,500 (after debiting bonus to employees ₹50,000, interest on bank loan ₹45,000 (unpaid), other expenses ₹40,000, salary to Uttar ₹4,88,000 & Dakshin ₹9,76,000, interest on capital @15% — Uttar ₹4,500 & Dakshin ₹6,000, depreciation ₹40,000; and crediting interest on drawings Uttar ₹2,000 & Dakshin ₹3,000). Treatment in the Hands of Partners

Remuneration to a representative partner is taxable in the HANDS OF SUCH PARTNER, not the organisation represented; sec. 40(b) still applies to the firm.

Share of profit: exempt in the partner's hands [Sec. 10(2A)] — taxed in the firm's hands only, and this holds even if the firm's taxable income becomes Nil due to any exemption/deduction under the Act.

Interest and remuneration to partner are taxable in the partner's hands only to the extent they were ALLOWED (exempted) in the firm's hands.

Example — Interest to Partners A, B, C @16%, Deed Silent Beyond 12%
PartnerAllowed to firm @12%Disallowed to firm (remaining)Business Income of the Partner
A12,0004,00012,000
B6,0002,0006,000
C24,0008,00024,000

Example: A, B, C run ABC & Co. with a loss of ₹4,00,000; remuneration paid A ₹1,50,000, B ₹2,00,000, C ₹1,00,000. Since the firm is in loss, maximum remuneration allowable to it is capped at ₹3,00,000, apportioned to each partner in the ratio of remuneration actually paid:

General Notes on Firm Assessment

Registration of the firm is not compulsory for its assessment as a firm for tax purposes.

Change in constitution or profit-sharing ratio: per sec. 184(3), a firm is assessed as a firm only if there is NO change in (a) the constitution of the firm, or (b) the profit-sharing ratio. Where such a change occurs during the P.Y., the firm must furnish a certified copy of the revised partnership instrument along with the ROI for the relevant A.Y. [Sec. 184(4)]. This applies even to a mere change in partner remuneration/interest terms — without a filed revised instrument, interest/remuneration is allowed only as per the OLD instrument.

"Change in constitution" means one or more partners cease to be partners, or one or more new partners are admitted.

Carry forward & set-off of firm loss on change in constitution [Sec. 78]: where a change occurs due to retirement or death of a partner, the proportionate loss attributable to that retired/deceased partner cannot be carried forward by the firm. This restriction does NOT apply to unabsorbed depreciation.

CONCEPT

2.4 Capital Gains ★★★ HIGH

As per sec. 45(1), profits or gains arising on transfer of a capital asset are chargeable under the head "Capital Gains."

Taxpoint — essential conditions to charge income under this head:

  1. There must be a capital asset.
  2. The assessee transfers such capital asset.
  3. There must be profit or gain (including negative profit or gain) on such transfer.

The transferred asset must be a capital asset at the time of transfer.

2.4.1 Basis of Charge

Capital gain is taxable in the previous year in which the asset is transferred. However, in some cases (e.g. compulsory acquisition by the Government), capital gain is taxable in the previous year in which consideration is received rather than the year of transfer.

2.4.2 Capital Asset [Sec. 2(14)]

Capital asset means — any kind of property held by an assessee, whether or not connected with his business or profession; any securities held by a Foreign Institutional Investor (invested per SEBI Act, 1992 regulations) or a specified investment fund u/s 115UB; and any unit linked insurance policy to which exemption u/s 10(10D) does not apply. "Property" includes any rights in or in relation to an Indian company, including rights of management or control.

Capital asset may be movable/immovable, tangible/corporeal (furniture, jewellery) or intangible/incorporeal (goodwill, tenancy right, copyright).

What is NOT a capital asset:

  • 1. Stock-in-trade — stock-in-trade, consumable stores or raw materials held for business/profession (profit on sale taxable under "Profits & gains of business or profession"). Exception: securities held by an FII per SEBI regulations are never treated as stock-in-trade.
  • 2. Personal effect — movable property held for personal use of the assessee or a dependent family member, excluding: (A) jewellery, (B) archaeological collections, (C) drawings, (D) paintings, (E) sculptures, (F) any work of art. Jewellery includes ornaments of gold/silver/platinum/precious metal (worked or not, set with stones or not) and loose precious/semi-precious stones. Income on transfer of a personal effect is a capital receipt — not taxed under any head. Taxpoint: an immovable property used for personal purpose is NOT a personal effect (still a capital asset); securities are not personal effect; intangible assets have no personal-effect status.
  • 3. Agricultural land in rural area — not a capital asset unless it falls within specified municipal/cantonment jurisdiction limits or the aerial-distance bands below. Profit on sale of true rural agricultural land is a capital receipt, not taxable under any head.
  • 4. Gold Bonds — 6.5% Gold Bond 1977; 7% Gold Bonds 1980; National Defence Gold Bond 1980.
  • 5. Special Bearer Bond, 1991 issued by the Central Government (need not be held by the initial subscriber).
  • 6. Gold Deposit Bonds issued under the Gold Deposit Scheme, 1999 or deposit certificates under the Gold Monetisation Scheme, 2015 (interest thereon exempt u/s 10(15)).
Rural agricultural land — aerial-distance test
Population of municipality/cantonment boardArea within aerial distance treated as non-rural (→ capital asset)
More than 10,000 but not exceeding 1,00,000Up to 2 km
More than 1,00,000 but not exceeding 10,00,000Up to 6 km
More than 10,00,000Up to 8 km

Population per last preceding published census before the 1st day of the previous year. If the land is outside India or is not truly agricultural, it is a capital asset irrespective of location.

2.4.3 Types of Capital Asset [Sec. 2(42A)/2(29A)]

Short-term Capital Asset [Sec. 2(42A)]Long-term Capital Asset [Sec. 2(29A)]
Held by an assessee for not more than 24 months immediately preceding the date of transfer.A capital asset which is not a short-term capital asset.
EXCEPTION — the following are STCA only if held for not more than 12 months: security listed in India; a unit of an equity oriented fund (quoted or not); Zero-Coupon Bonds (quoted or not); Units of UTI (quoted or not); units of a listed debt-oriented mutual fund. "Securities" includes shares/scrips/stocks/bonds/debentures/derivatives/Government securities/units of a pooled investment vehicle — but NOT a unit linked insurance policy.

Short-term capital gain (STCG) arises on transfer of a STCA; long-term capital gain (LTCG) arises on transfer of a LTCA.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: "24 MONTHS FOR EVERYTHING"

THE TRAP: assuming every asset needs >24 months to become long-term.

THE TWIST: listed securities, units of an equity-oriented fund, Zero-Coupon Bonds, UTI units and listed debt-oriented MF units flip to long-term after just >12 months. Everything else (unlisted shares, land, jewellery, gold, house property) needs >24 months.

Exceptions — asset stays short-term regardless of holding period:

  • Sec. 50: gain on transfer of a depreciable asset (WDV block u/s 32(1)(ii)) is always STCG, irrespective of period of holding.
  • Sec. 50AA: gain on transfer of market-linked debentures and units of a specified mutual fund is always STCG, irrespective of period of holding. "Market Linked Debenture" = a security with returns linked to market returns on other securities/indices (or so classified by SEBI). "Specified Mutual Fund" = a fund investing not more than 35% of its proceeds in equity shares of domestic companies.

2.4.4 Period of Holding

CaseRule
Shares held in a company in liquidationPeriod after the date of commencement of liquidation is excluded.
Date of transferExcluded while computing period of holding.
Conversion of preference shares into equity sharesIncludes the period the preference shares were held.
Gold converted into Electronic Gold Receipt (EGR) [sec. 47(viid)]Period gold was held prior to conversion is included.
EGR converted into gold [sec. 47(viid)]Period the EGR was held prior to conversion is included.

2.4.5 Transfer [Sec. 2(47)]

Transfer, in relation to a capital asset, includes:

  1. Sale, Exchange & Relinquishment of the asset.
  2. Extinguishment of any right in an asset.
  3. Compulsory acquisition of an asset under any law.
  4. Conversion of asset into stock-in-trade by the owner.
  5. Any transaction of immovable property u/s 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
  6. Any transaction having the effect of transferring or enabling enjoyment of immovable property.
  7. Maturity or redemption of a zero coupon bond.

Taxpoint: the definition is indicative, not exhaustive, and applies only to capital assets. It also includes disposing of/parting with an asset or interest, or creating any interest in any asset, directly/indirectly, absolutely/conditionally, voluntarily/involuntarily — even where characterised as flowing from transfer of shares of a foreign company (inserted w.r.e.f. 01-04-1962 by Finance Act, 2012, to nullify Vodafone International Holdings B.V. vs. UOI [2012] 204 Taxman 408).

  • Exchange includes barter (mutual transfer of ownership of one thing for another) — both parties incur tax liability; sale consideration = fair market value of the asset received.
  • Relinquishment = giving up/abandoning/surrendering a right in a property that continues to exist in someone else's hands; requires mutual consent (a unilateral write-off in the books is NOT relinquishment).
  • Extinguishment of right = ending the holder's right in the asset (not the asset itself). Incidences: reduction of share capital (deemed dividend u/s 2(22)(d) on the accumulated-profit portion; sec. 45 capital gain on the capital portion); forfeiture/surrender of shares (CIT vs Vania Silk Mills Pvt. Ltd. — treated as transfer despite no consideration).
  • Compulsory acquisition under any law in force is a transfer even without mutual agreement.
  • Conversion into stock-in-trade — a transfer even though only one party is involved [sec. 2(47)(iv)].
  • Sec. 53A, Transfer of Property Act — possession allowed against part performance of a contract is treated as transfer.
  • Enjoyment of immovable property — membership/shares in a co-operative society/company/AOP that entitle occupation of a building is treated as transfer; such a member is regarded as the deemed/legal owner of the allotted flat/building for all tax purposes.

2.4.6 Computation of Capital Gains [Sec. 48]

Short-term Capital Gain = gain on transfer of a short-term capital asset [Sec. 2(42B)]. Long-term Capital Gain = gain on transfer of a long-term capital asset [Sec. 2(29B)].

Capital Gain = Full value of consideration – Expenses on transfer – Cost of acquisition – Cost of improvement – Exemption u/s 54, 54B, 54D, etc.

No deduction is allowed for Securities Transaction Tax (STT) paid, in computing income under "Capital gains."

Computation of Capital Gain — format
ParticularsAmount
Sale consideration (Full value of consideration)****
Less: Expenses on transfer****
Net sale consideration****
Less: (i) Cost of acquisition (ii) Cost of improvement****
Short/Long Term Capital Gain****
Less: Exemption u/s 54, 54B, 54D, etc.(****)
Taxable Short/Long Term Capital Gain*****

Sale consideration: sale value in money or money's worth. If receivable in instalments across years, the entire value is taxable in the year of transfer. Sec. 50D: where consideration is not ascertainable/determinable, the fair market value of the asset on the date of transfer is deemed to be the full value of consideration.

Expenses on transfer: expenditure wholly & exclusively for the transfer (brokerage/commission, stamp & registration, travelling). Notes: must be necessary and not vague; may be incurred before or after completion; not allowable if already claimed under another head; STT is never deductible.

Cost of Acquisition [Sec. 55(2)]: expenditure to acquire the asset or complete title (e.g. sum paid to discharge a mortgage created by a previous owner; litigation cost to register shares). It excludes deductions already claimed on interest u/s 24(b) or under Chapter VI-A, and excludes STT.

Cost of Improvement [Sec. 55(1)(b)]: capital expenditure incurred to increase the productive quality of the asset (additions/alterations). Excludes any expenditure already deductible under another head (or Chapter VIA).

Assets acquired before 1/4/2001
ItemRule
Cost of acquisitionHigher of: (a) actual cost of acquisition (ignoring pre-1/4/2001 improvement cost); or (b) FMV of the asset as on 1/4/2001 [Sec. 55]. For land/building, FMV as on 1/4/2001 cannot exceed the stamp duty value (where available). Option NOT available for: assets depreciated u/s 32(1)(ii); self-generated assets (other than bonus shares).
Cost of improvementAny improvement cost incurred before 1/4/2001 (by assessee or previous owner) is ignored.

ILLUSTRATION 95 — basic capital gain computation

Mr. Divesh purchased a golden ring on 17/8/2024 for ₹20,000. On 1/05/2025 he sewed a diamond costing ₹25,000. On 1/08/2025 he sold the ring for ₹80,000, incurring brokerage ₹5,000.

Computation of capital gain of Mr. Divesh for A.Y. 2026-27
ParticularsAmount (₹)
Sale consideration80,000
Less: Expenses on transfer5,000
Net sale consideration75,000
Less: Cost of acquisition (20,000) + Cost of improvement (25,000)45,000
Short Term Capital Gain30,000

Answer: STCG ₹30,000 (held less than 24 months).

2.4.7 Tax on Capital Gain

Tax on STCG on transfer of certain assets where STT is charged [Sec. 111A]: taxed @ 20% + surcharge (if applicable) + Health & Education Cess.

Conditions: (1) asset is a short-term capital asset being an equity share in a company, or a unit of an equity oriented fund, or a unit of a business trust; (2) the transaction is chargeable to STT. Concessional rate also applies to a transaction in foreign currency on a recognised stock exchange in an IFSC even though STT is not charged there.

Notes: no Chapter VIA deduction against such STCG. For a resident individual/HUF, where total income (excluding such STCG) is below the exempted ceiling, such STCG is first reduced by the shortfall and tax @ 20% applies only on the balance:

Tax = 20% × [Such STCG – (Exempted ceiling – Total income excluding such STCG)]

Tax on LTCG in certain cases [Sec. 112A]

Applicable to all assessees where: total income includes capital gains; the gain is from transfer of a long-term equity share (including bonus shares) in a company, or unit of an equity-oriented fund, or unit of a business trust; and STT has been levied as follows:

Equity share in a companySTT paid on BOTH acquisition and transfer. Exception (STT-on-acquisition not required): equity share acquired before 01-10-2004; or acquisition notified (IPO, ESOP, etc. — Notification No. 60/2018 dated 01-10-2018).

*Unit of business trust is LTCA if held >24 months. STT condition (either case) is waived for transfer on a recognised stock exchange in an IFSC where consideration is received in foreign currency.

No indexation benefit is available; holding period runs from date of acquisition; loss is allowed to be carried forward. Bonus shares allotted before 31/01/2018 follow this same rule (FMV as on 31/01/2018 taken as cost, subject to the scenarios below).

2.4.8 Exception to Computation of Tax on LTCG — Land/Building

Applies where: transferor is a resident individual or resident HUF; LTCG arises on transfer of a long-term capital asset being land, building or both (residential, commercial or any other use); the asset was acquired before 23-07-2024; and is transferred on or after 23-07-2024. The assessee then has an option:

Option 1 — Pay tax @ 12.5% WITHOUT indexation benefit  |  Option 2 — Pay tax @ 20% AFTER considering indexation benefit

The option is only for computing the TAX on LTCG — the capital gain itself is always first computed WITHOUT index benefit; indexation only enters if Option 2 is chosen for tax purposes.

Index Benefit

Indexed cost of acquisition = Cost of acquisition × (CII of year of transfer ÷ CII of year of acquisition, or of F.Y. 2001-02, whichever is later)

Indexed cost of improvement = Cost of improvement × (CII of year of transfer ÷ CII of year of improvement)

"Cost Inflation Index" (CII): notified by the Central Government having regard to 75% of the average rise in the Consumer Price Index (urban) for the preceding previous year.

Indexed cost of acquisition is ascertained w.r.t. the date of acquisition (not the date the asset became a capital asset). If acquired before 1/4/2001, indexation benefit is available only from 2001-02.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: INDEXATION EVERYWHERE

THE TRAP: applying the indexed-cost formula to any long-term asset, or assuming Option 1/Option 2 is available to all LTCG.

THE TWIST: the 12.5%-no-index / 20%-with-index choice applies ONLY to a resident individual/HUF transferring land/building/both, acquired before 23-07-2024 and transferred on/after 23-07-2024. Every other LTCG (gold, jewellery, shares under 112(1), VDA, debentures) has no such option and no indexation at all in most cases; LTCG u/s 112A is always at 12.5% with NO indexation, full stop.

2.4.9 Transactions Not Regarded as Transfer [Sec. 46 & 47]

By virtue of sec. 46(1) and sec. 47, the following do NOT constitute a transfer for capital gain purposes:

SectionTransaction
46(1)Distribution of capital assets by a company to shareholders on liquidation (not a transfer in the company's hands).
47(i)Distribution of capital assets on total/partial partition of an HUF.
47(iii)Transfer by an individual/HUF under a gift, will or irrevocable trust. Exception: gift of ESOP shares IS treated as transfer.
47(iv)/(v)Transfer between a 100% holding company and its Indian subsidiary (either direction) — NOT exempt if transferred as stock.
47(vi)Transfer of a capital asset in a scheme of amalgamation, by amalgamating to amalgamated company, if the amalgamated company is Indian.
47(via)/(viab)Amalgamation of foreign companies transferring shares of an Indian company, if ≥25% of shareholders of the amalgamating foreign company continue as shareholders of the amalgamated foreign company, and the transfer attracts no capital gains tax in the amalgamating company's country.
47(viaa)Transfer by a banking company to a banking institution in an amalgamation scheme sanctioned u/s 45(7), Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
47(viiac)/(viiad)Transfer of assets by an "original fund" to a "resultant fund" (IFSC relocation scheme), or by a unit/share/interest holder therein, up to 31-03-2030, subject to prescribed conditions.
47(viiae)Transfer by India Infrastructure Finance Company Ltd to a notified infrastructure-financing institution.
47(viiaf)Transfer by a public sector company to another notified PSU/Central/State Government under a Central-Government-approved plan.
47(vib)/(vic)/(vicc)Transfer of a capital asset in a scheme of demerger, by demerged to resulting company, if resulting company is Indian; for foreign demergers, if shareholders holding ≥3/4th in value continue as shareholders of the resulting foreign company and no capital-gains tax attaches abroad.
47(vica)/(vicb)Transfer in a business reorganisation of co-operative banks, from predecessor to successor bank/converted banking company, or by a shareholder in consideration of shares in the successor.
47(vid)Transfer/issue of shares by the resulting company to shareholders of the demerged company, in consideration of the demerger.
47(vii)Transfer by a shareholder, in an amalgamation, of shares in the amalgamating company, in consideration of allotment of shares in the amalgamated (Indian) company.
47(viia)/(viiaa)/(viiab)/(viib)Transfer outside India, by a non-resident to another non-resident, of foreign currency convertible bonds, GDRs, rupee-denominated bonds, derivatives, notified securities or Government securities (various IFSC/IFSCA conditions apply).
47(viic)Redemption of a Sovereign Gold Bond (RBI scheme, 2015) by an individual.
47(viid)Conversion of gold into an Electronic Gold Receipt (EGR) issued by a Vault Manager, or EGR back into gold.
47(ix)Transfer of a work of art/archaeological/scientific collection, book, manuscript, drawing, painting, photograph or print to the Government/University/National Museum/Art Gallery/Archives or a notified institution of national importance.
47(x)/(xa)/(xb)Conversion of bonds/debentures/deposit certificates into shares/debentures of the same company; conversion of sec. 115AC(1)(a) bonds into shares/debentures; conversion of preference shares into equity shares.
47(xii)Transfer of land of a sick industrial company under a scheme sanctioned u/s 18, Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, where managed by a workers' co-operative.
47(xiii)Firm succeeded by a company — all assets/liabilities pass to the company; all partners become shareholders in the same capital-account proportion; partners receive only shares as consideration; aggregate partner shareholding ≥50% of voting power, maintained for 5 years from succession.
47(xiiia)Transfer of assets/membership rights to a company on demutualisation/corporatisation of a recognised stock exchange, per an SEBI-approved scheme.
47(xiiib)Private/unlisted public company converted into an LLP — all assets/liabilities pass to the LLP; shareholders become partners in the same capital/profit-sharing ratio; no consideration beyond LLP share/capital; aggregate profit-sharing ratio of erstwhile shareholders ≥50% for 5 years; company's turnover in any of the preceding 3 years ≤ ₹60 lakh; total assets ≤ ₹5 crore; no payment from accumulated profits to any partner for 3 years post-conversion.
47(xiv)Sole proprietary concern succeeded by a company — all assets/liabilities pass to the company; proprietor holds ≥50% of voting power for 5 years; proprietor receives only shares as consideration.
47(xv)Transfer under a securities-lending scheme per SEBI/RBI guidelines.
47(xvi)Transfer under a reverse mortgage scheme notified by the Central Government (loan amount received by senior citizen also exempt u/s 10(43)).
47(xvii)Transfer of an SPV share [sec. 10(23FC)] to a business trust in exchange for units allotted by that trust.
47(xviii)/(xix)Transfer by a unit holder of units in a consolidating scheme/plan of a mutual fund, in consideration of units in the consolidated scheme/plan (period of holding of the consolidating units carries forward).

Sec. 47(xiii) & (xiv) exempt capital gain on transfer of a capital ASSET, not on stock-in-trade — stock transferred at profit remains taxable as business income.

2.4.10 Deemed/Notional Cost of Acquisition [Sec. 49(1)]

(A) In the following cases, the cost of acquisition of the previous owner is deemed to be the cost of acquisition for the assessee:

  • Assets received on total/partial partition of HUF [49(1)(i)].
  • Assets received under a gift or will [49(1)(ii)].
  • Assets received by succession, inheritance or devolution [49(1)(iii)(a)].
  • Assets received on dissolution of a firm, BOI or AOP [49(1)(iii)(b)].
  • Assets received on liquidation of a company [49(1)(iii)(c)].
  • Assets received under a trust (revocable or irrevocable) [49(1)(iii)(d)].
  • Assets received under business reorganisation subject to conditions [49(1)(iii)(e)] — e.g. between a 100% Indian subsidiary and holding company, an amalgamated Indian company, or conversion of a company into an LLP.
  • Self-acquired property of a member received by an HUF [49(1)(iv)].

(B) Other deemed-cost rules: cost of preference shares carries over as cost of converted equity shares [Sec. 49(2AE)]; where the gain arises from property earlier taxed u/s 56(2)(x) (gift provision), cost = the value taken u/s 56(2)(x); inventory converted into a capital asset takes FMV as on date of conversion as cost; Electronic Gold Receipt / gold conversions carry over the cost of the underlying asset.

Aspects of Sec. 49(1)
ItemRule
Cost of acquisition — previous owner's cost ascertainableCost of acquisition of the previous owner.
Cost of acquisition — previous owner's cost unascertainableFMV of the asset on the date the previous owner acquired it.
Improvement expenditureIncludes improvement cost incurred by the previous owner.
Period of holdingPrevious owner's holding period counts for STCA/LTCA classification.
Indexation benefit (cost of acquisition)CIT vs. Manjula J. Saha 16 Taxmann 42 (Bombay): index benefit available from the year the previous owner first held the asset, or F.Y. 2001-02, whichever is later. Available only when computing tax on LTCG under Option 2 (resident individual/HUF, land/building).
Indexation benefit (cost of improvement)Available from the year the improvement cost was incurred (by current or previous owner) — same Option-2-only rider applies.

"Previous owner" = the last owner who acquired the asset through a mode OTHER than the sec. 49(1) modes above.

On 1/04/2009 Parminder incurred polish expenditure ₹5,000. Sold 1/04/2025 for ₹12,00,000; brokerage 1%. FMV as on 1/04/2001 ₹2,00,000; 1/04/2005 ₹5,00,000; 1/04/2025 ₹7,50,000.
