2.4.12 & 2.4.13 Advance Money Forfeited [Sec. 51] & Compensation Paid by the Transferor

W.e.f. A.Y. 2015-16, any sum received as advance/otherwise in the course of negotiations for transfer of a capital asset is taxable as "Income from Other Sources" if (a) it is forfeited AND (b) the negotiations do not result in transfer [Sec. 56(2)(ix)]. Such a sum, once taxed u/s 56(2)(ix), is NOT further deducted from the cost of acquisition/WDV/FMV when computing capital gain. (Pre-31-03-2014 advances retained by the assessee, not the previous owner, ARE still deducted from cost.)

Where the transferor defaults and the transferee receives compensation (over and above refund of advance), such compensation is treated as sale consideration for transfer (relinquishment) of the purchasing right — the right to purchase is the asset transferred, cost of acquisition is Nil, sale consideration is the compensation received.

2.4.14 Capital Gain on Insurance Claim [Sec. 45(1A)]

Overruling CIT vs Vania Silk Mills (P) Ltd. (which held insurance compensation for loss of capital assets non-taxable), Sec. 45(1A) (w.e.f. A.Y. 2000-01) treats compensation from an insurer for specified damages as a transfer, taxable in the year of RECEIPT of compensation. "Specified damages" = flood/typhoon/hurricane/cyclone/earthquake/natural calamity; riot/civil disturbance; accidental fire/explosion; enemy action (declared war or not).

ItemRule
Sale consideration — cash compensationCompensation received.
Sale consideration — compensation in kindFMV of assets received (as on date of receipt).
Cost of acquisition/improvement/expense on transferAs usual.
Indexation (if any)Till the year of destruction (available only where resident individual/HUF opt for Option 2).
Taxable inThe year of receipt of compensation, at that year's rate.

Machinery damage: compensation up to repair/renovation cost is treated u/s 41(1) (repair cost allowed u/s 31); excess over that is capital receipt, not taxable; Sec. 45(1A) does not apply as there's no transfer. Other damages (theft, road accident, ship loss) — capital receipt, not taxable. Damage to non-capital asset (e.g. stock) — taxable as business income u/s 28/56. No insurance at all — neither 45(1A) nor 45 applies; loss on the destroyed asset is not an allowable loss.

ILLUSTRATION 101 — fire destroys house, furniture and stock

Lucky's self-occupied house, acquired 18/08/2019 for ₹6,00,000, improved 18/08/2022 for ₹3,00,000, destroyed by accidental fire on 15/05/2025 along with furniture (₹5,00,000) and business stock. Insurance claim received 18/08/2025: house ₹1,00,000 cash + a new house (FMV ₹44,00,000); furniture ₹2,00,000; stock ₹80,000 (stock cost ₹1,00,000).

Computation of capital gain of Lucky for A.Y. 2026-27
ParticularsAmount (₹)
Sale consideration of house (₹1,00,000 + ₹44,00,000)45,00,000
Less: Expenses on transferNil
Net sale consideration45,00,000
Less: Cost of acquisition (6,00,000) + Cost of improvement (3,00,000)9,00,000
Long Term Capital Gain36,00,000

Answer: House — LTCG ₹36,00,000, taxable in A.Y. 2026-27 (year of receipt). Furniture — a personal effect, not a capital asset; compensation is a capital receipt, not taxable. Stock — loss of ₹20,000 (₹1,00,000 – ₹80,000) allowed under "Profits & gains of business or profession." If compensation had instead been received on 15/04/2026, the ₹36,00,000 gain would shift to A.Y. 2027-28.

2.4.15–2.4.20 Other Deemed-Transfer Computations

Capital gain on ULIP [Sec. 45(1B)]: any amount received under a ULIP (to which sec. 10(10D) exemption does not apply), including bonus allocated, is chargeable as "Capital gains" — deemed income of the year of receipt, computed in the prescribed manner. Where the ULIP is an equity-oriented unit, income is taxable u/s 112A.

Conversion of capital asset into stock-in-trade [Sec. 45(2)]
ItemRule
Sale considerationFMV as on date of conversion.
Cost of acquisition/improvement/expense on transferAs usual.
Taxable inThe year the converted stock is actually SOLD.
Difference on actual sale [Actual sale value – FMV on conversion – expenditure on transfer]Treated as business income.
Depreciable assets [Sec. 50]
ItemRule
MeaningCapital asset forming part of a WDV block on which depreciation is allowed u/s 32(1)(ii) (excludes goodwill of business/profession from any block).
Nature of gainAlways SHORT-term capital gain, irrespective of holding period.
IndexationNever available.
ComputationPer the "Profits & gains of business or profession" Depreciation (sec. 32) rules.
Transfer of dematerialised securities [Sec. 45(2A)]
ItemRule
Cost of acquisition & period of holdingDetermined on FIFO basis (per CBDT Circular No. 768 dated 24/6/1998: FIFO applies only to the demat portion if assessee holds both physical and demat forms; separate FIFO per demat account; the date of entry in the demat account governs, not the purchase date).
Sale consideration/expenditure on transferAs usual.

ILLUSTRATION 102 — capital contribution to a firm [Sec. 45(3)]

ABC & Co. admits D as partner (1/5th share) for capital of ₹2,00,000: furniture (personal, ₹50,000) + jewellery (FMV ₹2,00,000, recorded in books at ₹1,80,000; D's cost ₹45,000, acquired 7/07/2001).

Computation of capital gain in the hands of Mr. D for A.Y. 2026-27
ParticularsAmount (₹)
Sale consideration (books value)1,80,000
Less: Expenses on transferNil
Net sale consideration1,80,000
Less: Cost of acquisition45,000
Long Term Capital Gain1,35,000

Answer: furniture is a personal effect — not a capital asset, no gain; sale consideration for jewellery = the AMOUNT RECORDED IN BOOKS (₹1,80,000), FMV (₹2,00,000) is irrelevant.

Distribution on dissolution/reconstitution [Sec. 45(4) r.w.s. 9B]: A = B + C – D

A = income chargeable as capital gains of the specified entity (if negative, deemed Nil). B = money received by the specified person on the date of receipt. C = FMV of capital asset received by the specified person on that date. D = balance in the specified person's capital account in the entity's books at reconstitution, EXCLUDING any increase from revaluation of assets or self-generated goodwill/asset.

Sec. 9B separately deems the specified ENTITY to have transferred the asset/stock at FMV (income taxable as business income or capital gains, as the case may be); Sec. 45(4) taxes the specified entity again on the "A" formula above — the two provisions operate independently and in addition to each other.

2.4.21 Compulsory Acquisition [Sec. 45(5)]

Applies to compulsory acquisition of a capital asset (other than urban agro-land) under any law, or where consideration is determined/approved by the Central Government (not a State Government) or the RBI.

Initial compensation [Sec. 45(5)(a)]
ItemRule
Sale considerationTotal compensation/consideration received or receivable.
Cost of acquisition/improvementAs usual.
Expenditure on transferLegal expenditure to recover the claim is allowed.
Taxable inThe year compensation (or part) is FIRST received.
IndexationTill the year of compulsory acquisition (Option 2 only).
Enhanced compensation [Sec. 45(5)(b)]
ItemRule
Sale considerationTotal enhanced compensation received (taxable in the year of receipt only; part received → only that part taxed).
Expenditure on transferLitigation expenses to obtain the enhanced compensation are deductible.
Cost of acquisition/improvementNil.
Nature of gainSame as the initial compensation (STCG/LTCG).
Interest on enhanced compensationTaxable as "Income from Other Sources."

Interim-order compensation is deemed income of the year the FINAL order is passed. If the person entitled dies/otherwise before receipt, the gain is taxed in the hands of whoever actually receives the enhanced compensation. Reduced compensation [Sec. 45(5)(c)]: if a court/tribunal later reduces the compensation, the capital gain of that earlier year is RE-COMPUTED with the reduced figure.

ILLUSTRATION 103 — compulsory acquisition with enhanced compensation

Sunil's house, acquired 7/07/1995 for ₹3,00,000; improved ₹70,000 (16/08/2000) and ₹50,000 (17/07/2010); FMV as on 1/04/2001 ₹4,50,000. Compulsorily acquired 16/08/2024, compensation ₹81,50,000 (20% received 31/03/2026, balance 2/06/2026). Enhanced compensation ₹8,00,000 declared 16/08/2026 (litigation cost ₹11,000), received 18/08/2027.

Computation of capital gains of Sunil for A.Y. 2026-27
ParticularsAmount (₹)
Sale consideration (initial compensation)81,50,000
Less: Expenses on transferNil
Net sale consideration81,50,000
Less: Cost of acquisition (higher of actual ₹3,00,000 or FMV 1/4/2001 ₹4,50,000) + Cost of improvement (post-2001, ₹50,000)5,00,000
Long Term Capital Gain76,50,000

Answer: taxable in A.Y. 2026-27 — the P.Y. of RECEIPT (2025-26), not the P.Y. of acquisition (2024-25). Pre-1/4/2001 improvement cost (₹70,000) is ignored. A.Y. 2027-28: nothing taxable (no enhanced compensation received that year). A.Y. 2028-29: Sale consideration ₹8,00,000 – expenses ₹11,000 = ₹7,89,000 net; cost of acquisition/improvement Nil → LTCG ₹7,89,000 (nature follows the initial compensation's LTCG status).

Exemption — compulsory acquisition of urban agro-land [Sec. 10(37)]: for individual/HUF, where the land was used for agriculture by the assessee/parents/HUF for 2 years preceding transfer, transferred by compulsory acquisition (or Government/RBI-approved consideration), and compensation is received on/after 1/04/2004 — income is fully EXEMPT.

Exemption — transfer under Land Pooling Scheme [Sec. 10(37A)]: for individual/HUF owning land/building on 02-06-2014, transferred under the Andhra Pradesh Capital City Land Pooling Scheme — capital gain on the pooling transfer, on the land pooling ownership certificate, and on the reconstituted plot (if transferred within 2 years of possession) is EXEMPT. If the reconstituted plot is not transferred within that 2-year window, its cost of acquisition is deemed to be its stamp duty value as on the last day of the 2nd financial year after possession.

2.4.22 Joint Development Agreement (JDA) [Sec. 45(5A)]

Applies where an individual/HUF transfers land/building/both, under a REGISTERED "specified agreement," to a developer in consideration of a share (land/building) in the project, with or without part cash.

ItemRule
Sale considerationStamp duty value (on date of issue of completion certificate) of the assessee's share + cash consideration, if any.
Cost of acquisitionProportionate cost of the asset transferred.
IndexationUp to the year the completion certificate is issued (Option 2 cases only).
Taxable inThe year the completion certificate is issued.

If the assessee transfers his share BEFORE the completion certificate is issued, Sec. 45(5A) does not apply — gain is taxed in the ordinary year of transfer under normal rules.

2.4.23 & 2.4.24 Liquidation [Sec. 46] & Buy-back [Sec. 46A]

In the company's hands [Sec. 46(1)]: distribution of assets in specie to shareholders on liquidation is NOT a transfer. But if the company first SELLS the assets in the market and distributes proceeds, that sale IS a transfer chargeable in the company's hands (as usual sale consideration/cost, taxable in the year of sale) — the subsequent distribution of proceeds to shareholders is not itself taxed again.

In the shareholder's hands [Sec. 46(2)]: money/assets received on liquidation (excluding the amount taxed as deemed dividend u/s 2(22)(c)) is liable to capital gain — sale consideration = total received less deemed dividend; cost of acquisition/improvement as usual. Where distribution is less than total Shareholders' Funds, it is deemed to occur proportionately between share capital and accumulated profit. Instalment payments: cost of acquisition is absorbed against earlier instalments first; once absorbed, later instalments (less transfer expenses) are fully taxable. Even a non-capital asset distributed (e.g. rural agro-land) triggers sec. 46(2) capital gain, since the asset transferred (from the shareholder's perspective) is the SHARE in the company.

ILLUSTRATION 104 — liquidation distribution

Purva India (P) Ltd.: equity capital ₹8,00,000, preference capital ₹1,00,000, reserves ₹2,00,000. Liquidated; only building sold at book value, proceeds applied to liabilities/preference shareholders. Utkarsh holds 10% equity (acquired at face value, 16/08/2018) and 20% preference (subscribed at par, 1-04-2025); received land (MV ₹5,00,000) and cash ₹20,000 (for preference).

Computation of capital gain in the hands of Utkarsh for A.Y. 2026-27
ParticularsEquity share (₹)Preference share (₹)
Sale consideration [land ₹5,00,000 – deemed dividend ₹20,000 (10% of ₹2,00,000 reserves)]4,80,00020,000
Less: Cost of acquisition (10% of ₹8,00,000 / 20% of ₹1,00,000)80,00020,000
Capital Gain4,00,000 (LTCG)Nil (STCG)

Answer: no capital gain arises in the company's hands (building sold at book value). Utkarsh: LTCG ₹4,00,000 on equity, Nil STCG on preference shares.

Buy-back of specified securities other than shares [Sec. 46A]
ItemRule
Sale considerationDeemed Nil.
Cost of acquisition/improvementAs usual.
Taxable inThe year the securities are bought back.

Money received by a shareholder on buy-back of SHARES is taxable as dividend income under "Income from Other Sources" (company deducts TDS u/s 194) — not as capital gain. Any resulting nil/negative capital gains figure can still be adjusted against other capital gains, and unabsorbed capital loss carried forward u/s 74.

2.4.25–2.4.29 Further Special Computation Rules

HUF partition assets, subsequently transferred by member [Sec. 47(i) & 49(1)]
ItemRule
Sale considerationAs usual.
Cost of acquisitionCost of the assets in the HUF's hands.
Indexation on cost of acquisition/improvementFrom when the HUF held the asset / incurred the improvement (Option 2 cases only).
Nature of asset (STCA/LTCA)HUF's period of holding is considered.
Conversion of debentures into shares [Sec. 49(2A)] & Zero Coupon Bond [Sec. 2(48)]
ItemRule
Conversion of debentures/debenture stock/deposit certificate into shares/debenturesNOT a transfer. Cost of the old convertible debenture becomes cost of the new share; holding period runs from the date the debenture was acquired [Rule 8AA]. No indexation on debentures.
Zero Coupon Bond — definitionA bond issued by an infrastructure capital company/fund, infrastructure debt fund, PSU or scheduled bank, on which no payment/benefit is receivable before maturity/redemption, and notified by the Central Government.
NatureLTCA if held >12 months; redemption/maturity/sale is treated as transfer.
Tax rateLTCG on such bond — 12.5% WITHOUT indexation.
Issuer's treatmentDiscount (amount receivable by issuer less amount payable on maturity) is deductible u/s 36(1)(iiia) on a pro-rata basis over the bond's life.

ILLUSTRATION 105 — ESOP perquisite and capital gain

T Ltd. granted Rajat an ESOP option on 1/04/2021 for 100 shares @ ₹150; vesting 1/04/2023; exercised 31/05/2025, allotted 13/06/2025. FMV: 1/04/2021 ₹470; 1/04/2023 ₹890; 31/05/2025 ₹1,250; 13/06/2025 ₹1,470. On 31/12/2025 he gifted 25 shares and sold the rest @ ₹2,180/share.

Perquisite for A.Y. 2026-27
ParticularsAmount (₹)
FMV on exercise date (₹1,250 × 100)1,25,000
Less: amount paid (₹150 × 100)15,000
Value of perquisite1,10,000
Computation of capital gain in the hands of Mr. Rajat for A.Y. 2026-27
ParticularsAmount (₹)
Full value of consideration (₹2,180 × 100)2,18,000
Less: Cost of acquisition (FMV on exercise, ₹1,250 × 100)1,25,000
Short term Capital gain93,000

Answer: even the GIFTED 25 shares (via ESOP) are treated as a transfer for capital gains — only the outright gift-of-shares exemption u/s 47(iii) is disallowed for ESOP shares.

Market Linked Debentures [Sec. 50AA]: applies to units of a Specified Mutual Fund (acquired on/after 01-04-2023), Market Linked Debenture units, or unlisted bonds/debentures (transferred/redeemed/matured on/after 23-07-2024)

Full value of consideration – Expenses on transfer (STT not allowed) – Cost of acquisition = Short Term Capital Gain, irrespective of period of holding, taxable at regular slab rates. "Specified Mutual Fund" = a fund investing >65% of proceeds (annual average of daily closing figures) in debt/money market instruments, or ≥65% in units of such a fund.

2.4.30 Valuation of Consideration — Land/Building [Sec. 50C]

Applies where land/building/both is transferred and the stamp-duty value (adopted/assessed/assessable*) exceeds 110% of the actual consideration — the STAMP DUTY VALUE is then taken as the full value of consideration. If the stamp duty value does NOT exceed 110% of actual consideration (or is less than it), actual consideration is retained as full value of consideration.

*"Assessable" = the price the stamp authority would have adopted, had the matter been referred to it.

PROVISION ILLUSTRATED — Sec. 50C 110% tolerance band

Mr. Raj's self-occupied house, acquired 10 months ago for ₹5,00,000, sold to Rajshree for ₹6,00,000 (110% threshold = ₹6,60,000).

Computation of capital gain
ParticularsCase (a): stamp value ₹6,25,000Case (b): stamp value ₹6,75,000
Sale consideration taken6,00,000 (actual — stamp value within 110%)6,75,000 (stamp value — exceeds 110%)
Less: Cost of acquisition5,00,0005,00,000
Short Term Capital Gain1,00,0001,75,000

Reference to Valuation Officer: the AO may refer valuation to a Valuation Officer if the assessee claims the stamp-authority value exceeds fair market value AND that value has not been disputed in any appeal/revision/reference. If the Valuation Officer's figure EXCEEDS the stamp value, the stamp value is retained as full value of consideration; if it does NOT exceed the stamp value, the Valuation Officer's figure is taken instead. Taxpoint: sale consideration is thus always the MINIMUM of the stamp-duty value and the Valuation Officer's figure.

Agreement date vs. registration date: where these differ AND part/full consideration was received via account payee cheque/draft/ECS/specified electronic mode on or before the agreement date, the stamp value AS ON THE AGREEMENT DATE may be taken for computing full value of consideration. If that stamp value is later revised on appeal/revision/reference, the assessment is amended to recompute the gain using the revised value [Sec. 155].

PROVISION ILLUSTRATED — Valuation Officer reference

Mr. Rajesh's house, acquired 15/11/2024 for ₹6,00,000, sold to Jayshree 18/08/2025 for ₹5,00,000; stamp value ₹10,00,000; on reference, Valuation Officer determines ₹9,00,000.

Computation of capital gains in the hands of Mr. Raj for A.Y. 2026-27
ParticularsAmount (₹)
Sale consideration (lower of stamp value & Valuation Officer's figure)9,00,000
Less: Cost of acquisition6,00,000
Short Term Capital Gain3,00,000

Mr. A transfers land and building on 2-01-2026: net consideration ₹10 lakh; stamp value (uncontested) ₹12 lakh; Valuation Officer figure ₹13 lakh. Land received on HUF partial partition (1-04-2001, FMV ₹1,00,000); building constructed at cost ₹2,00,000 (completed 1-12-2004, F.Y. 2004-05).

Computation of capital gain of Mr. A for A.Y. 2026-27
ParticularsOption 1 (₹)Option 2 (₹)

2.4.31 Valuation of Consideration — Unquoted Shares [Sec. 50CA]

Where an unquoted company share is transferred for consideration less than its FMV, the FMV is deemed to be the full value of consideration. "Quoted share" = a share regularly quoted on a recognised stock exchange based on current ordinary-course transactions. Not applicable to transfers by prescribed classes of persons.

2.4.32 Self-Generated Assets [Sec. 55(2)(a)]

Cost of acquisition AND cost of improvement are treated as NIL for self-generated: goodwill of a business/profession; trademark/brand name; right to manufacture/produce/process any article; right to carry on business/profession; tenancy rights; stage carriage permits; loom hours or any other right. If such assets are NOT self-generated (acquired by purchase, or via sec. 49(1)(i)-(iv) from a previous owner who purchased), the actual/previous-owner purchase price is the cost. This Nil-cost rule applies even for assets developed/purchased before 1/4/2001 (the FMV-as-on-1/4/2001 option is NOT available here). Depreciable goodwill: where depreciation u/s 32(1) was claimed on goodwill up to A.Y. 2020-21, cost (purchase price) is reduced by the depreciation already obtained.

Mr. Rocky bought 1,000 shares of Azad (P) Ltd. @ ₹12 on 1/08/1998. Bonus 1:2 declared 31/03/2000 (500 shares). Gift of 500 shares from Rakesh on 7/07/2006 (Rakesh's cost ₹14/share, acquired 1/04/2001). Bonus 1:5 declared 1/03/2025 (400 shares, on the 2,000-share base). Sold all @ ₹50 on 1/01/2026.

Computation of capital gains in the hands of Mr. Rocky for A.Y. 2026-27

Answer: 2000-bonus tranche is long-term (allotted >12 months before sale); the 2025 bonus tranche (allotted 1/03/2025, sold 1/01/2026) is short-term. Total number of shares held builds up as 1,000 → 1,500 (bonus) → 2,000 (gift) → 2,400 (bonus).

2.4.34 Bonus Stripping [Sec. 94(8)]

Applies where a person: (a) buys securities/units within 3 months before the record date; (b) is allotted additional (bonus) securities/units without payment based on that holding; (c) sells all/any of the ORIGINAL securities/units within 9 months after the record date while continuing to hold the additional ones.

Loss on such purchase-and-sale of the original units is IGNORED for computing taxable income; the ignored loss instead becomes the deemed cost of acquisition of the bonus units still held.

ILLUSTRATION 109 — bonus stripping in a mutual fund

Mr. A bought 5,000 units @ ₹80 on 10/10/2025. Bonus 4:5 (record date 1/11/2025, 4,000 bonus units). Sold 2,500 original units @ ₹20 (1/12/2025); 1,000 bonus units @ ₹25 (10/01/2026); remaining 2,500 original @ ₹30 (12/02/2026); remaining 3,000 bonus @ ₹45 (14/03/2026).

Computation of capital gain of Mr. A for A.Y. 2026-27
TransactionSale consideration (₹)Cost of acquisition (₹)Result (₹)
2,500 original units @ ₹20 (1/12/2025)50,0002,00,000Loss ₹1,50,000 — IGNORED; becomes cost of 4,000 bonus units, i.e. ₹37.50/unit. Taxable gain: Nil
1,000 bonus units @ ₹25 (10/01/2026)25,00037,500 (@ ₹37.50)STCG (loss) ₹(12,500) — allowed, since these are bonus units, not original
2,500 original units @ ₹30 (12/02/2026)75,0002,00,000Loss ₹1,25,000 — IGNORED; becomes cost of remaining 3,000 bonus units (blended with earlier cost) i.e. ₹79.17/unit. Taxable gain: Nil
3,000 bonus units @ ₹45 (14/03/2026)1,35,0002,37,510 (@ ₹79.17)STCG (loss) ₹(1,02,510)

Answer: every loss on sale of ORIGINAL units is disallowed and instead loaded onto the bonus units' cost; only the bonus-unit sales generate a recognised (loss) figure.

2.4.35 Right Shares & Right Entitlement [Sec. 55(2)(aa)]

Right Share: where holding a financial asset entitles the assessee to subscribe to an additional financial asset, that additional asset is a "right share" — cost of acquisition = amount actually paid for it. Right Entitlement: the assessee's right to acquire the right share can be endorsed (renounced) to another person — cost of acquisition of the right entitlement itself is Nil.

Conversion of inventory into capital asset

Virtual Digital Assets [Sec. 115BBH r.w.s. 2(47A)]: VDA includes any crypto-token/code/number generated cryptographically representing value (with the promise of value/store of value/unit of account), specified NFTs or similar tokens, other notified digital assets, and crypto-assets on a distributed ledger. Excluded (Notification No. 74/2022): gift cards/vouchers, mileage/reward/loyalty points, website/platform subscriptions; also excluded — an NFT whose transfer legally transfers ownership of an underlying tangible asset.

Whether held as investment (taxable under "Capital Gains") or for trading (taxable as business income), computation and the 30% rate remain the same either way.

EXEMPTIONS

Deduction from Capital Gain — Sections 54 to 54GB

Several deductions are allowed from computed capital gain: Sec. 54, 54B, 54D, 54EC, 54EE, 54F, 54G, 54GA and 54GB. An assessee CAN claim exemption under more than one section simultaneously if each section's own conditions are independently satisfied [2.4.46] — e.g. claiming Sec. 54 on part of an LTCG (new residential house) and Sec. 54EC on the remainder (specified bonds).

2.4.38 Sec. 54 — Sale of Residential House Property

ItemRule
Applicable toIndividual or HUF.
ConditionsLong-term RESIDENTIAL house transferred (income taxable u/s 22); one new residential house acquired within the time limit, situated in India.
Alternate option (two houses)Where capital gain does not exceed ₹2 crore, assessee may purchase/construct TWO residential houses in India — option available only ONCE in a lifetime.
Time limit — purchase1 year BEFORE, or 2 years AFTER, the date of transfer.
Time limit — constructionWithin 3 years after the date of transfer (may start anytime, but must finish within the limit).
DeductionLower of: investment in new asset(s) (cost exceeding ₹10 crore is ignored), or the capital gain.
RevocationIf the new house is transferred within 3 years of its acquisition, the exemption is revoked and subtracted from the new asset's cost of acquisition.

Legal title need not be registered — substantial payment within the time limit suffices. Exemption applies to sale of an independent PART of a house. Cost of land is integral to the residential house. The benefit passes to a legal heir who independently satisfies the conditions.

Capital Gains Accounts Scheme (CGAS), 1988

If the new asset is not acquired by the due date of filing the return, the unutilised amount must be deposited in a CGAS account with a nationalised bank (proof filed with the return); the assessee later withdraws to acquire the new asset within the section's time limit. If unutilised, the amount becomes chargeable as capital gain (STCG/LTCG per the original transfer) in the year the time limit expires. For Sec. 54, 54B, 54D, 54G, 54GA — chargeable = unutilised amount. For Sec. 54F/54GB — chargeable = Unutilised amount × Capital gain ÷ Net sale consideration (excess over ₹10 crore ignored).

Due date of return: 31st October (audit cases) or 31st July (other cases) — sometimes 30th November. Maximum CGDS deposit for Sec. 54: lower of (capital gain) or (₹10 crore), reduced by amount already invested in the new asset by the return due date. The unutilised amount is withdrawable only after the time limit expires; the unutilised balance in a deceased assessee's CGAS cannot be taxed in the legal heir's hands [Circular No. 743 dated 6/5/1996].

ILLUSTRATION 111 — Sec. 54 exemption and its subsequent revocation

Mr. Sidhartha's residential house (taxable u/s 22), acquired 12/08/2022 for ₹2,00,000, sold 1/03/2026 for ₹25,00,000. New house acquired 31/03/2026 for ₹17,00,000 (self-occupation). Sold this new house 1/03/2027 for ₹30,00,000, and acquired yet another house 10/03/2027 for ₹35,00,000.

Computation of capital gain — A.Y. 2026-27
ParticularsAmount (₹)
Sale consideration25,00,000
Less: Cost of acquisition2,00,000
Long term capital gain23,00,000
Less: Exemption u/s 5417,00,000
Taxable Long term Capital gain6,00,000
Computation of capital gain — A.Y. 2027-28
ParticularsAmount (₹)
Sale consideration30,00,000
Less: Cost of acquisition (₹17,00,000 – earlier exemption ₹17,00,000 revoked)Nil
Short term capital gain30,00,000

Answer: the new house was sold within 3 years, so the Sec. 54 exemption is revoked (cost of acquisition reduced to Nil). No fresh Sec. 54 deduction is available against the house acquired on 10/03/2027, since this is a SHORT-term gain.

2.4.40 Sec. 54B — Transfer of Agricultural Land

ItemRule
Applicable toIndividual or HUF.
ConditionsAgricultural land (STCA or LTCA) transferred, used by the individual/parents/HUF for agriculture for ≥2 years before transfer; new agricultural land purchased (urban or rural).
Time limitWithin 2 years after the date of transfer.
DeductionLower of investment in new land, or the capital gain.
RevocationIf the new agricultural land is transferred within 3 years, exemption is revoked and subtracted from its cost.

Rural agricultural land is not a capital asset — its transfer generates no capital gain to exempt in the first place. Land held <2 years and used for agriculture from acquisition is NOT eligible. Tenancy period before purchase counts toward the 2-year test. Where an assessee sells urban agro-land and reinvests the gain into RURAL agro-land (to claim Sec. 54B) and then immediately resells that rural land within 3 years, the Sec. 54B exemption is revoked and subtracted from cost of the new asset, but the rural land itself is NOT liable to capital gain on its own resale (since it is not a capital asset). Compulsory acquisition of urban agro-land may separately qualify for the Sec. 10(37) exemption.

2.4.41 Sec. 54D — Compulsory Acquisition of Industrial Land/Building

ItemRule
Applicable toAll assessees.
ConditionsLand/building (or right therein), part of an industrial undertaking, compulsorily acquired under law; used for industrial purpose ≥2 years before transfer (tenancy period counts); new land/building purchased or constructed for shifting/re-establishing the undertaking.
Time limitWithin 3 years after receipt of compensation (or part thereof).
DeductionLower of investment in the new asset, or the capital gain.
RevocationIf the new land/building is transferred within 3 years, exemption is revoked and subtracted from its cost.

WDV of the block (3 buildings) as on 1/04/2025 was ₹7,50,000. New industrial building acquired for ₹2,00,000: Case A) 31/03/2026; Case B) 2/04/2026.

2.4.42 Sec. 54EC — Investment in Specified Bonds

ItemRule
Applicable toAll assessees.
ConditionsLong-term capital asset being LAND or BUILDING or both transferred; investment in "long-term specified assets" — 5-year redeemable bonds of NHAI, Rural Electrification Corporation Ltd., Power Finance Corporation Ltd., Indian Railway Finance Corporation Ltd., Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency (IREDA), or any other notified bond.
Time limitWithin 6 months after the date of transfer (from receipt of compensation for compulsory acquisition; from actual sale of stock, not conversion date, for stock-in-trade conversions — Circular No.791 dated 2/6/2000).
DeductionLower of investment in the new bond, or the capital gain — capped at investment of ₹50 lakh across the year of transfer and the following financial year combined.
RevocationIf the bond is transferred/converted to money, or a loan is taken against it as security, within 5 years, exemption is revoked (deemed conversion-to-money on the loan date) — treated as LTCG in the year of the new asset's transfer.
Scheme of depositNOT applicable (CGAS does not apply to Sec. 54EC).

CIT vs. Dempo Company Ltd. (2016) 387 ITR 354 (SC): Sec. 54EC benefit is available even on a depreciable asset held for more than the specified months. Investment already claimed for Sec. 80C is not further eligible for Sec. 54EC.

2.4.43 Sec. 54F — Transfer of an Asset Other Than a Residential House

ItemRule
Applicable toIndividual or HUF.
ConditionsLong-term capital asset (NOT a residential house) transferred; one new residential house acquired within the time limit, taxable u/s 22, situated in India; assessee owns NOT MORE THAN ONE other residential house (taxable u/s 22) on the date of transfer; assessee does not purchase (within 2 years) or construct (within 3 years) any OTHER residential house.
Time limit — purchase/constructionSame as Sec. 54 (1 year before/2 years after; or 3 years after, for construction).
DeductionLower of: [Investment in new asset × Capital gain ÷ Net sale consideration] (cost above ₹10 crore ignored); or the Capital gain itself.
RevocationNew house sold within 3 years of acquisition, OR another residential house purchased/constructed within the 2-year/3-year window — exemption is revoked, taxed as LTCG in the year of revocation.

Sec. 54F benefit is also available where the ORIGINAL asset transferred is a plot of land. CGAS max deposit = lower of (net consideration) or (₹10 crore), reduced by amount already invested by the return due date.

Already owns a self-occupied house; purchased ANOTHER house 17/03/2026 for ₹30,00,000 (let out). Purchased a further house 5/08/2026 for ₹15,00,000 (FMV ₹25,00,000, stamp value ₹14,00,000). Sold that house 7/04/2027 for ₹19,00,000 (stamp value ₹22,00,000, market value ₹26,00,000).

2.4.44 & 2.4.45 Sec. 54G / 54GA — Shifting Industrial Undertaking from Urban Area

2.4.47 & 2.4.48 Sec. 54H (Extension of Time) & Sec. 55A (Reference to Valuation Officer)

Sec. 54H: where the original asset is transferred by way of COMPULSORY ACQUISITION and the compensation is not received on the date of transfer, the time limit for acquiring the new asset (or depositing in CGAS) under Sec. 54, 54B, 54D, 54EC and 54F is reckoned from the date the compensation is actually RECEIVED — including, for enhanced compensation, from the date the enhanced amount is received.

CaseCondition to refer to Valuation Officer

Any other caseAO believes FMV exceeds the claimed value by MORE than 15% of the claimed value, OR by more than ₹25,000 — whichever is LESS; AND it is otherwise necessary having regard to the asset's nature.

Applies while ascertaining FMV under sec. 45(1A), 45(2), 45(4), 46(2), 55 and 2(47). "Valuation Officer" has the meaning under sec. 2(r) of the Wealth-tax Act, 1957.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: TREATING ALL SEC. 54-SERIES EXEMPTIONS ALIKE

THE TRAP: assuming every exemption uses "lower of investment or capital gain," or that the CGAS deposit scheme applies uniformly.

THE TWIST: Sec. 54EC has NO CGAS option and a hard ₹50 lakh investment ceiling; Sec. 54F's deduction is PROPORTIONATE to net sale consideration (not simply "lower of"), and is denied outright if the assessee owns more than one other residential house on the transfer date; Sec. 54B/54D/54G/54GA require actual prior USE of the asset for ≥2 years (agriculture/industry) — a freshly-acquired asset used from day one for less than 2 years fails the test even if used continuously thereafter, UNLESS an earlier tenancy period is added in.

CONCEPT

2.5 Income from Other Sources ★★★ HIGH

As per Sec. 56(1), any income which is not specifically exempted and not chargeable under any of the other four heads shall be chargeable under the head “Income from Other Sources.” This is the last and residuary head of income.

Taxpoint — a receipt is taxable under this head only if:

  • Such receipt is a taxable income; and
  • Such income does not specifically fall under any one of the other four heads (Salaries, Income from House Property, Profits and Gains of Business or Profession, or Capital Gains).

Sec. 56(2) lists incomes specifically taxable under this head — the list is not exhaustive. Apart from what Sec. 56(2) names, any other income fulfilling the two conditions above is still taxable here by virtue of Sec. 56(1).

The Sec. 56(2) List — Three Tiers of Chargeability

Tier 1 — Income absolutely chargeable under this head:

  1. Dividends [Sec. 56(2)(i)]
  2. Casual income — winnings from lotteries, etc. [Sec. 56(2)(ib)]
  3. Gift [Sec. 56(2)(x)]
  4. Income by way of interest received on compensation or enhanced compensation [Sec. 56(2)(viii)]
  5. Sum received as advance/otherwise in negotiations for transfer of a capital asset, if it is forfeited and the negotiations do not result in transfer [Sec. 56(2)(ix)]
  6. Any specified sum received by a unit holder from a business trust during the previous year, in respect of a unit held by him during that year [Sec. 56(2)(xii)]
  7. Any sum received under a life insurance policy [Sec. 56(2)(xiii)]

Tier 2 — Chargeable under this head only if NOT charged under ‘Profits and Gains of Business or Profession’:

  1. Sum received by the assessee from his employees as contribution to provident fund, etc. [Sec. 56(2)(ic)]
  2. Interest on securities [Sec. 56(2)(id)]
  3. Income from letting of machinery, plant or furniture [Sec. 56(2)(ii)]
  4. Composite Rent [Sec. 56(2)(iii)]

Tier 3 — Chargeable under this head only if NOT charged under ‘PGBP’ or under ‘Salaries’:

  1. Any sum (including bonus) received under a Keyman Insurance Policy [Sec. 56(2)(iv)] — a Keyman Insurance Policy is a life insurance policy taken by a person on the life of another who is his employee or otherwise connected with his business [Explanation to Sec. 10(10D)].
  2. Any compensation/payment due to or received in connection with the termination of employment or modification of its terms [Sec. 56(2)(xi)].

Apart from the above (by virtue of Sec. 56(1), an indicative — not exhaustive — list):

  • Income from sub-letting of a house property
  • Interest on bank deposits; interest on company deposits, loans, etc.
  • Remuneration for evaluation of answer scripts from a person other than the employer (if received from the employer, taxable as “Salaries” instead)
  • Rent from a vacant land
  • Insurance commission
  • Income from undisclosed sources
  • Income from private tuition
  • Interest on income-tax refund — Taxpoint: the income-tax refund itself is NOT an income, only the interest on it is.
  • Family pension received by family members of a deceased employee
  • Dividend received from a co-operative society
  • Directors’ sitting fee for attending Board Meetings
  • Income from the activity of owning and maintaining race-horses
  • Stipend to a trainee
  • Interest on employee’s contribution to an unrecognized provident fund, at the time of payment of the lump sum

2.5.1 Basis of Chargeability [Sec. 145]

Income under this head is chargeable on ‘accrual’ or ‘cash’ basis depending on the method of accounting regularly followed by the assessee (mercantile or cash system).

Exception: Dividend is charged as per the schedule laid down in Sec. 8 — NOT as per the assessee’s accounting method (see 2.5.13 below).

2.5.2 Casual Income — Winnings from Lotteries, Crossword Puzzles, etc. [Sec. 56(2)(ib)]

Winnings from the following are taxable under this head:

  1. Lotteries
  2. Crossword puzzles
  3. Races, including horse races
  4. Gambling and betting of any nature or form
  5. Online gaming
  6. Card games, game shows, or entertainment programmes on television/electronic mode, and any other game of any sort

Lottery includes winnings from prizes awarded by draw of lots or by chance or in any other manner, under any scheme/arrangement by whatever name called. Card game/other game of any sort includes any game show or TV/electronic entertainment programme where people compete to win prizes, or any similar game.

Tax Rate [Sec. 115BB]: flat 30% + applicable surcharge + HEC @ 4%

Exemption/deduction [Sec. 58(4)]: such income is FULLY taxable — no deduction is allowed against it, from any source.

Grossing-up: Lottery Income Received = Gross Lottery Income − TDS @ 30% on Gross Lottery Income = 70% of Gross Lottery Income

So: Gross Lottery Income = Lottery Income Received ÷ 70%. TDS under Sec. 194B/194BB is not deducted (hence no grossing-up needed) if: (a) the winning from lottery/horse race does not exceed ₹10,000; or (b) it is winning from gambling, betting, online gaming, or racing OTHER than horse racing (e.g. camel races).

Notes:

  • A jockey’s income from his profession is NOT treated as winning from horse races.
  • Winning from a motor car rally is a return for skill and effort — not casual income, taxable as normal income.
  • Winning from a lottery held as stock-in-trade (an agent/trader’s unsold tickets) is incidental to business — taxed as PGBP, not casual income.
  • No deduction can be claimed even if expenditure was incurred wholly and exclusively for earning such income.
  • Deductions u/s 80C to 80U are NOT available against such income.
  • Benefit of the unexhausted basic exemption limit is NOT available against such income.
  • Winnings from any online game are NOT taxed under Sec. 56(2)(ib)/115BB — they fall under the separate Sec. 115BBJ (2.5.13 below).
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: CASUAL INCOME “FEELS DEDUCTIBLE” BUT NEVER IS

THE TRAP: students assume that money genuinely spent buying lottery tickets, or the basic exemption slab, or Chapter VI-A deductions (80C–80U) can shave down a casual-income figure before the 30% rate is applied.

THE TWIST: Sec. 58(4) blocks EVERY deduction against casual income — no expenditure, no 80C–80U, and no unexhausted basic exemption limit. The entire gross amount is taxed flat @ 30% + surcharge + HEC @ 4% under Sec. 115BB, full stop. Also watch the ₹10,000 TDS-trigger threshold (Sec. 194B/194BB) — below it, no TDS is deducted, so no grossing-up is needed on that receipt.

2.5.3 & 2.5.4 Letting of Machinery/Plant/Furniture and Composite Rent [Sec. 56(2)(ii) & (iii)]

Income from letting machinery, plant or furniture on hire is charged under this head, if not chargeable as PGBP [Sec. 56(2)(ii)]. Generally, letting of a building alone is taxable as Income from House Property; but where such letting is inseparable from letting of machinery, plant or furniture (“Composite Rent”), the whole receipt is charged under this head if not taxed as PGBP [Sec. 56(2)(iii)].

Nature of LettingHead of Income
Building let out alone, separablyIncome from House Property
Building let out inseparably WITH machinery/plant/furniture (composite rent), not as part of a businessIncome from Other Sources [Sec. 56(2)(iii)]
Any asset let out as part of a business activity / as a commercial assetProfits & Gains of Business or Profession
Business assets leased out during a TEMPORARY discontinuance of business (no intention to close)Still PGBP
Mere separate quotation of rent for the building vs. the plant/furniture does NOT by itself make the letting “separable” — separability requires that the property is actually capable of being let separately.

2.5.5 Deductions Allowed Against Income u/s 56(2)(ii) & 56(2)(iii) [Sec. 57(ii) & (iii)]

Deductible from letting/composite-rent income under this head:

1. Current repairs [as per Sec. 30(a)(ii) or 31(i)]  ·  2. Insurance premium on machinery/plant/furniture/building [Sec. 30(c) or 31(ii)]  ·  3. Depreciation and unabsorbed depreciation [Sec. 32]  ·  4. Any other revenue expenditure incurred during the previous year, wholly and exclusively for earning such income.

2.5.6 Family Pension

Family pension means a regular monthly amount payable by the employer to a person belonging to the family of a deceased employee (e.g. the widow or legal heirs).

It is taxable under “Income from Other Sources” after allowing a standard deduction.

Standard Deduction [Sec. 57(iia)] = Minimum of: (i) 1/3rd of the family pension; or (ii) ₹15,000 — however ₹25,000 if the assessee is under the DEFAULT tax regime.

Relief u/s 89 is available on arrears of family pension received by the family member of a deceased employee, exactly as for arrears/advance of salary.

Notes:

  • A lump-sum payment made gratuitously or by way of compensation to the widow/legal heirs of an employee who dies while still in service is non-taxable.
  • An ex-gratia payment to the widow/legal heir of an employee who dies in active service is not taxable, provided it is paid by the Central Government, a State Government, a local authority, the Government, or a public sector undertaking.

ILLUSTRATION 118 — Family Pension, Standard Deduction Under Both Regimes

Given: Sunder died on 31-07-2025 while in Central Government service. His widow, Mrs. Sunder, is paid family pension of ₹10,000 p.m. plus dearness allowance @ 40% thereof. Compute her taxable income for A.Y. 2026-27 (assume no other income).

Computation of Gross Total Income of Mrs. Sunder for A.Y. 2026-27
ParticularsOld Regime (₹)Default Regime (₹)
Family pension [(₹10,000 + ₹4,000) × 8 months, 01-08-2025 to 31-03-2026]1,12,0001,12,000
Less: Standard deduction — minimum of (a) 1/3rd of pension = ₹37,333; or (b) statutory limit15,00025,000
Total Income97,00087,000
Tax on aboveNilNil

Answer: Total income ₹97,000 (Old Regime) / ₹87,000 (Default Regime); tax Nil under both.

2.5.7 Gift [Sec. 56(2)(x)] ★★★ HIGH

Sec. 56(2)(x) taxes five categories of receipt — cash, immovable property, and movable property, each received either without consideration or for inadequate consideration:

Cat.Nature of ReceiptTrigger ThresholdAmount Treated as Income
AAny sum of money (cash, cheque, draft, etc.) received without considerationAggregate value during the P.Y. exceeds ₹50,000Whole aggregate value of the sum(s) received
BAny immovable property (capital asset) received without considerationStamp duty value (SDV) exceeds ₹50,000SDV of the property
CAny immovable property (capital asset) received for considerationSDV exceeds consideration by more than the HIGHER of ₹50,000 or 10% of considerationSDV − consideration paid
DAny movable property (capital asset) received without considerationAggregate fair market value (FMV) during the P.Y. exceeds ₹50,000Whole aggregate FMV of property received
EAny movable property (capital asset) received for considerationAggregate FMV exceeds consideration paid by more than ₹50,000Aggregate FMV − consideration paid
Categories B & C (immovable property) are tested PER INCIDENCE — each gift/purchase judged separately. Categories A, D & E (cash and movable property) are tested by AGGREGATING all such receipts of that category received during the whole previous year. The ₹50,000 limit also applies separately, per category (e.g. ₹35,000 cash + ₹36,000 gift-in-kind in the same year attracts no tax at all).

“Relative” for an individual means: spouse; brother or sister; brother or sister of the spouse; brother or sister of either parent; any lineal ascendant or descendant (of the individual or of the spouse); and the spouse of any person just listed. For an HUF: any member thereof.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: “RELATIVE” IS NARROWER THAN IT SOUNDS

THE TRAP: students assume any family friend, cousin, or extended relation counts as a “relative” and treat gifts from them as automatically exempt. (The source’s own True/False set flags exactly this: a cash gift of ₹1,00,000 from an uncle’s son is NOT exempt — that relationship is outside the defined list.)

THE TWIST: the Sec. 56(2)(x) “relative” list is a closed, specific list (spouse; siblings of self/spouse; siblings of either parent; lineal ascendants/descendants of self or spouse; and their spouses). Anyone outside this exact list — a friend, a cousin, an uncle’s son — is a stranger for this section, however close the relationship feels socially.

ILLUSTRATION — Cash Gifts and the Aggregation Rule

Mr. Anand receives a cash gift of ₹1,00,000 from his friend Mr. Lathi on 10-10-2025. Mr. Ajay receives cash gifts of ₹25,000 each from 3 friends (one a non-resident) on 12-11-2025.

Answer: Anand — ₹1,00,000 taxable (single sum already exceeds ₹50,000). Ajay — entire ₹75,000 taxable, since the AGGREGATE of cash gifts in the year exceeds ₹50,000, even though no single gift did, and even though one donor is a non-resident (the donor’s residential status is irrelevant).

ILLUSTRATION — Gift of Immovable Property: Cost of Acquisition Under Sec. 49(4)

Mr. Pati receives a piece of land (SDV ₹75,000) from friend Mr. Raja without consideration on 10-01-2026; Raja had acquired it in 2001-02 for ₹10,000. SDV exceeds ₹50,000, so ₹75,000 is taxable to Pati u/s 56(2)(x) for A.Y. 2026-27. By Sec. 49(4), Pati’s cost of acquisition becomes ₹75,000 (the value already taxed) — NOT Raja’s original ₹10,000, since the normal “previous owner’s cost” rule of Sec. 49(1) does not extend to assets covered u/s 49(4). Pati sells the land on 03-06-2027 for ₹2,00,000 (SDV also ₹2,00,000).

Computation of Capital Gain in the hands of Mr. Pati for A.Y. 2028-29
Particulars₹
Sale Consideration2,00,000
Less: Expenses on transferNil
Less: Cost of acquisition75,000
Short-Term Capital Gain1,25,000

Answer: Short-term, because the holding period runs AFRESH from the date of gift — it does NOT carry forward Raja’s 2001-02 acquisition. Explanation 1 to Sec. 2(42A) lets a donee inherit the previous owner’s holding period only for assets covered u/s 49(1); an asset taxed u/s 56(2)(x) falls u/s 49(4) instead, so that carry-forward is lost. Mr. Raja himself pays no tax — a gift is not a “transfer” under Sec. 47.

ILLUSTRATION — Immovable Property Gifts Tested Per Incidence, Not Aggregated

Dipak receives land at Napasar (SDV ₹46,000) as a gift from Vikash on 10-07-2025 (Vikash acquired it in 2001 for ₹5,000), and land at Bikaner (SDV ₹30,000) without consideration from Anil on 01-11-2025 (Anil acquired it in 2024-25 for ₹10,000). Neither SDV individually exceeds ₹50,000, so Sec. 56(2)(x) is NOT triggered for either — immovable-property gifts are never aggregated across incidences. Because neither was taxed u/s 56(2)(x), Dipak inherits both the previous owner’s cost and holding period under the normal Sec. 49(1) rule. On 31-03-2026 Dipak sells Napasar to Kedar for ₹30,000 (SDV ₹50,000) and Bikaner to Nath for ₹90,000 (SDV ₹85,000).

Computation of Capital Gain in the hands of Mr. Dipak
ParticularsNapasar (₹)Bikaner (₹)
Sale Consideration (higher of actual consideration and SDV — Sec. 50C)50,00090,000
Less: Expenses on transferNilNil
Less: Cost of acquisition (previous owner’s cost)5,00010,000
Long-Term Capital Gain45,000—
Short-Term Capital Gain—80,000

Answer: Napasar is Long-Term (Vikash’s 2001 holding carries forward); Bikaner is Short-Term (Anil only acquired it in F.Y. 2024-25, so even with the carried-forward period, it stays short-term). Vikash and Anil (the donors) pay no tax on the gifts themselves.

The difference (₹45,000) does not exceed ₹50,000, so Sec. 56(2)(x) does NOT apply to Tipu; his cost of acquisition = the actual ₹30,000 paid. Tipu sells on 10-04-2027 for ₹1,75,000 (SDV ₹1,60,000).

The company sells on 10-04-2027 for ₹10,75,000 (SDV ₹12,50,000).

Answer: In a concessional PURCHASE (unlike an outright gift), the buyer’s holding period always runs afresh from the purchase date — never from the seller’s original acquisition — regardless of whether Sec. 56(2)(x) was triggered.

ILLUSTRATION — The “Higher of ₹50,000 or 10%” Safe-Harbour

Sonam buys land from Shweta (SDV ₹12,54,000) for ₹12,00,000 on 10-10-2025. The difference (₹54,000) exceeds ₹50,000 in absolute terms, BUT does not exceed 10% of consideration (10% of ₹12,00,000 = ₹1,20,000) — so Sec. 56(2)(x) is NOT attracted; Sonam’s cost of acquisition = ₹12,00,000 actually paid.

Separately, Priya buys land from Monica (SDV ₹4,45,000) for ₹4,00,000. The difference (₹45,000) does not exceed ₹50,000, so nothing is taxable to Priya u/s 56(2)(x). But on the SELLER’s side, Sec. 50C independently deems the ₹4,45,000 SDV as Monica’s full value of consideration for capital gains, because it exceeds 110% of the actual consideration (110% of ₹4,00,000 = ₹4,40,000, which is less than the ₹4,45,000 SDV).

Answer: Sec. 50C (seller-side capital gains) applies a 110%-of-consideration safe-harbour with no minimum-rupee floor; Sec. 56(2)(x) (buyer-side income) applies the higher-of-₹50,000-or-10% test. The two provisions can give different answers on the very same transaction.

ILLUSTRATION — Movable Property Gift: Aggregated for the Whole Year

Narendra receives a gold necklace (FMV ₹1,85,000) from Vivek without consideration on 10-01-2026 — FMV exceeds ₹50,000, so the entire ₹1,85,000 is taxable for A.Y. 2026-27; cost of acquisition = ₹1,85,000; holding period starts fresh from 10-01-2026.

Mohan receives shares (FMV ₹36,000, not via ESOP) from friend Uttam on 10-10-2025, and a gold chain (FMV ₹30,000) from another friend on 01-11-2025. Neither gift alone crosses ₹50,000.

Answer: Unlike immovable property, movable-property gifts are AGGREGATED across the whole previous year, not tested per incidence. Aggregate FMV of ₹66,000 exceeds ₹50,000, so the ENTIRE ₹66,000 is taxable to Mohan for A.Y. 2026-27. Cost of acquisition: ₹36,000 (shares) + ₹30,000 (chain); each asset’s holding period runs from its own gift date. Neither Vivek nor Mohan’s friends pay any tax — gift is not a “transfer” for the donor.

ILLUSTRATION — Movable Property at Concessional Value

Kamal buys jewellery (FMV ₹46,000) from Kishore for ₹30,000 on 10-10-2025 — difference ₹16,000 does not exceed ₹50,000, so nothing is taxable to Kamal; his cost of acquisition = ₹30,000 (Sec. 50C does not apply to movable property, so no “deemed higher value” adjustment for the seller either).

Capital Gain — Kishore (seller), jewellery acquired 10-04-2025 for ₹25,000
Particulars₹
Sale Consideration30,000
Less: Cost of acquisition25,000
Short-Term Capital Gain5,000

Janak buys jewellery (FMV ₹66,000) for ₹30,000, and separately a silver utensil (FMV ₹1,00,000) for ₹75,000. Aggregate FMV ₹1,66,000 less aggregate consideration ₹1,05,000 = difference ₹61,000, which exceeds ₹50,000.

Answer: ₹61,000 is taxable to Janak as Income from Other Sources; cost of acquisition of both assets = the FMV used in this computation. The concessional-value test for movable property, like the outright-gift test, is applied on an AGGREGATE basis for the year — not per incidence as for immovable property.

Exceptions — Sec. 56(2)(x) does NOT apply to any sum of money or property received:

  1. From any relative (as defined above).
  2. On the occasion of the marriage of the individual (whether from a relative or an outsider).
  3. Under a will or by way of inheritance.
  4. In contemplation of death of the payer or donor.
  5. From a local authority.
  6. By an individual, from any person, towards actual medical-treatment expenditure for himself/a family member for a COVID-19-related illness, subject to prescribed documentation (Notification No. 91/2022 dated 05-08-2022) and reporting to the Income-tax Department within 9 months of the financial year-end.
  7. By a family member of a deceased person whose death was COVID-19-related: without limit, from the deceased’s employer; up to an aggregate of ₹10 lakh, from any other person(s) — subject to conditions (payment within 12 months of death; death within 6 months of testing positive; prescribed medical/death documentation retained; reported within 9 months of the financial year-end). “Family” here means the spouse and children of the individual, plus parents/brothers/sisters wholly or mainly dependent on him.
  8. From/by any fund, foundation, university, other educational institution, hospital, other medical institution, or any trust/institution referred to u/s 10(23C) — provided not received by a person covered u/s 13(3).
  9. From/by any trust or institution registered u/s 12AA/12AB — provided not received by a person covered u/s 13(3).
  10. From an individual, by a trust created/established solely for the benefit of a relative of that individual.
  11. By way of distribution on total/partial partition of an HUF [Sec. 47(i)].
  12. By way of amalgamation/demerger transactions covered under the relevant sub-clauses of Sec. 47.
  13. From such class of persons and subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

Other Points:

  • FMV of a property other than immovable property means the value determined per the prescribed method.
  • “Property” (including virtual digital assets) covers: immovable property (land/building); shares & securities; archaeological collections; paintings; jewellery; drawings; sculptures; any work of art; bullion. It does NOT include furniture, clothes, etc. (unless they fall within “jewellery”). Assets received without consideration AS STOCK-IN-TRADE fall outside this section.
  • As per Sec. 2(47A), virtual digital asset covers any cryptographically-generated information/code/token representing value (not Indian or foreign currency), any non-fungible token or similar token, any Government-specified digital asset, and any crypto-asset based on a distributed ledger — the Central Government may exclude specific assets from this definition.
  • Stamp duty value means the value adopted/assessed/assessable by a Central or State Government authority for stamp duty purposes on an immovable property.

2.5.8 Interest on Compensation or Enhanced Compensation [Sec. 56(2)(viii)]

Interest received by an assessee on compensation or enhanced compensation is deemed to be the income of the YEAR IN WHICH IT IS RECEIVED (not the year to which it relates).

Taxable under this head after a standard deduction of 50% of such income.

Example: during P.Y. 2025-26, Mr. X receives ₹65,000 (of which ₹45,000 relates to P.Y. 2024-25) as interest on delayed compensation. The full ₹65,000 is taxed in P.Y. 2025-26 (irrespective of the year it pertains to); after the 50% standard deduction, ₹32,500 is the taxable income of P.Y. 2025-26.

2.5.9 Employee’s Contribution Towards Staff Welfare Fund or Scheme [Sec. 56(2)(ic)]

Any amount received/deducted by an employer from an employee towards Provident Fund, Superannuation Fund, a fund under the Employee’s State Insurance Act 1948, or any other employee-welfare fund is treated as income of the EMPLOYER under this head, if not taxable as PGBP. If the employer credits the sum to the employee’s account in the relevant fund on or before the due date under the relevant Act, an equal deduction is then available.

SituationTreatment
Employee’s contribution taken AND deposited within timeNo treatment (deduction offsets the receipt)
Employee’s contribution taken but NOT deposited within timeTaxable as Income from Other Sources, if not taxable as business income

2.5.10 Interest on Securities [Sec. 56(2)(id)]

As per Sec. 2(28B), “interest on securities” means interest on any Central/State Government security, and interest on debentures/other securities issued by a local authority, a company, or a corporation established by a Central, State or Provincial Act.

CaseTreatment
Securities held as stock-in-tradeInterest charged as PGBP
Securities held otherwise than as stock-in-tradeInterest charged as Income from Other Sources

Chargeability: cash or due basis per the assessee’s regular accounting method; where no method is followed, always on due basis.

Due date of interest: interest on securities does NOT accrue day-to-day — it accrues on the due date prescribed by the issuing authority, and the ENTIRE interest is charged to whoever holds the security on that date (irrespective of when they acquired it). Example: Mr. X acquires a debenture of A Ltd. on 07-09-2025; the due date of interest is 31st March every year — the whole year’s interest is taxable in Mr. X’s hands. Taxpoint: if the assessee dies before the due date, the whole year’s income is taxed in the hands of whoever actually receives it.

Grossing-up (interest given net of TDS): Gross income from interest = Interest received × 100 ÷ (100 − TDS rate, i.e. 10%)

TDS is required to be deducted @ 10% on interest on securities (certain cases are exempted from TDS — refer to the TDS chapter). Deductible expenditure under Sec. 57(i) & (iii): collection expenditure, interest on loan, and any other expenditure — but nothing hit by Sec. 58 can be deducted.

Avoidance of Tax by Transactions in Securities [Sec. 94]:

  • Bond-washing transactions [Sec. 94(1)]: because interest accrues wholly to whoever holds the security on the due date, an assessee could dodge tax by transferring securities to a low-income relative/friend just before the due date and reacquiring them after the interest is collected. Sec. 94(1) blocks this — if an assessee transfers securities before the interest due date and REACQUIRES the same securities, the interest received by the transferee is deemed the income of the TRANSFEROR. Example: Mr. X transfers 1,000 10% debentures (due date 31st March) to his brother Mr. Y on 27-03-2026 and repurchases them on 05-04-2026 — the interest for P.Y. 2025-26, though received by Y, is taxed in X’s hands.
  • Transactions resulting in less/no income [Sec. 94(2)]: where a person has had beneficial interest in securities at any time during the year, and any transaction relating to those securities results in no income (or less income than the day-to-day income from the securities) being received by him, the securities’ income for that year is deemed to be his income.
  • Exceptions [Sec. 94(3)]: Sec. 94(1) & (2) do not apply if the owner satisfies the Assessing Officer that (i) there was no tax avoidance, or it was exceptional and not systematic; and (ii) there was no Sec. 94 avoidance in the 3 years preceding the previous year.
  • The Assessing Officer may require any person, by written notice, to furnish (within not less than 28 days) particulars of securities he owned or had beneficial interest in during a specified period [Sec. 94(6)].

2.5.11 Sum Received Under a Life Insurance Policy [Sec. 56(2)(xiii)]

Any sum (including bonus) received during a previous year under a life insurance policy is taxable under this head if: (a) it is NOT exempt u/s 10(10D); (b) it is NOT received under a unit-linked insurance policy (ULIP); and (c) it is NOT received under a Keyman insurance policy.

Computation of income = Sum received during the previous year − aggregate premium paid over the policy’s term (not already claimed as a deduction under any other provision).

Sec. 10(10D) exemption conditions — sum received on death is always exempt; on maturity, exemption depends on the premium-to-sum-assured ratio for the year the policy was issued:

Life Insurance Policy issued duringInsured is disabled/specified disease (Sec. 80U/80DDB)Insured is any other person
Up to 31-03-2003No restrictionNo restriction
01-04-2003 to 31-03-201220% of capital sum assured20% of capital sum assured
P.Y. 2012-1310%10%
01-04-2013 to 31-03-202315%10%
On or after 01-04-202315%10%
Additional condition: aggregate premium must not exceed ₹5,00,000 in any previous year during the policy’s term. If any condition fails, the sum is taxable as Income from Other Sources.
ULIP issued duringInsured is disabled/specified disease (Sec. 80U)Insured is any other person
01-04-2003 to 31-03-201220%20%
P.Y. 2012-1310%10%
01-04-2013 to 31-01-202115%10%
On or after 01-02-202115%10%
Additional condition: aggregate premium must not exceed ₹2,50,000 in any previous year during the term. If conditions fail, a ULIP is taxable u/s 45(1B) as CAPITAL GAINS, not as Income from Other Sources — where it is a long-term capital asset, tax is computed u/s 112A WITHOUT indexation benefit (Circular No. 02 of 2022 dated 19-01-2022).

Keyman Insurance Policy: any sum received, in any circumstances, is taxable as salary, business income, or Income from Other Sources, as the case may be — Sec. 10(10D) exemption never applies to a Keyman policy.

Sum referred to in Sec. 80DD(3): where a dependent disabled person, for whom an individual/HUF member had paid amounts into an LIC/insurer scheme, predeceases that individual/member, the amount paid/deposited is deemed to be the income of the previous year in which it is received — and it is NOT exempt u/s 10(10D).

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: PENSION vs. FAMILY PENSION

THE TRAP: treating every kind of pension receipt as taxable the same way.

THE TWIST: a pension received by the EMPLOYEE HIMSELF (commuted or uncommuted) stays taxable as “Salaries.” Only FAMILY PENSION — paid to a deceased employee’s family after his death — falls under Income from Other Sources, with its own standard deduction under Sec. 57(iia) (minimum of 1/3rd of the pension or the statutory rupee ceiling) — a completely different mechanism from Sec. 16’s standard deduction on Salary.

2.5.13 Dividend [Sec. 2(22)]

Dividend generally means the amount received by a shareholder (cash or kind) in proportion to his shareholding, out of past/present, taxable/exempt, or revenue/capital income of the company. The Income-tax Act gives an INCLUSIVE definition — the following, to the extent of the company’s accumulated profits, are DEEMED dividends:

  1. Release of assets on distribution of accumulated profits (capitalized or not) [Sec. 2(22)(a)]. Bonus shares to equity shareholders are NOT dividend (no release of assets); the market value (not book value) of a non-cash asset released is what counts; not applicable on amalgamation.
  2. Distribution of debentures/deposit certificates to shareholders, or bonus shares to preference shareholders, to the extent of accumulated profits [Sec. 2(22)(b)]. Treated as dividend even without any release of assets; bonus shares to EQUITY shareholders remain outside this clause.
  3. Distribution on liquidation, to the extent of accumulated profits immediately before liquidation [Sec. 2(22)(c)]. Distribution to preference shareholders (issued for full cash consideration) is excluded; profits earned AFTER liquidation are excluded; not applicable on amalgamation.
  4. Distribution on reduction of capital, to the extent of accumulated profits [Sec. 2(22)(d)]. Distribution in respect of preference shares is excluded.
  5. Loan or advance by a closely-held company, out of accumulated profits (excluding capitalized profit), to: (i) an equity shareholder holding ≥10% voting power (a “specified shareholder”); (ii) a concern in which such shareholder has a “substantial interest” (≥20% share of income/voting power) as member/partner; or (iii) any person for the benefit of such shareholder [Sec. 2(22)(e)]. Deemed dividend even if the loan is later repaid; genuine trade advances (commercial transactions) are NOT “advance” for this clause [CBDT Circular No. 19/2017]; excluded if the loan is in the ordinary course of a money-lending business, or set off against a forthcoming dividend declaration, or between certain listed group finance entities.
  6. Buy-back of shares — any payment by a company purchasing its own shares [Sec. 2(22)(f)]. Example: XYZ Ltd. buys back 100 shares from Mr. A at ₹500 (purchase price ₹100/share) — Taxable Dividend = ₹50,000 (100 × 500); NO deduction for the cost of acquisition (₹100/share); the cost (₹10,000) is instead treated as a Capital Loss.
CaseAccumulated profit is measured
Company not in liquidationUp to the date of distribution/payment
Company in liquidationUp to the date of liquidation
Dividend under Sec. 2(22)(e)Up to the date of grant of the loan/advance
On amalgamation, the amalgamated company’s accumulated profits/loss are increased by the amalgamating company’s accumulated profits (capitalized or not) as on the date of amalgamation.

Basis of Charge [Sec. 8] — dividend is NOT taxed on the assessee’s accounting method; it follows a fixed schedule:

CaseYear of Taxability
Normal dividendYear in which declared by the company
Interim dividendYear in which unconditionally made available to the shareholder
Deemed dividendYear in which distributed or paid by the company

Place of accrual [Sec. 9(1)(iv)]: dividend is deemed to accrue/arise in India if declared by an Indian company.

Deduction available from dividend income [Sec. 57]: ONLY interest expense, capped at 20% of the dividend income (or income from units of a Mutual Fund) included in total income for the year — no other expenditure (collection charges, bank charges, etc.) is deductible.

This deduction is NOT available against dividend taxable under Sec. 2(22)(f) (buy-back of shares).

ILLUSTRATION — Dividend Income, Sec. 57 Interest-Deduction Cap

Given: During 2025-26, Mr. Ratnam received dividends from Sun Pharma Ltd. (Indian company) ₹11,00,000. He had invested in the shares using a loan and paid interest of ₹3,00,000 during the year. He also incurred collection charges of ₹50,000.

Computation of Taxable Dividend Income of Mr. Ratnam for A.Y. 2026-27
Particulars₹
Dividend11,00,000
Less: Interest expenditure, being lower of (Actual ₹3,00,000; 20% of dividend ₹2,20,000)2,20,000
Less: Collection chargesNil
Taxable Dividend8,80,000

Answer: ₹8,80,000. Apart from interest (capped at 20% of dividend), NO other expenditure — including collection charges — is allowed against dividend income.

Tax on Winnings from Online Games [Sec. 115BBJ]

AspectRule
Meaning of “online game”A game offered on the internet, accessible by a user through a computer resource including any telecommunication device
Tax rate30% + surcharge (if applicable) + HEC @ 4%
Expenditure/allowanceNone can be allowed against such income
Deduction under Chapter VI-ANot available
Benefit of unexhausted basic exemption limitNot available

Taxpoint: “Internet” means the combination of computer facilities, electromagnetic transmission media, related equipment and software comprising the interconnected worldwide network of computer networks transmitting information via a controlling protocol.

2.5.14 Specific Disallowances [Sec. 58]

The following are NEVER deductible from any income under this head:

  1. Any personal expenses of the assessee [Sec. 58(1)(a)(i)]
  2. Interest payable outside India on which tax has not been deducted at source [Sec. 58(1)(a)(ii)]
  3. Salary payable outside India on which tax has not been deducted at source [Sec. 58(1)(a)(iii)]
  4. 30% of any payment to a resident on which TDS provisions apply but TDS was not deducted [referred u/s 40(a)(ia)]
  5. Any amount paid as Wealth tax or Income tax [Sec. 58(1A)] — Taxpoint: interest paid on money borrowed to meet a tax liability is likewise NOT deductible.
  6. Amounts specified u/s 40A — payment to a relative in excess of requirement; payment exceeding ₹10,000 otherwise than by account-payee cheque/draft/specified electronic mode [Sec. 58(2)]
  7. Any expenditure against income by way of winnings from lotteries, crossword puzzles, races (including horse races), card games, other games of any sort, or gambling/betting of any form [Sec. 58(4)] — except this restriction does NOT apply to an assessee who owns and maintains race-horses, in respect of income from that activity.

2.5.15 Deemed Profits [Sec. 59]

Where (a) an allowance or deduction was allowed in an earlier year for a loss, expenditure, or trading liability incurred by the assessee, and (b) subsequently any amount is obtained — whether in cash or otherwise — as revocation of that loss/expenditure or remission of that liability, during any previous year, then such amount received or remitted is charged to tax. This holds good even in the case of succession or inheritance.

ILLUSTRATION 120 — Cash-Basis Assessee, Composite Letting

Given: Shri Anil (cash-basis accounting) for P.Y. 2025-26: interest on listed debentures of A Ltd. received ₹18,000 (net of TDS); letting of building & machinery @ ₹15,000 p.m. under a composite lease, received ₹1,50,000; paid collection charges ₹1,000, repairs ₹5,000, capital repairs ₹16,000, interest outside India (without TDS) ₹8,000; received gift from father ₹6,000; received ground rent ₹600 (relating to F.Y. 2024-25).   • Fill in the blank: Interest on enhanced compensation received by Mr. A, a resident individual, is ₹4,00,000, of which 75% pertains to an earlier financial year. The amount to be included in total income under “Income from Other Sources” is ₹_____. Answer: ₹2,00,000 — the entire ₹4,00,000 is taxed in the year of receipt, then reduced by the flat 50% standard deduction.
  • Fill in the blank: Total tax payable on a lottery income of ₹3,00,000 as per Sec. 115BB is _____. Answer: ₹90,000 + applicable surcharge and cess (flat 30% of ₹3,00,000).
  • True/False: Cash gift of ₹1,00,000 from uncle’s son is not taxable. Answer: False — an uncle’s son is outside the defined “relative” list.
  • True/False: Expenses of purchasing lottery tickets are deducted out of winning from lottery under Income from Other Sources. Answer: False — Sec. 58(4) blocks every deduction against casual income.
20 EXAM FACTS — HEADS OF INCOME (Module 2)

① Salaries (Sec. 15–17) taxes basic pay, allowances, perquisites and profits in lieu of salary — HRA exemption and perquisite valuation are its two most computation-heavy zones.

② A “specified employee” test, and whether the employer is Government or private, both change how a perquisite is valued.

③ Standard deduction and profession tax paid are the only two deductions Sec. 16 allows from Gross Salary to reach Taxable Salary.

④ House Property income runs GAV → less municipal tax paid → NAV → less Sec. 24 deductions (Sec. 22–24); a qualifying self-occupied property is deemed to have Nil annual value.

⑤ Interest on a housing loan splits into pre-construction-period interest (deferred, then spread over instalments) and the current year’s interest.

⑥ PGBP runs on the Sec. 28–44 scheme — Sec. 28 charges the income, Sec. 30–37 allow deductions, Sec. 40/40A/43B disallow or defer specific items.

⑦ Depreciation under Sec. 32 is computed on the Written Down Value of a “block of assets,” not asset-by-asset.

⑧ Presumptive-taxation schemes let eligible small businesses/professionals declare income at a prescribed percentage of turnover/receipts, without maintaining full books.

⑨ A “capital asset” (Sec. 2(14)) transferred is charged under Sec. 45 in the year of transfer; gains split into Short-Term and Long-Term by the period of holding.

⑩ Only Long-Term Capital Gains get the indexation benefit — Short-Term Capital Gains never do.

⑪ Exemption sections such as Sec. 54 relieve capital gains tax when sale proceeds/gains are reinvested in a specified manner, subject to conditions and a lock-in.

⑫ Income from Other Sources (Sec. 56(1)) is the residuary head — a receipt lands here only if it is taxable income AND does not fall under any of the other four heads.

⑬ Casual income (lottery, crossword, cards, gambling/betting, online gaming) is taxed flat @ 30% + surcharge + HEC @ 4% under Sec. 115BB — no deduction whatsoever, not even Sec. 80C–80U or the unexhausted basic exemption limit [Sec. 58(4)].

⑭ TDS on lottery/horse-race winnings is skipped only if the amount does not exceed ₹10,000; when only the net receipt is given, gross it up as Lottery Income Received = 70% of Gross Lottery Income.

⑮ Sec. 56(2)(x): immovable-property gifts are tested PER INCIDENCE against ₹50,000 stamp duty value; cash and movable-property gifts are AGGREGATED across the whole previous year against the same ₹50,000.

⑯ A concessional purchase of immovable property is taxable to the buyer only if stamp duty value exceeds consideration by more than the higher of ₹50,000 or 10% of consideration.

⑰ Gifts from a defined “relative,” on the individual’s own marriage, under a will/inheritance, in contemplation of death, or from a local authority are exempt from Sec. 56(2)(x) regardless of amount.

⑱ Family pension is taxed under this head after a standard deduction u/s 57(iia) of the lower of 1/3rd of the pension or a statutory rupee ceiling — a pension received by the employee himself, in contrast, stays taxable as Salary.

⑲ Interest on compensation/enhanced compensation is taxed in the year of RECEIPT, never accrual, after a flat 50% standard deduction [Sec. 56(2)(viii) with Sec. 57(iv)].

⑳ Deduction from dividend income is restricted to interest expense alone, capped at 20% of the dividend income for the year [Sec. 57] — and no deduction at all survives against dividend taxed under the buy-back clause, Sec. 2(22)(f).

Total Income and Tax
Liability of Individuals & HUF

This module moves from computing income under the five heads to computing the assessee's final tax liability — starting with the exceptions under which one person is taxed on another's income (clubbing, Sec. 60–65) and the machinery for adjusting losses against income (set-off and carry forward, Sec. 70–80), and continuing through deductions/rebate/relief, taxation of Individuals and HUF, advance tax, TDS/TCS, filing of return, PAN and self-assessment.

MUST NOT SKIP: intra-head set-off under Sec. 70 must be completed in full before inter-head set-off under Sec. 71 is attempted — get this sequence wrong and every subsequent set-off/carry-forward figure in the answer is wrong.

Module Learning Objectives

After studying this module, the students will be able to – identify the applicability of the provisions relating to clubbing of income; understand the relationship between various sources of income and heads of income; appreciate the provision relating to carry forward of losses; and appreciate the provisions relating to various compliances.

Glossary — Module 3, in Plain Words

The technical terms used across 3.1–3.2, explained simply.

Clubbing of Income [Sec. 60–65]Exceptions to the rule that a person is taxed only on his own income — certain income of another person (spouse, minor child, a transferee) is added into the assessee's own total income, to stop tax avoidance by shifting income or income-generating assets to a lower-taxed family member.
Revocable Transfer [Sec. 61–63]A transfer of an asset where the transferor keeps (or can regain) a right to re-assume power over the asset or its income, directly or indirectly — income from such an asset is clubbed in the transferor's hands even if the power to revoke is never actually used.
Substantial InterestBeneficially holding not less than 20% of a company's equity shares (or, in another concern, being entitled to not less than 20% of its profits) at any time during the previous year — alone or together with relatives.
Inadequate ConsiderationConsideration that is less than adequate, measured strictly in money — natural love and affection or a spiritual/religious benefit is never "adequate consideration" for clubbing purposes.
Accretion / Income on IncomeIncome earned on the accumulated income of a transferred asset (e.g. interest on income already clubbed once) — not clubbed further; it is taxable in the transferee's own hands.
Set-off [Sec. 70–71]Adjusting a loss from one source (or head) of income against income from another source (or head) of income in the SAME assessment year.
Intra-head / Inter-source Adjustment [Sec. 70]Setting off a loss from one source against income from another source under the SAME head of income.
Inter-head Adjustment [Sec. 71]Setting off a loss under one head of income against income under a DIFFERENT head, applied only after Sec. 70 (intra-head) is exhausted.
Carry Forward of LossWhere a loss cannot be fully set off in the current year for want of sufficient income, the unabsorbed balance is carried to future assessment year(s) for set-off there, subject to conditions (e.g. timely return filing u/s 139(3), and head-specific carry-forward periods).
Speculative Transaction [Sec. 43(5)]A contract for purchase/sale of a commodity (including stock/shares) that is settled otherwise than by actual delivery.
Specified Business [Sec. 35AD]Certain notified businesses (e.g. cold chain facility, cross-country natural gas pipeline) eligible for a capital-expenditure deduction — losses from such a business can be set off only against profits of another specified business.
Unabsorbed Depreciation [Sec. 32(2)]Depreciation that could not be fully absorbed for want of sufficient profit — added to next year's depreciation allowance and carried forward without any time limit, governed separately from Sec. 72 business-loss carry forward.
