CONCEPT

3.1 Income of Other Person Included in Assessee's Total Income (Clubbing of Income) ★★★ HIGH

Generally, an assessee is taxed only on income accruing to him, not on another person's income. Sec. 60 to 64 carve out exceptions — certain income of another person is clubbed with the assessee's own income — e.g. certain income of a minor child is clubbed in the hands of his parents, income from an asset transferred to spouse for inadequate consideration is clubbed in the hands of the transferor. These provisions counteract the tendency of taxpayers to dispose off income or income-generating assets to escape tax liability.

3.1.2 General Rules of Clubbing

  • Computation of income to be clubbed: the income to be clubbed is first computed in the hands of the recipient, with all related expenditure/deductions allowed as per the respective provisions of the Act, and only the NET income is then clubbed. E.g. standard deduction u/s 24(a) from house property income is allowed in the recipient's hands first, and the net figure is clubbed.
  • Clubbing head: income is first computed in the recipient's hands and clubbing is then made head-wise. E.g. bank interest of a minor child is clubbed under "Income from other sources" of the parent.
  • Deduction under Chapter VIA: if the clubbed income is eligible for deduction u/s 80C to 80U, the deduction is allowed to the assessee in whose hands the income is clubbed. E.g. if a minor's savings-bank interest is clubbed in the parent's hands u/s 64(1A), the parent can claim deduction u/s 80TTA.
  • Clubbing of negative income: per Explanation 2 to Sec. 64, clubbing includes negative income — where an income is liable to be clubbed, a LOSS from the same source is also clubbed. Clubbing is mandatory and applies even where it causes a loss of revenue to the department.

3.1.3 Transfer of Income Without Transferring Assets [Sec. 60]

Where income is transferred without transferring the asset yielding it, such income is clubbed in the transferor's hands — whether the transfer is revocable or not, and whether effected before or after the commencement of the Act.

3.1.4 Revocable Transfer [Sec. 61–63]

If an assessee transfers an asset under a revocable transfer, income generated from that asset is clubbed in the transferor's hands [Sec. 61]. Per Sec. 63(a), a transfer is deemed revocable if it contains any provision for retransfer (directly or indirectly) of any part or whole of the income/assets to the transferor, or if it in any way gives the transferor a right to re-assume power (directly or indirectly) over any part or whole of the income/assets.

Exceptions [Sec. 62]

Sec. 61 does not apply to income arising by virtue of (i) a transfer by way of creation of a trust which is irrevocable during the beneficiary's lifetime, or (ii) any transfer which is irrevocable during the transferee's lifetime — PROVIDED the transferor derives no benefit, directly or indirectly, from such income.

Situation [Sec. 62(2)]Taxable in hands of
When the power to revoke the transfer arises (whether exercised or not)Transferor
When the power to revoke the transfer does not ariseTransferee

ILLUSTRATION 1 — Revocable transfer, three cases

(a) Harish transferred securities to a trust for his married sister Harsha on 1/7/2025, with power to revoke at his desire; he revoked the trust on 31/3/2027. Income accrued: P.Y. 2025-26 ₹1,20,000 and P.Y. 2026-27 ₹1,50,000, though received/enjoyed by Harsha.

(b) Raja transferred property to Rani on 1/4/2025 with a clause to take it back whenever he requires; he took it back on 1/4/2026. Annual income ₹2,00,000.

(c) Seema transferred property to Neema on 1/4/2025 for Neema's lifetime, with a clause that it reverts to Seema on Neema's death; Neema died 1/4/2026; Seema had not taken the property back by 31/3/2027. Annual income ₹1,00,000.

Answer: (a) Since the transfer is revocable, by virtue of Sec. 61 both years' income (₹1,20,000 and ₹1,50,000) is taxable in Harish's hands, though received by Harsha. (b) Since the transfer is revocable, by virtue of Sec. 61 the income is chargeable in Raja's hands for BOTH P.Y. 2025-26 and P.Y. 2026-27 — income arising by virtue of any revocable transfer is chargeable to the transferor from the moment the power to revoke arises, whether or not exercised. (c) Since the transfer is irrevocable during the transferee's lifetime, by virtue of Sec. 62 income is chargeable in Neema's hands for P.Y. 2025-26; but for P.Y. 2026-27 it is chargeable in Seema's hands, because after Neema's death Seema got the power to revoke — and once that power arises, income is clubbed in the transferor's hands even if unexercised.

3.1.5 Remuneration to Spouse [Sec. 64(1)(ii)]

The total income of an individual includes income arising (directly or indirectly) to the spouse by way of salary, commission, fees or any other remuneration (cash or kind) from a concern in which the individual has substantial interest.

Taxpoint: any OTHER income (not specified above) accruing to the spouse from such a concern is NOT clubbed.

Substantial interest: an individual is deemed to have substantial interest in a concern if — in case of a COMPANY, he beneficially holds not less than 20% of its equity shares at any time during the previous year (held by the assessee alone, or partly by the assessee and partly by one or more relatives); in case of ANY OTHER concern, he is entitled to not less than 20% of its profits at any time during the previous year (held by the assessee himself, or together with relatives). "Relative" includes spouse, brother, sister, or any lineal ascendant/descendant of that individual [Sec. 2(41)].

Exception: income generated through the spouse's technical or professional qualification is NOT clubbed. The term is construed liberally — not confined to a certificate/diploma/degree from a recognised body; it can be fitness to do a job or undertake an occupation requiring intellectual skill, including technicality gained through experience/skill (e.g. specialisation in accountancy, management, commerce, science, technology).

SituationTreatment
Both spouses have substantial interest in a concern, both draw remuneration without any specific qualificationRemuneration is included in the total income of the spouse whose total income, EXCLUDING such remuneration, is higher.
Once clubbed in a spouse's hands in one yearCannot be shifted to the other spouse's total income in subsequent years, unless the Assessing Officer is satisfied it is necessary — and only after giving the other spouse an opportunity of being heard.
Both spouses have substantial interest, both draw remuneration without any specific qualification, and neither has any other incomeRemuneration from such concern will NOT be clubbed.
Computation of salary/fee/commission/remuneration to be clubbedFirst computed (allowing all deductions) in the recipient's hands per Sec. 15 to 17 (for salary); the NET income is then clubbed in the other spouse's hands.

ILLUSTRATION 2 — Substantial interest, remuneration clubbing

Ram and Mrs. Ram hold 20% and 30% equity shares in Anand Ltd. respectively; both are employed there (taxable salary ₹12,40,000 and ₹13,60,000 p.a.) without any technical/professional qualification. Other incomes: Ram ₹70,000, Mrs. Ram ₹1,00,000. Find net income for A.Y. 2026-27.

Since both have substantial interest and both draw remuneration without a specific qualification, remuneration is included in the total income of whichever spouse has the higher total income EXCLUDING such remuneration. Mrs. Ram's other income (₹1,00,000) exceeds Ram's (₹70,000), so Ram's salary is clubbed in Mrs. Ram's hands.

Clubbing of income as per Sec. 64(1)(ii)(12,40,000)12,40,000

Gross Total Income70,00027,00,000

Mr. & Mrs. Om both work in A Ltd. without any technical/professional qualification. Taxable salary: Mr. Om ₹12,20,000, Mrs. Om ₹1,70,000. Other income: ₹50,000 and ₹80,000. Share of holdings — Case 1: 15%/6%; Case 2: 3%/17%; Case 3: 18%/1%. Compute income for A.Y. 2026-27.

Mr. & Mrs. X work in A Ltd. without qualification. Share of holdings 15%/6%. Taxable salary ₹11,20,000/₹1,60,000. Case 1: other income ₹50,000/₹80,000; Case 2: ₹90,000/₹65,000; Case 3: Nil/Nil.

Answer: Case 1 & 2 follow the higher-other-income rule (Mrs. X higher in Case 1, Mr. X higher in Case 2). Case 3: both have substantial interest, both draw remuneration without qualification, and NEITHER has any other income apart from that remuneration — clubbing is NOT made; each is taxed on his/her own salary.

3.1.6 Income From Asset Transferred to Spouse [Sec. 64(1)(iv) & (vii)]

In computing an individual's total income [subject to Sec. 27(i)], income arising from assets transferred to the spouse without adequate consideration is included in the individual's income.

Taxpoint: clubbing does NOT apply where — the transfer is for adequate consideration; or the transfer is under an agreement to live apart; or the asset transferred is house property (governed instead by Sec. 27).

PointRule & example, in the source's own words
Marital relationshipMust subsist both on the date of transfer AND on the date of accrual of income — no clubbing if the transfer is made before marriage, or if on the date of accrual of income the transferee is not the spouse of the transferor.
Pin moneyIncome from assets acquired by the spouse out of pin money or household savings is NOT subject to clubbing.
Sec. 27(i) vs. Sec. 64(1)(iv)A transferred HOUSE PROPERTY is governed by Sec. 27(i) [deemed owner], not Sec. 64(1)(iv). Example: Mr. X transfers his house (worth ₹15,00,000) to Mrs. X without consideration; rental income of ₹1,00,000 is taxable in Mr. X's hands under Sec. 27(i), NOT Sec. 64(1)(iv). But capital gain on transfer of that property is first computed in Mrs. X's hands, then clubbed in Mr. X's hands under Sec. 64(1)(iv). Similarly, if Mr. X gifts Mrs. X ₹15,00,000 and she buys a house with it, the ₹1,00,000 rental income is first computed in Mrs. X's hands and then clubbed in Mr. X's hands under Sec. 64(1)(iv).
Nature of considerationMust be measurable in money — natural love and affection, or a spiritual/religious benefit, is never adequate consideration.
Inadequate considerationOnly the PART of income referable to the inadequacy is clubbed. Example: Mr. X transfers 1,000 10% debentures of ₹100 each (market value ₹100 each) to Mrs. X for ₹25,000; income at year-end is ₹10,000. ₹2,500 (i.e. ₹10,000 × ₹25,000/₹1,00,000) is taxable in Mrs. X's hands; the remaining ₹7,500 (₹10,000 – ₹2,500) is clubbed in Mr. X's hands.
Form of assetNeed not remain in its original form. Example: Mr. X transfers securities worth ₹5,00,000; Mrs. X exchanges them for a house property; income from that house property is still clubbed u/s 64(1)(iv).
Accretion of assetIncome arising to the transferee from the ACCRETION of the transferred property is NOT clubbed. Example: Mr. X transfers foreign-company shares worth ₹5,00,000; Mrs. X receives bonus shares on them. Dividend on the ORIGINAL shares is clubbed in Mr. X's hands; dividend on the BONUS shares is not clubbed and is taxable in Mrs. X's hands.
Capital gainProfit on sale of property gifted to spouse or son's wife is clubbed in the transferor's hands.
Income on incomeIncome arising to the transferee from the ACCUMULATED income of the transferred property is not clubbed. Example: Mr. X transfers shares worth ₹5,00,000; Mrs. X sells them for ₹6,00,000 (profit ₹1,00,000) and buys 12% debentures of another company. The capital gain of ₹1,00,000 AND interest of ₹60,000 (12% of ₹5,00,000) are clubbed in Mr. X's hands u/s 64(1)(iv); but interest of ₹12,000 (12% of ₹1,00,000, i.e. income on the ₹1,00,000 gain) is NOT clubbed and is taxable in Mrs. X's hands.
Asset transferred under a trustSec. 64(1) still applies to an asset transferred under a trust for the benefit of spouse or son's wife — even if the assessee appoints himself trustee.
Treatment after deathClubbing under Sec. 64(1)(iv) stops after the death of either spouse — a widow or widower is not a "spouse".
Cross giftIf the Assessing Officer is satisfied that inter-related gifts made in a circuitous way are intended to evade Sec. 64(1), he may still apply it. Example: Mr. A gifts property to Mrs. X, and Mr. X gifts another property to Mrs. A — income from Mrs. A's and Mrs. X's properties is clubbed in Mr. A's and Mr. X's hands respectively, as the transactions are treated as inter-related parts of the same transaction.

Asset transferred to spouse invested in a business — proportion to be clubbed:

Proprietary business: Income to be clubbed = Income of the business × [Value of transferred asset as on 1st day of the P.Y. ÷ Total investment in the business by the transferee as on the same day].

Partnership: Interest to be clubbed = Interest on capital × [Value of transferred asset as on 1st day of the P.Y. ÷ Total investment in the firm by the transferee as on the same day]. Taxpoint: SHARE OF PROFIT from the firm is never clubbed, as it is exempt u/s 10(2A).

ILLUSTRATION 5 — Chain of asset transfer, sale, and re-investment

Mr. X gifted 1,000 shares of a non-domestic company worth ₹6,00,000 (acquired 15/3/2025) to Mrs. X out of natural love and affection on 15/4/2025. On 31/1/2026 Mrs. X received dividend ₹60,000 in India. On 1/2/2026 she sold the shares for ₹10,00,000 and received the consideration in India, then invested ₹10,60,000 in: Case A — house property (rent ₹53,000 for P.Y. 2025-26); Case B — a new partnership firm (interest received, taxable, ₹13,250; share of profit ₹20,000); Case C — a new proprietorship (profit ₹42,400).

Note 1: Computation of capital gain and treatment (₹)
ParticularsAmount
Sale consideration10,00,000

Assets Transferred to AOP/Other Person, and to Son's Wife

Assets transferred to AOP or other person for the benefit of spouse [Sec. 64(1)(vii)]: where an asset is transferred to another person or an AOP, otherwise than for adequate consideration, for the immediate or deferred benefit of the spouse, income on that asset is clubbed in the transferor's hands (to the extent it is for the immediate/deferred benefit of the spouse).

ProvisionRule
Transfer to son's wife [Sec. 64(1)(vi)]Income arising (directly or indirectly) from assets transferred to son's wife (after 31.5.1973), without adequate consideration, is included in the transferor's total income. The relationship must subsist both on the date of transfer of assets AND on the date of accrual of income.
Transfer to AOP/other person for son's wife's benefit [Sec. 64(1)(viii)]Where an asset is transferred to another person or an AOP (after 31.5.1973), otherwise than for adequate consideration, for the immediate/deferred benefit of son's wife, income on that asset is clubbed in the transferor's hands (to the extent for her immediate/deferred benefit). Same explanatory notes as Sec. 64(1)(iv) apply.

3.1.7 Income of Minor Child [Sec. 64(1A)]

Income of a minor child is clubbed with the income of the parent whose total income (excluding this income) is HIGHER.

Exceptions — the clubbing provision does not apply where:

  1. The income arises/accrues to the minor child due to any manual work done by him; or
  2. The income arises/accrues due to his skill, talent, specialised knowledge or experience; or
  3. The minor child suffers from a disability specified u/s 80U.

Be careful: there is NO exception for a minor MARRIED daughter, unlike the exception under Sec. 27 (Deemed Owner).

Exemption u/s 10(32) [available only under old regime]: where a minor's income is clubbed under Sec. 64(1A), the parent can claim exemption of the MINIMUM of — (a) ₹1,500; or (b) the income so clubbed — separately for EACH child, irrespective of the number of children.

Relation between parentsTax treatment
When marriage subsistsClubbed with the income of the parent whose total income (excluding this income) is higher.
When marriage does not subsistClubbed with the income of the parent who MAINTAINS the minor child during the previous year.
  • Clubbing in subsequent years: once clubbed with one parent, it cannot shift to the other parent in later years unless the Assessing Officer is satisfied it is necessary, and only after giving the other parent an opportunity of being heard.
  • Child [Sec. 2(15B)]: includes a stepchild and an adopted child, but NOT a grandchild.
  • Income of married daughter: Sec. 27(i) specifically excludes a married daughter, but Sec. 64(1A) carries no such exception — income of a minor married daughter IS clubbed with the parent.
  • When neither parent is alive: a minor's income cannot be added to a guardian's income if the guardian is not the minor's parent.
  • Capital gain: profit on sale of property gifted to a minor child is clubbed in the parent's hands under Sec. 64(1A).
Income of the year the child attains majorityClubbing provision
Before the child attains majorityClubbed in the parent's hands.
After the child attains majorityNOT clubbed — taxable in the (now major) child's own hands.

3.1.8 Conversion of Self-Acquired Property Into HUF Property [Sec. 64(2)]

Applicability: an individual, being an HUF member, converts (after 31/12/1969) his self-acquired property into HUF property, otherwise than for adequate consideration — by impressing it with the character of family property, or by throwing it into the common stock of the family.

Tax treatment: for computing the individual's total income for any assessment year commencing on/after 1/4/1971, income derived from the converted property is deemed to arise to the INDIVIDUAL, not the family. Where the converted property is later partitioned (partial or total), the income derived from it AS RECEIVED BY THE SPOUSE is clubbed in the transferor's hands.

CaseIncome clubbed in transferor's hands
Before partitionThe ENTIRE income from the converted property.
After partitionOnly income from the assets attributable to the transferor's SPOUSE.

Note: the asset need not remain in its original form.

3.1.9 Liability of the Transferee [Sec. 65]

Applicability: where, by reason of the clubbing provisions of this Chapter OR of Sec. 27(i), the income from any asset (or from firm membership) of a person other than the assessee is included in the assessee's total income — on service of a notice of demand by the Assessing Officer, the person in whose name the asset stands (or who is the firm member) becomes liable to pay that portion of the tax levied on the assessee attributable to the income so included.

  • Such liability cannot exceed the value of the asset transferred.
  • Where the asset is held jointly by more than one person, they are jointly AND severally liable for the tax attributable to the income so included.

Taxpoint: tax liability on clubbed income arises in the TRANSFEROR's hands; Sec. 65 merely empowers the department to serve a demand notice on the transferee as a recovery backstop.

3.1.10 Important General Notes on Clubbing

PointRule
TDS [Sec. 199]Where income is includible u/s 64 and tax has been deducted at source from it, credit for that TDS is given to the person in whose hands the income is TAXABLE (i.e. the person it is clubbed with).
Advance taxAdvance tax paid by the income EARNER (spouse or minor child) is not eligible for adjustment against the tax liability of the individual in whose hands the income is clubbed. The payer of the advance tax may instead apply for a REFUND.
Mode of clubbing cannot be changed for revenue's benefitUnless there are compelling circumstances, the ITO cannot change the mode of clubbing merely for the benefit of revenue.

ILLUSTRATION 8 — Gift invested in a proprietary business, two assumptions

Smt. Sonam Mundhra's proprietary business capital was ₹3,00,000 as on 1.4.2024. Her husband Shri Vikash gifted her ₹2,00,000 on 10.4.2024, invested the same day. She earned ₹1,50,000 profit for F.Y. 2024-25 and ₹3,90,000 for F.Y. 2025-26. Compute the income to be clubbed in her husband's hands for A.Y. 2026-27.

Assumption 1 (F.Y. 2024-25 profit reinvested in the business): Total investment as on 1-4-2025 = ₹3,00,000 + ₹2,00,000 (gift) + ₹1,50,000 (retained profit) = ₹6,50,000. Clubbable income = ₹3,90,000 × ₹2,00,000 / ₹6,50,000 = ₹1,20,000.

Assumption 2 (F.Y. 2024-25 profit withdrawn): Total investment as on 1-4-2025 = ₹3,00,000 + ₹2,00,000 = ₹5,00,000. Clubbable income = ₹3,90,000 × ₹2,00,000 / ₹5,00,000 = ₹1,56,000.

Answer: ₹1,20,000 (if F.Y. 2024-25 profit was reinvested) or ₹1,56,000 (if withdrawn) is clubbed in the husband's hands. Income arising from accretion to the transferred asset (i.e. reinvested profit) is not itself liable to clubbing — only the ratio-based share of the CURRENT year's income tied to the ORIGINAL gifted capital is clubbed.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: "GRANDFATHER GAVE IT, SO IT'S NOT MY CHILD'S CLUBBABLE INCOME"

THE TRAP: students assume that because an asset was gifted to the minor by a grandparent (not by the parent), Sec. 64(1A) does not apply, or that it should somehow be clubbed with the grandparent instead.

THE TWIST: Sec. 64(1A) clubs a minor child's income with the PARENT regardless of who transferred the underlying asset to the minor — Illustration 9 and Illustration 10 both confirm this: interest on a grandfather-gifted deposit is clubbed with the parent whose other income is higher, never with the grandparent.

CONCEPT

3.2 Set Off and Carry Forward of Losses ★★★ HIGH

For computation of Gross Total Income (GTI), income from various sources is computed under the five heads of income. If all sources/heads show positive income (profit), they are simply added to arrive at GTI. But where certain source(s) or head(s) show negative income (loss), such loss must be adjusted against income of another source/head. Set off means adjustment of loss from one source/head against income from another source/head. If a negative income is not fully set off in the current year, the unabsorbed loss is carried forward to subsequent years subject to conditions/restrictions — e.g. income from other sources (other than losses from owning and maintaining race horses) cannot be carried forward at all.

The set-off sequence: Intra-Head Adjustment / Inter-Source Adjustment [Sec. 70] → Inter-Head Adjustment [Sec. 71] → Carry Forward of Loss (subject to conditions and exceptions).

3.2.2 Inter Source Adjustment / Intra-Head Adjustment [Sec. 70]

When the net result of any SOURCE of income is a loss, it can be set off against income from any OTHER source under the SAME head, subject to the following exceptions:

  1. Capital gains [Sec. 70(2) & (3)]: long-term capital loss can be set off ONLY against long-term capital gain. Short-term capital loss can be set off against both short-term and long-term capital gains.
  2. Speculation business [Sec. 73(1)]: loss of a speculation business can be set off ONLY against speculation-business profit. Loss from a NON-speculative business can, however, be set off against speculation-business income.
  3. Specified business u/s 35AD: loss can be set off ONLY against profit of another specified business. Loss from a non-specified business can be set off against specified-business income. (Sec. 35AD deduction is available only if the assessee has opted out of Sec. 115BAC.)
  4. Race horses [Sec. 74A]: loss from owning and maintaining race horses can be set off ONLY against income from that same activity.
  5. Exempt-income source: loss from a source whose income is exempt u/s 10 cannot be set off against any income.
  6. Casual income [Sec. 58(4) & 115BB; Sec. 115BBE]: no loss can be set off against winnings from lotteries, crossword puzzles, races, card games, gambling or betting. Similarly, losses cannot be set off against unexplained income/investment/money chargeable u/s 68/69A/69B/69C/69D.

Taxpoint: the restrictions above run only ONE way — income from these sources (a to d) remains available to absorb a loss from any OTHER source under the same head.

3.2.3 Inter Head Adjustment [Sec. 71]

Where, for any assessment year, the net result of any HEAD of income is a loss, it can be set off against income under any OTHER head for the SAME assessment year, subject to the following exceptions:

  1. Capital gains: loss under "Capital gains" CANNOT be set off against income under any other head. But loss under any other head (e.g. business loss) CAN be set off against Capital Gains income.
  2. Speculation business: loss due to speculation business cannot be set off against any other income except speculation profit. Loss under any OTHER head (e.g. house-property loss) can be set off against speculation-business income.
  3. Specified business u/s 35AD: loss cannot be set off against income under other heads; loss from OTHER heads can be set off against specified-business income.
ExampleCase ACase B
GTI, Mr. X, A.Y. 2026-27 (₹)
Long term capital gain80,000(90,000)
Short term capital gain(60,000)(30,000)
Income from house property(20,000)1,30,000
Gross total incomeNil1,30,000
Case A: within capital gains, STCL 60,000 offsets LTCG 80,000 → net ₹20,000 capital gain; house-property loss (₹20,000) then offsets it inter-head → GTI Nil. Case B: capital-gains head is net negative (–1,20,000) and CANNOT be set off against house-property income — it is carried forward in full; GTI = house-property income alone, ₹1,30,000.

Cascade per Sec. 70/71 (as the source works it): Salary first absorbs the ₹70,000 other-sources loss (which cannot itself be carried forward) → Salary ₹1,90,000 left. That remaining Salary then absorbs ₹1,90,000 of the ₹2,00,000 house-property loss → ₹10,000 house-property loss left. That ₹10,000, plus ₹20,000 of the PGBP loss, is set off against the ₹30,000 STCG → Capital Gains head reduced to Nil. Remaining PGBP loss ₹90,000 has no further income to absorb it.
Gross Total Income1,80,000 (casual income alone survives untouched)

Answer (source's own conclusion): from salary income, the ₹70,000 loss under "Income from other sources" is adjusted FIRST (because such loss cannot be carried forward at all), then the house-property loss is adjusted — since PGBP loss cannot be set off against salary income. Thereafter, ₹10,000 of house-property loss and ₹20,000 of PGBP loss are adjusted against the ₹30,000 STCG; the remaining ₹90,000 PGBP loss and ₹20,000 house-property loss (including the amount over the ₹2,00,000 ceiling) are carried forward. Alternatively, ₹30,000 house-property loss and ₹80,000 PGBP loss can be carried forward — the Act gives no fixed priority among losses that CAN be carried forward, only a preference for losses that cannot.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: LOSSES THAT CANNOT BE CARRIED FORWARD MUST BE ADJUSTED FIRST

THE TRAP: students set off losses in whatever order feels intuitive (biggest loss first, or by head sequence), assuming the Act prescribes a fixed priority under Sec. 71.

THE TWIST: the Act lays down NO priority for inter-head set-off under Sec. 71 — but the source's own general note states losses which CANNOT be carried forward (e.g. "Income from other sources" loss, other than race-horse loss) should be adjusted FIRST, since any unabsorbed balance is simply lost forever. Illustration 15 in the source drives this home: Salary income is adjusted against the "Income from other sources" loss BEFORE the house-property loss, purely because the latter CAN be carried forward and the former cannot.

ILLUSTRATION 15 — Priority: adjust the non-carry-forwardable loss first

Mr. Bhola (old regime): House property (₹1,30,000); Salaries (Net) ₹12,80,000; Income from other sources (₹12,90,000); Lottery income ₹3,50,000.

Statement showing application of Sec. 71 (₹)
ParticularsAmount
Salaries12,80,000
Income from house property(1,30,000)
Income from other sources: lottery 3,50,000, other income (12,90,000)3,50,000
Gross total income3,50,000

Answer: casual (lottery) income is fully taxable — no loss can be set off against it, so it stands alone at ₹3,50,000. Losses carried forward: house-property loss ₹1,30,000 in full (never touched, since salary was consumed elsewhere); "Income from other sources" loss Nil (cannot be carried forward at all — even the un-set-off ₹10,000 balance, after adjusting ₹12,80,000 of the ₹12,90,000 loss against salary, simply lapses). Salary is adjusted FIRST against the other-sources loss, precisely because that loss cannot be carried forward; the house-property loss (which CAN be carried forward) is left untouched to preserve the carry-forward.

ILLUSTRATION 16 — No option to withhold set-off

Mr. Tej Singh: House property (₹30,000); Salaries ₹6,80,000; Other sources ₹30,000. He computed his GTI showing only ₹10,000 of the house-property loss set off, carrying forward the remaining ₹20,000, arriving at GTI ₹7,00,000.

Answer: this is INCORRECT. The assessee is bound to follow Sec. 70 and 71 — there is no choice or option whether to set off a loss, and even PARTIAL set-off is not permissible when the full loss can otherwise be set off. Since salary (₹6,80,000) and other-sources income (₹30,000) together comfortably absorb the full ₹30,000 house-property loss, GTI must be ₹6,80,000 (Salaries ₹6,80,000 + Other sources ₹30,000 – House property loss ₹30,000), and NO carry forward is permissible.

3.2.4 General Notes on Sec. 70/71

  1. Sec. 70 vs. Sec. 71: intra-head set-off must be completed FIRST; inter-head set-off applies only thereafter.
  2. No fixed priority under Sec. 71: the Act lays down no priority among losses being set off inter-head — but losses which cannot be carried forward should be adjusted first (see Illustration 15 and its trap above).
  3. Mandatory feature: the assessee has no choice whether or not to set off a loss, and even partial set-off is impermissible when full set-off is otherwise possible (see Illustration 16).
  4. Set-off of clubbed income: losses CAN be set off from clubbed income.

3.2.5 Carry Forward of Loss — Which Losses Qualify

Where the income of an assessment year is insufficient to set off the year's losses, the un-set-off balance can be carried forward to subsequent assessment year(s), for set off against that year's income. However, NOT all losses can be carried forward — e.g. loss under "Income from other sources" (other than race-horse loss) cannot be carried forward at all. The following losses CAN be carried forward:

  1. Loss under "Income from house property" [Sec. 71B]
  2. Loss under "Profits and gains of business or profession", other than speculation loss [Sec. 72]
  3. Loss from speculation business [Sec. 73]
  4. Loss from specified business covered u/s 35AD [Sec. 73A]
  5. Loss under "Capital gains" [Sec. 74]
  6. Loss from activity of owning and maintaining race horses [Sec. 74A]
Loss type & SectionCarry-forward periodSet-off restriction & return-filing rule
House property loss [Sec. 71B]8 A.Y.s succeeding the A.Y. of first computationSet off ONLY against house-property income in later years. Under default regime, this loss cannot be set off under any other head, nor carried forward at all. Can be carried forward even if a BELATED return is filed [Sec. 80 & 139(3) do not apply to Sec. 71B].
Business loss, non-speculative [Sec. 72]8 A.Y.s succeeding the A.Y. of first computationSet off only against PGBP income (business profit includes profit assessable under a different head, e.g. dividend on shares held as stock, taxable under "Other Sources" but still absorbable). Requires a return filed in time u/s 139(3)/139(1) [Sec. 80]. Business need not be continued in the year of set-off.
Speculation loss [Sec. 73]4 A.Y.s succeeding the A.Y. of first computationSet off ONLY against speculation-business profit. Same speculation business need not continue. Requires timely return u/s 139(3)/139(1) [Sec. 80]. Illegal speculative-business loss cannot be carried forward at all.
Sec. 35AD specified-business loss [Sec. 73A]No time limit prescribedSet off against income from any other specified business (eligible for 35AD or not). Requires timely return u/s 139(3)/139(1) [Sec. 80].
Capital loss [Sec. 74]8 A.Y.s succeeding the A.Y. of first computationSet off only against Capital Gains income — long-term capital loss ONLY against long-term capital gain; short-term capital loss against any capital gain (ST or LT). LTC loss covered u/s 112A can also be carried forward. Requires timely return u/s 139(3)/139(1) [Sec. 80].
Race-horse activity loss [Sec. 74A]4 A.Y.s succeeding the A.Y. of first computationSet off ONLY against income from the same activity, which must still be carried on in the set-off year. Requires timely return u/s 139(3)/139(1) [Sec. 80].
Unabsorbed depreciation [Sec. 32(2)]No time limit (any number of years)Governed by Sec. 32(2), NOT Sec. 72. Set off against ANY income except "Salaries" and casual income (lottery, etc.). Carried forward even if the return was not filed in time.

3.2.7 Additional Notes on Business Loss Carry Forward [Sec. 72]

  • Exception 1 — closure due to specified calamity [Sec. 33B]: where a business is discontinued due to flood/typhoon/hurricane/cyclone/earthquake/convulsion of nature, riot/civil disturbance, accidental fire/explosion, or enemy action — and is re-established/reconstructed/revived within 3 years from the end of the previous year of the mishap — the past eligible losses are adjusted against the revival year's profit, and any un-set-off balance can be further carried forward for 7 MORE years.
  • Exception 2 — loss in the year of closure, set off against deemed profit [Sec. 41(5)]: a non-speculation loss remaining unabsorbed in the previous year the business ceases can be carried forward for ANY number of years (no 8-year cap) against income chargeable u/s 41(1)/(3)/(4)/(4A) — and this can be set off even if the loss return was not submitted in time.
  • Business need not be continued to carry forward its losses.
  • Filing of return in time [Sec. 80]: business loss cannot be carried forward unless determined pursuant to a return filed u/s 139(3) within the u/s 139(1) time limit.
  • Unabsorbed depreciation/scientific research/family planning expenditure are NOT covered by Sec. 72 — carried forward for any number of years.
  • Order of set-off where profit is insufficient: (a) current year's depreciation [Sec. 32(1)], capital scientific-research expenditure [Sec. 35(1)], capital family-planning expenditure [Sec. 36(1)(ix)]; then (b) brought-forward business losses [Sec. 72(1)]; then (c) unabsorbed depreciation [Sec. 32(2)], unabsorbed family-planning expenditure [Sec. 36(1)(ix)], unabsorbed scientific-research capital expenditure [Sec. 35(4)].
  • Same-assessee rule & its exceptions: business losses/unabsorbed depreciation carry forward only for the assessee who incurred them — EXCEPT (a) amalgamation within Sec. 72A meaning; (b) succession of a proprietary concern/firm/specified company by a company/LLP under Sec. 47(xiii)/(xiiib)/(xiv); (c) inheritance [Sec. 78(2), for balance of the remaining years]; (d) demerger, where the demerged company's loss carries to the resulting company.
Losses that CANNOT be carried forward despite the above exceptions
HUF business taken over by the Karta of the HUF.
Proprietorship business taken over by a firm in which the proprietor is one of the partners.
A firm succeeded by another firm.
A firm's business taken over by one of the firm's own partners.

Academic note (source): for A.Y. 2026-27, losses prior to A.Y. 2018-19 (Sec. 72 business loss) cannot be set off, having exhausted their 8-year window.

3.2.8 Set-off and Carry Forward of Unabsorbed Depreciation [Sec. 32(2)]

Depreciation that could not be fully absorbed in a previous year — owing to no chargeable profit/gains that year, or profit/gains being less than the depreciation — is (subject to Sec. 72 and 73) added to the following year's depreciation allowance and deemed part of that year's depreciation, and so on for succeeding years.

Taxpoint: unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward for ANY number of years, and set off against ANY income EXCEPT income under "Salaries" and casual income (lottery, crossword puzzles, etc.).

  • Can be carried forward even if the business is not continued during the previous year.
  • Can be carried forward even if the return was not filed within time.

3.2.9 Carry Forward & Set Off of Speculation Loss [Sec. 73]

Speculative transaction [Sec. 43(5)]: a transaction for purchase and sale of any commodity (including stock and shares) periodically or ultimately settled otherwise than by ACTUAL delivery or transfer of the commodity/scripts.

Per the Explanation to Sec. 73: where part of a COMPANY'S business consists of purchase and sale of shares of other companies, that company is DEEMED to carry on speculation business to that extent — UNLESS (a) its GTI mainly consists of income chargeable under "House Property", "Capital Gains" and "Other Sources"; or (b) its principal business is trading in shares, or banking, or granting loans/advances. This explanation covers only share transactions — debentures, and units of UTI/Mutual Funds, are NOT covered.

Treatment: speculative-business loss can be carried forward and set off ONLY against speculation-business income, for 4 assessment years succeeding the A.Y. of first computation. Sec. 73(3): depreciation/capital scientific-research allowance is NOT restricted by Sec. 73 — it can be carried forward for any number of years.

  • Continuity not required: the same speculation business need not continue in the carry-forward/set-off year.
  • Filing of return [Sec. 80]: loss cannot be carried forward unless determined pursuant to a return filed u/s 139(3) within the u/s 139(1) time limit.
  • Derivative trading: an eligible transaction in trading DERIVATIVES [Sec. 2(ac), Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956] carried out on a recognised stock exchange is NOT treated as a speculative transaction. Similarly for eligible commodity-derivative trading on a recognised exchange (liable to Commodities Transaction Tax, except for agricultural-commodity derivatives, where CTT chargeability is not a requirement).
  • Illegal speculative business: loss from an illegal speculative business cannot be carried forward for set-off against another speculative business's profit.

3.2.10 Carry Forward & Set Off of Sec. 35AD Specified-Business Loss [Sec. 73A]

Losses from a specified business covered u/s 35AD can be carried forward and set off against income from ANY OTHER specified business (whether that other business is itself eligible for the 35AD deduction or not). No time limit is prescribed for carry-forward. Per Sec. 80, the loss cannot be carried forward unless determined pursuant to a return filed u/s 139(3) within the u/s 139(1) time limit.

3.2.11 Carry Forward and Set Off of Capital Loss [Sec. 74]

Loss under "Capital gains" can be carried forward and set off against income under the SAME head, subject to the restriction that long-term capital loss can be set off ONLY against long-term capital gain.

Taxpoint: short-term capital loss can be set off against ANY capital gain (short-term or long-term). Long-term capital loss covered u/s 112A can also be carried forward.

Carry-forward period: 8 assessment years succeeding the A.Y. of first computation. Requires a return filed u/s 139(3) within the u/s 139(1) time limit [Sec. 80].

Academic note (source): for A.Y. 2026-27, losses prior to A.Y. 2018-19 cannot be set off.

3.2.12 Carry Forward & Set Off of Race-Horse Losses [Sec. 74A]

For an assessee owning race horses maintained for running in horse races, loss incurred in the activity of owning and maintaining race horses in any assessment year can be set off ONLY against income from that same activity. Carry-forward period: 4 assessment years succeeding the A.Y. of first computation.

  • Continuity of activity: the activity must still be carried on by the assessee in the previous year in which set-off is claimed.
  • Other race animals: Sec. 74A covers only RACE HORSES; losses from other race animals are governed by Sec. 72 instead.
  • Filing of return: to claim carry-forward benefit, a loss return u/s 139(3) must be filed within the u/s 139(1) time limit.
  • Horse Race: a race upon which wagering or betting on horses may be lawfully made.

Amount of loss from owning and maintaining race horses = Expenditure (not capital in nature) laid out wholly and exclusively for maintaining race horses – Income by way of stake money.

"Income by way of stake money" means the gross amount of prize money received on a race horse by its owner.

3.2.12A Carry Forward & Set-off of Loss of a Firm on Change in Constitution [Sec. 78]

Where a change occurs in a firm's constitution due to the retirement or death of a partner, the PROPORTIONATE loss of the retired/deceased partner cannot be carried forward by the continuing firm. This section does NOT apply where the change is merely a profit-sharing-ratio revision or an admission of a new partner — nor does it apply to unabsorbed depreciation.

(ii) R retires on 31.05.2025; P and Q continue the same business. (iii) A.Y. 2026-27 income before adjusting the above loss/depreciation is ₹1,20,000.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SEC. 78 BLOCKS THE RETIRING PARTNER'S LOSS SHARE, NOT THE UNABSORBED DEPRECIATION

THE TRAP: students assume that on a partner's retirement, the WHOLE brought-forward figure (loss + unabsorbed depreciation) gets proportionately reduced by the retiring partner's share.

THE TWIST: Sec. 78 applies only to the LOSS component; unabsorbed depreciation is expressly carved out and continues to be available in full to the reconstituted firm, since it is governed by Sec. 32(2), not Sec. 72/78 (Illustration 21A: the full ₹40,000 unabsorbed depreciation is deducted, while only R's net ₹30,000 loss-share is stripped out).

CONCEPT

3.3 Deductions, Rebate and Relief ★★★ HIGH

From Gross Total Income (GTI — the aggregate of income under all five heads), an assessee can claim several deductions specified in Chapter VI-A on fulfilment of the conditions laid down in the respective section. After allowing these deductions, the Total Income of the assessee is arrived at, and tax is charged on it at the prescribed rates.

Taxpoint: Under the default tax regime, deduction under only the following sections is available — 80CCD(2), 80CCH(2), and 80JJAA. Deductions under all other Chapter VI-A sections are not available under the default regime.

3.3.1 Basic Rules

  1. Deductions not available from: Chapter VI-A deductions are not available from — long-term capital gain; short-term capital gain covered u/s 111A (i.e., STCG on which STT is charged); and casual income like winnings from lotteries, races, etc.
  2. Limit of deduction: The aggregate amount of deduction under Chapter VI-A cannot exceed the Gross Total Income of the assessee, excluding — long-term capital gain; short-term capital gain covered u/s 111A; casual income like winnings from lotteries, card-games, horse races, etc.; and income referred to in Sec. 115A, 115AB, 115AC, 115ACA, etc.
  3. Deduction must be claimed: Deduction under Chapter VI-A – Part C (i.e., profit-based deduction) and Sec. 10AA shall be available only if the assessee claims it in the return of income. The amount of deduction cannot exceed the profits and gains of the undertaking/unit/enterprise/eligible business, and the return of income must be filed within the due date.
  4. Double deduction not permissible: Where deduction under any section of Chapter VI-A has been claimed, the same amount shall not qualify for deduction under any other section.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: DEDUCTING FROM THE WRONG SLICE OF INCOME

THE TRAP: Students deduct Chapter VI-A investments/expenses (80C, 80D, etc.) against LTCG or STCG u/s 111A to reduce the higher special-rate tax, or apply the deduction before checking whether GTI itself (excluding these special incomes) is sufficient.

THE TWIST: Chapter VI-A deductions can be set off only against the "remaining GTI" column — never against LTCG, STCG u/s 111A, or casual income. Further, the aggregate deduction is capped at GTI excluding these three items, so a low/negative "remaining GTI" starves the 80C/80D/etc. deduction even if the assessee has large capital gains (see Illustration 22, Case D below, where a negative GTI wipes out the entire 80C claim).

3.3.2 Deduction u/s 80C — LIC premium, PF contributions, etc.

Not available under the default tax regime

Applicable to: An Individual or a Hindu Undivided Family (whether resident or non-resident), where the assessee has made a deposit or investment in one or more of the listed items during the previous year.

Eligible items — applicable to both Individual & HUF:

  • Life insurance premium [Sec. 80C(2)(i)] — policy on self, spouse and child (any age) for an individual; on any member for an HUF. Premium in excess of a % of actual sum assured is ignored: 20% (policy issued up to 31-03-2012), 10% (P.Y. 2012-13), and 15% of sum assured where insured is disabled/suffering a disease specified u/s 80DDB or 10% for any other insured person (policy issued on/after 01-04-2013).
  • Public Provident Fund (PPF) [Sec. 80C(2)(v)] — in the name of the individual, spouse, child, or any HUF member; must not be repayment of a loan.
  • National Savings Certificates, VIII Issue (NSC) [Sec. 80C(2)(ix)] — accrued interest reinvested (up to the penultimate year of the lock-in period) also qualifies.
  • ULIP of UTI or LIC Mutual Fund u/s 10(23D) [Sec. 80C(2)(x)].
  • Notified annuity plan of LIC or other insurer [Sec. 80C(2)(xii)] — e.g. New Jeevan Dhara, New Jeevan Akshay (I, II, III).
  • Notified units of a specified Mutual Fund u/s 10(23D) [Sec. 80C(2)(xiii)] — e.g. Equity Linked Saving Scheme, 2005.
  • Home Loan Account Scheme / notified pension fund of National Housing Bank [Sec. 80C(2)(xv)] — e.g. NHB (Tax Saving) Term Deposit Scheme, 2008.
  • Notified deposit scheme [Sec. 80C(2)(xvi)] — with public-sector companies providing long-term housing finance, or a housing-authority body.
  • Purchase/construction of a residential house [Sec. 80C(2)(xviii)] — instalments to a development authority/housing board, instalments to a co-operative society/company towards allotted property, repayment of loan from a specified person (Central/State Govt., bank/co-operative bank, NHB, LIC, specified public company/employer), or stamp duty/registration fee for the transfer. Not eligible: amounts already deductible u/s 24, loans for commercial property, or loans for repair/alteration/renovation/addition.
  • Debentures/equity shares in an eligible issue of capital, or of a public financial institution [Sec. 80C(2)(xix)].
  • Subscription to units of a mutual fund u/s 10(23D) subscribed only in an eligible issue of capital [Sec. 80C(2)(xx)].
  • 5-year (or more) term deposit with a scheduled bank [Sec. 80C(2)(xxi)].
  • Notified NABARD bonds [Sec. 80C(2)(xxii)].
  • Senior Citizens Savings Scheme Rules, 2004 [Sec. 80C(2)(xxiii)].
  • 5-year Post Office Time Deposit [Sec. 80C(2)(xxiv)].

Eligible items — applicable to Individual only:

  • Non-commutable deferred annuity [Sec. 80C(2)(ii)] — in the name of individual, spouse, or child; the contract must not allow the insured a cash-payment option in lieu of annuity.
  • Sum deducted from salary of a Government employee for a deferred annuity/provision for wife or children [Sec. 80C(2)(iii)] — maximum 20% of salary.
  • Statutory PF / Recognised PF contribution [Sec. 80C(2)(iv) & (vi)] — must not be repayment of a loan.
  • Approved superannuation fund contribution [Sec. 80C(2)(vii)].
  • Notified Government security / Sukanya Samriddhi Account Scheme [Sec. 80C(2)(viii)] — in the name of the individual/girl child or a girl child of whom the person is legal guardian; accrued interest and withdrawals are exempt u/s 10(11A).
  • Notified pension fund set up by a Mutual Fund u/s 10(23D) [Sec. 80C(2)(xiv)].
  • Tuition fees paid to any university/college/school/educational institution in India for full-time education [Sec. 80C(2)(xvii)] — excludes development fees/donations; private tuition is not covered; restricted to a maximum of 2 children.
  • Contribution to NPS Tier-II account [notified u/s 80CCD] for a fixed period of not less than 3 years, by a Central Government employee.

Notes: (1) Deduction is not available against short-term capital gain u/s 111A and long-term capital gain. (2) Cash basis: the amount is allowed only on a payment basis — amounts due but unpaid by year-end are not eligible, even under the mercantile system of accounting.

Deduction u/s 80C = Minimum of — (a) Aggregate of eligible contributions/investments/expenditure; or (b) ₹ 1,50,000

Lock-in period: Life insurance policy — cannot be surrendered until 2 years' premium is paid. Housing loan — property cannot be transferred before 5 years from end of the financial year of possession. ULIP — participation cannot cease before 5 years' contribution is paid. Shares/debentures of infrastructure/power company or mutual fund — cannot be transferred within 3 years of allotment. Senior Citizen Savings Scheme / Post Office Time Deposit — cannot be withdrawn before 5 years (except on death of assessee, to nominee/legal heir). Consequence of violation: the entire deduction earlier allowed becomes taxable income in the year of default.

3.3.3 Deduction u/s 80CCC — Contribution to Pension Fund

Not available under the default tax regime

Applicable to: An individual (irrespective of residential status or citizenship), who during the previous year paid/deposited a sum under an annuity plan of LIC or any other insurer for receiving pension from the fund referred to in Sec. 10(23AAB), out of income chargeable to tax (need not relate to the current year).

Deduction u/s 80CCC = Minimum of — (a) Amount deposited; or (b) ₹ 1,50,000

Other points: Interest/bonus accrued on the fund is not eligible for deduction. Amount received as pension or on surrender [Sec. 80CCC(2)] is taxable in the year of receipt (including any interest/bonus received). Deduction u/s 80C is not available for an amount already claimed u/s 80CCC [Sec. 80CCC(3)].

3.3.4 Deduction u/s 80CCD — Contribution to Pension Scheme

Sec. 80CCD(1) and 80CCD(1B): Not available under default tax regime   Sec. 80CCD(2): Available under both tax regimes

Applicable to: An individual who, during the previous year, paid/deposited any amount in his account under a pension scheme notified by the Central Government (Atal Pension Yojna).

80CCD(1) — Salaried individual: Lower of (a) Amount paid/deposited, or (b) 10% of salary¹ for the previous year.

80CCD(1) — Any other individual: Lower of (a) Amount paid/deposited, or (b) 20% of Gross Total Income for the previous year.

80CCD(2) — Employer's contribution: whole of employer's contribution, up to a maximum of 10% of salary¹ (14% where contributed by Central/State Govt.); where the assessee is under the default regime, employer's contribution up to 14% of salary is allowed.

80CCD(1B) — Additional deduction for NPS/NPS Vatsalya contribution (over and above 80CCD(1)): Lower of (a) contribution, or (b) ₹ 50,000.

¹ "Salary" here means Basic + Dearness Allowance, if the terms of employment so provide.

RegimeGovernment EmployeeNon-Government Employee
Default regime14% of salary14% of salary
Old regime14% of salary10% of salary

Maximum deduction u/s 80CCD(2), by regime and employer type

Exemption on withdrawal: As per Sec. 10(12A), on closure/opting out of the NPS, 60% of the total amount payable is exempt (i.e., 40% is taxable). As per Sec. 10(12B)/(2BA), partial withdrawal up to 25% of the assessee's own contribution (or NPS Vatsalya) is fully exempt; the amount received on closure of an NPS Vatsalya account due to the minor's death is not deemed income of the parent/guardian. Amount used to purchase an annuity plan in the same year of withdrawal is not taxable. Amount received by the nominee on the death of the assessee is exempt in the nominee's hands.

Where any amount paid/deposited has been allowed as deduction u/s 80CCD, no deduction for the same amount is allowed u/s 80C.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: THE ₹1,50,000 CEILING DOESN'T CATCH EVERYTHING

THE TRAP: Students cap the entire 80C + 80CCC + 80CCD deduction (including employer's contribution and the additional NPS deduction) at ₹1,50,000.

THE TWIST: Sec. 80CCE's ₹1,50,000 ceiling applies only to 80C + 80CCC + 80CCD(1) (own contribution). Employer's contribution u/s 80CCD(2) (10%/14% of salary) and the additional ₹50,000 NPS deduction u/s 80CCD(1B) sit outside and above this ceiling — see Illustration 24, where total deduction reaches ₹1,95,000 even though the 80CCE-capped slice is only ₹1,50,000.

Deduction u/s 80CCH — Contribution to Agnipath Scheme

80CCH(1): Not available under the default tax regime   80CCH(2): Available under both tax regimes

Applicable to: Individual assessee enrolled in the Agnipath Scheme and subscribing to the Agniveer Corpus Fund, where he and/or the Central Government has contributed to his account in the Fund during the previous year.

ContributionOld RegimeDefault Regime
Own contribution to the corpusAmount so contributedNot available
Contribution by Central GovernmentAmount so contributedAmount so contributed

Taxpoint: The Central Government's contribution is included in the assessee's salary, but deduction u/s 80CCH(2) is available for the same amount. Payment from the Agniveer Corpus Fund to the enrolled person or nominee is exempt u/s 10(12C). Agnipath is a Central Government scheme (launched 2022) for enrolling Indian youth into the Armed Forces; the Agniveer Corpus Fund holds consolidated contributions of Agniveers plus matching Central Government contributions, with interest on both.

3.3.6 Deduction u/s 80D — Medical Insurance Premium

Not available under the default tax regime

Applicable to: An individual or HUF (irrespective of residential status/citizenship), for payment of health insurance/medical check-up as follows.

CategoryAssesseeExpenditure on behalf ofQuantum of deduction
1IndividualHimself/herself, spouse, or dependent childrenLower of — aggregate of (premium + Central Govt./notified health scheme contribution + preventive health check-up up to ₹5,000); or ₹25,000 p.a. (₹50,000 if the insured is a senior citizen)
2IndividualParents (dependent or not)Lower of — aggregate of (premium + preventive health check-up up to ₹5,000); or ₹25,000 p.a. (₹50,000 if the insured parent is a senior citizen)
3HUFAny member of the familyLower of premium paid, or ₹25,000 (₹50,000 if insured member is a senior citizen)
4Individual/HUFMedical expenditure (mediclaim not taken) on self/spouse/dependent children/parents (Individual) or any family member (HUF), who is a senior citizenLower of medical expenditure incurred, or ₹50,000

The deduction for preventive health check-up (self, spouse, dependent children, parents together) does not exceed ₹5,000 in aggregate, subject to the overall ₹25,000/₹50,000 limit. Category 4 is available only within the overall limit of Category 1/2/3 respectively — so maximum deduction under (1+4), (2+4), and (3+4) is ₹50,000 each.

Dependent children: children whose own resources are not sufficient to support them.

Other conditions: (i) Mode of payment — any mode other than cash (cash allowed only for preventive health check-up). (ii) Payment must be out of taxable income (need not relate to the current year). (iii) Lump-sum premium covering more than a year is allowed proportionately (total premium ÷ number of years).

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: "SENIOR CITIZEN" REFERS TO THE INSURED, NOT THE PAYER

THE TRAP: Students assume the assessee himself must be 60+ to claim the enhanced ₹50,000 limit.

THE TWIST: For claiming the higher ₹50,000 deduction under 80D (and, identically, 80DDB), the payer need not be a senior citizen — the person insured/treated must be. A senior citizen is a resident individual aged 60 years or more at any time in the relevant previous year.

3.3.7 Deduction u/s 80DD — Maintenance of Dependant Disabled Relative

Not available under the default tax regime

Applicable to: A resident individual (irrespective of citizenship) or resident HUF, having a dependant disabled relative (Individual: spouse, children, parents, brothers, sisters; HUF: any member) who wholly/mainly depends on the assessee for support, and where the disabled relative has not claimed benefit u/s 80U.

The assessee must either incur expenditure for medical treatment (incl. nursing)/training/rehabilitation of the dependant, or pay/deposit an amount in an approved LIC/insurer/UTI scheme for the dependant's maintenance. The deduction is statutory — not linked to actual expenditure incurred. A medical certificate from the prescribed medical authority must be filed with the return of income (re-filed on expiry/reassessment).

Relative suffering from severe disability (80% or more): ₹ 1,25,000

Relative suffering from disability but not severe (40% or more but less than 80%): ₹ 75,000

Sec. 80DD(3): Where the assessee deposited in an annuity plan for the disabled dependant's benefit and the dependant predeceases the assessee, the amount received from the annuity plan is deemed the assessee's income in the year of receipt — unless received by the dependant himself, before death, on attaining 60 years and discontinuation of the scheme.

3.3.8 Deduction u/s 80DDB — Medical Treatment of Specified Diseases

Not available under default tax regime

Applicable to: A resident individual or resident HUF who actually paid for medical treatment of a specified disease/ailment (rule 11DD) — for self or dependant relative (Individual: spouse, children, parents, brothers, sisters; HUF: any member) — on prescription from a neurologist/oncologist/urologist/haematologist/immunologist or other prescribed specialist.

General: Minimum of — (a) Actual expenditure incurred; or (b) ₹ 40,000

Where expenditure is for a senior citizen: enhanced ceiling of ₹ 1,00,000 (payer need not be a senior citizen; the patient must be).

Deduction is reduced by any amount received under an insurance policy or reimbursed by an employer for the treatment — in no case can the total deduction exceed ₹1,00,000.

Specified diseases (Rule 11DD): (1) Neurological diseases with 40%+ disability — Dementia, Dystonia Musculorum Deformans, Motor Neuron Disease, Ataxia, Chorea, Hemiballismus, Aphasia, Parkinson's Disease; (2) Cancer; (3) Full-blown AIDS; (4) Chronic Renal Failure; (5) Hemophilia; (6) Thalassaemia.

S — brother (88) is a resident senior citizen, but actual expenditure (₹72,000) is below the ₹1,00,000 cap, so deduction = actual expenditure. T — ₹40,000 general cap reduced by ₹8,000 mediclaim received = ₹32,000.

Note: If the assessee is under the default tax regime, deduction u/s 80DDB is not available.

3.3.9 Deduction u/s 80E — Interest on Loan for Higher Education

Not available under default tax regime

Applicable to: An individual (any residential status/citizenship) who took a loan from a financial institution (a banking company under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, or other specified institution) or an approved charitable institution (u/s 10(23C) or Sec. 80G(2)(a)), for pursuing higher education of himself, spouse, children (dependent or not), or a student for whom he is legal guardian. "Higher education" means any course of study after passing the Senior Secondary Examination (or equivalent) recognised by a Government/local/other authorised authority.

Deduction u/s 80E = Amount of interest actually paid during the year (no monetary ceiling).

Available for the initial assessment year + 7 immediately succeeding assessment years, or until interest is paid in full, whichever is earlier — i.e., a maximum of 8 consecutive years, starting from the year repayment of interest begins.

3.3.10 Deduction u/s 80EE — Interest on Loan for Residential House Property

Not available under the default tax regime

Applicable to: Individual (resident or non-resident) where — loan for acquiring a residential house property; sanctioned by a financial institution during P.Y. 2016-17; loan sanctioned amount does not exceed ₹35 lakhs; value of the property does not exceed ₹50 lakhs; and assessee owns no other residential house property on the date of sanction.

Deduction u/s 80EE = Minimum of — (a) Interest on loan payable for the previous year; or (b) ₹ 50,000.

Double deduction is not available — interest allowed here cannot also be claimed under any other provision. It is irrelevant whether the interest pertains to the pre-construction or post-construction period.

Deduction u/s 80EEA = Minimum of — (a) Interest on loan payable for the previous year; or (b) ₹ 1,50,000.

Not available under the default tax regime

Deduction u/s 80EEB = Minimum of — (a) Interest on loan payable for the previous year; or (b) ₹ 1,50,000.

Double deduction is not available under any other provision for interest already claimed here.

3.3.13 Deduction u/s 80G — Donations to Certain Funds, etc.

Not available under the default tax regime

Applicable to: All assessees (irrespective of residential status/citizenship), for donation (not in kind) to specified funds/organisations, subject to conditions: (1) donation in kind does not qualify; (2) donation in excess of ₹2,000 must be made by any mode other than cash (cash up to ₹2,000 qualifies); (3) proof of donation, in original, must be attached to the return.

Deduction u/s 80G = (100% or 50% of donation to Category A organizations) + (100% or 50% of donation to Category B organizations, subject to the 10%-of-Adjusted-GTI limit)

Adjusted GTI = Gross Total Income − Long-term capital gain − STCG covered u/s 111A − All deductions u/s 80C to 80U (other than 80G) − Income referred u/s 115A, 115AB, 115AC, etc. (Casual income like lottery winnings is included in Adjusted GTI.)

Category A (Items 1-23 — the 10% limit does NOT apply) vs Category B (Items 24-30 — the 10% limit DOES apply). Deduction under Sec. 80G(5) donee institutions (Category B, 50% rate) is allowed only on the basis of information furnished by the institution to the tax authority, subject to risk-based verification.

3.3.14 Deduction u/s 80GG — House Rent Paid

Not available under the default tax regime

Applicable to: An individual, where — he does not receive exempt HRA; he/spouse/minor child/his HUF owns no self-occupied residential property at the place of employment/business/profession; he has not claimed self-occupied treatment u/s 23(2)(a)/23(4)(a) for a house at any other place; and a declaration in Form 10BA is filed for the rent paid (residential house, furnished or unfurnished).

Deduction u/s 80GG = Minimum of — (i) ₹ 5,000 per month; (ii) 25% of Adjusted GTI for the year; or (iii) Rent paid − 10% of Adjusted GTI

Adjusted GTI = GTI − LTCG − STCG u/s 111A − all deductions u/s 80's other than 80GG − income u/s 115A/115AB/115AC, etc. (casual income is included).

Where the employer provides accommodation at a concessional rent, the rent actually paid by the assessee is both (a) deducted while valuing the perquisite, and (b) separately eligible for deduction u/s 80GG.

3.3.15 Deduction u/s 80GGA — Donations for Scientific Research, Rural Development, etc.

Not available under the default tax regime

Applicable to: An assessee having no income under "Profits & gains of business or profession," who paid a sum for — rural development (approved association/institution or notified Rural Development Fund), poverty eradication (notified National Urban Poverty Eradication Fund), scientific research (association/university/college/institution approved u/s 35(1)(ii)), social science/statistical research (u/s 35(1)(iii)), or other eligible projects approved by the National Committee (u/s 35AC(2)(a)). Payment in excess of ₹2,000 must be by a mode other than cash.

Deduction u/s 80GGA = 100% of the amount actually paid (fully deductible).

Deduction is not denied merely because approval/notification is subsequently withdrawn. Claims are subject to risk-based verification of information furnished by the payee.

3.3.16 & 3.3.17 Deductions for Contribution to Political Parties — Sec. 80GGB and 80GGC

Sec. 80GGBSec. 80GGC
Applicable toAn Indian company (not opting for Sec. 115BAA or 115BAB)All assessees except local authority and every artificial juridical person wholly/partly funded by Government. Not available under default regime for individual/HUF/AOP/BOI; not available if a co-operative society opts for Sec. 115BAD or 115BAE
ConditionContribution (by any mode other than cash) during the previous year, to any political party or an electoral trust
Quantum100% of such contribution made during the previous year

Taxpoint (80GGB): "Contribute" also deems as contribution — (a) a donation/subscription/payment given to a person for an activity likely to affect public support for a political party; (b) expenditure on advertisement in a souvenir/brochure/tract/pamphlet by or for a political party. There is a specific disallowance u/s 37(2B) for such advertisement expenditure while computing business income/GTI — but the same expenditure is separately allowable as a deduction from GTI under Sec. 80GGB.

3.3.18–3.3.24 Profit-linked deductions for industrial undertakings/enterprises [Sec. 80-IA, 80-IAB, 80-IAC, 80-IB, 80-IBA, 80-IE, 80JJA]

This cluster of deductions (typically for companies/enterprises, examined mainly for their identifying conditions, quantum %, and deduction period) shares several common "Other Points" across sections — return of income filed within the due date u/s 139(1); an audit report/certificate (Form 10CCB or as specified) furnished one month before the due date of filing return; the Assessing Officer's power to recompute profit where goods/services are transferred between an eligible and a non-eligible unit otherwise than at market value (Sec. 80A inter-unit transfer rule; arm's length price where a specified domestic transaction u/s 92BA is involved); double deduction is not allowed; and no deduction unless claimed in the return of income.

3.3.25 Deduction u/s 80JJAA — Employment of New Workmen

Available under both tax regimes

Applicable to: Any assessee subject to tax audit u/s 44AB, where the business is not formed by splitting up/reconstruction of an existing business (subject to the Sec. 33B natural-calamity exception) or acquired by transfer/business reorganisation, and the audit report is submitted one month before the due date of return filing. No deduction is allowed unless claimed in the return.

Deduction u/s 80JJAA = 30% of additional employee cost incurred during the previous year, for 3 assessment years including the year the employment is provided.

Additional employee excludes: an employee with emoluments exceeding ₹25,000 per month; one whose entire contribution is Government-paid under the Employees' Pension Scheme; one employed for less than 240 days (150 days for apparel/footwear/leather manufacturing) during the previous year (unless carried into the following year); and one who does not participate in the recognised provident fund. Emoluments exclude employer's contribution to pension/PF/other funds and lump-sum termination/superannuation/VRS payments (gratuity, severance pay, leave encashment, etc.). For an existing business, additional employee cost is Nil if there is no net increase in employee headcount, or if emoluments are not paid via account payee cheque/draft/ECS/specified electronic modes.

3.3.26 Deduction u/s 80LA — Certain Incomes of Offshore Banking Units

Applicable to: A scheduled bank owning an offshore banking unit (OBU) in an SEZ, any foreign-incorporated bank with an OBU in an SEZ, or a Unit of an International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) — with a certificate of a chartered accountant (Form 10CCF) and copy of the relevant permission/registration furnished with the return of income.

IFSC Unit: 100% of income for any 10 consecutive assessment years (assessee's option) out of 15, from the year permission/registration is obtained.

Any other case: 100% of income for the first 10 consecutive years from the year permission u/s 23(1)(a) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (or SEBI Act/other relevant law registration) is obtained.

Eligible income includes: income from an OBU in an SEZ; banking business (Sec. 6(1), Banking Regulation Act) with an SEZ undertaking; IFSC Unit business income; and income from transfer of an aircraft/ship leased by the unit (where the unit commenced operations on or before 31-03-2025).

3.3.27 Deduction u/s 80M — Inter-Corporate Dividend

Applicable to: A domestic company whose GTI includes dividend income from any other domestic/foreign company or a business trust, and which distributes dividend to its own shareholders within the due date (one month before the due date for furnishing the return of income).

Deduction u/s 80M = Minimum of — (a) Dividend received by the assessee; or (b) Dividend distributed by the assessee within the due date.

No double deduction: once allowed for a distributed dividend amount in one previous year, that amount cannot be claimed again in any other year.

3.3.28 Deduction u/s 80QQB — Royalty Income of Authors of Books

Not available under the default tax regime

Applicable to: A resident individual (any citizenship), being an author/joint author of a book of a literary, artistic, or scientific nature (excludes brochures, commentaries, diaries, guides, magazines, journals, newspapers, pamphlets, school textbooks, tracts, etc.), whose GTI includes a lump-sum consideration for assignment of copyright, or royalty/copyright fees, earned in India or from a source outside India.

For income earned outside India: it must be remitted to India in convertible foreign exchange within 6 months of the end of the previous year (or such further period as allowed), with a certificate in Form 10H. A certificate in Form 10CCD from the payer must accompany the return.

Lump-sum consideration for all rights: Minimum of — (a) 100% of such income; or (b) ₹ 3,00,000

Royalty/fee not exceeding 15% of book value: Minimum of — (a) 100% of such income; or (b) ₹ 3,00,000

Royalty/fee exceeding 15% of book value: Minimum of — (a) 100% of income re-computed by capping royalty at 15% of book value sold; or (b) ₹ 3,00,000

In all non-lump-sum cases, expenditure attributable to such income is first deducted from the receipts before applying the ceiling; for income earned outside India, substitute "money brought into India within the time limit" for "income earned."

Double deduction is not allowed; return of income must be filed on time; no deduction unless claimed in the return.

3.3.30 Deduction u/s 80RRB — Royalty on Patents

Not available under the default tax regime

Applicable to: A resident individual (any citizenship), being a patentee (true and first inventor, entered on the Patent register as owner/co-owner under the Patents Act, 1970), earning royalty (in India or outside India) for a patent registered on or after 1-4-2003. Royalty includes consideration for transfer of rights/licence, imparting information on the patent's working/use, use of the patent, or related services (incl. non-refundable advance royalty) — but excludes any capital sum on sale of the patent (taxable as capital gains) or consideration for sale of a product/article made using the patented process (commercial use).

Foreign-sourced income must be remitted in convertible foreign exchange within 6 months of year-end (Form 10H); a certificate in Form 10CCE from the Controller of Patents accompanies the return.

Income earned in India: Minimum of — (a) 100% of such income; or (b) ₹ 3,00,000

Income earned outside India: Minimum of — (a) money brought into India within the prescribed time; or (b) ₹ 3,00,000

Where a compulsory licence is granted under the Patents Act, 1970, the deduction cannot exceed the royalty settled by the Controller under that licence.

If the patent is later revoked and the assessee disqualified as patentee, the earlier deduction is deemed wrongly allowed, and the Assessing Officer may rectify the assessment within 4 years from the end of the previous year of revocation. Double deduction is not allowed.

3.3.31 & 3.3.32 Deduction on Interest on Deposits — Sec. 80TTA and 80TTB

Not available under the default tax regime (both sections)

Sec. 80TTASec. 80TTB
Applicable toIndividual (other than a senior citizen covered u/s 80TTB), or HUFSenior Citizen
Eligible interestInterest on deposits (not time deposits) in a savings account with a banking company, a co-operative society carrying on banking business (incl. co-operative land mortgage/development bank), or a Post OfficeInterest on deposits (savings and other deposits) with a banking company, a co-operative society carrying on banking business, or a Post Office
QuantumMinimum of — interest on such savings deposits, or ₹ 10,000Minimum of — interest on such deposits, or ₹ 50,000
Firm/AOP/BOI depositsNo deduction where the deposit is held by/on behalf of a firm, AOP, or BOI, in computing the total income of any partner/member

Note (80TTA): As per Notification No. 32/2011 (03-06-2011), interest on Post Office Savings Bank accounts is separately exempt u/s 10(15)(i) up to ₹3,500 (single account) / ₹7,000 (joint account) — this exemption operates before the 80TTA deduction is even considered.

3.3.33 Deduction u/s 80U — Person with Disability

Not available under the default tax regime

Applicable to: A resident individual (any citizenship) certified by the medical authority, at any time during the previous year, as a person with disability, who furnishes the certificate (prescribed form) with the return of income for the relevant assessment year.

Severe disability (80% or more): ₹ 1,25,000

Disability but not severe (40% or more but less than 80%): ₹ 75,000

Deduction is statutory, irrespective of actual expenditure. As with 80DD, a new medical certificate is required after expiry/reassessment of a prior certificate.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: 80DD vs 80U

THE TRAP: Students confuse the two disability sections and claim both for the same disability, or claim 80DD for the assessee's own disability.

THE TWIST: Sec. 80U is for a disability of the assessee himself (self); Sec. 80DD is for maintenance of a dependant disabled relative. The two can be claimed together in the same return for different persons (see Illustration 33, where Mr. X claims 80U for himself and 80DD for his dependant, disabled Mrs. X) — but 80DD is specifically barred if the disabled relative has separately claimed 80U for himself.

ILLUSTRATION 33 — Total income of Mr. X, Old Regime

Mr. X suffers low vision (certified severe disability). Net Salary ₹1,45,000; STCG ₹45,000; LTCG ₹1,50,000. Mrs. X, suffering leprosy (certified 50% disability), is fully dependant on Mr. X.

Computation of total income of Mr. X for A.Y. 2026-27
ParticularsAmount (₹)
Salaries1,45,000
Short-term capital gains45,000
Long-term capital gains1,50,000
Gross Total Income3,40,000
Less: 80DD (relative with disability, not severe)75,000
Less: 80U (assessee, severe disability)1,25,000
Total Income1,50,000

Both 80DD (₹75,000, dependant Mrs. X) and 80U (₹1,25,000, Mr. X himself) can be set off only against Salaries of ₹1,45,000 + whatever remaining GTI is available, not against LTCG/STCG covered u/s 111A. Total deduction here is capped by the basic rule at GTI excluding LTCG/STCG — i.e., against Salaries of ₹1,45,000 alone, but the illustration allows the full ₹1,90,000 since Total Income after deduction (₹1,50,000) is still positive within the LTCG/STCG portion left untouched.

Answer: Total Income = ₹1,50,000.

CONCEPT

3.3.34 Relief u/s 89 — Arrear/Advance Salary, Gratuity, Commuted Pension, etc.

When an assessee is charged for arrear or advance salary, or gratuity/commuted pension (profit in lieu of salary u/s 17(3)), or arrear family pension, he may fall into a higher tax slab than if the amount had been taxed in the year it related to (e.g., 20% instead of 30%). To compensate the assessee for this higher rate caused purely by the timing of receipt, Sec. 89(1) provides "Relief."

Applicable to: An assessee who receives — (a) arrear salary or advance salary, or otherwise receives salary for more than 12 months in one financial year; or (b) profit in lieu of salary u/s 17(3), e.g. gratuity, commuted pension; or (c) family pension paid in arrears. An assessee who receives leave encashment during continuation of service can also claim relief u/s 89.

Conditions: Due to such receipt, total income is assessed at a higher rate than it would otherwise have been; and the assessee has made an application to the Assessing Officer.

Quantum of relief: as computed under Rule 21A.

Method of computation — Rule 21A

Relief where salary/family pension is received in arrears or advance
StepParticulars
1Calculate tax for the previous year of receipt, on: (a) total income including additional salary; (b) total income excluding additional salary
2Calculate tax for the previous year to which the additional salary relates, on: (a) total income including additional salary; (b) total income excluding additional salary
3(a) Tax on receipt basis = Tax at 1(a) + Tax at 2(b); (b) Tax on accrual basis = Tax at 1(b) + Tax at 2(a)
4Relief u/s 89 = Tax on receipt basis − Tax on accrual basis

Relief when payment is taxable gratuity

Where past services extend over 15 years
StepParticulars
1Calculate total income and tax liability, considering the taxable gratuity of the relevant previous year
2Calculate total income and tax for each of the 3 previous years immediately preceding, adding 1/3rd of the taxable gratuity in each of those 3 years
3Average rate of tax (%) = (Tax + surcharge + cess after rebate of the respective year × 100) ÷ Total Income, for each year
4Calculate the average of the "average rate of tax" of the 3 preceding years
5Tax on taxable gratuity by applying the relevant previous year's average rate
6Tax on taxable gratuity by applying the average of average rates (Step 4)
7Relief u/s 89 = Tax as per Step 5 − Tax as per Step 6

Where past services extend over 5 to 15 years: same method, but the average rate is computed over the 2 immediately preceding years (not 3), and the taxable gratuity is apportioned into those 2 years (not 3).

Where past services do not extend over 5 years: Relief u/s 89 is not applicable.

Relief for compensation on termination of employment / commutation of pension

Compensation on termination: eligible for relief u/s 89 if — employment was terminated after continuous service of not less than 3 years, and the unexpired portion of the term of employment is also not less than 3 years. The calculation method mirrors the gratuity method for service extending over 15 years. However, where the assessee claims exemption u/s 10(10C) for the same compensation, relief u/s 89 is not available for it.

Commutation of pension: calculated the same way as gratuity where service extends over 15 years.

Other payments: in any other case, the Board may grant relief after examining the facts of the case.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: RELIEF u/s 89 IS NOT A DEDUCTION FROM INCOME

THE TRAP: Students subtract the "relief" figure from Total Income, treating it like a Chapter VI-A deduction.

THE TWIST: Relief u/s 89 is a reduction in tax liability, computed as (Tax on receipt basis − Tax on accrual basis) or (Tax at current year's average rate − Tax at the average of preceding years' average rate) — never a reduction to Total Income itself. It is deducted after the tax on Total Income (and after cess, per Illustration 37) has been computed, not before.

Applicable to: Individual / HUF / AOP / BOI / AJP. Under this section income tax is computed, at the option of the assessee, considering the special conditions and rate below.
