(ii) Without set-off of any loss: (a) brought forward loss/depreciation from an earlier A.Y. attributable to any of the deductions blocked above; (b) loss under "Income from house property" against any other head.

  • Basic exemption: ₹4,00,000 for every category of individual — senior citizen, super senior citizen and others alike — if this regime is opted.
  • Rebate u/s 87A: available to a resident individual whose total income does not exceed ₹12,00,000; marginal relief applies if income marginally exceeds ₹12,00,000. Rebate is not available against tax computed at any special rate.
  • Computed tax is further increased by applicable surcharge (subject to a maximum of 25%) and Health & Education cess.
  • Income taxable at a special rate u/s 110 to 115BBG [except 115BAC(1A)] is taxed at that special rate; rebate u/s 87A is not available against such tax.

Other points: Full effect of blocked loss/depreciation is deemed given — no further deduction is allowed in any subsequent year (block-of-asset WDV as on 01-04-2020 is adjusted where full effect wasn't given before A.Y. 2021-22). House Property loss cannot be carried forward.

Exercise of option [where person has business/profession income]Timing
Has income from business or professionWithin the due date u/s 139(1) for that A.Y.; once exercised, applies to subsequent A.Y.s.
Does not have such incomeAlong with the return u/s 139(1) for that A.Y.
Option to opt for OLD regime [Sec. 115BAC(6)]Timing
Person without business/profession incomeAlong with the return u/s 139(1); may pay under old regime one year and shift out in another year (freely, year to year).
Person with business/profession incomeWithin the due date u/s 139(1); once exercised, applies to subsequent A.Y.s. Withdrawal of this option is allowed only once, reverting to the default regime u/s 115BAC(1A) for a year other than the year of withdrawal — thereafter never eligible to opt out again, except on ceasing to have any business income.

Alternate Minimum Tax: where tax is computed as per Sec. 115BAC(1A), AMT u/s 115JC does not apply, and no AMT credit can be adjusted against tax computed u/s 115BAC(1A).

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SWITCHING BETWEEN REGIMES ISN'T A YEARLY FREEBIE FOR BUSINESS ASSESSEES

THE TRAP: students assume every individual/HUF can freely flip between the default regime and the old regime every single year, as if it were a checkbox on the return.

THE TWIST: that free-flip only applies to a person without business/profession income. A person with business/profession income who opts for the old regime u/s 115BAC(6) is locked in for subsequent years, may withdraw that option only once (reverting to default regime), and can never opt out of the default regime again thereafter — unless the business income itself ceases.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: REBATE u/s 87A DOES NOT TOUCH SPECIAL-RATE INCOME

THE TRAP: students compute total tax (slab tax + tax on casual income/LTCG/STCG at special rates) and apply the full ₹87A rebate against that combined figure whenever total income is within the rebate limit.

THE TWIST: rebate u/s 87A is available only against tax computed at slab rate — never against tax on casual income (30%), LTCG, STCG u/s 111A, or any other special-rate income. Illustration 36 (default regime) and Illustration 39/40 both show the special-rate tax surviving untouched even where slab-rate tax is fully wiped out by the rebate.

3.4.2 Alternate Minimum Tax (AMT) [Sec. 115JC] ★★ MEDIUM

Applicable to: all assessees (other than a company) who have claimed deduction under Sec. 80H to 80RRB (other than 80P), Sec. 10AA, or Sec. 35AD.

Exception: does not apply to an individual, HUF, AOP, BOI, or AJP if adjusted total income does not exceed ₹20 lakh.

  • The ₹20-lakh exception does not apply to a Firm or LLP — AMT applies to them (if claiming the above deductions) even below ₹20 lakh.
  • AMT applies only where the assessee is taxable under the old tax regime [i.e. exercised the option under Sec. 115BAC or 115BAC(6)]. If taxable under the default regime, AMT does not apply.
  • AMT does not apply to a co-operative society paying tax under Sec. 115BAE(5).
  • Not applicable to the specified fund referred to in clause (c) of the Explanation to Sec. 10(4D).

Scheme of AMT: Step 1 — Regular income tax liability before cess (A). Step 2 — Adjusted Total Income = Total Income (B) + deduction u/s 80H–80RRB other than 80P (C) + deduction u/s 35AD less depreciation u/s 32 (D) + deduction u/s 10AA (E) = (F). Step 3 — AMT = F × 18.5% (G). Step 4 — Income Tax liability = Higher of A & G, plus Health & Education Cess.

If C, D and E are all zero, AMT provisions don't apply at all. If F does not exceed ₹20 lakh, AMT does not apply to an Individual/HUF/AOP/BOI/AJP — but the provision still applies to an LLP/Firm regardless.

Where AMT applies (Step 3 value > Step 1 value): (a) Adjusted Total Income (Step 2) is deemed the assessee's total income; (b) tax liability = 18.5% (+ surcharge + cess) of adjusted total income.

AssesseeRate of AMT
Unit in an International Financial Services Centre, income solely in convertible foreign exchange9%
Co-operative society15%
Other (general rule)18.5%

A report in Form 29C from a Chartered Accountant must be uploaded one month prior to the due date of furnishing the return u/s 139(1). All other provisions of the Act — advance tax, interest, etc. — apply to such an assessee as usual.

Tax credit for Alternate Minimum Tax [Sec. 115JD]

  • The excess of AMT paid over the regular income-tax payable for that year is allowed as tax credit: Tax credit = Tax paid u/s 115JC – Regular Tax payable. No interest is payable on this credit.
  • The credit is carried forward and set off, but not beyond the 15th assessment year immediately succeeding the year in which the credit becomes allowable.
  • Set-off is allowed in a year when regular tax becomes payable, limited to the difference between AMT payable for that year and the balance credit — i.e. after set-off, tax liability for the year can never fall below that year's AMT.
  • Where foreign tax credit u/s 90/90A/91 allowed against AMT exceeds the credit admissible against regular tax, the excess is ignored while computing the Sec. 115JD credit.
  • If regular tax or AMT is revised by any order under the Act, the tax credit is varied accordingly.
  • Where the assessee computes tax under Sec. 115BAC(1A) (default regime) or Sec. 115BAE, brought-forward AMT credit cannot be adjusted.

EXAMPLES — AMT credit mechanics

(a) AMT liability ₹500; Regular tax liability ₹1,000.

Answer: ₹500 cannot be treated as credit — AMT liability is not greater than regular tax liability, so Sec. 115JC isn't even triggered that year.

(b) Year 1: AMT ₹2,000, Regular tax ₹1,000 → ₹1,000 credit carried forward.
Year 2: AMT ₹2,500, Regular tax ₹5,000 → difference ₹2,500; since regular liability now exceeds AMT, the carried-forward credit sets off to the extent of that difference, i.e. ₹2,500 (but only ₹1,000 credit exists, so only ₹1,000 is set off).

Year 2 — Tax Payable
ParticularsAmount
Regular Tax Liability5,000
Less: Set off of AMT credit1,000
Tax payable (before surcharge and cess)4,000

If the carried-forward credit had instead been ₹3,500: set-off is restricted to the permissible difference of ₹2,500 (Regular Tax ₹5,000 – AMT ₹2,500), leaving tax payable ₹2,500 and a balance credit of ₹1,000 (₹3,500 – ₹2,500) carried forward further. In other words, the excess of regular tax over AMT is the maximum set-off permissible in any year.

CONCEPT

Hindu Undivided Family (HUF)

3.4.4 Meaning of HUF: the term "Hindu Undivided Family" (or "Joint Hindu Family") is not defined in the Income-tax Act — it carries the same meaning as under Hindu law.

A Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) consists of all persons lineally descended from a common ancestor, including their wives and unmarried daughters.

Taxpoint: only those undivided families to which Hindu law applies are covered.

  • An HUF is not the creation of a contract — membership arises from status.
  • Jain families are treated as HUF for Income-tax purposes; a Muslim undivided family cannot be so treated.
  • Once a family is assessed as an HUF, it continues to be assessed as such until its partition.

3.4.5 Essential requirements of an HUF

1. Joint family property: ancestral property, or property acquired with the aid of ancestral property. Ancestral property is inherited from any of three immediate male ancestors — father, grandfather, or great-grandfather.

  • Property inherited from any other person (father-in-law, uncle, etc.) is not ancestral property.
  • Income of ancestral property is taxable as HUF income for: widow-mother and sons; husband and wife with no child; two or more brothers; uncle and nephew; mother, son and son's wife; a male and his late brother's wife.

2. Coparcener: a person who (a) acquires by birth an interest in joint family property, and (b) has the right to enforce partition.

Member of HUFCoparcener
Every coparcener must be a member of the family.A member may or may not be a coparcener — all coparceners are members, but not all members are coparceners.
May acquire membership in HUF otherwise than by birth.Acquires interest in HUF property by birth.
A member who is not a coparcener has no right to claim partition.Has the right to enforce partition. Taxpoint: a child in the mother's womb is entitled to a share of HUF property on partition.

3.4.6 School of Hindu Law

FeatureDayabhaga SchoolMitakshara School
Applicable toWest Bengal and AssamRest of India
Interest in propertyA child acquires interest in ancestral property only after the father's death.A child acquires interest in ancestral property as soon as he is born.
Right to claim partitionSon has no interest in ancestral property till father is alive, so cannot claim partition till then. Taxpoint: Father has an absolute right to dispose of family property.Son acquires interest by birth, so can claim partition at any time.
Fluctuation in coparcenary interestDoes not fluctuate on every birth/death of a male member — fluctuates only on the father's death.Fluctuates on every birth or death of a male member.
After the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005, a daughter (like a son) of a coparcener becomes a coparcener by birth in her own right and can demand partition of coparcenary property.

3.4.7 Computation of total income and tax liability of HUF

There is no specific provision in the Income-tax Act for computing HUF's total income — it is computed in the same manner as an individual.

ItemTreatment for HUF
Tax rate, Health & Education cessSame as an individual.
Computation under various headsAs usual — except HUF cannot have any income under "Salaries."
Clubbing of incomeAs usual; Sec. 64(1)/(1A) don't apply to HUF (they're individual-specific) — refer specially to Sec. 64(2).
Set-off & carry forward of lossesAs usual.
DeductionsAs per regime opted.
Advance taxAs in case of an individual.
Tax Regime u/s 115BAC(1A)/(6)Applicable.
  1. Remuneration to a member due to investment of HUF funds: where a joint fund is invested in a company/firm, fees or remuneration received by a member as director/partner by virtue of that investment is HUF income. If received by virtue of personal service rendered by the member, it is taxable in the member's own hands.
  2. Ancestral property income not always HUF income: under the Dayabhaga school, where the son has no right during the father's lifetime, income of ancestral property (father having no brother as coparcener) is the father's income, not the HUF's.
  3. Remuneration to Karta: genuine (not excessive) remuneration to the Karta for conducting HUF business is an allowable expenditure in the HUF's hands, provided paid under a bona fide agreement in the interest of the family business.
  4. Personal income of members: income acquired by a member in his personal capacity is not taxable in HUF's hands. Taxpoint: Stridhan is a woman's absolute property — income from it is not taxable in the hands of HUF.
  5. Income from impartible estate: though the estate belongs to the family, income from it is taxable in the hands of the holder of the estate, not the HUF.

3.4.8 Partition of HUF [Sec. 171]

CasePartition means
Where the property admits of physical divisionA physical division of the property. Taxpoint: mere division of income without physical division of the property is not deemed a partition.
Where the property does not admit of physical divisionSuch division as the property admits of. Taxpoint: mere severance of status is not deemed a partition.

Partial Partition is a partition that is partial as regards the persons constituting the HUF, or the properties belonging to it, or both.

CasePersons who can claim a share on partition
Any partitionAny coparcener; a child in the mother's womb at the time of partition.
Partition between sons after the father's deathMother gets an equal share to that of a son.
Partition between father and sonsWife gets an equal share to that of a son (apart from her share as husband's spouse).

3.4.9 Assessment after partition of a Hindu undivided family

An HUF assessed as such is deemed to continue as an HUF unless a finding of partition has been given under Sec. 171(1).

  1. Inquiry by AO [Sec. 171(2)]: where a member claims a total/partial partition has taken place, the AO makes an inquiry after notice to all family members.
  2. Record of findings [Sec. 171(3)]: on completing the inquiry, the AO records findings on whether a total/partial partition occurred and its date.
  3. Assessment up to the date of partition [Sec. 171(4)]: where a partition (during the previous year) is recorded, the HUF's total income up to the date of partition is assessed as if no partition had taken place, and each member is jointly and severally liable for tax on that income — liability of any member/group being computed per the portion of joint family property allotted to them at partition [Sec. 171(7)].
  4. Partition after expiry of the previous year [Sec. 171(5)]: total income of that previous year is assessed as if no partition had taken place.
  5. Notice of partition after assessment [Sec. 171(6)]: if the AO discovers a partition after completing HUF's assessment, tax is recovered from every person who was a member before partition, jointly and severally.
  6. Collection of penalty, interest, fine, etc. [Sec. 171(8)]: this section's provisions apply to levy/collection of penalty, interest, fine or other sums for the period up to the date of partition, just as they apply to tax.

Partial partition after 31-12-1978 [Sec. 171(9)]: where a partial partition takes place among HUF members after this date —

  • No claim of such partial partition shall be inquired into u/s 171(2), and no finding shall be recorded u/s 171(3).
  • The family continues to be assessed under the Act as if no such partial partition had taken place.
  • Each member/group of members immediately before the partial partition, and the family itself, are jointly and severally liable for any tax, penalty, interest, fine or other sum payable by the family — liability computed per the portion of property allotted at such partial partition — and this applies even to dues relating to the period before or after such partial partition.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: A "VALID" PARTIAL PARTITION UNDER HINDU LAW MAY BE TAX-INVISIBLE

THE TRAP: students treat any partial partition recognised under Hindu law as automatically splitting the HUF's tax assessment from that date onward.

THE TWIST: for a partial partition occurring after 31-12-1978, Sec. 171(9) bars the AO from even inquiring into or recording it — the family continues to be assessed as one HUF as if the partial partition never happened, while every member/group remains jointly and severally liable for the family's tax dues. Only a total partition (or a partial partition before that cut-off) gets AO recognition under Sec. 171.

CONCEPT

3.5 Advance Tax ★★★ HIGH

Ordinarily, tax on income earned in the previous year is paid in the corresponding assessment year. Under Advance Tax, an assessee must estimate the previous year's income and tax liability and pay tax on that estimate during the previous year itself — the scheme is built on "Pay as you earn." For instance, tax on income earned in P.Y. 2025-26 is ordinarily payable in A.Y. 2026-27, but under Advance Tax the assessee pays tax on the estimated income of P.Y. 2025-26 within that same previous year.

Applicable to: all assessees, irrespective of residential status and citizenship.

Scheme of Advance Tax [Sec. 208]: where the advance tax liability of the assessee is ₹10,000 or more, the assessee must pay such tax in the previous year itself, within the due dates u/s 211.

Advance tax liability [Sec. 209] — Estimated Gross Total Income; Less: Chapter VIA deductions as per regime opted = Estimated Total Income; Gross tax liability thereon; Less: Rebate u/s 87A as per regime opted = Tax liability after rebate; Add: Surcharge (if applicable) = Tax and surcharge payable; Add: Health & Education cess = Tax liability after cess; Less: TDS/TCS or other rebate & relief = Advance tax liability.

Due date of instalment [Sec. 211]

AssesseeDue date of instalmentMinimum amount payable (of advance tax liability)
Eligible assessee in respect of an eligible business u/s 44AD or 44ADAOn or before March 15100%
Other assesseeOn or before June 15Upto 15%
On or before September 15Upto 45%
On or before December 15Upto 75%
On or before March 15Upto 100%
  • Any amount paid u/s 211 on or before 31st March of the previous year is treated as advance tax paid during that financial year.
  • A senior citizen (or super senior citizen) with no income chargeable under "Profits and gains of business or profession" is not liable to pay advance tax at all.
  • Every income — including capital gains, lottery winnings, dividend, etc. — is subject to advance tax. But since capital gain/casual income/dividend (or business income arising for the first time) can't be estimated in advance, if the assessee pays the whole tax on such income either (i) as part of the remaining instalments still due, or (ii) by March 31 of the financial year (where no instalments remained due), then all advance-tax provisions are deemed complied with.
  • Net agricultural income is also considered while computing tax liability for advance tax purposes.
  • Failure to pay any instalment by its due date makes the assessee "an assessee in default" for that instalment [Sec. 218].
  • Any sum (other than penalty/interest) paid as advance tax is treated as a payment of tax, with credit given in the regular assessment [Sec. 219].
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: THE 44AD/44ADA PRESUMPTIVE ASSESSEE HAS ONLY ONE INSTALMENT

THE TRAP: students apply the usual 15%/45%/75%/100% four-instalment ladder to every assessee, including one declaring presumptive income u/s 44AD/44ADA.

THE TWIST: an eligible assessee in respect of an eligible business u/s 44AD/44ADA has just one instalment — 100% of the advance tax liability on or before March 15. Confusing this with "Other Assessee" produces a wrong instalment schedule even when the total liability figure is correct. Also watch the ₹10,000 threshold itself — below it, there is no advance-tax obligation at all (Illustration 41, Case 1).

3.5.1 Procedure to pay Advance Tax

(a) On assessee's own motion [Sec. 210(1)]

Procedure for 1st instalment:

  1. Estimate the current year's income, considering brought-forward losses, after deducting all allowable Chapter VIA deductions. (The estimate need not be filed with the tax authorities.)
  2. Compute tax liability on the estimated income at rates in force for the financial year, reduce rebate if any.
  3. Add surcharge (if applicable).
  4. Add Health and Education cess.
  5. Deduct tax deducted/collected at source.
  6. The resulting figure is the advance tax payable — where ₹10,000 or more, the appropriate percentage must be deposited.

Procedure for subsequent instalments:

  1. Check whether the earlier income estimate needs revision.
  2. If not, deposit the appropriate 2nd/3rd/4th instalment amount.
  3. If revision is needed, make a revised estimate and compute tax liability thereon.
  4. Determine advance tax payable in the subsequent instalment after deducting amounts already paid in earlier instalments.
  5. Deposit such advance tax.

(b) On receipt of order from the Assessing Officer [Sec. 210(3)/(4)]

The AO may pass an order and issue a demand notice u/s 156 requiring advance tax payment. Conditions: the assessee has already been regularly assessed in a prior year; the AO believes the person is liable to pay advance tax; the order can be passed any time during the financial year but not after the last day of February; it must be in writing and specify the amount and instalments. (Such an order may issue even if the assessee has already paid an instalment that the AO considers non-compliant with Sec. 211.)

Determination of advance tax by the AO — the higher of: tax on the latest assessed income per regular assessment; or tax on income declared by the assessee in the return for the previous year subsequent to the year of that regular assessment.

CaseAdvance tax to be paidIntimation to AO required?
AO's estimate of income is correctOn the basis of the AO's orderNo
Assessee estimates current income higher than the AO's estimateOn the basis of assessee's own estimateNo
Assessee estimates current income lower than the AO's estimateOn the basis of assessee's own estimateYes — submit own estimate in Form 28A

Per Sec. 210(4), the AO can revise the order to pay advance tax any time before 1st March of the relevant previous year.

Interest on non-payment of advance tax: an assessee who fails to pay advance tax, or defers payment beyond the specified date, is liable to interest u/s 234B & 234C.

CONCEPT

3.6 Tax Deducted at Source & Tax Collected at Source ★★★ HIGH

3.6.1 Meaning: TDS is a measure under which the person making payment of income is responsible for deducting tax from such income (at specified rates) and paying only the net amount to the payee. Tax so deducted must be deposited with the Government's treasury within the stipulated time. The payer issues a certificate in Form 16 or Form 16A to the payee, and the payee gets credit for the TDS, reducing his tax liability to that extent. In essence, the provisions are merely a mode of collection of income tax and a check on tax evasion through proper control and information.

Objects: quicker realisation of tax; effective realisation of tax. There are several provisions in the Act mandating TDS, spread across Sec. 192 to Sec. 206C, discussed below.

Sec. 206AA — Consequence of Non-Furnishing of PAN by the Deductee

If a resident payee fails to furnish PAN to the deductor, tax shall be deducted at the higher of: (i) the rate specified in the relevant TDS section; (ii) the rate(s) in force; or (iii) 20%. Exception: for non-PAN cases covered u/s 194-O or 194-Q, the rate of TDS is 5% (not 20%).

TDS on Salary & Employee Payments [Sec. 192, 192A]

  • Sec. 192 (Salary): tax is deducted at the average rate of tax at the time of payment. If an employee works with more than one employer simultaneously, he may (u/s 192(2)) furnish details of income from the other employer(s) in Form 12B to any one chosen employer, who then deducts tax on the aggregate salary. If the employee also has income under any other head (u/s 192(2B)), he may furnish those particulars — plus any tax already deducted/collected and any loss under "Income from house property" only — on plain paper; losses under any other head are not to be considered. Tax deducted shall be the higher of tax deductible after considering such other income/loss/TDS, or tax deductible on salary income alone (after adjusting the house-property loss) if the other income/loss is ignored.
  • Statement of perquisites: where salary exceeds ₹ 2,00,000, the employer furnishes a statement of perquisites in Form 12BA (particulars furnished if salary exceeds ₹ 1,50,000).
  • Non-monetary perquisites: the employer may, at his option, pay tax on non-monetary perquisites himself (at the average rate) without deducting it from the employee; such tax paid is not treated as income of the employee, and this amount is not required to be grossed up.
  • TDS on ESOP by eligible start-ups [u/s 80-IAC]: tax on the perquisite (taxed u/s 17(2) at the time of exercise) may be deducted/paid within 14 days of the earliest of: (a) expiry of 48 months from the end of the relevant assessment year; (b) date of sale of the specified security/sweat equity share; or (c) date the assessee ceases to be an employee of the start-up. Tax is deducted/paid at the rates in force for the FY in which the security is allotted or transferred.
  • Relief route: the recipient may apply to the Assessing Officer in Form 13 for a certificate authorising the payer to deduct tax at a lower rate or nil rate [Sec. 197].
  • Sec. 192A (Payment from Recognised Provident Fund): the trustees of the EPF Scheme, 1952 (or authorised person) deduct TDS at 10% (20% if no PAN) at the time of payment of the accumulated balance, but only where the payment is not exempt under Rule 8, Part A, Fourth Schedule (i.e., continuous service < 5 years and none of the saving conditions apply). No TDS if the aggregate payment is less than ₹ 50,000.

TDS on Interest, Dividend & Investment Income [Sec. 193, 194, 194A, 194EE, 194K]

  • Sec. 193 — Interest on securities: deducted at 10% (no surcharge, health & education cess) at the time of payment or crediting, whichever is earlier, if aggregate interest exceeds ₹ 10,000 in the FY. No TDS on interest on Central/State Government securities (except 8% Savings (Taxable) Bonds 2003, Floating Rate Savings Bonds 2020 (Taxable), 7.75% Savings (Taxable) Bonds 2018), interest to LIC/GIC and its 4 successor companies or other insurers on beneficially-held securities, interest to a business trust's SPV, or interest to a Regimental/non-Public Fund of the Armed Forces [exempt u/s 10(23AA)].
  • Sec. 194 — Dividends: the principal officer of a domestic company deducts 10% (no surcharge/cess) at the time of payment on dividend u/s 2(22) (money received on buy-back is also treated as dividend under this section). No TDS: dividend to an insurance company; dividend to a business trust's SPV; dividend to an individual shareholder paid other than in cash where the aggregate does not exceed ₹ 10,000; or dividend to any other notified person.
  • Sec. 194A — Interest other than on securities: deducted at 10% by (i) any person other than Individual/HUF, or (ii) an Individual/HUF whose turnover exceeds ₹ 1 crore (business) or ₹ 50 lakh (profession) in the preceding FY. General threshold ₹ 10,000; for a banking company, a co-operative society carrying on banking, or a post office, the threshold is ₹ 50,000 (₹ 1,00,000 for a senior-citizen payee) — computed branch-wise, except where Core Banking Solution (CBS) is adopted, in which case it is computed entity-wise. Interest to a firm's own partner, to a co-op society (other than a co-op bank) member, on deposits with a primary agricultural credit/land-mortgage/land-development society, and on notified schemes (NSC, Indira Vikas Patra, Kisan Vikas Patra, Post Office MIS) are all outside TDS. A co-operative society engaged in banking is nevertheless liable to deduct if its turnover exceeded ₹ 50 crore in the preceding FY and aggregate interest exceeds ₹ 1,00,000 (senior citizen) / ₹ 50,000 (others).
  • Sec. 194EE — NSS deposits: post office deducts 10% (resident) at the time of payment if aggregate exceeds ₹ 2,500; no TDS on payment to heirs of a deceased assessee.
  • Sec. 194K — Income from units: 10% at the time of payment/credit, if aggregate exceeds ₹ 10,000; not applicable where the income is in the nature of capital gains.
  • Common relief route for all of the above: Form 13 application to the AO for a lower/nil-rate certificate [Sec. 197], or a Form 15G/15H declaration (in duplicate) to the payer [Sec. 197A] where estimated tax on total income is nil.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SAME 30% RATE, DIFFERENT THRESHOLD RULES — SEC. 194B / 194BA / 194BB

THE TRAP: students assume the ₹ 10,000 per-transaction threshold that exempts small lottery/horse-race winnings from TDS also applies to online-gaming winnings under Sec. 194BA, since all three share the same 30% rate structure (Sec. 194B's rate table).

THE TWIST: Sec. 194BA (online gaming) has a Nil threshold — there is no minimum below which TDS is skipped, unlike Sec. 194B (lottery/crossword/card games, threshold ₹ 10,000 per single transaction) and Sec. 194BB (horse races, also ₹ 10,000 per single transaction). Also remember: if winnings are > ₹ 10,000 in aggregate under 194B (say ₹ 12,000), tax is deducted on the whole amount, not just the excess; and commission paid to a lottery agent is taxed u/s 194G, not u/s 194B.

TDS on Contracts, Commission & Professional/Technical Fees [Sec. 194C, 194D, 194DA, 194G, 194H, 194J, 194M]

  • Sec. 194C — Payment to contractor: deducted by a wide list of "specified persons" (Government, local authority, corporation, company, co-op society, society, trust, university, foreign Government/enterprise, firm, and an Individual/HUF/AOP/BOI whose turnover exceeds ₹ 1 crore business / ₹ 50 lakh profession in the preceding FY) at 1% (Individual/HUF payee) or 2% (other payee), at the time of payment or credit, whichever is earlier. No individual/HUF deducts tax on sums credited/paid exclusively for personal purposes. No TDS if a single contract sum ≤ ₹ 30,000 and the aggregate for the FY ≤ ₹ 1,00,000; also no TDS on payment to a transport operator owning ≤ 10 goods carriages who furnishes PAN and a declaration, even if the payment exceeds ₹ 1,00,000. "Work" includes advertising, broadcasting/telecasting, carriage of goods/passengers (other than by railway), catering, and certain manufacture/supply to customer specification — but excludes supply using material bought from a person other than the customer/its associate, and excludes anything covered by Sec. 194J.
  • Sec. 194D — Insurance commission: 10% (domestic company payee) or 2% (other payee), at payment/credit, whichever is earlier, if aggregate exceeds ₹ 20,000.
  • Sec. 194DA — Life insurance policy payment: 2% (no surcharge/cess) on the income portion, if the sum is not exempt u/s 10(10D) and aggregate payments are ₹ 1,00,000 or more.
  • Sec. 194G — Commission on lottery tickets: 2% at payment/credit, whichever is earlier; no TDS if commission ≤ ₹ 20,000.
  • Sec. 194H — Commission/brokerage (other than insurance): deducted by any person other than Individual/HUF, or an Individual/HUF whose turnover exceeds ₹ 1 crore business / ₹ 50 lakh profession in the preceding FY, at 2%; no TDS if aggregate ≤ ₹ 20,000. Where commission is retained by a consignee/agent while remitting sale proceeds, it is the consignor/principal who must deposit tax on that retained commission [Circular No. 619].
  • Sec. 194J — Professional/technical fees, royalty, Sec. 28(va) sums, director fees: deducted by any person other than Individual/HUF, or an Individual/HUF exceeding the same turnover thresholds as above, at 2% (fees for technical services where the payee's business is only call-centre operation; certain film royalty) or 10% (all other cases), at payment/credit whichever is earlier. No TDS if aggregate professional fees/FTS/royalty/28(va) sums ≤ ₹ 50,000 in the FY — but director's fees (not covered u/s 192) has no threshold at all. "Professional services" covers legal, medical, engineering, architectural, accountancy, technical consultancy, interior decoration, advertising and notified professions; "fees for technical services" covers managerial/technical/consultancy services but excludes construction/assembly/mining-type projects and amounts taxable as salary.
  • Sec. 194M — Certain sums by Individual/HUF (not otherwise covered u/s 194C, 194H, 194J): covers contract work payments, commission/brokerage (not insurance commission), and professional fees paid by an individual/HUF, at 2% (w.e.f. 01-10-2024), if the aggregate for the FY exceeds ₹ 50 lakh. The payer need not obtain a TAN and deposits tax using his own PAN.
  • Common relief route: Form 13 application to the AO under Sec. 197 for lower/nil TDS; Form 15G/15H under Sec. 197A where applicable (194D, 194DA, 194H not eligible for 15G/15H in this source's list — only 194, 194EE, 192A, 193, 194A, 194D, 194DA, 194-I are listed under Sec. 197A relief above).
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: 194C's PER-TRANSACTION LIMIT vs. 194J's AGGREGATE-ONLY LIMIT

THE TRAP: students apply the same "check each bill separately" logic to Sec. 194J that applies to Sec. 194C, and wrongly conclude that professional fees escape TDS as long as no single bill crosses ₹ 50,000.

THE TWIST: under Sec. 194C, the ₹ 30,000 limit is on the individual contract, with a separate ₹ 1,00,000 aggregate-for-the-year cap (both conditions must hold for TDS to be skipped). Under Sec. 194J, the ₹ 50,000 limit is not on the individual transaction — it is applied to the aggregate of all professional/technical fee bills during the year. If several bills together exceed ₹ 50,000, TDS must be deducted even though no single bill does.

TDS on Rent & Immovable Property [Sec. 194-I, 194-IA, 194-IB, 194-IC, 194LA]

Sec. 194-I — Rate Split by Asset Type

Machinery or plant or equipment → 2%. Land or building (incl. factory building) or land appurtenant to a building or furniture or fittings → 10%.

"Rent" = any payment under any lease, sub-lease, tenancy or other arrangement for the use of land, building, land appurtenant to a building, machinery, plant, furniture, fittings or equipment, whether or not owned by the payee.

  • Sec. 194-I: deducted by any person other than Individual/HUF, or an Individual/HUF exceeding ₹ 1 crore (business) / ₹ 50 lakh (profession) turnover in the preceding FY, at payment/credit whichever is earlier. No TDS if rent for a month or part of a month ≤ ₹ 50,000 (this limit applies to each co-owner separately where shares are known). No TDS where payee is Government/local authority [Sec. 10(20)]/statutory authority [Sec. 10(20A)], or where rent is paid to a REIT business trust for a directly-owned real estate asset [Sec. 10(23FCA)]. A lump-sum, non-adjustable upfront lease premium for long-term leasehold rights is not "rent" under Sec. 194-I and is outside TDS [Circular 35/2016].
  • Sec. 194-IA — Transfer of immovable property (other than rural agricultural land): the transferee deducts 1% of the consideration or the stamp duty value, whichever is higher, at payment/credit whichever is earlier. No TDS if both consideration and SDV are < ₹ 50 lakh. Consideration includes club membership, car parking, electricity/water facility, maintenance and similar incidental charges. With multiple transferors/transferees, the aggregate consideration across all of them is considered. The deductor need not obtain a TAN.
  • Sec. 194-IB — Rent by Individual/HUF not covered u/s 194-I: 2%, deducted at credit of rent for the last month of the previous year (or last month of tenancy if vacated during the year) or at payment, whichever is earlier. No TDS if rent for a month or part ≤ ₹ 50,000. No TAN required; if PAN is not furnished, TDS is at 20% u/s 206AA but capped at the rent payable for the last month.
  • Sec. 194-IC — Joint Development Agreement payment [Sec. 45(5A)]: 10%, at payment/credit whichever is earlier.
  • Sec. 194LA — Compensation on compulsory acquisition of immovable property (other than agricultural land): 10%, at the time of payment; no TDS if the aggregate for the FY ≤ ₹ 5,00,000. No deduction where the payment is exempt u/s 96 of the RFCTLARR Act, 2013.

TDS on Digital-Economy & Other Specific Payments [Sec. 194N, 194-O, 194P, 194Q, 194R, 194S, 194T]

  • Sec. 194N — Cash withdrawal: a banking company, a co-op society carrying on banking, or a post office deducts TDS on cash paid in aggregate exceeding ₹ 1 crore (₹ 3 crore for a co-op society) during the previous year, from accounts maintained with it. If the payee is a "defaulter" — has not filed returns of income for all 3 preceding assessment years for which the Sec. 139(1) time limit has expired — the threshold drops to ₹ 20 lakh. Tax deducted u/s 194N is not treated as deemed receipt of income. Not applicable to payments to the Government, banking companies/co-op societies/post offices themselves, banking correspondents, white-label ATM operators, or other notified persons; also inapplicable to certain exempt foreign diplomatic missions/UN agencies.
  • Sec. 194-O — E-commerce operator payment to participant: the e-commerce operator deducts 0.1% of the gross sale/service amount (5% if PAN not intimated) at payment/credit whichever is earlier. No TDS if the participant is an Individual/HUF, gross sales/services ≤ ₹ 5,00,000, and PAN/Aadhaar is furnished. A transaction on which 194-O tax was deducted (or which is exempt due to the threshold) is not subject to TDS under any other provision, except for amounts received for hosting advertisements/other unrelated services.
  • Sec. 194P — Specified senior citizens: a specified bank computes the total income (after Chapter VI-A deductions and Sec. 87A rebate) of a specified senior citizen (resident, age ≥ 75, income only from pension + interest from an account with the same bank, having furnished the prescribed declaration) and deducts income-tax at slab rates; such senior citizen need not file a return of income for that AY.
  • Sec. 194Q — Purchase of goods: a "buyer" (turnover > ₹ 10 crore in the preceding FY) deducts 0.1% of the sum exceeding ₹ 50 lakh in aggregate purchase value from a resident seller in a FY (5% if seller has no PAN), at payment/credit whichever is earlier. TDS is on the value exclusive of GST, except on advance payments (where GST cannot be identified separately, TDS applies to the whole amount) [Circular 13/2021]. Not applicable where seller is Central/State Government (but public sector undertakings/corporations are not exempt) [Circular 20/2021], nor to transactions in securities/commodities on recognised exchanges or electricity/REC/energy-saving certificates through power exchanges. Not applicable if tax is deductible under any other provision, or collectible u/s 206C.
  • Sec. 194R — Benefit or perquisite from business/profession: the provider deducts 10% of the value/aggregate value before providing the benefit/perquisite; no TDS by an Individual/HUF provider whose turnover does not exceed ₹ 1 crore (business) / ₹ 50 lakh (profession) in the preceding FY, and none at all if the aggregate value ≤ ₹ 20,000 in the FY.
  • Sec. 194S — Virtual digital asset transfer: 1% at credit or payment, whichever is earlier. No TDS if the aggregate consideration in the FY does not exceed ₹ 50,000 (where payable by a "specified person" — broadly, an individual/HUF with turnover ≤ ₹ 1 crore/₹ 50 lakh, or no business/profession income) or ₹ 10,000 (any other payer). Where tax is already deductible u/s 194-O, deduction is made u/s 194S instead.
  • Sec. 194T — Remuneration/interest to partner: the firm deducts 10% at credit (including to the capital account) or payment, whichever is earlier, if the aggregate paid/credited to that partner exceeds ₹ 20,000 in the FY; tax must be deducted on the entire sum even where such remuneration/interest is not taxable in the partner's hands.

EXAMPLE — TDS on Cash Withdrawal, Sec. 194N

A payee withdrew ₹ 3,50,00,000 (on different dates) in cash from his bank account. Compute the TDS in each scenario.

TDS Working u/s 194N on ₹ 3,50,00,000 Cash Withdrawal
Nature of PayeeDefaulter or NotTDS (₹)Working
Co-operative societyNo1,00,000₹ 50 lakh × 2%
Co-operative societyYes8,10,000₹ 2.80 crore × 2% + ₹ 50 lakh × 5%
Other personNo5,00,000₹ 2.50 crore × 2%
Other personYes14,10,000₹ 80 lakh × 2% + ₹ 2.50 crore × 5%

Answer: as tabulated above — the threshold before which TDS starts (₹ 50 lakh for co-op societies / non-defaulters generally computed against the base slab; ₹ 20 lakh once "defaulter" status applies; ₹ 1 crore for non-defaulters otherwise) drives which slice of the withdrawal is taxed at 2% and which at 5%.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: 194-O AND 194Q BOTH SEEM TO APPLY ON THE SAME E-COMMERCE SALE

THE TRAP: where a buyer purchases goods worth over ₹ 50 lakh from a seller through an e-commerce platform, students deduct TDS twice — once under Sec. 194-O (e-commerce operator on the participant) and again under Sec. 194Q (buyer on the seller).

THE TWIST: Sec. 194Q explicitly excludes transactions on which tax has been deducted by the e-commerce operator u/s 194-O (including transactions exempted under 194-O(2)) — such a transaction is not subjected to tax deduction u/s 194Q again. More generally, Sec. 194Q itself does not apply to any transaction on which tax is deductible under any other provision of the Act, or collectible u/s 206C.

Other TDS Provisions — Sec. 196, 197, 197A, 198, 199

  • Sec. 196 (No deduction from sums payable to Government/RBI/certain corporations): no TDS from sums payable to the Government, the Reserve Bank of India, a corporation established by/under a Central Act whose income is exempt from income-tax, or a Mutual Fund specified u/s 10(23D).
  • Sec. 197 (Certificate for lower/nil deduction): the AO, on a Form 13 application, issues a certificate for deduction at a lower rate or nil rate if satisfied that the person's existing and estimated tax liability justifies it. The certificate is valid only for the period specified, only for the named deductor, and is issued directly to the deductor (with advice to the applicant). Rule 28AA computation: estimated total income of the current year (A) → tax payable thereon (B) → less advance tax/TDS already paid for the current year (C) → balance liability (D = B − C) → average rate of tax (E = D/A × 100) → average of the average rate of tax of the preceding 3 years (F) → certificate rate = higher of E and F.
  • Sec. 197A (No deduction in certain cases): no TDS from payments to the New Pension System Trust [Sec. 10(44)]. No TDS u/s 194 (Dividend) and 194EE (NSS) where the payee is a resident individual, the aggregate income does not exceed the basic exemption limit, and Form 15G (Form 15H for senior citizen) is furnished declaring that tax on his estimated total income for the year will be nil. Similarly no TDS u/s 192A, 193, 194A, 194D, 194DA or 194-I on the same Form 15G/15H basis, where the payee is a person other than a company or firm.
  • Sec. 198 (Tax deducted is deemed income received): all sums deducted are, for computing the assessee's income, deemed to be income received — e.g. if Mr. X receives interest of ₹ 18,000 net of ₹ 2,000 TDS, his interest income is taken as ₹ 20,000. Exception: tax paid by the employer on non-monetary perquisites u/s 192(1A) and tax paid u/s 194N are not deemed income received. Where income is paid "net of tax," it must be grossed up for the purpose of deducting tax [Sec. 195A] — except for tax on non-monetary perquisites paid by the employer.
  • Sec. 199 (Credit for tax deducted): tax deducted and paid to the Central Government is treated as tax paid on behalf of the person from whose income it was deducted (credit passes to another person if the income is assessable in his hands). Sums under Sec. 192(1A) paid to the Central Government are treated as tax paid on behalf of the employee.

A correction statement may be filed to rectify mistakes/add/delete/update furnished information — but w.e.f. 01-04-2025, no correction statement can be delivered after 6 years from the end of the FY in which the original statement was due. Statements are processed u/s 200A by adjusting for arithmetical errors and incorrect claims apparent from the statement, computing interest and the Sec. 234E fee, and issuing an intimation to the deductor within 1 year from the end of the FY in which the statement was filed — determining sum payable by, or refund due to, the deductor.

Sec. 206A requires a banking company/co-op society/public company [referred to in Sec. 194A(3)] paying interest (other than on securities) not exceeding ₹ 50,000 (banking co./co-op society) or ₹ 10,000 (any other case) without deducting tax, to still file a statement of such payments to the prescribed income-tax authority.

TAN, PAN & Consequences of Default [Sec. 191, 201, 202, 203A, 206AA, Rule 125]

  • Sec. 203A (Tax deduction and collection account number): every deductor/collector without a TAN must apply in Form 49B, and must quote the TAN on all challans, certificates, statements and returns relating to TDS/TCS. Not applicable to a person deducting tax u/s 194-IA or 194-IB.
  • Sec. 206AA (PAN requirement, deductee): deductee must furnish PAN to the deductor, failing which tax is deducted at the highest of the section's specified rate, the rate(s) in force, or 20% (5% for non-PAN cases under 194-O/194-Q). No Form 15G/15H declaration or Sec. 197 certificate is valid unless it contains the applicant's PAN.
  • Rule 125 (Electronic payment of tax): a company, and any other person to whom tax-audit u/s 44AB applies, must pay tax (including TDS/TCS, interest, penalty) electronically — via internet banking or credit/debit cards. Payment can be made from another person's bank account, provided the challan clearly shows the PAN of the assessee on whose behalf it is paid.
  • Sec. 191 (Direct payment): where TDS provision is not made, or tax has not actually been deducted in accordance with the Chapter, tax remains payable by the assessee directly.
  • Sec. 202: deduction under this Chapter is only one mode of recovery of tax — the AO may use other prescribed recovery methods in addition.
  • Sec. 200(3A) note — GST-exclusive TDS: where the agreement/contract separately indicates the GST component within the amount payable to a resident, TDS under Chapter XVII-B is deducted on the amount excluding that GST component.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: NON-DEDUCTION/NON-DEPOSIT — "ASSESSEE IN DEFAULT" [SEC. 201]

THE TRAP: students assume that if a payer simply fails to deduct tax, he escapes any consequence as long as the recipient eventually pays his own tax — or, conversely, that any recipient-side tax payment automatically cures the payer's default.

THE TWIST: Sec. 201(1) deems any person required to deduct tax (or an employer u/s 192(1A)) who fails to deduct, or deducts but fails to pay, the whole or part of the tax, to be an "assessee in default" — without prejudice to any other consequences. The first proviso to Sec. 201(1) removes default status ONLY if all four conditions hold: (i) the resident recipient has filed his return u/s 139; (ii) he has included that sum in computing income in that return; (iii) he has paid the tax due on the income so declared; AND (iv) the payer furnishes a prescribed certificate to this effect from a chartered accountant, in Form No. 26A. Missing any one of the four — especially the CA-certified Form 26A, which students most often forget — keeps the payer in default. Separately, no penalty is charged u/s 221 unless the AO is satisfied the failure was without good and sufficient reason [second proviso to Sec. 201(1)].

TCS

Tax Collected at Source (TCS) [Sec. 206C] ★★ MEDIUM

Apart from TDS, another device for quicker collection of tax is Tax Collection at Source (TCS) u/s 206C.

3.6.41 Applicability — three categories:

  1. Every "seller" collects tax from the "buyer" of any specified goods, at the time of debiting the buyer's account or receipt of the amount, whichever is earlier.
  2. Every person granting a lease/licence/contract transferring rights in a parking lot, toll plaza, or mine or quarry (excluding mines/quarrying of mineral oil, which includes petroleum and natural gas) to another person (other than a public sector company), for business use, collects tax from the licensee/lessee at debit or receipt, whichever is earlier.
  3. (a) An authorised dealer receiving an amount for remittance out of India under RBI's Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), and (b) a seller of an overseas tour programme package receiving amount from the buyer — each collects at debit or receipt, whichever is earlier.

For category 3: not applicable to a non-resident buyer without a permanent establishment in India. The authorised dealer does not collect if aggregate remittance < ₹ 10,00,000 in the FY and is not for an overseas tour package (if remittance exceeds ₹ 10,00,000, say ₹ 11,00,000, tax is collected only on the excess, i.e. ₹ 1,00,000); nor where the seller has already collected tax on that amount; nor where the buyer has itself deducted TDS on the sum, or is Government/embassy/consulate/local authority/other notified person.

Meaning of key terms: "Seller" = Central/State Government, local authority, statutory corporation/authority, company, firm, co-op society, or an Individual/HUF whose turnover exceeds ₹ 1 crore (business) / ₹ 50 lakh (profession) in the preceding FY. "Buyer" (goods other than motor car) = one who obtains specified goods (or the right to receive them) by sale, excluding a public sector company/Government/embassy/club, and excluding a retail buyer for personal consumption; for motor vehicles/specified goods, "buyer" also excludes local authorities and passenger-carrying PSUs.

"Specified goods" include: alcoholic liquor for human consumption; tendu leaves; timber/forest produce (not tendu leaves) obtained under a forest lease; timber obtained otherwise than under a forest lease; scrap; specified minerals (coal, lignite, iron-ore); and motor car or other specified goods (wrist watch, art pieces/antiques/paintings/sculpture, collectibles like coin/stamp, yacht/rowing boat/canoe/helicopter, sunglasses, handbag/purse, shoes, sportswear/equipment, home theatre system, horse for racing/polo) of value exceeding ₹ 10 lakh.

TCS Rate Table [Sec. 206C]

Specified Goods / TransactionRate
Alcoholic liquor for human consumption1%
Tendu leaves5%
Timber or other forest produce (not tendu leaves) obtained under a forest lease2%
Timber obtained by any mode other than under a forest lease2%
Scrap1%
Specified minerals (coal, lignite, iron-ore)1%
Motor vehicle or other specified goods, value exceeding ₹ 10 lakh1%
Parking lot, toll plaza, mining and quarrying (lease/licence)2%
Where the purchaser/licensee/lessee is a non-resident non-corporate assessee or a non-domestic company, applicable surcharge and health & education cess also apply on top of the above rates.

"Scrap" means waste and scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials, definitely not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear, or other reasons.

Remittances under LRS / Overseas Tour Programme Package (point 3 above):

  • Loan obtained from a financial institution [Sec. 80E] remitted for pursuing education — 0%
  • Remittance for education (other than such a loan) or for medical treatment — 5% (after a threshold limit of ₹ 10 lakh)
  • Overseas tour programme package — up to ₹ 10 lakh: 5%; above ₹ 10 lakh: 20% (Non-PAN cases: 10% up to ₹ 10 lakh and 20% thereafter)
  • Any other case — 20% (after a threshold limit of ₹ 10 lakh)

Sec. 206CC — PAN Requirement by Collectee

A person paying a sum on which tax is collectible at source must furnish PAN to the collector, failing which tax is collected at the higher of: (i) twice the specified TCS rate; or (ii) 5%. If the PAN furnished is invalid or does not belong to the collectee, it is deemed as if PAN was not furnished at all. Exception: the higher-rate rule does not apply to a non-resident without a permanent establishment in India.

CONCEPT

3.7 Filing of Return of Income ★★★ HIGH

As per Sec. 139(1), the following persons must file a return of income in the prescribed form, within the prescribed time.

SectionAssesseeSize-of-income condition
139(1)(a)A company or a firmIrrespective of size of income — even where there is a loss
139(4A)TrustIrrespective of size of income — even where there is a loss (each entity type has its own trigger — see below)
139(4B)Political party
139(4C)Scientific research association; news agency; etc.
139(4D)Any university / college / other institution u/s 35(1)(ii) or (iii)
139(4E) / 139(4F)Business Trust / Investment Fund u/s 115UB
139(1)(b)Any other personWhere income, before giving effect to Sec. 54, 54B, 54D, 54EC, 54F, 54G, 54GA, 54GB and Chapter VIA (deductions u/s 80C to 80U), exceeds the maximum amount not chargeable to tax

The Central Government may, by notification, exempt any class(es) of persons from this filing requirement — Sec. 139(1C).

Compulsory Filing — Foreign Assets

A person, being resident other than not-ordinarily-resident, must furnish a return within the due date — irrespective of whether his total income exceeds the basic exemption limit or he has any taxable income at all — if he:

  • holds, as beneficial owner or otherwise, any asset (including any financial interest in any entity) located outside India, or has signing authority in any account located outside India; or
  • is a beneficiary of any asset (including any financial interest in any entity) located outside India.

Exception: an individual who is merely a beneficiary of a foreign asset is excused if the income arising from that asset is already includible in the income of the beneficial owner referred to above.

Beneficial owner — an individual who has provided, directly or indirectly, the consideration for the asset for the immediate or future benefit (direct or indirect) of himself or any other person. Beneficiary — an individual who derives benefit from the asset during the previous year, where the consideration for the asset was provided by someone other than himself.

Mandatory Filing — High-Value Transactions [7th proviso to Sec. 139(1)]

A person (other than a firm or company) not otherwise required to file, who during the previous year:

  • has deposited an aggregate amount exceeding ₹1 crore in one or more current accounts with a banking company or a co-operative bank; or
  • has incurred aggregate expenditure exceeding ₹2 lakh, for himself or any other person, on foreign travel; or
  • has incurred aggregate expenditure exceeding ₹1 lakh towards consumption of electricity; or
  • fulfils such other conditions as prescribed — the following, under Rule 12AB:
Condition (any one)Threshold
Total sales/turnover/gross receipts in business, during the previous yearExceeds ₹60 lakh
Total gross receipts in profession, during the previous yearExceeds ₹10 lakh
Aggregate of TDS and TCS during the previous year₹25,000 or more (₹50,000 or more for a senior citizen)
Deposit(s) in one or more savings bank account(s), in aggregate₹50 lakh or more during the previous year

Such a person must furnish a return on or before the due date, in the prescribed form and manner.

3.7.2 Tax Return Preparers (TRP) [Sec. 139B]

Under the TRP Scheme, 2006, an individual issued a "Tax Return Preparer Certificate" and a unique identification number is authorised to prepare and furnish returns of specified class(es) of persons and must also affix his signature on the return. Eligibility requires a bachelor's degree from a recognised Indian university/institution, or having passed the Intermediate examination of the ICAI, ICSI or ICMAI.

A TRP may act for any resident individual or resident HUF other than a company or a person whose accounts require audit u/s 44AB (tax audit) or any other law. An eligible person cannot file a revised return through a TRP unless the original return for that year was also filed through a TRP.

Not eligible to become a TRP: an accountant; a legal practitioner entitled to practise in a civil court; an officer of a scheduled bank (for an assessee maintaining a current account or other regular dealing with that bank); an employee of companies/persons whose accounts require audit u/s 44AB or other law.

3.7.7 Return of Loss [Sec. 139(3)]

An assessee is generally not compulsorily required to file a loss return. However, the following losses cannot be carried forward unless the loss return is filed within the time allowed u/s 139(1):

  1. Business loss (speculative or otherwise)
  2. Capital loss
  3. Loss from owning and maintaining race horses
  4. Loss from a specified business u/s 35AD
  • Loss declared in a belated return cannot be carried forward — but current-year set-off of losses while computing total income is not barred, even for a belated return.
  • Delay in filing a loss return may be condoned in certain cases.
  • Unabsorbed depreciation (Sec. 32) and loss under Income from House Property can be carried forward even if the loss return itself is filed after the due date.
  • If the current year's loss return is not filed on time, that year's loss cannot be carried forward — but losses of earlier years, if their own returns were filed on time, remain eligible to be carried forward.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: "LATE LOSS RETURN = NO SET-OFF AT ALL"

THE TRAP: assuming a late-filed loss return kills every kind of set-off for that loss.

THE TWIST: only carry-forward to future years is barred (for business/capital/race-horse/Sec. 35AD losses). Current-year set-off against other income is unaffected, and unabsorbed depreciation plus house-property loss can still be carried forward even from a late return.

Belated Return [Sec. 139(4)]: filed by the EARLIER of — 31st December of the relevant A.Y., OR before completion of assessment u/s 144

Available when the assessee misses the Sec. 139(1) due date or a Sec. 142(1) notice deadline. Consequence: liable to fee u/s 234F and interest u/s 234A; certain profit-linked deductions become unavailable; current-year losses cannot be carried forward.

A belated return (Sec. 139(4)) CAN be revised; a loss return CAN be revised. A return filed pursuant to a Sec. 142(1) notice CANNOT be revised.

3.7.16 Defective Return [Sec. 139(9)]

Where the Assessing Officer (AO) considers a return defective, he intimates the defect and gives the taxpayer an opportunity to rectify it.

  • Time limit: rectify within 15 days of intimation, or such extended time as the AO allows on application.
  • If not rectified in time: the AO treats the return as invalid — as if the taxpayer had never filed a return at all. If the assessee rectifies late but before the assessment is completed, the AO may condone the delay and treat the return as valid.

Taxpoint: a return is defective unless all annexures/statements/columns relating to computation of income under each head, gross total income and total income are duly filled in — and unless it is accompanied by proof of payment of taxes (advance tax or self-assessment tax).

3.7.18 Updated Return [Sec. 139(8A)]

Any person — whether or not he has already filed a return u/s 139(1), (4) or (5) — may furnish an updated return for the previous year relevant to an assessment year, within the prescribed form and manner.

Time limit: within 48 months from the end of the relevant assessment year. It cannot be furnished if a Sec. 148A show-cause notice was issued after 36 months from the end of the relevant AY — unless an order u/s 148A(3) has determined it is not a fit case to issue notice u/s 148.

An updated return cannot be filed if it:

  • is a return of loss; or
  • decreases the total tax liability already determined from an earlier return u/s 139(1)/(4)/(5) — i.e. it cannot be used to reduce tax liability; or
  • results in a refund, or increases a refund already due, for that assessment year.

No updated return may be furnished if: one has already been furnished for that AY; an assessment/reassessment/recomputation/revision proceeding is pending or completed for that year; or the person belongs to a notified class. It must be accompanied by proof of tax payment u/s 140B.

3.7.19 Tax on Updated Return [Sec. 140B]

Where no earlier return u/s 139(1)/(4) exists, the tax payable on the updated return — after adjusting advance tax, TDS/TCS, Sec. 89 relief, Sec. 90/90A/91 relief and Sec. 115JAA/115JD tax credit — must be paid together with interest, fee, and additional income-tax, before the return is furnished. Where an earlier return exists, an analogous computation applies (adjusting for credits already taken and any refund already issued), together with interest for default/delay in advance tax and additional income-tax net of interest already paid in the earlier return.

Updated return furnished after the Sec. 139(4)/(5) window, but before completion of…Additional income-tax
12 months from the end of the relevant assessment year25% of aggregate tax (+ surcharge + cess) and interest payable
24 months from the end of the relevant assessment year50%
36 months from the end of the relevant assessment year60%
48 months from the end of the relevant assessment year70%

Interest u/s 234C (where an earlier return exists) is computed after taking the updated return's total income as the "returned income"; interest u/s 234B is computed on the "assessed tax" — the tax on total income as declared in the updated return, adjusted for credit already taken, TDS/TCS on income not in the earlier return, and Sec. 115JD tax credit not already claimed, increased by any refund already issued.

3.8 PAN ★★ MEDIUM

Permanent Account Number (PAN) is an alpha-numeric, ten-character code allotted by the Income-tax Department to a person for identification of the assessee. A person can hold only one PAN.

3.8.1 Allotment of PAN — Compulsory Application [Sec. 139A & Rule 114]

Who must applyWhen to apply
Any person whose total income exceeds the maximum exempted limitOn or before 31st May of the relevant assessment year
Any resident person other than an individual entering into a financial transaction aggregating ₹2,50,000 or more in a financial year
The managing director, director, partner, trustee, author, founder, karta, CEO, principal officer or office bearer of such a person (or one competent to act on its behalf, or who intends to enter prescribed transactions)
Any person whose sales/turnover/gross receipts are likely to exceed ₹5,00,000 in any previous year
Any person required to file a return u/s 139(4A) (trust / charitable institution)On or before the end of the relevant financial year
Any person entitled to receive a sum on which tax is deductible in any financial year
Any person requiring an export-import codeBefore making any export or import
Assessee under GSTBefore applying for GST registration
Any person intending to enter a "specified transaction" *7 days before entering the transaction
Any other notified class of personsWithin the time prescribed

* Specified transactions (where PAN or Aadhaar must additionally be quoted on the related document): (1) cash deposit(s) aggregating ₹20 lakh or more in a financial year in one or more bank/co-operative bank/Post Office accounts; (2) cash withdrawal(s) aggregating ₹20 lakh or more in a financial year from such accounts; (3) opening a current account or cash-credit account with a banking company, co-operative bank, or Post Office. This rule does not apply to the Central/State Government or a Consular Office.

Voluntary application [Sec. 139A(3)]: anyone may apply for a PAN even without falling in the above categories — but a person already allotted a PAN cannot apply for another.

Where to apply: the Assessing Officer, or any other person assigned that function, or (failing either) the AO with jurisdiction over the person. Forms: Form 49A (Indian citizens/companies/entities incorporated in India); Form 49AA (other cases). (Companies may also apply via SPICe+ at incorporation, and LLPs via FiLLiP.)

Suo-motu allotment: the Central Government may, by notification, require any class of persons to apply for PAN [Sec. 139A(1B)]; the AO may also allot a PAN suo motu to any person not otherwise covered [Sec. 139A(2)].

3.8.2 Importance of PAN — Where It Must Be Quoted

A. On all returns, correspondence, documents and challans filed with an Income-tax authority, and on challans for payment of any sum due under the Act [Sec. 139A(5)].

B. On documents for prescribed transactions [Sec. 139A(5)(c) & Rule 114B] — PAN or Aadhaar must be quoted for, among others:

  1. Sale/purchase of a motor vehicle (other than a two-wheeler) requiring registration
  2. Opening a bank/co-operative bank account (other than a time deposit or Basic Savings Bank Deposit Account)
  3. Application for a credit or debit card
  4. Opening a demat account
  5. Cash payment exceeding ₹50,000 to a hotel or restaurant against a bill, at one time
  6. Cash payment exceeding ₹50,000 for foreign travel or foreign-currency purchase, at one time
  7. Payment exceeding ₹50,000 to a mutual fund for purchase of its units
  8. Payment exceeding ₹50,000 to a company/institution for debentures or bonds, or to RBI for its bonds
  9. Cash deposit exceeding ₹50,000 in one day with a bank/co-operative bank (and, under Rule 114BB, cash withdrawals aggregating ₹20 lakh or more in a financial year)
  10. Cash purchase of bank drafts/pay orders/banker's cheques exceeding ₹50,000 in one day
  11. A time deposit exceeding ₹50,000, or aggregating more than ₹5 lakh in a financial year, with a bank, Post Office, notified Nidhi, or NBFC
  12. Cash/draft/pay-order payment aggregating more than ₹50,000 in a financial year for pre-paid payment instruments
  13. Life insurance premium payment aggregating more than ₹50,000 in a financial year
  14. Contract for sale/purchase of securities (other than shares) exceeding ₹1 lakh in value
  15. Sale/purchase of unlisted company shares exceeding ₹1 lakh in value
  16. Sale/purchase of immovable property where the amount, or stamp value, exceeds ₹10 lakh
  17. Sale/purchase of any other goods or services exceeding ₹2 lakh in value

A minor with no taxable income quotes his father's/mother's/guardian's PAN instead. A person (other than a company or firm) without a PAN entering such a transaction must file Form No. 60. The Rule does not apply to the Central/State Governments, Consular Offices, or (for the items marked with an asterisk in the source) non-residents.

C. On TDS/TCS documents: the deductee must intimate his PAN to the deductor [Sec. 139A(5A)] — except where he furnishes Form 15G/15H declaring nil estimated tax or exemption from PAN. The deductor must quote the payee's PAN, his own PAN, and his TAN on all TDS statements/certificates [Sec. 139A(5B)]. Similarly for TCS, the collector quotes the buyer's/licensee's/lessee's PAN [Sec. 139A(5D)], and the buyer must intimate his PAN to the collector [Sec. 139A(5C)].

Every person entering a specified transaction must quote and authenticate his PAN/Aadhaar [Sec. 139(6A)]; every person receiving such a document must ensure it has been duly quoted and authenticated [Sec. 139(6B)].

Penalty [Sec. 272B]

DefaultPenalty
Failure to apply for PAN₹10,000
Failure to quote PAN/Aadhaar on prescribed documents, or to authenticate it; knowingly quoting a false number₹10,000 for each such default

3.8.4 Interchangeability & Quoting of Aadhaar [Sec. 139A(5E) & Sec. 139AA]

  • A person who has not been allotted a PAN but possesses an Aadhaar number may quote the Aadhaar number in lieu of PAN — a PAN is then allotted to him in the prescribed manner. (Per CBDT Notification No. 59/2019, this is deemed to be an application for PAN — no further documents are needed.)
  • A person already allotted a PAN, who has intimated his Aadhaar number, may quote the Aadhaar number instead of the PAN.
  • Every person eligible for Aadhaar must quote it in the PAN application form and in the return of income. A person allotted PAN before 1.7.2017 who is eligible for Aadhaar had to intimate it by 31.3.2022; linking is mandatory (w.e.f. 1.4.2019) unless specifically exempted — failure renders the PAN inoperative from 1.7.2023.

Consequences once PAN is inoperative (from 1.7.2023 until it becomes operative again):

  1. No refund of any tax due under the Act
  2. No interest payable on such refund, for the period the PAN stays inoperative
  3. Tax deductible at source on such person is deducted at a higher rate [Sec. 206AA]
  4. Tax collectible at source on such person is collected at a higher rate [Sec. 206CC]

Fee for default in Aadhaar intimation [Sec. 234H]: a fee (not exceeding ₹1,000, as prescribed) is payable at the time of intimation after the prescribed date; the PAN then becomes operative again within 30 days of Aadhaar intimation.

Sec. 139AA does not apply to notified persons/States — per CBDT Notification No. 37/2017 (effective 1.7.2017), it does not apply to an individual without an Aadhaar/Enrolment ID who is: (a) residing in Assam, Jammu & Kashmir or Meghalaya; (b) a non-resident; (c) aged 80 years or more at any time in the previous year; or (d) not a citizen of India.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: "PAN & AADHAAR ARE JUST TWO OPTIONS, PICK EITHER"

THE TRAP: treating PAN and Aadhaar as freely interchangeable in every context.

THE TWIST: Aadhaar can substitute for PAN only in the narrow situations of Sec. 139A(5E) (no-PAN-yet, or already-linked). Independently, Sec. 139AA makes Aadhaar quoting/linking to an existing PAN compulsory (subject to the notified exemptions) — skip that link and the PAN itself turns inoperative from 1.7.2023, with refund, interest and higher TDS/TCS consequences.

3.8.3 Intimation of Change

Every person must intimate the Assessing Officer, in the prescribed manner, of any change in his address, or in the name and nature of his business, on the basis of which the PAN was allotted [Sec. 139A(5)(d)].

CONCEPT

3.9 Self-Assessment & Intimation ★★★ HIGH

"Assessment" means deciding the assessee's income and tax liability, based on the return filed, information gathered, or the Department's best judgment. It begins with self-assessment — the assessee assessing himself.

3.9.1 Self-Assessment [Sec. 140A]: assessee computes his own taxable income and tax liability, and pays the tax due BEFORE filing the return

Tax payable = tax on returned income − relief/rebate − advance tax paid − TDS/TCS − MAT/AMT credit − tax/interest payable u/s 191(2). Interest u/s 234A (late filing) / 234B (advance-tax default) / 234C (advance-tax deferment) and fee u/s 234F (late filing) must be paid ALONG WITH the self-assessment tax — computed on the tax on the total income as declared in the return.

Order of adjustment where payment falls short of the aggregate of tax + interest + fee: FIRST fee, THEN interest, and the balance (if any) LAST towards tax. Any amount paid under Sec. 140A is later deemed paid towards the regular assessment. If the assessee fails to pay the tax/interest in full, he is deemed "an assessee in default."

ILLUSTRATION 46 — Self-assessment tax treatment u/s 140A

Mr. Gambhir Mitra paid ₹42,000 together with his return. Data: Tax liability ₹82,000; Interest u/s 234A ₹750; Interest u/s 234B ₹3,730; Interest u/s 234C ₹1,660; Fee u/s 234F ₹5,000; Advance tax paid ₹1,500; TDS ₹6,000.

3.9.2–3.9.5 The Assessment Framework

After a return is filed (or not filed), the Assessing Officer may assess the income by way of:

RouteSection
IntimationSec. 143(1)
Scrutiny AssessmentSec. 143(3)
Best Judgment AssessmentSec. 144
Income Escaping AssessmentSec. 147

Inquiry before assessment [Sec. 142]: the AO may serve notice on a person who has filed a return u/s 139, or whose Sec. 139(1) time limit has expired — to (i) submit a return [142(1)(i), only usable where no return has yet been filed — not mandatory before a best-judgment assessment]; (ii) produce accounts/documents [142(1)(ii), not for records more than 3 years before the previous year]; or (iii) furnish information in writing, including a statement of assets/liabilities [142(1)(iii), needing Joint Commissioner approval for assets outside the accounts]. Notice (i) can be issued only if no return has been filed; notices (ii) and (iii) can be issued whether or not a return has been filed.

The AO may also make any inquiry he considers necessary [Sec. 142(2) — from any source, unlike 142(1) which collects information from the assessee]; direct a special audit of accounts or valuation of inventory by a nominated accountant/cost accountant, with prior approval of the Pr. CCIT/Pr. CIT/CCIT/CIT [Sec. 142(2A)–(2D), report period capped at 180 days, form 6B, fees fixed by and paid by the Central Government; non-compliance triggers Best Judgment Assessment u/s 144 plus penalty/prosecution]; give the assessee an opportunity of being heard on material so gathered [Sec. 142(3), not applicable to a Sec. 144 assessment]; and refer valuation of an asset/property/investment to a Valuation Officer, who must report within 6 months from the end of the month of reference [Sec. 142A]. A faceless scheme for such notices/inquiries/directions/valuation may be notified [Sec. 142B].

3.9.6 Intimation [Sec. 143(1)]

Where a return is filed u/s 139, or in response to a Sec. 142(1) notice, it is processed as follows:

  1. Total income/loss is recomputed after adjusting for: (i) any arithmetical error in the return; (ii) an incorrect claim apparent from information in the return; (iii) any prescribed inconsistency with the preceding year's return; (iv) disallowance of a loss set-off claim where the loss-year's return was itself filed late; (v) disallowance of expenditure, or increase of income, flagged in the audit report but not reflected in the return; (vi) disallowance of a deduction u/s 10AA or Chapter VI-A "C" (deductions for certain incomes) where the return itself was filed late.
  2. Tax, interest and fee (if any) are computed on the recomputed total income.
  3. The sum payable (or refund due) is determined after adjusting TDS, TCS, advance tax paid, relief, self-assessment tax, and any other tax/interest/fee already paid.
  4. An intimation is generated and sent to the assessee stating the sum payable or refund due; a refund so determined is granted.
  5. An intimation is also sent where a declared loss is adjusted, even if no tax/interest/fee is payable and no refund is due.

Time limit: no intimation can be sent after 9 months from the end of the financial year in which the return is made — this period runs from the date of filing the latest revised return.

An "incorrect claim apparent from information in the return" means a claim, based on an entry in the return, that (a) is inconsistent with another entry in the same or another item of the return; (b) lacks the substantiating information required under the Act; or (c) is a deduction exceeding a specified statutory monetary/percentage/ratio/fraction limit.

Where refund becomes due u/s 143(1), but a notice has also been issued u/s 143(2) and the AO believes granting the refund would adversely affect revenue, he may — with reasons recorded in writing and prior approval of the Pr. CIT/CIT — withhold the refund until the assessment is made [Sec. 241A].

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: "NO LETTER = NO INTIMATION HAPPENED"

THE TRAP: assuming Sec. 143(1) processing is incomplete, or the return is still "open," if the assessee never receives a separate intimation letter.

THE TWIST: where no sum is payable and no refund is due (i.e. the return is accepted as filed with no adjustment), the acknowledgment of the return itself is deemed to be the intimation — no separate document issues. A fresh intimation is required only where an adjustment is made under (1) above, or where a declared loss is adjusted, and even then it is barred after 9 months from the end of the financial year of filing.

17 EXAM FACTS — TOTAL INCOME AND TAX LIABILITY OF INDIVIDUALS & HUF (Module 3)

① Clubbing provisions (Secs. 60–65) attribute certain third-party income back to the transferor-assessee — typically where income (without the asset) is transferred, or an asset is transferred to specified relatives without adequate consideration.

② Losses are set off intra-head, then inter-head, in the year they arise, subject to head-specific restrictions; unabsorbed losses can generally be carried forward only if the loss return was filed within the Sec. 139(1) due date.

③ Chapter VI-A deductions (Sec. 80C to 80U) reduce Gross Total Income to Total Income, subject to head-specific and aggregate ceilings, and several are unavailable under the default (new) tax regime.

④ Individuals/HUFs are taxed on slab rates that differ between the old and new tax regimes, with residential status governing the scope of total income brought to charge.

⑤ Advance tax is payable in instalments during the previous year itself once estimated tax liability crosses the prescribed threshold, with interest exposure under Secs. 234B/234C for shortfall or deferment.

⑥ TDS (Chapter XVII-B) and TCS (Sec. 206C) collect tax at the point of specified payments/receipts, at prescribed rates and thresholds, and are credited against the deductee's/collectee's final liability.

⑦ Companies and firms must file a return u/s 139(1)(a) irrespective of income size, even where there is a loss; trusts, political parties, and specified institutions/funds under 139(4A)–(4F) face a similar irrespective-of-size obligation.

⑧ "Any other person" must file only if pre-Chapter-VIA/pre-Sec.-54-series income exceeds the basic exemption limit — but a resident (other than NOR) with foreign assets/signing authority, or high-value transactions under the 7th proviso/Rule 12AB (e.g. turnover > ₹60 lakh, TDS+TCS ≥ ₹25,000), must file compulsorily regardless of income level.

⑨ Due dates (Explanation 2 to Sec. 139(1)): 30th November (Sec. 92E transfer-pricing report cases), 31st October (audit-required assessees / companies without international transactions), 31st July (any other case); late filing draws a fee u/s 234F of ₹1,000 (income ≤ ₹5 lakh) or ₹5,000 (above).

⑩ Belated return (Sec. 139(4)) and revised return (Sec. 139(5)) share the same outer window — 31st December of the A.Y. or completion of assessment/regular assessment, whichever is earlier; a Sec. 142(1)-notice return cannot be revised, but a belated or loss return CAN be.

⑪ Updated return (Sec. 139(8A)) is a much longer window — 48 months from the end of the relevant A.Y. — but cannot be a loss return, cannot reduce tax liability or create/increase a refund, and carries escalating additional income-tax of 25% / 50% / 60% / 70% under Sec. 140B depending on the delay slab.

⑫ A defective return (Sec. 139(9)) gives the assessee 15 days (extendable) to rectify; unrectified, the AO treats it as if no return was ever filed.

⑬ PAN is a 10-character alphanumeric code, one per person [Sec. 139A]; compulsory-application triggers include income above the exemption limit, turnover likely to exceed ₹5,00,000, and specified transactions (7 days' notice) — default draws a ₹10,000 penalty u/s 272B.

⑭ PAN/Aadhaar must be quoted on a long list of Rule 114B transactions (motor vehicle registration, bank a/c opening, immovable property > ₹10 lakh, cash deposits > ₹50,000/day, etc.); an unlinked PAN turns inoperative from 1.7.2023, blocking refunds/interest and triggering higher TDS/TCS u/ss. 206AA/206CC.

⑮ Self-assessment tax (Sec. 140A) must be paid BEFORE filing the return; a shortfall is adjusted first to fee, then interest, then tax — and non-payment makes the assessee "in default." An unpaid-self-assessment-tax return is itself a defective return.

⑯ Intimation u/s 143(1) recomputes income only for arithmetical errors, incorrect apparent claims, and similar listed adjustments — it must issue within 9 months from the end of the financial year of filing, and the bare acknowledgment is deemed the intimation when nothing is payable or refundable.

⑰ Beyond 143(1), assessment can proceed via Scrutiny (143(3)), Best Judgment (144), or Income Escaping Assessment (147) — each preceded, where relevant, by inquiry/notice under Sec. 142(1)/(2)/(2A).
