Concept of
Indirect Taxes

This module lays the conceptual foundation for the whole of Indirect Taxation — what makes a tax "indirect," how it differs from direct tax, the fragmented multiplicity of erstwhile Central and State levies (Excise, Service Tax, VAT, CST) that made pre-GST compliance so heavy, and the Constitutional route — Article 246, Schedule VII, and the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016 — through which GST was born.

MUST NOT SKIP: the Cascading Effect illustration — in the pre-GST VAT/CST/Excise chain, tax was charged on tax because input credit of Excise Duty and CST was NOT available to the next dealer, inflating a simple ₹1,00,000 + ₹10,000 transaction chain's tax outgo to ₹29,149; under GST, seamless Input Tax Credit collapses the same chain's tax outgo to ₹13,200. This is the single number that proves why GST exists.

4.1–4.4

Module Learning Objectives

After studying this module, the students will be able to – appreciate the difference between direct and indirect taxes, and understand the problems in the erstwhile (pre-GST) indirect taxes. The module is mapped against two SLOBs: acquiring knowledge of the legal provisions enshrined in the laws relating to GST and Customs Duty and appreciating their applicability in business operations, and gathering an understanding of the compliance-related legal provisions of these two indirect tax laws while conducting business operations.

Glossary — Module 4, in Plain Words

The technical terms used across 4.1–4.4, explained simply.

Direct TaxLevied on a person's income/wealth and paid directly to the Government by that same person. Incidence and impact fall on the same person — it cannot be shifted. Example given in the source: Income Tax.
Indirect TaxLevied at the point of supply/manufacture/purchase/sale/import/export of goods or services, but collected by the seller from the buyer and passed on to the Government — incidence and impact fall on different persons. Examples given in the source: GST, Customs Duty.
Regressive TaxAll persons — rich or poor — bear an equal percentage burden on the goods/services they consume, irrespective of their ability to pay. Describes indirect tax in the source.
Progressive TaxHigher tax is levied on a person earning higher income, and vice versa. Describes direct tax in the source.
Cascading Effect (Tax on Tax)Where tax is charged on a value that already includes an earlier stage's tax, because credit for that earlier tax was not available to the next dealer — the defining flaw of the pre-GST regime.
Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT)The Board dealing with levy and collection of all direct tax, constituted under the Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963.
Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC)The Board dealing with matters relating to levy and collection of Central indirect tax, constituted under the same 1963 Act.
Article 246 (with Schedule VII)Divides the subject matter of law made by the legislature into three lists — Union, State, and Concurrent.
Union List (List I)Subject matters on which only the Central Government has power of legislation.
State List (List II)Subject matters on which only the State Government has power of legislation.
Concurrent List (List III)Subject matters on which both Central and State Governments can pass legislation.
Central Excise ActTraced to Entry 84, Union List — duties of excise on tobacco and other goods manufactured/produced in India, excluding alcoholic liquor for human consumption and (with a medicinal/toilet-preparation carve-out) opium/narcotics.
Central Sales Tax (CST)Traced to Entry 92A, Union List — tax on sale/purchase of goods (other than newspapers) where the sale/purchase takes place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce.
State-Level VATTraced to Entry 54, State List — tax on sale/purchase of goods other than newspapers, subject to Entry 92A of the Union List.
Tax NakasCheck-posts at every inter-State border in the pre-GST regime, created to verify and collect CST/entry-related taxes — a major bottleneck to inter-State movement of goods.
One Nation One TaxThe idea underlying GST — subsuming the various indirect taxes levied separately by the Centre and the States into a single tax.
Dual GSTGST levied separately but concurrently by the Union (CGST) and the States/UTs with legislatures (SGST) or UTs without legislatures (UTGST).
CGST / SGST / UTGSTCentral tax / State tax / Union Territory tax — the three "intra" limbs of Dual GST under the 101st Amendment scheme.
IGSTIntegrated tax — levied by Parliament alone (exclusive power) on inter-State trade or commerce, including imports, in goods or services.
GST Council (GSTC)The constitutional body comprising the Union Finance Minister, the Minister of State (Revenue), and the State Finance Ministers, that recommends on GST rate, exemption, thresholds, taxes to be subsumed, and other features.
Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016The amendment that concurrently empowered the Centre and the States to levy and collect GST — assented to by the President on 8th September, 2016, effective 16th September, 2016.
CVD / SADAdditional duties of customs (Countervailing Duty / Special Additional Duty) that the Centre levies on imports, in addition to Basic Customs Duty, to counter-balance the excise duty/sales tax/State VAT levied on like domestic goods.

Module 4 Mind Map — read it now, redraw it from memory once you finish the module

Introduction — Why Government Levies Tax

In a Welfare State, the Government takes primary responsibility for the welfare of its citizens — health care, education, employment, infrastructure, social security and other development needs — and taxation is its primary source of revenue for incurring such public welfare expenditure. Taxes are a compulsory or enforced contribution to Government revenue by the public; the Government may levy tax on income, business profits or wealth, or add it to the cost of goods, services and transactions.

Basic reasons for imposing taxation, per the source: to provide basic facilities for every citizen (health care, electricity, roads, education, free housing for the poor, water supply, police, firefighters, judiciary, disaster relief, and other public welfare items); to finance multiple governments (local bodies such as village and block panchayats and municipal corporations receive funds via the Finance Commission); and protection of life (taxpayers receive protection of life and wealth from the Government against external aggression, internal armed rebellion or other such situations).

Taxpoint — Administration: both the CBDT and the CBIC have been constituted under the Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963. CBDT deals with the levy and collection of all direct tax, whereas matters relating to the levy and collection of Central indirect tax are dealt with by CBIC.

CONCEPT

4.1 Concept and Features of Indirect Taxes ★★ MEDIUM

Indirect tax is levied at the time of supply, manufacture, purchase, sale, import or export of goods, and is also levied on supply of services. The source sets out seven defining features.

  • Tax on goods and services: levied at the time of supply/manufacture/purchase/sale/import/export of goods, and also on supply.
  • Burden shifts: paid by the seller, but recovered by the seller from the buyer — the burden of indirect tax shifts from seller to buyer and is ultimately borne by the consumer of the goods or services.
  • Inflationary in nature: cost of goods and services increases due to the levy of indirect tax, so indirect taxes promote inflation.
  • Social welfare tool: useful for promoting social welfare by checking consumption of harmful or "sin" goods through a higher rate of tax.
  • Wider tax base: the majority of goods and services are liable to indirect tax with very low threshold limits, so the tax base is much wider than for direct tax.
  • Regressive in nature: all persons — rich or poor — bear an equal wrath of tax on the goods or services they consume, irrespective of their ability to pay; it creates no difference between rich and poor, so it may widen the disparity between them.
  • No pinch: the seller does not perceive a direct pinch of tax, since it is recovered from the buyer and then paid to Government; the buyer pays it built into the price, often without realising he is paying any tax to Government at all.
CONCEPT

4.2 Difference Between Direct & Indirect Taxes ★★★ HIGH

A frequently tested point-by-point distinction, reproduced from the source.

BasisDirect TaxIndirect Tax
MeaningReferred to as the tax levied on a person's income and wealth, and paid directly to the Government.Referred to as the tax levied on a person who consumes goods and services, and paid indirectly to the Government.
NatureProgressive — higher tax on a person earning higher income, and vice versa.Regressive — all persons bear equal wrath of tax on goods/services consumed, irrespective of their ability.
Incidence & ImpactFalls on the same person; the assessee himself bears such taxes — it pinches the taxpayer.Falls on different persons; tax is recovered from the assessee, who passes such burden to another person — it does not pinch the taxpayer.
ExampleIncome Tax.GST, Customs Duty.
EvasionTax evasion is possible.Tax evasion is hardly possible, because it is included in the price of goods and services.
InflationDirect tax helps in reducing inflation.Cost of goods and services increases due to the levy, so indirect taxes promote inflation — though sometimes usefully, to discourage sin-good consumption via a higher rate.
Imposition & CollectionImposed on and collected from the same person.Imposed on and collected from consumers of goods and services, but paid and deposited by the assessee.
BurdenCannot be shifted.Can be shifted.
EventTaxable income of the assessee.Supply of goods and services.
CONCEPT

4.3 Background of Erstwhile Indirect Taxes ★★★ HIGH

The Constitution of India is the supreme law of India — any tax law not in conformity with it is ultra vires the Constitution and held illegal and void. Article 246, read with Schedule VII, divides the subject matter of law made by the legislature into three categories: List I — Union List (only the Central Government has power of legislation on the subject matters covered), List II — State List (only the State Government has that power), and List III — Concurrent List (both Central and State Governments can legislate).

Union List (List I)State List (List II)
Entry 82 — Taxes on income other than agricultural income, i.e. Income-tax.Entry 54 — Taxes on the sale or purchase of goods other than newspapers, subject to Entry 92A of List I, i.e. State-level VAT.
Entry 83 — Duties of customs including export duties, i.e. Customs Act.Entry 46 — Taxes on agricultural income.
Entry 84 — Duties of excise on tobacco and other goods manufactured or produced in India (excluding alcoholic liquor for human consumption, and opium/Indian hemp/other narcotic drugs & narcotics except medicinal & toilet preparations containing them), i.e. Central Excise Act.Entry 60 — Taxes on professions, trades, callings and employments, i.e. Professional Tax.
Entry 86 — Taxes on the capital value of assets (exclusive of agricultural land) of individuals and companies, and the capital of companies, i.e. Wealth Tax.Entry 51 — Duties of excise on goods manufactured/produced in the State, and countervailing duties at the same or lower rates on similar goods manufactured elsewhere in India: alcoholic liquor for human consumption; opium/Indian hemp/other narcotic drugs and narcotics (excluding medicinal & toilet preparations containing them).
Entry 92A — Taxes on the sale or purchase of goods other than newspapers, where the sale/purchase takes place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce, i.e. Central Sales Tax.—
Entry 92C — Tax on services.—
Entry 97 — Any other matter not enumerated in List II or List III, including any tax not mentioned in either of those Lists.—

The Pre-GST Fragmentation Problem

  • In the pre-GST regime, Indian indirect tax was highly fragmented — the Centre and States separately taxed goods and services through many taxes: excise duty, service tax, VAT, CST, purchase tax, entertainment tax, octroi.
  • There was multiplicity of rates, laws and procedures, causing a heavy compliance burden.
  • Imposition of tax on tax was another serious problem — for example, VAT was levied on a value that included excise duty.
  • The Input Tax Credit chain broke as goods moved from one State to another, resulting in a hidden cost for business.
  • Pre-GST, there were tax nakas at every inter-State border, creating bottlenecks in inter-State transport of goods.
  • As a result, the logistics sector remained inefficient, adversely impacting businesses.
  • Every State was effectively a distinct market for both industry and consumer.
  • Industry's choice of locating factories or warehouses was heavily influenced by the prevailing tax regime rather than pure business considerations — making Indian industry uncompetitive.

To curb all this, GST was introduced with the idea of One Nation One Tax — the various indirect taxes levied by the Centre and the States were subsumed into one tax called GST.

ILLUSTRATION — Cascading Effect of Tax (Tax on Tax), Pre-GST vs. GST

Manufacturer "A" sells goods worth ₹1,00,000 to Dealer "B", from Gujarat to Haryana (an inter-State sale), liable to Excise Duty @12% and Central Sales Tax @2%. Dealer "B" in turn sells the goods to Dealer "C" in Haryana after adding ₹10,000, charging VAT @12% on that sale.

Pre-GST Regime — Excise Duty + CST + VAT
Transaction / ParticularsAmount (₹)Tax to Govt. (₹)
A to B: Sale price of goods1,00,000—
Add: Excise Duty @12%12,00012,000
Sub-total1,12,000—
Add: Central Sales Tax @2%2,2402,240
Total Invoice Value (A to B)1,14,240—
B to C: Sale price of goods [₹1,14,240 + ₹10,000]1,24,240—
Add: VAT @12%14,90914,909
Total Invoice Value (B to C)1,39,149—
Total tax to Government—29,149

Components inside the ₹14,909 VAT amount: on actual price ₹1,00,000 × 12% = ₹12,000; on Excise Duty ₹12,000 × 12% = ₹1,440; on CST ₹2,240 × 12% = ₹269; on value added by B ₹10,000 × 12% = ₹1,200. Total VAT = ₹14,909.

Since credit for Excise Duty and CST was NOT available to Dealer B, both were treated as a cost, and B was further liable to pay VAT on those tax components too. Such tax-on-tax is the cascading effect of tax, which leads to inflation.

If the Same Transactions Were Executed Under GST (rate assumed 12%)
Transaction / ParticularsAmount (₹)Tax to Govt. (₹)
A to B: Sale price of goods1,00,000—
Add: GST @12%12,00012,000
Total Invoice Value (A to B)1,12,000—
B to C: Sale price of goods [₹1,00,000 + ₹10,000]1,10,000—
Add: GST @12%13,200—
Total Invoice Value (B to C)1,23,200—
Amount payable to Government by B [₹13,200 − ₹12,000 ITC]—1,200
Total tax to Government—13,200

Answer: Total tax to Government — Pre-GST (cascading) regime = ₹29,149; under GST = ₹13,200. Since credit for the GST paid by B to A IS available to B, it is not treated as a cost — GST eliminates the cascading effect of tax, resulting in lower prices.

Why the Constitution Had to Change

Fiscal powers between the Centre and the States were clearly demarcated in the Constitution with almost no overlap. The Centre had power to levy tax on the manufacture of goods (except alcoholic liquor for human consumption, opium, narcotics, etc.), while the States had power to levy tax on the sale of goods. On inter-State sales, the Centre had power to levy a tax (Central Sales Tax), but the tax was collected and retained entirely by the originating States. For services, only the Centre was empowered to levy service tax. Since States were not empowered to tax the sale/purchase of goods in the course of import into or export from India, the Centre levied and collected this as additional duties of customs (CVD and SAD) — in addition to Basic Customs Duty — to counter-balance excise duty, sales tax, State VAT and other taxes levied on the like domestic product. Introducing GST required Constitutional amendment to concurrently empower the Centre and the States to levy and collect GST, and a unique institutional mechanism — with Constitutional force — to ensure decisions on GST's structure, design and operation were taken jointly.

CONCEPT

4.4 Constitutional Validity of GST ★★★ HIGH

4.4.1 Constitution (One Hundred and First) Amendment Act, 2016

To address the fiscal-power demarcation issue, the Constitution (122nd Amendment) Bill was introduced in the 16th Lok Sabha on 19.12.2014. The Bill provided for a levy of GST on supply of all goods or services, except Alcohol for human consumption.

  • The tax is levied as Dual GST — separately but concurrently — by the Union (central tax — CGST) and the States, including Union Territories with legislatures (State tax — SGST) / Union Territories without legislatures (Union territory tax — UTGST).
  • Parliament has the exclusive power to levy GST (integrated tax — IGST) on inter-State trade or commerce (including imports) in goods or services.
  • The Central Government has the power to levy excise duty in addition to GST on tobacco and tobacco products.
  • Tax on the supply of five specified petroleum products — crude, high speed diesel, petrol, air turbine fuel and natural gas — would be levied from a later date, on the recommendation of the GST Council.

The GST Council (GSTC)

A GST Council was to be constituted, comprising the Union Finance Minister, the Minister of State (Revenue), and the State Finance Ministers, to recommend on the GST rate, exemptions and thresholds, the taxes to be subsumed, and other features — ensuring a degree of harmonisation on GST between the Centre and the States, and across States.

GSTC Quorum: one-half of the total number of members.

GSTC Decision Rule: a majority of not less than three-fourth of weighted votes cast.

Centre's weightage = one-third of the total votes cast. All States taken together = two-third of the total votes cast. Consequence: BOTH the Centre AND a minimum of 20 States are required to form the majority.

Passage & Enactment Timeline

  • Constitution (122nd Amendment) Bill introduced in the 16th Lok Sabha — 19.12.2014.
  • Passed by the Lok Sabha — May, 2015.
  • Referred to the Select Committee of Rajya Sabha — 12.05.2015.
  • Select Committee submitted its Report on the Bill — 22.07.2015.
  • Bill, with certain amendments, finally passed in the Rajya Sabha and thereafter by the Lok Sabha — August, 2016.
  • Ratified by the required number of States and received the assent of the President — 8th September, 2016.
  • Enacted as the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016, with effect from 16th September, 2016.

QCorrectReason
1(c)Indirect taxes do not differentiate between the rich and the poor; both pay the same tax percentage on goods of mass consumption, which can increase wealth disparities.
2(b)Entry 84 of the Union List gives the Centre power to levy duties of excise on tobacco and other goods manufactured in India, excluding alcoholic liquor for human consumption.
3(b)Cascading effect refers to "tax on tax." In the pre-GST regime, VAT was often calculated on the invoice value inclusive of excise duty and CST, because credit for those taxes was not available to the dealer.
4(c)While the CBDT deals with direct taxes, the CBIC (Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs) handles the levy and collection of Central indirect taxes.
5(b)Article 246, read with Schedule VII, provides the three-fold distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States.
12 EXAM FACTS — CONCEPT OF INDIRECT TAXES (Module 4)

① Indirect tax's burden shifts from the seller (who pays it to Government) to the buyer/consumer (who ultimately bears it) — the "no pinch" feature.

② Indirect taxes are regressive (equal % burden on rich and poor alike); direct taxes are progressive (higher tax on higher income).

③ Incidence & Impact: Direct Tax falls on the SAME person (cannot be shifted, pinches the taxpayer). Indirect Tax falls on DIFFERENT persons (can be shifted, does not pinch the taxpayer).

④ Source's own examples: Income Tax = Direct Tax; GST and Customs Duty = Indirect Tax. Taxable event: Direct = taxable income of the assessee; Indirect = supply of goods and services.

⑤ Article 246, read with Schedule VII, divides legislative subject matter into three lists — Union List (List I), State List (List II), Concurrent List (List III).

⑥ Entry 84 (Union List) = Central Excise Act (tobacco/other manufactured goods, alcohol & most-narcotics excluded); Entry 92A (Union List) = Central Sales Tax (inter-State sale/purchase).

⑦ Entry 54 (State List) = State-level VAT; Entry 51 (State List) = State excise on alcohol/opium/narcotics manufactured in the State.

⑧ Pre-GST indirect tax was fragmented across excise duty, service tax, VAT, CST, purchase tax, entertainment tax and octroi — with multiplicity of rates/law/procedure and tax nakas at every inter-State border.

⑨ Cascading effect ("tax on tax") arose because ITC of Excise Duty and CST was NOT available to the next dealer — source's illustration: pre-GST total tax = ₹29,149 vs. ₹13,200 under GST on the identical ₹1,00,000 + ₹10,000 transaction chain.

⑩ GST was introduced as "One Nation One Tax," subsuming Central and State indirect taxes and eliminating cascading via seamless Input Tax Credit.

⑪ Constitution (122nd Amendment) Bill introduced 19.12.2014 → passed Lok Sabha May 2015 → Rajya Sabha Select Committee report 22.07.2015 → passed both Houses August 2016 → President's assent 8th September 2016 → enacted as Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016, effective 16th September 2016.

⑫ GST is Dual GST: CGST + SGST/UTGST concurrently (Centre + States/UTs), plus IGST (Parliament's exclusive power) on inter-State supply/imports; GSTC decisions need ≥3/4 weighted votes, Centre = 1/3 weightage, all States together = 2/3 weightage — so Centre + a minimum of 20 States are needed for a majority.

Goods and Services
Tax (GST) Laws

By amalgamating a large number of Central and State taxes into a single tax, GST mitigates cascading (tax-on-tax) and paves the way for a common national market — a destination-based, dual GST (CGST + SGST/UTGST on intra-State supply, IGST on inter-State supply) levied on the single taxable event of “supply,” in force with effect from 01-07-2017. This module runs from the Constitutional foundation and GST Council through to the charging section, the meaning of supply, composite/mixed supply, reverse charge, and exemptions.

MUST NOT SKIP: the meaning of “Supply” under Sec. 7 — every rupee of GST liability starts here, since “supply” (not manufacture, sale, or entry into a State) is now the ONE taxable event. Getting Schedule I (deemed supply without consideration), Schedule II (goods vs. services classification), Schedule III (neither goods nor services) and the composite-vs-mixed-supply test wrong is this module's single most repeated error pattern — and at 35% weight, this is by far the highest-value module in the paper.

5.1–5.2

Module Learning Objectives

SLOB mapped against the module: to acquire knowledge of the legal provisions enshrined in laws relating to GST and Customs Duty and appreciate their applicability in business operations; and to gather understanding of the legal provisions of these two indirect tax laws on matters of compliance while conducting business operations.

After studying this module, the student will be able to – appreciate the Constitutional aspects of GST; understand the basic features of the Indian model of GST; appreciate the meaning of supply; understand the provisions relating to charge, exemption and composition levy; appreciate the provisions relating to time and value of supply; appreciate the concepts of input tax credit and its utilisation; apply the knowledge in computing GST liability; and appreciate the various compliance provisions of the GST laws.

Glossary — Module 5, in Plain Words

Foundational GST terms used across 5.1–5.2, explained simply.

Supply [Sec. 7]The ONE taxable event under GST — replaces manufacture, sale, rendering of service, purchase, entry into a State, etc. An inclusive (not exhaustive) definition covering sale, transfer, barter, exchange, licence, rental, lease, disposal for consideration in the course/furtherance of business, plus certain things treated as supply even without consideration.
Dual GSTCentre and States simultaneously tax the same transaction — intra-State supply attracts CGST (Centre) + SGST/UTGST (State/UT); inter-State supply attracts IGST (Centre, shared with the destination State).
CGSTCentral Goods and Services Tax — levied & collected by the Centre under the CGST Act, 2017 on intra-State supply.
SGST / UTGSTState/Union Territory GST — levied & collected by the respective State/UT under its own SGST Act, 2017 on intra-State supply.
IGSTIntegrated GST — levied & collected by the Centre on every inter-State supply (and on imports); IGST rate = CGST rate + SGST rate; the levy is shared equally between Centre and the destination State.
GST Council [Art. 279A]The joint Centre-State forum (Union FM as Chairperson) that recommends rates, exemptions, thresholds and model GST law. Decisions need a 3/4 majority of weighted votes present and voting — Centre's vote = 1/3 weight, all States together = 2/3 weight; quorum is half the total members.
GSTNGoods and Services Tax Network — the non-profit, Government-owned Special Purpose Vehicle running the common IT portal (www.gst.gov.in) for registration, returns, payments and IGST settlement; each taxpayer gets a 15-digit PAN-based GSTIN.
Taxable Person [Sec. 2(107)]A person who is registered, or liable to be registered, u/s 22 or Sec. 24 — even a voluntarily-registered person qualifies.
Taxable Supply [Sec. 2(108)]A supply of goods or services or both which is leviable to tax under the Act.
Consideration [Sec. 2(31)]Any payment (money or otherwise) or the monetary value of any act/forbearance, made for the supply — excludes Government subsidies; a mere deposit is not consideration unless the supplier applies it as such.
Composite Supply [Sec. 2(30)]Two or more taxable supplies naturally bundled and supplied together in the ordinary course of business, one of which is a principal supply — taxed at the principal supply's rate.
Mixed Supply [Sec. 2(74)]Two or more individual supplies made together for a single price that do NOT constitute a composite supply — taxed at the highest rate among the constituents.
Principal Supply [Sec. 2(90)]The predominant element of a composite supply, to which the other (ancillary) supplies are incidental.
Related Persons / Distinct Persons [Sec. 25(4)]Related persons: officers/directors of each other, legal partners, employer-employee, 25%+ common ownership/control, family members, etc. Distinct persons: separately-registered branches of the same PAN in different States/UTs (or multiple registrations within one State) — supply between them is taxable even without consideration.
Reverse Charge [Sec. 2(98)]The liability to pay GST shifts from the supplier to the RECIPIENT, in notified categories of supply u/s 9(3)/9(4) (CGST) or Sec. 5(3)/5(4) (IGST).
Electronic Commerce Operator (ECO) [Sec. 2(45)]Any person who owns, operates or manages a digital/electronic platform for e-commerce; under Sec. 9(5), for specified services the ECO itself is deemed the supplier liable to pay tax.
Zero Rated Supply [Sec. 16, IGST Act]Export of goods/services, or supply to an SEZ developer/unit for authorised operations — ITC may be availed and unutilised ITC refunded, even though the outward supply itself bears no tax.
Exempt Supply [Sec. 2(47)]Supply attracting a nil rate of tax, or wholly exempted u/s 11 (CGST)/Sec. 6 (IGST), and includes non-taxable supply.
Non-taxable Supply [Sec. 2(78)]A supply that is not leviable to tax at all under the CGST Act or the IGST Act (e.g. alcoholic liquor for human consumption).
Schedule IActivities treated AS supply even without consideration (if in the course/furtherance of business) — e.g. ITC-availed asset disposal, supply between related/distinct persons, principal-agent goods transfer.
Schedule IIActivities/transactions classified as EITHER supply of goods OR supply of services — e.g. renting is always a service; transfer of title in goods is always goods.
Schedule IIIThe negative list — activities treated as NEITHER supply of goods NOR supply of services (no GST at all) — e.g. employee services to employer, court/tribunal services, sale of land, sale of a completed building.
Compensation CessLevied under the GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 on notified goods (pan masala, tobacco, coal, aerated water, motor cars, etc.) to compensate States for revenue loss on GST implementation — extended up to 31/03/2026.
