CONCEPT

Introduction ★★ MEDIUM

Under the earlier indirect tax system, numerous indirect taxes were levied and collected at multiple rates by both the Central and State Governments, adding compliance complexity and multiple points of interaction with tax authorities. The idea of moving towards GST in India was first mooted by the Union Finance Minister in the Budget for 2006-07, with introduction originally proposed from 1st April, 2010. The Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers (which had designed State VAT) was asked to develop the GST roadmap; Joint Working Groups of Centre and State officials examined exemptions, thresholds, taxation of services and inter-State supplies. A First Discussion Paper (FDP) on GST was released in November, 2009, forming the basis for further Centre-State discussion.

CONCEPT

5.1 Introduction to GST Law ★★★ HIGH

The introduction of GST was a very significant step in Indian indirect tax reform. By amalgamating a large number of Central and State taxes into a single tax, it mitigates cascading (double taxation) and paves the way for a common national market. For the consumer, the biggest advantage is a reduction in the overall tax burden on goods; GST also makes Indian products more competitive domestically and internationally.

5.1.1 Amendments by the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016 — GST Council [Article 279A]

The President, within 60 days of the commencement of the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016, was to constitute, by order, a Goods and Services Tax Council [Art. 279A(1)] — and has since done so.

Composition — a joint forum of Centre and States: (a) Union Finance Minister — Chairperson; (b) Union Minister of State in-charge of Revenue/Finance — Member; (c) the Minister in-charge of finance/taxation (or any Minister nominated) from each State Government — Members, who choose a Vice-Chairperson from amongst themselves.

Recommends to Union & States on — taxes/cesses/surcharges that may be subsumed into GST; goods/services to subject to or exempt from GST; model GST laws, principles of levy and apportionment of inter-State IGST, and place-of-supply principles; the threshold turnover below which exemption applies; rates including floor rates with bands; special rate(s) for a specified period during a natural calamity/disaster; special provisions for Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, J&K, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand; the date from which GST applies to petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit (petrol), natural gas and aviation turbine fuel; and any other GST matter.

Decision rule: ≥ 3/4 of the weighted votes of Members present & voting, at a meeting

Centre's vote = 1/3 weight of total votes cast  ·  all States together = 2/3 weight of total votes cast

Quorum = one-half of the total number of Members. No act/proceeding of the Council is invalid merely for a vacancy, defect in constitution/appointment, or a procedural irregularity not affecting merits.

Taxpoint: Per Art. 366(12A), “goods and services tax” means any tax on supply of goods, or services, or both — EXCEPT tax on supply of alcoholic liquor for human consumption. For inter-State supply, only the Centre can make law; for intra-State supply, both Centre and State can. Earlier, Art. 246 distributed indirect-tax powers between Centre and States separately; Art. 246A now empowers BOTH to levy GST concurrently.

Levy & Collection on Inter-State Supply [Article 269A]

GST on supplies in the course of inter-State trade or commerce is levied & collected by the Government of India and apportioned between the Union and the States as Parliament may provide by law, on the GST Council's recommendation. The amount so apportioned to a State does NOT form part of the Consolidated Fund of India; nor does an amount collected as IGST but used for paying SGST (or vice versa). Parliament may, by law, formulate the principles for determining place of supply and when a supply is inter-State.

Taxpoint: Supply of goods, services, or both in the course of import into India is deemed to be supply in the course of inter-State trade or commerce.

5.1.3 GST Network (GSTN)

Government established a common GST Electronic Portal (www.gst.gov.in), managed by the Goods and Services Network (GSTN), as the common IT infrastructure for the Centre and States. GSTN is a non-profit, Government-owned Special Purpose Vehicle. Its functions include: facilitating registration; forwarding returns to Central and State authorities; computation and settlement of IGST; matching tax-payment details with the banking network; providing MIS reports to Governments; profiling taxpayers; and running the ITC matching/reversal/reclaim engine. Each taxpayer receives a 15-digit alpha-numeric PAN-based Goods and Service Tax Identification Number (GSTIN) on registration.

Salient features of GSTN

  • Incorporated in March 2013 as a Sec. 25 (100% Government-owned) company with paid-up capital of ₹ 10 crore.
  • Functions as a common pass-through portal for taxpayers to submit registration applications, file returns, and make tax payments; also develops back-end modules for States.
  • Infosys Ltd. appointed as Managed Service Provider (MSP); more than 70 GST Suvidha Providers (GSPs) appointed.

5.1.4 Need for GST

Under the pre-GST regime, multiple taxes were collected differently by State and Central Governments with rates differing State to State, leading to a high-cost, inefficient structure. Specifically: (a) tax levied by one Government was generally not available for set-off against tax levied by another; (b) cascading effect (tax on tax) — e.g. State VAT levied on Central excise duty — fuelled inflation; (c) the lower CST rate (vs. VAT) was used for tax arbitrage; (d) each State's separate VAT law fragmented the nation into economic silos; (e) entry tax/octroi hindered free flow of business. GST, effective 01-07-2017, removed these inefficiencies.

Taxes Subsumed vs. NOT Subsumed into GST

Numerous Central and State indirect taxes were subsumed into GST (see FAQ list below). The following, however, remain OUTSIDE GST:

Central Taxes (NOT subsumed)State Taxes (NOT subsumed)
Basic Customs DutyState Excise Duty
Research and Development CessStamp Duty
Export DutyProfession Tax
Anti-Dumping DutyMotor Vehicle Tax
Safeguard Duty—

Taxes subsumed — Centre: Central Excise duty; Duties of Excise (Medicinal & Toilet Preparations); Additional Duties of Excise (Goods of Special Importance / Textiles & Textile Products); Additional Duties of Customs (CVD); Special Additional Duty of Customs (SAD); Service Tax; Central Surcharges & Cesses relating to supply of goods/services. State: State VAT; Central Sales Tax; Luxury Tax; Entry Tax (all forms); Entertainment & Amusement Tax (except when levied by local bodies); Taxes on advertisements; Purchase Tax; Taxes on lotteries, betting and gambling; State Surcharges & Cesses relating to supply of goods/services.

Benefits of GST (Summary)

  • Seamless flow of credit: the buyer (other than the ultimate consumer) credits tax paid at purchase against output tax liability — eliminating multiplicity/cascading of taxes.
  • Competitive prices: lower embedded taxes reduce the amount end consumers pay, boosting demand and consumption.
  • Increase in revenue: a simple tax structure widens the taxpayer base.
  • Easy, uniform tax structure: one tax to pay instead of many — less paperwork, lower compliance cost.
  • One Nation One Tax: uniform tax on supplies turns India into one market.
  • For business & industry: easy IT-driven compliance, uniform rates/structures, removal of cascading, improved competitiveness, and gains to manufacturers/exporters from full input set-off and CST phase-out.
  • For Centre & States: simpler administration, better anti-leakage controls via ITC-chain transparency, higher revenue efficiency, and a boost to ‘Make in India’.
  • For the consumer: a single transparent tax from manufacturer to consumer (replacing multiple hidden taxes) and relief in overall tax burden.

5.1.6 Salient Features of GST

  • Destination-based tax: a value-added tax on consumption, levied at every stage from manufacture to final consumption, with credit of taxes paid at earlier stages available as set-off — only value addition is taxed, and the final consumer bears the burden. Tax revenue accrues to the CONSUMING State (e.g. goods produced in Gujarat and sold to Rajasthan — tax accrues to Rajasthan, not Gujarat; under the pre-GST origin-based system it would have accrued to Gujarat).
  • One Nation One Tax: a single tax on supply across all of India, including Jammu & Kashmir, right from manufacturer to consumer.
  • Import & Export: import is treated as inter-State supply, chargeable to IGST along with Basic Customs Duty; export is a Zero Rated Supply — no IGST payable.
  • Tax on value of supply: GST is computed on the transaction value of the supply, subject to certain exceptions.
  • Registration: every supplier making a taxable supply (subject to threshold limits) must register under GST.
  • Other features: self-supply in specified situations is taxable; supply without consideration is, in a few cases, still liable to GST; a notified list of exempted goods/services exists; alcoholic liquor for human consumption, petroleum crude, high speed diesel, petrol, natural gas and ATF are outside GST's purview; GST collection procedure is uniform across States; and a common return serves both Centre and State.

Dual GST Model

Centre and States impose tax on goods and services simultaneously:

Nature of SupplyTax(es) & Who Levies/Administers
Intra-State supplyCGST (Centre) + SGST/UTGST (State/UT where consumed)
Inter-State supplyIGST — payable to the Centre, which levies and administers it

IGST rate = CGST rate + SGST rate

For intra-State supply, the IGST rate is split 50:50 into CGST and SGST/UTGST — e.g. IGST rate 18% on inter-State supply ⇒ intra-State CGST = 9%, SGST/UTGST = 9%.

Rates of GST: in general, 0%, 5%, 18% and 40%. A few supplies attract 0.25% (rough precious/semi-precious stones), 3% (Gold, Silver, Jewellery), 1.50% (silver filigree, handmade imitation jewellery) or 28% (Pan masala, tobacco products, etc.). Compensation cess is additionally payable on pan masala, tobacco & tobacco products, coal, lignite, aerated water and motor-cars.

ILLUSTRATION I — CGST/SGST on an Intra-State Supply of Goods

GIVEN: Hypothetically, CGST rate = 10%, SGST rate = 10%. A steel wholesaler in Uttar Pradesh supplies steel bars/rods (basic price ₹ 100) to a construction company in the same State.

WORKING: The dealer charges CGST ₹ 10 and SGST ₹ 10 in addition to the basic price — CGST deposited to the Central Government account, SGST to the State Government account. He need not pay the full ₹ 20 in cash — he can set off this liability against CGST/SGST already paid on his purchases (inputs).

ANSWER: For paying CGST he may use ONLY CGST credit on his purchases; for SGST, ONLY SGST credit. CGST credit cannot, in general, be used for SGST payment, nor SGST credit for CGST payment.

ILLUSTRATION II — CGST/SGST on an Intra-State Supply of Services

GIVEN: Same hypothetical rates (CGST 10%, SGST 10%). An advertising company in Mumbai supplies advertising services (basic value ₹ 100) to a soap manufacturer, also in Maharashtra.

WORKING: CGST ₹ 10 and SGST ₹ 10 are charged on the basic value; CGST deposited to Central account, SGST to State account. Set-off is available against CGST/SGST paid on the ad company's own purchases (stationery, office equipment, artist services, etc.).

ANSWER: Same rule applies — CGST credit only against CGST, SGST credit only against SGST; no cross-utilisation between the two.

Input Tax Credit — Utilisation Order & Seamless Credit Flow

  • IGST credit: first utilised for IGST payment; balance, if any, utilised towards CGST and SGST/UTGST.
  • CGST credit: first utilised for CGST payment; balance may be utilised towards IGST.
  • SGST/UTGST credit: first utilised for SGST/UTGST payment; balance may be utilised towards IGST.

Seamless inter-State credit flow: the exporting-State's inter-State supplier sets off available IGST/CGST/SGST credit against IGST payable on his inter-State supply; the importing-State buyer avails IGST-paid credit against his own output tax; the exporting State transfers to the Centre the SGST/UTGST credit utilised for IGST payment; and the Centre transfers to the importing State the IGST credit used for SGST/UTGST payment.

ActRules
The Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (similar law made by States/UTs)Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017
The Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017Integrated Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017
The Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act, 2017Goods and Services Tax Compensation Cess Rules, 2017
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: CGST/SGST CROSS-UTILISATION & “WHAT'S OUTSIDE GST”

THE TRAP: students assume CGST credit can be freely used against SGST liability (or vice versa) since both arise on the same intra-State invoice; and separately assume that GST replaced EVERY pre-existing indirect tax.

THE TWIST: per Illustrations I & II, CGST credit can be used ONLY against CGST, SGST credit ONLY against SGST — never cross-utilised. And Basic Customs Duty, Export Duty, Anti-Dumping/Safeguard Duty, R&D Cess (Central), plus State Excise Duty, Stamp Duty, Profession Tax and Motor Vehicle Tax (State) all continue OUTSIDE GST — alongside alcoholic liquor for human consumption and (temporarily) the five specified petroleum products.

5.1.7 Goods and Services Tax Compensation Cess

The GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 levies Compensation Cess to compensate States for revenue loss on GST implementation, with effect from 01-07-2017, for five years or such extended period as the GST Council recommends (extended up to 31/03/2026). Taxable persons selling notified goods — Pan masala; Tobacco & tobacco products; Cigarettes, cigar; Coal, lignite; Aerated water; and Motor-cars — must collect and pay GST Cess.

  • Cess is computed on the value of taxable supply, levied IN ADDITION to CGST + SGST/UTGST (intra-State) or IGST (inter-State, including import of goods).
  • ITC of Cess may be used only against output Cess liability — never against output CGST, SGST or IGST.
  • Cess does not apply to outward supplies of a taxpayer registered under the composition levy.
  • Cess is not levied on exports — the exporter may claim refund of ITC of cess paid on purchases.

Compensation payable to a State = Projected Revenue for the FY − Actual Revenue earned (incl. IGST share)

Step 1: Base Revenue = State's tax revenue in FY 2015-16.

Step 2: Assumed growth rate = 14% p.a. → Projected Revenue for FY 2018-19 (if base year revenue = ₹ 100) = 100 × (1 + 14/100)3.

At the end of the transition period, 50% of the unutilised Fund balance transfers to the Consolidated Fund of India (Centre's share); the balance 50% is distributed among States in the ratio of their total State-tax/UTGST revenues in the last transition year.

FAQ by CBIC (15-12-2018) — Selected, on 5.1

  • What is GST? A destination-based tax on consumption, levied at all stages with credit of taxes paid at previous stages as set-off — only value addition is taxed and the final consumer bears the burden.
  • Destination-based consumption tax means? Tax accrues to the taxing authority with jurisdiction over the place of consumption (= place of supply).
  • Commodities kept outside GST? Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is excluded by the Constitutional definition of GST itself [Art. 366(12A)]; five petroleum products (petroleum crude, motor spirit, high speed diesel, natural gas, ATF) are TEMPORARILY kept out until the GST Council notifies a date — the existing VAT & Central Excise regime continues on them meanwhile.
  • Tobacco under GST? Leviable to GST; the Centre additionally retains power to levy Central Excise duty on tobacco products.
  • Why Dual GST? India's federal structure assigns tax powers to both Centre and States, each with distinct constitutional responsibilities — dual GST keeps faith with fiscal federalism.
  • CGST vs. SGST chargeability difference? Location of supplier/recipient within the country is immaterial for CGST; SGST is chargeable ONLY when both supplier and recipient are located within the same State.
  • Overall tax-burden reduction estimate? Currently estimated at 25%–30% on goods.

Quick MCQ — 5.1

1. Which Constitutional Amendment Act paved the way for GST in India?

(a) 122nd Amendment Act(b) 101st Amendment Act(c) 115th Amendment Act(d) 102nd Amendment Act

Answer: (b). The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 (enacted 8th September 2016) provided the legal framework for GST.

2. Which Article was inserted to grant concurrent powers to Centre and States to levy GST?

(a) Article 246(b) Article 269A(c) Article 246A(d) Article 279A

Answer: (c). Article 246A provides a unique mechanism where both Parliament and State Legislatures may make GST law.

3. For inter-State supply of goods/services, who has EXCLUSIVE power to make GST law?

(a) State Government(b) Both Centre and State concurrently(c) Parliament (Central Government)(d) GST Council

Answer: (c). Article 246A(2) — Parliament has exclusive power where supply takes place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce.

4. Under the dual GST model, which tax is levied by the Centre on an intra-State supply?

(a) SGST(b) IGST(c) UTGST(d) CGST

Answer: (d). CGST is levied by the Centre on intra-State supplies; SGST/UTGST is levied by the State/UT.

5. Which of the following was NOT subsumed into GST at the State level?

(a) State VAT(b) Luxury Tax(c) Professional Tax(d) Entertainment Tax (levied by the State)

Answer: (c). VAT, Luxury Tax and State Entertainment Tax were subsumed; Professional Tax remains outside GST (as does Entertainment Tax levied by local bodies).

6. The GST Council is chaired by:

(a) The Prime Minister of India(b) The Union Finance Minister(c) The Governor of the RBI(d) The Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue

Answer: (b). Article 279A — the Council is headed by the Union Finance Minister as Chairperson.

7. GST is a value-added tax levied on the ________ of goods and services.

(a) Manufacture(b) Sale(c) Supply(d) Movement

Answer: (c). GST shifts the taxable event from manufacture/sale to the act of “supply.”

8. Which Central tax has been subsumed into GST?

(a) Basic Customs Duty(b) Central Excise Duty(c) Property Tax(d) Income Tax

Answer: (b). Central Excise Duty, Service Tax and Additional Duties of Customs (CVD/SAD) merged into GST; Basic Customs Duty continues separately.

9. Per Article 279A, within how many days must the President constitute the GST Council?

(a) 30 days(b) 90 days(c) 60 days(d) 120 days

Answer: (c). Article 279A(1) — within 60 days of commencement of the Amendment Act.

10. What is the primary objective of the “Dual GST” model adopted in India?

(a) Centre collects all taxes and distributes at its discretion(b) Centre and States can concurrently levy and collect tax on a common base(c) Eliminate the need for State-level tax departments(d) Apply GST only on imports, keeping domestic sales under VAT

Answer: (b). Given India's federal structure, Dual GST lets Centre and States simultaneously tax the supply of goods and services.

CONCEPT

5.2 Levy and Collection of CGST and IGST ★★★ HIGH

5.2.1 Application of CGST/IGST Laws — GST is a multi-stage value added tax on consumption of goods or services or both. A “dual GST” model applies:

Nature of SupplyTax Payable
A. Intra-State Supply — within a State/UTCentral tax (CGST) under the CGST Act, 2017 (Parliament) + State tax (SGST) under the respective SGST Act, 2017 (State legislature)
B. Inter-State SupplyIntegrated GST (IGST) — levied by the Centre; the levy is shared equally between Central and the respective State Government

Determining whether a supply is inter-State or intra-State decides which tax applies:

Intra-State SupplyInter-State Supply
Supply of goods within the State/UTSupply of goods from one State/UT to another State/UT
Supply of services within the State/UTSupply of services from one State/UT to another State/UT
—Import of goods till they cross the customs frontier
—Import of service
—Export of goods or service
—Supply of goods/services to/by SEZ
—Any other supply in the taxable territory not being intra-State

Sec. 20 of the IGST Act provides that CGST Act provisions relating to scope of supply; composite & mixed supply; time & value of supply; input tax credit; registration; tax invoice, credit/debit notes; accounts & records; returns (other than late fee); payment of tax; TDS/TCS; assessment; refunds; audit; inspection/search/seizure/arrest; demands & recovery; liability in certain cases; advance ruling; appeals & revision; presumption as to documents; offences & penalties; job work; electronic commerce; transitional provisions; and interest/penalty — shall apply, mutatis mutandis, to integrated tax as if enacted under the IGST Act itself.

5.2.2 Concept of Supply, including Composite and Mixed Supplies ★★★ HIGH

The taxable event in GST is “supply of goods or services or both.” Multiple earlier taxable events (manufacture, sale, rendering of service, purchase, entry into a territory of State, etc.) are replaced by this ONE event. The GST law gives an inclusive definition.

Supply [Sec. 7(1)] includes — (a) all forms of supply of goods or services or both such as sale, transfer, barter, exchange, licence, rental, lease or disposal, made or agreed to be made for a consideration by a person in the course or furtherance of business; (aa) activities/transactions by a person (other than an individual) to its members or constituents or vice-versa, for cash/deferred payment/other valuable consideration — the person and its members are deemed to be two separate persons for this purpose; (b) import of services for a consideration, whether or not in the course or furtherance of business; and (c) activities specified in Schedule I, made or agreed to be made WITHOUT consideration.

Sec. 7(1)(a) — All Forms of Supply for Consideration, in the Course/Furtherance of Business

  • Supply must be OF GOODS OR SERVICES — supply of anything else (e.g. money or securities) is not covered.
  • Illustrative inclusions: Sale (lawful, absolute transfer of ownership for money, no rights left with the transferor); Transfer (lawfully conveying property, consent/capacity of parties may be absent); Barter (consideration is goods/services, not money — involves two supplies); Exchange (giving/taking one thing for another); Licence (permission to enter/use property, or to act); Rental; Lease (money paid to use land/building/vehicle/equipment for an agreed period); Disposal (getting rid of something).
  • Includes agreeing to supply in future — e.g. advance received for a future service triggers GST at the time of receipt.
  • “Consideration” [Sec. 2(31)] includes any payment made/to be made (money or otherwise) and the monetary value of any act or forbearance in respect of the supply, whether by the recipient or any other person — but EXCLUDES any Government subsidy. A mere deposit is not consideration unless the supplier applies it as such.
  • The transaction must be “in the course” or “furtherance of business” — non-business supplies do not qualify as “supply” for GST.
  • Goods [Sec. 2(52)]: every kind of movable property other than money and securities, but includes actionable claim, growing crops, grass and things attached to/forming part of the land agreed to be severed before/under a contract of supply. Taxpoint: only SPECIFIED actionable claims (lottery, betting, gambling) are taxable supply — others are not.
  • Services [Sec. 2(102)]: anything other than goods, money and securities — includes activities relating to use of money/its conversion (for a separate consideration) and facilitating/arranging securities transactions.
  • Taxable Person [Sec. 2(107)]: a person registered or liable to be registered u/s 22 or Sec. 24 — supply must be BY a taxable person, but the recipient need not be one.
  • Person [Sec. 2(84)]: individual; HUF; company; firm; LLP; AOP/BOI (incorporated or not); any corporation under Central/State/Provincial Act or Government company; body corporate under foreign law; co-operative society; local authority; Central/State Government; society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860; trust; and every artificial juridical person.
  • Business [Sec. 2(17)]: trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure, wager or similar (whether or not for pecuniary benefit); connected/incidental/ancillary activities; activities without volume/frequency/continuity/regularity; supply/acquisition of goods (incl. capital goods)/services at commencement or closure of business; club/association facilities to members for consideration; admission of persons to premises for consideration; services by an office-holder in the course of trade/profession/vocation; race-club activities; and activities of Government/local authority as public authorities.

A transaction is “supply” only if ALL of these hold:

Supply of goods or services or both · for consideration (subject to exceptions) · in the course/furtherance of business (subject to exceptions) · a TAXABLE supply · in a taxable territory · by a taxable person

Sec. 7(1)(b) & (c) — Import of Services; Schedule I (Supply Without Consideration)

Import of service for consideration [Sec. 7(1)(b)]: import of a service (not goods) made for consideration, whether or not in the course/furtherance of business — so even a paid import for PERSONAL consumption is “supply,” liable to tax.

Schedule I activities, without consideration [Sec. 7(1)(c)] — treated as supply (if in the course/furtherance of business):

  1. Permanent transfer/disposal of business assets where ITC was availed on the asset. Taxpoint: if ITC was NOT availed, disposal without consideration is NOT a supply. E.g. availed-ITC beauty products taken for personal family use, or ITC-availed furniture donated to an NGO — both are supply.
  2. Supply between related persons or distinct persons [Sec. 25(4)] in the course/furtherance of business — even without consideration. Exception: gifts up to ₹ 50,000 in value per financial year by an employer to an employee are NOT treated as supply. “Related persons” [explanation to Sec. 15(5)] — officers/directors of each other's business, legal partners, employer-employee, 25%+ common voting-stock ownership/control, one controls the other, both controlled by a third person, together control a third person, or members of the same family [Sec. 2(49): spouse, children; and dependent parents/grandparents/siblings]. Employer-employee ARE related, but services by an employee to employer in the course of employment are NOT supply. Distinct person [Sec. 25(4)]: a person with more than one GST registration (same or different States/UTs) is treated as a distinct person for each registration. Providing a Corporate Guarantee to a subsidiary is a supply of service even without consideration [Rule 28(2)].
  3. Supply of goods between principal and agent where the agent undertakes to supply (on behalf of the principal) or to receive (on behalf of the principal) such goods — applicable ONLY to goods, ONLY between principal and agent. Agent [Sec. 2(5)]: a factor, broker, commission agent, arhatia, del credere agent, auctioneer, or other mercantile agent carrying on business of supply/receipt of goods or services on another's behalf. Principal [Sec. 2(88)]: the person on whose behalf the agent acts.
  4. Import of services by a person from a related person or from his own establishment outside India, in the course/furtherance of business — even without consideration (contrast: Sec. 7(1)(b) needs consideration; this Schedule I entry does not, but needs a RELATED-party/own-establishment import).

Buy One Get One Free [Circular No. 92/11/2019-GST]: goods/services supplied free of cost are NOT “supply” under Sec. 7(1)(a) (except Schedule I activities). A “Buy One Get One Free” offer is, in substance, NOT an individual free supply but two or more supplies for a single combined price — effectively two goods for the price of one.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: “NO CONSIDERATION = NO GST” IS NOT ALWAYS TRUE

THE TRAP: students assume that because consideration is a normal ingredient of “supply” [Sec. 7(1)(a)], any transaction without money or valuable consideration changing hands automatically escapes GST — e.g. a free “bonus” item, an inter-branch stock transfer, or a donated asset.

THE TWIST: Schedule I lists four specific situations that ARE deemed supply even WITHOUT consideration — ITC-availed asset disposal; supply between related/distinct persons (e.g. inter-State branch stock transfer, since separately-registered branches are “distinct persons”); principal-agent goods transfer; and import of services from a related person/own foreign establishment. The determining test is NOT “was money paid?” but “does this fall in Schedule I, and was it in the course/furtherance of business?” The ONLY carve-out is ITC NOT availed on the asset being disposed of, and gifts ≤ ₹ 50,000/year to an employee.

Illustrations — Meaning of Supply [Sec. 7]

ILLUSTRATION 1 — Sec. 7(1)(a): Supply for Consideration (Barter)

'TechGizmo Ltd.' exchanges 100 old laptops with a dealer for 50 new printers; open market value of the old laptops is ₹ 10 Lakhs.

ANSWER: Barter — transfer of title in goods for consideration in kind, in the course of business ⇒ Supply of Goods u/s 7(1)(a).

ILLUSTRATION 2 — Sec. 7(1)(b): Import of Services (Personal vs. Business)

Mr. Ankit, an architect, imports interior design services from a US firm: ₹ 1 Lakh to design his office, and ₹ 50,000 to design his personal bedroom.

ANSWER: Office design — import for consideration in the course of business is a Supply. Bedroom design — import for consideration, even for personal use, is ALSO a Supply u/s 7(1)(b) (consideration alone suffices for import of services).

ILLUSTRATION 3 — Schedule I: Deemed Supply — Permanent Disposal of Business Assets

'Alpha Motors' donates an old delivery van to an NGO, having claimed ITC on the van 5 years ago.

ANSWER: Since ITC was availed, permanent disposal (even by donation, without consideration) is a Deemed Supply under Schedule I.

ILLUSTRATION 4 — Corporate Guarantee to Subsidiary

'HoldCo Ltd.' issues a corporate guarantee to a bank for a loan taken by subsidiary 'SubCo Ltd.', with no guarantee fee charged.

ANSWER: HoldCo and SubCo are Related Persons — supply of services between related persons in the course of business is a taxable supply even without consideration.

ILLUSTRATION 5 — Principal-Agent Supply

Mr. A (Principal, Gujarat) sends goods to agent Mr. B (Maharashtra); B sells the goods on A's behalf and issues the invoice to the final customer in his OWN name.

ANSWER: Since the agent invoices in his own name, he falls under the Schedule I Agent definition — the A-to-B transfer is a Deemed Supply of goods, liable to GST.

ILLUSTRATION 6 — Schedule II: Software Development

'SoftSolutions' develops customized ERP software for a client, charging ₹ 50 Lakhs.

ANSWER: Development/design/programming/customization of IT software is a Supply of Services (Schedule II).

ILLUSTRATION 7 — Renting of Immovable Property

Mrs. Mehta rents her commercial shop to a CMA firm, and her residential flat to a registered business entity for use as a guest house.

ANSWER: Shop renting — Supply of Services. Renting of immovable property is always Supply of Service if rented to a Registered Person, regardless of purpose.

ILLUSTRATION 8 — Schedule III: Sale of Land vs. Works Contract

Case A: Builder sells a flat where the ENTIRE consideration is received after issuance of the Completion Certificate (CC). Case B: Builder sells an under-construction flat with part payment received BEFORE CC.

ANSWER: Case A — sale of a building after completion is Neither Goods nor Services (Schedule III); no GST. Case B — a Works Contract, Supply of Service (Schedule II); GST applies.

ILLUSTRATION 9 — Actionable Claims

Transaction X: transfer of an unsecured debt (loan assignment). Transaction Y: purchase of a lottery ticket.

ANSWER: X — actionable claims are generally in Schedule III (No Supply); unsecured debt is NOT a supply. Y — lottery, betting, gambling and online money gaming are the exception, treated as Supply of Goods.

ILLUSTRATION 10 — SEZ Warehousing

'Global Importers' warehouses goods in an SEZ; before clearing for home consumption, they sell the goods to 'Local Processors Ltd.'

ANSWER: Supply of SEZ-warehoused goods to any person before clearance for home consumption is Neither Goods nor Services (Schedule III) — no GST (though Customs duties apply on eventual clearance).

ILLUSTRATION 11 — Stock Transfer Between Branches

'Omega Retail Ltd.' transfers 500 shirts from its registered Mumbai showroom to its registered Surat showroom, by delivery challan (no sale invoice).

ANSWER: Under Sec. 25, branches in different States are “Distinct Persons”; per Schedule I, supply between distinct persons in the course/furtherance of business is Supply even without consideration — Omega Retail (Mumbai) must pay IGST on the value of the transfer.

ILLUSTRATION 12 — Agreeing to Tolerate an Act (Schedule II)

Tenant 'Alpha Traders' terminates a 5-year lease early; the landlord agrees but charges a ₹ 2 Lakh “Cancellation Fee”/“Early Exit Penalty.”

ANSWER: Schedule II classifies “agreeing to tolerate an act” as Supply of Services — the fee is consideration for tolerating early exit — a taxable supply of service.

ILLUSTRATION 13 — High Sea Sales (Schedule III)

'India Oil Corp' imports crude oil from Saudi Arabia; while still on the high seas (before crossing customs frontiers), it sells the consignment to 'Reliance Industries' by endorsing documents of title.

ANSWER: Schedule III specifically excludes such “supply of goods by the consignee to any other person by endorsement of documents of title, after dispatch from a port outside India but before home-consumption clearance” — a High Sea Sale, Neither Goods nor Services; no GST on this specific transaction (IGST is paid by the final buyer at the Bill of Entry stage).

Schedule II — Classified as Supply of Goods OR Supply of Services [Sec. 7(1A)]

Schedule II settles activities historically taxed ambiguously (e.g. works contract, under earlier VAT + Service Tax law) by expressly classifying them.

ParticularsClassified As
Any transfer of the title in goods (e.g. sale of readymade garments)Supply of Goods
Any transfer of right in goods / undivided share in goods WITHOUT transfer of title (e.g. renting a weaving machine)Supply of Services
Transfer of title in goods under an agreement that property passes at a future date upon full payment (e.g. hire-purchase-style car sale)Supply of Goods
Any lease, tenancy, easement, licence to occupy landSupply of Services
Any lease/letting out of a building (commercial/industrial/residential complex), wholly or partly, for business or commerceSupply of Services
Any treatment or process applied to another person's goods (e.g. job work)Supply of Services
Business assets transferred/disposed so as no longer to form part of business assetsSupply of Goods
Business goods put to private use / made available to any person for a non-business purposeSupply of Services
Where a person ceases to be a taxable person, goods forming part of business assets are deemed supplied immediately before cessation (exceptions: going-concern transfer, or business continued by a personal representative)Supply of Goods
Renting of immovable property (any purpose) — renting a residential dwelling as residence to an UNREGISTERED person is exempt [Entry 12] but still a “supply”Supply of Services
Construction of a complex/building/civil structure for sale — UNLESS entire consideration is received after completion certificate OR first occupation, whichever earlier (then NOT a supply at all)Supply of Services
Temporary transfer/permitting use of Intellectual Property Right (IPR) — permanent transfer of IPR ownership is GoodsSupply of Services
Development, design, programming, customization, upgradation, enhancement, implementation of IT softwareSupply of Services
Agreeing to refrain from an act / to tolerate an act or situation / to do an act (non-compete fee; charges for non-supply of a desired product)Supply of Services
Transfer of the right to use any goods for a purpose (cash/deferred payment/other consideration), e.g. hire purchaseSupply of Services
Works contract [Sec. 2(119): building/construction/fabrication/erection/installation/repair/renovation of immovable property involving transfer of property in goods]Supply of Services
Supply of food/other article for human consumption or drink (other than alcoholic liquor), as part of any service, for considerationSupply of Services

Per Circular No. 178/10/2022-GST (03.08.2022), taxability of “agreeing to tolerate an act” (Sch. II Para 5(e)) requires an EXPRESS or IMPLIED contractual promise to tolerate, against consideration — a mere flow of money does not by itself create a supply. NOT taxable (mere “flow of money”/penalty, not consideration): liquidated damages compensating breach; cheque dishonour fines; penalties for law violations (traffic, mining, pollution); forfeiture of salary/employee bond on early exit; forfeiture of earnest money for non-serious bidding. Taxable (ancillary service naturally bundled with the principal supply): late-payment surcharge/fee; cancellation charges for tickets/bookings.

Sec. 7(2) — Negative List: Neither Supply of Goods Nor Services

The following are treated as NEITHER supply of goods NOR supply of services — hence NO GST at all: (a) activities/transactions specified in Schedule III; or (b) activities by Central/State Government/local authority as public authorities, as notified by the Government on the GST Council's recommendation.

Schedule III activities:

  1. Services by an EMPLOYEE to the employer in the course of/relating to employment. (Gifts ≤ ₹ 50,000/year employer-to-employee are not supply; benefits under the employment contract don't attract GST; but services by an employee in some OTHER capacity are not covered by this exclusion.)
  2. Services by any court or Tribunal established under any law.
  3. Functions performed by Members of Parliament/State Legislature/Panchayats/Municipalities/local authorities; duties performed by any person holding a Constitutional post (e.g. President, Vice-President, PM, Chief Justice, Speaker Lok Sabha, CAG, UPSC Chairman, Chief Election Commissioner, Attorney General); and duties of a Chairperson/Member/Director in a Government-established body (not deemed an employee before this clause commenced).
  4. Services of funeral, burial, crematorium or mortuary, including transportation of the deceased.
  5. Sale of land, and (subject to Schedule II para 5(b)) sale of building — i.e. excluding under-construction premises where part/full consideration was received before completion certificate/first occupation. Taxpoint: sale of a ready flat (post-completion) is not taxable.
  6. Actionable claims, OTHER than SPECIFIED actionable claims. Specified actionable claim [Sec. 2(102A)]: betting; casinos; gambling; horse racing; lottery; or online money gaming [Sec. 2(80A)/2(80B)] — these ARE taxable (Supply of Goods).
  7. Supply of goods from a non-taxable territory to another non-taxable territory without entering India (merchant trading / Out-and-Out transactions).
  8. (a) Supply of customs-bonded warehoused goods before clearance for home consumption; (aa) supply of SEZ/FTWZ-warehoused goods before clearance for export or to DTA; (b) high-sea sale — supply by the consignee, by endorsement of title documents, after dispatch from a foreign port but before home-consumption clearance.
  9. Apportionment of co-insurance premium by the lead insurer to co-insurers (subject to the lead insurer paying CGST/SGST/UTGST/IGST on the entire premium).
  10. Ceding/reinsurance commission deducted by an insurer from reinsurance premium paid to the reinsurer (subject to CGST/SGST/UTGST/IGST being paid by the reinsurer on the gross premium inclusive of that commission).

Notified u/s 7(2)(b): services by way of any activity relating to a function entrusted to a Panchayat (Art. 243G) or Municipality (Art. 243W); and grant of an alcoholic liquor licence against a licence/application fee.

Clarified by circular as “not supply”: inter-State movement of conveyances (trains, buses, trucks, tankers, trailers, vessels, containers, aircraft) between distinct persons, EXCEPT when the movement is for further supply of the conveyance itself; and inter-State movement of rigs, tools, spares and wheeled goods (e.g. cranes) — though repairs/maintenance of such goods remains taxable.

Sec. 7(3): the Government, on the Council's recommendation, may by notification specify transactions to be treated as (a) supply of goods and not services, or (b) supply of services and not goods.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: WHICH SCHEDULE III ITEMS ARE REALLY “NO GST”

THE TRAP: students over-generalise Schedule III — assuming ALL actionable claims are outside GST, or that a director's every payment from a company is a Schedule III employment payment, or that any land/building sale escapes GST.

THE TWIST: Schedule III excludes actionable claims OTHER THAN specified ones — lottery, betting, gambling, horse racing and online money gaming are carved BACK IN as taxable Supply of Goods. A whole-time director's SALARY is a Schedule III employment payment (no GST), but sitting fees for attending board meetings are services BY a director TO the company outside an employment contract — taxable under Reverse Charge. And “sale of building” is Schedule III ONLY for a COMPLETED building (consideration received after completion certificate/first occupation); an under-construction sale with part payment received earlier is a Works Contract under Schedule II, fully taxable.

Composite and Mixed Supply [Sec. 7(1), Sec. 8] ★★★ HIGH

GST is payable on every supply unless exempted, and different goods/services attract different notified rates. Where a supply is a single, clearly identifiable good/service, rate application is simple — but many real supplies COMBINE goods and/or services, each potentially at a different rate. GST law resolves this via composite and mixed supply.

Tax liability on composite/mixed supply [Sec. 8]

Composite supply (one of the constituents being a principal supply) ⇒ taxed as a supply of that PRINCIPAL SUPPLY, at its rate.

Mixed supply (two or more supplies, not composite) ⇒ taxed as a supply of whichever constituent attracts the HIGHEST rate of tax.

“Composite supply” [Sec. 2(30)] means a supply by a taxable person to a recipient consisting of two or more taxable supplies of goods/services/both, naturally bundled and supplied in conjunction with each other in the ordinary course of business, one of which is a principal supply. “Principal supply” [Sec. 2(90)] is the predominant element of a composite supply, to which any other supply is ancillary.

Examples of composite supply: goods packed, transported and insured together (principal supply = goods); a laptop sold with warranty + pre-installed OS/Office (principal supply = laptop); food supplied to in-patients as advised by the doctor/nutritionist, as part of composite healthcare supply (but food to non-admitted patients/attendants/visitors is separately taxable); and printing of content-supplied-by-recipient using the printer's own paper (principal supply = the printing service).

Taxpoint: works contract and restaurant services are classic composite supplies, but the GST Act itself separately identifies BOTH as “supply of services” chargeable to a specific notified rate against each — so for these two, no separate “is-it-composite” test is needed.

“Mixed supply” [Sec. 2(74)] means two or more individual supplies of goods/services/any combination, made in conjunction for a SINGLE PRICE, where such supply does NOT constitute a composite supply.

Example of mixed supply: a package of canned foods, sweets, chocolates, cakes, dry fruits, aerated drinks and fruit juices sold for a single price — each item is independently supplyable, so it is a mixed supply (it would NOT be a mixed supply if the items were sold separately). The test order is: first rule out composite supply — only if the transaction fails the “naturally bundled” test does it become a mixed supply, classified at the highest applicable rate.

A house rented, one floor for residence and another for a printing press, under a single rent deed — renting for two different purposes is NOT naturally bundled; the entire bundle is treated as the higher-liability category (commercial renting), since that attracts the higher tax.

Is a Bundle “Naturally Bundled”? — Indicators

  • The consumer/service-receiver's perception — if most receivers reasonably expect the package as one, it's naturally bundled (e.g. hotel package with breakfast).
  • Majority of service providers in that line of business offer a similar bundle (e.g. on-board catering + air transport, offered by most airlines).
  • Nature of the services — a main service plus incidental/ancillary services that aid its better enjoyment (e.g. hotel stay + free laundry of 3–4 items/day).
  • Other indicators (not determinative alone): a single price regardless of how much of the package is used; advertised as a package; elements not available separately; elements integral to one overall supply — removing one changes the nature of the supply.

A hotel booked for a 100-delegate conference at a lump-sum package (accommodation, breakfast, tea/coffee, fitness room, conference room, business centre) — no single constituent captures the essential character alone, but “convention service” does; the bundle is judged as convention service, chargeable at its full rate. It remains open to the hotel to charge individually for services, provided value is not off-loaded from a higher-rated to a lower/concessional-rated item.

Composite vs. Mixed Supply — Comparison

DescriptionComposite SupplyMixed Supply
Naturally bundledYesNo
Each supply available individuallyNoYes / No
One is the predominant supply for the recipientYesYes / No
Other supply(ies) ancillary to, or received because of, the predominant supplyYesNo
Each supply priced separatelyYes / NoNo
Supplied togetherYesYes
All supplies can be of goods; all can be of services; or a combination of one/more goods with one/more servicesYesYes
No infallible test exists — every supply must be independently analysed against these indicators; there is no straight-jacket formula.

Illustration 14 — Composite or Mixed? (Case-by-Case)

Identify Composite vs. Mixed Supply
CaseNature of Supply
Air ticket Delhi–Mumbai, including on-board meals and insuranceComposite Supply [Sec. 2(30)] — passenger transportation is the principal supply.
Refrigerator sold with Tupperware bottles + a separate stabilizer, for a single priceNot naturally bundled in the ordinary course of business — Mixed Supply [Sec. 2(74)].
“Conference Executive Kit” (leather bag + fountain pen + notebook + calculator) at ₹ 2,500Not naturally bundled nor a necessity together; sold for a single price, each sellable separately — Mixed Supply.
Luxury hotel room + 2 pieces of laundry/day included in room rent, non-optionalComposite Supply — laundry is incidental to and aids better enjoyment of the room stay (frequent practice); Principal Supply = hotel accommodation.
Specialized machine + delivery + installation + 3-day mandatory technical trainingInstallation & training are essential and ancillary to the machine in heavy-machinery trade — Composite Supply; Principal Supply = the machine.
Diwali gift hamper: dry fruits + tinned juices + chocolates + decorative diya, single priceNo natural bundle — independent taxable supplies happening to be sold together — Mixed Supply.
55-inch LED TV with a single price including 1-year warranty + 2-year AMCStandard practice to bundle warranty/AMC with high-value electronics; TV is predominant — Composite Supply.

ILLUSTRATION 15 — Mixed Supply: Rate & GST Computation

GIVEN: “FitLife Traders” sells a pre-packaged “Starter Fitness Kit” for a single price of ₹ 20,000 (excl. GST), containing: Product A (market value ₹ 18,300, GST 18%), Product B (market value ₹ 500, GST 5%), Product C (market value ₹ 1,200, GST 5%). Items can be sold separately.

STEP 1 (nature of supply): the items are distinct, not naturally bundled in the ordinary course of business, sold together for a single price ⇒ Mixed Supply [Sec. 2(74)].

STEP 2 (rate): for a mixed supply, the rate is the HIGHEST rate among the constituents [Sec. 8(b)] — Product A 18%, Product B 5%, Product C 5% ⇒ applicable rate = 18%.

ANSWER: Taxable Value = ₹ 20,000; GST Payable = ₹ 20,000 × 18% = ₹ 3,600.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: COMPOSITE vs. MIXED SUPPLY CLASSIFICATION

THE TRAP: students treat “sold together for one price” as sufficient, by itself, to call something a composite supply — or wrongly tax a mixed supply at the LOWEST constituent rate, or at the rate of whichever item has the highest individual value.

THE TWIST: a single price is common to BOTH composite and mixed supply (see the comparison table) — it is NOT the deciding factor. The real test is whether the items are “naturally bundled in the ordinary course of business” with one predominant/principal element (composite ⇒ taxed at the PRINCIPAL supply's rate) versus independent items merely sold together (mixed ⇒ taxed at the HIGHEST rate among constituents, regardless of which item is highest in VALUE — Illustration 15's Product A is both the highest-value AND highest-rate item, but that is coincidence, not the rule).

FAQ by CBIC (15-12-2018) — Composite & Mixed Supply

How do composite and mixed supply differ? Composite supply = two or more taxable supplies naturally bundled in the ordinary course of business, one being a principal supply — e.g. a TV sold with warranty and a maintenance contract (TV = principal; warranty/AMC = ancillary). Mixed supply = a combination of individual supplies made for a single price, which CAN ordinarily be supplied separately — e.g. storage water bottles sold along with a refrigerator (both easily priced/sold separately).

Tax treatment? Composite supply is taxed as the principal supply; mixed supply is taxed at whichever constituent good/service attracts the highest rate.

Quick MCQ — Supply / Composite & Mixed Supply

1. Which of the following is NOT considered a ‘Supply’ under GST?

(a) Import of services for consideration, personal use(b) Permanent transfer of ITC-availed business assets(c) Services by an employee to employer in the course of employment(d) Rental of commercial property

Answer: (c). Schedule III — services by an employee to the employer in the course of/relating to employment are treated as neither supply of goods nor services.

2. Mr. X imports architectural services from his brother (related person) in London, for no consideration, to design his new office in Mumbai. This transaction is:

(a) Not a supply, no consideration(b) A supply of service under Schedule I(c) A supply of goods(d) Exempt from GST

Answer: (b). Import of services from a related person outside India, in the course/furtherance of business, is a supply even without consideration [Schedule I].

3. Which “Actionable Claim” is a taxable supply of goods under GST?

(a) Unsecured Debts(b) Bill of Exchange(c) Lottery, Betting, Gambling, Online Money Gaming(d) Promissory Notes

Answer: (c). Most actionable claims are in the Schedule III negative list, but specified claims (lottery, betting, gambling, online money gaming) are the exception, taxed as Supply of Goods.

4. ‘Development, design, programming, customization, upgradation, enhancement, implementation of IT software’ is:

(a) Supply of Goods(b) Supply of Services(c) Both Goods and Services(d) Neither Goods nor Services

Answer: (b). Schedule II specifically classifies IT-software development/customization as Supply of Services.

5. Gifts exceeding ________ in value in a financial year by an employer to an employee are treated as supply.

(a) ₹ 25,000(b) ₹ 50,000(c) ₹ 1,00,000(d) ₹ 5,000

Answer: (b). Per the Schedule I proviso, gifts up to ₹ 50,000/year are not treated as supply; any excess is taxable.

6. Which renting activity is a ‘Supply of Service’?

(a) Residential dwelling to an unregistered person, for residence(b) Employee services to employer in employment(c) Renting of a commercial complex(d) Both (a) and (c)

Answer: (d). Renting of immovable property is always Supply of Service (Schedule II) — residential-to-unregistered-person renting is EXEMPT but still a “supply”; commercial-complex renting is a taxable supply.

7. Mr. A transfers business assets (on which NO ITC was availed) to friend Mr. B without consideration. This transaction is:

(a) A Supply of Goods(b) A Deemed Supply under Schedule I(c) Not a Supply(d) A Mixed Supply

Answer: (c). Permanent transfer of business assets without consideration is a deemed supply under Schedule I ONLY if ITC was availed — since it was not, it is not a supply.

8. Under Sec. 2(30), a composite supply must consist of taxable supplies that are:

(a) Artificially bundled(b) Naturally bundled(c) Sold for different prices(d) None of the above

Answer: (b).

9. In a mixed supply, the applicable tax rate is:

(a) The rate of the principal supply(b) The lowest rate among the items(c) The highest rate among the items(d) 18% flat

Answer: (c).

10. ‘Principal supply’ is defined under which section of the CGST Act?

(a) Section 2(30)(b) Section 2(74)(c) Section 2(90)(d) Section 8

Answer: (c).

11. A supplier provides a “Stay + Breakfast” package in a hotel. This is a case of:

(a) Mixed Supply(b) Composite Supply(c) Exempt Supply(d) Continuous Supply

Answer: (b).

CONCEPT

5.2.3 Charge of Tax, including Reverse Charge ★★★ HIGH

Article 265 of the Constitution mandates that no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law — the charging section is the essential provision of any tax law. Before a tax can be imposed, the transaction must fall within the taxable event (supply), and the person on whom tax is imposed must fall within the charging section. Sec. 9 is the charging provision of the CGST Act (Sec. 5 for the IGST Act) — it covers all four aspects of levy: taxable event, tax rate, manner of collection, and person liable to pay.

Tax Payable on Forward Charge [Sec. 9(1) & 9(2)]

CGST is levied on all intra-State supplies of goods/services/both, EXCEPT supply of alcoholic liquor for human consumption / un-denatured extra neutral alcohol / rectified spirit used for manufacturing such liquor

— on the value determined u/s 15, at rates NOT exceeding 20% (as notified by the Government on the Council's recommendation), collected as prescribed, and paid by the taxable person.

  • Per Sec. 5 of the IGST Act, IGST is levied on all inter-State supplies and on goods imported into India — maximum IGST rate = 40% (20% CGST-equivalent + 20% SGST/UTGST-equivalent). SGST/UTGST is also levied on all intra-State supplies.
  • Central tax on petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit (petrol), natural gas and aviation turbine fuel applies only from a date the Government notifies on the Council's recommendation — i.e. GST is NOT currently leviable on these. [Sec. 2(78): “non-taxable supply” = a supply not leviable to tax under the CGST Act or IGST Act.]
  • Taxable Person [Sec. 2(107)]: registered or liable to be registered u/s 22 or Sec. 24 — even a voluntarily-registered person qualifies. Supplier [Sec. 2(105)]: the person supplying the goods/services, including an agent acting on the supplier's behalf; a person organising/arranging supply of specified actionable claims (incl. a digital-platform manager) is deemed the supplier of those claims.
  • “India” [Sec. 2(56)]: the territory per Art. 1 of the Constitution, its territorial waters/seabed/sub-soil/continental shelf/exclusive economic zone/other maritime zones, and the air space above.

Rate of GST: 0%, 5%, 18% and 40% in general (this is the IGST rate, i.e. combined CGST + SGST/UTGST rate). Rough precious/semi-precious stones = 0.25%; Gold, Silver, Jewellery = 3%; tobacco products and Pan masala = 28%. Services not covered under any specific heading are taxable @ 18%.

Tax Payable on Reverse Charge [Sec. 9(3)]

Ordinarily the supplier pays GST; under Reverse Charge Mechanism (RCM), the liability shifts to the RECIPIENT for notified categories. Reverse Charge [Sec. 2(98)]: liability to pay tax by the recipient instead of the supplier, u/s 9(3)/9(4) (or Sec. 5(3)/5(4) IGST Act). The Government, on the Council's recommendation, notifies such categories of goods/services.

Reverse Charge from Unregistered Suppliers [Sec. 9(4)] & on E-Commerce [Sec. 9(5)]

Sec. 9(4): the Government may notify a class of registered persons who must pay tax on reverse charge basis in respect of specified goods/services received from an UNREGISTERED supplier. Notified: (i) specified goods/services (other than development-rights/long-term-lease/FSI transfers) forming the shortfall from a promoter's minimum required purchase from registered suppliers, in a financial year up to completion certificate/first occupation; (ii) cement required for project construction, similarly; (iii) capital goods supplied to a promoter for project construction — in each case, Supplier = unregistered person, Recipient (liable) = the Promoter.

Sec. 9(5) — tax via Electronic Commerce Operator (ECO): the Government may notify categories of services where the person liable to pay tax is NEITHER the supplier NOR the recipient, but the ECO through whom the supply is effected. If the ECO has no physical presence in the taxable territory, any person representing it there is liable; if there is no representative either, the ECO must appoint one to pay tax. Notified services: (1) passenger transport by radio-taxi/motorcab/maxicab/motorcycle/other motor vehicle except omnibus; (2) passenger transport by omnibus, unless the supplier-through-ECO is itself a company; (3) hotel/inn/guest-house/club/campsite accommodation, unless the supplier is liable for registration u/s 22(1) [aggregate turnover exceeds ₹ 20 lakh, or ₹ 10 lakh for special category States]; (4) housekeeping (plumbing, carpentry, etc.), unless the supplier is liable for registration u/s 22(1); (5) restaurant service, other than at “specified premises” (hotel accommodation tariff above ₹ 7,500/unit/day); (6) local delivery, unless the supplier is liable for registration u/s 22(1).

Inter-State vs. Intra-State Supply — IGST Act Provisions

ProvisionRule
Intra-State supply of goods [Sec. 8(1), IGST Act]Location of supplier and place of supply in the SAME State/UT. Exceptions (treated as inter-State): supply to/by an SEZ developer/unit; goods imported until they cross customs frontiers; supplies to a tourist [Sec. 15 — a non-resident staying ≤ 6 months for legitimate non-immigrant purposes].
Intra-State supply of services [Sec. 8(2), IGST Act]Location of supplier and place of supply in the SAME State/UT. Exception: supply to/by an SEZ developer/unit is NOT intra-State.
Inter-State supply of goods [Sec. 7(1) & 7(2), IGST Act]Supplier and place of supply in two different States, two different UTs, or a State and a UT. Goods imported into India (till crossing customs frontiers) are also inter-State supply.
Inter-State supply of services [Sec. 7(3) & 7(4), IGST Act]Same cross-State/UT test as goods; services imported into India are also inter-State supply.
Other inter-State supply [Sec. 7(5), IGST Act]Supplier in India, place of supply outside India; supply to/by an SEZ developer/unit; or any other taxable-territory supply not covered elsewhere and not intra-State.

For inter-State supply, IGST is collected/paid by the supplier; for intra-State supply, CGST + SGST/UTGST is collected/paid by the supplier.

Zero Rated Supply [Sec. 16, IGST Act]

“Zero rated supply” means: (a) export of goods/services/both; or (b) supply of goods/services/both for authorised operations to an SEZ developer or SEZ unit.

  • ITC (subject to blocked credit u/s 17(5)) may be availed for zero-rated supplies, even though such supply may otherwise be an exempt supply.
  • A registered person making zero-rated supply may claim refund of unutilised ITC, without payment of IGST, under bond/Letter of Undertaking (Sec. 54) — EXCEPT no refund of unutilised ITC/IGST is allowed if the zero-rated goods supply is subject to export duty.
  • If sale proceeds are not realised within the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 time limit, the refund received (with Sec. 50 interest) must be deposited back within 30 days of expiry of that time limit.
  • The Government may notify a class of persons who may make zero-rated supply ON payment of IGST and claim refund of the tax paid, and a class of goods/services exportable on IGST payment with refund.

Illustrations — Charge of Tax & Reverse Charge

ILLUSTRATION 16 — Extra Neutral Alcohol

M/s Spirit Link supplies un-denatured ENA to a liquor distillery for manufacturing alcoholic liquor for human consumption, and industrial-grade rectified (denatured) spirit to a chemical factory, in the same month.

ANSWER: Per Sec. 9(1), supply of un-denatured ENA for manufacturing alcoholic liquor is outside GST; industrial-grade spirit remains taxable. GST is NOT leviable on the distillery supply; GST IS leviable on the chemical-factory supply.

ILLUSTRATION 17 — Taxable Event & Forward Charge

A registered wholesaler in Maharashtra supplies 100 electric fans to a retailer in Gujarat.

ANSWER: Inter-State supply [Sec. 7, IGST Act]; tax is payable on forward charge by the supplier u/s 5(1) IGST Act (equivalent to Sec. 9(1) CGST). The wholesaler is liable to pay IGST at the applicable rate.

ILLUSTRATION 18 — Government Services (RCM)

The Department of Posts provides speed post services to M/s Alpha Ltd. (a private corporate entity).

ANSWER: Government-to-business services are generally under RCM, but specific Department of Posts services (speed post, express parcel post, life insurance, agency services) to a non-Government person are under Forward Charge. The Department of Posts is liable to pay GST under Forward Charge.

ILLUSTRATION 19 — Renting of Residential Dwelling (RCM)

Mr. X (unregistered) rents his residential flat to M/s Zee Ltd. (registered company) for use as a guest house.

ANSWER: Entry 5AA of Notification 13/2017-CT(R) — renting a residential dwelling to a REGISTERED person is under Reverse Charge. M/s Zee Ltd. (recipient) is liable to pay GST under RCM.

ILLUSTRATION 20 — GTA Services

M/s Speed-Trucks (a GTA) invoices a registered factory, pays GST under forward charge and declares this on the invoice.

ANSWER: Once a GTA opts for forward charge and fulfils the declaration requirements, RCM is NOT triggered. The GTA (supplier) is liable to pay tax; the factory cannot pay under RCM.

ILLUSTRATION 21 — Electronic Commerce Operator

Mr. A books a Bangalore hotel room through “Stay-Easy” (an online travel portal/ECO); the hotel is NOT registered under GST.

ANSWER: Under Sec. 9(5), for accommodation services provided through an ECO by an unregistered person, the ECO is deemed the supplier. “Stay-Easy” (ECO) is liable to pay GST.

ILLUSTRATION 22 — Director's Remuneration

Mr. Kapoor, a director of Shine-Star Ltd., receives sitting fees for board meetings, AND a monthly salary as a Whole-time Director (WTD).

ANSWER: Salary to a WTD is a “contract of service” (Schedule III — neither goods nor services). Sitting fees are for director services NOT in the course of employment, hence taxable under RCM — the Company (recipient) is liable to pay GST on the sitting fees.

ILLUSTRATION 23 — Import of Services (RCM)

M/s Tech-Logic (India) receives legal consultancy from a London law firm for its Indian operations.

ANSWER: Import of service for consideration in the course of business is a supply; services from a non-taxable territory to a taxable territory are under RCM. M/s Tech-Logic (recipient) is liable to pay IGST under RCM.

ILLUSTRATION 24 — Specified Actionable Claims (ECO)

A user plays an online money game on “Win-Big,” an electronic platform managed by a platform manager.

ANSWER: The person organising/managing the digital platform for specified actionable claims (betting, gambling, online gaming) is deemed the supplier u/s 2(105). The platform manager is liable to pay GST on the full value of the bets.

ILLUSTRATION 25 — Legal Services by Advocate

Senior Advocate Mr. Mehta provides legal representational services to M/s Heavy-Lift Ltd. (aggregate turnover ₹ 80 Lakhs in the previous year).

ANSWER: Advocate services to a business entity above the registration threshold are covered under RCM. M/s Heavy-Lift Ltd. (recipient) is liable to pay GST under RCM.

ILLUSTRATION 26 — Passenger Transport via Uber

Mr. Y books a ride in an air-conditioned motorcab (Uber Premier) through the Uber App, within Mumbai.

ANSWER: Under Sec. 9(5), for motorcab passenger transport through an ECO, the ECO is deemed the supplier, liable to pay tax. Uber (the ECO) is liable to pay GST; the individual driver is not liable for tax or registration for this supply.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: FORWARD CHARGE IS THE DEFAULT — RCM/ECO ARE THE NOTIFIED EXCEPTION

THE TRAP: once students learn RCM exists, they start assuming it applies broadly — e.g. that ALL Government services to business, or ALL GTA transport, are automatically RCM, or that the individual service-provider (the driver, the hotel) always ends up paying.

THE TWIST: Sec. 9(3)/(4)/(5) apply ONLY to specifically NOTIFIED categories, each with its own carve-outs — Dept. of Posts speed-post/parcel/insurance/agency services to non-Government persons stay on FORWARD charge (Illustration 18); a GTA that opts for forward charge and declares it on the invoice takes RCM off the table entirely (Illustration 20); and under Sec. 9(5), it is the ECO itself — not the underlying driver/hotel/restaurant — who is deemed the supplier and pays tax for the five/six notified ECO categories (motorcab/omnibus transport, hotel accommodation below the registration threshold, housekeeping, restaurant service outside “specified premises”, local delivery).

Quick MCQ — Charge of Tax & Reverse Charge

1. As per Sec. 9(1) of the CGST Act, which is specifically excluded from the levy of GST?

(a) Tobacco and tobacco products(b) Un-denatured ENA used for manufacturing alcoholic liquor for human consumption(c) Motor Car(d) Aerated waters containing added sugar

Answer: (b). Sec. 9(1) specifically excludes ENA used for manufacturing alcoholic liquor for human consumption from GST.

2. Under RCM, the liability to pay tax is on:

(a) The Supplier(b) The Recipient(c) The Electronic Commerce Operator(d) Both, in equal proportion

Answer: (b). Sec. 2(98) — reverse charge means liability on the recipient instead of the supplier.

3. Which service, when provided through an ECO, makes the ECO liable to pay GST u/s 9(5)?

(a) Food/beverages by a GST-registered restaurant(b) Passenger transport by radio taxi(c) CA professional consultancy(d) Sale of mobile phones by a registered dealer

Answer: (b). Under Sec. 9(5), for radio-taxi passenger transport via an ECO, the ECO is deemed the supplier, liable to pay tax.

4. The maximum rate of Central Tax (CGST) prescribable under Sec. 9(1) is:

(a) 12%(b) 18%(c) 20%(d) 40%

Answer: (c). Sec. 9(1) caps CGST at 20%; the 40% figure is the total IGST (CGST + SGST) equivalent.

5. Supply of which item is taxable under GST only from a date to be notified on the GST Council's recommendation?

(a) Alcoholic liquor for human consumption(b) Extra Neutral Alcohol (ENA)(c) Natural Gas and Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF)(d) All of the above

Answer: (c). Sec. 9(2) — five petroleum products (incl. Natural Gas and ATF) are temporarily outside GST; alcoholic liquor is Constitutionally outside GST altogether.

6. When a Director provides services to a company as an employee (contract of service), the treatment is:

(a) Outside GST (Schedule III)(b) Taxable under RCM(c) Taxable under Forward Charge(d) Exempt via Notification

Answer: (a). Employee services to the employer in employment are covered by Schedule III.

7. Services by a GTA to a registered factory, where the GTA has NOT opted for Forward Charge:

(a) The GTA is liable to pay tax(b) The Factory is liable to pay tax under RCM(c) The transaction is exempt(d) The Government is liable to pay tax

Answer: (b). Where a GTA has not opted for forward charge, the specified recipient (e.g. registered factory) pays under RCM u/s 9(3).

8. For Sec. 9(5), if an ECO has no physical presence in the taxable territory:

(a) Exempt from paying GST(b) The recipient must pay under RCM(c) Any person representing the ECO in the taxable territory is liable(d) The supplier must register and pay tax

Answer: (c). Per the Sec. 9(5) proviso, an ECO's representative in the taxable territory is liable; if none exists, the ECO must appoint one.

FAQ by CBIC (15-12-2018) — Charge of Tax

  • Are all goods and services taxable? Yes, except alcoholic liquor for human consumption; petroleum crude, HSD, petrol, natural gas and ATF become taxable only from a future notified date.
  • What is Reverse Charge? Liability to pay tax on the recipient instead of the supplier, for notified categories of supply.
  • Does RCM apply only to services? No — RCM applies to BOTH goods and services, as notified.
  • Can a person other than supplier/recipient be liable? Yes — the Government can make an ECO liable to pay tax on services supplied through it, as if the ECO were the supplier.
CONCEPT

5.2.4 Exemption from Tax ★★ MEDIUM

“Exempt supply” [Sec. 2(47)] means supply of any goods/services/both which attracts a NIL rate of tax, or which is wholly exempt from tax u/s 11 (CGST Act) or Sec. 6 (IGST Act), and INCLUDES non-taxable supply. “Non-taxable supply” [Sec. 2(78)] means a supply of goods/services/both which is NOT leviable to tax under the CGST Act or the IGST Act at all.

Power to grant exemption [Sec. 11, CGST Act; Sec. 6, IGST Act]: the Government, on the Council's recommendation, by notification, may exempt (absolutely, or subject to conditions) goods/services of any specified description from the whole or part of the tax leviable, with effect from a specified date; and, by special order in exceptional circumstances, may exempt payment of tax on specific goods/services on which tax is leviable. For clarifying scope/applicability, an explanation may be inserted by notification within 1 year of the earlier notification/order — such explanation has retrospective effect, as if always part of the original notification/order.

  • Unconditional exemption is MANDATORY; conditional exemption is OPTIONAL.
  • Where an exemption is granted absolutely, the registered person supplying such goods/services must NOT collect tax in excess of the effective rate.
  • Exemption may be granted on the basis of: activities; suppliers; recipients; or a combination of specified suppliers and specified recipients.

Goods Exempt from Tax [Notification No. 10/2025-CT (Rate) dt. 17/09/2025, as amended]

Around 170 items are exempted from GST. Commonly-tested examples: cereals (other than in unit containers bearing a registered brand name); fresh/chilled edible vegetables, roots and tubers (potatoes, tomatoes, onions, garlic, cabbages, etc.); fresh fruits (coconuts, bananas, dates, figs, mangoes, etc.); meat/fish/aquatic invertebrates (taxable if frozen and in unit containers); dairy produce, birds' eggs, natural honey (if not pre-packaged and labelled); coffee beans (not roasted) and unprocessed green tea leaves; jaggery/khandsari sugar/rab (other than pre-packaged and labelled); puffed/flattened/parched rice, khakhra, bread/roti/chapathi/paratha (other than pre-packaged and labelled, where applicable); prasadam supplied by religious places; electrical energy; salt; human blood and its components; organic manure (unbranded, loose); contraceptives; printed books, newspapers and maps; raw silk, wool (uncarded), jute fibre (raw/processed but not spun); Indian National Flag; agricultural implements (manually/animal operated); handloom weaving machinery; hearing aids; and slates, slate pencils and chalk sticks. (Selected list — the full Notification lists ~170 items.)

Services Exempt from Tax [Notification No. 12/2017-CT(R), as amended]

Entry 1 — Charitable activities by an entity registered u/s 12AA/12AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961. “Charitable activities” means activities relating to: (i) public health — care/counselling of terminally-ill persons, persons with severe disability, persons with HIV/AIDS, or persons addicted to a dependence-forming substance; or public awareness of preventive health, family planning, or HIV-infection prevention; (ii) advancement of religion, spirituality or yoga; (iii) advancement of educational programmes/skill development for abandoned/orphaned/homeless children, physically/mentally abused and traumatized persons, prisoners, or persons over 65 residing in a rural area; (iv) preservation of environment (watershed, forests, wildlife). Taxpoint: where a charitable/religious trust merely provides accommodation or serves food/drink against consideration (e.g. donation), that activity IS taxable; fitness camps/aerobics/dance/music classes are also taxable. A school/college run by a trust is NOT covered by Entry 1 (covered instead under a separate entry); hostel accommodation and medical facilities have their own separate entries; religious yatra service is generally NOT exempt.

Entry 2 — services by way of transfer of a going concern, as a whole or an independent part thereof.

Entry 3 (as far as covered) — pure services (excluding works contract or other composite supplies involving goods) provided to the Central Government, State Government, UT or local authority by way of any activity relating to a function entrusted to a Panchayat under Article 243G of the Constitution, or…

Some individual entries carry conditions that recur heavily in illustrations and MCQs — captured below with their exact figures.

Services by Government / Local Authority — Entries 4–9G

  • Entries 4 & 5: any activity entrusted to a Municipality (Art. 243W) or Panchayat (Art. 243G) is exempt when performed by Central/State Govt., UT, local authority or governmental authority.
  • Entry 6: services by Central/State Govt., UT or local authority are exempt except (a) Dept. of Posts & Ministry of Railways; (b) services re an aircraft/vessel inside or outside port/airport precincts; (c) transport of goods or passengers; (d) any other service to business entities.
  • Entry 7: services by Government to a business entity are exempt if the entity’s aggregate turnover in the preceding FY is within the registration-exemption threshold — but never for (a) Posts/Railways, aircraft/vessel services, transport of goods/passengers, and (b) renting of immovable property.
  • Entry 8: Government-to-Government services are exempt, except Posts/Railways, aircraft/vessel and transport-of-goods/passengers services.
  • Entry 9: Government services where consideration does not exceed ₹ 5,000 are exempt (same three exclusions as Entry 8); for a continuous supply, the ₹ 5,000 ceiling applies per financial year.
  • Entry 9D: old age home run by Government or a Sec. 12AA entity — exempt up to ₹ 25,000 per month per member, inclusive of boarding, lodging and maintenance.
  • Entry 9E: Railways — platform tickets, retiring/waiting rooms, cloak room, battery-operated car services.

Entry 52A exempts a tour operator’s service performed partly outside India, to the extent so performed, for a foreign tourist. The exempt value = lower of (i) total consideration × (days of tour outside India ÷ total days), or (ii) 50% of total consideration. A day ≥ 12 hours counts as one full day; < 12 hours as half a day.

Entry 52A exempt value = LOWER OF [ Total Consideration × (Days outside India ÷ Total tour days) ] OR [ 50% × Total Consideration ]

Example (Case A): 3 days India + 2 days Nepal, consideration ₹ 2,00,000. Lower of ₹ 80,000 (= 2,00,000 × 2/5) and ₹ 1,00,000 (50%) → ₹ 80,000 exempt.
Case B: 2 days India + 3 nights Nepal, consideration ₹ 1,00,000. Lower of ₹ 60,000 (= 1,00,000 × 3/5) and ₹ 50,000 (50%) → ₹ 50,000 exempt.
Case C: 2.5 days India + 3 days Nepal (rounded to 5.5 total days since 2.5 rounds to 3 as it is ≥ 12 hrs), consideration ₹ 1,00,000. Lower of ₹ 54,545 (= 1,00,000 × 3/5.5) and ₹ 50,000 (50%) → ₹ 50,000 exempt.

Exemptions under the IGST Act — Notification No. 9/2017-Integrated Tax (Rate)

  • Entry 10: services received from a provider located in a non-taxable territory by (a) Government/local authority/individual for a non-business purpose, (b) a Sec. 12AA charitable entity, (c) supply of online educational journals to an educational institution (other than one covering pre-school to higher-secondary or vocational education), or (d) a person located in a non-taxable territory — but the exemption does NOT extend to OIDAR services received by (a)/(b), nor to transport of goods by vessel from outside India up to the customs station received by the specified persons.
  • Entry 10F: services from an Indian establishment to its own distinct-person establishment outside India (Sec. 8 IGST Act, Explanation 1), where the place of supply is outside India.
  • Entries 10G & 10H: import of services by the UN / a specified international organization; and by a foreign diplomatic mission, consular post, diplomatic agents or career consular officers in India.
  • Entry 10L: import of services by a foreign airline company’s Indian establishment from a related person/other establishment outside India, made without consideration (subject to certain restrictions).
  • Entry 12AA: intermediary services where both supplier and recipient are located outside the taxable territory.
  • Entry 42: services received by RBI from outside India for management of foreign exchange reserves.
  • Entry 54: tour operator service provided to a foreign tourist for a tour conducted wholly outside India.

Other exemptions: services imported by a unit/developer in an SEZ; the Central Government’s share of profit-petroleum; services supplied by the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and International Finance Corporation (IFC); and royalty/licence fee to the extent it is re-included in the transaction value on which customs duty has already been paid.
