Power Not to Recover GST Not Levied or Short-Levied as a Result of General Practice [Sec. 11A]

Sec. 11A empowers the Government to grant exemption from GST on the basis of prevailing trade practices, so that traders are not unduly burdened with unnecessary taxes. This applies especially where a taxpayer did not pay GST wrongly but in line with a normal, widely-followed trade practice — the section also protects against retrospective demands based on such widely-accepted practices.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: RENTING RESIDENTIAL DWELLING — "ALWAYS EXEMPT" IS WRONG

THE TRAP: students assume Entry 12 (renting of residential dwelling for use as residence) exempts every such rental, so a firm renting a flat as a guest house pays nothing.

THE TWIST: Entry 12 exempts renting to an unregistered person for use as residence. Renting the same dwelling to a registered person (e.g., as a company guest house) is taxable under Reverse Charge Mechanism on the recipient (Illustration 38). Entry 12 also excludes student-residence accommodation and Hostel/Camp/PG accommodation.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: ENTRY 81 “RIGHT TO ADMISSION” ≠ ALL ENTERTAINMENT

THE TRAP: assuming the ₹ 500-per-person exemption under Entry 81 covers admission to a cinema/multiplex, since it “sounds like” a right-to-admission event.

THE TWIST: Entry 81 lists specific categories only — circus, dance/theatrical performance/drama/ballet, award function/concert/pageant/musical performance/non-recognised sporting event, recognised sporting event, and planetarium. Movie/multiplex admission is NOT in this list and is taxable regardless of ticket value.

10(c)Entry 81 covers circus, dance, theatre, award functions, concerts, pageants, sporting events and planetariums — not cinema/multiplex admission.
CONCEPT

5.2.5 Composition Levy ★★★ HIGH

The composition levy is an alternative, optional method of levying tax designed for small taxpayers whose turnover is up to a prescribed limit. It brings simplicity, eases the compliance burden, and reduces compliance cost — essentially a turnover-tax regime with lighter compliance.

An eligible person opting for the composition scheme pays tax at a prescribed percentage of turnover, instead of paying tax on every invoice at the specified rate.

Advantages: lesser compliance (returns, books, invoices); limited tax liability; higher liquidity as tax is levied at a lower rate.

Disadvantages:

  • Limited territory of business — the dealer is barred from inter-State transactions.
  • No Input Tax Credit available to composition dealers.
  • Cannot supply non-taxable goods under GST, such as alcohol.
  • Cannot supply goods through an e-commerce portal (subject to the ECO nuance below for intra-State supply).
  • No ITC to the buyer of goods from a composition supplier — this increases the buyer’s cost.

Composition Levy [Sec. 10]: a registered person whose aggregate turnover in the preceding FY did not exceed the threshold limit may opt to pay, in lieu of tax u/s 9(1), an amount of tax calculated at the prescribed rate.

Taxpoint: the option can be exercised in the current FY if turnover of the preceding FY did not exceed the limit.

Threshold Limit [Notification No. 14/2019-CT dated 07-03-2019]

Composition scheme — eligibility threshold
CaseThreshold Limit
Supply of goods and restaurant service (restaurant, mandap keeper, outdoor caterer — food/drink other than alcoholic liquor for human consumption): Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura, Uttarakhand₹ 75 lakh
Other States / UTs₹ 1.5 crore
Manufacturers and Traders — supply of services along with supply of goods and/or restaurant serviceHigher of: 10% of turnover in the State/UT in preceding FY, OR ₹ 5,00,000
Supplier of service (other than restaurant services)₹ 50 lakh

Manufacturers of the following goods are not eligible for the composition scheme: (a) ice cream and other edible ice, whether or not containing cocoa; (b) Pan masala; (c) Tobacco and manufactured tobacco substitutes; (d) aerated water; (e) fly ash bricks / fly ash aggregate with ≥ 90% fly ash content / fly ash blocks; (f) bricks of fossil meals or similar siliceous earths; (g) building bricks; (h) earthen or roofing tiles.

The value of exempt supply of services provided by extending deposits, loans or advances (where consideration is interest/discount) is excluded from turnover in a State/UT for determining the value of turnover.

Rates of GST for Composition Suppliers [Rule 7]

Composition scheme — rate table
CaseRate of GST
Manufacturers other than manufacturers of ice cream, pan masala, tobacco, aerated water, etc.1% (0.5% CGST + 0.5% SGST) of turnover in the State/UT
Traders1% (0.5% CGST + 0.5% SGST) of turnover of taxable supplies of goods and services in the State/UT
Restaurant Services5% (2.5% CGST + 2.5% SGST) of turnover in the State/UT
Services other than restaurant services6% (3% CGST + 3% SGST) of turnover of supplies of goods and services in the State/UT

For manufacturers, “turnover” for rate purposes includes both exempted and taxable supplies. The composition supplier must pay tax at the rate applicable on the supply for every inward supply liable under reverse charge — regardless of his own composition rate on outward supplies — but the value of such inward RCM supplies is not included in his aggregate turnover, even though the liability is discharged by him.

Restrictions on Eligibility

Supplier of goods and restaurant services [Sec. 10(2)] — eligible only if the person:

  • is not engaged in the supply of services (except up to the limit noted above);
  • is not engaged in supplying goods/services not leviable to tax under the Act (dealing in exempt supply is, however, allowed);
  • is not engaged in any inter-State outward supply of goods or services;
  • is not engaged in supplying services through an e-commerce operator required to collect TCS u/s 52 (Taxpoint: the restriction applies only to services supplied through an ECO);
  • is not a manufacturer of the notified goods listed above;
  • is neither a casual taxable person nor a non-resident taxable person.

Supplier of services [Sec. 10(2A)] — eligible only if the person:

  • is not engaged in supplying goods/services not leviable to tax under the Act;
  • is not engaged in any inter-State outward supply of goods or services;
  • is not engaged in supplying services through an ECO required to collect TCS u/s 52;
  • is not a manufacturer of notified goods or supplier of notified services; and
  • is not a casual taxable person or non-resident taxable person.

Same-PAN rule (both categories): where more than one registered person shares the same PAN, none of them is eligible for the scheme unless ALL such registered persons opt for it.

Example: a company has two separately-registered businesses — mobile-device sale (Kerala) and a branded-restaurant franchisee (Goa). Both units must opt for composition together, or neither can — the company cannot use composition for Kerala while remaining regular for Goa.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: THE SAME-PAN RULE POISONS EVERY UNIT

THE TRAP: a group with multiple GST registrations under one PAN assumes it can put its “clean” units on composition even if one unit is disqualified (e.g., an ice-cream manufacturing unit).

THE TWIST: ALL registered persons under the same PAN must opt in together. If even one unit is ineligible (e.g., manufactures a notified negative-list good like ice cream), every unit under that PAN is disqualified from composition and must pay tax under the regular scheme u/s 9(1).

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: RCM UNDER COMPOSITION IS AT THE NORMAL RATE, NOT THE COMPOSITION RATE

THE TRAP: a composition dealer computes tax on reverse-charge inward supplies at their own composition rate (say 1%) since “everything is at composition rate for us.”

THE TWIST: RCM liability must be discharged at the NORMAL applicable rate for that supply (e.g., 18%), in cash, with NO Input Tax Credit available to offset it — regardless of the composition rate applicable to the dealer’s own outward supplies. The value of such RCM inward supplies is also excluded from the dealer’s aggregate turnover.

Aggregate Turnover for Composition Purposes

As per Sec. 2(6), aggregate turnover = (a) all taxable supplies (excluding inward supplies taxed under reverse charge), + (b) exempt supplies (excluding exempt interest/discount on deposits/loans/advances), + (c) exports of goods or services, + (d) inter-State supplies of persons with the same PAN (e.g., branch stock transfers) — computed on an all-India basis, but excluding CGST, SGST, UTGST, IGST and cess.

For eligibility, aggregate turnover includes supplies made from 1st April of a FY up to the date of becoming liable to registration, but still excludes exempt interest/discount income.

For computing the actual tax payable (“turnover in State/UT”), the following are excluded: (i) supplies from 1st April of the FY up to the date of becoming liable to registration; and (ii) exempt interest/discount income.

Lapse, Collection Bar & Penalty

  • Lapse of option [Sec. 10(3)]: the composition option lapses from the day aggregate turnover during the FY exceeds the threshold limit.
  • Bar on collecting tax [Sec. 10(4)]: a composition taxpayer cannot collect tax from the recipient on his supplies, nor claim any input tax credit — he pays tax from his own pocket.
  • Penalty for wrongful availment [Sec. 10(5)]: if the proper officer believes a person paid tax under composition despite ineligibility, that person is liable to a penalty in addition to any tax payable, with Sec. 73/74/74A applied mutatis mutandis for determination of tax and penalty.

Procedural Rules

  • Intimation [Rule 3]: option given in Part B of Form GST REG-01 at the time of applying for registration; a registered person opts via Form GST CMP-02, filed electronically before the commencement of the FY for which the option is exercised, plus Form GST ITC-03 (per Rule 44(4)) within 60 days of the start of that FY. Intimation for any one place of business is deemed intimation for all places of business on the same PAN.
  • Effective date [Rule 4]: if registration is applied for within 30 days of becoming liable, the option is effective from the date the person becomes liable to registration; if applied after 30 days, effective from the date of grant of registration.
  • Conditions [Rule 5]: not a casual/non-resident taxable person; stock held was not purchased from an unregistered supplier (or, if it was, tax has been paid under Sec. 9(4) reverse charge); tax paid u/s 9(3)/9(4) on inward supplies; was not a manufacturer of notified goods in the preceding FY; must print “composition taxable person, not eligible to collect tax on supplies” at the top of every bill of supply; must display “composition taxable person” at every place of business.
  • Validity [Rule 6]: the option remains valid so long as conditions are satisfied; the person becomes liable to pay tax u/s 9(1) from the day he ceases to satisfy any condition, must then issue tax invoices, and must file Form GST CMP-04 (withdrawal intimation) within 7 days of that event. The proper officer may issue a show-cause notice in Form GST CMP-05 (reply in 15 days via GST CMP-06); the officer then passes an order in Form GST CMP-07 within 30 days. A stock statement in Form GST ITC-01 must follow within 30 days of withdrawal/denial.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: EXPORT SEEMS “ZERO-RATED, SO HARMLESS” — IT ISN’T FOR COMPOSITION ELIGIBILITY

THE TRAP: a composition dealer assumes exports are safe to make because they are zero-rated (no tax on the export itself), so composition status is unaffected.

THE TWIST: exports are treated as inter-State supplies, and Sec. 10 bars a composition taxpayer from ANY inter-State outward supply. A single export transaction disqualifies the taxpayer from composition for the entire period, forcing regular-scheme tax on ALL outward supplies made in that quarter (Illustration 52) — not just the export.

FAQs by CBIC (dated 15-12-2018, as amended)

  • Crossing the threshold mid-year: the composition option lapses from the day aggregate turnover exceeds ₹ 150 lakh / ₹ 75 lakh — NOT allowed to continue till 31st March. The taxpayer must file Form GST CMP-04 (withdrawal) within 7 days, then Form GST ITC-01 (stock statement) within 30 days.
  • Computing aggregate turnover: computed on an all-India PAN basis, per the Sec. 2(6) definition; exempt services by way of extending deposits/loans/advances (interest/discount) do not make a person ineligible and are excluded from the turnover computation for eligibility.
  • ITC on inward supplies: not available — a composition taxpayer is out of the credit chain.
  • ITC to the buyer from a composition dealer: not available.
  • Tax invoice: a composition taxpayer cannot issue a tax invoice.
  • Returns: no monthly return; annual return in Form GSTR-4 by 30th April of the following year, plus Form CMP-08 by the 18th of the month succeeding each quarter.
  • Opting in after registration: yes, via Form GST CMP-02, filed electronically before commencement of the FY.
  • Multi-State registration: a person cannot opt for composition in one State and not in another — any intimation for one place of business is deemed intimation for all places of business on the same PAN.
  • Voluntary withdrawal: permitted, via Form GST CMP-04 before the date of withdrawal, followed by Form GST ITC-01 (stock statement) within 30 days.

Other clarifications: the scheme is available even if the taxable person has inter-State inward supplies — only inter-State outward supplies are barred. “Person having the same PAN” means all units across India under that PAN. If a composition taxpayer crosses the ₹ 1.50 crore threshold during the year, the permission granted earlier is deemed withdrawn from that day, and the person becomes liable to pay tax under the regular scheme (Sec. 9) from that day.

CONCEPT

5.3 Basic Concepts of Time, Place and Value of Supply ★★★ HIGH

To calculate and discharge GST liability, three questions must be answered for every supply: WHEN does the liability arise (Time of Supply), WHERE is the supply deemed to occur, i.e. which State/UT gets the SGST share and whether CGST+SGST or IGST applies (Place of Supply), and HOW MUCH is taxable (Value of Supply). GST law gives separate, detailed provisions for each — and separately for goods vs services, and forward charge vs reverse charge.

5.3.1 Time of Supply

Time of supply is the point in time when goods/services are considered as supplied — it fixes the due date for payment of tax. GST law provides separate rules for goods and for services, and separately again for forward charge and reverse charge.

Time of Supply of Goods – Forward Charge [Sec. 12(2)] = EARLIER of — (a) date of issue of invoice by the supplier; or (b) the last date on which he is required to issue the invoice u/s 31.

(c) "date supplier receives payment" is listed in the Section but is NOT relevant in practice — see Taxpoint below.

Taxpoint: Per Notification No. 66/2017-CT dated 15/11/2017, a registered person NOT under composition levy pays tax on outward supply of goods only at Sec. 12(2)(a) time — i.e. no GST on advances received against supply of goods. This relaxation does NOT apply to supply of services or specified actionable claims, and NOT to goods under reverse charge.

Where the supplier receives up to ₹1,000 in excess of the invoice amount, time of supply for that excess is, at the supplier's option, the date of the next invoice. "Date of receipt of payment" = date entered in supplier's books OR date credited to bank, whichever is earlier. Supply is deemed made only to the extent covered by the invoice or payment.

Tax Invoice [Sec. 31]

SituationInvoice must issue before/at time of
Supply involves movement of goodsRemoval of goods for supply to recipient
Supply does not involve movement of goodsDelivery of goods / making available to recipient
Continuous supply of goods [Sec. 31(4)]Each successive statement of accounts issued, or each successive payment received
Goods sent on approval for sale or return, removed before supply takes place [Sec. 31(7)]Before/at time of supply, OR 6 months from date of removal — whichever is EARLIER

ILLUSTRATION 54 — Excess Receipt Against Goods

Ramesh issues an invoice of ₹54,200 for goods on 10/04/2025; receives ₹55,000 by NEFT same date, credited to his books on 11/04/2025.

Answer: (a) Time of supply of the goods = 10/04/2025 (date of payment irrelevant — Notification No. 66/2017-CT). (b) ₹800 excess received — time of supply of the excess is the date of issuance of the next invoice (adjusted against it). (c) If ₹75,000 received instead (excess ₹20,800), the excess amount is still not immediately taxable — time of supply of the excess is again the date of issuance of the next invoice, assuming adjustment there.

ILLUSTRATION 55 — Sale on Approval / Return

Goods sent by Mr. X on sale-on-approval basis to Mr. Y on 22 April 2025. Case 1: invoice issued 20 Aug 2025. Case 2: invoice issued 22 Nov 2025. Payment in both cases 23 Nov 2025 (irrelevant, ignored).

Rule: time of supply = earlier of date of issuance of invoice OR last date of issuance of invoice (= earlier of confirmation of supply or 6 months from removal).

Answer: Case 1 — 6-month period expires after confirmation, so last date = 20 Aug 2025 = actual invoice date → Time of Supply = 20 Aug 2025. Case 2 — the 6-month period expired 21 Oct 2025 (before confirmation/invoice); invoice was issued late on 22 Nov 2025, so Time of Supply = the last date, 21 Oct 2025.

Time of Supply of Goods – Reverse Charge [Sec. 12(3)] = EARLIEST of — (a) date of receipt of goods; (b) date of payment entered in recipient's books; (c) date payment is debited in recipient's bank; (d) day immediately following 30 days from date of supplier's invoice (or other document).

Taxpoint: if time of supply cannot be determined as above, it is the date of entry in the recipient's books of account. Notification No. 66/2017-CT relief (no GST on advance) does NOT apply to reverse charge.

ILLUSTRATION 56 — Reverse Charge, Goods

01.04.2025 order placed · 10.04.2025 goods received · 15.04.2025 invoice issued · 20.04.2025 payment by cheque, recorded in books · 25.04.2025 payment debited from bank.

Earliest of: (a) 10.04.2025 receipt of goods; (b) 20.04.2025 books entry; (c) 25.04.2025 bank debit; (d) 15.04.2025 + 30 days + 1 day = 16.05.2025.

Answer: Time of Supply = 10.04.2025. Alternate case (goods received 30.04.2025 instead): earliest of 30.04.2025 / 20.04.2025 / 25.04.2025 / 16.05.2025 → Time of Supply = 20.04.2025.

Time of Supply of Goods – Residual Cases [Sec. 12(5)]: where a periodical return is to be filed → the date such return is due; in any other case → the date the tax is paid.

Example: a raid detects removal of goods with no invoice issued and no accounts maintained; since no return covers this transaction, Time of Supply = date the tax (penalty) is finally paid.

Enhancement in value — interest/late fee/penalty [Sec. 12(6)]: Time of Supply for the addition in value = date the supplier RECEIVES that addition.

ILLUSTRATION 57 — Late Payment Charge on Goods

Contract dated 10 Apr 2025 for goods worth ₹10,00,000; invoice dated 12 Apr 2025; goods removed 13 Apr 2025; late-payment charge ₹20,000 if payment delayed beyond 60 days. Mr. Nath pays ₹10,00,000 + ₹20,000 late fee on 15 July 2025.

Answer: For ₹10,00,000 — Sec. 12(2): earlier of invoice date (12 Apr) and last date of issuance = date of removal (13 Apr) → Time of Supply = 12 April 2025 (date of payment is immaterial per Notification No. 66/2017-CT). For the ₹20,000 late fee — Sec. 12(6): Time of Supply = date supplier receives the addition = 15 July 2025.

Time of Supply of Services – Forward Charge [Sec. 13(2)]

SituationTime of Supply
Invoice issued within the period prescribed u/s 31Earlier of — (a) date of issue of invoice; (b) date of receipt of payment
Invoice NOT issued within the prescribed periodEarlier of — (a) date of provision of service; (b) date of receipt of payment
Neither (a) nor (b) above appliesDate the recipient shows receipt of services in his books of account

"Date of receipt of payment" = entered in supplier's books OR credited to bank, whichever is earlier. Supply deemed made only to extent covered by invoice/payment. Excess receipt up to ₹1,000 over invoice value — at supplier's option, time of supply of the excess = date of the invoice for that excess.

EXAMPLE — Telephone Company, Excess Receipt

Telephone company invoices ₹3,800 on 23 July 2025, receives ₹4,000 on 27 July 2025 — ₹200 excess can be adjusted against next month's invoice; Time of Supply arises only for ₹3,800 on 23 July 2025, and the ₹200 may (at supplier option) not arise on 27 July but be adjusted next month.

Variant: if ₹5,000 received instead of ₹4,000, the excess (₹1,200) exceeds ₹1,000 so the supplier has NO option — supply is deemed made to the extent of the ₹3,800 invoice (23 July) and the balance ₹1,200 is taxable on 27 July 2025 (date of receipt).

Time Limit for Issuance of Invoice for Services [Sec. 31 r.w. Rule 47]

SituationTime limit
General casesWithin 30 days from date of supply of service (45 days for insurance/banking company or financial institution, including NBFC)
Supply of services ceases before completionAt the time supply ceases (invoice to extent of supply made before cessation)
Continuous supply, due date ascertainable from contractOn or before the due date of payment
Continuous supply, due date NOT ascertainableBefore/at the time supplier receives payment
Continuous supply, payment linked to completion of an eventOn or before date of completion of that event
Insurance/banking/financial institution (incl. NBFC), telecom operator, or notified supplier making supplies between distinct persons u/s 25Before/at the time such supplier records it in books, or before expiry of the quarter in which the supply was made

ILLUSTRATION 59 — Advance + Balance, Invoice Timing

Mr. Kedar's consultancy worth ₹50,000 to Mr. Nath. 08.04.2025 advance ₹10,000 received; 10.04.2025 service provided; 16.05.2025 balance ₹40,000 received & booked.

Situation 1 — invoice issued 15.04.2025 (within 30 days of supply): rule = earlier of invoice date/payment date. For ₹10,000: earlier of 15.04.2025 and 08.04.2025 → ToS = 08.04.2025. For ₹40,000: earlier of 15.04.2025 (invoice) and 16.05.2025 (payment) → ToS = 15.04.2025.

Situation 2 — invoice issued 15.05.2025 (beyond the 30-day period, so rule = earlier of completion-of-service date/payment date). For ₹10,000: earlier of 08.04.2025 (advance receipt) → ToS = 08.04.2025. For ₹40,000: earlier of 10.04.2025 (completion of service) and 16.05.2025 (payment) → ToS = 10.04.2025.

ILLUSTRATION 61 — No Invoice, No Books (Investigation Case)

Mr. X provided catering services worth ₹1,00,000 to Mr. Y, paid in cash; Mr. X issued no invoice and recorded nothing. Mr. Y recorded the ₹1,00,000 cash payment in his books on 28 April 2025.

Answer: Since neither payment date nor invoice date is available from the supplier, the date the RECIPIENT records the payment in his books becomes the fallback trigger → Time of Supply = 28 April 2025.

ILLUSTRATION 62 — Cessation of a Continuous Service Contract

Professional-services contract for ₹10,00,000 over 3 months, entered 20 July 2025. On 16 Aug 2025 recipient stops the contract; services rendered till then mutually valued at ₹3,50,000. Invoice issued 20 Aug 2025 (after the cessation date); payment made 25 Aug 2025.

Answer: Since the invoice (20 Aug) is after the required date (cessation date, 16 Aug), the fallback rule applies — Time of Supply = earlier of date of completion of service (16 Aug 2025) and date of payment (25 Aug 2025) = 16 August 2025.

Time of Supply of Services – Reverse Charge [Sec. 13(3)] = EARLIER of — (a) date of payment entered in recipient's books; (b) date payment debited in recipient's bank; (c) day immediately following 60 days from date of supplier's invoice (where supplier must issue it); (d) date of invoice issued BY THE RECIPIENT (where the recipient must issue it).

If undeterminable — date of entry in recipient's books. For associated enterprises where the service supplier is located outside India — time of supply = earlier of date of entry in recipient's books or date of payment. "Associated Enterprises" has the Sec. 92A Income-tax Act, 1961 meaning.

Time of Supply of Services – Residual Cases [Sec. 13(5)]: periodical return due → its due date; otherwise → date tax is paid.

Enhancement in value — interest/late fee/penalty [Sec. 13(6)]: Time of Supply for the addition = date supplier receives that addition — identical structure to Sec. 12(6) for goods.

Change in Rate of Tax [Sec. 14]

Three events matter: (i) the supply itself; (ii) issuance of invoice; (iii) receipt of payment.

SupplyEvents (invoice/payment)Time of SupplyRate
Before changeAny event occurred before changeOccurrence of the 1st eventOld
After changeAny event occurred before changeOccurrence of the 2nd eventNew
Before changeBoth events occurred after changeDate of receipt of payment or date of issue of invoice, whichever earlierNew
After changeBoth events occurred before changeDate of receipt of payment or date of issue of invoice, whichever earlierOld
Rate rule shortcut: if AT LEAST 2 of the 3 events occur after the rate change → NEW rate applies; if at least 2 occur before → OLD rate applies.

Taxpoint: "date of receipt of payment" = entered in books OR credited to bank, whichever earlier — BUT the bank-credit date is used instead only if that credit occurs more than 4 working days after the date of the rate change. For goods, Notification No. 66/2017-CT (no tax on advance) still applies.

ILLUSTRATION 67 — Time of Supply of Goods (Forward Charge)

M/s. ABC Manufacturers (Pune) supplies machinery to XYZ Ltd. (Nasik): 25-Sep-2025 advance ₹2,00,000 received; 01-Oct-2025 machinery removed; 15-Oct-2025 invoice issued; 20-Oct-2025 balance received.

Rule [Sec. 12(2) r.w. Notification No. 66/2017-CT]: earlier of invoice date and last date to issue invoice (date of removal) — payment date irrelevant. Invoice date 15-Oct is later than removal date 01-Oct.

Answer: Time of Supply for the ENTIRE amount (including the ₹2,00,000 advance) = 01-Oct-2025. No tax payable at the time the advance was received (25-Sep).

ILLUSTRATION 68 — Time of Supply of Services (Forward Charge & Advances)

Mr. Consultant (CA) — service completed 10-Nov-2025. Advance ₹50,000 received 30-Oct-2025; balance ₹1,50,000 received 20-Dec-2025. Invoice due within 30 days of supply, i.e. by 10-Dec-2025.

Case A — invoice issued 25-Nov-2025 (within time): rule = earliest of invoice/payment. Advance (₹50k): earlier of 25-Nov and 30-Oct → ToS = 30-Oct-2025. Balance (₹1.5L): earlier of 25-Nov and 20-Dec → ToS = 25-Nov-2025.

Case B — invoice issued 15-Dec-2025 (late): rule = earliest of provision-of-service/payment. Advance (₹50k): earlier of 10-Nov and 30-Oct → ToS = 30-Oct-2025. Balance (₹1.5L): earlier of 10-Nov (provision) and 20-Dec → ToS = 10-Nov-2025.

ILLUSTRATION 69 — Change in Rate of Tax [Sec. 14]

GST rate on a service changed from 12% to 18% w.e.f. 01-Nov-2025. Supply: 28-Oct-2025 (Before). Invoice: 05-Nov-2025 (After). Payment: 10-Nov-2025 (After).

Supply Before, but both Invoice and Payment After → New Rate applies; Time of Supply = earliest of Invoice or Payment.

Answer: Time of Supply = 05-Nov-2025 (date of invoice). Applicable rate = 18% (New Rate).

ILLUSTRATION 70 — Reverse Charge (GTA-type Service)

Alpha Traders receives a reverse-charge service on 15-Jan-2026; invoice date 15-Jan-2026; payment made 20-Mar-2026.

Rule for RCM services: earlier of (i) date of payment, (ii) 61st day from invoice date. 61st day: Jan (remaining) 16 days + Feb 28 days + Mar 17 days = 61 → 17-Mar-2026.

Answer: Compare 20-Mar (payment) vs 17-Mar (61st day) → Time of Supply = 17-Mar-2026.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: ADVANCE ON GOODS vs ADVANCE ON SERVICES

THE TRAP: students assume an advance payment always fixes the time of supply, for goods and services alike.

THE TWIST: Notification No. 66/2017-CT dated 15/11/2017 relieves GOODS ONLY — no GST is payable at the time an advance for goods is received; time of supply is fixed by the invoice/removal date instead. This relief does NOT extend to services (advances on services remain taxable when received) or to goods under reverse charge (Sec. 12(3) still counts date of receipt of goods/payment).

1. What is the time of supply for a registered person for the outward supply of goods under forward charge?

(a) Date of receipt of payment or date of invoice, whichever earlier (b) Date of issue of invoice or last date it is required to be issued u/s 31 (c) Date of delivery of goods only (d) Date of entry in the supplier's books

2. For a supply of services, if the invoice is issued within 30 days from the date of supply, time of supply is:

(a) Date of issue of invoice or date of receipt of payment, whichever earlier (b) Date of completion of service or date of payment, whichever earlier (c) Date of entry in the recipient's books (d) Date of filing the return

3. If a supplier receives an advance of ₹800 in excess of invoice value for a supply of services, what is the time of supply for this excess amount?

(a) Must be the date of receipt of payment (b) At the supplier's option, date of invoice for such excess, or receipt of payment (c) Always the 30th day of the next month (d) No GST is payable on excess amounts below ₹1,000

4. What is the "Date of receipt of payment" defined as for GST purposes?

(a) Date of realization in the bank (b) Date of entry in supplier's books, or date of bank credit, whichever earlier (c) Date on the cheque (d) Date of filing the return

5. For goods sent on "approval for sale or return," the invoice must be issued at the latest by:

(a) 3 months from the date of removal (b) 6 months from the date of removal (c) 1 year from the date of removal (d) The end of the financial year

6. Mr. A supplies taxable goods to Mr. B: goods removed 20 Oct 2025, invoice issued 25 Oct 2025, advance already paid by Mr. B on 15 Oct 2025. What is the Time of Supply?

(a) 15 Oct 2025 (Date of Payment) (b) 20 Oct 2025 (Date of Removal) (c) 25 Oct 2025 (Date of Invoice) (d) 20 Oct for the goods and 15 Oct for the advance

7. A Cost Accountant completes a service on 10 Nov 2025; invoice issued 15 Dec 2025; payment received 20 Dec 2025. What is the Time of Supply?

(a) 15 December 2025 (b) 20 December 2025 (c) 10 November 2025 (d) 10 December 2025 (30 days from completion)

8. Mr. X supplied goods to Mr. Y on credit; due to delay Mr. X charged a ₹5,000 penalty, paid by Mr. Y on 15 July 2025. When does the Time of Supply arise for this ₹5,000?

(a) The date of the original supply of goods (b) The date the penalty was agreed upon (c) 15 July 2025 (date of receipt of penalty) (d) The last day of the financial year
QCorrectReason
1bNotification No. 66/2017-CT — GST on outward supply of goods is payable only at invoice date / last required-invoice date; advances for goods are not taxable at receipt.
2aSec. 13(2) — invoice within the prescribed period → earlier of invoice date or payment date.
3bProviso to Sec. 13(2) — up to ₹1,000 excess, supplier may treat time of supply as the date of the invoice issued for that excess.
4bExplanation 2 to Sec. 12(2)/13(2) — earlier of books-entry date or bank-credit date.
5bSec. 31(7) — invoice before/at time of supply or 6 months from removal, whichever earlier.
6b) 20 Oct 2025Earlier of invoice date/removal date; Notification No. 66/2017-CT makes the payment date irrelevant. Removal (20 Oct) is earlier than invoice (25 Oct).
7c) 10 Nov 2025Invoice (15 Dec) is beyond the 30-day limit from completion (10 Nov), so time of supply = earlier of provision-of-service date / payment date — 10 Nov is earlier than 20 Dec.
8c) 15 July 2025Sec. 12(6)/13(6) — time of supply for interest/late fee/penalty = date the supplier receives that addition in value.

Notable CBIC FAQ Points (15-12-2018) Not Already Covered Above

  • Part payment / part invoice: for SERVICES, the supply is deemed made only to the extent covered by the invoice or the part payment. For GOODS, tax must be paid on the FULL invoice value at the time of issue of invoice, irrespective of whether advance/part payment was received.
  • Worked rate-change example (goods, 18%→20% w.e.f. 1.9.2017): goods supplied and invoice issued AFTER the change (September 2017), but full advance payment already received BEFORE the change (July 2017) → the NEW rate of 20% applies, since goods are supplied and invoiced after the change date.
  • Worked rate-change example (services, 18%→20% w.e.f. 1.9.2017): services provided and invoice issued BEFORE the change (July 2017), but payment received AFTER the change (September 2017) → the OLD rate of 18% applies, since the services were provided prior to the change.

5.3.2 Place of Supply

Place of supply determines the KIND of tax charged. As per Sec. 7 of the IGST Act — if the location of supplier and the place of supply are in two different States (or UTs), it is an inter-State supply and IGST is chargeable; if they are in the same State (or UT), it is an intra-State supply and CGST/SGST is chargeable. Place of supply is a legal term, not a matter of common understanding — it is exactly what the legislature has appointed, and it determines the State/UT to which the SGST portion of revenue accrues.

Place of Supply of Goods (not imported/exported) [Sec. 10, IGST Act]

SituationPlace of Supply
Supply involves movement of goods, by supplier, recipient, or any other person [Sec. 10(1)(a)]Location of the goods at the time movement TERMINATES for delivery to the recipient. E.g. supplier in Kolkata, recipient in Delhi → POS = Delhi.
Goods delivered by supplier to a recipient/other person on the direction of a THIRD person (Bill-to-Ship-to), before/during movement, by transfer of documents of title or otherwise [Sec. 10(1)(b)]Principal place of business of the THIRD person. E.g. Burman (W. Bengal) supplies to Raman (Tamil Nadu); Raman instructs Burman to deliver to Chaman (Kerala) → POS = Tamil Nadu (Raman's location).
Supply does NOT involve movement of goods [Sec. 10(1)(c)]Location of the goods at the time of delivery to the recipient. E.g. Ramesh installs a centralized AC in Raja's rented building and leaves it behind on vacating → POS = where the AC is fixed.
Goods purchased over-the-counter in one State and transported to another State by an UNREGISTERED buyer [Sec. 10(1)(ca)]Address of the person recorded in the invoice; if no address recorded, location of the supplier. Recording the State name alone is deemed sufficient recording of the address. Circular No. 209/3/2024-GST: where delivery address differs from billing address on the invoice, POS = the DELIVERY address recorded on the invoice.
Goods assembled or installed at site [Sec. 10(1)(d)]Location of such installation or assembly. E.g. lift purchased by a Karnataka company from a Karnataka vendor, installed at its Chennai office → POS = Chennai.
Goods supplied on-board a conveyanceLocation at which the goods are taken ON BOARD. E.g. Mr. Jain boards a train at Kolkata carrying goods, sells them when the train reaches Tatanagar → POS = Kolkata (where taken on board).

Place of Supply of Goods Imported into / Exported from India [Sec. 11, IGST Act]

CasePlace of Supply
ImportLocation of the importer
ExportLocation outside India

Place of Supply of Services — Supplier & Recipient both in India [Sec. 12, IGST Act]

Service CategoryPlace of Supply
General rule(a) To a registered person — location of such person. (b) To any other person — location of the recipient where the address on record exists, else location of the supplier. E.g. Mr. Aman (Mumbai) provides architect services to a Bengaluru registered company → POS = Bengaluru. A beauty parlour with no customer records → POS = location of the parlour; if it does keep records → POS = location of the recipient.
Immovable property services (architects, interior decorators, engineers, estate agents, grant of rights to use immovable property, construction; hotel/inn/guest house/homestay/houseboat lodging; accommodation for marriage/reception/functions; ancillary services)Location where the immovable property/boat/vessel is located or intended to be located. If located in more than one State/UT, POS is apportioned across each State/UT in proportion to value per the contract, or as prescribed. If the property/boat/vessel is located OUTSIDE India, POS = location of the recipient.
Restaurant & catering, personal grooming, fitness, beauty treatment, health service (incl. cosmetic/plastic surgery)Location where the services are actually performed
Training & performance appraisal(a) Registered person — location of such person. (b) Other — location where actually performed
Admission to a cultural/artistic/sporting/scientific/educational/entertainment event or amusement parkWhere the event is actually held / where the park is located
Organization of such an event (conference, fair, exhibition, celebration) or ancillary services / sponsorship(i) Registered person — location of such person. (ii) Other — where the event is actually held; if held outside India — location of the recipient. If held across multiple States/UTs with a consolidated charge — apportioned by value per State/UT.
Transportation of goods (incl. mail/courier)(a) Registered person — location of such person. (b) Other — location where the goods are handed over for transportation
Passenger transportation service(a) Registered person — location of such person. (b) Other — place where the passenger embarks for a continuous journey (return journey treated as a SEPARATE journey even if booked together)
Services on board a conveyance (vessel, aircraft, train, motor vehicle)Location of the FIRST scheduled point of departure of that conveyance for the journey
Fixed telecom line, leased circuit, cable/dish antennaLocation where the line/circuit/connection is installed for receipt of service
Mobile connection, post-paidBilling address of the recipient on the supplier's records
Mobile/internet/DTH connection, pre-paid via voucher/agent(a) Sold through selling agent/re-seller/distributor — address of that agent on supplier's record at the time of supply. (b) Sold directly to final subscriber — location where prepayment is received / voucher sold
Banking & other financial services incl. stock broking, to any personLocation of the recipient on the supplier's records
Insurance services(i) Registered person — location of such person. (ii) Other — location of recipient on supplier's records
Advertisement services to Central/State Government, a statutory body, or a local authorityLocated in EACH such State, apportioned by value attributable to dissemination in each State

Place of Supply where Supplier OR Recipient is Outside India [Sec. 13(1), IGST Act]

SituationPlace of Supply
General ruleIf location of recipient is available in ordinary course of business → location of the recipient; if not available → location of the supplier
Goods physically made available by recipient to supplier to perform the service [Sec. 13(3)(a)]Where the services are actually performed
Services provided electronically in relation to tangible goods [Sec. 13(3)(a)]Actual location of the goods
Services requiring the physical presence of the recipient (or someone acting for the recipient) [Sec. 13(3)(b)]Where the services are actually performed
Services directly relating to immovable property (lease/right to use, hotel accommodation, construction, architects, interior decorators, renting, real estate agents, engineers etc.) [Sec. 13(4)]Where the immovable property is located or intended to be located
Admission to / organization of cultural, artistic, sporting, scientific, educational, entertainment events, celebrations, conferences, fairs, exhibitions, and ancillary services [Sec. 13(5)]Where the event is actually held
Any Sec. 13(3)/(4)/(5) service supplied at more than one location, incl. one in the taxable territory [Sec. 13(6)]The location in the taxable territory
Sec. 13(3)/(4)/(5) service performed in more than one State/UT [Sec. 13(7)]Deemed in each such State/UT in proportion to value of services provided there
Specified services — banking/financial/NBFC to account holders; intermediary services; hiring of means of transport (other than aircraft, and vessels except yachts) up to 1 month [Sec. 13(8)]Location of the supplier of services
Passenger transportation services [Sec. 13(10)]Where the passenger embarks on the conveyance for a continuous journey
Service provided on board a conveyance (aircraft, vessel, rail, roadways bus)First scheduled point of departure of that conveyance for the journey
Online information & database access or retrieval servicesLocation of the recipient of service

Circular No. 242/36/2024-GST dated 31-12-2024: for online services supplied to an unregistered person, POS = location of the recipient; the supplier must record the recipient's State on the invoice, and this State is deemed to be the recipient's address.

Inter-State Supply [Sec. 7, IGST Act]

  • Supply of goods where supplier's location and place of supply are in two different States, two different UTs, or a State and a UT — inter-State trade or commerce.
  • Goods imported into India, till they cross the customs frontiers of India — deemed inter-State supply.
  • Supply of services under the same "two different States/UTs" test — inter-State trade or commerce.
  • Services imported into India — deemed inter-State supply.
  • Supply of goods/services where (a) supplier is in India and POS is outside India; (b) to/by an SEZ developer or SEZ unit; or (c) in the taxable territory, not being intra-State and not covered elsewhere — treated as inter-State.

Intra-State Supply [Sec. 8, IGST Act]

  • Supply of goods where supplier's location and POS are in the SAME State/UT — intra-State, EXCEPT: (i) supply to/by an SEZ developer or SEZ unit; (ii) goods imported into India till they cross the customs frontiers; (iii) supplies to a tourist referred to in Sec. 15.
  • Supply of services under the same "same State/UT" test — intra-State, except supply to/by an SEZ developer or SEZ unit.
  • Taxpoint: an establishment in India + another outside India, or an establishment in one State/UT + another outside that State/UT (even if in the same PAN), or two establishments both registered in the same State/UT — are treated as establishments of DISTINCT PERSONS. A branch, agency, or representational office in any territory is treated as an establishment in that territory.

Supplies in Territorial Waters [Sec. 9, IGST Act]: where the supplier's location OR the place of supply is in the territorial waters, it is deemed to be in the coastal State/UT where the nearest point of the appropriate baseline is located.

ILLUSTRATION 71 — Bill-to-Ship-to Model (Goods)

Mr. Alpha (Maharashtra) orders 100 laptops from Mr. Beta (Gujarat); Alpha instructs Beta to deliver directly to his client Mr. Gamma in Karnataka.

Answer: Per Sec. 10(1)(b), goods delivered on the direction of a third person (Alpha) → POS = principal place of business of the third person = Maharashtra. Supplier (Beta) = Gujarat; POS = Maharashtra → Inter-State Supply, IGST.

ILLUSTRATION 72 — Immovable Property Services (Architect)

Mr. Design (architect, New Delhi) provides consultancy to Global Hotels Ltd. (Mumbai) for a hotel project located in Goa.

Answer: Sec. 12(3) — POS = location of the immovable property = Goa (recipient's Mumbai location is irrelevant here). Supplier in Delhi, POS in Goa → IGST applicable.

ILLUSTRATION 73 — Supply to Unregistered Person, Billing vs Delivery Address

Mr. John (unregistered, Odisha) buys a study table from Furniture World (West Bengal); billing address Odisha, delivery address Jharkhand.

Answer: Sec. 10(1)(ca) & Circular No. 209/3/2024 — where delivery address differs from billing address for an unregistered recipient, POS = the DELIVERY address recorded on the invoice = Jharkhand. IGST (West Bengal → Jharkhand) applies.

ILLUSTRATION 74 — Event Management: Admission vs Organization

Case A: Rock Events (Delhi) sells tickets to Mr. X (unregistered, Punjab) for a concert held in Haryana. Case B: Rock Events (Delhi) organizes a conference for Tech Solutions Ltd. (registered, Bangalore) held in Goa.

Answer: Case A — admission to an event, Sec. 12(6) → POS = where the event is held = Haryana (IGST). Case B — organization service to a registered person, Sec. 12(7) → POS = location of such person = Bangalore (IGST).

ILLUSTRATION 75 — Telecommunication & Internet Services

Case 1 (Pre-paid voucher): Mr. Fast (distributor, Karnataka) sells a pre-paid voucher to Mr. Slow (unregistered, Tamil Nadu) at his Bangalore shop. Case 2 (Post-paid): Connect Telecom provides a post-paid connection to Tech Startups Pvt. Ltd. (registered, Hyderabad); billing address Hyderabad.

Answer: Case 1 — Sec. 12(11)(b), pre-payment via distributor → POS = address of the distributor = Karnataka. Case 2 — Sec. 12(11)(a), post-paid → POS = billing address = Telangana (Hyderabad).

ILLUSTRATION 76 — Goods Supplied on Board a Conveyance

Rajdhani Express departs New Delhi for Mumbai; food packets loaded at Kota (Rajasthan); Mr. Passenger boards at Vadodara (Gujarat) and buys a food packet during the journey.

Answer: Sec. 10(1)(e) — POS = location where the goods were TAKEN ON BOARD = Rajasthan (Kota), regardless of where the passenger bought/consumed it.

ILLUSTRATION 77 — Architect Service, Property Outside India

Global Architects (Chennai) hired by Resort Chains Ltd. (Kerala) to design a resort in Dubai (UAE).

Answer: General immovable-property rule is proviso'd — if the property is outside India and BOTH supplier and recipient are in India, POS = location of the recipient = Kerala. This is NOT an export of service (POS is in India); it is an Inter-State supply, IGST applicable.

ILLUSTRATION 78 — Telecom Services (Prepaid vs Postpaid), GST Computation

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: BILL-TO-SHIP-TO — WHOSE LOCATION COUNTS?

THE TRAP: students assume the place of supply for a Bill-to-Ship-to transaction is either the supplier's location or the PHYSICAL delivery point (where the goods actually land).

THE TWIST: under Sec. 10(1)(b), when goods are delivered to a recipient/other person on the direction of a THIRD person, the third person is DEEMED to have received the goods — POS = the third person's PRINCIPAL PLACE OF BUSINESS, not the physical delivery address (Illustration 71: delivery in Karnataka, but POS = Maharashtra, the third party's location). Similarly for unregistered buyers under Sec. 10(1)(ca), POS follows the DELIVERY address recorded on the invoice, not the billing address (Illustration 73).

1. Mr. A (Kolkata) orders a laptop from a supplier in Delhi. The supplier ships the goods to Mr. A's branch in Mumbai. What is the Place of Supply?

(a) Delhi(b) Kolkata(c) Mumbai(d) Either Delhi or Kolkata

2. U/s 10(1)(ca), if an unregistered person's delivery address is recorded on the invoice, the POS is:

(a) Location of the Supplier(b) Location of the recipient's billing address(c) The delivery address recorded on the invoice(d) The State where the goods were manufactured

3. For the purposes of Sec. 10(1)(ca), what is deemed to be the "recording of the address"?

(a) Full postal address with Pincode(b) Recording the name of the State(c) Mentioning the PAN of the buyer(d) Mentioning the Aadhaar of the buyer

4. X (Tamil Nadu) instructs Y (Karnataka) to deliver goods to Z (Gujarat). Y bills X. What is the POS?

(a) Karnataka(b) Gujarat(c) Tamil Nadu(d) No GST is applicable

5. A hotel in Goa provides accommodation to a guest from Delhi. The POS is:

(a) Delhi(b) Goa(c) Maharashtra (nearest hub)(d) Union Territory

6. An event organizer in Delhi organizes a corporate seminar in New Delhi for a company registered in Haryana. The POS is:

(a) New Delhi(b) Haryana(c) Chandigarh(d) Mumbai

7. Same event organizer, but for an UNREGISTERED person in Haryana. The POS is:

(a) Haryana(b) New Delhi(c) Location of the organizer(d) Exempt from GST

8. For Export of Services, if the recipient is outside India and the supplier is in India, the POS is generally:

(a) Location of the Supplier(b) Location of the Recipient(c) Customs Frontier(d) Port of Exit

9. If a supplier fails to record the address of an unregistered person on the invoice, the POS becomes:

(a) The recipient's home state (if known)(b) The location of the supplier(c) The nearest GST Suvidha Kendra(d) Always Delhi (Central Registry)

10. "Place of Supply" is primarily determined to decide:

(a) The date of payment of tax(b) Whether the supply is Intra-state or Inter-state(c) The valuation of the goods(d) The eligibility of ITC for the supplier
QCorrectReason
1cSec. 10(1)(a) — POS is where movement terminates for delivery to the recipient (Mumbai).
2cSec. 10(1)(ca) — delivery address on invoice determines POS.
3bRecording the State name on the invoice is deemed sufficient.
4cBill-to-Ship-to u/s 10(1)(b) — POS is the principal place of business of the third person (X = Tamil Nadu).
5bSec. 12(3) — POS for immovable property (hotels) is the property's location.
6bSec. 12(7)(a) — registered recipient → POS = location of such person (Haryana).
7bSec. 12(7)(b) — unregistered recipient → POS = where the event is actually held (New Delhi).
8bSec. 13(2) — POS = location of the recipient of the service.
9bDefault of Sec. 10(1)(ca) — no recorded address → POS = location of the supplier.
10bSec. 7 & 8, IGST Act — supplier location + POS together fix intra-State vs inter-State.

5.3.3 Value of Supply

GST is computed as a percentage of the value of taxable supply — so valuation is central to the tax liability itself.

Value of a supply of goods or services or both shall be the TRANSACTION VALUE, which is the price actually paid or payable for the supply, where (a) the supplier and recipient are NOT related, and (b) the price is the SOLE consideration for the supply — Sec. 15(1).

Related Persons & Key Definitions

Persons are deemed "related" if: (a) officers/directors of one another's businesses; (b) legally recognised business partners; (c) employer and employee; (d) any person directly/indirectly owns, controls or holds 25% or more of the outstanding voting stock/shares of both; (e) one directly/indirectly controls the other; (f) both directly/indirectly controlled by a third person; (g) together they directly/indirectly control a third person; or (h) members of the same family. Also, a sole agent / sole distributor / sole concessionaire relationship is deemed "related."

Sec. 2(75) "money" — Indian legal tender or any foreign currency, cheque, promissory note, bill of exchange, letter of credit, draft, pay order, traveller cheque, money order, postal/electronic remittance, or any RBI-recognised instrument, but EXCLUDES currency held for its numismatic value.

Sec. 2(31) "consideration" — includes any payment made/to be made (money or otherwise), and the monetary value of any act/forbearance, in respect of the supply, whether by the recipient or any other person — but EXCLUDES any subsidy given by Central or State Government. A deposit is NOT "payment" unless the supplier applies it as consideration for that supply.

Value of Taxable Supply = Transaction Value + Inclusions [Sec. 15(2)] – Exclusions [Sec. 15(3)]

ADD (Sec. 15(2)): • Taxes/duties/cesses/fees under any law OTHER than GST, if charged separately (Taxpoint: TCS under the Income-tax Act is NOT included — it is an interim levy, not final tax) • amounts the supplier was liable to pay but the RECIPIENT paid on their behalf (third-party payments) • incidental expenses charged by the supplier before delivery (packing, commission, inspection, freight) • interest/penalty for delayed payment of consideration • subsidies received from NON-Government bodies, directly linked to the price (Central/State Government subsidies are NOT included).

LESS (Sec. 15(3)): • Pre-supply discount — given before/at the time of supply and recorded in the invoice • Post-supply discount — only if (a) agreed upon before supply, (b) linked to specific invoices, and (c) the recipient has reversed the proportionate ITC (a CA/CMA certificate, or an undertaking if the tax involved is under ₹5,00,000/FY, may evidence the reversal). Taxpoint: interest-free refundable deposits attract no GST.

Illustrative Points from the Source (Compact Examples)

  • Value inclusive of tax ₹100, GST 18% → tax component = (100 × 18) ÷ 118 = ₹15.25.
  • Mr. X sells to Mr. B for ₹1,000, unrelated, price is sole consideration → value of supply = ₹1,000.
  • Supplier's goods worth ₹5,00,000: ₹3,00,000 paid directly by the recipient, ₹2,00,000 paid by the recipient's debtor — BOTH amounts are included in the value.
  • Goods worth ₹20,000 + packing charges ₹1,000 + freight ₹3,000 (paid by supplier) → taxable value = ₹24,000 (packing & freight both included).
  • Cafeteria sells lunch at ₹120/plate; vendor also receives ₹70/plate subsidy from the corporate host (a non-Government body) → taxable value = ₹120 + ₹70 = ₹190. Had the subsidy come from GOVERNMENT (e.g. mid-day meal scheme), the ₹70 would NOT be included.
  • Contract for goods worth ₹2,00,000; late penalty ₹10,000 for payment beyond 2 months, actually charged → ₹10,000 is includible; if GST not separately charged on it, the ₹10,000 is treated as INCLUSIVE of GST.
  • M/s Nanda Bakery: MRP ₹200/cake, 10% discount, 600 cakes sold → value of supply = 90% × (₹200 × 600) = ₹1,08,000.
  • Goods sold for ₹2,50,000; buyer pays the ₹2,500 freight that was the seller's contractual obligation → value of taxable supply = ₹2,52,500 (seller's obligation discharged by the buyer is included).

EXAMPLE — RG Pvt. Ltd. to GK Pvt. Ltd., Full Sec. 15(2) Walk-through

List price (excl. tax/discount) ₹10,00,000; Municipal Authority tax ₹1,00,000; CGST+SGST chargeable ₹2,00,880; packing charges (not in list price) ₹20,000; NGO subsidy ₹40,000 (already reflected in the ₹10,00,000 list price); 2% discount on list price, recorded in invoice.

Computation of Value of Taxable Supply
Particulars₹
List price (excl. tax/discount)10,00,000
Add: Municipal Authority tax [includible — Sec. 15(2)(a)]1,00,000
Add: CGST/SGST chargeable [NOT includible — Sec. 15(2)(a)]—
Add: Packing charges [includible — Sec. 15(2)(c)]20,000
Add: NGO subsidy (non-Government) [includible — Sec. 15(2)(e)]40,000
Total11,60,000
Less: Discount @ 2% on ₹10,00,000(20,000)
Value of taxable supply11,40,000

Discounts — Circular No. 92/11/2019 dated 07.03.2019 & Circular No. 251/08/2025 dated 12.09.2025

  • Staggered "Buy more, save more" discounts (e.g. 10% above ₹5,000, 20% above ₹10,000, 30% above ₹20,000) — shown on the invoice itself — EXCLUDED from value of supply.
  • Periodic/year-end "volume" discounts (e.g. additional 1% for 10,000 pieces/year, 2% for 15,000 pieces/year) — established by an agreement entered into at/before supply, though the exact quantum crystallises only at year-end and is passed via credit notes — still EXCLUDED, provided the Sec. 15(3) conditions (incl. ITC reversal by recipient) are satisfied. The supplier remains entitled to full ITC on inputs/input services/capital goods used for such supplies.
  • Secondary discounts (not known at the time of supply, offered afterwards — e.g. re-valuing biscuits from ₹10/packet to ₹9/packet after supply) — a financial/commercial credit note CAN still be issued under Sec. 34(1) even if Sec. 15(3)(b) conditions are not met, but such secondary discounts shall NOT be excluded while determining value of supply, since the Sec. 15(3)(b) conditions are not satisfied. There is no impact on the supplier's own ITC in this case.

Circular No. 251/08/2025-GST: (1) if a post-sale discount is passed via a FINANCIAL credit note (no GST adjustment), the buyer is still entitled to FULL ITC of the tax on the original invoice, provided the buyer pays the reduced value plus the full tax amount. (2) Post-sale discounts to boost sales (target incentives) are pure discounts, NOT consideration for a service by the dealer — UNLESS the dealer is explicitly required to run a specific advertisement/co-branding campaign, in which case it becomes a separate taxable service.

FeatureScenario A — Sec. 15(3)(b) DiscountScenario B — Circular 251/2025
Type of discountCash discount with pre-agreementFinancial/commercial discount (target incentive, no pre-agreement)
Document issuedGST Credit Note (with tax adjustment)Financial Credit Note (without tax adjustment)
Supplier's tax liabilityReduced (pays less tax)Not reduced (pays full tax)
Recipient's actionMust reverse ITC proportionate to discountNo reversal required — can claim full ITC
Legal authoritySec. 15(3)(b)Circular No. 251/08/2025-GST

Consideration Not Wholly in Money [Rule 27]

CaseValue of Supply
Open market value (OMV) is availableOMV (money value excluding IGST/CGST/SGST/UTGST/cess, between unrelated parties, sole consideration, same time)
OMV not availableMoney consideration + further amount in money equivalent to the non-money consideration, if known at the time of supply
Not determinable under (a)/(b)Value of supply of goods/services of LIKE KIND AND QUALITY
Not determinable under (a)/(b)/(c)Value per Rule 30 or Rule 31, in that order

Examples: new phone for ₹20,000 + exchange of old phone; price of new phone WITHOUT exchange = ₹24,000 → OMV = ₹24,000. Laptop for ₹40,000 + barter of a printer valued ₹4,000, laptop's OMV unknown → value of laptop supply = ₹44,000. Jaya's TV: shop's quoted price ₹81,000, settled at ₹78,000 via a ₹85,000 exchange offer with an old TV worth ₹8,000; since price is NOT the sole consideration, OMV of ₹85,000 is taken as the value of supply.

Supply Between Distinct/Related Persons, Other Than Through an Agent [Rule 28]

CaseValue of Supply
OMV available, recipient NOT eligible for full ITCOpen market value
OMV available, recipient eligible for full ITCValue declared in the invoice deemed to be OMV (tax-neutral transaction)
OMV not available, goods not for further supply as suchValue of supply of like kind and quality
OMV not available, goods intended for further supply as suchAt supplier's option — value of like kind and quality, OR 90% of the price charged by the recipient to his (unrelated) customer

Where value is still not determinable, Rule 30 or Rule 31 applies in that order. A person with multiple registrations (one State/UT or across States/UTs) is treated as a DISTINCT PERSON for each registration [Sec. 25(4)/(5)].

Corporate guarantee override: value of supply of services by a related-person supplier providing a corporate guarantee to a banking company/financial institution on behalf of the recipient (both in India) = DEEMED to be 1% of the guarantee amount per annum, OR the actual consideration, whichever is HIGHER — this overrides the general related-party valuation rules EVEN IF the recipient is eligible for full ITC (invoice value cannot be substituted as OMV here).

"Agent" [Sec. 2(5)] — a factor, broker, commission agent, arhatia, del credere agent, auctioneer, or other mercantile agent carrying on business of supply/receipt of goods or services on behalf of another.

Supply of Goods Through an Agent [Rule 29]

CaseValue of Supply
OMV availableAt supplier's option — OMV, OR 90% of the price charged by the recipient (agent) to his unrelated customer, where intended for further supply
OMV not determinableRule 30 or Rule 31, in that order

Example: principal supplies groundnut to agent; agent re-sells like-kind groundnut at ₹5,000/quintal on the day of supply; an independent supplier sells like-kind groundnut to the same agent at ₹4,550/quintal. Value = ₹4,550/quintal (like-kind price), or, if the supplier exercises the option, 90% × ₹5,000 = ₹4,500/quintal.

Value Based on Cost [Rule 30] = 110% of the cost of production/manufacture or cost of acquisition of goods, or cost of provision of services — used only where preceding rules fail.

Residual Method [Rule 31]: where value cannot be determined under Rules 27–30, use REASONABLE MEANS consistent with Sec. 15's principles. For SERVICES ONLY, the supplier may opt for Rule 31 directly, skipping Rule 30.

Lottery, Betting, Gambling, Horse Racing & Online Gaming [Rule 31A / 31B / 31C]

Lottery [Rule 31A(2)]: deemed value = HIGHER of (a) 100/140 of face value of ticket, or (b) 100/140 of the price notified by the Organising State. ("Lottery run by State Govt." = not sold outside the organising State; "Lottery authorised by State Govt." = also sold in other States.)

Betting/gambling/horse racing actionable claim in a race club [Rule 31A(3)]: value = 100% of the face value of the bet, or the amount paid into the totalisator.

Online gaming, incl. online money gaming [Rule 31B]: value = TOTAL amount paid/payable to or deposited with the supplier (money or money's worth, incl. virtual digital assets), by or on behalf of the player. Amounts refunded/returned are NOT deductible from this value. Winnings re-used for further play (without withdrawal) are NOT treated as a fresh deposit.

Casino [Rule 31C]: value = total amount paid/payable for purchase of tokens/chips/coins/tickets, OR for participating where no token is required. Refunds on returned tokens are NOT deductible.

"Online gaming" [Sec. 2(80A)] — offering a game on the internet/electronic network, incl. online money gaming. "Online money gaming" [Sec. 2(80B)] — players pay/deposit money or money's worth expecting to win money or money's worth, whether skill- or chance-based, whether or not permissible under other law. "Specified actionable claim" — betting, casinos, gambling, horse racing, lottery, or online money gaming.

EXAMPLE — Lottery Valuation, Rule 31A(2)

Face value per ticket ₹1,000; official-gazette notified price ₹600 (or, alternately, ₹1,050).

ParticularsNotified price ₹600Notified price ₹1,050
100/140 of face value (₹1,000 × 100/140)714.28714.28
100/140 of notified price428.57750.00
Value of supply (higher of the two)714.28750.00

Value in Respect of Certain Specified Supplies [Sec. 15(5) & Rule 32] — determined at the option of the supplier

Purchase/sale of foreign currency, incl. money changing [Rule 32(2)]: Option 1 — where one currency is INR: value = (buying/selling rate – RBI reference rate) × total units of currency; if RBI reference rate unavailable, value = 1% of the gross INR amount. Where NEITHER currency is INR: value = 1% of the lesser of the two amounts obtainable by converting either currency to INR at the RBI reference rate. Option 2 (based on gross amount exchanged): up to ₹1,00,000 — higher of 1% of gross amount OR ₹250; over ₹1,00,000 up to ₹10,00,000 — ₹1,000 + 0.5% of the excess over ₹1,00,000; over ₹10,00,000 — lower of [₹5,500 + 0.1% of the excess over ₹10,00,000] OR ₹60,000. The option chosen under Rule 32(2), once exercised for a financial year, cannot be withdrawn during that year.

EXAMPLES — Money-Changing Valuation, Rule 32(2)

  • US$100 sold at ₹78/USD, RBI reference rate ₹77/USD → taxable value = (₹78–₹77) × 100 = ₹100.
  • INR 90,000 changed into GBP at ₹90; RBI reference rate for GBP ₹89 → taxable value = ₹1,000 [(90–89) × 1,000 GBP]; if RBI rate unavailable, value = 1% of ₹90,000 = ₹900.
  • USD 100 at ₹65/USD, gross ₹6,500 → value = higher of ₹250 and 1% of ₹6,500 = ₹250.
  • USD 1,000 at ₹65/USD, gross ₹65,000 → value = 1% × ₹65,000 = ₹650.
  • USD 3,000 at ₹65/USD, gross ₹1,95,000 → value = ₹1,000 + [(1,95,000–1,00,000) × 0.5%] = ₹1,475.
  • USD 20,000 at ₹65/USD, gross ₹13,00,000 → value = ₹5,500 + [(13,00,000–10,00,000) × 0.1%] = ₹5,800.

EXAMPLE — Air Travel Agent, Rule 32(3)

Deemed value = 5% of basic fare (domestic booking) or 10% of basic fare (international booking). "Basic fare" = the portion of air fare on which commission is normally paid to the agent by the airline.

Mr. Ram, Travel Agent

Life Insurance Business [Rule 32(4)]

CaseValue of Supply
Policy has investment features, amount intimated to policyholderGross premium LESS the amount allocated for investment/savings. E.g. gross premium ₹60,000, of which ₹55,000 invested → value = ₹5,000.

Taxpoint: this rule does NOT apply where the entire premium is only towards risk cover (pure term insurance).

Second-Hand Goods (Margin Scheme) [Rule 32(5)]: for a dealer in used goods (as such, or after minor processing not changing their nature) who has availed NO ITC on purchase — value of supply = Selling Price – Purchase Price. If this margin is NEGATIVE, it is IGNORED (no GST on a loss-making sale).

Taxpoint: for a repossessed defaulting-borrower's goods, purchase value = defaulting borrower's original purchase price REDUCED by 5% per quarter (or part) between the purchase date and the disposal date.

Sl.Purchase (₹)Sale (₹)Profit (₹)
1 (Bihar)80,0001,20,00040,000
2 (Bihar)75,00065,000Ignored — negative margin

EXAMPLE — Repossessed Car Valuation

Mr. X takes a ₹3,00,000 car loan on 1 Sep 2022 (entirely for the car); defaults; car repossessed by the bank 1 Jan 2023; sold by the bank 30 Mar 2023 for ₹2,50,000.

Deemed purchase value = ₹3,00,000 – (5% × 3 quarters, Sep–Mar × ₹3,00,000) = ₹3,00,000 – ₹45,000 = ₹2,55,000.

Answer: sale value ₹2,50,000 is below ₹2,55,000 → margin ignored, no GST. If sold instead for ₹2,70,000 → taxable value = ₹2,70,000 – ₹2,55,000 = ₹15,000.

Vouchers, Tokens, Coupons, Stamps (redeemable against goods/services) [Rule 32(6)]: value = the MONEY VALUE of the goods/services redeemable against it, not its purchase/issue price.

Example: Mr. X buys a voucher for ₹200, redeemable against a ₹500 wallet → valuation taken = ₹500 (redemption value), NOT ₹200 (purchase value).

Notified Class of Service Providers, Sch. I Distinct Persons [Rule 32(7)]: where ITC is available, value of taxable services between such distinct persons is DEEMED NIL.

Pure Agent [Rule 33]: expenditure/costs incurred by a supplier as a PURE AGENT of the recipient are EXCLUDED from value of supply, if ALL conditions are met — (a) acts as pure agent when paying the third party on the recipient's authorisation; (b) the payment is separately indicated on the invoice to the recipient; (c) the procured supplies are IN ADDITION to the services supplied on the agent's own account.

"Pure agent" — enters a contract to incur such expenditure as agent; neither intends to hold nor holds title to the goods/services procured; does not use them for his own interest; recovers only the ACTUAL amount incurred (plus his own separate fee).

Example: Firm A handles Company B's incorporation; besides its own fee, A recovers ROC registration/approval fees (compulsorily levied on B) from B. A is a pure agent for those fees — the recovery is a disbursement, NOT part of A's value of supply.

Rate of Exchange for Non-INR Consideration [Rule 34]: for GOODS — the rate notified by the Board u/s 14 Customs Act, 1962, for the time-of-supply date under Sec. 12. For SERVICES — the rate per generally accepted accounting principles, for the time-of-supply date under Sec. 13.

ILLUSTRATION 88 — Comprehensive Sec. 15(2) Value Computation

S Ltd. sells a machine to A Ltd., Feb 2026, list price ₹8,50,000 (excl. tax/discount). Municipal taxes ₹55,000; outward freight (F.O.R. contract) ₹75,000. S Ltd. normally charges 1% p.m. interest beyond a 30-day credit period; A Ltd. paid after 45 days but S Ltd. WAIVED the interest. S Ltd. received ₹50,000 subsidy from an NGO, not linked to the machine's price and not reflected in the ₹8,50,000 list price. A Ltd. deducted an unauthorised ₹15,000 discount at final payment (not per agreement). S Ltd. collected ₹8,500 as TCS under the Income-tax Act.

ILLUSTRATION 89 — Intra-State Supply with Invoice Discount

Ms. Sonam (Mumbai), March 2026 — intra-State supplies: list price ₹3,30,000; packing expenses (charged separately in invoice) ₹10,800; discount of 1% on list price (recorded in the invoice).

⚠ TRAP: WHICH SUBSIDY, WHICH DISCOUNT?

THE TRAP: students assume ALL subsidies are excluded from value and ALL post-supply discounts are automatically deductible.

THE TWIST: only Central/State GOVERNMENT subsidies are excluded [Sec. 15(2)(e)] — a subsidy from an NGO, trade association, or any non-Government body that is directly linked to the price MUST be added back into the value (Illustrations 88, 90, 92). Similarly, a post-supply discount is deductible ONLY if it satisfies all three Sec. 15(3)(b) conditions together — pre-agreed before supply, linked to specific invoices, AND the recipient has reversed proportionate ITC; a discount passed later via a bare financial/commercial credit note (Circular No. 251/08/2025), without a pre-existing agreement, is NOT deductible from value even though the buyer may still claim full ITC on the original invoice.
