For GSTR-4, delayed filing draws a late fee of ₹50 per day up to a maximum of ₹2,000; where the tax liability is Nil, the maximum late fee is ₹500. † A TDS return under GSTR-7 must be furnished for every calendar month whether or not any deduction was made in that month.

B. Furnishing Details of Outward Supplies — GSTR-1 [Sec. 37]

Every registered person (including a casual registered person) must electronically furnish the details of outward supplies of goods/services made during a tax period, in Form GSTR-1, on or before the 10th day of the succeeding month (presently extended to the 11th). "Tax period" means the period for which the return is to be furnished – Sec. 2(106).

  • Scope: "Details of outward supplies" covers invoices, debit notes, credit notes and revised invoices issued for outward supplies made during the tax period.
  • Exceptions — Sec. 37 does NOT apply to: (a) Input Service Distributor; (b) non-resident taxable person; (c) a person paying tax u/s 10 (composition), s. 51 (TDS) or s. 52 (TCS).
  • Communication to recipient: details in GSTR-1 are auto-drafted and communicated to the recipient — in GSTR-2A (normal registered recipient), GSTR-4A (composition-scheme recipient), or GSTR-6A (Input Service Distributor recipient).
  • Extension of due date: the Commissioner may extend the time limit by notification, for reasons recorded in writing; a Commissioner of State/UT tax's extension is deemed notified by the Commissioner as well.
  • Rectification [Sec. 37(3)]: a registered person who discovers any error or omission in furnished details must rectify it, and pay tax with interest if there is short payment, in the return for the tax period in which the correction is made. No rectification is allowed after 30th November following the end of the financial year to which the details pertain, or the actual filing of the annual return — whichever is earlier.
  • Restriction [Sec. 37(4)]: a registered person cannot furnish GSTR-1/IFF for a tax period if GSTR-1 for any earlier tax period is outstanding; GSTR-1 is also now blocked if GSTR-3B for the preceding month has not been furnished. (The Government may, by notification, relax this for specified classes.)
  • Maximum time limit: GSTR-1 for a tax period cannot be furnished after the expiry of 3 years from its due date (subject to Government-notified extension for specified classes).
  • A Nil GSTR-1 can be filed by SMS using the taxpayer's registered mobile number.
  • Small taxpayers under the Quarterly Return Monthly Payment (QRMP) Scheme may opt to file GSTR-1 quarterly.

C. Form GSTR-1A and the Invoice Furnishing Facility (IFF) [Rule 59]

Every registered person (other than one covered by Sec. 14 of the IGST Act) files GSTR-1 electronically through the common portal, directly or via a Facilitation Centre. After furnishing GSTR-1 for a tax period but before filing GSTR-3B for that period, the person may, at their own option, amend or add outward-supply details in Form GSTR-1A for that same period.

IFF for QRMP taxpayers [Rule 59(2)]: a registered person filing GSTR-1 quarterly (proviso to Sec. 39(1)) may furnish outward-supply details for the first and second months of the quarter, up to a cumulative value of ₹50 lakh in each month, using the Invoice Furnishing Facility (IFF), electronically, from the 1st day of the succeeding month till the 13th day of that month.

QRMP Taxpayer — What Is Filed Instead of Monthly GSTR-1
FilingCoverageTime Limit
Invoice Furnishing Facility (IFF)First two months of the quarterWithin the 13th day of the following month
GSTR-1Entire quarterWithin the 13th day of the following quarter

Details furnished via IFF for the first and second months of a quarter are NOT to be furnished again in GSTR-1 for that quarter.

  • Details to be given in GSTR-1/1A [Rule 59(4)/(4A)]: (a) invoice-wise inter-State & intra-State supplies to registered persons, and inter-State supplies with invoice value > ₹1,00,000 to unregistered persons; (b) consolidated intra-State supplies to unregistered persons per tax rate, and State-wise inter-State supplies up to ₹1,00,000 to unregistered persons per tax rate; (c) debit/credit notes issued during the month for earlier invoices.
  • Details to be given in IFF [Rule 59(5)]: (a) invoice-wise inter-State & intra-State supplies to registered persons; (b) debit/credit notes issued during the month for such invoices.

Restrictions on Furnishing GSTR-1 or IFF [Rule 59(6)]

Notwithstanding anything else in Rule 59, a registered person shall NOT be allowed to furnish GSTR-1/IFF where:

  1. GSTR-3B has not been furnished for the preceding month (for a monthly filer);
  2. GSTR-3B has not been furnished for the preceding tax period (for a quarterly filer under the proviso to Sec. 39(1));
  3. an intimation under Rule 88C (liability mismatch between GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B) is pending and neither the amount has been deposited nor a reply explaining the unpaid amount has been furnished;
  4. an intimation under Rule 88D (excess ITC availed vs. GSTR-2B) is pending and neither the excess amount has been paid nor a reply has been furnished;
  5. bank account details have not been furnished per Rule 10A.

Separately, Rule 67A allows a registered person required to furnish a Nil GSTR-3B, a Nil GSTR-1, or a Nil CMP-08 statement to do so via SMS using their registered mobile number, verified by an OTP.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: THE GSTR-1 BLOCKING CHAIN

THE TRAP: students assume GSTR-1 can be filed on schedule as long as its OWN data is ready, treating it as an isolated monthly task.

THE TWIST: GSTR-1/IFF filing is gated on FIVE separate conditions being clear — all previous GSTR-1s filed, the PRECEDING month's GSTR-3B filed, no unresolved Rule 88C liability-mismatch intimation, no unresolved Rule 88D excess-ITC intimation, and bank details furnished under Rule 10A. Any one unresolved item blocks the CURRENT GSTR-1, even if that period's own outward-supply data is complete and correct.

D. Communication of ITC — GSTR-2B and the Invoice Management System (IMS) [Sec. 38]

Details furnished by suppliers u/s 37(1), along with an auto-generated statement of input tax credit, are made available electronically to the recipient. The auto-generated statement covers: (a) inward supplies where ITC may be available; and (b) supplies where credit cannot be availed (wholly or partly) — e.g. where the supplier is newly registered, has defaulted in paying tax for a prescribed period, has output tax payable exceeding output tax paid by a prescribed limit, has availed ITC exceeding the permissible credit by a prescribed limit, or has defaulted under Sec. 49(12).

Generation of the auto-drafted statement (Form GSTR-2B) is now inextricably linked to the Invoice Management System (IMS) on the GST Portal: recipients may mark supplier-furnished invoices (from GSTR-1/IFF/GSTR-1A) as 'Accept', 'Reject' or 'Pending'. Only 'Accepted' invoices (or those deemed accepted where no action is taken) populate GSTR-2B as eligible ITC; 'Rejected' invoices never form part of eligible ITC; 'Pending' invoices roll forward to the next tax period.

E. Furnishing of Returns — GSTR-3B [Sec. 39, Rule 61]

Every registered person must, for every calendar month (or part thereof), electronically furnish a return of inward/outward supplies, ITC availed, tax payable and tax paid — even a Nil return is mandatory.

  • Exceptions — Sec. 39(1) does NOT apply to: (a) an Input Service Distributor (files GSTR-6); (b) a non-resident taxable person (files GSTR-5); (c) a person paying tax u/s 10/composition (files GSTR-4), s. 51/TDS (files GSTR-7), or s. 52/TCS (files GSTR-8).
  • Maximum time limit: a return for a tax period cannot be furnished after the expiry of 3 years from its due date (subject to Government-notified extension).
Due Dates for Form GSTR-3B [Rule 61]
Filing FrequencyDue Date
Monthly (non-QRMP)20th day of the month succeeding such month
Quarterly (QRMP) — Category 1 States*22nd day of the month succeeding such quarter
Quarterly (QRMP) — Category 2 States*24th day of the month succeeding such quarter

* Category 1 and Category 2 are the two notified groups of States/UTs used consistently for GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B QRMP due dates.

Discharge of liability before filing return [Rule 61(2)]: a registered person discharges tax, interest, penalty, fee or any other amount payable by debiting the Electronic Cash Ledger or Electronic Credit Ledger, and includes the details in GSTR-3B.

Monthly Payment for Quarterly Filers [Rule 61(3)/(4)]

A registered person filing GSTR-3B quarterly must pay the tax due for each of the first 2 months of the quarter by depositing the amount in Form GST PMT-06, by the 25th day of the succeeding month (the Commissioner may extend this by notification). While depositing:

  1. for the 1st month of the quarter, the balance in the Electronic Cash Ledger may be taken into account;
  2. for the 2nd month, the balance may be taken into account excluding the tax due for the 1st month.

The amounts deposited in months 1 and 2 are debited only when the quarter's GSTR-3B is filed; any refund of a balance out of such deposits is permitted only after that quarterly GSTR-3B has been filed.

F. Returns by Composition Taxpayer, ISD, and Non-Resident Taxpayer

  • Composition taxpayer [Sec. 39(2), Rule 62]: furnishes a quarterly statement of self-assessed tax in Form CMP-08, by the 18th day of the month succeeding the quarter, discharging liability by debiting the Electronic Cash Ledger; and a return for each financial year in Form GSTR-4, by 30th June following the end of that year. The GSTR-4 return covers invoice-wise inter-State & intra-State inward supplies (registered and unregistered), plus consolidated outward-supply details.
  • Input Service Distributor [Sec. 39(4)]: furnishes a monthly return in Form GSTR-6, within 13 days after the end of the month.
  • Non-resident taxable person [Sec. 39(5)]: furnishes a monthly return in Form GSTR-5, within 13 days after the end of the calendar month, or within 7 days after the last day of the registration period u/s 27(1) — whichever is earlier. The Commissioner may extend this time limit by notification.

G. Rectification, Restriction, First Return, ITC Availment, Final Return

  • Rectification of mistake [Sec. 39(9)]: a registered person who discovers an omission or incorrect particular in a filed return (other than from scrutiny/audit/inspection/enforcement) rectifies it in the return for the month/quarter of discovery, subject to payment of interest. No rectification is allowed after 30th November following the end of the relevant financial year, or the actual date of filing the annual return — whichever is earlier.
  • Restriction on filing [Sec. 39(10)]: a return for a tax period cannot be furnished if the return for any earlier tax period, or the GSTR-1 details for the same tax period u/s 37(1), remains unfurnished (the Government may relax this by notification).
  • First return [Sec. 40]: a registered person who made outward supplies between the date they became liable to register and the date registration was actually granted must declare those supplies in the first return furnished after registration.
  • Availment of ITC [Sec. 41]: a registered person is entitled to avail eligible input tax, as self-assessed, in their return — credited to the Electronic Credit Ledger. Where the supplier has not paid the tax payable on such supplies, the credit availed must be reversed by the recipient along with applicable interest; if the supplier subsequently pays that tax, the recipient may re-avail the reversed credit.
  • Final return [Sec. 45]: a registered person required to file returns u/s 39(1) whose registration has been cancelled must furnish a final return in Form GSTR-10, within 3 months of the date of cancellation or the date of the cancellation order — whichever is later.

H. Quarterly Return, Monthly Payment of Taxes (QRMP) Scheme

QRMP simplifies compliance for small taxpayers: those with aggregate PAN-level turnover up to ₹5 crore in the preceding financial year may opt for quarterly GSTR-1 filing (with IFF available for the first two months, by the 13th of the next month) and quarterly GSTR-3B filing, paying tax for the first two months via a simple PMT-06 challan. The system automatically assigns quarterly frequency to eligible small taxpayers.

  • If aggregate turnover exceeds ₹5 crore during any quarter of the current financial year, the registered person becomes ineligible for the Scheme from the next quarter.
  • The option is exercised GSTIN-wise — some GSTINs under one PAN may be eligible while others are not.
  • New registration: if registration is granted during the first month of a quarter, QRMP is available from the start; if granted during either of the latter two months, QRMP becomes available only from the next quarter.
  • Other registered persons can opt in for a quarter any time from the 1st day of the second month of the preceding quarter to the last day of the first month of that quarter. Once exercised, the option continues for future periods without needing to be repeated each quarter.
  • Under IFF, up to ₹50 lakh of invoices can be uploaded in each of the first two months of the quarter, from the 1st till the 13th of the succeeding month; uploaded details flow through to the recipient's GSTR-2A and GSTR-2B.
  • Quarterly GSTR-3B is due by the 22nd/24th of the month succeeding the quarter (Category 1/Category 2 States) or such notified date; excess payment may be claimed as refund after filing that quarter's GSTR-3B, or carried forward.
MethodHow the Monthly Payment (Months 1 & 2) Is Fixed
Fixed Sum MethodPortal generates a pre-filled challan in Form GST PMT-06 — commonly known as the "35% challan".
Self-Assessment MethodActual tax due is paid through PMT-06, computed by considering the tax liability on inward and outward supplies and the ITC available for the period, as per law.
Both routes deposit into the same PMT-06 challan; the amount so deposited in months 1&2 is debited only when the quarter's own GSTR-3B is filed.

ILLUSTRATION 131 — Correcting a Missed Invoice Before GSTR-3B Is Filed

Mr. Sharma, a registered dealer, furnishes GSTR-1 for October 2025 on 11th November. On 15th November he realises he omitted a high-value B2B invoice of ₹5 lakh issued to M/s. Alpha Ltd. He has not yet filed GSTR-3B for October. Can he add the invoice now, or must he wait for the November GSTR-1?

Analysis: under the proviso to Rule 59(1), a registered person may amend or furnish additional details in Form GSTR-1A after furnishing GSTR-1 but before filing GSTR-3B for the same tax period.

Answer: Mr. Sharma need not wait for the next month — he can voluntarily file Form GSTR-1A to add the missed invoice. This lets M/s. Alpha Ltd. see the credit in its GSTR-2B immediately, with the liability correctly auto-populated into Mr. Sharma's GSTR-3B before he pays tax.

ILLUSTRATION 132 — GSTR-1 Blocked by an Unfiled Preceding GSTR-3B

XYZ Pvt. Ltd. filed its GSTR-1 for November 2025 on time but, due to a cash-flow crunch, has not filed GSTR-3B for November 2025. On 11th January 2026 it attempts to file GSTR-1 for December 2025. Will the portal allow this?

Analysis: per Sec. 37(4) and Rule 59(6), a registered person is not allowed to furnish GSTR-1 for a tax period if GSTR-3B for the preceding month has not been furnished.

Answer: Filing of GSTR-1 for December is blocked. XYZ Pvt. Ltd. must first file the pending November GSTR-3B (and pay the tax/interest) to "unlock" the facility to file the December GSTR-1.

ILLUSTRATION 133 — Rectification Deadline Missed

During a December 2026 year-end audit, Beta Enterprises' accountant notices an invoice for F.Y. 2025-26 was entered with the wrong GSTIN. Can this be rectified in the December 2026 GSTR-1?

Analysis: per Sec. 37(3), no rectification of errors for a financial year is allowed after 30th November following the end of that financial year, or the actual date of filing the Annual Return, whichever is earlier. Since the F.Y. 2025-26 Annual Return had not been furnished earlier, the deadline was 30th November 2026.

Answer: The rectification is time-barred — the 30th November 2026 deadline has passed, so the GSTIN cannot be corrected in GSTR-1.

ILLUSTRATION 134 — Ignoring a Rule 88C Liability-Mismatch Intimation

M/s. Gamma Tech's GSTR-1 showed a tax liability of ₹10 lakh but its GSTR-3B declared only ₹2 lakh, without valid reason. It received a Rule 88C intimation on the portal but ignored it. Ten days later it tries to file GSTR-1 for the next month. What is the consequence?

Analysis: under Rule 59(6)(c), if a Rule 88C intimation (liability mismatch) is issued and the person fails to either deposit the difference or furnish a satisfactory reply within 7 days, GSTR-1 for the subsequent period is blocked.

Answer: M/s. Gamma Tech cannot file the next GSTR-1. It must first resolve the Rule 88C intimation — either by paying the differential ₹8 lakh (with interest) or by filing a reply explaining the difference.

ILLUSTRATION 135 — Ignoring a Rule 88D Excess-ITC Intimation

M/s. Delta Traders availed ITC of ₹10,00,000 in its December 2025 GSTR-3B, but GSTR-2B for that period showed only ₹2,00,000 available. On 25th January 2026 it received a Rule 88D intimation for the excess ₹8,00,000, believed it to be a system error, and neither responded nor paid. On 11th February 2026 it attempts to file GSTR-1 for January 2026. Will the portal allow this?

Analysis: Rule 88D triggers when ITC availed in GSTR-3B exceeds ITC available in GSTR-2B by a prescribed limit. Rule 59(6)(d) blocks GSTR-1/IFF for a subsequent tax period unless the excess ITC has been paid, or a reply explaining the reasons has been furnished.

Answer: Filing of GSTR-1 for January 2026 is blocked. M/s. Delta Traders must respond to the Rule 88D intimation — either pay the differential amount, or file a satisfactory explanation on the portal — to restore its filing rights.

I. Payment of Tax — Who Pays, and When Liability Arises ★★★ HIGH

For an intra-State supply, the taxes payable are Central GST (CGST, to the Central Government) and State/UT GST (SGST, to the concerned State Government). For an inter-State supply, the tax payable is Integrated GST (IGST), which carries components of both CGST and SGST. Additionally, specified registered persons must pay TDS/TCS to the Government, and Interest, Penalty, Fees and other amounts may also fall due.

Persons liable to pay GST:

  • The supplier of goods or services is ordinarily liable to pay GST.
  • In specified cases (imports and other notified supplies) liability shifts to the recipient under the reverse charge mechanism.
  • In notified intra-State supplies of services, liability may be cast on e-commerce operators through whom the services are supplied.
  • Government Departments paying vendors above ₹2.5 lakh under one contract [Sec. 51(1)(d)] must deduct tax (TDS).
  • E-commerce operators must collect tax (TCS) on the net value (aggregate taxable supplies made through them, excluding value on which the operator itself is liable u/s 9(5)) and deposit it with the Government.

When does liability arise? At the time of supply of goods (Sec. 12) or services (Sec. 13) — generally the earliest of receiving payment, issuance of invoice, or completion of supply.

J. Electronic Ledgers and the Electronic Liability Register

On the common portal (gst.gov.in), every registered taxpayer maintains ONE electronic register — the Electronic Liability Register — and TWO electronic ledgers — the Electronic Cash Ledger and the Electronic Credit Ledger. Together these show the taxpayer's liabilities and the cash/credit balance available to settle them, viewable at any time by logging into the common portal. Any discrepancy in any of the three must be communicated to the jurisdictional officer, through the common portal, in Form GST PMT-04.

Each register/ledger carries separate sub-ledgers for: (a) CGST, (b) SGST, (c) UTGST, (d) IGST, and (e) Cess.

K. Electronic Cash Ledger [Sec. 49(1)]

Every deposit made on account of tax, interest, penalty, fee or any other amount — via internet banking, UPI, IMPS, credit/debit card, NEFT/RTGS, or another prescribed mode — is credited to the Electronic Cash Ledger, maintained in Form GST PMT-05 for each registered person. An unregistered person can pay on the basis of a temporary identification number generated through the common portal.

  • A challan is generated in Form GST PMT-06, valid for 15 days. There is a single challan prescribed for all tax, fee, penalty, interest and other payments — a manual challan is not allowed.
  • Deposit modes: (a) Internet Banking through authorised banks; (b) Credit/Debit card through the authorised bank; (c) NEFT or RTGS from any bank; (d) Over-the-Counter (cash, cheque, or demand draft) through authorised banks, capped at ₹10,000 per challan per tax period.
  • Where payment is via NEFT/RTGS, a mandate form is generated alongside the challan and is also valid for 15 days from the date the challan was generated.
  • On successful credit to the Government account, the collecting bank generates a Challan Identification Number (CIN), shown on the challan; on the portal receiving the CIN, the amount is credited to the Electronic Cash Ledger and a receipt is made available.
  • If the bank account was debited but the CIN was not generated (or not communicated to the portal), the person represents electronically in Form GST PMT-07 to the bank/gateway through which the deposit was initiated.
  • Amounts deducted u/s 51 (TDS) or collected u/s 52 (TCS) are credited to the Electronic Cash Ledger of the person from whom they were deducted/collected.
  • Refund of a balance in the Electronic Cash Ledger can be claimed under Sec. 54, but only after all return-related liabilities for that tax period have been discharged.

L. Electronic Credit Ledger [Sec. 49(2)]

The Electronic Credit Ledger is maintained in Form GST PMT-02 for each registered person. Input tax credit, as self-assessed in the return per Sec. 41, is credited here — the only way this ledger can be credited is through filing of returns; no direct entries are ever allowed except as specifically provided. The balance may be used only for payment of output tax (never interest, penalty or fee) under CGST/SGST/UTGST/IGST.

  • Where a refund of unutilised credit is claimed under Sec. 54, the claimed amount is debited from this ledger; if the refund is rejected (wholly or partly), the rejected amount is re-credited by the proper officer in Form GST PMT-03.
  • Discrepancies are communicated to the jurisdictional officer in Form GST PMT-04, same as for the other ledgers.
  • With the IMS linkage, ITC credited to this ledger is now subject to the recipient's action on IMS — only invoices marked 'Accepted' (or deemed accepted) are available for utilisation towards payment of output tax.

Order of Utilisation of Input Tax Credit [Sec. 49(5) r.w.r. Rule 88A]

ITC Available OnUtilisation Order
IGSTFirst fully towards payment of IGST; then the remaining balance, if any, towards CGST/SGST/UTGST — in any order and any proportion.
CGSTFirst towards payment of CGST; then the remaining balance, if any, towards IGST — but only after ITC on account of IGST is fully exhausted. ITC of CGST shall NEVER be utilised towards SGST/UTGST.
SGST / UTGSTFirst towards payment of SGST/UTGST; then the remaining balance, if any, towards IGST — but only where the balance of CGST credit is not available for payment of IGST. ITC of SGST/UTGST shall NEVER be utilised towards CGST.

Sec. 49A: ITC on account of CGST, SGST or UTGST can be utilised towards payment of IGST, CGST, SGST or UTGST only after the ITC available on account of IGST has first been utilised fully towards such payment. ITC on account of CGST must be exhausted towards IGST before ITC on account of SGST is used towards IGST.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: CROSS-HEAD ITC UTILISATION

THE TRAP: students assume that if CGST liability is fully paid and CGST credit is still left over, that surplus can be used to pay an SGST shortfall (or vice versa).

THE TWIST: CGST credit can NEVER be utilised against SGST/UTGST liability, and SGST/UTGST credit can NEVER be utilised against CGST liability — there is no direct CGST↔SGST route. The only cross-head route for either is via IGST, and IGST credit must be fully exhausted first before any CGST or SGST/UTGST credit can even be applied towards IGST liability.

M. Other Provisions of Sec. 49 — Discharge Order, Liability Register, Transfer, Restriction

  • Order of discharge [Sec. 49(8)]: (a) self-assessed tax and other dues of previous tax periods; (b) self-assessed tax and other dues of the current tax period; (c) any other amount payable, including demands determined u/s 73, 74 or 74A.
  • Recording of liability [Sec. 49(7)]: all liabilities are recorded in the Electronic Liability Register, maintained in Form GST PMT-01 for each liable person, with all payable amounts debited to it.
  • Deemed pass-on [Sec. 49(9)]: a person who has paid tax on goods/services is, unless the contrary is proved by them, deemed to have passed on the full incidence of that tax to the recipient.
  • Inter-Act transfer [Sec. 49(10)]: a registered person may transfer any amount (tax, interest, penalty, fee, or other amount) available in the Electronic Cash Ledger under the CGST Act to the Electronic Cash Ledger for IGST/CGST/SGST/UTGST/Cess, or to a "distinct person" u/s 25(4)/(5) — using Form GST PMT-09. Such transfer is deemed a refund from the CGST cash ledger. No transfer to a distinct person is permitted if the transferor has any unpaid liability in their own Electronic Liability Register. A transferred amount is deemed deposited in the receiving ledger – Sec. 49(11).
  • Usage cap [Sec. 49(12)]: the Government may, on Council recommendation, specify the maximum proportion of output tax liability that may be discharged through the Electronic Credit Ledger by any registered person or class of persons.

Restriction on Use of Electronic Credit Ledger [Rule 86B]

A registered person cannot use the Electronic Credit Ledger to discharge more than 99% of output tax liability, where the value of taxable supply (other than exempt and zero-rated supply) in a month exceeds ₹50 lakh. This restriction does NOT apply where:

  • (a) the person, or their proprietor/karta/managing director/certain office-bearers, has paid more than ₹1 lakh as income tax in each of the last two financial years for which the Sec. 139(1) filing deadline has expired; or
  • (b) the person received a refund of more than ₹1 lakh in the preceding financial year on account of unutilised ITC under the first proviso to Sec. 54(3)(i); or
  • (c) the person received a refund of more than ₹1 lakh in the preceding financial year under the first proviso to Sec. 54(3)(ii); or
  • (d) the person has discharged output tax liability through the Electronic Cash Ledger for an amount exceeding 1% of total output tax liability, applied cumulatively up to that month in the current financial year; or
  • (e) the person is a Government Department, Public Sector Undertaking, local authority, or statutory body.

The Commissioner (or an authorised officer) may remove the restriction after such verification and safeguards as deemed fit.

N. Interest on Delayed Payment of Tax [Sec. 50]

Interest on unpaid tax: rate not exceeding 18% (present rate), as notified by the Government on Council recommendation, for the period the tax (or any part) remains unpaid.

Calculated in the prescribed manner, running from the day succeeding the day the tax was due to be paid.

Interest on wrongly availed AND utilised ITC: rate not exceeding 24%, as notified by the Government on Council recommendation.

  • Cash-ledger-only rule: interest is generally payable ONLY on the portion of tax paid by debiting the Electronic Cash Ledger (i.e. the Net Tax Liability) — NOT on the portion of tax discharged by utilising ITC. This relaxation is, however, NOT available in proceedings under Sec. 73 or Sec. 74A.
  • Wrongly availed AND utilised ITC: a registered person must pay interest (up to 24%) on such ITC, calculated in the prescribed manner — this is distinct from the ordinary 18% interest on unpaid tax.
  • CBIC clarification (Rule 88B): for calculating interest on wrongly-availed-and-reversed IGST credit, the combined balance of ITC under IGST, CGST and SGST heads taken together — not any single head — decides whether the credit was "utilised." If that combined balance never fell below the wrongly availed amount between availment and reversal, no interest arises under Sec. 50(3), even if the IGST head's own balance individually fell below that amount. Interest arises only to the extent, and for the period, that the combined balance actually falls below the wrongly-availed amount.
  • Compensation Cess excluded: per the proviso to Sec. 11 of the GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017, Cess credit can be utilised only against Cess liability. It is therefore excluded when computing the combined credit-ledger balance for Rule 88B(3) interest purposes on wrongly availed/utilised IGST, CGST or SGST credit.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: INTEREST ON GROSS TAX LIABILITY, NOT NET

THE TRAP: on a delayed return, students calculate interest at 18% on the FULL/gross tax liability shown in the return, including the part that was already covered by available ITC.

THE TWIST: under the proviso to Sec. 50(1), interest applies only to the portion of tax actually paid by debiting the Electronic Cash Ledger (the Net Tax Liability) — the ITC-covered portion draws NO interest under this general rule. The one place this relief disappears is in proceedings under Sec. 73 or Sec. 74A, where interest on the gross liability is not relaxed.

ILLUSTRATION 136 — Interest Computed Only on the Cash-Ledger Portion

M/s. ABC Ltd. filed its GSTR-3B for November 2025 on 15th January 2026 (due date was 20th December 2025 — a delay of 26 days). Total tax liability: ₹10,00,000. ITC available & utilised: ₹8,00,000. Balance paid through the Electronic Cash Ledger: ₹2,00,000. On what amount is interest payable?

Analysis: per the proviso to Sec. 50(1), interest is payable only on the portion of tax paid by debiting the Electronic Cash Ledger (Net Tax Liability), where the return is filed after the due date. No interest is payable on the portion discharged via ITC.

Interest is calculated only on the cash component (₹2,00,000): ₹2,00,000 × 18% × 26/365 = ₹2,564.

Answer: Interest payable = ₹2,564, on the ₹2,00,000 cash-ledger portion only. No interest is payable on the ₹8,00,000 paid via ITC.

ILLUSTRATION 137 — Wrongly Availed IGST Credit, Combined-Balance Test

M/s. Zenith Ltd. wrongly availed IGST credit of ₹1,00,000 in January 2025 and reversed it in June 2025. During the January–June period, the balance in its Electronic Credit Ledger (IGST + CGST + SGST combined) never fell below ₹5,00,000. Is it liable to pay interest on the wrong availment?

Analysis: interest u/s 50(3) applies only when ITC is wrongly availed AND utilised. Per the CBIC clarification, if the combined balance across IGST, CGST and SGST never falls below the wrongly availed amount, the wrong ITC was never "utilised."

Answer: Since the combined balance (₹5 lakh) always exceeded the wrongly availed amount (₹1 lakh), no utilisation occurred and no interest is triggered — interest under Rule 88B(3) applies only to the extent, and period, the combined balance falls below the wrongly availed amount.

ILLUSTRATION 138 — Cash Ledger Transfer Between Distinct Persons (PMT-09)

"Global Traders" has two GST registrations (distinct persons under one PAN) — Maharashtra and Gujarat. The Maharashtra branch has an excess balance of ₹50,000 in its Electronic Cash Ledger (CGST head). The Gujarat branch has a pending liability of ₹40,000 (IGST head) and no cash balance. Can the Maharashtra branch help the Gujarat branch pay its dues without claiming a refund?

Analysis: u/s 49(10), a registered person may transfer any amount available in the Electronic Cash Ledger to the Electronic Cash Ledger of a distinct person (same PAN, different GSTIN), using Form GST PMT-09 — provided the transferor has no unpaid liability in its own Electronic Liability Register.

Answer: Yes. The Maharashtra branch can file Form GST PMT-09 to transfer ₹40,000 from its CGST Cash Ledger to the IGST Cash Ledger of the Gujarat branch; this is deemed a deposit in the Gujarat branch's ledger, provided Maharashtra has no unpaid liability of its own.
