22 EXAM FACTS — GOODS AND SERVICES TAX (GST) LAWS (Module 5)

① GST is a destination-based, multi-stage, dual-structure tax — CGST + SGST/UTGST apply concurrently on intra-State supply, IGST applies on inter-State supply and imports, all administered through one common portal.

② GST is levied as a value-added tax at each stage of the supply chain — tax paid at the previous stage is available as credit at the next, so only the value addition at each stage is ultimately taxed.

③ The charge of GST is anchored in the definition of "supply" under Sec. 7 of the CGST Act, tested by scope, consideration, and the course or furtherance of business.

④ Reverse Charge Mechanism shifts the liability to pay GST from the supplier to the recipient in specified/notified cases — the recipient then discharges the tax directly, generally via the Electronic Cash Ledger.

⑤ Time of Supply fixes WHEN tax becomes payable — generally the earliest of receipt of payment, issue of invoice, or completion of supply, per Sec. 12 (goods) and Sec. 13 (services).

⑥ Place of Supply decides WHETHER a transaction is intra-State (CGST + SGST/UTGST) or inter-State (IGST) — it does not by itself decide the rate or the taxability of the supply.

⑦ Value of Supply u/s 15 is ordinarily the transaction value, provided price is the sole consideration and the supplier and recipient are not related persons.

⑧ ITC is blocked for the specific categories listed under Sec. 17(5), regardless of otherwise-eligible use.

⑨ ITC eligibility under Sec. 16 requires the recipient to hold a valid tax invoice/debit note, have received the goods/services, have the supplier's tax actually paid to Government, and have furnished their own return — all conditions apply together, not in the alternative.

⑩ GST liability is computed supply-wise and head-wise (CGST/SGST/UTGST/IGST/Cess) before being set off, first against the Electronic Credit Ledger and then the Electronic Cash Ledger.

⑪ Net GST payable in cash for a tax period equals the gross output tax liability for that period, less eligible Input Tax Credit available for set-off, computed per head.

⑫ GST registration is PAN-based and State/UT-wise — operating from multiple States requires a separate GSTIN (and hence a separate set of electronic ledgers) for each State.

⑬ Once granted, a GSTIN carries ongoing compliance obligations — return filing, invoicing, and record-keeping — that continue until the registration is validly cancelled or surrendered.

⑭ The tax invoice is the foundational document for claiming ITC — no valid tax invoice or debit note, no ITC — and its time of issue is tied directly to the time-of-supply rules.

⑮ An E-Way Bill accompanies the movement of goods above the prescribed consignment-value threshold and must be generated before commencement of movement.

⑯ GSTR-1 is due on the 11th of the next month (non-QRMP) or by the 13th of the month following the quarter (QRMP); GSTR-3B is due on the 20th of the next month for monthly filers, or by the 22nd/24th of the month following the quarter (Category 1/Category 2 States) for QRMP filers.

⑰ GSTR-1/IFF is blocked if the previous period's GSTR-1, or the preceding month's GSTR-3B, has not been filed, or if a Rule 88C/88D intimation remains unresolved [Sec. 37(4), Rule 59(6)].

⑱ Rectification of any error/omission in GSTR-1 or GSTR-3B is barred after 30th November following the end of the financial year, or the date of filing the annual return, whichever is earlier.

⑲ Every registered taxpayer maintains ONE Electronic Liability Register (PMT-01) and TWO ledgers — Electronic Cash Ledger (PMT-05, funded by deposit) and Electronic Credit Ledger (PMT-02, credited ONLY through self-assessed ITC in a filed return, never by direct entry).

⑳ Order of ITC utilisation: IGST credit must fully exhaust IGST liability first, then the balance is usable against CGST/SGST/UTGST in any order/proportion; CGST credit and SGST/UTGST credit can never be cross-utilised against each other directly.

㉑ Interest under Sec. 50 is capped at 18% and — except in proceedings u/s 73/74A — is charged only on the portion of tax paid by debiting the Electronic Cash Ledger (Net Tax Liability), never on the ITC-covered portion; interest on wrongly availed AND utilised ITC runs up to 24%.

㉒ GSTR-10 (Final Return) is due within 3 months of the date of cancellation of registration or the date of the cancellation order, whichever is later; the maximum time limit to furnish GSTR-1/GSTR-3B for any tax period is 3 years from its due date.

MODULE 5 CLOSING DRILL (retrieval practice — do not skip, ~10–12 minutes — this is the largest module in the paper): put this document down and, on rough paper, write from memory: (1) the dual-GST structure and exactly when CGST+SGST applies versus IGST; (2) the Sec. 7 tests for "supply" and when the reverse charge mechanism shifts the liability to the recipient; (3) the three earliest-of events that fix time of supply, and how place of supply serves a different purpose from time of supply; (4) the four cumulative conditions for ITC under Sec. 16, and the Sec. 17(5) blocked-credit categories; (5) the sequence — gross output tax, less eligible ITC head-wise, balance through the cash ledger — used to compute net GST payable; (6) why GST registration is State-wise even under a single PAN; (7) the tax-invoice time-of-issue rules for goods versus services, and when an E-Way Bill becomes mandatory; (8) the GSTR-1/GSTR-3B due-date grid for monthly versus QRMP filers, and the five conditions that can block GSTR-1/IFF; (9) the IGST→CGST→SGST/UTGST utilisation order for ITC, and exactly which portion of unpaid tax draws interest u/s 50. Check against the notes only after finishing — answering from memory is what converts today's reading into exam-day marks. Anything you could not retrieve, star it and re-attempt tomorrow morning.

MODULE 6 OF 6 · SECTION B · WEIGHT 10% · ≈10 MARKS · THE FINAL MODULE

Customs Act
& Rules

Customs, as a major source of revenue, plays a very important role in the economy of our country — Entry No. 83 of List I to Schedule VII of the Constitution empowers the Union Government to legislate and collect duties on imports and exports, and the Customs Act, 1962, effective from 1-2-1963, provides vide its section 12 for the levy of duties on goods imported into or exported from India. This module carries you from the basic concepts and Sec. 2 definitions, through the several types of customs duty, the Sec. 14 valuation scheme and the Valuation Rules, 2007, to the actual computation of assessable value and duty liability.

MUST NOT SKIP: the assessable-value and duty ladder. Build FOB → add freight (actual; if unascertained 20% of FOB; by AIR always capped at 20% of FOB) → add insurance (actual; if unascertained 1.125% of FOB) = CIF = Assessable Value [A]. Then Basic Customs Duty [B = rate × A] → Social Welfare Surcharge [C = 10% of B] → Value for IGST [D = A + B + C] → IGST [E = 18% × D] → Compensation Cess [F = rate × D]. Total duty payable = B + C + E + F. Every computation illustration in 6.4 is this one ladder wearing a different hat.

6.1–6.4

Module Learning Objectives

After studying this module, the students will be able to – appreciate the Constitutional power; understand the basic concepts of the Customs Act; appreciate the different types of duties; understand the provision relating to determination of assessable value; and apply the knowledge in computing duty liability. The module is mapped against two SLOBs: acquiring knowledge of the legal provisions enshrined in laws related to GST and Customs Duty and appreciating their applicability in business operations, and gathering an understanding of the legal provisions of these two indirect tax laws about matters of compliance while conducting business operations.

Where the law lives. The Customs Act, 1962 contains the provisions governing the import and export duty imposed on imports and exports of goods. The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 contains the rate of customs duty levied on imports or exports of goods. Beneath them sit the Rules and Regulations — among them the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007; the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007; the Baggage Rules, 2016; and the Re-export of Imported Goods (Drawback of Customs Duties) Rules, 1995.

Glossary — Module 6, in Plain Words

The technical terms used across 6.1–6.4, explained simply.

Customs DutyThe duty levied u/s 12 of the Customs Act, 1962 on goods imported into, or exported from, India — at the rate specified under the Customs Tariff Act, 1975. It is a tax on the GOODS, not on the person importing or exporting them.
First Schedule / Second ScheduleFirst Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act = goods chargeable to IMPORT duty (21 Sections, 98 Chapters, built on the HSN). Second Schedule = goods chargeable to EXPORT duty.
HSNHarmonized Commodity Description and Coding System (“Harmonized System of Nomenclature”), developed by the World Customs Organization and applied uniformly by more than 137 countries — the classification skeleton of the First Schedule.
Heading / Sub-heading / Tariff ItemEvery 4-digit code is a “heading”; every 6-digit code a “sub-heading”; every 8-digit code a “Tariff Item”. Read left to right: first 2 digits Chapter, next 2 Heading, next 2 Sub-heading, last 2 Tariff Item.
Ad valorem vs Specific dutyAd valorem = duty as a percentage of the assessable value (the predominant mode). Specific = duty based on a measure such as quintal or metre. Some goods carry specific-cum-ad valorem duty.
Standard rate / Preferential rateStandard rate (column 4 of the Schedule) applies generally and is the higher one. Preferential rate (column 5) is the concessional rate for imports from a notified preferential area — the importer must specifically claim it and satisfy the conditions, failing which the standard rate applies anyway.
Territorial WatersExtends 12 nautical miles into the sea from the baseline on the coast of India (1 nautical mile = 1.1515 miles = 1.852 km), including any bay, gulf, harbour, creek or tidal river — and covering the seabed, subsoil and airspace as well. India has full sovereignty here, so the whole Customs Act applies.
BaselineThe lower water mark along the coast — the line every maritime distance is measured from.
Exclusive Economic Zone of India (EEZI)The area beyond and adjacent to the territorial waters, extending to 200 nautical miles from the baseline.
Continental Shelf of India (CSI)The seabed and subsoil of the submarine areas extending beyond the territorial waters through the natural prolongation of India's land territory to the outer edge of the continental margin, or to 200 nautical miles from the baseline where that margin does not reach so far.
Indian Customs Waters [Sec. 2(28)]Water extending into the sea up to the limit of the Exclusive Economic Zone — i.e. 200 nautical miles — and including any bay, gulf, harbour, creek or tidal river. Wider than territorial waters; do not confuse the two.
Goods [Sec. 2(22)]Includes vessels, aircraft and vehicles; stores; baggage; currency and negotiable instruments; and any other kind of movable property.
Import / Imported goodsImport [Sec. 2(23)] = bringing into India from a place outside India. Imported goods [Sec. 2(25)] = goods brought into India from outside, but NOT including goods already cleared for home consumption.
Importer [Sec. 2(26)]In relation to goods, at any time between importation and clearance for home consumption, includes any owner or any person holding himself out to be the importer — so it catches the person who clears goods from a warehouse even though he is not the actual importer.
Export / Export goods / ExporterExport [Sec. 2(18)] = taking out of India to a place outside India. Export goods [Sec. 2(19)] = goods to be taken out of India to a place outside India. Exporter [Sec. 2(20)] = the owner, or any person holding himself out to be the exporter, between entry for export and actual export.
Dutiable goods [Sec. 2(14)]Goods chargeable to duty on which duty has NOT been paid. Once the duty is paid, the goods stop being “dutiable”.
Beneficial owner [Sec. 2(3A)]Any person on whose behalf the goods are being imported or exported, or who exercises effective control over them.
Assessment [Sec. 2(2)]Determination of the dutiability of goods and the amount of duty/tax/cess payable — with reference to classification, value, exemption, quantity, origin and any other factor — and it INCLUDES provisional assessment, self-assessment, re-assessment, and even an assessment where the duty assessed is nil.
Adjudicating authority [Sec. 2(1)]Any authority competent to pass an order or decision under the Act, but NOT the Board, the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Appellate Tribunal.
Bill of Entry [Sec. 2(4) r.w.s. 46]The document by which an importer (other than for transit/transhipment) makes entry of goods — presented electronically on the customs automated system, for home consumption or for warehousing.
Bill of Export / Shipping Bill [Sec. 2(5) r.w.s. 50]The exporter's entry document — a shipping bill for goods leaving by vessel or aircraft, a bill of export for goods leaving by land.
Board [Sec. 2(6)]The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC), constituted under the Central Boards of Revenue Act, 1963.
Conveyance [Sec. 2(9)]Includes a vessel (sea), an aircraft (air) and a vehicle (land). “Vehicle” means any conveyance used on land and includes a railway vehicle [Sec. 2(42)].
Person-in-charge [Sec. 2(31)]Vessel → the master; aircraft → the commander or pilot-in-charge; railway train → the conductor, guard or person having chief direction; any other conveyance → the driver or person-in-charge.
Customs Station / Port / Airport / AreaCustoms station [Sec. 2(13)] = any customs port, customs airport, international courier terminal, foreign post office or land customs station. Customs port [Sec. 2(12)] and customs airport [Sec. 2(10)] are places appointed u/s 7 (and include an inland container depot / air freight station). Customs area [Sec. 2(11)] = the area of a customs station or warehouse, plus any area where imported/export goods are ordinarily kept before clearance.
Coastal goods [Sec. 2(7)]Goods, OTHER than imported goods, transported in a vessel from one port in India to another.
Foreign-going vessel or aircraft [Sec. 2(21)]Any vessel/aircraft engaged in carrying goods or passengers between a port or airport in India and one outside India — whether or not it touches an intermediate Indian port — and includes a foreign naval vessel in naval exercises, a vessel fishing or operating outside territorial waters, and any vessel/aircraft proceeding abroad for any purpose.
Arrival manifest / import report [Sec. 2(24) r.w.s. 30]The document the person-in-charge must deliver to the proper officer. Vessel or aircraft → arrival/import manifest, electronically, BEFORE arrival (export: departure manifest before departure). Vehicle → import report WITHIN 12 HOURS after arrival at the customs station (export: before departure).
Prohibited goods [Sec. 2(33)]Goods whose import/export is prohibited under this or any other law — but NOT goods for which the permitting conditions have actually been complied with.
Stores [Sec. 2(38)]Goods for use in a vessel or aircraft, including fuel, spare parts and other equipment, whether or not for immediate fitting.
Transit [Sec. 53] / Transshipment [Sec. 54]Transit = goods stay on the SAME conveyance to a place outside India or to another customs station; the proper officer may allow it without payment of duty. Transshipment = goods are moved to a different conveyance; a bill of transshipment must be presented.
Clearance for home consumptionCustoms duty on the imported goods has been paid and the goods can be taken out by the importer for utilisation or consumption within the country.
WarehousingGoods stored in a bonded warehouse remain in customs bond; payment of duty is DEFERRED until clearance from the warehouse, and import is treated as taking place only when the goods are cleared for home consumption.
Pilferage [Sec. 13]Stealing something typically of small value or in small quantities — petty theft. Not total destruction and not complete loss.
Abatement [Sec. 22]Proportionate reduction of duty where imported goods are damaged or deteriorated in the specified circumstances.
Remission [Sec. 23(1)]Giving up the duty entirely where the goods have been lost (otherwise than by pilferage) or destroyed before clearance for home consumption.
Relinquishment of title [Sec. 23(2)]The owner abandoning his title to the imported goods — unconditionally, and before the order for clearance for home consumption or for deposit in a warehouse — whereupon he is not liable to pay duty.
Derelict / Wreck / Jetsam / Flotsam [Sec. 21]Derelict = property abandoned at sea without hope of recovery. Wreck = property cast ashore by tide after shipwreck. Jetsam = goods cast into the sea to lighten a ship and prevent it sinking. Flotsam = goods separated from the ship by some peril that continue to float.
Basic Customs Duty (BCD)The core duty levied u/s 12 of the Customs Act read with Sec. 2 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, at the tariff rate.
Social Welfare Surcharge (SWS)A surcharge @ 10% of total customs duties (3% for gold and silver, including that plated with platinum, unwrought or in semi-manufactured form or in powder form) on IMPORTED goods only — never on export.
IGST on imports [Sec. 3(7), Customs Tariff Act]Integrated tax charged in addition, at the rate leviable u/s 5 of the IGST Act, 2017 on a like article supplied in India — on a value of (Sec. 14 value + BCD + other customs-like sums), but excluding the IGST itself and the Compensation Cess. ITC of this IGST is available under GST law.
GST Compensation Cess [Sec. 3(9), Customs Tariff Act]Cess on luxury products such as high-end cars and demerit goods such as pan masala, tobacco and aerated drinks, to compensate States for revenue loss — originally for 5 years, now extended up to 31-03-2026. Same value base as IGST.
AIDCAgriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess — levied on the import of specified goods (apples, kabuli chana, urea, various coals, gold and silver) at notified rates, computed on the Sec. 14 value, and levied IN ADDITION to other customs duties.
Safeguard measures [Sec. 8B, Customs Tariff Act]Duty, tariff-rate quota or other measure applied where an article is imported in INCREASED QUANTITIES so as to cause or threaten serious injury to domestic industry. Product specific, and in addition to any other duty.
Tariff-rate quotaA safeguard measure fixing a quota; it cannot be set lower than the average level of imports in the last 3 representative years for which statistics are available, unless a different level is needed to prevent or remedy serious injury.
Countervailing Duty on subsidized articles [Sec. 9]Duty not exceeding the amount of the SUBSIDY paid or bestowed by the exporting country on manufacture, production, exportation or transportation of the article.
Dumping / Anti-Dumping Duty [Sec. 9A]Dumping = exporting to another country at a price LOWER than normal value — an unfair trade practice. Anti-dumping duty rectifies its trade-distortive effect and cannot exceed the margin of dumping.
Margin of dumpingNormal Value LESS Export Price. (Not the other way round — the direction is examined.)
Normal valueThe comparable price in the ordinary course of trade for the like article destined for consumption in the exporting country; failing which, the comparable representative export price to an appropriate third country, or the cost of production in the country of origin plus reasonable administrative, selling and general costs and profits.
Export priceThe price of the article exported from the exporting country; where there is none or it is unreliable because of association or a compensatory arrangement, it may be constructed from the first resale price to an independent buyer or on such other reasonable basis as the rules provide.
Landed valueIn the source's anti-dumping computation, Assessable Value + Basic Customs Duty + Social Welfare Surcharge — the figure the notified value is compared against to find the anti-dumping duty.
Transaction Value [Sec. 14(1)]The price actually paid or payable for the goods, when sold for export to India (or from India), for delivery at the time and place of importation (or exportation), where buyer and seller are not related and price is the sole consideration.
Tariff Value [Sec. 14(2)]A value CBIC may fix for a class of imported or export goods having regard to the trend of value of such or like goods; where fixed, duty is charged with reference to it. Presently fixed for crude palm oil, crude palmolein, crude soyabean oil, brass scrap, poppy seeds, etc.
FOBFree on Board — cost of production + manufacturer's profit + freight in the foreign country + local taxes + loading charges + export duty and cess. The starting block of the valuation ladder.
CIF / Assessable ValueCost, Insurance and Freight — FOB as per Customs plus freight plus insurance. This IS the assessable value on which BCD is charged.
Buying commissionFees paid by an importer to HIS OWN agent for the service of representing him abroad in the purchase of the goods being valued — specifically NOT added to value.
Lighterage / barging chargesCharges for bringing goods from outer anchorage to the jetty, where the ship cannot come up to the jetty (deep draught, busy port). These ARE added.
Demurrage chargesCharges payable to port trust authorities for delay in clearing goods — these are NOT added. (But ship demurrage on chartered vessels IS added.)
Related personsOfficers/directors of one another's businesses; legally recognised partners; employer and employee; anyone owning, controlling or holding 5% or more of the voting rights of both; one controlling the other; both controlled by a third; together controlling a third; members of the same family. A sole agent/distributor/concessionaire also counts if within these criteria.
Identical goods [Rule 4]Imported goods the SAME in all respects — physical characteristics, quality and reputation — barring minor appearance differences that do not affect value; produced in the same country; by the same producer or, if unavailable, a different one.
Similar goods [Rule 5]Imported goods not alike in all respects, but with like characteristics and like component materials letting them perform the same function and be commercially interchangeable, having regard to quality, reputation and trade mark.
Deductive Value [Rule 7]Working BACKWARDS from the Indian selling price: take the unit price at which the goods are sold in the GREATEST AGGREGATE QUANTITY to unrelated persons in India, then strip out Indian commission/profit and general expenses, Indian transport and insurance, and the customs duty and Indian taxes.
Greatest aggregate quantityThe price at which the greatest NUMBER of units is sold to unrelated persons at the first commercial level after importation — not the largest single sale, and not the average price.
Computed Value [Rule 8]Building the value FORWARDS: cost or value of materials and fabrication/processing + general expenses and profit of producers in the exporting country for export to India + Rule 10(2) transport and insurance.
Residual method [Rule 9]Value determined by reasonable means consistent with the principles and general provisions of the Rules, using data available in India — the last resort, with seven expressly forbidden bases.
Rate of exchangeThe rate determined by, or ascertained as directed by, CBIC. Import → rate in force on the date the bill of entry is presented u/s 46 (selling rate). Export → rate in force on the date the shipping bill is presented u/s 50 (buying rate). RBI's rate is irrelevant for customs.
Goods of like kind and qualityUnder the Export Goods Valuation Rules, 2007 — export goods identical or similar in physical characteristics, quality and reputation, performing the same functions or commercially interchangeable, produced by the same person OR a different person.

Module 6 Mind Map — read it now, redraw it from memory once you finish the module

Introduction — Where Customs Comes From

The term “customs” derives its colour and essence from the term “custom” — a habitual practice or course of action characteristically repeated in like circumstances. Collection of revenue through Customs has been known in India from time immemorial; laws for collection of revenue and punishment for their violation appear as early as Kautilya's Arthasasthra. The modern system, however, is a British legacy: in England, in the days of King John in the 13th century, the customary dues till then collected by local sheriffs and chieftains as protection money for police service rendered to foreign traders came to be collected as revenue of the State. Excise and Income Tax were conceived much later, in the 17th century.

In India, Customs in its modern form arrived soon after the consolidation of British rule. Trade was then mainly by sea, with England and other European countries, and the Sea Customs Act, 1878 was enacted for collection of revenue and control of the movement of goods. About 50 years later came the Land Customs Act, 1924 for goods arriving by land routes, and the Indian Aircraft Act, 1934 for export/import by air. Those laws had been designed with an eye to protecting British interests only, but independent India allowed them to continue in force until 1963, when the Customs Act, 1962, repealing all the earlier enactments, was passed.

CONCEPT

6.1 Customs Act — Basic Concepts and Definitions ★★★ HIGH

Entry No. 83 of List I to Schedule VII of the Constitution empowers the Union Government to legislate and collect duties on imports and exports. Accordingly the Customs Act, 1962, effective from 1-2-1963, provides vide its section 12 for the levy of duties on goods imported into or exported from India. The items and the rates of duties leviable are specified in two Schedules to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975.

  • First Schedule: the various import items in systematic and well-considered categories, in accordance with the international scheme of classification of internationally traded goods known as the “Harmonized System of Commodity Classification”, and the rates of import duties thereon as prescribed by the legislature.
  • Second Schedule: items subject to export duties and the rates thereof.
  • Duties on imported items are usually levied on a specific or ad-valorem basis; in a few cases specific-cum-ad valorem duties are also levied. Levy on the ad-valorem basis (with reference to value) is the predominant mode.
  • For ad-valorem levy the value of imported goods is determined per Sec. 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 read with the Customs Valuation (Determination of Prices of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007; these provisions are essentially the adoption of the GATT-based valuation system, now termed the WTO Valuation Agreement, that is followed internationally. For export goods, value is determined per Sec. 14 read with the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007.

Applicability: the Customs Act, 1962 extends to the whole of India. Save as otherwise provided in the Act, it applies also to any offence or contravention thereunder committed outside India by any person.

6.1.1 India, Territorial Waters, EEZ and Indian Customs Waters

  • India includes the territorial waters of India [Sec. 2(27)].
  • As per sec. 3 of the Territorial Water, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zone Act, 1976, territorial water extends to 12 nautical miles (1 nautical mile = 1.1515 miles = 1.852 km) into the sea from the baseline on the coast of India, and includes any bay, gulf, harbour, creek or tidal river. India includes not only the surface of the sea but also the seabed and subsoil underlying it and the air space over such waters.
  • India has sovereignty in its territorial waters — all provisions of the Customs Act and the rules and regulations apply in Indian territorial waters.
  • Baseline: the lower water mark along the coast.
  • Exclusive Economic Zone of India (EEZI): an area beyond and adjacent to the territorial waters, the limit of such zone being 200 nautical miles from the baseline.
  • Continental Shelf of India (CSI): the seabed and subsoil of the submarine areas that extend beyond the limit of the territorial waters throughout the natural prolongation of India's land territory to the outer edge of the continental margin, or to a distance of 200 nautical miles from the baseline where the outer edge of the continental margin does not extend up to that distance.

Extension of the Customs Act, 1962 and the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 to EEZ and Continental Shelf. The Acts have been extended to (i) the notified designated areas in the CSI and EEZI; and (ii) the whole of the EEZ and Continental Shelf of India for the purposes of (a) the prospecting for extraction or production of mineral oils (including petroleum and natural gas) in the CSI and EEZI, and (b) the supply of any goods in connection with any of those activities.

Taxpoint — implication: bringing any goods from any other country to any place in the EEZ or Continental Shelf of India in connection with any activity related to extraction or production of mineral oils shall be treated as import under the Customs Act, 1962 and charged to duty accordingly. Further, mineral oils produced in the EEZ or CSI would be deemed to be produced in India and subject to levy of central excise duties under the Central Excise Act, 1944.

Indian Customs Waters [Sec. 2(28)] means the water extending into the sea upto the limit of the Exclusive Economic Zone u/s 7 of the Territorial Water, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zone Act, 1976, and includes any bay, gulf, harbour, creek or tidal river.

Maritime zoneDistance from baselineWhat India has there
Territorial Waters12 nautical milesFull sovereignty — the entire Customs Act and its rules and regulations apply. Included within the meaning of “India” [Sec. 2(27)]. Covers seabed, subsoil and airspace.
Indian Customs Waters [Sec. 2(28)]200 nautical miles (up to the limit of the EEZ)Customs jurisdiction extends this far, plus any bay, gulf, harbour, creek or tidal river.
Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ)200 nautical milesSovereign rights for exploration, exploitation, conservation and management of natural resources (living and non-living) and for producing energy from tides, winds and currents; exclusive rights and jurisdiction for construction/maintenance/operation of artificial islands, off-shore terminals, installations and other structures; exclusive jurisdiction to authorise, regulate and control scientific research; exclusive jurisdiction to preserve and protect the marine environment and prevent and control marine pollution; and such other rights as are recognised by International Law.
Continental Shelf of IndiaTo the outer edge of the continental margin, or 200 nautical miles where the margin falls shortSovereign rights for exploration, exploitation, conservation and management of ALL resources; exclusive rights and jurisdiction for artificial islands, off-shore terminals, installations and structures; exclusive jurisdiction over scientific research; exclusive jurisdiction to preserve and protect the marine environment and prevent and control marine pollution.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: 12 NAUTICAL MILES QUOTED FOR “INDIAN CUSTOMS WATERS”

THE TRAP: the candidate remembers “12 nautical miles” as the customs figure and writes it against Indian Customs Waters u/s 2(28).

THE TWIST: 12 nautical miles is territorial waters (and it is territorial waters, not customs waters, that are included in “India”). Indian Customs Waters u/s 2(28) run to the limit of the EEZ — 200 nautical miles from the baseline. The source's own MCQ tests exactly this substitution.

6.1.2 Chargeability [Sec. 12] and the Taxable Event

Sec. 12: Duties of customs shall be levied at the rate specified under the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 (or any other law for the time being in force) on goods imported into or exported from India.

Duty of customs is leviable on the GOODS and not on the person importing / exporting them · the goods must be such as are imported to or exported from India · the rate shall be that specified under the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 — import rates in the First Schedule, export rates in the Second Schedule.

  • Goods [Sec. 2(22)] includes (a) vessels, aircraft and vehicles; (b) stores; (c) baggage; (d) currency and negotiable instrument; and (e) any other kind of movable property.
  • Import [Sec. 2(23)] means bringing into India from a place outside India. Imported goods [Sec. 2(25)] means goods brought into India from a place outside India but does not include goods which have been cleared for home consumption.
  • Dutiable goods [Sec. 2(14)] means any goods which are chargeable to duty and on which duty has not been paid.
  • Importer [Sec. 2(26)], in relation to any goods at any time between their importation and the time when they are cleared for home consumption, includes any owner or any person holding himself out to be the importer. Taxpoint: the term also includes a person who cleared the goods from a warehouse even though he is not the actual importer.
  • Export [Sec. 2(18)] means taking out of India to a place outside India. Export goods [Sec. 2(19)] means any goods which are to be taken out of India to a place outside India. Exporter [Sec. 2(20)], at any time between entry for export and the time of export, includes the owner or any person holding himself out to be the exporter.
  • The provision applies also to goods belonging to the Government. However, imports by the Indian Navy, specific equipment required by police, Ministry of Defence, Coastal Guard, etc. are fully exempt from duty by virtue of specific notifications, subject to fulfilment of the conditions and/or procedure set out in those notifications.
  • The object of the Act is to tax only those goods which get mixed up with the mass of goods in India — M. Jamal Co. vs Union of India (1985) 21 ELT 369 (Mad.).
SituationTaxable event — when it happens
Imports (general)Import of goods commences when they cross the territorial waters but continues and is completed when they become part of the mass of goods within the country — Garden Silk Mills Ltd. vs UOI (1999) 113 ELT 358 (SC).
Goods cleared for home consumptionThe taxable event is reached at the time when the goods reach the customs barriers and the bill of entry for home consumption is filed.
Goods cleared for warehousingIf imported goods are taken into a warehouse, the goods continue to be in customs bond. Thus in the case of a warehouse also, import takes place when the goods are cleared for home consumption — payment of duty is deferred till clearance from the warehouse.
ExportsExport of goods is complete when they cross the territorial waters. That means, if goods sink within the territorial waters, export is not complete.

6.1.3 Some Important Definitions — Sec. 2 of the Customs Act, 1962

Learn these as a block. One-mark and MCQ questions are drawn straight from this table.

Sec.TermDefinition
2(1)Adjudicating authorityAny authority competent to pass any order or decision under this Act, but does NOT include (i) the Board, (ii) Commissioner (Appeals), or (iii) the Appellate Tribunal.
2(2)AssessmentDetermination of the dutiability of any goods and the amount of duty, tax, cess or any other sum so payable under this Act / the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 / any other law in force, with reference to: (a) the tariff classification as determined under the Customs Tariff Act; (b) the value as determined under this Act and the Customs Tariff Act; (c) exemption or concession consequent upon any notification; (d) the quantity, weight, volume, measurement or other specifics where duty is leviable on that basis; (e) the origin of the goods, if the amount payable is affected by origin; (f) any other specific factor which affects the sum payable — and includes provisional assessment, self-assessment, re-assessment and any assessment in which the duty assessed is nil.
2(3)BaggageIncludes unaccompanied baggage but does NOT include motor vehicles.
2(3A)Beneficial ownerAny person on whose behalf the goods are being imported or exported, or who exercises effective control over the goods being imported or exported.
2(4)Bill of entryA bill of entry referred to in sec. 46. Sec. 46 provides that the importer of any goods, other than goods intended for transit or transhipment, shall make entry thereof by presenting electronically on the customs automated system to the proper officer a bill of entry for home consumption or warehousing, in such form and manner as may be prescribed.
2(5)Bill of exportA bill of export referred to in sec. 50. Sec. 50 provides that the exporter shall make entry by presenting electronically on the customs automated system to the proper officer — a shipping bill where goods are to be exported in a vessel or aircraft, and a bill of export where goods are to be exported by land.
2(6)BoardThe Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) constituted under the Central Boards of Revenue Act, 1963.
2(7)Coastal goodsGoods, other than imported goods, transported in a vessel from one port in India to another.
2(9)ConveyanceIncludes a vessel (for sea), an aircraft (for air) and a vehicle (for land). Taxpoint: vehicle means conveyance of any kind used on land and includes a railway vehicle [Sec. 2(42)].
2(10)Customs airportAny airport appointed u/s 7(a) to be a customs airport, and includes a place appointed u/s 7(aa) to be an air freight station.
2(11)Customs areaThe area of a customs station or a warehouse, and includes any area in which imported goods or export goods are ordinarily kept before clearance by Customs Authorities.
2(12)Customs portAny port appointed u/s 7(a) to be a customs port, and includes a place appointed u/s 7(aa) to be an inland container depot.
2(13)Customs stationAny customs port, customs airport, international courier terminal, foreign post office or land customs station.
2(21)Foreign-going vessel or aircraftAny vessel or aircraft for the time being engaged in the carriage of goods or passengers between any port or airport in India and any port or airport outside India, whether touching any intermediate port or airport in India or not, and includes — (i) any naval vessel of a foreign Government taking part in any naval exercises; (ii) any vessel engaged in fishing or any other operations outside the territorial waters of India; (iii) any vessel or aircraft proceeding to a place outside India for any purpose whatsoever.
2(24)Arrival manifest / import manifest / import reportThe manifest or report required to be delivered u/s 30. Sec. 30 requires the person-in-charge (or any other notified person) of a vessel, aircraft or vehicle carrying imported goods or export goods to deliver to the proper officer, in the prescribed form and manner — Vessel or aircraft: an arrival manifest or import manifest (for export, a departure manifest or export manifest), presented electronically PRIOR to the arrival (for export, before departure) of the vessel or aircraft. Vehicle: an import report (for export, an export report) WITHIN 12 HOURS after its arrival in the customs station (for export, before departure).
2(31)Person-in-charge(a) vessel → the master of the vessel; (b) aircraft → the commander or pilot-in-charge; (c) railway train → the conductor, guard or other person having the chief direction of the train; (d) any other conveyance → the driver or other person-in-charge.
2(33)Prohibited goodsAny goods the import or export of which is subject to any prohibition under this Act or any other law for the time being in force, but does NOT include any such goods in respect of which the conditions subject to which the goods are permitted to be imported or exported have been complied with.
2(38)StoresGoods for use in a vessel or aircraft, and includes fuel and spare parts and other articles of equipment, whether or not for immediate fitting.
53Transit of goodsWhere any goods imported in a conveyance and mentioned in the arrival manifest / import manifest / import report as for transit in the SAME conveyance to any place outside India or to any customs station, the proper officer may allow the goods and the conveyance to transit without payment of duty, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.
54Transshipment of goodsWhere any goods imported into a customs station are intended for transshipment, a bill of transshipment shall be presented to the proper officer in such form and manner as may be prescribed.

6.1.4 Sets of Articles [Sec. 19] and Re-importation [Sec. 20]

Determination of duty where goods consist of articles liable to different rates [Sec. 19]. Where the goods consist of a set of articles, duty is calculated as follows.

ArticlesBasis of chargeability
1. Articles liable to duty on the basis of quantityChargeable on the basis of quantity.
2. Articles liable to duty on the basis of value — if liable at the SAME rateChargeable at that rate.
2. Articles liable to duty on the basis of value — if liable at DIFFERENT ratesChargeable at the highest of such rates.
3. Articles not liable to dutyChargeable on the basis mentioned in (2) above.
Two riders. (i) Accessories of, and spare parts or maintenance and repairing implements for, any article are chargeable at the SAME rate as that article — e.g. where a machine is chargeable at 30%, repairing implements with that machine are also charged at 30%. (ii) Where the importer produces evidence to the satisfaction of the proper officer (or the evidence is available) regarding the value of any of the articles liable to different rates, such article shall be chargeable to duty separately at the rate applicable to it.

Re-importation of goods [Sec. 20]. If goods are imported into India after exportation therefrom, such goods shall be liable to duty and be subject to all the conditions and restrictions, if any, to which goods of the like kind and value are liable or subject on importation.

Goods exported for repairs abroad and re-imported → duty is NOT charged on the full value, but only on: Fair cost of repairs + Insurance and Freight both ways

Condition: the ownership of the goods must not have changed.

6.1.5 Goods Derelict, Wreck, Jetsam and Flotsam [Sec. 21]

TermMeaning
DerelictProperty abandoned at sea without hope of recovering.
WreckProperty cast ashore by tide after shipwreck.
JetsamWhere goods are cast into the sea to lighten the ship to prevent it from sinking.
FlotsamGoods separated from the ship by some peril, which continue to float on the sea.
Treatment: goods being derelict, wreck, jetsam and flotsam brought or coming into India shall be dealt with as if they were imported into India. However, where it is shown to the satisfaction of the proper officer that they are entitled to be admitted duty-free, the proper officer may admit them as duty-free.

6.1.6 Customs Duty Not Leviable, or Leviable at a Reduced Amount

Four rescue provisions sit side by side. Fix in mind which loss each one deals with, and at which moment the loss must have happened — that pair of facts decides the answer to almost every question on this topic.

ProvisionTriggerEffect on duty
Sec. 13 — Pilfered goodsGoods pilfered after unloading, before the clearance/warehousing order, and not re-stored.No duty leviable on the importer.
Sec. 22 — Damaged or deteriorated goodsDamage/deterioration in the specified circumstances.Reduced (proportionate) duty.
Sec. 23(1) — Lost or destroyed goodsGoods lost (otherwise than by pilferage) or destroyed before clearance for home consumption.Remission of duty.
Sec. 23(2) — Relinquishment of titleOwner relinquishes title before the clearance/warehousing order.Not liable to pay duty thereon.

No Duty on Pilfered Goods [Sec. 13]

Conditions — all three must hold: (a) imported goods are pilfered; (b) such goods are pilfered after the unloading thereof and before the proper officer has made an order for clearance for home consumption or deposit in a warehouse; and (c) the pilfered goods are not re-stored.

Treatment: the importer shall not be liable to pay the duty leviable on such pilfered goods. Where imported goods are pilfered while in custody, the custodian is required to pay duty on such goods.

  • Pilfer means to steal something, typically of small value or in small quantities — petty theft. It does not mean total destruction or complete loss.
  • If such goods are re-stored to the importer after pilferage, the importer becomes liable to pay duty.
  • The governing principle: “when the goods are not in the control of the importer, he is not liable to pay duty thereon.”
  • Sec. 13 does not deal with: (a) goods lost or destroyed; (b) goods pilfered before unloading (the importer must prove pilferage occurred before the clearance order; once proved, no burden to pay duty); (c) goods pilfered after the order for clearance for home consumption or deposit in a warehouse.
  • Where Sec. 13 is applicable, Sec. 23(1) is not applicable.

Abatement of Duty on Damaged or Deteriorated Goods [Sec. 22]

Circumstances — where it is shown to the satisfaction of the Assistant Commissioner of Customs or Deputy Commissioner of Customs that:

  1. any imported goods had been damaged or had deteriorated at any time before or during the unloading of goods in India; or
  2. any imported goods (other than warehoused goods) had been damaged at any time after unloading but before examination, on account of any accident not due to any wilful act, negligence or default of the importer, his employee or agent; or
  3. any warehoused goods had been damaged at any time before clearance for home consumption, on account of any accident not due to any wilful act, negligence or default of the owner, his employee or agent.

Duty on damaged goods = [Value of damaged / deteriorated goods ÷ Value of goods before damage / deterioration] × Duty on goods before damage

In words: the duty to be charged on the goods shall bear the same proportion to the duty chargeable on the goods before the damage or deterioration, as the value of the damaged or deteriorated goods bears to the value before the damage or deterioration.

Value of the damaged / deteriorated goods — ascertained by EITHER method, at the option of the owner:

(a) the value may be ascertained by the proper officer; or (b) the goods may be sold by the proper officer by public auction or by tender, or with the consent of the owner in any other manner, and the gross sale proceeds shall be deemed to be the value of such goods.

“Damage” denotes physical damage — goods are not fit for the purpose for which they are intended. “Deterioration” denotes reduction in the quality of goods due to natural cause.

Sec. 22 in Figures — the Source's Own Example
Particulars₹
Value of goods before damage1,00,000
Duty liability before damage10,000
Value of goods after damage40,000
Revised duty liability after damage [₹10,000 × ₹40,000 ÷ ₹1,00,000]4,000

Remission on Lost or Destroyed Goods [Sec. 23(1)] and Relinquishment of Title [Sec. 23(2)]

Sec. 23(1). Where it is shown to the satisfaction of the Assistant Commissioner or Deputy Commissioner that any imported goods have been lost (otherwise than as a result of pilferage) or destroyed at any time before clearance for home consumption, the Assistant Commissioner or Deputy Commissioner shall remit the duty on such goods.

  • Remission is permissible only when there is total loss, or the loss is forever and beyond recovery — e.g. imported goods destroyed due to fire in the warehouse before clearance for home consumption.
  • In case of pilferage, Sec. 13 (not Sec. 23(1)) applies.

Sec. 23(2). The owner of any imported goods may, before an order for clearance of the goods for home consumption or an order permitting the deposit of goods in a warehouse, relinquish his title to the goods, and thereupon he shall not be liable to pay the duty thereon.

  • “Relinquish” literally means to withdraw from, to abandon, to give up anything or any right, to cease to hold, to surrender, to give over the possession or control of, to leave off.
  • Such relinquishment must be unconditional.
  • The importer may exercise this option at any time before the passing of the order for clearance for home consumption, or before the order permitting deposit of goods in a warehouse.
  • However, the owner shall not be allowed to relinquish title to goods regarding which an offence appears to have been committed under this Act or any other law.
  • Situations where an importer is unwilling or unable to take delivery: (a) the imported goods are not according to the specifications; (b) the goods are so damaged during the voyage as to be of no use to the importer; (c) there may be breach of contract.
Point of differencePilferage of goods u/s 13Loss or destruction of goods u/s 23(1)
MeaningPilferage denotes stealing in small quantities, i.e. petty theft.Loss or destruction denotes total loss, or loss forever and beyond recovery.
Duty liabilityThe importer is not made liable to pay the duty on pilfered imported goods. However, if goods are restored, the importer is liable to pay the duty.The duty paid on the goods shall be remitted to the importer.
Time of occurrenceThe imported goods must have been pilfered after the unloading, but before the proper officer has made an order for clearance for home consumption.Imported goods have been lost or destroyed at any time before physical clearance of the goods for home consumption.
Warehoused goodsSec. 13 is not applicable where goods are pilfered after warehousing.The provision is applicable to warehoused goods also.
Burden to proveNo such burden is cast on the importer u/s 13.U/s 23(1) the burden is cast on the importer to satisfy the Assistant / Deputy Commissioner that the imported goods have been lost or destroyed at any time before physical clearance for home consumption.
Source of the distinction: Hindustan Petroleum Corporation vs. CC 1984 (18) ELT 358 (Tri Mumbai).
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: TREATING PILFERAGE AND DESTRUCTION AS THE SAME RELIEF

THE TRAP: answering “remission u/s 23(1)” whenever goods go missing, or applying Sec. 13 to warehoused goods stolen after warehousing.

THE TWIST: the two provisions occupy different ground. Sec. 13 is petty theft, no duty at all, no burden of proof on the importer, and it does NOT apply once goods are warehoused or once the clearance order is passed — and if the pilfered goods are re-stored, duty revives. Sec. 23(1) is total, irrecoverable loss or destruction, the duty is remitted, the burden of satisfying the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner rests on the importer, and it DOES cover warehoused goods. Where Sec. 13 applies, Sec. 23(1) does not.

Denaturing / Mutilation [Sec. 24] and Exemption from Duty [Sec. 25]

Sec. 24. The Central Government may make rules for permitting, at the request of the owner, the denaturing or mutilation of imported goods which are ordinarily used for more than one purpose, so as to render them unfit for one or more of such purposes; where goods are so denatured or mutilated they shall be chargeable to duty at such rate as would be applicable if the goods had been imported in the denatured or mutilated form.

Sec. 25 — Power to grant exemption. If the Central Government is satisfied that it is necessary in the public interest so to do — (a) it may, by notification in the Official Gazette, exempt generally (either absolutely or subject to certain conditions) goods of any specified description from the whole or any part of duty; (b) it may, by special order, exempt from payment of duty, under circumstances of an exceptional nature stated in such order, any goods on which duty is leviable.

  1. An exemption may be granted by providing for levy of duty at a rate expressed in a form or method different from that in which duty is leviable; such duty shall in no case exceed the original duty. “Form or method” means the basis — valuation, weight, number, length, area, volume or other measure — with reference to which duty is leviable.
  2. Duty shall not be collected where the amount of duty leviable does not exceed ₹100.
  3. Such exemption shall, unless otherwise specified or varied or rescinded, be valid up to the 31st day of March falling immediately after 2 years from the date of such grant or variation.

Classification of Imported / Export Goods

Import and export of goods are required to be assessed to duty — which may include an assessment of nil duty. For this purpose it is necessary to determine the classification of the goods, i.e. the categorisation of the goods in a specific heading or sub-heading of the Schedules to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975.

Why classification matters: (i) for determining the rate of duty; (ii) for determining eligibility for an exemption notification, which is with reference to the tariff heading or sub-heading — wrong classification would either cause loss of revenue to the Central Government or impose unjustifiable loss on the assessee; (iii) for applicability of other duties on goods like anti-dumping duty, safeguard duty, etc.; (iv) for applicability of any restriction and control on import or export of goods.

First Schedule structure: 21 Sections · 98 Chapters, on the HSN developed by the World Customs Organization and applied uniformly by more than 137 countries.

A Section is a group of Chapters codifying a particular class of goods; Section notes explain the scope of chapters/headings. Chapters consist of chapter notes and brief descriptions of commodities arranged at four-, six- and eight-digit levels.

4-digit code = HEADING · 6-digit code = SUB-HEADING · 8-digit code = TARIFF ITEM

Reading an 8-digit code left to right: first 2 digits → Chapter; next 2 → Heading; next 2 → Sub-heading; last 2 → Tariff Item. The Second Schedule contains the description of goods chargeable to export duty.

ILLUSTRATION 1 — Degraded Chemicals: Can the Importer Escape the Duty?

ABC Ltd. imported a consignment of chemicals. Upon arrival, they discovered that the chemicals were chemically degraded and not suitable for their industrial use. The duty assessed on these goods is ₹2,00,000. The goods have not yet been cleared for home consumption. ABC Ltd. does not want to pay the duty or take delivery. The Customs Officer insists that since the goods were imported, duty must be paid. Can ABC Ltd. avoid paying the duty?

Provision: u/s 23(2), the owner of any imported goods may, at any time before the order for clearance for home consumption is passed, relinquish his title to the goods.

Condition: the relinquishment must be unconditional, and no offence should have been committed regarding the goods.

Answer: ABC Ltd. CAN avoid paying the duty. If ABC Ltd. formally relinquishes the title to the Customs authorities before the clearance order, they shall not be liable to pay the duty thereon — the ₹2,00,000 assessed duty is not payable.

ILLUSTRATION 2 — Glass Sheets Damaged by a Crane Accident During Unloading [Sec. 22]

M/s. Safe Imports Ltd. imported a consignment of high-grade glass sheets valued at ₹10,00,000. The applicable Basic Customs Duty (BCD) is 10%. During the unloading of goods at the port (before examination by the proper officer), a crane accident occurred and the glass sheets were heavily damaged. The accident was not due to any negligence or wilful act of the importer or his agent. The Proper Officer assessed the value of the damaged goods (scrap value) at ₹2,00,000. Calculate the actual customs duty payable.

Provision: u/s 22, if imported goods are damaged or deteriorated at any time before or during unloading, or before examination (provided it is not the importer's fault), the duty is reduced proportionately. Formula: Duty on Damaged Goods = (Value of Damaged Goods ÷ Value of Goods before Damage) × Total Duty Leviable.

Computation of Customs Duty Payable after Damage
Particulars₹
1. Original duty liability [₹10,00,000 × 10%]1,00,000
2. Value before damage10,00,000
   Value after damage2,00,000
3. Revised duty [(₹2,00,000 ÷ ₹10,00,000) × ₹1,00,000 = 0.2 × 1,00,000]20,000

Answer: the importer is liable to pay only ₹20,000 as customs duty.

ILLUSTRATION 3 — “Professional Grooming Kit”: A Set of Articles at Different Rates [Sec. 19]

Mr. Kumar imports a “Professional Grooming Kit” from the USA valued at ₹5,000. The kit is a single retail package containing items otherwise liable to duty at different rates if imported separately — Electric Trimmer: 20%; Shaving Gel: 10%; After-Shave Cologne: 30%; Plastic Comb (Exempt): Nil. Mr. Kumar contends that since the comb is exempt and the gel is at 10%, the average rate should apply. Determine the rate of duty applicable.

Provision: u/s 19 of the Customs Act, 1962, where goods consist of a set of articles liable to duty at different rates — (a) articles liable to duty at the same rate are charged at that rate; (b) articles liable to duty at different rates are chargeable at the highest of such rates.

Analysis: since the items are imported as a set and have different rates (Nil, 10%, 20%, 30%), the entire value of the set will be taxed at the highest rate applicable to any of the ingredients.

Answer: the entire “Grooming Kit” valued at ₹5,000 will be chargeable to duty at 30% — the rate applicable to the After-Shave Cologne. There is no averaging.

10. An importer can relinquish his title to the goods and avoid paying duty, provided:

QCorrectReason
1(d)Indian Customs Waters means the waters extending into the sea up to the limit of the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), which is 200 nautical miles from the baseline.
2(b)As per sec. 25, conditional exemptions are valid up to the 31st day of March falling immediately after 2 years from the date of such grant or variation.
3(c)While import commences upon crossing territorial waters, the taxable event is reached when the goods reach the customs barriers and the bill of entry for home consumption is filed.
4(b)For goods exported for repairs and re-imported, duty is charged only on the (fair cost of repairs + insurance and freight both ways), provided ownership has not changed.

8(b)The Customs Act, 1962 became effective from 1-2-1963.
