CONCEPT

6.2 Types of Duties ★★★ HIGH

An imported consignment rarely bears one duty. It bears a stack — and each layer of the stack is computed on a different base. Learn the duty first, then the base, and the computation questions in 6.4 become mechanical.

Duty / levyCharging provisionRate and base — as the source states it
Basic Customs Duty (BCD)Sec. 12 of the Customs Act, r.w.s. 2 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975At the tariff rate — specific (based on measures like quintal, metres) or ad valorem (a percentage of assessable value), or specific-cum-ad valorem. Two basic rates: standard (column 4, applies generally, the higher one) and preferential (column 5, concessional, for imports from a notified preferential area). Base: the assessable value.
Social Welfare Surcharge (SWS)Levied on imported goods; not levied on export@ 10% of total customs duties (with exclusions below). 3% in the case of goods being gold, silver including that plated with platinum, unwrought or in semi-manufactured form or in powder form. Base: the customs duties, i.e. in the standard computation, the BCD.
Integrated Tax (IGST)Sec. 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975At the rate leviable u/s 5 of the IGST Act, 2017 on a like article on its supply in India. Base: Sec. 14(1) value / Sec. 14(2) tariff value + any duty of customs chargeable u/s 12 + any sum chargeable under any law as an addition to, and in the same manner as, a duty of customs (like anti-dumping duty, safeguard duty) — but NOT including the IGST itself and the Compensation Cess. ITC of this IGST is available under GST law.
GST Compensation CessSec. 3(9) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975At the rate leviable u/s 8 of the GST (Compensation to States) Cess Act, 2017 on a like article on its supply in India. Charged on luxury products like high-end cars and demerit commodities like pan masala, tobacco and aerated drinks — for 5 years to compensate States for loss of revenue, now extended up to 31-03-2026. Base: identical to the IGST base — and it too excludes the IGST and this cess. ITC available under GST law.
Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess (AIDC)Levied on the import of specified goods at notified ratesFinances the improvement of agriculture infrastructure and other development expenditures. Notified goods include apples, kabuli chana, urea, various types of coal, and precious metals like gold and silver (including imports by eligible passengers). Base: the value of goods determined u/s 14 of the Customs Act, 1962. Levied in addition to other customs duties; all provisions of the Act on assessment, refund, exemptions, interest, appeals and penalties apply mutatis mutandis.
Safeguard measures (incl. Safeguard Duty)Sec. 8B of the Customs Tariff ActWhere an article is imported into India in increased quantities so as to cause or threaten to cause serious injury to the domestic industry. Product specific; in addition to any other duty. Measures include safeguard duty, tariff-rate quota, or such other measure as the Central Government considers appropriate.
Countervailing Duty on subsidized articlesSec. 9 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975Where a country pays or bestows, directly or indirectly, a subsidy on manufacture, production or exportation (including a subsidy on transportation). Quantum: not exceeding the amount of such subsidy. In addition to any other duty.
Anti-Dumping DutySec. 9A of the Customs Tariff ActWhere an article is exported to India at less than its normal value. Quantum: not exceeding the margin of dumping (= Normal Value less Export Price). In addition to any other duty.
Export DutySecond Schedule of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975In general, no duty is payable on export. However, Government has imposed export duty on certain goods like leather goods, ferrous waste and scrap, snake skins, etc.
Apart from these, additional duty, countervailing duty or special additional duty is also applicable on certain goods. Generally these duties are subsumed in GST; however, they are still applicable for goods outside the purview of GST, like alcoholic liquor for human consumption. Government also imposes certain surcharges or cesses on specific goods from time to time — e.g. Road and Infrastructure cess on motor spirit and high speed diesel, Health cess on medical equipment.

6.2.1 Social Welfare Surcharge — the 10% That Sits on the Duty, Not on the Value

Social Welfare Surcharge = 10% of total customs duties (3% for gold / silver, incl. platinum-plated, unwrought, semi-manufactured or powder form)

SWS applies to imported goods only — such surcharge is not levied on export.

For the purpose of computing SWS, the following are NOT to be considered:

Safeguard Duty · Countervailing duty on subsidized article · Anti-dumping duty · IGST · GST Compensation cess · Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess (AIDC).

Source Example — BCD + SWS Only
Particulars₹
Assessable Value1,00,000
Basic Customs Duty @ 10%10,000
Add: Social Welfare Surcharge @ 10% of the aforesaid1,000
Total duty payable11,000

6.2.2 IGST on Imports [Sec. 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975]

  • Any article which is imported into India shall, in addition, be liable to integrated tax.
  • IGST shall be levied at such rate as is leviable u/s 5 of the Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 on a like article on its supply in India.

Value for levying IGST = Sec. 14(1) value / Sec. 14(2) tariff value + Customs duty chargeable u/s 12 + any sum chargeable under any law as an addition to, and in the same manner as, a duty of customs (anti-dumping duty, safeguard duty, etc.)

… but does NOT include the IGST itself and the Compensation Cess. In the standard computation this works out to: Value for IGST [D] = Assessable Value [A] + Basic Customs Duty [B] + Social Welfare Surcharge [C].

Source Example — Assessable Value ₹1,00,000, BCD 10%, IGST 18%
Particulars₹
Assessable Value [A]1,00,000
Basic Customs Duty [B = 10% of A]10,000
Add: Social Welfare Surcharge [C = 10% of B]1,000
Value for computing IGST [D = A + B + C]1,11,000
Add: IGST [E = D × 18%]19,980
Total Duty payable [B + C + E]30,980

For the aforesaid payment of IGST, ITC under GST law is available.

Taxpoint — warehoused goods sold before clearance. Where goods deposited in a warehouse under the Customs Act, 1962 are sold to any person before clearance for home consumption or export, the value of such goods for calculating the integrated tax shall be —

SituationValue for IGST
Where the whole of the goods is soldThe value determined as per the aforesaid provision or the transaction value of such goods, whichever is higher.
Where any part of the goods is soldThe proportionate value of such goods as per the aforesaid provision or the transaction value of such goods, whichever is higher.
Where the whole of the warehoused goods or any part thereof are sold more than once before such clearance for home consumption or export, the transaction value of the last such transaction shall be the transaction value for the aforesaid purposes.

6.2.3 GST Compensation Cess [Sec. 3(9) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975]

Under the GST regime, Compensation Cess is charged on luxury products like high-end cars and demerit commodities like pan masala, tobacco and aerated drinks, for a period of 5 years, in order to compensate States for loss of revenue — now extended up to 31-03-2026. Any article imported into India shall, in addition, be liable to the GST compensation cess at such rate as is leviable u/s 8 of the Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Cess Act, 2017 on a like article on its supply in India.

Where the cess is leviable at a percentage of value, value of the imported article = Sec. 14(1) value / Sec. 14(2) tariff value + customs duty chargeable u/s 12 + any sum chargeable under any law as an addition to, and in the same manner as, a duty of customs (anti-dumping duty, safeguard duty, etc.)

… but does NOT include the IGST or this cess. In respect of warehoused goods, a provision similar to that for IGST applies.

Source Example — AV ₹1,00,000, BCD 10%, IGST 18%, Compensation Cess 22%
Particulars₹
Assessable Value [A]1,00,000
Basic Customs Duty [B = 10% of A]10,000
Add: Social Welfare Surcharge [C = 10% of B]1,000
Value for computing IGST [D = A + B + C]1,11,000
Add: IGST [E = D × 18%]19,980
Add: Compensation Cess [F = D × 22%]24,420
Total Duty payable [B + C + E + F]55,400

For the aforesaid payment of IGST and compensation cess, ITC under GST law is available.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: COMPUTING THE COMPENSATION CESS ON THE POST-IGST FIGURE

THE TRAP: the candidate adds IGST to the sub-total and then applies the Compensation Cess to that grand figure — here, 22% on (₹1,11,000 + ₹19,980) = ₹28,816.

THE TWIST: IGST and Compensation Cess sit side by side on the SAME base, not one on top of the other. Sec. 3(9) expressly excludes both the IGST and the cess itself from the cess's value base. So the cess is ₹1,11,000 × 22% = ₹24,420, and the total duty payable is B + C + E + F = ₹55,400. Two parallel branches from one node [D] — not a chain.

6.2.4 Safeguard Duty and Safeguard Measures [Sec. 8B of the Customs Tariff Act]

Condition to impose. Where the Central Government is satisfied that — (a) an article is imported into India in increased quantities; and (b) such article is imported so as to cause or threaten to cause serious injury to the domestic industry — then it may apply such safeguard measures on that article as it deems appropriate.

  1. Safeguard measures include imposition of safeguard duty, application of tariff-rate quota, or such other measure as the Central Government may consider appropriate, to curb the increased quantity of imports and prevent serious injury to domestic industry.
  2. Developing-country carve-out. Safeguard duty shall NOT be imposed if (a) the article originates from a developing country or countries; and (b) the aggregate import does not exceed the limits below.
  3. Where tariff-rate quota is used as a safeguard measure, the Central Government shall not fix such quota lower than the average level of imports in the last 3 representative years for which statistics are available, unless a different level is deemed necessary to prevent or remedy serious injury. The Government may allocate such tariff-rate quota to supplying countries having a substantial interest in supplying the article concerned, in such manner as may be provided by rules.
  4. Provisional Safeguard Duty. Pending determination of safeguard measures, the Central Government may apply provisional safeguard measures on the basis of a preliminary determination that increased imports have caused or threatened serious injury. Any provisional safeguard measure shall not remain in force for more than 200 days from the date on which it was applied. Where, on final determination, the Government is of the opinion that increased imports have not caused or threatened serious injury, it shall refund the safeguard duty so collected.
  5. Duration. Safeguard duty ceases to have effect on the expiry of 4 years (unless revoked earlier) from the date of its imposition. However, the Central Government may extend the period of levy to 10 years.
  6. 100% EOU / SEZ. Safeguard duty or provisional safeguard duty shall not apply to articles imported by a 100% export-oriented undertaking or a unit in a special economic zone unless (a) it is specifically made applicable in such notification or to such undertaking or unit; or (b) such article is either cleared as such into the domestic tariff area, or used in the manufacture of any goods that are cleared into the domestic tariff area — in which case safeguard measures apply on the portion so cleared or used, as was applicable when it was imported into India.
  7. The safeguard duty is product specific and is in addition to any other duty imposed under this Act or any other law for the time being in force. The provisions of the Customs Act, 1962 and all rules and regulations made thereunder apply to this duty also.
Where the article originates from…Safeguard duty is not imposed if…
One developing countryThe share of imports of that article from that country does not exceed 3% of the total imports of that article into India.
More than one developing countryThe aggregate of the imports from all such countries does not exceed 9% of the total imports of that article into India.
However, the Central Government may exempt such quantity of any article, when imported from any country or territory into India, from payment of the whole or part of the safeguard duty leviable thereon.

Sec. 8B definitions to reproduce verbatim in an answer

Developing country = a country notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette. Domestic industry = the producers (a) as a whole of the like article or a directly competitive article in India, or (b) whose collective output of the like article or a directly competitive article in India constitutes a major share of the total production of the said article in India. Serious injury = an injury causing significant overall impairment in the position of a domestic industry. Threat of serious injury = a clear and imminent danger of serious injury.

6.2.5 Countervailing Duty on Subsidized Articles [Sec. 9 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975]

Conditions to impose — all four: (a) any country or territory pays or bestows, directly or indirectly, any subsidy upon the manufacture or production therein, or the exportation therefrom, of any article, including any subsidy on transportation of such article; (b) such article is imported into India; (c) such article is imported directly or indirectly from the country of manufacture or production; and (d) the article is imported in the same condition as when exported from the country of manufacture or production, or has been changed in condition by manufacture, production or otherwise.

Quantum: the Central Government may impose a countervailing duty not exceeding the amount of such subsidy.

Duration: in force for 5 years (unless revoked earlier) from the date of imposition, extendable for another 5 years. Where a review initiated before expiry of the 5-year period has not concluded before such expiry, the duty may continue pending the outcome of the review for a further period not exceeding 1 year. If the duty is revoked temporarily, the period of such revocation shall not exceed 1 year at a time. Such countervailing duty is in addition to any other duty imposed under this Act or any other law.

When a subsidy is deemed to exist. (a) There is a financial contribution by a Government, or any public body in the exporting or producing country or territory — i.e. where (i) a Government practice involves a direct transfer of funds (including grants, loans and equity infusion), or a potential direct transfer of funds or liabilities, or both; (ii) Government revenue that is otherwise due is foregone or not collected (including fiscal incentives); (iii) a Government provides goods or services other than general infrastructure, or purchases goods; (iv) a Government makes payments to a funding mechanism, or entrusts or directs a private body to carry out one or more of the functions in (i) to (iii) which would normally be vested in the Government, the practice in no real sense differing from practices normally followed by Governments. Or (b) a Government grants or maintains any form of income or price support which operates directly or indirectly to increase export of any article from, or to reduce import of any article into, its territory, and a benefit is thereby conferred.

  • Circumvention [Sec. 9(1A)]: where the Central Government is of the opinion that circumvention of the imposed countervailing duty has taken place — by altering the description, name or composition of the article, by import in an unassembled or disassembled form, by changing the country of origin or export, or in any other manner whereby the duty is rendered ineffective — it may extend the countervailing duty to such other article also, from a date not earlier than the date of initiation of the inquiry.
  • Absorption [Sec. 9(1B)]: where absorption of the imposed countervailing duty has taken place, rendering it ineffective, the Government may modify the duty to counter that effect, from a date not earlier than the date of initiation of the inquiry. Absorption is said to have taken place (a) if there is a decrease in the export price of an article without any commensurate change in the resale price in India of such article imported from the exporting country or territory; or (b) under such other circumstances as may be provided by rules.
  • Provisional duty [Sec. 9(2)]: pending determination of the amount of subsidy, the Government may impose a countervailing duty not exceeding the subsidy as provisionally estimated. If the duty so imposed exceeds the subsidy as finally determined, the Government shall reduce the duty and refund the excess collected.
  • 100% EOU / SEZ: a notification or countervailing duty shall not apply to an article imported by a 100% export-oriented undertaking or an SEZ unit, unless (i) specifically made applicable in the notification or to such undertaking/unit; or (ii) the article is cleared as such into the domestic tariff area or used in the manufacture of goods cleared into the DTA — in which case duty is imposed on that portion so cleared or used, as was applicable when imported into India.
  • Threshold condition: countervailing duty shall not be levied unless it is determined that (a) the subsidy relates to export performance; (b) the subsidy relates to the use of domestic goods over imported goods in the export article; or (c) the subsidy has been conferred on a limited number of persons engaged in manufacturing, producing or exporting the article — unless such subsidy is for (i) research activities conducted by or on behalf of such persons, (ii) assistance to disadvantaged regions within the exporting country's territory, or (iii) assistance to promote adaptation of existing facilities to new environmental requirements.
  • Retrospective levy: where injury to domestic industry that is difficult to repair is caused by massive imports in a relatively short period of the subsidised article, and retrospective levy is necessary to preclude recurrence of such injury, the Government may levy countervailing duty from a date prior to the date of imposition, but not beyond 90 days from the date of such notification.
  • The amount of subsidy is ascertained and determined by the Central Government from time to time after such inquiry as it considers necessary; the Government may make rules for the identification of such articles and for assessment and collection of the duty. The provisions of the Customs Act, 1962 and its rules and regulations apply to this duty also.

6.2.6 Anti-Dumping Duty [Sec. 9A of the Customs Tariff Act]

Dumping is said to occur when the goods are exported by a country to another country at a price lower than its normal value. This is an unfair trade practice which can have a distortive effect on international trade. Anti-dumping is a measure to rectify the situation arising out of the dumping of goods and its trade-distortive effect — to re-establish fair trade. Its use as an instrument of fair competition is permitted by the WTO. Anti-dumping is an instrument for ensuring fair trade and is not a measure of protection per se for the domestic industry; it provides relief to the domestic industry against the injury caused by dumping.

Conditions to impose: (a) any article is exported by an exporter or producer from any country or territory to India at less than its normal value; and (b) such article is imported into India.

Anti-dumping duty ≤ Margin of Dumping  ·  Margin of Dumping = Normal Value − Export Price

Watch the direction. It is Normal Value LESS Export Price — not the reverse. The Central Government may impose an anti-dumping duty not exceeding the margin of dumping in relation to such article.

Export price means (a) the price of the article exported from the exporting country or territory; and (b) where there is no export price, or the export price is unreliable because of association or a compensatory arrangement between the exporter and the importer or a third party, the export price may be constructed on the basis of the price at which the imported articles are first resold to an independent buyer — or, if not resold to an independent buyer or not resold in the condition as imported, on such reasonable basis as may be determined under rules made u/s 9A(6).

Normal value means (i) the comparable price, in the ordinary course of trade, for the like article when destined for consumption in the exporting country or territory, as determined under rules made u/s 9A(6); or (ii) where there are no sales of the like article in the ordinary course of trade in the exporting country's domestic market, or where because of the particular market situation or low volume of such sales a proper comparison is not permitted — either (a) the comparable representative price of the like article when exported from the exporting country to an appropriate third country, or (b) the cost of production of the article in the country of origin along with a reasonable addition for administrative, selling and general costs and for profits. Where the article is imported from a country other than the country of origin and has been merely transhipped through the country of export, or is not produced in the country of export, or there is no comparable price in the country of export — normal value is determined with reference to its price in the country of origin.

  • Duration: in force for 5 years (unless revoked earlier) from the date of imposition. If, in a review, the Central Government is of the opinion that cessation of the duty is likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of dumping and injury, it may from time to time extend the period for a further period up to 5 years, such further period commencing from the date of the order of extension. Where a review initiated before expiry of the 5-year period has not concluded before such expiry, the duty may continue pending the outcome of the review for a further period not exceeding 1 year. If the duty is revoked temporarily, the period of such revocation shall not exceed 1 year at a time. The duty is in addition to any other duty.
  • Circumvention: where circumvention has taken place — by altering the description, name or composition of the article, by import in unassembled or disassembled form, by changing the country of origin or export, or in any other manner rendering the duty ineffective — the Government may extend the anti-dumping duty to such article, or to an article originating in or exported from such country, from a date not earlier than the date of initiation of the inquiry.
  • Absorption: where absorption has taken place rendering the duty ineffective, the Government may modify the duty from a date not earlier than the date of initiation of the inquiry. Absorption is said to have taken place (a) if there is a decrease in the export price of an article without any commensurate change in the cost of production of such article, or in the export price to countries other than India, or in the resale price in India of such article imported from the exporting country; or (b) under such other circumstances as may be provided by rules.
  • Provisional anti-dumping duty: pending determination of normal value and margin of dumping, the Government may impose duty on a provisional estimate; if it exceeds the margin as finally determined, the Government shall reduce the duty and refund the excess collected.
  • 100% EOU / SEZ: same carve-out as for countervailing duty — the duty does not apply to articles imported by a 100% EOU or an SEZ unit unless specifically made applicable, or unless the article is cleared as such into the DTA or used in the manufacture of goods cleared into the DTA (in which case duty is imposed on that portion, as was applicable when imported).
  • Retrospective effect: where (i) there is a history of dumping which caused injury, or the importer was or should have been aware that the exporter practises dumping and that such dumping would cause injury; and (ii) the injury is caused by massive dumping of an article imported in a relatively short time which, in light of the timing and volume dumped and other circumstances, is likely to seriously undermine the remedial effect of the duty — the Government may levy anti-dumping duty retrospectively from a date prior to the date of imposition, but not beyond 90 days from the date of the notification, at such rate and from such date as specified. The provisions of the Customs Act, 1962 and its rules and regulations apply to this duty also.

Refund of anti-dumping duty [Sec. 9AA]. Where, upon determination by an officer authorised by the Central Government, an importer proves to the satisfaction of the Central Government that he has paid anti-dumping duty imposed u/s 9A on any article in excess of the actual margin of dumping, the Central Government shall reduce such duty as is in excess of the actual margin so determined, and the importer shall be entitled to a refund of such excess duty. Such importer shall NOT be entitled to refund of so much of the excess duty as is refundable u/s 9A(2). The Central Government may make rules to (i) provide the manner and time for the importer's application; (ii) authorise the officer who shall dispose of the application within the time specified; and (iii) provide the manner in which the excess duty shall be (A) determined by such officer, and (B) refunded by the Deputy Commissioner or Assistant Commissioner of Customs after such determination.

No levy u/s 9 or 9A in certain cases [Sec. 9B]. (a) No article shall be subjected to both countervailing duty and anti-dumping duty to compensate for the same situation of dumping or export subsidization. (b) The Central Government shall not levy countervailing or anti-dumping duty (i) by reason of exemption of such articles from duties or taxes borne by the like article when meant for consumption in the country of origin or exportation, or by reason of refund of such duties or taxes; (ii) under sub-section (1) of each of those sections, on import from a WTO member country or a country with which India has a most-favoured-nation agreement (a “specified country”), unless a determination has been made under the rules that import of such article into India causes or threatens material injury to an established industry in India, or materially retards the establishment of any industry in India; and (iii) under sub-section (2) of each of those sections, on import from specified countries unless a preliminary finding has been made of subsidy or dumping and consequent injury to domestic industry, and a further determination has been made that a duty is necessary to prevent injury during the investigation. Sub-clauses (ii) and (iii) do not apply where a countervailing or anti-dumping duty has been imposed to prevent injury or threat of injury to the domestic industry of a third country exporting the like articles to India. (c) The Central Government may not levy (i) countervailing duty u/s 9, at any time, upon receipt of satisfactory voluntary undertakings from the Government of the exporting country to eliminate or limit the subsidy or take other measures concerning its effect, or from the exporter to revise the price of the article, if satisfied that the injurious effect of the subsidy is thereby eliminated; (ii) anti-dumping duty u/s 9A, at any time, upon receipt of a satisfactory voluntary undertaking from any exporter to revise its prices or to cease exports to the area in question at a dumped price, if satisfied that the injurious effect of dumping is eliminated by such action.

ILLUSTRATION 4 — Anti-Dumping Duty Alongside Normal Duties [Sec. 9A]

A commodity is imported into India from a country covered by a notification issued by the Central Government u/s 9A of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975. Assessable Value for levying Basic Customs Duty: ₹12,62,500. Quantity imported: 500 kgs. Basic customs duty: 10%. IGST: 18%. As per the notification, the anti-dumping duty will be equal to the difference between the cost of the commodity calculated @ US$ 40 per kg (exchange rate 1 USD = INR 90) and the landed value of the commodity as imported. Appraise the liability on account of normal duties and the anti-dumping duty.

Computation of Customs Duty, SWS, Anti-Dumping Duty and IGST
ParticularsDetails₹
Assessable Value—12,62,500
Basic Customs Duty @ 10% on ₹12,62,500 [A]—1,26,250
Add: SWS @ 10% [B]—12,625
Landed value of imported goods [C]—14,01,375
Rate of commodity as per Anti-Dumping Notification, per kg.US$ 40—
Quantity imported500 kg—
Value as per notification (500 kg × US$ 40)US$ 20,000—
Exchange rate 1 US$₹90—
Market Value in ₹ [D]—18,00,000
Add: Anti-dumping Duty [E = D − C]—3,98,625
Value for levying IGST [F]—18,00,000
Add: IGST @ 18% of [F]—3,24,000
Total Customs Duty Payable [A + B + E + IGST]—8,61,500

Answer: Basic Customs Duty ₹1,26,250 + SWS ₹12,625 + Anti-dumping Duty ₹3,98,625 + IGST ₹3,24,000 = ₹8,61,500. Note the mechanics: the “landed value” against which the notified value is compared is Assessable Value + BCD + SWS (₹14,01,375); the anti-dumping duty is the shortfall to the notified market value; and because anti-dumping duty is a sum chargeable in the same manner as a duty of customs, it sits inside the IGST base — here the base becomes ₹18,00,000.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: COMPUTING SWS ON THE WRONG DUTIES

THE TRAP: the candidate totals every duty on the paper — BCD, anti-dumping duty, safeguard duty, IGST, cess — and takes 10% of that grand total as Social Welfare Surcharge.

THE TWIST: six items are expressly excluded from the SWS base — Safeguard Duty, Countervailing duty on subsidized article, Anti-dumping duty, IGST, GST Compensation cess and AIDC. In every illustration in this module SWS therefore comes out at exactly 10% of the Basic Customs Duty. And SWS is 3%, not 10%, for gold and silver (including platinum-plated, unwrought, semi-manufactured or powder form). Note also that SWS is levied on imports only — never on export.

CONCEPT

6.3 Valuation Rules ★★★ HIGH

The rate of customs duty leviable on imported or exported goods is either on a specific basis, or on an ad valorem basis (i.e. as a percentage of the value of goods), or at times specific-cum-ad valorem. Where the duty is ad valorem, the valuation of the goods may be determined either as transaction value u/s 14(1) or as tariff value u/s 14(2).

Valuation of Imported Goods [Sec. 14(1)] — the value of the imported goods shall be the transaction value of such goods, that is to say: the price actually paid or payable for the goods; when sold for export to India; for delivery at the time and place of importation; where the buyer and seller of the goods are not related; and where price is the sole consideration for the sale — subject to such other conditions as may be specified in the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007.

Taxpoint — what the transaction value must include. In addition to the price as aforesaid, any amount paid or payable for costs and services, including: commissions and brokerage (excluding buying commission); engineering, design work; royalties and licence fees; costs of transportation to the place of importation; insurance; and loading, unloading and handling charges — to the extent and in the manner specified in the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007.

Valuation of Export Goods [Sec. 14(1)] — the value of the exported goods shall be the transaction value of such goods, that is to say: the price actually paid or payable for the goods; when sold for export FROM India; for delivery at the time and place of EXPORTATION; where the buyer and seller of the goods are not related; and where price is the sole consideration for the sale — subject to such other conditions as may be specified in the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007.

Valuation on the basis of Tariff Value [Sec. 14(2)]. CBIC may fix tariff values for any class of imported or export goods, having regard to the trend of value of such or like goods; where any such tariff values are fixed, the duty shall be chargeable with reference to such tariff value. At present, tariff value has been fixed in respect of import for crude palm oil, crude palmolein, crude soyabean oil, brass scrap, poppy seeds, etc.

6.3.1 Date Relevant for Determination of the Rate of Exchange

The price shall be calculated with reference to the rate of exchange as in force on the date on which a bill of entry is presented u/s 46, or a shipping bill of export is presented u/s 50, as the case may be.

Import → date on which the bill of entry is presented u/s 46. Export → date on which the shipping bill of export is presented u/s 50.

Rate of exchange [Explanation to sec. 14] means the rate of exchange (i) determined by the Board (i.e. CBIC), or (ii) ascertained in such manner as the Board may direct, for conversion of Indian currency into foreign currency or foreign currency into Indian currency.

Rates are notified by (i) CBIC; (ii) RBI; and (iii) the Foreign Exchange Dealers' Association of India. For the purpose of customs, the rate notified by CBIC shall be considered. The selling rate is considered for import and the buying rate for export.

6.3.2 The Sequential Valuation Methods for Imported Goods

The methods must be followed in hierarchical order — you may only move down one rung when the rung above genuinely fails.

Primary Method — Transaction Value [Rule 3]

Secondary Methods, in order: (1) Transaction value of identical goods [Rule 4] → (2) Transaction value of similar goods [Rule 5] → (3) Deductive value [Rule 7] → (4) Computed value [Rule 8] → (5) Residual method [Rule 9].

The one permitted swap: on the request of the importer (and, per Rule 6, with the approval of the proper officer), the order of application of Rule 7 (Deductive value) and Rule 8 (Computed value) shall be reversed. No other pair can be swapped.

RuleMethodWhat it does — in one line
Rule 3Transaction valueThe price actually paid or payable for THESE goods when sold for export to India, adjusted per Rule 10. The default.
Rule 4Transaction value of identical goodsBorrow the accepted transaction value of goods the SAME in all respects, sold for export to India and imported at or about the same time.
Rule 5Transaction value of similar goodsBorrow the accepted transaction value of goods with like characteristics and like component materials, commercially interchangeable, at or about the same time.
Rule 6Bridge provisionIf value cannot be determined under Rules 3, 4 and 5, determine it under Rule 7 or, failing that, Rule 8 — the order being reversible at the importer's request with the proper officer's approval.
Rule 7Deductive valueWork BACKWARDS from the Indian selling price in the greatest aggregate quantity to unrelated persons, stripping out Indian commission/profit and general expenses, Indian transport and insurance, and the customs duty and Indian taxes.
Rule 8Computed valueBuild FORWARDS from the producer's own costings: materials and fabrication + general expenses and profit + Rule 10(2) transport and insurance.
Rule 9Residual methodReasonable means consistent with the principles and general provisions of these Rules, using data available in India — subject to a ceiling and seven forbidden bases.
Rule 10Cost and servicesNot a valuation method — the list of additions to the price actually paid or payable, and the Rule 10(2) freight/insurance rules.
Rule 11Declaration by importerProcedure — the importer's declaration and supporting documents.
Rule 12Rejection of declared valueProcedure — not a valuation method at all; a mechanism for rejecting the declared value, after which one proceeds sequentially through Rules 4 to 9.
Rule 13Interpretative notesThe notes in the Schedule to the Rules apply for their interpretation.

6.3.3 Transaction Value [Rule 3] — the Five Acceptance Conditions

Transaction value shall be accepted as price provided the following conditions are satisfied.

  1. The sale is in the ordinary course of trade under fully competitive conditions.
  2. There are no restrictions as to the disposition or use of the goods by the buyer, other than restrictions which (a) are imposed or required by law or by public authorities in India; or (b) limit the geographical area in which the goods may be resold; or (c) do not substantially affect the value of the goods.
  3. The sale or price is not subject to a condition or consideration for which a value cannot be determined.
  4. No part of the proceeds of subsequent resale, disposal or use of the goods by the buyer will be shared with the seller, unless an appropriate adjustment is made.
  5. The buyer and seller are not related.

Related persons — persons shall be deemed to be related if:

1. they are officers or directors of one another's businesses; 2. they are legally recognized partners in business; 3. they are employer and employee; 4. any person owns, controls or holds 5% or more of the voting rights of both of them; 5. one of them controls the other; 6. both of them are controlled by a third person; 7. together they control a third person; 8. they are members of the same family.

(a) “Person” also includes legal persons. (b) Persons associated in business such that one is the sole agent, sole distributor or sole concessionaire of the other, howsoever described, shall be deemed to be related for the purpose of these rules if they fall within the criteria of this sub-rule. Note to rule 2: one person shall be deemed to control another when the former is legally or operationally in a position to exercise restraint or direction over the latter.

When a related-party price is STILL accepted. The transaction value shall be accepted even where the buyer and seller are related, in the following cases:

  • the examination of the circumstances of the sale of the imported goods indicates that the relationship did not influence the price; or
  • the importer demonstrates that the value of the goods being valued closely approximates to one of the following values ascertained at or about the same time — (i) the transaction value of identical goods, or of similar goods, in sales to unrelated buyers in India; (ii) the deductive value for identical goods or similar goods; (iii) the computed value for identical goods or similar goods.

Notes. While comparing prices, due account shall be taken of differences in commercial levels, quantity levels and costs incurred by the seller in sales to an unrelated buyer — e.g. the price of 1,000 units is not comparable with the price of 1,00,000 units. While determining the value of identical or similar goods, a substitute value shall not be taken. In determining whether one value “closely approximates” another, factors include the nature of the imported goods, the nature of the industry, the season in which the goods are imported, and whether the difference in values is commercially significant — so no uniform standard such as a fixed percentage can be applied. Where a test under Rule 3(3)(b) is met, it is not necessary to examine the question of influence under Rule 3(3)(a).

Note to rule 3 — price actually paid or payable. This is the total payment made or to be made by the buyer to or for the benefit of the seller for the imported goods. The payment need not take the form of a transfer of money — it may be by letters of credit or negotiable instruments, and may be made directly or indirectly (an example of an indirect payment being the settlement by the buyer, in whole or in part, of a debt owed by the seller). Activities undertaken by the buyer on his own account, other than those for which an adjustment is provided in Rule 10, are not considered an indirect payment to the seller, even though they might be regarded as of benefit to him. The value shall not include the following charges, provided they are distinguished from the price actually paid or payable: (a) charges for construction, erection, assembly, maintenance or technical assistance undertaken after importation on imported goods such as industrial plant, machinery or equipment; (b) the cost of transport after importation; (c) duties and taxes in India. The flow of dividends or other payments from the buyer to the seller that do not relate to the imported goods are not part of the customs value.

6.3.4 Rule 10 — Additions to the Price Actually Paid or Payable

The transaction value of imported goods shall be the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to India, adjusted in accordance with the provisions of rule 10. As per Rule 10, the following costs or values (being not already included in the price) shall be ADDED.

  1. The following costs and services, to the extent they are incurred by the buyer — (a) commission and brokerage, except buying commissions; (b) the cost of containers; (c) the cost of packing, whether for labour or materials.
  2. The appropriate value of the following goods and services supplied by the buyer free of charge or at reduced cost for use in the production and sale for export of the imported goods — (a) materials, components, parts and similar items incorporated in the imported goods; (b) tools, dies, moulds and similar items used in the production of the imported goods; (c) materials consumed in the production of the imported goods; (d) engineering, development, art work, design work, plans and sketches undertaken elsewhere than in India and necessary for the production of the imported goods.
  3. Royalties and licence fees related to the imported goods that the buyer is required to pay as a condition of the sale of such goods.
  4. The value of any part of the proceeds of any subsequent resale, disposal or use of such goods that accrues to the seller.
  5. All other payments actually paid or payable by the buyer to the seller, or by the buyer to a third party to satisfy an obligation of the seller.

Additions under this rule shall be made on the basis of objective and quantifiable data. Where objective and quantifiable data do not exist for the required additions, the transaction value cannot be determined under Rule 3.

Note to Rule 10(1)(c) — royalties and licence fees. These may include, among other things, payments in respect of patents, trademarks and copyrights. However, charges for the right to reproduce the imported goods in the country of importation shall not be added. Payments made by the buyer for the right to distribute or resell the imported goods shall not be added if such payments are not a condition of the sale for export to the country of importation.

Note to Rule 10(1)(b)(ii) — apportioning a mould or tool. Two factors are involved: the value of the element itself, and the way that value is apportioned to the imported goods. If the importer acquires the element from an unrelated seller at a given cost, the value is that cost; if he produced it himself or through a related person, the value is the cost of producing it; if it had been previously used, the original cost must be adjusted downward to reflect its use. As an illustration — an importer provides the producer with a mould to be used in producing the imported goods and contracts to buy 10,000 units. By the time of arrival of the first shipment of 1,000 units, the producer has already produced 4,000 units. The importer may request the proper officer of customs to apportion the value of the mould over 1,000 units, 4,000 units or 10,000 units — the method of apportionment used will depend upon the documentation provided by the importer.

6.3.5 Price for Delivery at the Time and Place of Importation [Rule 10(2)]

The value of imported goods shall be the price for delivery at the time and place of importation. Hence it includes (a) the cost of transport, loading, unloading and handling charges associated with the delivery of the imported goods to the place of importation; and (b) the cost of insurance to the place of importation.

Where the cost is NOT ascertained — the deemed additions

Cost of transport = 20% of the FOB value of goods.
Cost of insurance = 1.125% of the FOB value of goods.

Where goods are imported by AIR, the cost of transport — whether ascertained or not — shall be restricted to 20% of the FOB value of goods.

So for air imports the 20% figure is a ceiling, not merely a fallback: even a known, actual air freight above 20% of FOB is cut down to 20%.

FOB value = Cost of production + Profit of the manufacturer + Freight in foreign country + Local taxes + Loading charges + Export duty and cess

The two reverse-working rules under Rule 10

Where the FOB value is not ascertainable but the sum of (FOB + insurance) is → the transport cost shall be 20% of such sum. Where the FOB value is not ascertainable but the sum of (FOB + transport cost) is → the insurance cost shall be 1.125% of such sum. Where CIF value is given but transport cost is not available → Cost of transport = CIF Value × 20/120. Where CIF value is given but insurance cost is not available → Cost of insurance = CIF Value × 1.125/101.125.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: THE THREE FREIGHT-AND-INSURANCE MISTAKES

THE TRAP: (i) applying the actual air freight because it is “given in the question”; (ii) computing insurance at 1.125% of the CIF or of the plain price rather than of FOB as per Customs; (iii) using 20% of FOB for sea freight even when the actual sea freight IS given.

THE TWIST: for air transport the 20%-of-FOB figure is a hard ceiling — whether the actual freight is ascertained or not, it is restricted to 20% of FOB (so a stated air freight of $3,500 on a $10,000 FOB becomes $2,000). For sea transport, 20% is only a fallback when the actual is unascertained — if the actual is given, use the actual. Insurance is 1.125% of FOB value as per Customs and only when the actual is unascertained; if the actual insurance figure is given (even in rupees), take the actual.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: DESIGN CHARGES — ADDED OR NOT?

THE TRAP: a candidate either adds every design/development figure in the question, or drops all of them as “post-shipment”.

THE TWIST: the test is WHERE the work was undertaken. Rule 10 adds engineering, development, art work, design work, plans and sketches undertaken elsewhere than in India and necessary for the production of the imported goods — so Illustration 7's 60,000-Yen Japanese designing charge and Illustration 11's $2,000 USA design charge are both added, and Illustration 9's 500-UKP U.K. engineering charge is added too. Work done in India (Illustration 7's ₹2,00,000 development activity, Illustration 11's ₹50,000 Indian development work, Illustration 18's ₹15,000 designing charges incurred in India) is never added.

6.3.6 Transaction Value of Identical Goods [Rule 4] and of Similar Goods [Rule 5]

Rule 4. The value of imported goods shall be the transaction value of identical goods sold for export to India and imported at or about the same time as the goods being valued. Rule 5. The value shall be the transaction value of similar goods sold for export to India and imported at or about the same time as the goods being valued.

BasisIdentical goods [Rule 4]Similar goods [Rule 5]
Core testImported goods which are same in all respects, including physical characteristics, quality and reputation, as the goods being valued — except for minor differences in appearance that do not affect the value.Imported goods which, although not alike in all respects, have like characteristics and like component materials which enable them to perform the same function, and which are commercially interchangeable with the goods being valued, having regard to quality, reputation and the existence of a trade mark.
CountryProduced in the country in which the goods being valued were produced.Produced in the country in which the goods being valued were produced.
ProducerProduced by the same person who produced the goods; where no such goods are available, goods produced by a different manufacturer.Produced by the same person who produced the goods; where no such goods are available, goods produced by a different manufacturer.
ExclusionDo NOT include goods where engineering, development, art work, design work, plan or sketch was done by the buyer in India free of charge or at a reduced cost.Do NOT include goods where engineering, development, art work, design work, plan or sketch was done by the buyer in India free of charge or at a reduced cost.
Commercial / quantity levelShall be sold at the same commercial and quantity level; where no such sale is found, the transaction value of identical goods sold at a different commercial level, or in a different quantity, or both, shall be used with certain adjustment.Shall be sold at the same commercial and quantity level; where no such sale is found, the transaction value of similar goods sold at a different commercial level, or in a different quantity, or both, shall be used with certain adjustment.
Multiple valuesWhere more than one transaction value is found, the LOWEST of such values shall be used.Where more than one transaction value is found, the LOWEST of such values shall be used.

Notes to Rule 4 (applying mutatis mutandis to Rule 5). The proper officer shall, wherever possible, use a sale of identical goods at the same commercial level and in substantially the same quantities. Where no such sale is found, a sale under any ONE of three conditions may be used — (a) same commercial level but different quantities; (b) different commercial level but substantially the same quantities; (c) different commercial level AND different quantities — with adjustments then made for (a) quantity factors only, (b) commercial level factors only, or (c) both. The transaction value of identical imported goods means a value already accepted under Rule 3, adjusted as provided in Rule 4. Any adjustment for different commercial levels or quantities — whether it increases or decreases the value — must be made only on demonstrated evidence clearly establishing its reasonableness and accuracy, e.g. valid price lists containing prices for different levels or quantities. Example: if the goods being valued are a shipment of 10 units and the only identical goods with a transaction value involved a sale of 500 units, and the seller is recognised to grant quantity discounts, the adjustment may be made by resorting to the seller's price list and using the price applicable to a sale of 10 units — it is not necessary that a sale in quantities of 10 had actually been made, so long as the price list is bona fide. In the absence of such an objective measure, a Rule 4 determination is not appropriate.

Rule 6 — the bridge. If the value cannot be determined under Rules 3, 4 and 5, it shall be determined under Rule 7 or, when it cannot be determined under that rule, under Rule 8. However, at the request of the importer and with the approval of the proper officer, the order of application of Rules 7 and 8 shall be reversed.

6.3.7 Deductive Value [Rule 7]

Where the goods being valued, or identical or similar imported goods, are sold in India at or about the time of determination of value, the value of imported goods shall be based on the unit price at which such goods are sold in the greatest aggregate quantity to unrelated persons in India, as REDUCED by —

  • (a) the commission usually paid or payable, or the additions usually made for profits and general expenses, for sales in India;
  • (b) the cost of transport and insurance and other costs incurred within India;
  • (c) the customs duty and other taxes payable in India by reason of importation or sale of the goods.
  1. Where such goods are not sold at or about the same time of importation of the goods being valued, the value shall be based on the unit price at which the imported goods (or identical or similar imported goods) are sold in India at the earliest date after importation but before the expiry of 90 days after such importation.
  2. Where such goods are sold in India after further processing, the value shall be based on the unit price at which the imported goods after processing are sold in the greatest aggregate quantity to unrelated persons in India, as reduced by the processing and other costs incurred in India.

“Unit price at which goods are sold in the greatest aggregate quantity” = the price at which the greatest NUMBER of units is sold, in sales to persons not related to the persons from whom they buy such goods, at the first commercial level after importation at which such sales take place.

It is not the largest single sale, and not the average price. Group the sales by PRICE, total the units at each price, and pick the price attached to the largest total.

Working equation used in the source's Rule 7 computation:

Assessable Value + Customs duty = Unit sale price in the greatest aggregate quantity − Expenditure incurred in India — and since customs duty is itself a percentage of assessable value, this resolves to (100% + duty rate) × Assessable Value = the net figure.

Further points from the notes to Rule 7. Any sale in India to a person who supplies, directly or indirectly, free of charge or at reduced cost, any of the Rule 10(1)(b) elements for use in connection with the production and sale for export of the imported goods should not be taken into account in establishing the unit price. “Profit and general expenses” must be taken as a whole, determined on information supplied by or on behalf of the importer unless his figures are inconsistent with those obtaining in sales in India of imported goods of the same class or kind. “General expenses” include the direct and indirect costs of marketing the goods in question. Local taxes payable by reason of the sale of the goods, for which a deduction is not made under Rule 7(1)(iii), shall be deducted under Rule 7(1)(i). Whether goods are “of the same class or kind” must be determined case by case — the narrowest group or range of imported goods of the same class or kind which includes the goods being valued should be examined; for Rule 7 this includes goods imported from the same country as the goods being valued as well as goods imported from other countries. The “earliest date” under Rule 7(2) is the date by which sales are made in sufficient quantity to establish the unit price. Under Rule 7(3), deductions for the value added by further processing shall be based on objective and quantifiable data relating to the cost of such work, using accepted industry formulas, recipes, methods of construction and other industry practices. Rule 7(3) would normally not apply where the imported goods lose their identity as a result of further processing — though there can be instances where, although identity is lost, the value added can be determined accurately without unreasonable difficulty; and equally, instances where the goods keep their identity but form so minor an element of the goods sold in India that this method would be unjustified. Each such situation must be considered case by case.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: PICKING THE BIGGEST SINGLE SALE, OR FORGETTING THE 90-DAY CUT-OFF

THE TRAP: the candidate scans the sale list, spots the largest single transaction (2,000 units at ₹100 on 7-5-2026, or 2,000 units at ₹98 on 10-1-2026) and takes that unit price; or averages the prices; or includes every sale in the table.

THE TWIST: first strike out any sale after 90 days from importation (the 7-5-2026 sale goes). Then total the units at each PRICE across all remaining dates — ₹98 carries 4,000 units, more than any other price — and take ₹98. Then remember the second half: what remains after deducting Indian expenditure is Assessable Value PLUS duty, so you must gross down by (100% + 25%), not simply take ₹80 as the assessable value.

6.3.8 Computed Value [Rule 8] and Residual Method [Rule 9]

Rule 8 — Computed Value. The value of imported goods shall consist of — (a) the cost or value of materials and fabrication or other processing employed in producing the imported goods; (b) an amount for general expenses and profit made by producers in the country of exportation for export to India; (c) the cost of transport, insurance, etc. as referred to in Rule 10(2). This method is normally possible when the importer in India and the foreign exporter are closely associated and the foreign exporter is willing to give the necessary costing.

Computed Value Proforma [Rule 8]
Particulars₹
Cost of materials and general expenses for producing the imported goodsxx
Add: Profit of the exporterxx
Add: All expenditure as per Rule 10xx
Assessable Valuexx

Notes to Rule 8. As a general rule, value is determined on the basis of information readily available in India; to determine a computed value, however, it may be necessary to examine the costs of producing the goods and other information obtained from outside India, and in most cases the producer is outside the proper officer's jurisdiction. Use of the computed value method will therefore generally be limited to cases where buyer and seller are related and the producer is prepared to supply the necessary costings and to provide facilities for subsequent verification. The “cost or value” is determined on information supplied by or on behalf of the producer, based on his commercial accounts, provided those accounts are consistent with the generally accepted accounting principles applied in the country of production; it shall include the cost of the elements specified in Rule 10(1)(a)(ii) and (iii), and the apportioned value of any Rule 10(1)(b) element supplied by the buyer — with elements under Rule 10(1)(b)(iv) undertaken in India included only to the extent charged to the producer, and no cost or value counted twice. The “amount for profit and general expenses” is determined from the producer's information unless inconsistent with that usually reflected in sales of goods of the same class or kind made by producers in the country of exportation for export to India; it must be taken as a whole, so a low profit offset by high general expenses may still be consistent (for example where a product is being launched in India). “General expenses” under Rule 8 covers the direct and indirect costs of producing and selling the goods for export not already included under clause (a). For Rule 8, “goods of the same class or kind” must be from the same country as the goods being valued.

Rule 9 — Residual method. Where the value of imported goods cannot be determined as per any preceding rule, the value shall be determined using — reasonable means consistent with the principles; the general provisions of these rules; and data available in India.

Ceiling: the value so determined shall not exceed the price at which such or like goods are ordinarily sold or offered for sale for delivery at the time and place of importation in the course of international trade — where the seller or buyer has no interest in the business of the other and price is the sole consideration for the sale or offer for sale.

Seven bases on which NO value shall be determined under Rule 9:

(a) the selling price in India of goods produced in India; (b) a system which provides acceptance of the value being the higher of two alternative values; (c) the price of the goods on domestic markets of the country of exportation; (d) the cost of production (other than computed value) for identical or similar goods; (e) the price of the goods for export to a country other than India; (f) minimum customs values; (g) arbitrary or fictitious values.

Notes to Rule 9. Value under Rule 9 should, to the greatest extent possible, be based on previously determined customs values. The methods employed may be those laid down in Rules 3 to 8 inclusive, but a reasonable flexibility in their application would be in conformity with the aims and provisions of Rule 9 — for example: for identical goods, the “at or about the same time” requirement could be flexibly interpreted, identical goods produced in a country other than the country of exportation could be the basis, and customs values of identical goods already determined under Rules 7 and 8 could be used; the same flexibility applies for similar goods; and for the deductive method, the “condition as imported” requirement in Rule 7(1) could be flexibly interpreted and the ninety-days requirement administered flexibly.

6.3.9 Declaration by the Importer [Rule 11] and Rejection of Declared Value [Rule 12]

Rule 11. The importer or his agent shall furnish — (a) a declaration disclosing full and accurate details relating to the value of imported goods; and (b) any other statement, information or document, including an invoice of the manufacturer or producer of the imported goods (where the goods are exported by a person other than the manufacturer or producer), as considered necessary by the proper officer for determination of the value. The declaration inter alia includes: the relationship between buyer and seller; the basis of the declared value; conditions and restrictions attached with the sale; and costs not included in the invoice. The provisions of the Customs Act, 1962 relating to confiscation, penalty and prosecution apply to cases where a wrong statement, information, document or declaration is furnished under these rules.

Rule 12. When the proper officer has reason to doubt the truth or accuracy of the value declared, he may ask the importer to furnish further information including documents or other evidence. Where, even after receiving such information — or in the absence of a response — the proper officer has reasonable doubt about the truth or accuracy of the value declared, then it shall be deemed that the value cannot be determined under transaction value. At the request of an importer, the proper officer shall intimate the importer in writing the grounds for doubting the truth and accuracy of the declared value, and provide a reasonable opportunity of being heard before taking a final decision.

Rule 12 does NOT by itself provide a method for determination of value — it provides a mechanism and procedure for rejection of the declared value where there is reasonable doubt that it does not represent the transaction value. Where the declared value is rejected, the value shall be determined by proceeding sequentially in accordance with rules 4 to 9.

The declared value shall be ACCEPTED where the proper officer is satisfied about its truth and accuracy after the said enquiry in consultation with the importer.

Grounds on which the proper officer may raise doubts include: (a) the significantly higher value at which identical or similar goods imported at or about the same time in comparable quantities in a comparable commercial transaction were assessed; (b) the sale involves an abnormal discount or abnormal reduction from the ordinary competitive price; (c) the sale involves special discounts limited to exclusive agents; (d) the misdeclaration of goods in parameters such as description, quality, quantity, country of origin, year of manufacture or production; (e) the non-declaration of parameters such as brand, grade, specifications that have relevance to value; (f) fraudulent or manipulated documents.

Rule 13 — Interpretative notes. The interpretative notes specified in the Schedule to these rules shall apply for the interpretation of these rules. The General Note explains that “generally accepted accounting principles” refers to the recognised consensus or substantial authoritative support within a country at a particular time as to which economic resources and obligations shall be recorded as assets and liabilities, which changes should be recorded, how they should be measured, what information should be disclosed and how, and which financial statements should be prepared — standards that may be broad guidelines of general application as well as detailed practices and procedures.

6.3.10 Valuation of EXPORT Goods

The value of export goods shall be deemed to be the price at which such or like goods are ordinarily sold or offered for sale for delivery at the time and place of exportation in the course of international trade.

That price is taken into consideration only when the following conditions are satisfied — (a) the seller and the buyer have no interest in the business of each other; (b) one of them has no interest in the business of the other; and (c) the price is the sole consideration for the sale or offer for sale.

  • Price shall be calculated with reference to the rate of exchange in force on the date on which a shipping bill or bill of export is presented. The rate determined by the Board shall be considered.
  • Generally, the free on board value shall be considered as the price for export. If the export sale contract is a CIF contract, then post-exportation elements like insurance and freight are required to be adjusted (i.e. stripped out).

Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007 — they came into force on the 10th day of October, 2007 and apply to export goods.

RuleProvision
Rule 2 — Definitions(a) Goods of like kind and quality means export goods which are identical or similar in physical characteristics, quality and reputation as the goods being valued, and perform the same functions or are commercially interchangeable with the goods being valued, produced by the same person OR a different person. (b) Transaction Value means the value of export goods within the meaning of sec. 14(1) of the Customs Act, 1962.
Rule 3 — Determination of the method of valuation(1) Subject to rule 8, the value of export goods shall be the transaction value. (2) The transaction value shall be accepted even where the buyer and seller are related, provided that the relationship has not influenced the price. (3) If the value cannot be determined under sub-rules (1) and (2), it shall be determined by proceeding sequentially through rules 4 to 6.
Rule 4 — Determination of export value by comparison(1) The value shall be based on the transaction value of goods of like kind and quality exported at or about the same time to other buyers in the same destination country of importation, or in its absence another destination country of importation, adjusted per sub-rule (2). (2) The proper officer shall make such adjustments as appear reasonable, taking into consideration — (i) difference in the dates of exportation; (ii) difference in commercial levels and quantity levels; (iii) difference in composition, quality and design between the goods to be assessed and the goods compared; (iv) difference in domestic freight and insurance charges depending on the place of exportation.
Rule 5 — Computed value methodIf the value cannot be determined under rule 4, it shall be based on a computed value which shall include — (a) cost of production, manufacture or processing of export goods; (b) charges, if any, for the design or brand; (c) an amount towards profit.
Rule 6 — Residual methodSubject to rule 3, where the value cannot be determined under rules 4 and 5, it shall be determined using reasonable means consistent with the principles and general provisions of these rules — provided that the local market price of the export goods may not be the ONLY basis for determining the value of export goods.
Rule 7 — Declaration by the exporterThe exporter shall furnish a declaration relating to the value of export goods in the manner specified in this behalf.
Rule 8 — Rejection of declared value(1) Where the proper officer has reason to doubt the truth or accuracy of the declared value, he may ask for further information, documents or evidence; if, after receiving it, or in the absence of a response, he still has reasonable doubt, the transaction value shall be deemed not to have been determined in accordance with rule 3(1). (2) At the exporter's request, the proper officer shall intimate in writing the ground for doubting the declared value and provide a reasonable opportunity of being heard before taking a final decision.
Explanation to Rule 8. This rule by itself does not provide a method for determination of value — it provides a mechanism and procedure for rejection of the declared value; where the declared value is rejected, the value shall be determined by proceeding sequentially in accordance with rules 4 to 6. The declared value shall be accepted where the proper officer is satisfied about its truth or accuracy after the said inquiry in consultation with the exporter. Grounds for doubt may include — (a) significant variation in the value at which goods of like kind and quality exported at or about the same time in comparable quantities in a comparable commercial transaction were assessed; (b) a significantly higher value compared to the market value of goods of like kind and quality at the time of export; (c) the declaration of goods in parameters such as description, quality, quantity, year of manufacture or production.
BasisIMPORT goodsEXPORT goods
Governing RulesCustoms Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007.Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007 — in force from 10th October, 2007.
Sec. 14(1) framingPrice actually paid or payable, when sold for export TO India, for delivery at the time and place of importation.Price actually paid or payable, when sold for export FROM India, for delivery at the time and place of exportation.
Sequence of fallback methodsRule 3 → 4 (identical) → 5 (similar) → 7 (deductive) → 8 (computed) → 9 (residual); Rules 7 and 8 reversible on request.Rule 3 (transaction value) → 4 (comparison) → 5 (computed) → 6 (residual). Only four rungs.
Related partiesRelationship is a bar to transaction value under Rule 3, unless the circumstances show the relationship did not influence the price, or a “test value” is closely approximated.Transaction value is accepted even where buyer and seller are related, provided the relationship has not influenced the price.
Relevant date for exchange rateDate on which the bill of entry is presented u/s 46 (CBIC selling rate).Date on which the shipping bill of export is presented u/s 50 (CBIC buying rate).
Freight and insuranceAdded up to the place of importation to build CIF = assessable value.FOB is generally the price; under a CIF contract the post-exportation insurance and freight are adjusted out.
Social Welfare SurchargeApplicable @ 10% (3% for gold/silver).Not levied on export.
Duty scheduleFirst Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975.Second Schedule — and in general no duty is payable on export, except on notified goods such as leather goods, ferrous waste and scrap, snake skins.
CONCEPT

6.4 Computation of Assessable Value and Duties ★★★ HIGH

This is the most heavily examined topic of the module. Two questions have to be answered before a single figure is written: which date fixes the rate of duty, and which date fixes the rate of exchange. They are not always the same date. Then the ladder is applied.

Date for determination of rate of duty and tariff valuation of IMPORTED goods [Sec. 15]. The rate of duty and tariff valuation (if any) applicable to any imported goods shall be the rate and valuation in force —

CaseRate and Tariff Value, if any, in force on…
Goods entered for home consumption u/s 46Date on which the bill of entry is presented.
Goods cleared from a warehouse for home consumptionDate on which the bill of entry for home consumption is presented.
In any other caseDate on which duty is paid.

The deeming rule for an early bill of entry

Where a bill of entry has been presented BEFORE the date of — entry inwards of the vessel: the bill of entry shall be deemed to have been presented on the date of such entry inwards. Arrival of the aircraft or vehicle: the bill of entry shall be deemed to have been presented on the date of arrival of the aircraft or vehicle.

BUT — for determining ASSESSABLE VALUE, the rate of exchange in force on the actual submission of the bill of entry shall be taken.

So the deeming fiction moves the RATE OF DUTY date forward; it does not move the EXCHANGE RATE date. Two different dates can therefore govern one computation.

Example (from the source): if the bill of entry is presented on 10-10-2025 and the aircraft arrived on 20-10-2025, the relevant date for determination of rate of duty and tariff valuation is 20-10-2025. Though the bill of entry is presented on 10-10-2025 for procedural purposes, for the purpose of determination of rate of duty and tariff valuation the bill of entry will be deemed to have been filed on 20-10-2025.

  • The provisions of Sec. 15 shall not apply to baggage and goods imported by post.
  • Social Welfare Surcharge @ 10% of the basic customs duty is also applicable.
  • Integrated tax (IGST) is also payable at the applicable rate on assessable value + basic duty + social welfare surcharge. Import is considered an inter-State supply under GST laws and liable for reverse charge.

Date for determination of rate of duty and tariff valuation of EXPORT goods [Sec. 16].

CaseRate and Tariff Value, if any, in force on…
When goods are entered for export u/s 50Date on which the proper officer makes an order permitting clearance and loading of the goods for exportation u/s 51.
In any other caseDate on which duty is paid.
The provisions of this section shall not apply to baggage and goods imported by post.
⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: USING ONE DATE FOR BOTH THE DUTY RATE AND THE EXCHANGE RATE

THE TRAP: the bill of entry is filed on 20.01.2026 and entry inwards is granted on 25.01.2026, so the candidate deems the bill of entry filed on 25.01.2026 and uses the 25.01.2026 CBIC exchange rate (₹87) as well as the 25.01.2026 duty rate.

THE TWIST: the deeming fiction u/s 15 is confined to the rate of duty and tariff valuation. For determining assessable value, the rate of exchange in force on the actual submission of the bill of entry applies — in Illustration 14 that is the 20.01.2026 CBIC rate of ₹86, which is why the assessable value is $5,080 × ₹86 = ₹4,36,880. And note the mirror image: where the bill of entry is presented AFTER entry inwards (Illustrations 15 and 20), there is nothing to deem — the bill-of-entry date governs the duty rate too, so it is 10%, not the 20%/15% in force on the earlier date.

6.4.1 The Master Computation Ladder

STAGE 1 — Build the Assessable Value

FOB (or CIF less air freight less insurance, when CIF is what you are given) → add Rule 10 items not already inside (commission & brokerage except buying commission, packing, foreign design/engineering, royalties & licence fee as a condition of sale, buyer's free-issue materials, resale proceeds accruing to the seller) = FOB value as per Customs → add freight (actual; if unascertained 20% of FOB; by AIR capped at 20% of FOB) → add lighterage/barge charges and ship demurrage on chartered vessels → add insurance (actual; if unascertained 1.125% of FOB) = CIF = ASSESSABLE VALUE [A]. Convert foreign currency at the CBIC rate on the date of actual presentation of the bill of entry.

STAGE 2 — Stack the Duties

[B] Basic Customs Duty = A × BCD rate
[C] Social Welfare Surcharge = B × 10% (3% for gold/silver)
[D] Value for computing IGST = A + B + C (plus anti-dumping/safeguard duty and AIDC where levied)
[E] IGST = D × IGST rate
[F] GST Compensation Cess = D × cess rate
TOTAL DUTY AND TAX PAYABLE = B + C + E + F

Two shortcuts the source itself uses. (i) Where only BCD and SWS are in play, the combined effective rate can be written directly — e.g. BCD 12% + SWS 10% of BCD = 13.20% of assessable value (Illustration 16). (ii) The IGST charged here is creditable — ITC under GST law is available for the IGST and the Compensation Cess paid on import.

ILLUSTRATION 12 — The Ladder in Its Simplest Form

Assessable value of an item imported is ₹2,00,000. Basic customs duty is 10%, integrated tax is 18%, and social welfare surcharge is 10% on duty. Compute the amount of total customs duty and integrated tax payable. Ignore GST Compensation Cess.

Computation of Customs Duty
Particulars₹
1. Assessable Value2,00,000
2. Basic customs duty @ 10%20,000
3. Add: Social Welfare Surcharge @ 10% on ₹20,0002,000
4. Sub-total2,22,000
5. Integrated tax @ 18% of ₹2,22,00039,960
6. Total customs duty and integrated tax payable [(2) + (3) + (5)]61,960

Answer: total customs duty and integrated tax payable = ₹61,960. Note what is NOT in the total: the assessable value itself and the sub-total are working figures only — only lines (2), (3) and (5) are duty or tax.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: STACKING THE DUTIES IN THE WRONG ORDER, ON THE WRONG BASE

THE TRAP: the four commonest wrong ladders — (i) computing SWS on the assessable value instead of on the BCD; (ii) computing IGST on the bare assessable value, leaving BCD and SWS out of its base; (iii) computing IGST on a base that already contains the Compensation Cess, or the cess on a base that already contains the IGST; (iv) adding the assessable value or the sub-total into the “total duty payable” figure.

THE TWIST: the order is fixed and each rung has its own base. BCD is on the assessable value. SWS is 10% of the BCD (and excludes safeguard duty, countervailing duty on subsidized articles, anti-dumping duty, IGST, GST Compensation Cess and AIDC from its base). IGST is on A + B + C — Sec. 3(7) requires the Sec. 14 value plus customs duty plus any sum chargeable in the same manner as a duty of customs (so anti-dumping and safeguard duty enter this base, as in Illustration 4), but expressly excludes the IGST itself and the Compensation Cess. The Compensation Cess is on that SAME base, parallel to the IGST, not on top of it. And the total duty payable is only B + C + E + F — the assessable value and the intermediate sub-totals are working figures, never part of the answer.

10. If more than one transaction value of identical goods is found at the same commercial level and quantity, which value shall be used?

(a) The highest value.(b) The average value.(c) The lowest of such values.(d) The latest value.
QCorrectReason
1(c)The price is calculated with reference to the rate of exchange in force on the date on which the bill of entry is presented u/s 46.
2(c)Where goods are imported by air, the cost of transport (whether ascertained or not) shall be restricted to 20% of the FOB value of the goods.
3(d)Transaction value includes commissions and brokerage but specifically excludes buying commission.
4(b)Rule 10 requires the addition of the value of engineering, development, art work and design work undertaken elsewhere than in India and necessary for the production of the imported goods.
5(b)Where the cost of insurance is not ascertained, 1.125% of the FOB value of the goods shall be added.
6(b)The value shall be based on the unit price at which such goods are sold in the greatest aggregate quantity to unrelated persons in India.
7(b)If the bill of entry has been presented before the date of entry inwards, the bill of entry shall be deemed to have been presented on the date of such entry inwards. Thus, the rate in force on that later date applies.
8(b)On the request of the importer, the order of application of Rules 7 (Deductive value) and 8 (Computed value) shall be reversed.
9(b)In case of export, the price shall be calculated with reference to the rate of exchange in force on the date on which a shipping bill of export is presented u/s 50.
