Every wrong figure and every misplaced Section number traces back to one of these confusions. The first four are this paper's signature traps — they run right across both halves. Read once, slowly, the morning of the exam.

1. The same Section number means different things in three different statutes — always name the Act before the number. Sec. 14 is the five heads of income under the Income-tax Act, valuation under the Customs Act, and change in rate of tax under the CGST Act. Sec. 15 is the "due or receipt, whichever is earlier" basis of charge for Salaries, the value of supply under CGST, and the date determining the rate of duty on imports under Customs. Sec. 16 is the two deductions from Gross Salary, the ITC eligibility conditions under CGST, and zero-rated supply under the IGST Act. Sec. 22, 23 and 24 are the house-property charge, annual value and deductions under the Income-tax Act, but persons liable / not liable / compulsorily liable to register under CGST, and abatement, remission and denaturing under Customs. Sec. 50 is the always-short-term rule for depreciable assets under the Income-tax Act and interest on delayed payment under CGST.

2. Almost every deduction and exemption you know is regime-dependent, and the DEFAULT regime is the one that applies unless the assessee opts out. Blocked under Sec. 115BAC(1A): Sec. 10(5) LTC, 10(13A) HRA, 10(14) special allowances, 10(17), 10(32) minor-child exemption, 10AA SEZ, the Sec. 16(ii) entertainment allowance and 16(iii) professional tax, Sec. 24(b) interest on a SELF-OCCUPIED house, additional depreciation, Sec. 32AD, 33AB/33ABA, 35AD, 35CCC and the whole of Chapter VI-A except 80CCD(2), 80CCH(2), 80JJAA and 80LA. Surviving: the ₹75,000 standard deduction u/s 16(ia), and Sec. 24(b) interest on a LET-OUT or deemed-let-out property.

3. Exempt, nil-rated, zero-rated and non-GST are four separate categories and only one of them preserves the credit chain. Zero-rated [Sec. 16, IGST Act] — exports and SEZ supplies: no tax on the outward supply, but ITC may be availed and refunded. Nil-rated — taxable in principle at a nil rate. Exempt [Sec. 2(47)] — nil-rated or wholly exempted u/s 11 CGST / Sec. 6 IGST, and it expressly INCLUDES non-taxable supply; no ITC. Non-taxable [Sec. 2(78)] — outside the levy altogether, such as alcoholic liquor for human consumption.

4. The customs duty stack has a fixed order and each rung has its own base. BCD is on the assessable value. SWS is 10% of the BCD alone — never on the assessable value, and its base excludes safeguard duty, countervailing duty on subsidized articles, anti-dumping duty, IGST, GST Compensation Cess and AIDC. IGST is on A + B + C. The Compensation Cess sits on the SAME base D as the IGST, in parallel, never on a figure that already contains the IGST. And the total is B + C + E + F — the assessable value and the sub-total are working figures, not duty.

5. A large one-time payment is not automatically a capital receipt, and expenditure that enhances an asset is not automatically capital. A ₹3,60,000 lump sum accepted instead of ₹10,000 a month for three years is still salary; a TENANT's renovation spend on a rented building stays revenue because the tenant acquires no capital asset of his own.

6. Residence is a strict TWO-STAGE test. Sec. 6(1) alone decides Resident versus Non-resident; only if Resident does Sec. 6(6) run, and BOTH its conditions (resident in 2 of the preceding 10 P.Y.s, and 730 days in the preceding 7) must be met for "Ordinarily Resident." A Non-resident never reaches Stage 2 at all.

7. Income earned on a farm is not automatically agricultural income. The test is whether it is DERIVED FROM LAND by agricultural operations — poultry, dairy, fisheries and livestock breeding all fail it, and interest, whether on a mortgage of agricultural land or on arrears of its rent, is a return on money rather than on land.

8. Sec. 10AA is not available under the default tax regime — and separately not available to a company or co-operative society that has opted for Sec. 115BAA / 115BAB / 115BAD / 115BAE. Check the regime before computing the SEZ export deduction at all.

9. Salary "due" is not salary "accrued" — read the due date, not the months worked. Where salary falls due on the 1st of the following month, an employee joining on 1st December 2025 has only December, January and February salary taxable in P.Y. 2025-26; March's salary is due on 1/4/2026 and belongs to the next previous year.

10. The two "completed year" rules for gratuity are opposite. Under the Payment of Gratuity Act a fraction in excess of 6 months counts as a full year, so 29 years 6 months 15 days = 30 years; where the Act does not cover the employee any fraction is simply ignored, so the identical service is 29 years. The salary base differs too.

11. The 10-month average window shifts between gratuity and leave encashment. For gratuity not covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act the 10 months are those PRECEDING the month of retirement; for leave encashment the 10 months END on the date of retirement itself.

12. The commuted-pension fraction applies to 100% commutation, not to the amount actually received. Where 80% commutation fetched ₹1,20,000, gross it up to ₹1,50,000 first, then exempt one-half or one-third of that figure.

13. HRA's 50%/40% limb looks at where the HOUSE is, not where the employee works. An employee posted in a metro but renting outside it gets 40%; one posted elsewhere but renting a metro house gets 50%. Recompute the whole three-limb test separately for each period when salary, rent, city or the fact of renting changes mid-year.

14. Rent-free accommodation is valued for the period OCCUPIED, not the period ALLOTTED. A house allotted from 1/5/2025 but occupiable only from 1/6/2025 carries 10 months of perquisite, not 11. Free refreshment, mobile/telephone and computer facilities never enter the RFA salary base.

15. Where the STATUTORY car value applies, the amount recovered from the employee is NOT subtracted. ₹2,400 + ₹900 a month stays ₹39,600 for the year even where ₹15,000 was charged to the employee; the deduction for the employee's contribution exists only where the value is built up from actual maintenance and depreciation.

16. The ₹20,000 concessional-loan figure is a gateway, not a deduction. Once the aggregate loan crosses it, notional interest is charged on the ENTIRE loan — on the maximum outstanding monthly balance, at the SBI rate prevailing on the FIRST day of the previous year for a loan of that same purpose.

17. Depreciation on a transferred perquisite asset runs in completed years from the DATE OF PURCHASE, not from 1st April. A computer bought on 1/7/2022 and sold to the employee on 18/8/2025 depreciates for three completed years ending 30/6/2025 — the stub after that earns nothing.

18. A URPF withdrawal splits four ways, across two heads. The employer's contribution and the interest on it are taxed as Salaries; the employee's own contribution is not taxable at all; the interest on the employee's contribution is taxed under Income from Other Sources.

19. Entertainment allowance goes IN first as a fully taxable allowance, and only then comes out as a Sec. 16(ii) deduction — and only for a Government employee, only under the old regime, with the ₹5,000 limb almost always binding.

20. Standard Rent is a CEILING on Reasonable Expected Rent, never a target. RER = lower of [higher of Gross Municipal Value and Fair Rent] and [Standard Rent]. Standard Rent can only pull RER down or leave it untouched — it can never push it up.

21. Municipal tax is deductible only if actually PAID, by the OWNER, and only after it has been levied. Outstanding tax, tax paid by the tenant and tax paid in advance of the levy are all inadmissible.

22. The ₹2,00,000 interest ceiling is ONE aggregate cap across both self-occupied houses, not ₹2,00,000 per house — and it exists only under the old regime. Under the default regime the self-occupied NAV stays Nil and no interest is deductible at all, so the income from that house is Nil, never negative. A company or firm can never claim the self-occupied benefit.

23. Capital and revenue expenditure have OPPOSITE defaults under PGBP. Capital expenditure is disallowed unless expressly allowed (Sec. 35, 35AD); revenue expenditure is allowed unless expressly barred (Sec. 40, 40A, 43B).

24. Sec. 30 and Sec. 31 do not cover every building or asset cost. They reach only rent, rates, taxes, repairs and insurance for buildings and repairs and insurance for plant, machinery and furniture. Rent paid to USE plant, machinery or furniture falls under the residuary Sec. 37(1).

25. The 180-day depreciation rule tests "acquired," not merely "used." Half-rate applies only where the asset was BOTH acquired in the current P.Y. AND put to use for less than 180 days in it. An asset carried over from an earlier year gets full depreciation however late it is used this year, and the date of SALE is irrelevant throughout.

26. The Explanation 5 "cost less notional depreciation" rule for personal-to-business conversion is BUILDING-ONLY. For any other personal asset brought into the business — a car, a laptop, jewellery — the ORIGINAL COST is simply taken as the actual cost.

27. Sec. 43A and Sec. 43AA are not interchangeable. Sec. 43A is narrow — it adjusts the actual cost of a specific imported asset for exchange movement at the time of payment. Sec. 43AA is general — it taxes or allows forex gain or loss across all foreign-currency transactions per ICDS, and steps aside wherever 43A already applies.

28. Interest paid to a proprietor, a partner and a relative follow three different rules. Interest to a sole proprietor is fully disallowed; interest to a partner is allowed only within the Sec. 40(b) cap in the firm's own hands; interest to any other related lender is allowed subject to Sec. 40A(2).

29. The employer's own PF contribution and the employees' contribution it withholds follow different due dates. Sec. 36(1)(iv)/(v) contributions are deductible if paid by the RETURN-FILING due date under Sec. 43B; money withheld from employees' wages under Sec. 36(1)(va) is deductible only if credited to the fund by the due date fixed under the relevant labour law.

30. Splitting a cash bill escapes Sec. 40A(3) only across DIFFERENT DAYS. Splitting the same bill on the same day, at different times, still disallows the entire sum.

31. The Sec. 43B "pay by the return due date" relief does not extend to MSME dues. Category A items get that relief; Category B dues to micro and small enterprises beyond the Sec. 15 MSMED Act time limit are deductible only in the P.Y. of actual payment.

32. There is no single ₹1-crore tax-audit line. The Sec. 44AB threshold rises to ₹2 crore, ₹3 crore or ₹10 crore depending on whether income is declared u/s 44AD and how much turnover moves through cash — and even a presumptive assessee can be dragged into audit for declaring income below the prescribed percentage.

33. Only Sec. 44AD splits its rate by payment mode. 6% for turnover received through account payee cheque/DD, ECS or prescribed electronic modes and 8% for everything else; Sec. 44ADA is a FLAT 50% however the receipts came in; Sec. 44AE is not a rate on turnover at all but a fixed monthly figure per vehicle.

34. Nothing at all is set off against Sec. 68 to 69D income. Sec. 115BBE taxes it at a flat 60% plus surcharge and cess and expressly bars every deduction for expenditure or allowance and every set-off of loss.

35. Not every asset needs more than 24 months to turn long-term. Listed securities, units of an equity-oriented fund, Zero-Coupon Bonds, UTI units and units of a listed debt-oriented mutual fund flip after just 12 months; everything else — unlisted shares, land, jewellery, gold, house property — needs more than 24.

36. Indexation is not available everywhere. The 12.5%-without-index versus 20%-with-index choice belongs only to a resident individual or HUF transferring land, building or both, acquired before 23-07-2024 and transferred on or after that date. No other long-term gain carries that option, and LTCG u/s 112A carries no indexation at all.

37. The Sec. 54-series exemptions are not interchangeable. Sec. 54EC has NO Capital Gains Accounts Scheme option and a hard ₹50 lakh ceiling; Sec. 54F's relief is PROPORTIONATE to net sale consideration, and is denied outright where the assessee owns more than one other residential house on the transfer date; Sec. 54B/54D/54G/54GA all require actual prior USE of the asset for at least 2 years.

38. Casual income feels deductible and never is. Sec. 58(4) blocks the cost of the lottery tickets, every Sec. 80C to 80U deduction, and the unexhausted basic exemption limit — the entire gross amount is taxed flat at 30% plus surcharge and cess under Sec. 115BB.

39. "Relative" under Sec. 56(2)(x) is a closed list — spouse; siblings of self or spouse; siblings of either parent; lineal ascendants and descendants of self or spouse; and their spouses. A friend, a cousin or an uncle's son is a stranger to this section however close the family feels.

40. Pension and family pension sit under different heads. A pension received by the employee himself, commuted or uncommuted, stays taxable as Salaries; only FAMILY pension paid to a deceased employee's family falls under Income from Other Sources, with its own Sec. 57(iia) standard deduction.

41. A minor's income is clubbed with the PARENT whose income is higher, whoever gifted the asset. A grandfather-funded deposit changes nothing — Sec. 64(1A) never clubs with the transferor.

42. Adjust the losses that cannot be carried forward FIRST. Sec. 71 lays down no priority for inter-head set-off, but any unabsorbed "other sources" loss (other than a race-horse loss) is simply lost forever, so it must be used before losses that will survive to next year.

43. Sec. 78 reduces only the LOSS component on a change in a firm's constitution. Unabsorbed depreciation is expressly carved out, is governed by Sec. 32(2) rather than Sec. 72/78, and continues in full to the reconstituted firm.

44. A late loss return does not kill every set-off. Only carry-forward of business, capital, race-horse and Sec. 35AD losses is barred; current-year set-off is unaffected, and unabsorbed depreciation and house-property loss can still be carried forward from a belated return.

45. Chapter VI-A deductions attach only to the "remaining GTI" column. They can never be set against LTCG, STCG u/s 111A or casual income, and the aggregate is capped at GTI excluding those three — large capital gains do not create room for 80C.

46. The ₹1,50,000 ceiling does not catch everything. Sec. 80CCE caps only 80C + 80CCC + 80CCD(1); the employer's contribution under 80CCD(2) and the additional ₹50,000 under 80CCD(1B) sit outside and above it.

47. Under Sec. 80D and Sec. 80DDB the enhanced ₹50,000 / ₹1,00,000 limit turns on the age of the person INSURED or TREATED, not the payer. And Sec. 80U (the assessee's own disability) and Sec. 80DD (a dependant disabled relative) are separate sections claimable together for different people — never both for the same disability.

48. Relief u/s 89 is a reduction in TAX, not a deduction from Total Income — computed after the tax and the cess have been worked out, never subtracted from income like a Chapter VI-A item.

49. Rebate u/s 87A never touches special-rate income. It applies only to tax computed at slab rates — not to casual income at 30%, not to LTCG, not to STCG u/s 111A — so that tax survives even where the slab-rate tax has been wiped out entirely.

50. Switching regimes is not a yearly freebie for a business assessee. Only a person WITHOUT business or profession income may flip freely each year; one with business income who opts for the old regime u/s 115BAC(6) is locked in, may withdraw only ONCE, and can never opt out again unless the business income itself ceases.

51. A presumptive assessee u/s 44AD or 44ADA has only ONE advance-tax instalment — 100% on or before 15th March — not the 15%/45%/75%/100% ladder that applies to every other assessee. And below the ₹10,000 threshold there is no advance-tax obligation at all.

52. Sec. 194BA has a NIL TDS threshold. Online-gaming winnings carry the same 30% rate as lottery and horse-race winnings, but not their ₹10,000 per-transaction exemption — there is no floor below which deduction is skipped.

53. Sec. 194C tests each contract; Sec. 194J tests only the aggregate. Under 194C, TDS is skipped only where the single contract is ₹30,000 or less AND the year's aggregate is ₹1,00,000 or less; under 194J the ₹50,000 limit applies to the aggregate of all professional and technical payments for the year, so no single bill needs to reach it.

54. Sec. 194-O and Sec. 194Q never apply to the same transaction twice. Sec. 194Q expressly excludes transactions on which the e-commerce operator has deducted u/s 194-O, and does not apply to any transaction on which tax is deductible under another provision.

55. A partial partition of an HUF after 31-12-1978 is tax-invisible. Sec. 171(9) bars the Assessing Officer from even inquiring into or recording it — the family continues to be assessed as one HUF, with every member jointly and severally liable.

56. Aadhaar does not substitute for PAN generally. It works only in the narrow Sec. 139A(5E) situations; separately, Sec. 139AA makes Aadhaar linking to an existing PAN compulsory, and an unlinked PAN turns inoperative from 1.7.2023, blocking refunds and interest and triggering higher TDS/TCS u/ss. 206AA/206CC.

57. No intimation letter does not mean no intimation. Where nothing is payable and no refund is due, the acknowledgment of the return is itself DEEMED to be the Sec. 143(1) intimation — a separate document issues only where an adjustment is made or a declared loss is altered.

58. "No consideration" does not mean "no GST." Schedule I deems four situations to be supply even without consideration — disposal of an ITC-availed asset, supply between related or DISTINCT persons (so an inter-State branch stock transfer is taxable), a principal-agent goods transfer, and import of services from a related person or one's own foreign establishment.

59. Schedule III is narrower than it looks. It excludes actionable claims OTHER than the specified ones — lottery, betting, gambling, horse racing and online money gaming are carved back in as taxable supply of goods. A whole-time director's SALARY is a Schedule III employment payment, but sitting fees for board meetings are services by a director to the company outside employment.

60. A single price does not make a bundle composite. One price is common to both composite and mixed supply; the test is whether the items are naturally bundled in the ordinary course of business with one predominant element. Composite → the PRINCIPAL supply's rate; mixed → the HIGHEST constituent rate, never the lowest and never the rate of the highest-value item.

61. Forward charge is the default; reverse charge is the notified exception. Sec. 9(3), 9(4) and 9(5) reach only specifically notified categories, each with its own carve-outs — Department of Posts speed-post, parcel, insurance and agency services to non-Government persons stay on forward charge, and a GTA that opts for forward charge and declares it on the invoice takes reverse charge off the table entirely.

62. Renting a residential dwelling is not always exempt. Entry 12 exempts renting to an UNREGISTERED person for use as a residence; renting the same dwelling to a registered person, for instance as a company guest house, is taxable under reverse charge on the recipient. Student-residence and hostel/camp/PG accommodation are excluded from the entry too.

63. The ₹500-per-person "right to admission" exemption is a closed list. Entry 81 covers circus, dance/theatrical performance/drama/ballet, award functions, concerts, pageants, musical performances, non-recognised sporting events, recognised sporting events and planetariums — cinema and multiplex admission is not in it and is taxable at any ticket value.

64. Composition is all-or-nothing across a PAN. Every registered person under the same PAN must opt in together, so one ineligible unit — an ice-cream manufacturer, say — disqualifies every other unit under that PAN.

65. A composition dealer's reverse-charge liability is discharged at the NORMAL rate, in cash, with no ITC — never at his own 1% or 5% composition rate. The value of those inward supplies is nonetheless excluded from his aggregate turnover.

66. Exports destroy composition eligibility. Exports are inter-State supplies and Sec. 10 bars a composition taxpayer from ANY inter-State outward supply — one export transaction forces regular-scheme tax on ALL outward supplies for that period, not merely on the export.

67. The relief on advances applies to GOODS ONLY. Notification No. 66/2017-CT dated 15/11/2017 means no GST is payable when an advance for goods is received; advances on SERVICES remain taxable on receipt, and the relief never extends to goods under reverse charge, where Sec. 12(3) still counts the date of receipt of goods.

68. In a bill-to-ship-to transaction the place of supply is the THIRD PERSON's principal place of business, not the supplier's location and not the physical delivery address — Sec. 10(1)(b) deems that third person to have received the goods.

69. Only GOVERNMENT subsidies are excluded from the value of supply. A subsidy from an NGO, a trade association or any non-Government body that is directly linked to the price must be ADDED BACK under Sec. 15(2)(e). Similarly, a post-supply discount is deductible only where all three Sec. 15(3)(b) conditions are met together.

70. The Sec. 17(5) blocked list is exhaustive, not intuitive. "Used for business" is never enough — it is a standalone override of Sec. 16(1). Beyond motor vehicles and food and catering, remember CSR expenditure under (fa), construction on own account under (d) even where wholly for business, and the 13-seat carve-out under (a). "Plant and machinery" in the (c)/(d) exception excludes land, buildings, other civil structures, telecommunication towers and pipelines laid outside the factory premises.

71. CGST credit and SGST/UTGST credit can NEVER be cross-utilised against each other. There is no direct route in either direction; the only bridge is through IGST, and Sec. 49A requires IGST credit to be fully exhausted before any CGST or SGST/UTGST credit is touched at all.

72. "Special category State" has two different lists. Article 279A(4)(g) names eleven, but for GST REGISTRATION only Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura carry the ₹10 lakh threshold — Assam, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand and the rest follow the general limit.

73. ₹40 lakh is not a universal goods threshold. It applies only to an exclusive supplier of goods outside the specified-goods list (ice cream, pan masala, tobacco, fly ash and clay bricks, roofing tiles) and outside the ten named States — everyone else sits at ₹20 lakh. And aggregate turnover for the test is computed all-India, including exempt supplies and exports, not just taxable turnover.

74. Invoice timing for goods is EVENT-based; for services it is TIME-based. Goods: before or at removal, or before or at delivery where the goods do not move. Services: within 30 days of the supply, stretched to 45 days only for insurance and banking companies, financial institutions and NBFCs. There is no 45-day rule for goods and no "removal" concept for services.

75. The 4-digit and 6-digit HSN rules do not mirror each other. At turnover up to ₹5 crore, 4-digit HSN is mandatory for B2B invoices only; the moment turnover EXCEEDS ₹5 crore the requirement jumps to 6 digits and widens to ALL transactions, B2B and B2C alike.

76. The ₹50,000 e-way bill threshold is not absolute. Two movements require an e-way bill even below it — inter-State movement to or from a job worker, and inter-State transport of handicraft goods by a registration-exempt dealer — and one may always be generated voluntarily below the threshold.

77. Keep this topic's rupee figures apart. ₹200 is the value below which no tax invoice is compulsory for an unregistered, non-requesting recipient; ₹50,000 is both the value at which an unregistered recipient's name and address must appear on the invoice and the e-way bill trigger; ₹5 crore is the e-invoicing and 6-digit-HSN line. Swapping them is exactly what the options are built to reward.

78. GSTR-1 is not an isolated monthly task. Its filing is gated on five separate conditions being clear — all previous GSTR-1s filed, the PRECEDING month's GSTR-3B filed, no unresolved Rule 88C or Rule 88D intimation, and bank details furnished under Rule 10A. Any one of them blocks the current return however complete its own data is.

79. Interest under Sec. 50 runs on the NET cash liability, not the gross. The proviso to Sec. 50(1) confines it to the portion of tax actually paid by debiting the Electronic Cash Ledger; the ITC-covered portion draws none. The one place this relief disappears is in proceedings under Sec. 73 or Sec. 74A. Interest on ITC wrongly availed AND utilised runs up to 24%.

80. The Electronic Credit Ledger can only be credited through self-assessed ITC in a filed return — never by direct entry, and never by a cash deposit, which reaches the Electronic Cash Ledger (PMT-05) instead.

81. 12 nautical miles is territorial waters, not Indian Customs Waters. It is territorial waters that are included in "India"; Indian Customs Waters under Sec. 2(28) run to the limit of the EEZ — 200 nautical miles from the baseline.

82. Pilferage and destruction attract different reliefs. Sec. 13 is petty theft — no duty at all, no burden of proof on the importer — but it does not apply once goods are warehoused or the clearance order is passed, and duty revives if the pilfered goods are re-stored. Sec. 23(1) is total, irrecoverable loss or destruction, giving remission, with the burden on the importer, and it does cover warehoused goods.

83. Social Welfare Surcharge is not 10% of every duty on the paper. Six items are expressly outside its base — safeguard duty, countervailing duty on subsidized articles, anti-dumping duty, IGST, GST Compensation Cess and AIDC — so in practice it comes to exactly 10% of the Basic Customs Duty. And it is 3%, not 10%, for gold and silver.

84. Three freight-and-insurance mistakes recur. For AIR transport the 20%-of-FOB figure is a hard CEILING even where the actual freight is known and higher; for SEA transport 20% is only a fallback where the actual is unascertained, so a stated actual must be used; and insurance is 1.125% of FOB, never of CIF or of the bare price.

85. Design charges are added or dropped according to WHERE the work was done. Rule 10 adds engineering, development, art work, design work, plans and sketches undertaken ELSEWHERE THAN IN INDIA and necessary for the production of the imported goods — Indian design and development work is never added.

86. Deductive value is not the biggest single sale and not an average. Strike out any sale made more than 90 days after importation, then group the remaining sales by PRICE and total the units at each price — the greatest aggregate quantity to UNRELATED persons wins. Then remember the residue is Assessable Value PLUS duty and gross it down accordingly.

87. One date does not serve for both the duty rate and the exchange rate. The Sec. 15 deeming fiction for an early bill of entry is confined to the rate of duty and tariff valuation; the assessable value always uses the CBIC rate in force on the ACTUAL date the bill of entry was presented — and the rate is CBIC's, never RBI's or the inter-bank market's.

88. Sec. 19 taxes a set of articles at the HIGHEST applicable rate, not at each item's own rate. A ₹5,000 grooming kit containing Nil, 10%, 20% and 30% items is taxed wholly at 30%, and accessories, spare parts and repair implements take the main article's rate.

The Last 48 Hours — Revision Plan for This Document
WhenWhat
48 hours outRe-read Module 5 (Goods and Services Tax Laws) end to end — the module-divider through all eight sub-topics, from the levy under Sec. 9 to returns and payment under Sec. 37 to 50. At 35% it is the single largest module in this paper and nothing else earns back the hours lost here. Rehearse three things from memory afterwards and check them against the module: the six-limb test of "supply" under Sec. 7 with Schedules I, II and III; the whole Sec. 17(5) blocked-credit list; and the Sec. 49(5)/49A order of ITC utilisation, written out head by head.
36 hours outRe-read Module 2 (Heads of Income) — 25%, the second largest, and the most computation-dense. Rebuild four formats cold, on paper: the three-limb HRA exemption, the two gratuity cases side by side, the GAV → NAV → Sec. 24 house-property ladder, and the Sec. 48 capital-gains computation with the indexation fraction. With Module 5, this is 60% of the paper — these two days are not negotiable.
24 hours outSweep Module 3 (Total Income & Tax Liability of Individuals & HUF) — 15%, and the module that converts everything else into a number. Prioritise the carry-forward table (which loss, how many years, against what, and whether a timely return is required), the Chapter VI-A ceilings, the default-versus-old-regime blocked list, and the Sec. 211 advance-tax instalments. Then re-read the TDS ready-reckoner once, straight through, for the rate-and-threshold pairings alone.
18 hours outSweep Module 6 (Customs Act & Rules) — 10%, and the most mechanically scorable module in the paper because its questions are nearly always the same ladder. Write out the assessable-value build-up and the B–C–D–E–F duty stack from memory twice, with the base beside each rung. Then Module 1 (10%) — the Sec. 6 day-tests, the Sec. 5 incidence grid and the agricultural-income splits, all of which are pure recall and cost nothing to secure.
12 hours outModule 4 (Concept of Indirect Taxes) — 5%, and the fastest module in the document to finish. The Constitutional entries, the direct-versus-indirect contrast, the cascading illustration and the GST Council's voting arithmetic are the whole of it; one careful pass is enough, and it also underpins every Module 5 answer that opens with why GST exists.
6 hours outRead The Final Ladder above, start to finish, once, slowly.
2 hours outRead the Master Trap List above, start to finish, once, slowly. Nothing new after this point.
In the hallThe paper is 100 marks — 30 marks of MCQs and 70 marks descriptive, seven questions of 14 marks each, of which any five are attempted. There is no negative marking on the MCQs, so no MCQ is ever left blank. Do the MCQ section first while recall is sharpest, then read all seven descriptive questions before choosing your five — the choice itself is worth marks. Open every computation with the correct statement heading and the assessment year ("Computation of Total Income of ... for the A.Y. ...", "Computation of GST Liability for the tax period ...", "Computation of Assessable Value and Customs Duty"), and cite the Section number with the Act named beside it. Show the working for every figure; a correctly-laid computation earns marks even where one later figure goes wrong. Never abandon a part-worked numerical for a fresh question — a half-built ladder in the right format outscores a blank page.

Weight-based priority if time runs out anywhere in this plan: Module 5 (35%) and Module 2 (25%) are 60% of the paper between them and are never the ones you cut — if only one day remains, it belongs entirely to those two. Module 3 (15%) is the arithmetic that turns Module 2's heads into a tax figure, so it is revised third and never skipped outright; a pass over its carry-forward table and Chapter VI-A ceilings alone recovers most of its marks. Module 6 (10%) repays revision out of all proportion to its weight because its questions are formula-driven and repetitive — the assessable-value ladder and the duty stack are worth more than any equivalent hour spent elsewhere. Module 1 (10%) is pure recall of day-tests, incidence and Section numbers and can be secured in a single focused hour. Module 4 (5%) is the smallest weight in the paper and the last thing to touch — but it is also the shortest, so shore it up rather than abandoning it.

This page is exam strategy, not syllabus content — every fact it points to lives in the verified module pages above, condensed strictly from ICMAI's own Paper 7 Study Notes (Syllabus 2022).
